summary: Africa is home to over 800 golf courses, with South Africa alone hosting more than half, and several countries emerging as top golf-travel destinations. The article highlights ten standout courses across the continent, including designs by Gary Player and Bernhard Langer in Egypt, Mauritius, Morocco, Namibia, Seychelles, South Africa, Tunisia, and Zimbabwe. These courses are noted for their scenic settings, challenging hazards, and variety, with many attached to luxury resorts and offering green fees ranging from around $30 to over $280. Overall, the piece positions Africa as a compelling and diverse destination for golf holidays, blending sport with distinctive landscapes and wildlife.

The article highlights the long-standing connection between James Bond and luxury hotels, noting that the latest novel, "Solo," opens at London's Dorchester. It then showcases several iconic properties featured in Bond films, such as the Peninsula Hong Kong, Tokyo's New Otani, the One&Only Ocean Club in the Bahamas, and Venice's Hotel Cipriani. Other notable locations include London's Langham, Hamburg's Atlantic Kempinski, India's Taj Lake Palace, Miami's Fontainebleau, Sardinia's Cala di Volpe, and the Four Seasons at Canary Wharf. Each hotel is tied to memorable scenes, from rooftop chases to romantic encounters, reinforcing the franchise's glamorous travel appeal.

The article declares that craft beer has shifted from a passing trend to a mainstream global movement, with demand rising sharply across Asia Pacific. It highlights a selection of standout craft beer bars in Asian cities such as Bangkok, Beijing, Shanghai, Tokyo, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Kuala Lumpur. These venues range from pioneering microbreweries and experimental taprooms to local adaptations of international brands, reflecting a growing appetite for diverse and high-quality beers. The piece also notes that while some Asian markets are still developing their craft beer culture, interest is steadily expanding beyond mass-produced lagers.

The article highlights ten of Scotland’s most remarkable castles, chosen in honor of National Tartan Day, ranging from iconic fortresses like Edinburgh Castle to scenic Highland landmarks such as Eilean Donan. It notes that many of these historic sites offer unique attractions, including royal jewels, whisky-region settings, Shakespearean and film connections, and family histories. Several castles remain private residences, while others invite visitors to explore period furnishings, gardens, and interactive experiences. Overall, the piece showcases Scotland’s rich architectural heritage and the fairy-tale appeal of its ancient strongholds.

The article highlights ten remote and pristine wilderness destinations around the world, from Tasmania’s ancient rainforests and Scotland’s rugged peninsula to Bolivia’s salt flats and Canada’s Great Bear Rainforest. Each location offers immersive nature experiences such as guided treks, kayaking, wildlife viewing, and cultural encounters. The piece emphasizes the appeal of escaping modern life and finding solitude, adventure, and spiritual renewal in these wild landscapes. It also provides practical travel details, including tour operators, prices, and trip options for each destination.

The article highlights exceptional global destinations for observing rare wildlife, ranging from accessible sites like Florida’s alligator courtship dances and California’s diverse marine mammals to remote adventures in Guyana, Madagascar, and Siberia. It also covers spectacular African wildlife viewing in Namibia and Ethiopia, as well as the scenic but risky Karakoram Highway and the biologically rich yet conflict-affected regions of the Democratic Republic of Congo. The author emphasizes that while some locations are easy to visit, others require careful planning and a tolerance for challenging conditions.

South Africa offers far more than its famous safaris and Cape Town beaches, with ten lesser-known destinations that showcase the country’s diversity. Highlights include Johannesburg’s vibrant creative districts, the prehistoric Cradle of Humankind, scenic mountain and battlefields regions, and the coastal charm of Umhlanga and the Wild Coast. The Garden Route and Cape Town also hold hidden gems, from rugged hikes and kayak adventures to full-moon picnics and rooftop trailer stays. Meanwhile, the vast Northern Cape draws visitors with superb stargazing and spectacular spring wildflowers.

Medical errors are a widespread and often preventable problem in U.S. hospitals, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths each year and ranking as a leading cause of mortality. The article highlights common mistakes such as wrong-patient treatment, retained surgical tools, patient wandering, fake doctors, ER delays, air bubbles in lines, wrong-site surgery, infections from poor hand hygiene, tube mix-ups, and waking during anesthesia. To reduce risk, patients and families are urged to actively verify identities, surgical sites, and tubes, confirm doctor credentials, ask about anesthesia, and insist that staff wash hands. These simple precautions can help prevent serious harm and even save lives.

Canada’s standout qualities go far beyond its scenery and politeness, encompassing a mix of cultural quirks and everyday pleasures. The country is known for constant apologizing, an abundance of lakes and cottage retreats, and serving as a popular stand-in filming location for Hollywood. It also ranks high for clean air, produces famous comedians, offers distinctively creamier chocolate, and boasts world-class ski destinations. Other national traits include the ubiquitous maple leaf as a symbol, beloved roadside food chains, and uniquely Canadian slang and expressions.

Hong Kong stands out for its unique blend of urban living and cultural strengths, from the complex Cantonese language and exceptionally low crime rates to its world-class public transit and iconic skyline. The city is also known for its financial appeal, with low taxes, as well as its legendary contributions to kung fu cinema, a highly awarded airport, and a vibrant food culture. Its energetic nightlife, centered on Lan Kwai Fong, has become so influential that other Chinese cities have sought to replicate it. Overall, the article celebrates Hong Kong as a dynamic, competitive global city with distinctive advantages across safety, infrastructure, entertainment, and everyday life.

Taiwan stands out for its unique cultural and social offerings, from hundreds of bustling night markets and quirky themed restaurants to free public WiFi and the world’s largest collection of Chinese artifacts. It also excels in areas like satirical animated news, convincing mock meat, and a record 17 Little League World Series titles. The island is praised for its affordable universal healthcare and a deep obsession with Hello Kitty, including themed flights and beer. It has also become a global force in dumpling culture, with Din Tai Fung earning Michelin recognition.

The article highlights ten uniquely American strengths, ranging from friendly greetings and epic road trips to demolition derbies, innovative craft beer, and diverse landscapes. It also celebrates the country’s national parks, adventurous food culture, major sports scene, and influential film and television industry. The author notes that while China may soon surpass the U.S. in several of these categories, America still leads in these distinctive areas for now.

Honolulu and Oahu can be pricey, but budget-conscious travelers can still enjoy the island by using TheBus instead of renting a car and seeking out affordable local eateries for traditional Hawaiian dishes. Many iconic experiences are inexpensive or free, including hiking Diamond Head, visiting Pearl Harbor, and browsing the Aloha Stadium Swap Meet for souvenirs. The article also highlights low-cost treats like shave ice and udon noodles, plus free attractions such as "Lost" filming locations and the Dole Plantation's gardens. Overall, it shows that with a little planning, visitors can experience Oahu's beauty and culture without overspending.

Brazil is a country of contrasts, having lifted tens of millions into the middle class while still struggling with deep inequality, as seen in mass protests. Known for its outgoing, expressive culture, it values outdoor life, music, and social warmth, with customs like cheek-kissing and a relaxed approach to personal space. The article also highlights everyday realities such as limited English, excellent juice bars, and the vast natural wonders from the Amazon to Iguazu Falls. It closes by dispelling myths like the danger of piranhas while noting practical concerns like crime and the gap between rich and poor.

New Mexico is a vast, sparsely populated state with an eclectic mix of beauty and strangeness, from UFO lore and atomic history to its unique bilingual culture. It is full of surprising attractions, including restaurants serving red or green chile year-round, monks who brew craft beer, and a wine industry that predates California’s. Visitors can also find quirky landmarks like a self-crossing stretch of Route 66, a miraculous staircase in Santa Fe, and a Wild West atmosphere where open gun carrying is still common. The state also offers natural and historical wonders, such as gypsum sand dunes, thousands of ancient Pueblo sites, a lightning-inspired art installation, and geothermal hot springs used for centuries.

The article highlights lesser-known Caribbean experiences beyond the typical tourist crowds, from hidden hiking trails and national parks to local food and drink spots. It showcases destinations like Martinique’s historic Route de la Trace, Dominica’s volcanic Valley of Desolation, and Aruba’s desert-like Arikok National Park. The piece also features authentic cultural encounters, such as community tours in Cuba, turtle diving in Bonaire, and the famous Killer Bee cocktail in Nevis. Overall, it encourages travelers to seek out quieter, more genuine corners of the Caribbean that retain their old-world charm.

The article presents a range of women’s perspectives on the “having it all” debate, sparked by Sheryl Sandberg’s book and Marissa Mayer’s telecommuting policy. The contributors reflect on their own experiences, emphasizing that success is defined personally rather than by a single standard. Several highlight the importance of workplace flexibility, family support, and making deliberate choices, while others argue that true progress requires broader structural changes like equal pay and childcare. Overall, the piece reframes the question from achieving everything at once to having the freedom and support to pursue one’s own version of a fulfilling life.

Ten years into the U.S. intervention in Afghanistan, the conflict has become America’s longest war, with the Taliban gaining strength and Kabul suffering a series of high-profile attacks, including the assassination of former President Burhanuddin Rabbani. The killing underscored the collapse of Karzai’s peace initiative and deepened suspicions about the roles of the Haqqani network and Pakistan’s ISI. However, the article argues that military victory is impossible and that all insurgencies ultimately end through negotiation, with the Taliban already showing interest in direct talks with Washington rather than Kabul. The key challenge is to engage moderate Taliban elements and ensure any future power-sharing arrangement prevents a return to ethnic civil war.

Russia’s intervention in Crimea could lead to Western economic isolation, yet deep trade ties make that difficult. Beyond trade, wealthy Russians hold major stakes in global luxury assets, including top sports teams, high-end real estate, and valuable art collections. Russian involvement also extends to critical areas like space, where NASA depends on Russian spacecraft, and technology, with investments in major companies and globally recognized cybersecurity firms. These far-reaching holdings illustrate how intertwined Russian wealth is with Western economies and institutions.

The article announces that the world’s first artificial surfing lake will open in Wales in summer 2015, featuring a large lagoon with machine-generated waves. It then highlights a variety of unconventional surfing destinations around the globe, including tidal bores in Brazil and the UK, standing river waves in Germany and Canada, and remote spots in Antarctica, Namibia, Bangladesh, Oman, Ghana, Iceland, and even Lake Michigan. These locations offer unique challenges such as cold water, strong currents, wildlife risks, and limited access, appealing to surfers seeking extraordinary experiences beyond typical ocean waves.

The article marks the Panama Canal’s 100th anniversary but emphasizes that the country offers far more than this engineering marvel. It highlights a range of attractions, including historic Panama City neighborhoods, tropical islands like Bocas del Toro and San Blas, coffee-growing highlands, indigenous Embera culture, a chocolate farm, wildlife-rich Gatun Lake, and a new biodiversity museum. The piece also points to colonial ruins, vibrant local food markets, and eco-adventures as key draws. Overall, it presents Panama as a diverse destination blending history, nature, and culture beyond the famous waterway.

Hungary is a small, history-obsessed country with a strong cultural identity, known for its vast Lake Balaton, abundant thermal baths, and remarkable intellectual achievements, including numerous Nobel laureates and inventions like the ballpoint pen and Rubik's cube. Its cuisine centers on goulash as a soup and the ubiquitous use of paprika, while its famous sweet wine, Tokaji, has royal acclaim. Social customs are distinctive, such as avoiding clinking beer glasses in remembrance of past defeat, and Hungarians take pride in their equestrian traditions, sports excellence, and resourceful "little gate" approach to life.

Spain’s cultural influence stems from its remarkable regional diversity, which flourished after Franco’s death and gave rise to distinct languages, traditions, and cuisines. The country is unified by iconic symbols like bullfighting, though this tradition faces growing opposition, while its daily rhythm is marked by late meals and vibrant tapas culture. Beyond famous coasts, Spain offers unspoiled landscapes, snowy mountains, and a deep layered history visible in churches built over mosques and Roman ruins. Its calendar is filled with eccentric festivals, and its culinary pride ranges from prized acorn-fed ham to avant-garde gastronomy, with Catalonia’s independence movement adding a modern political edge.

American Airlines attributed recent seat detachment issues to sticky residue from spilled drinks and food debris, but passengers and online commenters responded with heavy skepticism and mockery. Many found the explanation implausible, joking that if beverage gunk could break seats, highchairs and theater seats would constantly fall apart. Others sarcastically suggested the airline might ban sodas, charge extra for locked seats, or blame coffee for unrelated problems like lost luggage. Overall, the public reaction framed the excuse as a transparent attempt to shift blame onto customers.

In 2014, a wave of luxury hotels is set to open worldwide, offering far more than standard upscale amenities. These new properties feature unique attractions such as marine conservation centers, private cinemas, oxygen lounges, and thermal baths, all set in distinctive locations ranging from historic mansions and mountain gorges to private islands and city centers. The hotels span the globe, including notable debuts in Los Angeles, Kyoto, Amsterdam, Oman, Doha, New York, Beijing, Bali, Lhasa, Bath, London, and Paris, each emphasizing local culture and architectural heritage. From a canyon-side retreat in Oman to a private island in Doha and a property with direct access to thermal waters in Bath, these openings redefine the luxury travel experience.

The article highlights a trend of historic European and Asian palaces, castles, and chateaus being transformed into luxury hotels, offering guests a chance to stay in richly storied surroundings. It features a diverse selection of properties, from a Roman palace restored by an oil tycoon and a hotel within Diocletian's Palace in Croatia to a Beijing retreat near the Summer Palace and a Venetian palace once home to a Doge. Other notable examples include a French chateau tied to the Hundred Years' War, an English castle with a working portcullis, and opulent options in Vienna, Prague, Istanbul, Lisbon, St. Petersburg, and Malta. The piece emphasizes the blend of historical authenticity with modern amenities, while deliberately excluding India's well-known palace hotels.

The article highlights a roundup of unusual cocktails from around the world, published to coincide with the 2013 World Cocktail Championship in Prague. It features inventive and bizarre drinks, such as a margarita with Cointreau pearls, a cocktail served in an eggshell, a camel milk-based non-alcoholic drink, and a cocktail containing a preserved amputated toe. Other notable entries include a flaming rum drink, a gunpowder-infused gin served in a smoking cloche, a chocolate piña colada served in a toilet bowl, and a luxury cocktail with gold flakes and diamonds. The list also includes a royal-birth-inspired summer drink, a hangover-curing Bloody Mary with bacon and a grilled cheese sandwich, a molecular cocktail with test tubes, and an Earl Grey caviar martini.

At the 86th Academy Awards, “12 Years a Slave” took home Best Picture, along with Best Supporting Actress for Lupita Nyong’o and Best Adapted Screenplay, with the film’s message about slavery and survival emphasized in acceptance speeches. “Gravity” led the night with seven wins, including Best Director for Alfonso Cuarón, the first Latin American to win that category. “Dallas Buyers Club” earned acting honors for Matthew McConaughey and Jared Leto, while Cate Blanchett won Best Actress for “Blue Jasmine.” Host Ellen DeGeneres made history with a star-studded selfie that became the most retweeted photo ever, and “American Hustle” was notably shut out despite leading nominations.

The article highlights a collection of thrilling, high-altitude observation platforms around the world, including a newly opened deck in the Austrian mountains. It describes various structures such as glass-bottomed walkways, skywalks, and open-air ledges that offer dramatic views from bridges, towers, and cliffs. Notable examples range from Austria’s Dachstein Stairway to Nothingness and Canada’s CN Tower EdgeWalk to the Grand Canyon Skywalk and London’s The Shard. Each platform provides unique adrenaline-filled experiences, with details on heights, glass features, and visitor information.

The article highlights a collection of hotels around the world that are themed around famous authors and literary works. These properties range from historic New York landmarks like The Algonquin and The Plaza to quirky options such as a Hobbit-themed motel in New Zealand and book-focused boutiques in Portland and Paris. Many offer unique features like lending libraries, book-themed decor, and even "book butlers" to immerse guests in literary culture. Overall, the piece showcases how travel accommodations can celebrate storytelling and the legacy of celebrated writers.

The article highlights legendary bars and cafés around the world that served as creative haunts for famous writers and artists, from Hemingway’s favorite spots in Paris, Madrid, and Havana to Beat Generation hangouts in San Francisco. It notes that many of these establishments still welcome visitors, preserving memorabilia, dedicated tables, and the atmosphere that inspired literary works. Iconic locations include Paris’s Les Deux Magots, Oxford’s Eagle and Child where the Inklings met, and Dublin pubs tied to figures like Oscar Wilde and W.B. Yeats. The piece also mentions modern cultural touches, such as literary prizes, filming locations, and ongoing traditions that keep these historic venues relevant.

Thai authorities insist they are not targeting Cambodian migrant workers, but roughly 180,000 to 200,000 have left the country since last week amid panic fueled by rumors of arrests and persecution. The exodus has caused severe crowding at border towns, prompting Cambodian and Thai officials to meet and set up a hotline. Thai officials are trying to reassure workers that they can continue their jobs and return if they left, while urging employers to register their staff. The fear appears linked to uncertainty following Thailand's recent military coup and its stated focus on tackling illegal migration.

A powerful blizzard sweeping across New England has caused at least one death and left over 600,000 customers without power, with heavy snow and fierce winds creating hazardous conditions. The storm, which combined two weather systems, dumped more than a foot of snow in parts of Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Massachusetts, with gusts near 75 mph along the coast. Widespread flight cancellations, road closures, and suspended rail service disrupted travel, while officials warned of possible coastal flooding at high tide. States of emergency were declared across the region, and residents were urged to stay off the roads as crews worked to manage the storm’s impact.

Yosemite National Park has confirmed a second hantavirus death and a probable fourth case, all tied to visitors who stayed in Curry Village's tent cabins in mid-June. Officials are reaching out to guests who used those cabins from June through the recent deep cleaning, urging them to seek medical attention if symptoms appear. Hantavirus is a rare but often fatal respiratory illness spread through rodent droppings and urine, with symptoms emerging one to six weeks after exposure, and it does not transmit between people.

A consolidated federal lawsuit filed on behalf of more than 2,000 former NFL players accuses the league of concealing the long-term neurological dangers of repeated head trauma and failing to protect players from those risks. The complaint merges over 80 existing cases and cites conditions such as dementia, early-onset Alzheimer’s, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy as consequences of the league’s alleged deception. Families and former players, including the widow of Ray Easterling and ex-running back Kevin Turner, argue the NFL must provide care and make the sport safer. The NFL responded that player safety has long been a priority and dismissed the allegations of misleading players as meritless.

London 2012 organizers admitted that they had sold more tickets than available for four synchronized swimming sessions. After reviewing seating plans against ticket orders, they notified about 3,000 applicants and offered replacement tickets for other events they had originally requested. It remains unclear whether similar overselling occurred for other competitions. The affected events were to be held at the Aquatics Centre, which relies on temporary seating wings for most spectators.

At the 2014 Golden Globes, “12 Years a Slave” took best drama and “American Hustle” won best comedy or musical, positioning both as strong Oscar contenders. “Gravity” earned Alfonso Cuarón the best director prize, while acting honors went to Matthew McConaughey, Cate Blanchett, Leonardo DiCaprio, Amy Adams, Jennifer Lawrence, and Jared Leto. On the TV side, “Brooklyn Nine-Nine” and “Breaking Bad” were among the night’s big winners, and hosts Tina Fey and Amy Poehler drew laughs with sharp Hollywood jokes. The ceremony also sparked criticism over a lack of diversity among winners, prompting the hashtag #notbuyingit.

The Golden Globes drew their largest TV audience in a decade, averaging 20.9 million viewers on NBC—an increase from last year and the show’s best numbers since 2004. It also saw a slight uptick in the key 18–49 demographic, reinforcing the continued appeal of live award shows. Social media engagement was strong, with millions of Twitter messages reaching over 10 million users. Returning hosts Tina Fey and Amy Poehler received credit for the ratings boost, and NBC’s red carpet pre-show also performed well, far outpacing E!’s competing special.

The article examines the possibility of a 2016 presidential matchup between Jeb Bush and Hillary Clinton, which would extend the Bush and Clinton families' decades-long dominance of American politics. It highlights a family divide over Jeb's potential run, with Barbara Bush publicly urging him to sit out while his father, George H.W. Bush, reportedly supports the idea. The piece also explores broader concerns about political dynasties, noting both the advantages of name recognition and fundraising power and the public fatigue with familiar political families. Ultimately, supporters argue that both Jeb and Hillary should be judged on their own ideas and qualifications rather than their last names.

Qatar is building Lusail, a high-tech planned city from scratch on the Persian Gulf coast, designed to house 250,000 people with smart infrastructure, underground utilities, solar cooling, and futuristic transit. It will include a stadium meant to host the 2022 World Cup final, but the project faces criticism over extreme heat, alleged migrant labor abuses, and corruption concerns. Qatar has announced labor reforms and promised advanced cooling systems to address these issues. Despite uncertainty about the World Cup, developers say construction will continue regardless of FIFA's decisions.

The article celebrates familiar global chains and franchises as comforting travel anchors, offering reliability, recognizable food, and clean facilities in unfamiliar places. It highlights a diverse range of favorites, from Cinnabon and McDonald's to Din Tai Fung and 7-Eleven, noting their global reach and localized adaptations. The list also includes hotels, rental car companies, and unique concepts like KidZania, emphasizing how these brands provide a sense of security and convenience for travelers. Ultimately, the piece acknowledges that while chains may lack exotic charm, their predictability can be a welcome relief on the road.

A large recall of over 22,000 pounds of ready-to-eat meat products, including chicken and ham salads and beef items, has been issued due to possible Listeria contamination. The products were shipped to numerous U.S. states and Canada, and the issue was identified through testing by Canadian food safety officials, with no reported illnesses so far. Consumers are advised to either return the affected items for a refund or throw them away, as Listeria can cause serious infection, especially in vulnerable groups.

Kevin Kane, a Pennsylvania financial adviser, has visited Ireland six times since his first trip in 2000 and considers the Dingle Peninsula his favorite spot, while also praising places like the Ring of Kerry and Galway. He advises first-time visitors not to pack too much into their itinerary, since travel between towns can be slow and challenging. He also recommends chatting with locals in pubs, exploring lesser-known sites such as island ferries and abbey ruins, and keeping a flexible, unhurried pace. Ultimately, he suggests leaving room to soak in the experience and planning for a return trip, as Ireland tends to draw visitors back.

A suicide car bombing in Kabul killed three NATO service members, including two Americans and one Polish soldier, with the Taliban claiming responsibility for the attack on a foreign military convoy. The blast also wounded at least 13 Afghan civilians and damaged numerous vehicles, prompting alarms at the U.S. Embassy. The incident followed a separate attack the previous day in which an Afghan soldier opened fire on international forces. These attacks occur as NATO troops prepare to withdraw from Afghanistan and the country deals with political tensions from its presidential election.

A former apparel designer who had been laid off fatally shot a former colleague near the Empire State Building before being killed in a shootout with police. Nine bystanders were wounded, mostly by ricocheting bullets, though none of their injuries were life-threatening. The gunman had a history of disputes with the victim and had filed harassment complaints against each other. Police confirmed the shooting was not terrorism-related, and the landmark building remained open as the investigation continued.

An overpass under construction collapsed in Belo Horizonte, a World Cup host city, killing two people and injuring 22 others, while also crushing vehicles and buses. The bridge was near the Mineirao stadium and had been intended to be finished before the tournament. The incident adds to criticism of Brazil’s World Cup preparations, which have been marked by high spending and worker fatalities on stadium projects. Belo Horizonte is still set to host a semifinal match this week.

A federal grand jury has charged two foreign nationals, Parviz Khaki and Zongcheng Yi, with conspiring to illegally send U.S. equipment and materials to Iran for use in uranium-enrichment gas centrifuges. The indictment includes export violations, smuggling, defrauding the U.S. government, and money laundering, with Khaki also accused of trying to obtain radioactive source materials for Iranian customers. Khaki was arrested in the Philippines, while Yi remains at large. The case reflects U.S. efforts to block goods that could support Iran's nuclear program, which Iran maintains is peaceful but Western nations suspect could be used for weapons.

A second federal lawsuit has been filed against Kevin Clash, the former voice of Elmo, alleging he had a sexual relationship with a teenage boy in 2000 after meeting him through a gay chat line and providing alcohol. The accuser, now an adult, says the relationship continued into his early adulthood and caused emotional harm. This follows an earlier lawsuit from another man making similar allegations, though one prior accuser has since recanted. Clash has denied the claims through his lawyer and resigned from Sesame Street, though his voice will still appear on the show through 2014.

Two Secret Service supervisors assigned to President Obama’s protective detail are under internal investigation following allegations of misconduct. The case emerged after one supervisor left ammunition in a hotel room belonging to a woman he met at a bar and later tried to regain access; investigators also found sexually suggestive emails involving both supervisors. The probe was reportedly triggered by press inquiries rather than a formal complaint. The incident echoes the 2012 Cartagena prostitution scandal, and a senator has alleged similar misconduct occurred in 17 countries, raising concerns about security risks and the agency’s culture.

Voters in Colorado and Washington approved ballot measures legalizing recreational marijuana, while Massachusetts passed a medical marijuana initiative, marking major victories for legalization advocates. Supporters hailed the results as a turning point in the long campaign against cannabis prohibition, but federal authorities quickly reiterated that marijuana remains illegal under national law. Colorado’s governor cautioned that state officials must still navigate conflicting federal rules before legal sales can begin, leaving the future of enforcement uncertain. The outcome highlights a growing tension between state-level legalization and federal drug policy.

An attack on residential apartments in eastern Baghdad, reportedly used as a brothel, left at least 28 women and six men dead. The assailants, dressed in military-style clothing, left a note warning that this was the fate of prostitution. Residents blamed the Shiite militia Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq, though the group denied involvement. Elsewhere, ISIS militants launched an assault on Haditha that was repelled by Iraqi forces and tribal fighters, while airstrikes targeted a bridge near Falluja and a roadside bomb wounded police in Kirkuk.

Armed militants linked to al-Shabaab stormed an upscale Nairobi shopping mall, killing dozens and taking hostages in a siege that left security forces battling the gunmen for hours. Kenyan officials reported at least 39 dead, including relatives of the president, and hundreds wounded, with foreigners among the casualties. The attackers claimed to still hold ground and refused negotiations, while Kenyan authorities said they had isolated the gunmen and vowed to hunt down those responsible. The assault shattered the mall’s image as a safe haven and drew widespread international condemnation.

Despite a newly extended ceasefire, pro-Russian separatists attacked a Ukrainian military base in Slovyansk, killing three and wounding four others. The truce, prolonged by 72 hours until Monday night, was meant to pave the way for hostage releases and the withdrawal of separatist forces, but violence continues. The broader conflict stems from former President Yanukovych’s rejection of an EU deal, which led to his ouster, Russia’s annexation of Crimea, and the ongoing separatist insurgency. Ukrainian President Poroshenko insists on negotiations, hostage freedom, and Russia’s reversal of the Crimea annexation, while reserving the right to use force where the ceasefire is violated.

A shooting at a North Carolina lumber company left three people dead and one person wounded, with the suspected gunman also critically injured. The suspect, a 50-year-old employee, was found at his home with a self-inflicted gunshot wound and a rambling note. Authorities said all five individuals involved worked at the business, and while harassment at work is possible, no motive has been confirmed. The wounded victim and the suspect were both airlifted to a hospital for treatment.

President Obama’s pledge that Americans could keep their health plans is being challenged in Virginia, Kentucky, and Idaho, where regulators are requiring insurers to cancel policies that don’t meet Affordable Care Act standards. These states decided it was simpler to replace existing plans than to update them with the new required benefits, leaving many policyholders to find new coverage. While some consumers may pay more, others could qualify for subsidies that lower costs. The White House maintains that plans unchanged since before the law took effect are grandfathered, but in practice insurers are moving away from such policies, causing confusion and frustration.

New Caledonia briefly held the title of world’s largest marine protected area with its Coral Sea park, covering its entire economic zone and safeguarding a unique, highly endemic reef ecosystem. Though the U.S. soon established an even larger marine monument, New Caledonia’s park stands out as the most accessible. The article highlights three ways to explore it: surfing remote reef breaks from a small camp, joining a relaxed multi-day yacht regatta among the lagoon’s many islands, and snorkeling near Noumea at Signal Island, where vibrant, unbleached coral teems with diverse marine life.

A shooting at a Chicago park during a basketball game wounded 13 people, including a 3-year-old boy who was shot in the head and is expected to survive. Police believe the attack was gang-related and involved an assault-style rifle with a high-capacity magazine. The boy's grandmother made an emotional plea for an end to the violence, while officials, including the police superintendent and mayor, condemned the shooting and renewed calls for stricter gun laws. The incident highlights Chicago's persistent struggle with gun violence, as the city continues to record the highest number of homicides in the nation.

Governor Chris Christie used his State of the State address to press Congress for swift, unencumbered Hurricane Sandy relief, noting that tens of thousands of New Jersey residents remain displaced and criticizing the lengthy delay in federal assistance. He highlighted the storm’s massive toll, including billions in damages and hundreds of thousands of damaged homes, while lawmakers had only approved a fraction of the requested aid, with a larger package still pending. The speech also reflected Christie’s political standing, as his handling of the crisis boosted his approval ratings and likely influenced Newark Mayor Cory Booker’s decision to pursue a U.S. Senate seat rather than challenge him for governor. Despite bipartisan praise for his leadership, Christie continues to face resistance from the state’s Democratic legislature on other policy priorities.

A 4.2-magnitude earthquake near Guthrie, Oklahoma, early Tuesday was widely felt across the area, with many residents reporting being shaken awake or noticing items rattling. Experts said significant damage was unlikely, though the quake stood out because so many people noticed it. Oklahoma has experienced a sharp rise in seismic activity since 2009, recently recording more quakes than California, and longtime residents say minor structural issues like cracked door frames are becoming more common.

Scientists have confirmed that a tiny zircon crystal from Western Australia is the oldest known piece of Earth’s crust, dating back about 4.4 billion years. Its oxygen isotope composition suggests the early Earth cooled quickly enough to support liquid water, and possibly life, much earlier than previously thought. The age was verified using advanced atom-probe tomography, which showed that lead atoms within the crystal had not shifted enough to distort radioactive dating. This finding sheds new light on the planet’s mysterious early history, when conditions were once believed to be hellish and inhospitable.

More than 450,000 people have been displaced in northwestern Pakistan over the past two weeks due to a military offensive targeting militant groups in North Waziristan and other tribal areas. Many have moved to camps in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, where authorities are distributing food and supplies. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has assured displaced families of government support during the crisis. The army reports that over 250 insurgents have been killed, including dozens in recent airstrikes.

Raw milk from a Utah dairy has been linked to 45 cases of campylobacteriosis, with most infections in Utah residents and a couple in neighboring states. The dairy’s license was suspended after inspectors found that an employee’s failure to properly clean cow udders introduced manure contamination into the milk. The bacterial illness can cause diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain, and may lead to serious complications for vulnerable people. Health officials stress that raw, unpasteurized milk can carry harmful bacteria and advise consumers to avoid it.

Texas health officials reported 48 new cases of cyclospora infection this week, mostly in the Dallas/Fort Worth area, with the source still under investigation. The outbreak may be connected to similar cases in Iowa and Nebraska, and past U.S. outbreaks have been linked to imported fresh produce. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, and nausea, though the illness is not highly contagious. Officials advise thoroughly rinsing fruits and vegetables to reduce risk, and medication is available for those infected.

The article reports the deaths of four young cousins from the Bakr family, killed by Israeli shelling while playing on a Gaza City beach. The Israeli military claims the strike targeted Hamas operatives and is under review, but the incident highlights the heavy toll on children, who make up about 40 of the more than 200 Palestinians killed in the recent bombardment. Journalists nearby witnessed the attack and helped the wounded, underscoring the tragedy. The story also conveys the shared fears of parents on both sides of the conflict, as well as the grief and anger at the boys' funeral.

A predawn fire tore through eight rowhouses in Philadelphia, killing four young children and displacing dozens of residents. The blaze, which began on a porch couch and spread through wooden porch roofs, also sent several people to the hospital, including minors. The victims, all from the home where the fire started, were a 1-month-old boy, twin 4-year-old girls, and a 4-year-old boy. A shelter was set up for those forced from their homes.

Eating more vegetables offers benefits beyond weight control and disease prevention. They can reduce bloating by flushing out excess sodium and supporting digestion, while their water and nutrient content promotes hydrated, youthful skin. Vegetables also help manage stress by supplying minerals and vitamins that stabilize blood sugar and calm the body. Additionally, certain vegetables contribute to bone health through calcium, vitamin K, and other bone-supporting nutrients.

The House is unlikely to pass immigration reform this year, despite President Obama’s openness to breaking the legislation into smaller pieces. Republicans remain divided, with many conservatives opposing any path to citizenship, and the party is hesitant to act while it sees political advantage in focusing on Obamacare. Timing is a key factor: some strategists suggest 2014 could offer a "sweet spot" before primaries, but deep partisan mistrust after the government shutdown and a lack of incentives for Republican lawmakers make progress difficult. Ultimately, without stronger Republican support and a deadline, immigration reform is expected to keep stalling.

Up to 500 migrants are believed to have drowned in the Mediterranean after traffickers deliberately rammed and sank their overcrowded vessel, according to survivor accounts. The migrants had refused to transfer to a smaller boat they considered unsafe, which enraged the smugglers, who then attacked the ship and left after ensuring it had gone under. The International Organization for Migration called it one of the worst migrant shipwrecks in years, describing the act as a deliberate killing by criminal gangs. The disaster pushes the estimated migrant death toll off Europe’s coasts this year to nearly 3,000.

Fifty years after John F. Kennedy's assassination, his presidency remains globally inspiring despite a mixed record of successes and failures. His key insight was that Cold War leadership required both military strength and the persuasive power of ideas, which he used to renew American influence and ease tensions with the Soviet Union. That lesson still applies today: the United States should balance hard and soft power, cooperate with China where interests align, and rebuild its standing in the Middle East by winning hearts and minds. Kennedy's emphasis on international engagement and measured leadership continues to offer relevant guidance for contemporary foreign policy.

The U.S. Department of Education has publicly released its first-ever list of 55 colleges and universities currently under federal investigation for possible mishandling of sexual violence and harassment complaints under Title IX. Officials said the move aims to increase transparency and encourage public dialogue, while noting that being listed does not mean a school has violated the law. Several institutions acknowledged the probes and emphasized their commitment to improving policies and supporting victims. The announcement follows a sharp rise in federal complaints and growing student activism pressing for stronger campus responses to sexual assault.

Heavy monsoon flooding across Pakistan has killed at least 58 people, with Balochistan province suffering the worst impact, including 15 deaths and over 20,000 displaced. The flooding has destroyed homes and overwhelmed dozens of villages, prompting army helicopters to deliver aid and tents to stranded residents. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, floodwaters are receding after killing 17 people, while officials say flooding in Karachi is largely under control. Additional fatalities have also been reported in Punjab, Fata, and Azad Jammu Kashmir.

The U.S. launched surprise airstrikes in Syria, joined by several Arab nations, to hit both ISIS and the al Qaeda-linked Khorasan Group, which was reportedly plotting an imminent attack on the West. The involvement of Arab states helps counter the narrative that the campaign is a war against Muslims, while targeting Khorasan also reflects intense rivalry among jihadist factions competing to strike American interests. Syria did not retaliate, though a Syrian jet was shot down after briefly crossing into Israeli airspace, underscoring the conflict’s volatility. The strikes came just before President Obama’s U.N. speech, highlighting both strategic timing and the awkward irony of acting a year after he backed away from attacking Assad.

Travelers often struggle to eat healthily during the hectic holiday season, which can contribute to weight gain. In response, airports and airlines are expanding their menus with more nutritious choices like salads, hummus, and whole-grain options. To stay on track, experts recommend planning meals around your schedule, researching healthy options at your airport and on your airline, choosing foods in their natural state while avoiding fried items and heavy sauces, and packing portable snacks for delays.

A Georgia father is charged with felony murder and child cruelty after allegedly leaving his 22-month-old son in a hot car all day while he went to work; the child died from hyperthermia. Police say the case goes beyond simple negligence, noting the father had recently searched online about children dying in hot vehicles. His wife and some friends have defended him, saying he was a caring father. He is being held without bond and is due in court in early July.

Brazilian churrascarias offer an abundant, meat-centric dining experience rooted in the gaucho barbecue tradition of southern Brazil. Servers circulate with skewers of slow-roasted meats, slicing off portions of more than 20 different cuts directly at the table. The most prized cut is picanha, a juicy rump cap, while other popular options include baby beef, top sirloin, filet mignon, and Parmesan-crusted pork loin. The rodizio style allows diners to sample a wide variety of meats, each cooked to their preferred level of doneness.

Dark tourism, or travel to sites associated with death and tragedy, is growing in popularity as people seek authentic, unvarnished experiences over conventional attractions. The article highlights several such destinations, including Dachau, Hanoi’s Hoa Lo Prison, Bangkok’s forensic medicine museum, Cambodia’s Killing Fields, Malaysia’s Penang War Museum, and Thailand’s tsunami memorials. These places serve both as historical lessons and sites of remembrance, though they also raise questions about the line between education, commemoration, and commercialization. Ultimately, dark tourism offers visitors a powerful, visceral connection to history while prompting reflection on how death and suffering are remembered and presented.

At the dedication of George W. Bush’s presidential library in Dallas, all five living former presidents gathered, with Democrats Jimmy Carter and Bill Clinton praising Bush’s Africa policy, particularly his role in the Sudan peace agreement. Bush defended his record, saying he stayed true to his convictions even when unpopular, and expressed confidence that history would judge his actions fairly. The museum’s exhibits highlight his early priorities and the transformative impact of the September 11 attacks, symbolized by World Trade Center beams. Bush said he is at peace with his presidency, while his mother, Barbara Bush, noted she would prefer to see other families in the White House rather than another Bush run.

Justin Bieber was arrested in Miami Beach on charges including DUI, resisting arrest, and driving without a valid license after police caught him street racing. The 19-year-old admitted to drinking alcohol, smoking marijuana, and taking prescription medication, raising questions about how he obtained them and rented the Lamborghini he was driving. Additional charges could follow, but deportation is unlikely since the current offenses are misdemeanors. There is no evidence he received preferential treatment, though three officers were suspended over unauthorized escorting of his caravan.

The deadly train derailment in Santiago de Compostela has put a spotlight on high-speed rail safety and the role of excessive speed. While high-speed trains are common in Europe and Asia, the U.S. lags behind, with only Amtrak’s Acela Express offering limited service. American safety regulations are far stricter than European standards, requiring heavier, more rigid train cars, which critics say drives up costs and slows the adoption of modern high-speed systems. These regulatory differences may help explain why the U.S. has struggled to build the kind of fast, widespread rail networks seen elsewhere.

Before surgery, patients should feel empowered to ask their healthcare team questions to reduce anxiety and prepare effectively. Key concerns include whether the procedure is truly necessary, what alternatives exist, and whether the chosen hospital or surgical center has sufficient experience with the specific case. Patients should also clarify how to prepare physically and mentally, discuss anesthesia options and risks, and understand what recovery will involve, including pain management and needed support. Relying on doctors and nurses rather than general online information is emphasized, since every patient’s situation is unique.

Bathurst, a small village in South Africa's Eastern Cape, is known for its quirky, creative spirit rather than typical town amenities. Its main attractions include the world's largest pineapple, which contains a museum, and the Pig and Whistle, the country's oldest continuously licensed pub. The village also features eccentric vintage shops, playful British-style humor, and an agricultural museum showcasing over 1,300 pieces of farming history. Home to artists and free spirits, Bathurst is especially lively on Sundays when its farmers market draws a crowd.

Philip Seymour Hoffman was a highly acclaimed and prolific actor known for memorable roles in both major films and independent theater, earning an Oscar for his portrayal of Truman Capote. Despite his Hollywood success, he remained down-to-earth, living modestly in New York, taking the subway, and prioritizing family life. He was equally respected for his stage work and his willingness to take on small, eccentric, or villainous characters. His heartfelt Oscar speech, in which he thanked his mother, further reflected the humble and genuine nature that made him beloved.

The article highlights common mistakes made by beginner triathletes and offers five key rules for improvement. It emphasizes developing enjoyment for swimming, biking, and running, while avoiding overcomplication with gadgets and trends. Beginners should not neglect their weakest discipline, should follow a structured training plan, and focus on the present rather than the finish line. The overall message is to keep training balanced, simple, and mentally manageable.

The article looks ahead to the 2014 midterm elections, focusing on the Senate battleground where Republicans need a net gain of six seats to take control. It highlights five key races—Kentucky, Alaska, Louisiana, Wyoming, and Georgia—each featuring competitive incumbents, primary challenges, or open seats. Other notable contests in New Hampshire, Iowa, Arkansas, North Carolina, Montana, West Virginia, and South Dakota could also shape the balance of power. Overall, the piece suggests that while many races may not be close, the cumulative results could significantly shift control in Washington.

President Obama’s Asia tour aimed to reaffirm U.S. commitment to the region, primarily by reassuring allies and signaling resolve toward China through military agreements, including a new defense pact with the Philippines. However, progress on trade was limited, as talks with Japan over the Trans-Pacific Partnership stalled. The trip also highlighted challenges to sustaining the “pivot,” with other global crises like Ukraine competing for attention. Alongside policy efforts, Obama offered condolences in South Korea and Malaysia after disasters and emphasized people-to-people ties as a key part of U.S. strategy.

Bradley Manning, the former U.S. soldier imprisoned for leaking classified material, has publicly declared she is a transgender woman named Chelsea and hopes to begin hormone therapy soon. The article also clarifies that gender identity differs from sexual orientation, explaining that transgender people may or may not choose medical transitions like hormone treatment or surgery. It notes that reliable data on the transgender population is limited, and that the latest psychiatric manual no longer classifies being transgender as a mental disorder, though it still recognizes gender dysphoria for access to care. Additionally, gender nonconforming behavior in children is relatively common and usually fades, but it is distinct from a lasting transgender identity.

The Senate is beginning debate on a bipartisan immigration overhaul that would offer most undocumented immigrants a 13-year path to citizenship while boosting border security and adjusting visa programs. The bill’s authors remain united, but conservative critics argue it has serious flaws and needs major changes. Its chances in the House are uncertain, where many Republicans view the citizenship pathway as amnesty. Public polls show majority support for a conditional path to citizenship, though most Americans doubt Congress can pass comprehensive reform.

Pope Francis, the first Jesuit and Latin American pope in modern times, is known for his humility and connection with ordinary people, often choosing public transit, simple living, and a pastoral approach. His papal name honors St. Francis of Assisi, reflecting a commitment to the poor and marginalized. While he is the first non-European pope in recent history, he is not the first overall. His papacy also faces challenges, including past controversies in Argentina, church scandals, and the need to address shifting Catholic views worldwide.

Hurricane Sandy has forced both presidential campaigns to scale back their activities, with President Obama returning to Washington to oversee the federal response and Mitt Romney canceling rallies and shifting to storm-relief efforts. The storm creates an opportunity for Obama to appear presidential, but also carries political risk if the government’s handling is seen as inadequate. Campaign advertising, early voting, and public polling in affected battleground states are all being disrupted, potentially freezing the race in place just days before the election.

Newt Gingrich’s decisive South Carolina victory reshaped the Republican race, showing that high-profile endorsements had little impact on voters. While Mitt Romney continued to attract moderates and educated voters, he struggled with conservatives, raising doubts about his strength in the South. The results also underscored the outsized influence of debates, which helped Gingrich surge late among late-deciding voters. The contest now heads to Florida, where a more aggressive and negative battle is expected, with the nomination fight likely to stretch well into the spring.

The explosion of TWA Flight 800 off Long Island in 1996, which killed all 230 people aboard, immediately raised fears of terrorism due to eyewitness reports of a possible missile and a series of recent attacks. The massive multi-year investigation considered state sponsors like Libya, Iraq, and Iran, and involved hundreds of witness interviews before ultimately ruling out a criminal act. The NTSB concluded that a spark in the center fuel tank caused the explosion, but investigators never determined the exact source of that spark. Despite the extensive effort, lingering questions about the official explanation have persisted for years.

The author reflects on how Brown v. Board of Education shaped her family’s history, from her parents fleeing Southern segregation to their eventual return to a transformed South. Despite the progress made since the Civil Rights era, she notes that U.S. schools are now resegregating, largely due to housing patterns and court rulings that weakened desegregation efforts. This trend harms students of color by concentrating them in under-resourced, high-poverty schools, while white students increasingly lack real-world cross-racial contact. She argues that fulfilling Brown’s promise requires equitable resources and deliberate education on race and social justice for all students.

Sixty-three women and girls recently abducted by Boko Haram managed to escape while their captors were away fighting security forces, and they returned to their destroyed village. However, the militant group is still believed to hold more than 200 schoolgirls taken from Chibok, a case that sparked global outrage. Boko Haram, which opposes Western education and seeks to impose strict Sharia law, has intensified kidnappings and attacks in northeastern Nigeria. The ongoing insurgency has caused widespread death and destruction, with the military and local vigilantes struggling to contain the violence.

Six British soldiers from the Scots Guard, all Fiji nationals, face third-degree assault charges after a fight outside a Manhattan bar left an off-duty NYPD officer and a friend injured. The altercation began as a verbal dispute and escalated into violence, with one soldier also accused of attempting to steal the officer’s phone. The soldiers were in New York for a rugby match, and three are scheduled to appear in court this week. The British Ministry of Defence said it is aware of the incident and will take disciplinary action, including possible discharge, if warranted.

The article highlights several destinations that offer macabre attractions throughout the year, not just at Halloween. Ohio features funeral and mortuary museums with historic hearses, celebrity death memorabilia, and even a former funeral parlor turned bed-and-breakfast. Other eerie locales include New Orleans for voodoo culture and haunted hotels, Charleston for Civil War relics and a bloodstained manuscript, Sleepy Hollow and Salem for literary and witch-trial history, and Edinburgh for underground tours and dark legends. It also notes the growing popularity of haunted attractions, now supported by an industry association.

A court in India has sentenced six men to life imprisonment for the gang rape and robbery of a Swiss tourist who was attacked while camping with her husband. The incident fueled political protests in Madhya Pradesh, where opposition leaders accused authorities of failing to maintain law and order. The case is part of a broader national reckoning over sexual violence, which intensified after the deadly 2012 Delhi gang rape and has continued with subsequent high-profile assaults.

The article reports that the United States accuses Russia of launching a full-scale military intervention in eastern Ukraine, providing arms, training, and funding to separatists, while Moscow denies direct involvement and claims the accusations are false. It traces the conflict back to Ukraine’s 2013 decision to abandon an EU trade deal, which sparked protests, the ouster of President Yanukovych, and Russia’s annexation of Crimea. The West has responded mainly with diplomatic pressure and economic sanctions, but experts say military action by NATO or the U.S. is not a realistic option. The situation may continue as a stalemate, with Russia willing to risk further sanctions to pursue its interests in the region.

Punjab offers an offbeat and vibrant travel experience in India, with its top draw being the stunning Golden Temple in Amritsar, known for its golden dome, healing pool, and massive free community kitchen. The region is also a food lover’s paradise, featuring iconic dishes like buttery tandoori bread, rich dal makhani, fried catfish, and creamy lassi at historic local eateries. Other highlights include the dramatic daily flag-lowering ceremony at the Wagah border, a peaceful rural stay at Punjabiyat Lodge, and historic sites like the Mughal-era Sarai Amanat Khan inn. Travelers can also unwind at the heritage hotel Ranjit's Svaasa, which offers luxurious rooms, spa treatments, and cooking classes in a charming 200-year-old setting.

A six-year-old Colorado boy was suspended from school after kissing a classmate on the hand, with the school labeling the act sexual harassment. His mother is outraged, arguing the punishment is far too harsh for a child his age and is seeking to have the term removed from his record. School officials defend the decision, citing their policy on unwanted touching and the need to protect the girl involved. The case has sparked public debate, with many seeing it as an overreaction to innocent childhood behavior while a few support the school's stance.

The article reframes disgust as more than just a fear of death, arguing that confronting gross things can lead to fascinating discoveries and even enjoyment. It highlights seven unusual American attractions that embrace this idea, including a Philadelphia medical museum with odd specimens, Oregon’s massive underground fungus, a California town where the dead vastly outnumber the living, and a Montana toxic pit lake. Other featured spots include an Indiana brain collection, a Missouri museum dedicated to Victorian hair art, and a Brooklyn library offering classes in whimsical taxidermy. Together, these places turn repulsion into curiosity about nature, history, and the human body.

The article highlights seven top U.S. destinations for summer wildlife watching, from Alaska’s Arctic Refuge with its massive caribou herd to Washington’s San Juan Islands for orcas, Montana’s Glacier National Park for elk and bighorn sheep, and Yellowstone for its ancient bison herds. It also features the spectacular bat flights at Carlsbad Caverns, nesting sea turtles along Florida’s coast, and wild ponies and migratory birds on Assateague and Chincoteague Islands. These locations offer prime opportunities to observe animals as they raise young and prepare for fall migrations. The piece closes with a reminder to keep a safe distance from wildlife and research potential risks before venturing into the wild.

Eric Cantor’s unexpected primary defeat stunned political observers and revealed deep dissatisfaction with his leadership style. Analysts attributed the loss to his perceived arrogance, excessive ambition, and failure to stay connected with his district, compounded by very low voter turnout. Conservative media and activists rallied behind challenger Dave Brat, while some Democrats also crossed over to vote against Cantor. The result sent a strong warning to Republican leaders that compromise and establishment politics could be punished by the party’s base.

Beth Pratt, a wildlife advocate and National Wildlife Federation California director, shares her favorite American nature destinations for Earth Day. Her picks range from Yosemite’s Gaylor Lakes and Yellowstone’s Mount Washburn to the salamander-rich Great Smoky Mountains and San Francisco’s coastal Lands End trail. She also highlights the scenic Beartooth Highway, Nebraska’s Platte River during the massive sandhill crane migration, and Cape Cod, where her childhood fascination with horseshoe crabs began. Throughout, she emphasizes seasonal wildlife viewing, wildflowers, and personal connections to these landscapes.

The article playfully suggests that modern video games offer virtual worlds so immersive that even Alexander the Great might have stayed home to explore them instead of conquering real lands. It highlights seven game settings—such as Hyrule, San Andreas, Rapture, and Minecraft—as dream destinations, praising their visual appeal and escapist appeal. For each fictional place, the piece offers a real-world alternative, like horseback riding in Mongolia or cruising Los Angeles in a luxury car. Overall, it celebrates gaming as a way to experience fantastical travel while also pointing to comparable real-life adventures.

A high-speed train derailed on a sharp curve in northwestern Spain, killing at least 80 people, including an American woman, and injuring dozens more, several critically. The crash occurred near Santiago de Compostela as the train approached the station, and authorities suspect excessive speed was the cause. The driver, who survived with minor injuries, is under police investigation, while officials have opened formal inquiries into the disaster. Spain declared national mourning as rescue crews worked through the wreckage and families awaited news of the victims.

Hotels have not always offered the modern comforts guests now take for granted. Over the past century, pioneering properties introduced innovations such as electric Christmas trees, en-suite bathrooms, in-room radios, room service, minibars, air conditioning, and complimentary toiletries, each eventually becoming industry standards. These breakthroughs transformed guest expectations and pushed hospitality toward greater convenience and luxury. More recently, eco-conscious resorts have also led the way by proving that sustainability and high-end comfort can coexist.

Brazil’s vast tropical coastline offers an extraordinary range of beaches, from iconic urban stretches like Rio’s Ipanema to secluded, unspoiled shores. The article highlights several standout destinations, including private, tranquil Praia dos Carneiros, car-free Caraiva, turquoise reef pools at Taipus de Fora and Porto de Galinhas, and the cliff-accessed Praia do Sancho. These beaches showcase Brazil’s beach culture, natural beauty, and variety, appealing to both relaxation seekers and adventure travelers.

Hotel pillows are more complex than they seem: their legally required tags date back to 19th-century efforts to prevent contaminated materials from spreading disease, and hotels replace them regularly for hygiene. Housekeepers use a quick "hot dog bun" technique to change pillowcases, and guests who bring their own pillows are a notable annoyance. Some hotels offer extensive pillow menus—one Singapore property has 16 options, including porcelain—while luxury properties may monogram pillowcases for VIPs. Ultimately, the article suggests it's better not to dwell on how many previous guests have used the same pillow.

The article suggests eight travel resolutions for the new year, encouraging readers to make their trips more adventurous and fulfilling. Key recommendations include spending some time exploring alone even when traveling with others, not letting language barriers prevent travel, and being open to organized tours or cruises. It also advises using all earned vacation days and truly disconnecting from work, saving money specifically for travel, and pushing personal boundaries by doing something slightly frightening. Finally, travelers should make their own choices based on their values rather than being held back by other people's fears.

The article describes the ancient stone city of Great Zimbabwe, a remarkable archaeological site in southern Zimbabwe known for its massive granite walls and unique dry-stone construction. Built by the Shona people, it was the capital of a prosperous trading empire from the 11th to 15th centuries and remains the largest pre-colonial structure in sub-Saharan Africa. The site, a UNESCO World Heritage landmark, features three main zones, including the impressive Great Enclosure with its curved granite walls. Its enduring cultural significance is reflected in the nation's name, "Zimbabwe," which comes from the Shona term meaning "big houses of stone."

The article celebrates milestones for the Channel Tunnel and showcases remarkable tunnels worldwide, highlighting their engineering achievements and unique features. It notes the Channel Tunnel as the longest undersea tunnel, the Laerdal Tunnel as the longest road tunnel, and other notable examples like Japan’s deep Seikan Tunnel and Malaysia’s dual-purpose SMART Tunnel. The piece also emphasizes human stories, such as the hand-built Guoliang Tunnel in China and the role of Colorado’s Eisenhower Tunnel in women’s rights. Overall, it underscores how these structures overcome geographic and technical challenges while transforming travel and communities.

The article highlights that while most Americans haven't served, everyone can support the over 23 million veterans through simple acts of kindness. Suggested actions include providing transportation to medical appointments, donating frequent flier miles for families to visit injured troops, and supporting programs that train service dogs for those with PTSD. Other ways to help involve building accessible homes for severely injured veterans, assisting homeless veterans through Stand Down events, and sending care packages or handwritten letters. Finally, people can volunteer with Honor Flight to take veterans to memorials, help preserve their stories through the Veterans History Project, or simply express gratitude by saying thank you.

Molly is widely misperceived as pure MDMA, but law enforcement reports that most samples actually contain dangerous, unregulated synthetic chemicals rather than the original compound. These lab-made stimulants can cause severe physical and psychological effects, including panic attacks, psychosis, seizures, and even death, with potency varying wildly between batches. The problem is fueled by clandestine chemists, primarily in China, who constantly tweak formulas to evade bans, making regulation difficult. Users, especially young people and electronic music fans, are essentially taking untested substances with no reliable way to know what or how much they are ingesting.

Two associates of former Patriots player Aaron Hernandez were indicted on murder charges in the 2013 shooting death of Odin Lloyd, after previously facing lesser accessory counts. Hernandez, already held on first-degree murder and weapons charges, allegedly picked up Lloyd with the two men, and surveillance showed the group near the crime scene. Defense lawyers for the newly indicted men questioned the timing and basis of the charges, suggesting they may be politically motivated. Related legal actions have also targeted Hernandez’s fiancée and cousin for alleged perjury and conspiracy.

Families of two men killed in a 2012 Boston drive-by shooting have filed $6 million wrongful death lawsuits against former Patriots player Aaron Hernandez, alleging he recklessly and maliciously fired into their vehicle. Hernandez has not been criminally charged in that case, but he remains jailed awaiting trial for a separate murder. The lawsuits come as Hernandez was moved to a higher-security jail unit following an altercation with another inmate. He also faces other civil actions, including suits from the family of Odin Lloyd and a man who says Hernandez shot him in the face.

The article contrasts historic maritime heroism, like captains who stayed aboard sinking ships to save passengers, with recent cases where captains abandoned their vessels. It focuses on South Korean Captain Lee Joon-seok of the Sewol ferry and Italian Captain Francesco Schettino of the Costa Concordia, both of whom face criminal charges for leaving passengers behind. Experts emphasize that a captain’s primary duty is passenger safety and that early departure creates a dangerous leadership vacuum during evacuations. While international law does not explicitly require captains to go down with their ships, abandoning passengers is widely considered a serious breach of duty.

A yearlong investigation by the Tampa Bay Times and the Center for Investigative Reporting found that dozens of U.S. charities, led by Kids Wish Network, raise hundreds of millions of dollars by exploiting sympathetic causes while giving almost nothing to those in need. These nonprofits often hire for-profit telemarketers, who keep the vast majority of donations, while some operators also pay themselves or family-run companies through consulting fees and other arrangements. Many of the worst offenders use misleading names similar to well-known charities, employ aggressive fundraising scripts, and rely on accounting tricks to hide how little reaches beneficiaries. In total, the 50 worst charities diverted nearly $1 billion over a decade that could have gone to charitable programs, highlighting a stark contrast with well-run nonprofits that spend most donations directly on their missions.The investigation revealed that America’s 50 worst charities, led by Kids Wish Network, raise over $1.3 billion but divert nearly $1 billion to for-profit solicitors, leaving less than 4% for direct aid. These groups often mimic reputable charity names, use deceptive telemarketing scripts, and enrich their own operators through salaries, consulting fees, and family contracts. Many employ accounting tricks and inflate donated goods to hide how little reaches those in need. The findings contrast sharply with well-managed nonprofits, which typically spend most donations on their actual programs.

Abu Dhabi is emerging from Dubai’s shadow as a rich and diverse travel destination, blending its deep maritime heritage with modern attractions. Visitors can enjoy the scenic Corniche waterfront, the opulent Emirates Palace hotel, and the lively fish market, which offer insight into both local life and luxury. The city also preserves its cultural roots through the Heritage Village and Cultural Foundation, while future plans for Louvre and Guggenheim branches aim to boost its arts scene. With landmarks like the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque and nearby Al Ain’s historic fort, Abu Dhabi offers a compelling mix of tradition and contemporary appeal.

A United Nations inquiry has documented systematic atrocities in North Korea, including murder, torture, starvation, and sexual violence, concluding that such abuses constitute crimes against humanity orchestrated at the highest levels of the government. The commission recommended referring the case to the International Criminal Court and warned leader Kim Jong Un he could face prosecution, though China, a key ally and Security Council member, has opposed such action. North Korea dismissed the report as a political fabrication, while the U.S. and human rights groups urged accountability and international action. The investigation, based on testimony from over 300 witnesses, highlighted harrowing accounts of prison camp brutality and called on the world to respond.

Ariel Castro has been ruled mentally competent to stand trial after a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation, with both prosecutors and defense agreeing on the finding. The judge accepted the sealed report and scheduled the next pretrial hearing for late July, with jury selection expected to begin in early August. Castro was also denied visitation with his young daughter, whose mother is one of his alleged victims. Prosecutors plan to seek a new grand jury indictment, while Castro faces hundreds of charges, including aggravated murder.

NASA researchers have proposed that Jupiter’s moon Ganymede may contain a layered internal structure resembling a “club sandwich,” with a salty ocean directly above its rocky core. This arrangement could allow chemical reactions between rock and water, potentially creating conditions favorable for life. The moon’s vast ocean, possibly 25 times larger than Earth’s, is thought to be dense enough due to salts that it sinks to the seafloor, with multiple ice layers and slush in between. While the model is uncertain, Ganymede joins several other icy moons considered promising targets in the search for subsurface oceans and habitability.

India’s Supreme Court has recognized transgender people as a third gender, a historic step against long-standing discrimination. The ruling offers hope to individuals like Abhina Aher, who faced family rejection, isolation, and social stigma before finding acceptance within the Hijra community. However, the court also reinstated a colonial-era law criminalizing consensual gay relationships, creating fear and confusion among LGBTQ activists. Despite legal progress, many transgender people still struggle with limited employment opportunities and deep-rooted social prejudice.

Creativity and innovation are not limited to the young; adults can also rediscover their creative path, though it becomes harder as distractions multiply. The article highlights that pursuing passion and purpose later in life requires making intentional choices, such as accepting less money for greater fulfillment and redefining failure as a necessary part of growth. Key advice includes shutting out external noise, continuing to learn, embracing iteration, making time for play and reflection, and seeking diverse perspectives. Ultimately, the drive to create is ageless, and anyone can reignite their innovative spirit by committing to self-discovery and sustained effort.

Acting Veterans Affairs Secretary Sloan Gibson visited the Phoenix facility at the center of the waiting-list scandal and announced the start of reforms, including contacting affected veterans and scheduling their appointments. He said a nationwide audit will be released Monday to reveal how widespread the problems are, and the department will use temporary staff, mobile units, and outside providers to speed up care. Gibson also suspended executive bonuses and removed the 14-day scheduling target from performance plans to prevent manipulation. Meanwhile, Senate negotiators reached a bipartisan deal to fund new VA facilities, hire more medical staff, and expand access to non-VA care for rural veterans.

The article describes how a low-budget desert adventure film secretly became an anti-Islam movie, shocking its cast and crew who say they were deceived about the script and purpose. The filmmaker, identified as convicted felon Nakoula Basseley Nakoula using the alias Sam Bacile, provoked violent protests across the Muslim world and was linked to the deadly attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi. Cast members expressed betrayal and sadness over the tragedies, while authorities investigated whether Nakoula violated his probation by using false names and accessing the internet. The film’s inflammatory portrayal of the Prophet Mohammed was amplified after Arabic-dubbed trailers aired on Egyptian television, fueling widespread outrage.

James Gandolfini, the acclaimed actor best known for playing Tony Soprano on HBO’s “The Sopranos,” died suddenly on Wednesday while vacationing in Rome; he was 51, and his managers said the cause may have been a heart attack. He won three Emmys for the role that made him a star, and the news prompted an outpouring of grief from colleagues, friends, and fans who remembered him as a deeply kind and talented man. Tributes highlighted both his powerful on-screen presence and his warmth and generosity off screen. He is survived by his wife, their young daughter, and a son from a previous marriage.

James Rebhorn, a prolific character actor known for many film and TV roles, passed away on Friday at age 65, according to his representative. He was widely recognized for appearances in movies like *Scent of a Woman* and *Independence Day*, as well as TV shows including *Seinfeld*, *White Collar*, and *Homeland*. His career also spanned soap operas and stage work, and he became a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2007.

Actress Ellen Page publicly came out as gay during an emotional speech at a Las Vegas conference supporting LGBTQ youth.
