She said she was tired of hiding and hoped her announcement could help others, and she received a standing ovation. Page also praised football player Michael Sam, who had recently come out as gay. The Human Rights Campaign, which helped organize the event, applauded her decision to live openly.

A Canadian woman was convicted of stalking and harassing actor Alec Baldwin and sentenced to 210 days in jail, along with a five-year protection order barring contact with him and his wife. The case stemmed from her repeated unwanted contact, including emails and an attempt to visit his apartment, which she claimed were attempts to find closure after a brief romantic encounter. Baldwin denied the relationship and testified that her behavior left him anxious and fearful. The judge also added time for contempt after the woman disrupted court proceedings with outbursts.

Adam Gadahn, an American-born al Qaeda spokesman, released a video urging attacks on U.S. ambassadors worldwide and praising the killing of Ambassador Chris Stevens in Libya. He also encouraged wealthy Muslims to fund rewards for assassinations, specifically mentioning a bounty on the U.S. ambassador to Yemen. Although several U.S. embassies in the region had recently been closed over general al Qaeda threats, officials said this particular video was not the direct cause. Gadahn, who has a U.S. bounty on his own head, has previously made similar calls for attacks on American diplomats.

Petra Vujevic, a 20-year-old Croatian computer science student, is spending a year away from university to try modeling in New York during Fashion Week. Though she juggles numerous castings and jobs with varied styles—from intimate presentations to a large Avril Lavigne show—her agency believes she has a special spark that could make her stand out. Vujevic remains down-to-earth, treating modeling as a temporary experiment rather than a lifelong career. She plans to return to her studies in Croatia in October and is unsure whether she would come back for another New York Fashion Week.

Chinese outbound travel has grown dramatically, with nearly 100 million trips in 2013 and projections of 200 million by 2018, driven by a rising middle class, easier visas, and more flight options. Today’s Chinese tourists are increasingly tech-savvy, booking online, favoring smaller groups or independent travel, and balancing a love of shopping with a growing desire for authentic experiences. The travel and hospitality industry must adapt by understanding Chinese cultural preferences and behaviors, as illustrated by Hilton’s “Huanying” program and efforts to educate guests on local customs and environmental care. Building strong brand recognition within China is also essential to earning the trust and loyalty of these travelers as they explore the world.

The Obama administration blocked Texas’s new voter ID law, citing concerns that it would disproportionately harm Hispanic and other minority voters. The Justice Department found little evidence of widespread voter fraud in the state and said the law could disenfranchise eligible voters. Texas officials condemned the decision as federal overreach, while civil rights groups praised it. The move follows a similar rejection of South Carolina’s voter ID law, and Texas’s new electoral maps are also facing separate legal challenges.

A&E has reversed its suspension of “Duck Dynasty” star Phil Robertson, announcing that filming will resume with the entire family after discussions with the Robertsons and advocacy groups. The network also plans to air public service announcements promoting unity and acceptance. The decision came after widespread conservative backlash and petitions supporting Robertson, while some LGBTQ and civil rights groups expressed cautious approval or continued criticism. The controversy highlights how the show has become a flashpoint in the broader culture wars over free speech, religion, and tolerance.

The article highlights a range of aerial and high-altitude experiences across Africa, making dramatic views more accessible to travelers. It features helicopter flights over Victoria Falls, private flying safaris over the Kalahari and Okavango, and a rotating cable car up Table Mountain. Other adventures include bungee jumping at the Nile’s source, skydiving in Kenya, hot-air ballooning over Zambia’s Busanga Plains, and microlight flights above Kruger National Park. The list also covers mountain treks, a Cairo observation tower, and a zipline through a South African gorge, with prices and practical details for each activity.

Newly revealed cockpit recordings from Air France Flight 447 show the crew’s confusion and panic in the final minutes before the 2009 crash, as they struggled to understand why the plane was not responding despite pulling back on the controls. The transcript captures frantic exchanges and repeated stall warnings just before the aircraft plunged into the Atlantic, killing all 228 people on board. French investigators and Air France have criticized the disclosure as a breach of regulations and sensationalized, arguing it adds little to the official inquiry. The episode has renewed focus on pilot training for high-altitude stalls and the broader challenges of flying modern airliners in extreme conditions.

A whistleblower at the Phoenix VA revealed that managers maintained a secret, off-the-books waiting list to conceal months-long delays in care for roughly 1,400 to 1,600 veterans. The scheme involved destroying records and reporting false wait times to Washington, while at least 40 veterans died waiting for appointments, including a Navy veteran with urgent bladder cancer. Internal emails showed top VA officials knew about and defended the practice. The revelations have prompted a congressional investigation and orders to preserve all records.

The article examines how the film "Zero Dark Thirty" centers on a fictional female CIA analyst, Maya, and argues this portrayal reflects the significant but often overlooked role real women played in the hunt for Osama bin Laden. It highlights historical figures such as Jennifer Matthews, Gina Bennett, and other female analysts who were instrumental in tracking al Qaeda, noting that the CIA's bin Laden unit was largely staffed by women. The piece also acknowledges that the movie makes creative choices, such as compressing the contributions of many individuals and dramatizing events, while noting that some torture scenes were toned down after expert feedback. Ultimately, it suggests that while the film takes liberties, the central image of a determined woman finishing the mission is grounded in historical reality.

Education is a crucial driver of personal and national development, particularly for girls, yet millions of children—especially in sub-Saharan Africa—remain out of school or lack basic literacy and math skills. Investing in girls' education yields significant economic and social returns, including higher earnings, reduced child marriage and mortality, and stronger GDP growth. However, simply increasing school enrollment is not enough; improving actual learning outcomes requires better funding, data, and accountability. African leaders and global partners are being urged to commit more resources to education, with young people demanding action at upcoming summits.

The Hadza are one of the world’s last hunter-gatherer communities, living in Tanzania with a unique language and ancient DNA tied to humanity’s roots. Their traditional lifestyle, based on foraging and hunting without permanent homes or food storage, is increasingly endangered by land loss to farmers and herders, as well as the disappearance of local wildlife and plants. Despite these pressures, some Hadza have gained official land rights, and a community spokesperson is working to secure similar protections for his own people.

The African diaspora, though diverse in background and experience, holds significant potential to drive Africa’s development by acting as cultural ambassadors, influencing foreign policy, and contributing skills and investment. Many diasporans maintain strong ties to the continent and can help counter negative stereotypes while promoting a more accurate, hopeful image of Africa. They are also increasingly returning or investing in African markets, helping to close skills gaps and create economic opportunities. Organizations like The Africa-America Institute have long facilitated this connection by training African professionals and fostering leadership that benefits both Africa and its diaspora.

After 15 years on Louisiana’s death row, Damon Thibodeaux was exonerated and released after DNA and other evidence proved his confession to a 1996 rape-murder was false. His case, championed by the Innocence Project, marked the 300th DNA-based exoneration in the U.S. Thibodeaux urged law enforcement to ensure they have the right suspect before pursuing execution, and advocates highlighted the need to videotape interrogations and reconsider the death penalty, which they argue risks putting innocent people to death.

Nepal is opening 104 previously unclimbed Himalayan peaks, bringing the total available to 414, in an effort to draw mountaineers back after a deadly avalanche killed 16 Sherpas on Everest. The move responds to climbers' requests and aims to revive interest following the cancellation of most Everest expeditions this season. Among the newly opened mountains are peaks named after Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay Sherpa. Although nearly all foreign climbers abandoned Everest this year out of respect for the victims, a few are still attempting the summit.

A five-year-old Alabama boy, Ethan, survived a six-day kidnapping in an underground bunker after his abductor killed the bus driver, and while he is currently eating and playing normally, experts say the long-term psychological impact remains uncertain. Drawing on parallels with the 1976 Chowchilla bus kidnapping, survivors emphasize that children cannot simply return to a carefree childhood after such life-threatening events, making a strong support system essential. Mental health professionals stress that Ethan, along with other children who witnessed the trauma, needs a stable, reassuring environment, consistent routines, and extra patience and attention to rebuild a sense of safety. Since Ethan also has Asperger’s syndrome and attention deficit disorder, experts note that familiar routines and specialized therapeutic interventions may be especially important for his recovery.

The release of Bowe Bergdahl has drawn renewed attention to other Americans still held captive in the region, sparking debate over the prisoner swap and why other cases were not included. Among them is Bob Levinson, a former FBI agent and alleged CIA contractor who has been missing in Iran for over seven years, making him the longest-held American hostage. Warren Weinstein, an aid worker kidnapped in Pakistan, remains in al Qaeda custody, and his family worries the political fallout from Bergdahl’s deal may reduce chances of future negotiations. Also unaccounted for are Caitlin Coleman and her Canadian husband, who disappeared in Afghanistan and appeared in videos pleading for help from the U.S. government.

The recent deaths of three young football players in different states have reignited the national debate over whether the sport is too dangerous for children. While some parents refuse to let their kids play due to concussion risks and the game's violent nature, others feel safer because of improved safety training programs like Heads Up Football. Though opinions differ on acceptable risk, there is broad agreement that prioritizing player safety and proper coaching is essential.

Germany is pushing ahead with an ambitious shift from nuclear power and fossil fuels to renewables, aiming for 35% clean electricity by 2020 and 80% by 2050. However, critics warn the transition is impractical and extremely expensive, citing high consumer energy bills, grid instability, and the high cost of wind and solar compared to conventional plants. Supporters acknowledge the upfront costs but argue that offshore wind can create jobs, reduce reliance on coal, and bring long-term economic and environmental benefits.

The conflict left a mixed outcome for key players: Israel achieved a tactical military success by degrading Hamas capabilities and showcasing its Iron Dome system, but analysts argue it emerged politically weaker amid a changed, post-Arab Spring landscape. Hamas gained greater legitimacy and attention for the Palestinian cause, though the killing of its military leader may lead to more instability. The Palestinian Authority and Mahmoud Abbas lost ground, appearing sidelined and without leverage over Hamas. Egypt’s President Morsi emerged as a pivotal broker, strengthening his regional standing, while Iran’s influence was somewhat diminished despite its ongoing role in supporting Hamas.

Smartphone users are expected to download fewer native apps in the coming years, as improved mobile web technology and faster networks make browser-based services a smoother experience. News and media apps are predicted to decline most sharply, since publishers can deliver content more cheaply and efficiently through the mobile web than through platform-specific apps. However, native apps will remain dominant in categories like games and utilities, where user experience depends on app-level performance. Overall, the shift points not to the end of app-like experiences, but to their evolution beyond traditional downloadable apps.

Federal health officials reported a fourth infant case of a rare Cronobacter infection linked to powdered formula, but stress there is no evidence connecting the cases and no recall is needed. The newest case was in Florida, joining infections in Missouri, Illinois, and Oklahoma, with two infants dying. Testing found no contamination in factory-sealed products, and bacterial DNA from the Missouri and Illinois cases differed, indicating unrelated sources. Officials advise parents to continue using powdered formula as directed, while noting Cronobacter can be serious in newborns and recommending breastfeeding when possible.

Morten Storm, a Danish former radical Islamist, became a double agent for Western intelligence after losing his faith, using his trusted position inside al Qaeda to work with the CIA. He gained the confidence of senior militants, including Anwar al-Awlaki, and even helped arrange a marriage as part of a spy operation. Storm claims his intelligence work led to al-Awlaki’s death, but he was denied the promised $5 million reward and later broke with his handlers. Now facing death threats from former comrades, including from ISIS, he lives in hiding.

The George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum in Dallas opens with exhibits highlighting his early agenda—tax cuts, education reform, and faith-based initiatives—before shifting focus to the September 11 attacks, which redefined his presidency. Central artifacts include World Trade Center steel and the bullhorn he used at Ground Zero, with visitors encouraged to touch the wreckage to connect with that historic day. An interactive “Decision Points” theater lets guests wrestle with his toughest calls, including the Iraq War and Hurricane Katrina, without offering apologies for controversial policies. While public opinion on his presidency remains divided, the museum reflects Bush’s confidence that history will judge him fairly.

Three friends in Baghdad created a comedy talk show to bring some humor to Iraqis living through years of conflict and hardship. The show, built around jokes from their personal banter, became popular with many viewers but also sparked outrage for addressing taboo subjects like sex and relationships. It faced protests, censorship complaints, and even threats against the host, forcing the team to soften its content and remove a female DJ. Despite these restrictions, the creators accept the limits imposed by conservative society as long as they can still make people smile.

Airbus has filed a patent for a futuristic airplane seat design that resembles a narrow saddle, with upright posture and minimal back support. The concept aims to increase passenger capacity by fitting four seats in the space currently used for three, potentially making flying more affordable on short routes. The design has drawn comparisons to a similar concept from an Italian firm and has been widely mocked as extremely uncomfortable. Airbus, however, says it files many patents and has no current plans to turn this particular idea into a real product.

Samoa Air has introduced a new extra-wide seat with additional legroom and a boarding ramp to better accommodate larger passengers, complementing its existing pay-as-you-weigh pricing model. The airline, which serves a population with high rates of obesity, says the larger seat is meant to give heavier travelers who pay more a more comfortable experience. While the weight-based fare system has drawn criticism as a “fat tax,” the airline defends it as a practical weight-management issue, not a health judgment. Industry analysts say the approach makes sense for a small carrier, but major U.S. airlines are unlikely to adopt it due to negative publicity and logistical challenges.

The Persian Gulf carriers are now reshaping the global airline alliance system, having already upended traditional European carriers. With Qatar Airways joining oneworld while Emirates and Etihad pursue separate partnerships with other oneworld members, loyalty within alliances has become blurred. These strategic deals, such as Etihad’s link to Air Berlin and Emirates’ tie-up with Qantas, undermine the coherence of alliances and expose their limits in today’s competitive market. The Gulf airlines’ growing power suggests alliances will continue to weaken as carriers pursue individual commercial interests.

A government watchdog report links a sharp rise in air traffic controller errors near airports and on approach paths to a 2009 policy that lets controllers report mistakes without punishment. While the FAA and controller unions argue the rule improves safety by encouraging transparency, investigators suggest it may reduce accountability and encourage riskier behavior. The increase in reported errors coincides with an unusually safe period for U.S. commercial aviation, with no fatal airline crashes since the rule began. Experts caution that the reporting change explains part of the spike, but not all of it, leaving safety concerns about near misses.

Air New Zealand has released a new in-flight safety video featuring Sports Illustrated swimsuit models, sparking mixed reactions. Critics argue it is sexist and a creative step backward from the airline’s earlier quirky and clever safety videos, while supporters praise it as effective marketing. The airline defends the video as tasteful and part of its strategy to make safety messages engaging and memorable.

A French air traffic controller strike has caused major flight disruptions across Europe, with thousands of passengers facing delays and cancellations. Eurocontrol described the situation as unstable, and major airlines such as British Airways, EasyJet, and Ryanair were affected, with Ryanair canceling about 15% of its scheduled flights. Brussels Airport also halted all flights after Belgian controllers joined the action, prompting frustration among travelers. Airlines advised passengers to check flight statuses, while EU rules entitle affected travelers to refunds or alternative arrangements.

Venezuela’s main airport in Caracas has introduced a controversial fee of about $18 for all departing passengers, supposedly to cover a new air-conditioning system that also releases ozone. The charge has sparked widespread mockery on social media, with travelers questioning its benefits and noting the airport’s poor conditions. This comes as several international airlines have cut back flights to Venezuela due to currency control disputes, though the government denies owing carriers money. The airport, a key regional hub, is also undergoing renovations.

A U.S. airship company and Icelandair Cargo have partnered to explore using a new type of hybrid airship for freight transport across the Arctic. The aircraft can take off and land vertically without runways, making it ideal for delivering standard cargo containers to remote, infrastructure-poor regions like Siberia, Alaska, and northern Canada. It also runs on diesel, offering significant fuel savings compared to traditional aviation fuel. The partnership could eventually turn Iceland into a major logistics hub and open up new economic opportunities in the region.

Genealogy enthusiast A.J. Jacobs is working to create a massive global family tree, showing that people are connected to famous figures like Barack Obama, Albert Einstein, and celebrities. He is organizing a world family reunion in New York City, aiming to break the record for the largest gathering, with proceeds going to fight Alzheimer’s disease. His project highlights the idea that all humans share common ancestors, and he even notes that DNA testing reveals many spouses, including himself and his wife, are distant cousins.

Akira Ioane, an 18-year-old New Zealand rugby player, has made a strong early impression on the international sevens circuit, drawing comparisons to All Blacks legend Jonah Lomu. Despite his rapid rise, Ioane dismisses such hype, emphasizing that he is still adjusting to the professional game, including a strict new diet and fitness regime. His Japanese name reflects his childhood in Tokyo, where his father played professional rugby, and he comes from a deeply athletic family. While his parents are proud, they also stress the importance of education as a safeguard against the uncertainties of a sports career.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad warned that foreign military intervention would have severe consequences for the entire region, insisting that Syria would not yield to international pressure. Meanwhile, tensions rose over an Arab League plan to send observers, as Syria demanded changes that the League rejected, accusing Damascus of trying to undermine the initiative. The ongoing crackdown has left thousands dead, though Assad disputed casualty figures and blamed armed groups rather than government forces for the violence. He also announced plans for elections and a new constitution, while vowing to resist any foreign attempt to remove him.

Alec Baldwin lashed out at a Daily Mail reporter over a story claiming his wife had been posting on social media during James Gandolfini’s funeral. Baldwin insisted his wife had left her phone in the car and called the report disgraceful, unleashing a series of angry tweets that included threats and derogatory language. He later deleted his Twitter account and issued a statement through GLAAD clarifying that his remarks were not homophobic. The article also notes this was not Baldwin’s first public outburst, referencing his 2011 removal from an American Airlines flight.

Actor Alec Baldwin and a photographer are in a dispute over an incident outside New York City’s marriage license office, where Baldwin had just obtained a license with fiancée Hilaria Thomas. Baldwin claims the photographer nearly struck him with a camera and used a Twitter post to criticize paparazzi, while the New York Daily News alleges Baldwin angrily hit photographer Marcus Santos in the chin. The newspaper published photos showing the confrontation, and Baldwin’s representative said the photographer was aggressive and that Baldwin only acted to protect himself.

An arbitrator has largely upheld Alex Rodriguez’s 211-game suspension for performance-enhancing drug use, meaning the Yankees slugger will miss the entire 2014 season and postseason and lose about $25 million in salary. The ruling, the harshest doping penalty in baseball history, stems from Rodriguez’s ties to the Biogenesis clinic and further tarnishes his once Hall of Fame-caliber career. Rodriguez responded defiantly, denying any failed drug test and accusing Major League Baseball of bias, and he is expected to appeal the decision in federal court.

Al Feldstein, the longtime editor of Mad magazine, has died at age 88 in Montana. He led the publication from 1955 to 1984, shaping its satirical voice and recruiting legendary contributors who influenced generations of comedy. After leaving Mad, he returned to his original passion and became a painter of Western wildlife and landscapes.

Alfredo Di Stefano, the legendary former Real Madrid forward, has passed away at the age of 88 after suffering a heart attack near the Bernabeu. Considered one of football’s all-time greats, he led Real Madrid to five consecutive European Cup titles and won numerous domestic honors. He also had a unique international career, representing Argentina, Colombia, and Spain without ever playing in a World Cup. Tributes poured in from across the football world, including from Sir Alex Ferguson, who praised his extraordinary balance and poise.

The article highlights a gap in planetary exploration: after the Curiosity rover, no funded missions are currently in development to search for habitable environments beyond Earth. It points to the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn—especially Europa—as the most promising targets, since they harbor vast subsurface liquid water oceans that could support microbial life. Exploring Europa could help answer whether life arises easily and whether biology can exist beyond the DNA-based chemistry found on Earth. The article argues that continued exploration, including of Earth’s own oceans, is essential to humanity’s pursuit of knowledge and should be a priority.

Egyptian authorities detained four Al Jazeera journalists in Cairo, alleging that one of them had contact with the banned Muslim Brotherhood and used a hotel as a base to broadcast negative coverage. Al Jazeera condemned the arrests as arbitrary and accused Egyptian security forces of ongoing harassment, including raids and equipment seizures. The detentions came as a press freedom group highlighted Egypt among the deadliest countries for journalists, with many killed in the previous year. The arrests reflect the intensified crackdown on dissent following the ouster of Mohamed Morsy and the government’s designation of the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization.

Fourteen alleged members of the white supremacist group American Front were arrested in Florida on charges including paramilitary training and conspiracy to shoot at a building. The group’s leader, Marcus Faella, allegedly planned disruptive protests to attract media attention and recruit new members, and investigators say he spoke of killing minorities during a predicted race war. The group, which has a violent history and declined after its former leader’s death, was operating from a fortified compound where members trained with weapons and made body armor. The arrests followed a two-year investigation aided by a confidential informant who had infiltrated the group.

The prosecution’s final witness testified that Jerry Sandusky sexually abused him in the coach’s basement during visits, saying he screamed for help but no one came and that he avoided looking at Sandusky when identifying him. Other accusers described inappropriate touching during showers and overnight stays, with one saying he stayed silent because he enjoyed the gifts and attention. A former police investigator testified that charges should have been filed after a 1998 complaint, but prosecutors declined at the time. Sandusky, who denies the allegations, faces 52 counts involving multiple boys over 15 years.

An all-female jury has been chosen for George Zimmerman’s second-degree murder trial, with opening statements set to begin Monday. Zimmerman, who fatally shot 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012, claims self-defense, while prosecutors argue he profiled and killed the teenager. The case has drawn national attention over race and gun laws, and the jury’s composition has raised questions about equal justice. Pretrial proceedings will also address whether audio analysis of screams from a 911 call can be admitted as evidence, a ruling that could affect the credibility of Zimmerman’s defense.

Iraq’s outgoing Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki has defiantly insisted he will not drop his bid for another term, rejecting claims that he had agreed to step aside in exchange for political concessions. His refusal deepens a political deadlock as Iraq’s newly elected parliament struggles to convene and form a government amid intense pressure to include Sunni leaders. The country’s top Shiite cleric has condemned the failure to reach an agreement as a serious setback during a critical time. Meanwhile, violence continues, including a suicide bombing near Samarra, while Iraqi forces claim to have retaken Saddam Hussein’s birthplace and Indian nurses held by militants have been freed.

Fernando Alonso secured pole position for the German Grand Prix with a strong performance in wet qualifying at Hockenheim, edging out Sebastian Vettel. Alonso credited a smart pit-stop strategy for giving him fresher tires at the crucial moment. Mark Webber qualified third but dropped to eighth due to a gearbox penalty, promoting Michael Schumacher to third. Heavy rain in the earlier session eliminated Felipe Massa and Nico Rosberg, who also faced a separate penalty.

A newly formed al Qaeda affiliate in South Asia claimed responsibility for an attempted hijacking of a Pakistani naval vessel, which it said was meant to attack U.S. ships in the Indian Ocean. The plot failed after a firefight, and Pakistani officials acknowledged that insider help may have been involved. The attack marked the first major operation by the group, announced by al Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri to counter the rise of ISIS. The two rival extremist networks are increasingly competing over who can legitimately establish and lead a global caliphate.

The leader of al-Nusra Front has issued an ultimatum to ISIS, demanding it halt internal fighting and submit to religious arbitration within five days or face expulsion from Iraq and Syria. This comes after al Qaeda’s central leadership already disavowed ISIS, which has clashed with rival rebels and alienated civilians through brutal tactics. The feud stems from disagreements over whether toppling the Syrian government or building an extremist state should come first. The infighting is diverting resources away from the fight against President Assad and ultimately strengthening his position.

Al Qaeda has publicly disowned its former affiliate, the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant, citing the group’s brutal tactics and the destructive infighting among Syrian rebel factions. The split follows months of clashes between ISIL and other jihadist groups, which have killed thousands and weakened the opposition to President Bashar al-Assad. Al Qaeda’s leadership had previously ordered ISIL to stand down and defer to the al-Nusra Front, but ISIL openly defied that command. Despite the rupture, ISIL remains a formidable force, attracting many foreign fighters and deepening the broader rift within the global jihadist movement.

The Westgate Mall attack in Nairobi demonstrates Al-Shabaab's increased capacity for complex, high-profile operations beyond Somalia, closely mirroring al Qaeda's guidance on targeting Western interests, taking hostages, and minimizing Muslim casualties. The assault was partly retaliation for Kenya's military intervention in Somalia, and the group's loss of key territory like Kismayo removed earlier restraints on striking Kenya. Nairobi's vulnerability is heightened by Al-Shabaab's ties to the local militant network al Hijra and the large Somali refugee community. The attack also reflects the tightening control of hardline leader Ahmed Abdi Godane, raising concerns about further regional violence and potential domestic backlash against Somali and Kenyan Muslims.

Althea Gibson was a trailblazing Black athlete who broke racial barriers in tennis, becoming the first African-American to win major titles like Wimbledon and the U.S. Nationals in the 1950s. Despite her success, she faced segregation, financial struggles after retiring, and was often overlooked by history. She later became the first Black woman on the professional golf tour, and her achievements inspired future stars such as Arthur Ashe, Zina Garrison, and the Williams sisters. Billie Jean King, who idolized Gibson, helped raise money for her in later years and continues to advocate for preserving her legacy.

Mom2Mom is a unique 24/7 helpline in the U.S. designed specifically for mothers of children with special needs, staffed by peer counselors who have lived through similar experiences. Founded by Cherie Castellano, the program offers emotional support, ongoing follow-up, in-person meetings, and referrals, helping mothers feel less isolated and more able to care for themselves. It also connects callers with support partners whose children have similar conditions, and although funded for New Jersey residents, it has helped families from over 20 states. For mothers like Suzanne Jablonski and Debra Lee, the service has been transformative, easing feelings of shame and crisis while building a sense of community and self-worth.

Amanda Bynes was arrested early Sunday on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs after failing field sobriety tests in Sherman Oaks, California. Police noted her disheveled appearance but said she was cooperative during the arrest. The arrest is the latest in a series of legal and personal struggles, including a prior DUI charge that was reduced to reckless driving, an involuntary psychiatric hold, and a period under her parents' custody. She had recently appeared to be doing better, focusing on fashion school and posting positive updates on social media.

Amanda Bynes was arrested in Manhattan after police responded to reports of her smoking in her apartment building and allegedly saw her toss drug paraphernalia out a 36th-floor window. She now faces charges including felony tampering with evidence, reckless endangerment, and misdemeanor marijuana possession. The arrest adds to her ongoing legal troubles, which include a pending DUI case in California and a recent three-year probation sentence for driving on a suspended license.

Amanda Knox says she is afraid to go back to Italy for a retrial in the murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher, but she is open to returning. She insists there is no evidence linking her to the crime and defends her right to speak out, rejecting criticism that she acted coldly after the killing. Knox also dismisses prosecutors’ claims of a sexual motive as absurd and says she has faced death threats since returning to the U.S., which is why she has taken self-defense training.

An Italian court has convicted Amanda Knox and Raffaele Sollecito again in the murder of Meredith Kercher, increasing Knox’s sentence to 28 years and Sollecito’s to 25 years. The retrial followed Italy’s Supreme Court overturning their 2011 acquittals due to unresolved evidence and testimony issues. Knox, who remains in the U.S., is expected to contest any extradition, while Sollecito, an Italian citizen, had his passport revoked. Kercher’s family welcomed the verdict, though further appeals could prolong the case.

Amanda Knox has vowed to keep fighting her renewed murder conviction, saying she was shocked by the verdict and will never willingly return to Italy. Her lawyer argues there is no evidence against her and that extradition talks are premature while appeals continue. Meanwhile, her co-defendant Raffaele Sollecito was briefly stopped near Italy’s border, though his lawyer said he was not trying to flee. Meredith Kercher’s family acknowledged the painful reality that they may never know exactly what happened, but they hope the case can finally reach a conclusion.

Amazon’s “Sell” link opens a global marketplace for small merchants, who can store inventory in Amazon’s international warehouses and reach customers in roughly 180 countries. The Fulfillment by Amazon program lets entrepreneurs like Bernie Thompson of Plugable Technologies ship in bulk to hubs abroad, cutting costs and enabling fast local delivery. This system gives small sellers access to hundreds of millions of potential buyers while allowing them to focus on product development and customer service. Amazon also benefits from a flexible network of independent sellers who can quickly shift inventory in response to shifting global demand.

Amazon unveiled its first smartphone, the Fire, which is built to deepen users’ ties to Amazon’s shopping ecosystem. Its standout feature, Firefly, uses image, text, and audio recognition to identify products, songs, movies, and more, then instantly directs users to buy them from Amazon. The phone is priced like other high-end smartphones and comes with a free year of Amazon Prime, reflecting Amazon’s strategy of using hardware to drive ongoing purchases. While its success is uncertain, Firefly could make it even easier for shoppers to compare prices and buy through Amazon on the go.

Amber Rose has publicly denied allegations that she cheated on her estranged husband, Wiz Khalifa, and instead suggested that he was unfaithful. She has filed for divorce and is seeking full custody of their young son. The couple, who married just over a year ago, separated earlier this week, with Rose saying she is heartbroken but focused on their child.

Amelia Rose Earhart, a 31-year-old pilot who recently learned she is not actually related to her famous namesake, plans to fly around the world in a single-engine plane later this month. Her goal is to become the youngest woman to complete such a journey and to symbolically “close the flight plan” that Amelia Earhart left open when she disappeared in 1937. The trip will begin and end in Oakland, California, spanning about two and a half weeks with 17 stops across 14 countries. She says she is not afraid of the legendary pilot’s fate, citing modern technology and advanced navigation systems, though she remains mindful of challenging weather conditions.

American Airlines has joined other carriers in discontinuing special bereavement fares, citing the availability of cheaper last-minute tickets and more flexible options. Delta and United still offer some form of bereavement discounts, though the benefits are often minimal. Critics argue the move reflects broader industry consolidation, which tends to reduce consumer choices and services. Many travelers may find better deals online anyway, but the policy shift is seen by some as a sign of declining compassion from airlines.

A U.S. citizen infected with Ebola in Sierra Leone has been transported to Emory University Hospital in Atlanta for treatment, though officials have not confirmed whether this patient is the WHO doctor who recently tested positive. Meanwhile, another American doctor, Rick Sacra, continues to improve at a Nebraska medical center. The outbreak has now infected more than 4,200 people and killed over 2,200, with cases rising rapidly, especially in Liberia. In response, the U.S. has pledged additional millions in funding and plans to send more health care workers to West Africa to help contain the crisis.

The U.S. men’s hockey team suffered a crushing 5-0 defeat to Finland in the Olympic bronze-medal game, ending their hopes for a podium finish in Sochi. The Americans appeared flat and were still affected by their earlier semifinal loss to Canada, which had forced them into the consolation match. Finland took control in the second period and pulled away in the third, showcasing their NHL-heavy roster. Meanwhile, the U.S. women’s team had a better outcome, earning a silver medal after a narrow overtime loss to Canada.

Oracle Team USA staged a remarkable comeback in the America’s Cup, erasing an 8-1 deficit to tie Emirates Team New Zealand at 8-8, forcing a winner-take-all final race. The defending champions won both races on Tuesday, aided by improved boat performance and a tactical change that brought in Ben Ainslie. New Zealand had a chance to delay the decider but chose to race instead. The dramatic turnaround sets up what could be the most thrilling finish in the event’s 162-year history.

New mapping technology has revealed that North America’s tallest mountain, Mount McKinley in Alaska, is 83 feet shorter than previously recorded, with its official height now set at 20,237 feet instead of 20,320 feet. The old measurement, which had stood since 1952, was based on photogrammetry, while the new figure comes from a radar mapping system used by state and federal agencies. Climbers who have scaled the peak, also known as Denali, said the change does not matter to them, noting the climb remains just as difficult and the air just as thin. The mountain still stands well above Canada’s Mount Logan, the continent’s second-highest peak.

A breakaway Amish leader in Ohio was sentenced to 15 years in prison for orchestrating hate crimes against fellow Amish who had left his community. He and his followers forcibly cut the beards and hair of victims, acts that carry deep religious significance in Amish culture. The attacks, carried out in 2011, were described as revenge against families who departed over religious disagreements. Sixteen people were convicted overall, with followers receiving prison terms ranging from about one year to seven years.

Amnesty International has warned that China’s decision to shut down its re-education through labor camps may be largely symbolic, as authorities appear to be replacing them with other forms of arbitrary detention. These include unofficial “black jails,” forced drug rehabilitation facilities, and so-called brainwashing centers, where abuses reportedly continue. The report highlights cases of detainees being re-detained upon release and says the system has long been used to punish political and religious dissent. Amnesty is urging China to end all arbitrary detention and bring its laws in line with international human rights standards.

Punjab offers an offbeat and vibrant travel experience in India, with its top draw being the stunning Golden Temple in Amritsar, known for its golden dome, healing pool, and massive free community kitchen. The region is also a food lover’s paradise, featuring iconic dishes like buttery tandoori bread, rich dal makhani, fried catfish, and creamy lassi at historic local eateries. Other highlights include the dramatic daily flag-lowering ceremony at the Wagah border, a peaceful rural stay at Punjabiyat Lodge, and historic sites like the Mughal-era Sarai Amanat Khan inn. Travelers can also unwind at the heritage hotel Ranjit's Svaasa, which offers luxurious rooms, spa treatments, and cooking classes in a charming 200-year-old setting.

Amtrak has introduced a free writer residency program on its long-distance train routes, offering selected writers sleeper accommodations and scenic travel to focus on their work. The idea originated from a tweet by writer Jessica Gross, inspired by novelist Alexander Chee’s comment about wanting such a residency, which led to a trial trip and eventually a formal application process. Up to 24 writers will be chosen annually for trips lasting two to five days, with no requirement to produce or publish anything about Amtrak. The program aims to generate organic buzz and rekindle the romantic appeal of train travel while giving writers a unique space to create.

The article reflects on the cultural and historical significance of American railroads, arguing that trains were essential in building the nation by connecting regions and fueling economic growth. It explains how rail travel declined with the rise of cars and planes, leading to the creation of Amtrak in 1971 to preserve passenger service. Despite ongoing political debates over subsidies, Amtrak remains highly successful in the Northeast, while also offering scenic long-distance routes like the California Zephyr. The piece concludes that traveling by train still provides a unique and meaningful way to experience America, especially during election season.

Mitt Romney selected Paul Ryan as his running mate in a bold and early announcement, a choice that surprised many political observers. Ryan is known for his controversial proposals to overhaul Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security, which has made the pick both risky and potentially energizing for the Republican base. Supporters argue that Ryan’s focus on fiscal issues helps frame the election around big national questions, while the Obama campaign quickly attacked the ticket, claiming it would harm the middle class and the elderly. The unusually early timing was also seen as a strategic move to shift attention away from Romney’s recent missteps and falling poll numbers.

John Kerry has brought an unusually hands-on, high-energy approach to his first months as secretary of state, traveling extensively and personally negotiating agreements on issues like Syria aid and Middle East peace. He pushed international backers to channel military support through the moderate Syrian opposition and sought commitments against extremism, while also working to revive Israeli-Palestinian talks and ease tensions with North Korea. His direct, sometimes outspoken style has impressed foreign leaders but also raised concerns in Washington about whether he is overpromising or straying from White House policy. Ultimately, Kerry’s success may depend on maintaining President Obama’s trust and staying within the bounds of White House control.

As the primary race winds down, Mitt Romney and President Obama are already turning their attention to the general election, exchanging early attacks. Obama criticized Romney by name over his support for the Ryan budget, while Romney blamed the president for high gas prices. Although Romney swept the latest primaries, exit polls revealed lingering weaknesses with working-class, rural, and evangelical voters, as well as doubts among some Republicans. Still, these issues are seen as challenges for the fall rather than threats to his nomination.

A new Deloitte report shows that the English Premier League’s record revenue, boosted by a lucrative new television deal, could give its clubs a significant financial edge over European rivals in the Champions League. However, much of that income is being absorbed by rising player wages, with the league’s wages-to-revenue ratio hitting a record 71% and operating profits remaining thin. Despite this, the Premier League remains the top-earning European league, far ahead of Germany, Spain, Italy, and France, while the Bundesliga stands out for stronger profitability and stricter cost control.

The Dubai Mall is an extraordinary shopping destination, drawing more visitors annually than major global landmarks and featuring immense scale with over a thousand stores, an ice rink, an aquarium, and even a flight simulator. Operating this massive complex requires a workforce comparable to a small army, including a large night cleaning crew that works quickly to maintain the vast space before reopening. Outside, the adjacent artificial lake and fountain demand daily attention to combat sand accumulation, aided by robotic vacuums. Despite its success, the mall’s leadership acknowledges that continuous effort is needed to fully achieve their vision of excellence.

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have officially married in a private ceremony at their French estate, with their six children playing key roles in the wedding. The couple, who met in 2004 and got engaged in 2012, had long delayed tying the knot, partly in support of same-sex marriage rights. Their marriage license was obtained in California and legally recognized under state law.

The acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting of Trayvon Martin triggered widespread anger and grief, with many viewing the verdict as a painful confirmation of racial injustice and the devaluation of Black lives. Peaceful protests erupted in several cities, while social media campaigns using hoodie imagery and hashtags like #JusticeforTrayvon expressed solidarity with the slain teenager. Critics argued the case highlighted the dangers of racial profiling and "stand your ground" laws, drawing parallels to other victims and the conviction of Marissa Alexander. Despite the despair, some voices urged continued struggle and nonviolent action for change.

Internet activist Aaron Swartz, known for helping create Reddit and RSS, died by suicide at age 26 while facing federal prosecution for allegedly downloading millions of academic papers from MIT. His family blamed the harsh charges and MIT’s involvement for contributing to his death, prompting MIT to review its role in the case. The incident sparked widespread online tributes, including researchers sharing papers in his honor, and Anonymous briefly defaced MIT websites in protest. Federal prosecutors dropped the charges after his death.

Democratic lawmakers criticized an all-male witness panel at a House hearing on religious freedom and contraception, demanding to know why no women were included. Rep. Carolyn Maloney specifically objected to the exclusion of Georgetown law student Sandra Fluke, who had sought to testify about a classmate harmed by lack of contraceptive coverage. Committee Chairman Darrell Issa defended the decision, citing procedural rules and arguing the hearing was focused on religious liberty rather than the contraception mandate. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi echoed the criticism, questioning how a panel on women’s health could exclude women.

The trial of the Sewol ferry captain and 14 crew members has begun in Gwangju, where grieving relatives confronted them over the disaster that killed 292 people, mostly schoolchildren. The captain pleaded not guilty to murder, with his defense arguing that he was not primarily responsible for the overloaded and poorly secured cargo that caused the sinking. Prosecutors, however, contend that the crew ignored rescue requests and prioritized their own safety, amounting to murder. Meanwhile, authorities continue searching for the ferry company’s alleged owner, Yoo Byung Eun, who is wanted in connection with financial irregularities linked to the tragedy.

A Chinese animal protection group rescued nearly 800 dogs from being transported to restaurants in southern China, paying a dog trader about 83,000 yuan after a standoff. The animals, many severely dehydrated, were being packed in cramped cages, and volunteers are now providing care, reuniting some with owners, and seeking new homes. The rescue highlights the growing opposition to China’s dog meat trade, though activists note the lack of a national animal welfare law makes enforcement difficult. Similar rescues, such as one in April involving 520 dogs, have fueled debate over animal rights in the country.

Rising inequality is a central concern of modern capitalism, as progress often leaves many behind while benefiting a fortunate few. The future of work, shaped by automation and digital innovation, may favor creativity and talent over traditional capital, prompting debates about capitalism’s survival. However, individual success still depends heavily on public investment in physical and social infrastructure, from roads to education and care. To counter inequality, societies should adopt a “leg-up state” approach that invests in human potential and enables more people to create their own opportunities.

The article criticizes the pervasive message in professional sports that players must avoid being distractions, which pressures gay athletes to hide their identity to keep their jobs. The author argues that sexual orientation has no bearing on athletic performance and that an openly gay player should not be seen as a disruption. He calls on teammates, coaches, and the media to grow up and treat gay players with the same respect as anyone else, focusing on their on-field contributions. Most importantly, he assures the first gay player to come out that he will have support and allies.

A United Airlines 787 Dreamliner was forced to return to Houston on Sunday because of a brake indicator issue, marking the third diversion involving the aircraft type in less than a week. The two earlier incidents were related to oil filter and low oil indications, and all flights landed safely with no injuries. These mechanical issues follow the global grounding of the Dreamliner earlier this year over battery problems. Despite the setbacks, United has shown confidence in the plane by ordering 20 additional 787-10s, while rival Airbus recently flew its competing A350 for the first time.

The article criticizes the Obama administration for consistently failing to support pro-democracy movements abroad, citing Hong Kong as the latest example after similar situations in Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela. It argues that U.S. officials offered only vague statements about general rights while avoiding explicit backing for democratic aspirations. The piece attributes this reluctance to Obama’s desire to distance himself from George W. Bush’s freedom agenda, a self-image of pragmatic realism, and progressivism’s skepticism toward liberty. It concludes that even symbolic moral support from the United States is deeply meaningful to oppressed groups, and that withholding it betrays America’s founding principles.

U.S. officials are weighing whether to authorize a drone strike against an American al Qaeda operative in Pakistan, with the final decision resting with President Obama. The debate centers on whether to strike immediately or continue surveillance to gather more intelligence, while also considering the sensitivity of U.S.-Pakistan relations and the challenges of maintaining drone operations after 2014. The article also highlights concerns about growing ties between al Qaeda in Pakistan and Somalia’s Al-Shabaab, including an American citizen linked to the group. Legal experts remain divided, with some defending the president’s authority to kill American terrorists abroad, while civil liberties groups argue such secretive targeted killings violate due process and constitutional limits.

Huma Abedin publicly stood by her husband, Anthony Weiner, after he admitted to new explicit online exchanges following the scandal that forced him from Congress. She said forgiving him required significant effort and therapy, but she chose to stay in the marriage and support his New York City mayoral campaign. Abedin, a longtime close aide to Hillary Clinton, is known for being private, making her decision to speak out especially notable. She acknowledged his “horrible mistakes” but expressed love, forgiveness, and belief in him as they move forward.

Ukraine is experiencing its largest protests since the 2004 Orange Revolution, triggered by President Viktor Yanukovich’s decision to abandon a trade deal with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Russia. Demonstrators have occupied government buildings and Independence Square, demanding Yanukovich’s resignation and early elections, with opposition leaders urging peaceful, unified action. The government has responded with force, including tear gas and batons, while Yanukovich warns against radicalization and Putin dismisses the unrest as politically motivated. Despite calls for dialogue, protesters say they have passed the point of no return and view the movement as a revolution.

A Kansas City-area shooting at two Jewish facilities left three people dead, with police arresting 73-year-old Frazier Glenn Cross, a longtime white supremacist who had been active in hate movements since the 1970s. The attack came just after the Anti-Defamation League had warned of heightened risk around Passover and Hitler’s birthday. Although overall anti-Semitic incidents in the U.S. have declined, violent assaults against Jewish people rose significantly in 2013, underscoring concerns about emboldened extremists. Cross, who had a history of paramilitary activity and had previously cooperated with federal prosecutors, was known for virulent anti-Semitic rhetoric and had long been involved in white supremacist groups.

French footballer Nicolas Anelka sparked widespread controversy by using the “quenelle” gesture—popularized by comedian Dieudonné—to celebrate a goal, with critics linking it to an inverted Nazi salute and rising anti-Semitism in France. Anelka defended it as an anti-system tribute to his friend, while other French athletes who made the gesture apologized. The incident intensified debate over free speech and anti-Semitism, especially amid reports of increasing anti-Jewish attacks in France. Anelka was asked by his club not to repeat the gesture and now faces possible disciplinary action from English football authorities.

Gabby Giffords and her husband Mark Kelly reflect on life after the 2011 Tucson shooting that killed six and left her with severe injuries. Though she still struggles with aphasia, limited vision, and paralysis on her right side, Giffords says she feels stronger and remains determined to move forward. The couple notes that the tragedy brought their family closer together, including improving her relationship with Kelly’s daughters, and they express empathy for the shooter’s parents while acknowledging his untreated mental illness. Despite ongoing challenges and uncertainty about having children, Giffords shows no resentment, focusing instead on recovery and the future.

Ryanair’s CEO, Michael O’Leary, sparked controversy by claiming seat belts are useless because they wouldn’t save passengers in a major crash. He proposed introducing standing-room-only sections on planes, offering very cheap standing tickets to budget travelers. However, the article points out that seat belts are essential for turbulence, not just crashes, and that European safety regulations requiring seat belts make his plan unlikely to happen. O’Leary dismissed the regulators, but his idea remains more provocative than practical.

People often ruin live concerts by filming them on their phones, even though they will never rewatch the footage, and this habit has become a widespread annoyance. The Yeah Yeah Yeahs recently asked fans to stop watching shows through screens, and the author recalls how many people at a Roger Waters concert missed an incredible spectacle because they were staring at their devices. A positive example came at Wanee Festival, where poor cell service led most attendees to simply enjoy the music. The article ultimately urges concertgoers to put their phones away and be present in the moment.

According to the article, a new study supports the "Cheerleader Effect," the idea that people appear more attractive when seen in a group than when viewed alone. Researchers at the University of California, San Diego found that being surrounded by others helps average out unattractive or unusual facial features, making individuals look better overall. The effect applied to both men and women, with people in group photos rated about 5.5% more attractive than in solo shots. Essentially, having companions in social settings can boost your perceived appearance by minimizing flaws.

A couple brought their eight-month-old baby to Alinea, a high-end Chicago restaurant, sparking an online debate after the infant cried and other diners complained. The chef, Grant Achatz, tweeted about the situation, questioning whether parents should bring small children to such upscale establishments. The discussion highlighted a general view that there is a certain level of fine dining where young kids don’t belong, though the exact line is debatable. The story gained further attention when a parody Twitter account appeared for the baby, and the chef later responded with a joke about the child’s food preferences.

A fan determined that the “good day” described in Ice Cube’s 1992 song likely occurred on January 20, 1992, and his research inspired a crowdfunding campaign called the Good Day Blimp. The project aims to raise $25,000 for a South Central Los Angeles youth charity while pressuring Goodyear to fly its blimp on that date displaying the message “Ice Cube’s a Pimp.” Goodyear has responded cautiously, noting it cannot accommodate every request but expressing willingness to support the charity directly. Ice Cube himself endorsed the effort, calling it “dope” and encouraging donations.

A teenager named Zach Belden created an Instagram account to document the life of his 80-year-old great-grandmother, Betty Jo Simpson, who has lung cancer. The account quickly gained hundreds of thousands of followers because of her charming personality, leading to media attention, fan letters, and even a custom logo. Beyond the viral fame, the story highlights the deep bond between generations and how social media can create meaningful connection. It contrasts sharply with the narrator’s own trivial posts, showing the positive potential of sharing genuine moments online.

Keurig is introducing a new 2.0 brewer with digital rights management technology that uses a camera to read proprietary markers on pods, meaning only Keurig-branded cups will work. The company claims this ensures performance and safety, but competitors argue it is an anti-competitive move to lock out cheaper third-party options. This has already sparked legal challenges, with at least one lawsuit filed and another company considering action. The new machines also add the ability to brew full carafes, not just single cups.

Tech investor Tim Draper is pushing a ballot initiative to split California into six separate states, arguing that the state’s size leaves it poorly represented in Washington and that smaller states would foster better governance and business competition. The proposal has gained attention as Draper prepares to submit it to state officials, though getting it on the ballot faces major legal and financial hurdles. The article also notes that the idea isn’t entirely unprecedented, referencing a pre-Civil War vote to divide California, but treats the plan with humor and skepticism. Ultimately, any real change would take years, and the proposal remains more of a provocative talking point than a likely outcome.

A humorous article discusses a study suggesting that penis size does matter to heterosexual women, contradicting the comforting idea that it doesn’t. Researchers used computer-generated male figures and found that while body shape and height were the most important factors, larger genital size boosted attractiveness ratings. Taller men benefited more from size due to proportion, and fit body type remained the strongest overall influence. The piece ends by noting that real-life appeal involves more than the traits measured in the study.

Scientists uncovered the oldest known sperm, estimated at 17 million years old, remarkably preserved in bat guano within an Australian cave. The fossilized sperm was found inside tiny crustaceans called ostracods, or seed shrimp, and was surprisingly large—about the length of the shrimp itself. A retired paleontologist spotted the specimens in museum sediment, and further analysis with a specialist confirmed the discovery. The findings were published in a scientific journal, highlighting an extraordinary example of long-term preservation.

A federal appeals court has dismissed a lawsuit brought by the now-defunct Al-Haramain Islamic Foundation, which claimed the government illegally wiretapped its communications without warrants under a secret surveillance program. The court ruled that Congress had not waived the government’s immunity from lawsuits over the collection of intelligence, even if constitutional rights were violated, though it noted claims over the use of such information might still be possible. The decision overturned a lower court’s $2.5 million attorney fee award and effectively ended the group’s long-running legal challenge. The judges also rebuked Justice Department lawyers for accusing the plaintiffs of “game-playing,” calling such criticism careless given the serious civil liberties concerns involved.

A federal appeals court narrowly ruled that Michigan’s voter-approved ban on using race and gender in college admissions is unconstitutional, saying it unfairly burdened minority students seeking policy changes. The state plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, with officials defending the ban as a matter of merit and equal opportunity. Supporters of the ruling called it a major victory and hope the Supreme Court will use the case to strike down similar affirmative action bans in other states. The decision applies only to college admissions, not to the ban’s effects on public hiring or contracting.

Apple’s iPhone 4S introduces Siri, a voice-controlled virtual assistant that can answer questions, set reminders, schedule appointments, and send messages by interpreting natural language. The feature is expected to be a major selling point, as it goes far beyond earlier voice command systems by integrating with services like Yelp and WolframAlpha. Siri originated from an AI research project at SRI International, was later developed into a standalone app, and was acquired by Apple in 2010. Initially, the enhanced Siri will be available only on the iPhone 4S, which Apple is betting will draw customers to the new device.

Afghan women have seen real gains since the Taliban’s fall, including access to education, jobs, and legal protections, yet serious abuses like forced marriage, domestic violence, and imprisonment for “moral crimes” remain widespread. With foreign troops set to withdraw and peace talks with the Taliban approaching, many women fear their rights will be sacrificed. Concerns deepened when President Karzai appeared to endorse a conservative religious council’s statement that women should not travel without male chaperones, avoid mixing with men, and accept secondary status. The article urges international backers to insist that any negotiated settlement protect women’s rights and to press Karzai to clearly reject such rollbacks.

The deadliest Ebola outbreak on record has killed more than 1,200 people in West Africa, where panic and misinformation are spreading faster than the virus itself. Widespread rumors and superstition have led to attacks on treatment centers, patients avoiding care, and dangerous practices such as drinking salt water, which has already proven fatal. Deep distrust of government and aid workers, worsened by weak infrastructure and past conflicts, makes it difficult to counter false beliefs and enforce quarantine measures. Experts stress that containing the outbreak requires grassroots health education, community engagement, and emergency food aid to support isolated populations.

Experts say recent earthquakes, including Sunday's Northern California temblor, do not necessarily indicate an unusual global increase, and there is no sign the long-feared "Big One" on the San Andreas Fault is imminent. The Napa-area quake occurred on a different fault, though part of the same tectonic system. While the rate of major quakes was above average early in 2014, scientists caution that the time frame is too short to draw firm conclusions, and some increased activity in the central U.S. may be linked to fracking. A massive San Andreas quake remains a serious long-term threat, but moderate, damaging quakes can strike California at any time.

Bahia’s cultural identity is deeply rooted in drumming, with Salvador at the center of Brazil’s Afro-Brazilian traditions. Percussion groups like Olodum and Ile Aiye have shaped Carnival and popular music, while artists such as Carlinhos Brown rose from street drumming to national fame. Local genres like axe and samba reggae blend Afro-Brazilian beats with Caribbean and global influences, creating a vibrant musical laboratory. Drums also carry spiritual meaning in Candomblé ceremonies and street processions like afoxe, making rhythm a powerful link between heritage, faith, and celebration.

Two hit-and-run deaths of Black men in rural Mississippi illustrate serious flaws in how hate crimes are tracked nationwide. In one case, authorities declined to pursue a hate crime charge despite witness accounts, while in the other, police failed to investigate for years. The article highlights that FBI hate crime data is vastly underreported—Mississippi reported zero hate crimes for several years—and that federal statistics differ sharply from victim-based surveys, which estimate far more incidents. This weak reporting system makes it difficult for law enforcement to understand and respond to bias-motivated violence.

Sleep is essential for physical and mental health, yet many adults and teens are not getting enough, with the CDC labeling insufficient sleep a public health epidemic. Recent research shows that poor sleep in young children can harm their physical, emotional, and social well-being, including raising the risk of weight problems. Sleep needs vary by age, and parents can gauge adequacy by whether a child wakes easily and stays cheerful without late-day meltdowns. Key strategies include making sleep a priority, maintaining consistent bedtime routines, scheduling exercise earlier, and keeping electronic screens out of the bedroom.

Many Americans are so exhausted by busy schedules, stress, and constant screen time that they regularly choose sleep over sex. Beyond simple fatigue, low libido and boredom can also dampen desire, affecting both men and women. To revive intimacy, experts recommend prioritizing sleep, scheduling sex, exploring daytime opportunities, and pushing past tiredness to rediscover pleasure. Once couples re-establish the habit, sex often becomes more frequent and fulfilling.

Arianna Huffington, despite leading a major media company, advocates for a slower, less stressful life through practices like meditation and prioritizing sleep, which she credits for her success. Her company is capitalizing on this message by expanding its lifestyle coverage and launching a stress-reduction app. Reflecting on her career, she emphasizes the importance of embracing failure and taking risks, which helped her overcome early setbacks. She also voices concerns about youth unemployment and encourages women to reject self-imposed pressure, hoping younger generations feel less burdened than she did.

The jury in Jodi Arias’s murder trial failed to reach a unanimous decision on whether she should receive the death penalty, leading to a hung jury and a scheduled retrial for the sentencing phase. The jury foreman described the deliberations as emotionally draining, noting that hearing from the victim’s family was especially difficult and that jurors had to suppress their feelings in court. He also said that while the jury rejected Arias’ self-defense claim, he personally believed she had been mentally and verbally abused by the victim, though that did not excuse her actions. Prosecutors plan to pursue the death penalty again in the next phase of the trial.

Ariel Castro, the Ohio man convicted of kidnapping, raping, and imprisoning three women for nearly a decade, took his own life in his prison cell by hanging. He had been serving a life sentence plus 1,000 years and was found unresponsive despite being in protective custody with regular checks. The three survivors were informed of his death but chose not to comment publicly. While some family members felt relief, his attorney argued that prison officials should have done more to prevent the suicide, and investigations into the death were launched.

An Arkansas circuit judge has struck down the state's constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, deeming it a violation of equal protection and privacy rights. The ruling, which came in response to a lawsuit filed by 21 same-sex couples, was not immediately stayed, leaving the door open for marriages to begin, though the state is expected to appeal. This decision adds to a recent wave of court victories for marriage equality, bringing the total to 17 states plus the District of Columbia. The judge's reasoning echoed the U.S. Supreme Court's Windsor decision, emphasizing that the nation's commitment to freedom should extend to all citizens.

Army Private Naser Jason Abdo has been sentenced to life in prison for plotting to bomb a restaurant near Fort Hood, Texas, that was likely to be full of soldiers and their families. The federal judge imposed two life terms plus an additional 60 years for related weapons and attempted murder charges. Abdo, who went AWOL after refusing deployment to Afghanistan, said his Muslim beliefs conflicted with U.S. military operations there. He represented himself during sentencing, and the Justice Department later emphasized the case as a reminder to remain vigilant against extremists.

A former U.S. soldier who was accused of fighting alongside a terrorist group in Syria has been released after pleading guilty to a reduced weapons-export charge and receiving a time-served sentence. He had faced life in prison on the original conspiracy charge, which involved using rocket-propelled grenades with the al-Nusra Front. In an unusual move, U.S. authorities removed him from the no-fly list so he could travel from Turkey to the U.S., where he was arrested upon arrival. The case was complicated by the fact that he had been fighting the Syrian government, which the U.S. also opposed, though Washington still designated the group as a terrorist organization.

A California judge struck down the state’s teacher tenure, dismissal, and layoff laws as unconstitutional, arguing they protect ineffective teachers and disproportionately harm poor and minority students. U.S. Education Secretary Arne Duncan praised the ruling as a chance to reform the teaching profession, while teachers unions condemned it as an attack on public education and announced plans to appeal. The decision could prompt major changes to how California hires, evaluates, and fires teachers.

A 1974 cold-case murder in Massachusetts has been solved after DNA evidence linked a Georgia man to the stabbing death of 21-year-old Eileen Ferro. The suspect, 69-year-old Lonzo Guthrie, had been at her home as a furniture deliveryman the day before the killing but was never originally investigated. The breakthrough came when crime-scene evidence was re-tested and matched a DNA sample Guthrie was required to provide after a parole violation. He is now in custody without bond and is contesting extradition to Massachusetts.

A missing Arkansas realtor, Beverly Carter, disappeared after showing a home, prompting an arrest warrant for Aaron Lewis, who remains at large. Hundreds of volunteers joined the search while authorities focused on rural farmland and asked landowners to check their property. Carter’s family expressed anguish, and her case sparked widespread discussion among realtors about safety, with many advocating for precautions like the buddy system.

Police in Atlanta have issued an arrest warrant for rapper Gucci Mane after he allegedly struck a man with a champagne bottle at a nightclub. The victim said he approached the rapper to ask for a photo and was suddenly hit, leaving a deep cut on his head, and another man then punched him. The incident occurred in the VIP area during a mixtape release party in mid-March. Gucci Mane, whose real name is Radric Davis, is now wanted on an aggravated assault charge.

A London regatta debuted on the Thames, merging competitive sailing with contemporary art by displaying works from British artists on the sails of ten boats. Organizers call it a first-of-its-kind collaboration and already plan to expand the concept to venues like Moscow, San Francisco, and Miami. Artists noted the unusual challenges of working on lightweight, constantly shifting sailcloth, but viewed the format as an exciting new artistic medium. Participants also hope the event will draw fresh audiences to sailing by adding a cultural element to the sport.

A petition with over 142,000 signatures is urging Mars to eliminate synthetic dyes from M&Ms sold in the United States, pointing to a mother’s observation that her son’s behavior improved after removing artificial coloring from his diet. In Europe, similar additives carry warning labels about potential effects on children’s attention and activity, prompting many manufacturers to switch to natural colorings. The FDA has acknowledged that some children with behavioral issues may be affected by synthetic dyes but has not banned them. Mars maintains that its ingredients are safe while saying it continually reviews its formulations.

Artist Heather Dewey-Hagborg collects discarded genetic material like hair, gum, and cigarette butts from public spaces, then extracts DNA to infer physical traits such as gender, eye color, and facial structure. She uses this information to generate 3-D portrait sculptures that resemble the unknown donors, though they are approximate likenesses rather than exact replicas. The project, called "Stranger Visions," is intended to spark conversation about genetic surveillance and privacy in an age where personal biological traces are easily left behind. While some find the work unsettling, the artist embraces that reaction as part of its provocative purpose.

Thomas Heatherwick criticizes Abu Dhabi for importing European park designs instead of embracing its desert identity. His proposed Al Fayah Park features a cracked, earth-like mound that shelters gardens, streams, cafes, and a library beneath it, offering residents an outdoor social space beyond shopping malls. The design also incorporates desert sand concrete and uses shade to cut irrigation water in half, while giving the flat city its first hill-like landmark.

Andrew Dawson and neuroscientist Jonathan Cole created "The Articulate Hand," a performance blending theater and science that explores how people cope with losing hand function. Through movement and storytelling, Dawson portrays real patients, such as a quadriplegic woman who regained some independence using a bionic hand system. The project aims to give both medical audiences and art lovers fresh insight into the human experience of disability without reducing it to a clinical condition. Dawson’s own agile hands serve as the medium, illustrating how deeply our sense of self is tied to the body’s capabilities.

Asiana Airlines is offering $10,000 to every passenger on the crashed Flight 214, independent of any medical compensation, and accepting the payment does not forfeit their right to sue. The July 6 crash at San Francisco International Airport killed three people and injured over 180. One victim, a Chinese teenager, initially survived the impact but was fatally struck by a rescue vehicle, prompting an apology from the San Francisco fire chief. The NTSB is continuing its investigation into the accident.

The U.S. Department of Transportation has fined Asiana Airlines $500,000 for failing to properly assist families after its 2013 crash in San Francisco, marking the first penalty issued under a 1997 law requiring airlines to have family assistance plans. The airline was criticized for being slow to publicize a contact number, taking two days to reach most families, and not notifying some relatives until five days after the accident. Asiana defended its response, citing limited airport staff, privacy restrictions at hospitals, and the dispersal of injured passengers across multiple medical centers.
