Most of the fine is due immediately, while a portion will fund industry training to improve future emergency response.

Asiana Airlines Flight 214 was traveling well below the recommended landing speed as it approached San Francisco International Airport, triggering a stall warning just before the crash. Investigators say the crew increased engine power and attempted a last-second go-around, but there was not enough altitude to recover. The NTSB is examining pilot actions, training, automation use, and other possible contributing factors, while noting that crashes often result from multiple issues. Two Chinese teenagers were killed, and many passengers were injured, though most aboard survived.

Bangkok’s nahm has been named Asia’s best restaurant, though chef David Thompson jokes that he lost money betting against himself. He hopes the recognition will support Bangkok during Thailand’s political unrest and highlight the resilience of Thai culture. The awards also reflect a broader shift toward Asian culinary identity, with chefs drawing on local traditions to create modern dishes. Japan led this year’s list with ten entries, while Singapore, Hong Kong, and mainland China also featured prominently.

Vice President Joe Biden is visiting East Asia to help defuse rising territorial tensions, particularly between Japan and China over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The trip also highlights his deep foreign policy experience, which has long been seen as one of his key strengths and a reason he was chosen as Obama’s running mate. While the visit boosts his credentials amid speculation about a possible 2016 presidential bid, polls show Hillary Clinton would be the overwhelming Democratic frontrunner if she runs, though Biden would lead the field if she does not.

Boko Haram militants raided a girls’ boarding school in northeastern Nigeria, abducting as many as 200 students after a gun battle with soldiers guarding the campus. The attackers arrived in a convoy of trucks, buses, and vans, loaded the girls onto vehicles, and fled into the bush, burning homes and businesses along the way. A few students managed to escape when one of the vehicles broke down, but most remained captive. The abduction followed a recent video threat by the group’s leader to target schoolgirls, and came amid a wave of attacks that had already forced the closure of many secondary schools in the region.

Julian Assange, speaking remotely from the Ecuadorian embassy in London, told the South by Southwest festival that mass digital surveillance of every person on Earth will soon become a reality. He criticized the U.S. National Security Agency as a rogue power and argued that tech giants like Facebook and Google are exploiting users by harvesting their data for profit. Assange also described his own confinement as prison-like and framed online privacy advocates as freedom fighters against government overreach. The event was marred by technical difficulties, turning what was meant to be a Q&A into a lengthy monologue.

Charges against Chris Brown and his bodyguard were downgraded from felonies to misdemeanor simple assault after a weekend altercation in Washington, D.C. Both were released without bail, though Brown must keep 100 yards away from the alleged victim and report to his California probation officer within 48 hours. The incident could complicate Brown’s probation stemming from his 2009 assault on Rihanna, as any legal trouble may be treated as a violation. His lawyer maintained that Brown committed no crime and that the bodyguard was acting in self-defense.

Obama enters his second term with far lower expectations than his historic first inauguration, facing an unfinished agenda that includes trillion-dollar deficits, entitlement reform, and immigration, now compounded by new battles over gun control. The political landscape is deeply polarized, with resistance from Republicans and divisions within his own party, while the economy will largely determine how much he can achieve. Historical precedent suggests he has a narrow window—roughly 18 months—before lame-duck status takes hold, and past second-term presidents all suffered major political setbacks. He also must contend with staff turnover and a volatile global environment, even as both critics and aides disagree over whether gridlock stems from his own approach or GOP obstruction.

A Ukrainian military transport plane was shot down near the Luhansk region close to the Russian border, killing none? Actually all eight on board were Ukrainians; four escaped, two were taken hostage, and two remain missing. Ukrainian officials claimed the aircraft was struck by a powerful missile launched from Russian territory, not a portable ground-fired system. Russia declined to confirm that any missile originated from its side. The incident comes amid ongoing clashes between Ukrainian forces and pro-Russian separatists in the area.

The death toll from the collapse of a guesthouse at a Lagos church owned by prominent Nigerian televangelist T.B. Joshua has climbed to at least 70, with 131 people rescued and search efforts still underway. The two-story building came down on Friday while additional floors were being constructed, and officials suspect the foundation was not reinforced to support the new stories. Many of the victims were South Africans, prompting President Jacob Zuma to call it an unprecedented loss of South African lives abroad. An official investigation into the cause has not yet begun.

At the 2013 Netroots Nation conference, progressive activists expressed deep frustration with President Obama, acknowledging he is better than a Republican alternative but criticizing his record on issues like NSA surveillance, Wall Street reform, foreclosures, the Keystone XL pipeline, and job creation. Many attendees felt Obama has not delivered on campaign promises and lacks bold leadership, with some saying he is "treading water" and failing to champion progressive causes. The conference highlighted the left's historical restlessness and weak allegiance to the Democratic Party, though disappointment stopped short of outright anger. Even as Obama addressed the gathering via video, most activists remained unimpressed, with only LGBT advocates offering notable praise for his actions.

The shooting of Pakistani schoolgirl Malala Yousufzai by the Taliban has sparked widespread public outrage in Pakistan, with many citizens demanding government action against extremists. Officials have vowed to intensify efforts against the Taliban, announced protective measures for girls' schools, and reported progress in the investigation. While condemnation is broad, some political figures and commentators have deflected blame onto U.S. drone strikes or questioned the official narrative. Meanwhile, Malala is recovering in a British hospital, where doctors say she is showing strength and making progress despite needing further surgery.

George Zimmerman’s defense attorney, Mark O’Mara, has ended his representation of Zimmerman for the domestic dispute and upcoming divorce, though he will stay involved in the defamation lawsuit against NBC and in recovering trial costs from Florida. Since being acquitted of murder in July, Zimmerman has faced several legal and personal issues, including a brief detention after a confrontation with his estranged wife and her father, who declined to press charges. He also helped people escape from an overturned SUV and received two traffic citations in separate stops. Despite the acquittal, Zimmerman’s legal troubles and public scrutiny continue.

Jerry Sandusky, the former Penn State coach convicted of 45 counts of child sexual abuse, plans to appeal, arguing he received ineffective legal representation and that prosecutors improperly referenced his post-arrest silence. His defense team will file the appeal after sentencing, which is expected in about 90 days and could result in life in prison. The case has also triggered broader fallout, including pending charges against two former university administrators and the possibility of additional accusations against Sandusky. Penn State has indicated it may seek to compensate the victims as it tries to move forward.

A Philadelphia church official on trial for allegedly covering up child sex abuse is seeking dismissal of all charges after a newly discovered 1994 memo reportedly shows that the late Cardinal Anthony Bevilacqua ordered the destruction of a secret list naming 35 abusive priests. The memo, written by Monsignor James Molloy, states that he shredded the lists on the cardinal’s directive. Defense attorneys argue this evidence proves Lynn was following orders and should not be prosecuted. The case is notable as the first U.S. prosecution of a church administrator for failing to stop abuse, rather than only the abusers themselves.

In the Aurora theater shooting, three young men—Jon Blunk, Alex Teves, and Matt McQuinn—died while shielding their girlfriends from gunfire, saving the women’s lives. Their selfless acts are framed as genuine heroism rooted in a code of honor, not mere chivalry. The article argues these everyday men should be celebrated as real-life role models, especially at a time when traditional manhood is often seen as lacking. Their stories remind us that courage and goodness can prevail over evil in real life, not just in movies.

Australia placed federal police in charge of parliamentary security after a major counter-terrorism sweep in Sydney, prompted by intelligence about possible attacks linked to militant sympathizers. The prime minister said an Australian ISIS operative in Syria had encouraged supporters at home to carry out violence. Meanwhile, Muslim leaders warned against rising Islamophobia and called for social cohesion, as peaceful protests backed the community. Most detainees were released, though one man was charged with conspiracy, and Australia moved forward with plans to join the international coalition against ISIS.

UNESCO has granted Australia a one-year extension to demonstrate stronger protection for the Great Barrier Reef, warning that failure could lead to an “in danger” listing. The decision follows ongoing concerns about coastal development, particularly new ports and liquefied natural gas projects, as well as the dumping of dredge spoil near Abbot Point. Environmental groups argue that dredging pollutes reef waters and have called for an immediate ban, while the Australian government defends its environmental assessments and significant annual spending on reef health. The reef’s condition has also worsened due to cyclones, coral bleaching, crown-of-thorns starfish, and decades of neglect, with scientists emphasizing the need to boost coral resilience.

Australian officials now believe Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 was most likely flying on autopilot when it ended up in the southern Indian Ocean, with the crew possibly incapacitated due to oxygen deprivation. This conclusion is based on the plane’s steady satellite-tracked path, suggesting no human control in its final hours. The underwater search is being moved to a new 60,000-square-kilometer zone deemed the most probable crash site, though officials warn the operation will be difficult and could take up to a year. Meanwhile, families of the passengers remain skeptical and frustrated by the lack of definitive answers.

Jack Brabham, the Australian Formula One legend and three-time world champion, has died at age 88. He made history as the only driver to win the championship in a car bearing his own name, achieving that feat in 1966 after earlier titles with Cooper. Tributes from figures across motorsport and Australian public life honored his pioneering engineering skill and lasting influence. His family confirmed he passed away peacefully at home on the Gold Coast.

An Australian missionary has been detained in North Korea after reportedly carrying Korean-language Gospel tracts during a tour. His wife says authorities questioned him about who sent him and who translated the materials, though Pyongyang has not confirmed the arrest. Since Australia has no diplomatic ties with North Korea, Sweden is assisting with consular matters. The detention echoes past cases like Kenneth Bae’s, reflecting North Korea’s harsh stance on independent religious activity.

The extreme heat at the 2014 Australian Open has sparked player complaints, but sports scientist Ross Tucker argues that athletes who properly acclimatize, such as through Bikram yoga, can perform well in such conditions. While players like Andy Murray and Frank Dancevic have voiced safety concerns, tournament officials maintain that the health risks are minimal and that dehydration is less dangerous than overdrinking. Critics have also questioned the rule allowing heat breaks only for women, noting that larger male players may face greater heat challenges. Ultimately, experts believe the heat is uncomfortable but not life-threatening, and the tournament should continue as scheduled.

Australia raised its national terrorism threat level to “high” for the first time since the system was created in 2003, indicating an attack is considered likely though no specific plot has been identified. Officials said the increased alert would mainly mean tighter security at airports, ports, government sites, and major public events. The decision reflects growing concern about Australians recruited by ISIS, with dozens believed to be fighting abroad and many more supporting such activities at home. The move follows a similar threat-level increase in the United Kingdom amid broader worries about returning foreign fighters.

A failed satellite phone call from ground staff to Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has provided new clues, suggesting the jet may have turned south earlier than previously believed. This refined analysis has shifted focus to the southern portion of the existing search zone in the Indian Ocean, though the overall search area remains unchanged. An underwater search involving three ships is set to begin next month, with seabed mapping already revealing challenging terrain, including volcanoes and steep drops. Malaysia has agreed to match Australia’s financial contribution to the search, while the cause of the plane’s disappearance remains unknown.

Australian officials are preparing to announce a revised search zone for the missing jet, following a re-analysis of satellite data that could shift the area hundreds of kilometers south. In a separate development, Malaysian police have dismissed a British newspaper report claiming the captain was the primary suspect, emphasizing that the investigation is still ongoing with no definitive conclusions. The disputed report pointed to deleted flight simulator routes and the pilot's lack of future commitments, but investigators stress the evidence is circumstantial and an FBI review found no conclusive proof. The next phase of the underwater search, which will be managed by a private company, is expected to begin no earlier than August, with contractor proposals due by the end of June.

Arizona state Senator Russell Pearce, the chief sponsor of the state’s strict immigration enforcement law, was defeated in a recall election by fellow Republican Jerry Lewis. The vote was widely viewed as a public judgment on Pearce’s hard-line immigration policies, with Lewis winning about 53% of the vote. Pearce framed his ouster as the cost of keeping his promises, while critics called the result a warning against divisive politics. Lewis, who argued the law harmed Arizona’s reputation, advocated for a more cooperative approach with the federal government on immigration.

Esi Edugyan’s novel “Half-Blood Blues,” a Man Booker finalist, follows a fictional jazz band in late-1930s Berlin and Paris, centering on the brilliant black German trumpeter Hieronymus Falk, who is arrested by the Gestapo and vanishes. Decades later, the band’s bassist and narrator, Sid, returns to Berlin for a documentary about Falk and is forced to confront a long-hidden secret. Edugyan drew inspiration from her own experiences as a Black Canadian of Ghanaian descent and from the little-known history of Afro-Germans persecuted under Nazism. The story explores themes of identity, loyalty, and betrayal, capturing both the jazz era’s energy and the racial tensions of prewar Europe.

A newly published study claiming that African-American boys face a higher autism risk if given the MMR vaccine before age two has reignited the vaccine-autism debate. The study’s author alleges that CDC researchers knew about this link in 2004 but concealed it, while the CDC maintains its original finding that vaccines do not cause autism. The study was quickly withdrawn by the journal due to serious concerns about its conclusions, and experts have questioned its methodology. The broader scientific consensus remains that vaccines are safe and do not cause autism, with prior research linking autism to factors present before birth.

The CDC reports that autism prevalence has risen to 1 in 68 U.S. children, up from 1 in 88 two years earlier, with boys affected far more often than girls. The increase is especially notable among children with average or above-average intelligence, though the average age of diagnosis remains above four years despite the possibility of earlier detection. Experts attribute part of the rise to greater awareness and broader diagnostic practices, while also cautioning that some cases may involve similar conditions rather than autism itself. The findings highlight ongoing concerns about disparities in access to care, the need for better services, and the importance of a coordinated national strategy to support affected families.

A year after the 5.8-magnitude earthquake struck the U.S. capital, officials announced that the Washington Monument is structurally sound and would survive even a worst-case quake, though it remains closed for extensive repairs to cracked marble and interior damage. The National Cathedral, also badly damaged, faces restoration costs exceeding $50 million and a decade of work, aided by a recent $5 million donation. Officials also promoted an upcoming regional drill aimed at teaching people to drop, cover, and hold on during an earthquake, noting that many had evacuated unsafely during the 2011 tremor.

Research into preverbal infants suggests that morality is innate rather than purely learned. In one study, babies consistently chose a larger snack, but often rejected it when offered by a mean character, showing they value fairness over self-interest. However, if the larger reward was big enough, they would accept it even from the wrongdoer. This indicates that even babies experience moral dilemmas, balancing compassion against personal gain.

Prince George made his first public appearance in three months at his christening, held at St. James's Palace in a deliberately small ceremony attended by close family, including the Queen and Prince Charles. He wore a replica of a historic royal christening gown, and the service was led by the Archbishop of Canterbury, who noted that while all babies are special, George’s baptism carried extra significance because he is destined to become king and head of the Church of England. The event also featured traditional elements such as water from the River Jordan and a silver font used in royal christenings since 1841. Additionally, George became the first royal baby honored with an official christening coin from the Royal Mint.

Former Bachelor contestant Gia Allemand has died at age 29, two days after being found unconscious in what appeared to be a suicide attempt. Her boyfriend, NBA player Ryan Anderson, discovered her at her New Orleans home, and she was later taken off life support surrounded by family and friends. Allemand was known for appearing on season 14 of The Bachelor and on Bachelor Pad, and was remembered for her kindness and love of animals. Tributes poured in from the show’s creator, host, and fellow contestants, who expressed shock and grief over her passing.

The discovery and DNA confirmation of Richard III’s remains beneath a parking lot have reignited debate over his vilified reputation. Historians and the Richard III Society argue that his negative image was largely Tudor propaganda, amplified by Shakespeare’s portrayal of him as a deformed, murderous tyrant. New skeletal evidence challenges some of those physical caricatures, showing severe scoliosis rather than a withered arm or hump. The findings have also renewed efforts to reassess his reign, give him a proper burial, and separate historical fact from myth.

The article explains that while most Americans and lawmakers from both parties support expanding background checks for gun purchases, there is sharp disagreement over the details. It outlines the current system, which screens buyers through the FBI’s NICS database but only applies to sales by licensed dealers, leaving private transactions—about 20% of gun sales—unchecked. Democrats are pushing to close this loophole by requiring checks for all sales, including at gun shows and online, but opponents worry about government record-keeping and argue the system is ineffective due to incomplete state data and the ease of buying guns illegally. Despite these concerns, polls show roughly 90% of Americans favor background checks on every gun sale.

Bahrain has declared a senior U.S. diplomat, Tom Malinowski, persona non grata, accusing him of interfering in domestic affairs by meeting selectively with certain political groups. The U.S. State Department rejected the claim, noting the visit was pre-arranged and that meeting a broad range of recognized groups is standard practice. The dispute comes amid ongoing tensions in Bahrain, where authorities have faced criticism for suppressing pro-democracy protests. Bahrain also recently enacted a law imposing prison sentences and fines for publicly insulting the king.

AC Milan striker Mario Balotelli has said he will leave the field if he faces racist abuse again, after being targeted with monkey chants during a Serie A match against Roma. He nearly walked off but was persuaded by teammate Kevin Prince-Boateng, who had previously left a match over racism. Roma was fined $65,000, a penalty FIFA president Sepp Blatter sharply criticized as too lenient. The incident highlights ongoing problems with racism in Italian football, which has seen several clubs fined this season.

William Guarnere, the World War II veteran known as "Wild Bill" and featured in the miniseries "Band of Brothers," has passed away at age 90. He died Saturday night from a ruptured aneurysm, according to his son. Guarnere lost a leg during the war while attempting to save a comrade, and his story was brought to television in the HBO series based on Stephen Ambrose's book. His funeral is scheduled for this week in his hometown of Philadelphia.

The 20-day recovery operation at Bangladesh’s Rana Plaza factory collapse has ended, with the confirmed death toll reaching 1,127 and 2,438 people rescued alive, though dozens remain missing and many bodies are unidentified or unclaimed. The disaster has sparked widespread anger and accountability efforts, including the arrest of the building owner and legal action against factory owners. In response, the government has pledged to raise garment workers’ minimum wage and approved a draft law mandating life insurance, while several international retailers signed a safety agreement requiring independent inspections and funding for factory upgrades. Despite these reforms, many workers remain fearful, and numerous factories have been shut down after employees refused to return over safety concerns.

Barbie’s appearance in the Sports Illustrated swimsuit edition has sparked backlash, with critics arguing that placing a children’s toy alongside sexualized adult models promotes unhealthy beauty standards and blurs the line between objectification and play. Mattel defends the campaign as empowering and says it is not aimed at girls, emphasizing Barbie’s legacy as a cultural icon. However, many commentators and experts contend that the partnership reinforces narrow ideals of femininity and undermines positive messages about women’s achievements.

Barcelona coach Tito Vilanova is returning to Spain after two months of cancer treatment in New York, giving the team a lift ahead of their Champions League quarterfinal against Paris Saint-Germain. Assistant Jordi Roura had been handling first-team duties while staying in close contact with Vilanova. The coach had been treated for a recurrence of parotid gland cancer, which first required surgery in 2011. During his absence, Barcelona faced some setbacks but recovered strongly, including a decisive comeback against AC Milan in the previous round.

European Commission President José Manuel Barroso has argued that a federal Europe is inevitable if the euro is to survive the ongoing debt crisis. He advocates for greater shared sovereignty, including giving the European Central Bank regulatory authority over eurozone banks, as a necessary step to strengthen the currency. Barroso also welcomed the new European Stability Mechanism as a European equivalent of the IMF and insisted that closer integration does not mean a loss of national sovereignty but rather a pooling of it. He believes that only through unity can European countries compete globally and that Greece remains committed to reforms and staying in the eurozone.

Earl Weaver, the fiery Hall of Fame manager of the Baltimore Orioles, passed away at 82 from an apparent heart attack. Over 17 seasons, he led the team to four pennants and a 1970 World Series championship, amassing 1,480 wins. Known for his confrontations with umpires and players, he was also an early adopter of computers and radar guns to analyze pitchers. He is remembered as the greatest manager in Orioles history and a beloved figure in Baltimore.

Mo’ne Davis, a 13-year-old pitcher for Philadelphia’s Taney Dragons, has captured national attention as the first girl to throw a shutout in Little League World Series history and the first Little Leaguer featured on the cover of Sports Illustrated. Her success is inspiring young girls to pursue sports traditionally dominated by boys and challenging outdated gender stereotypes, as seen in the phrase “throws like a girl” taking on a new, positive meaning. Supporters believe her visibility helps normalize girls excelling alongside boys and could boost interest in baseball among younger audiences. Despite her pitching fame, Davis dreams of becoming a point guard for UConn and eventually playing in the WNBA.

Bashar al-Assad came to power in 2000 with promises of democratic and economic reform, but his rule soon became marked by state-controlled media, censorship, and continued repression. Former insiders describe him as indecisive and easily influenced, while the regime remains dominated by his family and the Alawite minority, which acts out of fear of losing power. Despite a brutal crackdown on protests that has killed thousands, Assad denies giving orders to use force, claiming the military acts independently. The opposition, having lost faith in his ability to reform, now demands his removal and genuine democratic elections.

Hall of Fame coach John “Dr. Jack” Ramsay has died at 89 after a long battle with cancer. He was best known for leading the Portland Trail Blazers to their only NBA championship in 1977. Ramsay also had a distinguished college and pro coaching career, amassing more than 860 NBA wins, and later became a longtime basketball broadcaster for ESPN. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1992.

The article explores how many modern women still struggle with intense perfectionism, a trait the author fears passing on to her daughters. It highlights Debora Spar’s book, which argues that feminism has morphed into an unrealistic quest to have it all effortlessly. Spar offers practical advice for breaking this cycle, including being honest about struggles, learning to say no, letting go of guilt, accepting good enough options, and allowing men to share domestic responsibilities. The overall message is that women can ease the pressure by embracing imperfection and redefining success.

Bayern Munich executive Karl-Heinz Rummenigge backs moving the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to the winter, but insists any disruption to the football calendar must be limited to that single season. Speaking for the European Clubs Association, he notes that summer heat in Qatar makes the usual timing unworkable and that clubs prefer a November or January start. However, he warns that a January tournament would clash with the Winter Olympics and stresses the need to protect other major events. The article also touches on his continued support for Bayern president Uli Hoeness amid the latter’s tax evasion trial.

Bayern Munich overwhelmed Barcelona 3-0 at the Nou Camp to complete a dominant 7-0 aggregate victory and book their place in the Champions League final. Without the injured Lionel Messi, Barcelona had no answer to Bayern’s second-half surge, which included goals from Arjen Robben, a Gerard Pique own goal, and Thomas Mueller. Bayern will now face domestic rivals Borussia Dortmund at Wembley, with coach Jupp Heynckes aiming to cap his final season by winning the treble. The result marked one of Barcelona’s heaviest European defeats and underlined Bayern’s status as favorites for the title.

Bayern Munich and Real Madrid will meet in the Champions League semifinals, while Atletico Madrid face Chelsea in the other tie. Bayern aim to become the first team to retain the title in the modern era, and Real are chasing a record tenth European crown. The Chelsea-Atletico matchup is complicated by goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who is on loan at Atletico from Chelsea, though UEFA has ruled any agreement restricting his availability invalid. The first legs are scheduled for late April, with the final set for Lisbon in May.

Katmai National Park in Alaska offers visitors a rare chance to observe brown bears in the wild, especially at Brooks Camp, where dozens gather each July to fish for salmon. The park’s remote location on the Alaskan Peninsula means it is accessible only by plane or boat, but admission is free and the wilderness remains largely unspoiled. Ranger Roy Wood highlights the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, formed by a massive 1912 volcanic eruption, as a must-see for solitude and dramatic scenery. He also stresses the importance of keeping at least 50 yards from bears, which are powerful, unpredictable animals despite their calm appearance.

British singer-songwriter Jackie Lomax has died at 69 after a brief illness. Despite a five-decade career and collaborations with major figures like the Beatles, he never achieved widespread commercial success. His work with Apple Records, including a 1969 album produced by George Harrison, showcased his R&B and blue-eyed soul style. He remained devoted to music until the end, having just completed a new album scheduled for release.

The writer expresses pride in both English and British identity and supports Scotland remaining part of the UK, backing the "Let's Stay Together" campaign. They emphasize that many across the UK care deeply about the union and would feel a profound sense of loss if Scotland left. While fully respecting Scots' right to decide, they argue Scotland can enjoy both strong self-governance and the security of UK membership. Ultimately, they believe the shared history, emotional bonds, and future cooperation make the union stronger together.

David Beckham will play his final game for the LA Galaxy in the MLS Cup on December 1, ending a six-year stint with the club. His arrival in 2007 significantly boosted Major League Soccer’s visibility in the U.S., and he helped the Galaxy win the league championship in 2011. While his next move is unclear, Beckham said he is seeking one last career challenge and hopes to eventually become an MLS owner. The league credited him with greatly increasing soccer’s popularity and importance in North America.

A roundup of recent health studies highlights several notable findings: a compound in beer may support brain function in young mice, though only at impractically high doses; e-cigarettes did not prove more effective than regular cigarettes for quitting among cancer patients; dry-roasted peanuts triggered stronger allergic reactions in mice than raw ones, possibly explaining regional allergy differences; and people tended to drink more alcohol on days they exercised. Another study found that men who followed five healthy habits—eating well, exercising, staying fit, not smoking, and drinking moderately—could prevent most heart attacks.

Rio’s preparations for the 2016 Olympics face serious challenges, including construction delays at key venues, severe water pollution in Guanabara Bay, and ongoing security issues in the favelas. An IOC official called the situation the worst he had seen, though local organizers insist the delays are exaggerated and that venues will be ready in time. Environmental experts warn that athletes could be exposed to raw sewage, and city officials admit the cleanup will not be finished before the Games. Public concern over spending is also high, but officials argue that much of the money is going toward lasting infrastructure like transportation and sanitation.

China’s top legislature has approved changes to Hong Kong’s leadership election rules, allowing only candidates screened by a nominating committee to run for chief executive, with an emphasis on loyalty to the country. Hong Kong’s current leader welcomed the move as a step toward universal suffrage, but pro-democracy activists condemned it as an unfair restriction that undermines genuine elections. The Occupy Central movement and other demonstrators have vowed continued protests and civil disobedience, while Beijing insists the changes comply with Hong Kong’s basic law and are necessary for stability. The decision has intensified concerns that Hong Kong’s promised autonomy and civil liberties are gradually being eroded.

Belgium’s new king, Philippe, was sworn in after his father, Albert II, abdicated due to age and health concerns. Philippe, a former fighter pilot educated in both French and Flemish, became monarch alongside his wife, Queen Mathilde. Albert’s departure follows similar abdications in the Netherlands and at the Vatican, and he was praised by European officials for his dedication to Belgium and European unity. However, the monarchy continues to face challenges from separatist movements, particularly in the economically stronger Flemish region.

Ben Ainslie, Britain’s most decorated Olympic sailor, has set his sights on winning the America’s Cup, a title his country has never claimed. After retiring from Olympic competition with four golds, he is now helming high-speed catamarans and building his own British team, while also serving as a reserve helmsman for Oracle. His Olympic journey was marked by fierce rivalries, especially with Brazil’s Robert Scheidt, and a dramatic gold-medal win at London 2012 under intense home pressure. Despite the sport’s elite image and the physical toll of years of training, Ainslie remains deeply devoted to sailing and dreams of a relaxed retirement at sea.

The article recounts the deadly September 11, 2012, attack on the U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya, which resulted in the deaths of Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. It details the sequence of events, from the initial breach and fire at the compound to the later mortar assault on a nearby CIA annex. The piece also highlights the ensuing controversy over whether the Obama administration failed to provide adequate security and whether it attempted to conceal what happened.

HGTV has canceled the upcoming series “Flip It Forward” starring twin brothers David and Jason Benham, following public scrutiny over David’s past remarks on homosexuality and abortion. The controversy began when a watchdog site surfaced recordings of David leading a prayer rally and discussing what he called “demonic ideologies” and an “agenda” attacking the nation. The brothers defended themselves, insisting they do not hate or discriminate against anyone and that their Christian faith was the real reason for the backlash. Supporters have since launched a petition urging HGTV to reverse its decision.

A senior Democratic Party official has warned that Silvio Berlusconi returning as Italy’s prime minister would be disastrous, arguing that the election is now a two-way contest between Berlusconi and the center-left candidate Pier Luigi Bersani. The comments come as Berlusconi gains ground in polls despite having left office amid economic crisis and legal troubles. His allies reject the warning, insisting that a Berlusconi victory would not alarm financial markets and that a Bersani government poses a greater risk to recovery. Analysts, however, caution that investors are too complacent and that a Berlusconi win could trigger a sharp bond market sell-off.

Formula One chief Bernie Ecclestone has publicly backed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s controversial anti-gay legislation, arguing that critics have misrepresented the policy and claiming most people worldwide would agree with it. He also praised Russia’s preparations for the Sochi Olympics and expressed admiration for Putin’s outspokenness. The article additionally touches on Ecclestone’s own legal troubles, including a recent court ruling that cleared him in a civil case while questioning his credibility, and discusses upcoming Formula One changes such as quieter hybrid engines and a new points system that he hopes will keep the championship competitive.

Celebrity chefs are increasingly opening restaurants in airports, transforming them into dining destinations rather than just transit hubs. High-profile examples include Heston Blumenthal’s new Heathrow eatery and Gordon Ramsay’s long-running Plane Food, alongside ventures by other renowned chefs worldwide. These operations face unique challenges such as restrictions on gas cooking, strict security protocols, and diners with very limited time, though advances in electric cooking and approved suppliers have eased some difficulties. With air travel nearly doubling over the past decade, airports now see millions of potential customers, making the trade-offs worthwhile for chefs seeking exposure and travelers expecting higher-quality food.

The article highlights a range of New Year’s Eve celebrations across the globe, from Australia’s Byron Bay music festival and India’s Goa beach parties to Prague’s fireworks and Harbin’s ice sculptures. It also features large public events in Niagara Falls and Reykjavik, as well as themed festivities at Whistler, Walt Disney World, and Chiang Mai. For those seeking variety, cruise lines offer multi-destination parties with special onboard events. Overall, the piece emphasizes diverse ways people ring in the new year, from family-friendly countdowns to massive concerts and cultural traditions.

Oman is positioning itself as a more understated alternative to its flashy Gulf neighbors, emphasizing heritage, natural beauty, and authentic experiences over rapid modernization. The country blends traditional charm with high-end comfort, offering luxury stays like the Chedi Muscat and a hilltop resort in the green mountains, as well as cultural attractions such as its own Royal Opera House. Visitors can also explore dramatic coastlines by boat, camp in the Wahiba Sands desert, and enjoy the slow-cooked lamb dish shuwa, all within a distinctly Omani setting.

The article highlights several of the most secluded spots in the continental United States, chosen for their distance from human activity and signs of civilization. It features destinations such as Montana’s Bob Marshall Wilderness, New York’s High Peaks, California’s Wildcat Beach, Utah’s Wasatch Mountains, Florida’s Everglades, Arizona’s Mooney Falls, Minnesota’s Angle Inlet, and Nevada’s U.S. Route 50, each paired with a suggested activity like hiking, canoeing, or fishing. It also makes an exception for Alaska’s Little Diomede Island, noting its extreme isolation and proximity to Russia. Overall, the piece emphasizes that true solitude can still be found within the U.S. without traveling far abroad.

A blog post by writer Seth Adam Smith about his father’s advice on marriage went viral, drawing over 24 million views within days. The father’s message was that marriage is not about personal happiness but about selflessly serving your spouse and future children. Smith expressed shock and gratitude at the overwhelming response, which also led to media appearances. The article notes that while many people avoid marriage for various reasons, heartfelt relationship wisdom like this can still resonate widely.

The Beverly Hills City Council unanimously passed a resolution condemning Brunei’s harsh Sharia laws, which include stoning for homosexuality and adultery, and called on the sultan to sell the Beverly Hills Hotel and other local properties he controls. The vote took place despite opposition from hotel workers, who warned that a boycott would threaten their livelihoods. The action followed celebrity-led protests, including by Jay Leno, against the hotel’s ownership, while the hotel’s management argued that targeting the property unfairly punishes innocent employees. U.S. officials also expressed serious concerns about Brunei’s human rights record.

The article discusses how the popularity of "Fifty Shades of Grey" has sparked greater public interest in sexual exploration, while cautioning that the novel is not a realistic guide to BDSM. To provide reliable guidance, the author gathers recommendations from sex experts, who suggest a range of educational and enlightening books on topics such as male sexuality, erotic fantasies, spicing up routine relationships, sexual history, and women's desires. The piece emphasizes the value of sex-positive literature for learning, overcoming shame, and improving intimacy, and it also highlights the author’s own popular book on female pleasure. Overall, it encourages readers to seek out credible resources to enhance their sexual knowledge and relationships.

Lebanon’s food culture is central to daily life, with eating and debating among the nation’s favorite pastimes, and meals often turning into long, abundant gatherings. The author, a Lebanese native, explores the country’s culinary diversity beyond familiar staples, highlighting Beirut’s mix of traditional restaurants, street food, and bakeries, as well as regional specialties like kibbeh, fresh seafood, and local pastries in places such as Tripoli, Batroun, Byblos, and Tyre. The article also emphasizes that home-cooked meals are a vital part of the experience, with hosts encouraging guests to eat generously. Ultimately, visitors should come hungry and surrender to the hospitality and rich flavors Lebanon offers.

Italy offers many underrated small towns and islands that rival its famous cities, from Ischia’s thermal baths and Matera’s ancient cave dwellings to Lecce’s Baroque architecture and Mantova’s Renaissance heritage. The article highlights destinations like Pienza, Syracuse, Turin, and Ventotene for their history, local cuisine, and unique sights, including UNESCO sites, Roman ruins, and natural landscapes. These places provide authentic experiences, often with fewer crowds and lower prices, while still delivering rich culture, food, and charm. Travelers seeking alternatives to Rome, Florence, or Milan will find plenty of hidden gems worth exploring.

Associated Press journalist Jean H. Lee recently became the first person to send a mobile tweet from North Korea, using a new 3G network that is available only to foreigners. Speaking at South by Southwest, she described two separate digital realities: foreign visitors can access the open internet, while North Koreans are limited to a state-controlled intranet with no social media. Although the country is taking small steps toward openness, such as allowing foreigners to bring in cellphones, digital life for residents remains heavily monitored and restricted. Lee and a colleague have been sharing rare glimpses of daily life in Pyongyang through social media, but she notes that true online freedom is still far off.

Vice President Joe Biden apologized to President Barack Obama after his public remarks on same-sex marriage forced Obama to announce his support for the issue sooner than intended. Obama acknowledged that Biden had gotten ahead of him but said the outcome was positive, noting that his views had evolved partly because of his daughters' exposure to same-sex couples. The announcement created political tensions, with some aides frustrated with Biden, while Obama faced criticism from opponents like Mitt Romney and some African-American leaders. Despite the controversy, the White House is reaching out to key groups, and recent polls show Americans are nearly evenly divided on the issue.

Vice President Joe Biden says his most comfortable role is closing deals, citing trusted personal relationships across party lines, as seen in his last-minute fiscal cliff agreement with Mitch McConnell. He will lead the administration’s push for gun control, acknowledging the need to counter NRA opposition but expressing optimism after Newtown. Biden also stresses his strong, candid rapport with President Obama, noting they disagree on tactics but never policy. He hints at a possible 2016 presidential run while insisting his immediate focus is helping Obama succeed.

Scientists at the University of Nottingham are launching a five-year, $1.58 million project to develop a "cellular operating system" for living cells, similar to how computers run an OS. The goal is to create a generic biological platform that can be easily reprogrammed for different tasks, such as producing biofuels, cleaning up pollution, or fighting disease. This would simplify synthetic biology by avoiding the need to redesign cells from scratch for every new application. While the project could be transformative, researchers acknowledge it is high-risk, and outside experts remain skeptical that a single technical breakthrough can overcome the field's many complexities.

Scientists announced a major discovery that may confirm the rapid expansion of the universe just after the Big Bang, a process known as inflation. Using the BICEP2 telescope in Antarctica, researchers detected a distinct polarization pattern in ancient light that serves as the first direct evidence of gravitational waves—ripples in space-time predicted by Einstein. This finding supports the idea that the universe expanded faster than light in its earliest moments, but experts caution that the results must be verified by other experiments before being fully accepted.

Former President Bill Clinton stated that U.S. involvement in Syria will be prolonged due to the threat from ISIS, but he does not foresee it escalating into a ground war. He emphasized that the coalition airstrikes, which included several Middle Eastern nations, mean the effort is not solely America's responsibility. Clinton expressed support for President Obama's strategy, saying it has a real chance to succeed, though he cautioned that results will not come quickly and that not all threats can be eliminated.

Former President Bill Clinton said his wife, Hillary Clinton, needs time to carefully consider both whether to run for president in 2016 and what unique vision she would bring to the race. He stressed that she should not enter the campaign without a clear sense of purpose, and he insisted he would support whatever decision she makes, praising her as an exceptionally capable public servant. The interview also touched on the recent controversy over Hillary’s “dead broke” comment, which Bill dismissed as a fabricated political distraction and defended the couple’s paid speaking fees as a means to ensure their family could continue in public service. Meanwhile, Hillary has grown more open about her possible candidacy during her book tour, though no formal decision has been made.

Bill de Blasio was inaugurated as New York City’s 109th mayor on New Year’s Day 2014, with Bill Clinton administering the oath. In his speech, he pledged to tackle economic inequality, which he described as a “tale of two cities,” and outlined a progressive agenda including higher taxes on the wealthy to fund universal pre-K and expanded paid sick leave. He also promised to reform the controversial stop-and-frisk policy and address record homelessness. The ceremony marked a Democratic return to City Hall after two decades of Republican leadership.

Billionaire publisher Richard Mellon Scaife has died at 82 after recently revealing he had terminal cancer. A heir to the Mellon fortune, he used his wealth to fund major conservative institutions and causes, including efforts to investigate Bill Clinton during his presidency, which Hillary Clinton once described as a “vast right-wing conspiracy.” Though a staunch conservative, he diverged from the GOP on issues like abortion, same-sex marriage, and the Iraq War, and later supported Clinton-related initiatives. He was also remembered for his deep passion for newspapering, particularly through the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review.

Saudi Prince Alwaleed bin Talal has again voiced support for allowing women to drive, arguing on Twitter that the move would benefit the economy and cut the need for roughly 500,000 foreign drivers. However, women’s rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider dismissed his remarks as symbolic, noting that similar statements have not led to real change. The issue remains sensitive in Saudi Arabia, where women are effectively barred from driving despite no explicit traffic law, and where authorities have recently cracked down on illegal foreign workers. Activists have campaigned for reform, including through the Women2Drive movement, which gained attention after a woman was detained for driving in 2011.

Bindi Irwin, daughter of the late Steve Irwin, is urging teenage girls to dress more modestly and age-appropriately. In a recent interview, she expressed sympathy for peers who wear revealing outfits, warning they may regret those choices later. She described herself as an old soul with a simple, conservative personal style, and suggested that basic clothing like jeans and a T-shirt can look classier than trying too hard.

Pakistan is experiencing a severe polio outbreak, with cases at a 15-year high, and the disease has paralyzed young children like 17-month-old Ikra. Vaccination efforts are being undermined by widespread distrust stemming from the CIA’s fake vaccination campaign used to locate Osama bin Laden, which has led some parents to refuse the drops as a Western plot. Aid organizations are now working with religious leaders to reassure families and rebuild confidence in immunization. Although an emergency vaccination drive has reduced cases this year, health officials stress that near-universal immunization is still needed to fully stop transmission.

Amid Washington gridlock and the government shutdown, a bipartisan group of 14 moderate senators quietly crafted a compromise to reopen the government and avert default. Led by Republican Susan Collins, the group included senators from both parties and independents, many from politically mixed states. Although their initial plan was rejected, key elements made it into the final deal struck by Senate leaders. The group pledged to keep working together on future crises, arguing that real leadership means risking criticism to achieve bipartisan progress.

A newly identified avian influenza strain, seal H3N8, jumped from birds to harbor seals and caused the deaths of over 160 seals along the New England coast, mostly young pups. The virus has adapted to infect mammalian respiratory systems and may have increased ability to spread among mammals, though further testing is needed. Scientists warn that because animal-borne diseases have previously crossed to humans, this strain could pose a public health risk. The findings were published in the journal mBio.

BlackBerry CEO John Chen is prioritizing enterprise clients as the core of his turnaround plan, while still keeping an eye on the consumer market for future growth. The company introduced two new devices, the Z3 and Q20, developed through its manufacturing partnership with Foxconn, with the Z3 set to reach consumers within four months. Chen also highlighted BBM as a key strategic asset, especially with the launch of BBM Protected for business security, though he acknowledged he must consider any option that benefits shareholders. He stressed that rebuilding confidence among employees and investors is his biggest challenge, as the company must prove its financial and product progress.

The article explores the heated debate among parents about whether to take children to SeaWorld after the documentary "Blackfish" raised concerns about keeping killer whales in captivity. It highlights the film's impact, including one mother canceling a planned family trip, while presenting contrasting viewpoints: some parents value SeaWorld for its educational and conservation efforts, while others refuse to support animal performances on ethical grounds. A third group remains uncertain, weighing the joy and learning opportunities for kids against the moral implications of captivity. Ultimately, the piece captures the emotional and ethical complexity parents face in deciding what is best for their children and the animals involved.

A year ago, the author saw encouraging progress in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea after years of conflict and instability, but the Ebola outbreak now threatens to undo that progress. The leaders of these countries are asking for three kinds of help: urgent resources to contain the crisis, support to rebuild health, education, and economies afterward, and long-term assistance in strengthening government capacity to handle future emergencies. The world has begun to respond, but action must be swift and sustained to prevent a major humanitarian disaster. With proper support, these nations can overcome the crisis as they have overcome past hardships.

A car bomb outside a restaurant in Mosul killed at least four people and wounded 14 others, while violent clashes erupted in Anbar province after Sunni tribal fighters seized several police stations, freed detainees, and confiscated weapons. The unrest in Anbar followed government attempts to dismantle protest camps and the arrest of a Sunni lawmaker, prompting further tensions with the army. The United Nations reported that 2013 was Iraq’s deadliest year for civilians since 2008, with nearly 7,800 killed and almost 18,000 injured. The UN envoy urged Iraqi leaders to address the root causes of violence and prevent sectarian conflict from escalating further.

Daniel Kish, who is blind, uses tongue clicks and the resulting echoes to navigate and form mental images of his surroundings, a technique he calls human echolocation. Through his nonprofit, World Access for the Blind, he has taught hundreds of blind children this skill to promote independence and reduce reliance on sighted people. His methods have drawn criticism from some colleagues and disability advocates who worry about overemphasis or unrealistic portrayals, but Kish argues the approach expands everyday opportunities. Despite limited interest from U.S. schools and agencies, he remains committed to spreading the technique worldwide.

Guinness World Records is opening an office in Dubai to handle a surge in record applications from the Middle East, where submissions have grown by 300 to 400 percent in recent years. The organization emphasizes that all attempts must be measurable, verifiable, breakable, and based on a single variable. To attract younger audiences, Guinness is expanding its digital presence through social media and user-generated video submissions. The region has already produced notable records, including a massive gold ring, a solar-powered wheelchair journey, and the world's tallest residential tower.

The U.S. government announced that direct enrollment through HealthCare.gov is now available to all individual-market customers, not just those who do not qualify for subsidies. This process lets consumers shop on insurance company websites or private exchanges, then use HealthCare.gov to verify eligibility for tax credits before completing a purchase. Officials said most technical fixes are in place, though insurers still need to test the system before full use. Separately, they acknowledged that about 30% of the marketplace—mainly payment and accounting functions—remains unfinished but is expected to be ready for coverage starting in January.

A second blood moon will occur Wednesday morning, visible across the western United States, and will appear slightly larger than the previous one because the moon is near its closest point to Earth. It is part of a rare tetrad—four consecutive total lunar eclipses spaced about six months apart—with the next events set for April and September 2015. Unlike partial eclipses, a total eclipse gives the moon its reddish-orange color as sunlight filters through Earth’s atmosphere. Although some link these events to religious holidays, astronomers note the connection is simply a result of the lunar calendar, not a mystical sign.

Actor Ryan O’Neal won a legal battle to keep an Andy Warhol portrait of his late partner Farrah Fawcett, which the University of Texas claimed belonged to her estate. He learned of the jury’s favorable verdict while undergoing surgery to remove skin cancer, and he broke down in tears of relief. The trial involved painful testimony about his relationship with Fawcett, but supporters and jurors ultimately believed the portrait was his. O’Neal says the artwork is priceless to him and will be passed down to their son, Redmond.

A designer has proposed a futuristic transit concept that removes traditional train stations entirely. Instead, city trams would travel in continuous loops and briefly dock with high-speed trains while both are moving, allowing passengers to transfer seamlessly between vehicles. This integrated system would let people travel from their neighborhoods to other cities without using cars, buses, or taxis, with RFID technology replacing paper tickets. Although the idea is far from being built, it is intended as a bold rethinking of the entire rail travel experience.

Bob Bergdahl, father of freed U.S. soldier Bowe Bergdahl, underwent a profound personal transformation during his son’s five-year Taliban captivity, immersing himself in Afghan history and the Pashto language to better understand and connect with his son’s captors. His journey drew both support and criticism, especially after a since-deleted tweet suggested he wanted to help free Guantanamo Bay prisoners, reflecting his belief that wars end through negotiation and reconciliation. While the prisoner swap that secured Bowe’s release sparked political backlash, Bergdahl’s Idaho community stood firmly behind the family, who had campaigned relentlessly for years. The elder Bergdahl also prepared a remote mountain campsite for his son’s recovery, noting that Bowe, too, had absorbed his captors’ language and now struggles with English.

After more than five decades and seven nominations, 84-year-old Bob Newhart finally won his first Emmy, taking home the award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series for his role on “The Big Bang Theory.” He credited the show’s writers for giving him strong material and remained humble, saying that in past years the nominees who beat him were simply better. Newhart also joked that he hopes to keep acting until he dies on a soundstage. The Creative Arts Emmys ceremony airs later this month, ahead of the main Primetime Emmy telecast.

The bodies of Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans killed in the Benghazi consulate attack were returned to the U.S. in a solemn ceremony attended by President Obama and Secretary Clinton, who vowed to pursue justice and continue American diplomatic leadership. Libyan officials announced several arrests linked to the assault, though the suspects are not directly tied to the attack and are believed to belong to extremist groups operating in eastern Libya. Investigators remain divided over whether the attack was premeditated, with the U.S. deploying warships, drones, and Marines to track those responsible. The incident occurred amid anti-American protests over an anti-Islam film, and questions persist about the exact circumstances of the ambassador's death.

Joe Weider, the influential fitness and bodybuilding pioneer, passed away at age 93 in a Los Angeles hospital. He built a publishing empire, founded major competitions like Mr. Olympia, and helped transform global attitudes toward exercise and health. Arnold Schwarzenegger, whom Weider mentored and brought to the U.S., praised him as a generous father figure and a titan of the industry. Even after a heart condition diagnosis, Weider remained active and dedicated to his work until nearly the end.

Boeing has announced the completion of its first 787-9 Dreamliner, a longer version of the 787-8 that can carry more passengers and fly farther while maintaining the same 20% fuel efficiency advantage. The aircraft has moved to the flight line in Washington state and is scheduled for delivery to launch customer Air New Zealand in mid-2014. This milestone offers a bright spot after a difficult year for Boeing, which included a global grounding of Dreamliners following a battery fire and several other technical incidents. Despite these setbacks, the company reports strong demand, with the 787-9 accounting for about 40% of all 787 orders.

Boeing opened the Dubai Air Show with a record-breaking launch of its 777X jet, securing 259 orders and commitments valued at over $95 billion, largely from Gulf carriers like Emirates, Qatar Airways, Etihad, and Lufthansa. The article places this milestone within Boeing’s history of transformative aircraft, from the 707 and 747 to the 777 and the troubled 787 Dreamliner. The 777X is designed as a more efficient evolution of the proven 777, blending new engines and wings with existing fuselage technology to compete with Airbus while avoiding the delays of an all-new design. Middle Eastern airlines have become the key drivers of Boeing’s latest strategy, shaping demand for long-range, fuel-efficient wide-body jets.

Boko Haram, whose name roughly translates to “Western education is forbidden,” has become a major threat in Nigeria through bombings, kidnappings, and assassinations, including the mass abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok. Founded over a decade ago by Mohammed Yusuf, the group grew more violent after his death and now operates under the elusive leader Abubakar Shekau, who has repeatedly survived claims of his demise. While it claims to seek strict Sharia law, its attacks also target Muslims who oppose it, and it exploits northern poverty and distrust of a corrupt government to gain sympathy. The group’s ties to regional extremists and threats against the West have drawn international concern, though foreign involvement remains limited.

Boko Haram militants attacked villages in northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, abducting at least 97 men and boys, killing 28 people, and burning numerous homes. The assault occurred days earlier but was only reported later because previous attacks had destroyed local cell towers, cutting off communication. The group, known for its violent campaign to impose strict Sharia law, has also been responsible for the mass abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls from Chibok and recently seized the wife of Cameroon’s deputy prime minister.

Boko Haram’s leader has released a video claiming the group will sell more than 200 abducted Nigerian schoolgirls, intensifying fears for their safety. Nigerian officials insist the threat will not weaken their resolve and say they are committed to finding the girls, though they face criticism over the slow response. The kidnapping has sparked global protests and social media campaigns, with world leaders and activists demanding action. Authorities now believe 276 girls were taken, but 53 escaped, leaving 223 still missing.

Suspected Boko Haram militants on motorcycles attacked four Christian villages near Chibok in northeastern Nigeria, killing at least 30 people and burning homes and churches. The gunmen also chased down residents who fled into the bush, making the death toll likely higher. A local priest and vigilante members reported that the military response was delayed, allowing the attackers to cause widespread destruction before escaping. Survivors have fled to nearby towns and the state capital, Maiduguri.

Boko Haram militants killed at least 35 people in coordinated dawn attacks on three villages in Borno State, dressing in military uniforms and using guns and firebombs. The deadliest assault left 26 dead in one village, while the other two raids claimed nine lives and injured several others. These attacks follow a recent assault on a military base and police station in neighboring Yobe State that killed dozens of security personnel. The group, which continues to hold over 200 abducted schoolgirls, has intensified its violent campaign in Nigeria's northeast.

Boko Haram stands out among terrorist groups for its extreme brutality, carrying out mass killings, bombings, and kidnappings across northern Nigeria, including the abduction of hundreds of schoolgirls. Its leader, Abubakar Shekau, justifies such acts with a medieval interpretation of Islam, including slavery and child marriage, while the group recruits young men by exploiting poverty, unemployment, and government neglect. Nigerian security forces have failed to stop the insurgency, and the group has splintered into factions with growing ties to al Qaeda affiliates in the region. Experts warn that without serious political and economic reforms, these militant groups could become even more dangerous and destabilize the wider Sahel area.

Three men were sentenced in Moscow for the acid attack that severely injured Bolshoi Ballet artistic director Sergei Filin, including a lead soloist who orchestrated the assault. Filin, speaking in Germany after the verdict, said he cannot forgive the perpetrators because no punishment can restore the eyesight he lost. Though surgeries have partially recovered his vision, he remains in pain and emotionally scarred. The attack exposed deep rivalries and turmoil within the famed ballet company.

Bonnaroo’s 2014 lineup spans a wide range of genres, featuring headliners like Elton John and Kanye West alongside acts such as Lionel Richie, Jack White, and Vampire Weekend. The four-day festival takes place June 12–15 in Manchester, Tennessee, with over 125 bands performing across 13 stages around the clock. In addition to music, more than 20 comedians are scheduled, and special all-star “superjam” collaborations are planned. Tickets become available Saturday through the festival’s website.

Former NFL star Boomer Esiason sparked backlash after suggesting that Mets player Daniel Murphy should have arranged for his wife to have a scheduled C-section so he wouldn’t miss Opening Day. Critics condemned the remark as insensitive and sexist, emphasizing that major surgery should not be scheduled for convenience. Esiason later apologized, saying he never meant to dictate women’s health decisions or drag the Murphys into controversy. Murphy defended his choice to prioritize his wife and child, and medical experts noted that purely elective C-sections are uncommon and generally discouraged.

A lawyer involved in the historic Bosman ruling has joined a Belgian agent in filing a complaint against UEFA’s Financial Fair Play regulations, arguing that the break-even requirement stifles competition and violates EU laws on free movement. They claim the rules could reduce player transfers and lower wages, thereby hurting agents’ earnings. UEFA has defended FFP as a measure promoting financial sustainability and expects the European Commission to dismiss the challenge. The complaint follows UEFA’s recent ban on Malaga for breaching the rules, a decision the Spanish club is appealing.

A friend of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev has admitted guilt to charges of obstructing the Boston Marathon bombing investigation by taking items from Tsarnaev’s dorm room after the attack. Under a plea agreement, the Kazakh national faces a recommended seven-year prison sentence and will be deported afterward. The charges stem from his disposal of a backpack containing fireworks and gunpowder, as well as his removal of Tsarnaev’s computer. A separate roommate involved in the case was previously convicted and is awaiting sentencing.

Defense attorneys for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev have asked to move his Boston Marathon bombing trial to Washington, D.C., arguing that local surveys show widespread pretrial bias, with many potential jurors already believing he is guilty and favoring the death penalty. They compared the case to Timothy McVeigh’s Oklahoma City bombing trial, saying the Boston community’s deep involvement and trauma make a fair local jury unlikely. Separately, the judge rejected prosecutors’ use of Tsarnaev’s immigrant status and alleged betrayal of the U.S. as an aggravating factor for seeking execution, calling such a distinction inappropriate.

At a congressional hearing, lawmakers questioned whether the Boston Marathon bombing could have been prevented, focusing on the FBI’s decision to close its investigation of Tamerlan Tsarnaev after a Russian tip. While some officials defended the intelligence community’s actions, Boston’s police commissioner acknowledged that having that information beforehand would have prompted a second look. The hearing also highlighted the need to improve intelligence sharing and protect soft targets, though officials cautioned against overly intrusive surveillance. The discussion is expected to continue as more congressional hearings on the attack are planned.

Botswana’s economy has been transformed by diamonds since the late 1960s, thanks to a unique 50/50 partnership with De Beers that gives the state a direct share of profits, not just taxes. This arrangement has funded major investments in education and healthcare, making Botswana one of Africa’s most prosperous nations. The industry is set to expand further as De Beers relocates its rough diamond trading to Gaborone, bringing billions in sales, banking activity, and new jobs. However, officials warn that the country must reduce its dependence on diamonds, since the resource is finite and recent market downturns have highlighted the risks.

Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl is nearing the end of his reintegration process and will soon be assigned to a new military unit. As part of his gradual return to normal life, he has made supervised trips off the Texas base to places like restaurants and stores. His release in exchange for five Taliban prisoners has sparked criticism, especially from former unit members who believe he deserted and endangered others. While the circumstances of his disappearance remain under investigation, military officials have emphasized his physical and mental recovery.

Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl is expected to meet soon with the general leading the investigation into the circumstances of his 2009 capture by the Taliban. After five years in captivity, he was released in exchange for senior Taliban detainees, but his return sparked criticism and accusations that he deserted his post. An earlier Army inquiry reportedly found he left his outpost intentionally, though officials have not made a definitive desertion determination. Bergdahl has since returned to regular duty in Texas, where he is assigned to a homeland defense unit.

A celebrity boxing promoter has proposed a $1 million-per-fighter exhibition match between Chris Brown and Drake following their alleged nightclub altercation. The promoter also plans to donate $1 million to a women’s charity and has jokingly invited Rihanna to serve as a ring girl, though he expects she will decline. The offer comes as police investigate the brawl, which left Brown injured and also led San Antonio Spurs player Tony Parker to sue the nightclub over an eye injury. Neither Brown nor Drake has publicly responded to the proposal.

An 11-year-old boy who wandered off from his mother at a shopping center in Manchester made his way to the airport and managed to bypass passport and boarding pass checks before boarding a flight to Rome. He was only noticed by the crew while the plane was in the air, and he was sent back home on the same aircraft. Airport staff have been suspended while an investigation takes place, though officials maintain that security was not compromised since the boy passed through full screening. No criminal charges were filed.

A teenager appeared in juvenile court in San Diego County for a small fire tied to last week’s wildfires, though proceedings were closed and few details were released. A 19-year-old arrested alongside him was let go after prosecutors decided there wasn’t enough evidence to file charges. Separately, 57-year-old Alberto Serrato was charged with arson in connection with another small fire and has pleaded not guilty. The wildfires scorched nearly 26,000 acres, were mostly contained, and have prompted task forces to investigate possible patterns and warn residents about disaster-related scams.

A 12-year-old boy in California has been formally charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing death of his 8-year-old sister, Leila Fowler. He appeared in juvenile court, acknowledged the charges, and remained in custody without entering a plea. Authorities had initially pursued reports of an intruder, but the boy was arrested days after the attack. It was also reported that he had been suspended from school for bringing a knife shortly before the killing.

Seven-year-old Timmy Tyrrell, who loves racing go-karts, turned his hobby into a charity effort called Mini’s Mission after his friend Ella was diagnosed with cancer. He collects donations at weekly races to support families of children with cancer through the Jeffrey Virostek Fund. So far, he has raised more than $22,000, and his friend Ella has since recovered. Timmy says he wants to keep racing and helping children for as long as he can.

At age six, Jeff Franzen witnessed the assassination of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, mistaking the gunfire for firecrackers. He recalled seeing what looked like confetti burst from the car, but was too young to understand that a killing was taking place. Decades later, he reflected on the experience as a remarkable piece of history he happened to witness.

New research presented at a reproductive medicine conference suggests that everyday chemicals like BPA and phthalates may contribute to fertility problems and pregnancy loss. One study found that men with higher phthalate levels had a 20% reduction in fertility, while another linked elevated BPA levels in early pregnancy to a greater risk of miscarriage. Although the studies do not prove cause and effect, experts say the findings add to concerns about environmental impacts on reproduction. They recommend reducing exposure by avoiding microwaving plastics, limiting canned foods, and handling fewer paper receipts.

BP is taking its fight over Gulf oil spill compensation to the U.S. Supreme Court after a lower appeals court upheld a ruling that allows businesses to claim losses without proving direct harm from the 2010 disaster. The company argues the settlement was never meant to cover unrelated damages and says it will continue challenging what it calls excessive or unjustified claims. BP has already paid billions in compensation and cleanup costs, but faces billions more in potential payouts. The company is also asking the court to pause payments while the Supreme Court decides whether to hear the case.

South Africa’s braai is a culturally unifying barbecue tradition that brings together people of all backgrounds around an open fire. Its popularity has grown through the TV show “The Ultimate Braai Master,” which has introduced the practice to a global audience. The cuisine is diverse, ranging from common meats like chicken and sausage to wild game and organ meats, with regional specialties and marinades. Braais are relaxed, social events, and communal spots like Mzoli’s in Cape Town have become popular destinations for both locals and tourists.

Prosecutors challenged Bradley Manning’s claims of mistreatment in military custody, pointing to weekly check-in forms that recorded no complaints and his own ratings of the treatment as “excellent” and “professional.” Manning responded that he did raise concerns verbally, but officers often wrote down “no issues” after discussing them. The hearing also revisited his testimony about harsh conditions, including isolation, sleep restrictions, and a humiliating naked head count, which he partially walked back under questioning. The defense is seeking dismissal or a reduced sentence, while prosecutors argue the detention was justified and Manning could face life in prison if convicted.

Army intelligence analyst Bradley Manning will face a court-martial on charges connected to the massive leak of classified U.S. documents to WikiLeaks, including aiding the enemy, which could result in life imprisonment but not the death penalty. Prosecutors allege he used his top-secret clearance in Iraq to download sensitive material and pass it to Julian Assange. His defense has pointed to weak security protocols and the Army’s failure to address his emotional struggles. The case has also highlighted ongoing U.S. intelligence community efforts to prevent insider leaks while improving information sharing.

Army Private Bradley Manning testified publicly for the first time about his harsh military confinement, describing severe isolation, sleep disruption, and suicidal thoughts during his detention in Kuwait and at Quantico. His defense argued that the treatment amounted to punishment and should lead to dismissal or a reduced sentence if he is convicted. Manning faces charges related to leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, including aiding the enemy, and could receive a life sentence. A psychiatrist also testified that Manning was a suicide risk and that recommendations to ease his restrictions were ignored.

The court-martial of Pfc. Bradley Manning centers on opposing portrayals: prosecutors argue he knowingly aided enemies by leaking massive volumes of classified U.S. documents to WikiLeaks, while his defense contends he was a disillusioned idealist who exposed wrongdoing. Manning admitted to lesser charges but denied the most serious accusation of aiding the enemy, which carries a possible life sentence. The case involves hundreds of thousands of leaked military reports and diplomatic cables, including the "Collateral Murder" video, and the trial has also highlighted disputes over whether the disclosures truly harmed national security or mainly caused embarrassment. A military judge is now set to deliver the verdict, determining Manning's guilt or innocence in what is considered the largest classified leak in U.S. history.

Brad Pitt issued a blunt warning to Vitalii Sediuk, saying the man would be stomped if he ever tried to look up a woman’s dress again.
