It includes underwater caves and a transparent viewing tunnel for spectators, and was inaugurated by Italian freediving champions. The goal is to turn the area into an international diving destination while also welcoming beginners under supervision.

Humorist Dave Barry’s latest book is a collection of essays that humorously touches on parenting, though he insists it offers no real advice. He shares personal stories about raising his teenage daughter, including taking her to a Justin Bieber concert and dealing with her constant social media use. In an interview, he jokes about being wary of boys, admits parents should “lighten up,” and mentions his next project, a novel about a disastrous middle school class trip.

David Beckham transcended football to become a cultural icon, reshaping ideas of modern masculinity with his stylish, metrosexual image while remaining unquestionably straight. Though never the world's best player, he became a pioneering celebrity athlete, known more for being himself than for his sporting achievements. His mystique grew through his silence and carefully managed public persona, which allowed the public to project their own ideas onto him. Even a denied affair scandal only enhanced his status, adding a hint of edge to his otherwise clean-cut image and cementing his lasting place in popular culture.

Prime Minister David Cameron has sparked controversy by suggesting Tottenham fans should not be prosecuted for using the word "Yid" when self-identifying, arguing that hate speech should only be punished when motivated by hatred. Anti-racism groups and legal figures condemned his remarks as legitimizing anti-Semitism, insisting that reclaiming the term is not justified and that the law should apply equally. Meanwhile, some commentators defended Spurs fans, arguing that the real problem is the anti-Semitic abuse from rival supporters, such as chants about Auschwitz, and that the FA is targeting the wrong people. The debate highlights the deep division over whether the word can be reclaimed in a football context or whether its use only sustains racism.

The article reflects on this year’s Davos theme, which centers on how the world is being reshaped after years of crisis. The author initially dismisses the jargon but comes to see its relevance, noting that rapid changes—such as the spread of the internet, social media, emerging economies, and a shift in power eastward—have upended long-held assumptions. The piece argues that Davos must move beyond crisis management and focus on how societies, governments, and businesses should make decisions in this new, uncertain landscape. Ultimately, it suggests the summit will be worthwhile only if leaders set aside narrow interests and genuinely confront these transformative issues.

The World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Davos brings together global leaders, executives, and public figures to discuss a broad theme about reshaping the world amid rapid technological, social, and economic change. Against a backdrop of conflicts in Syria, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic, as well as fragile recoveries in major economies, speakers will address issues from Iran’s role to U.S. engagement abroad. While the global economy shows signs of improvement, persistent problems like high youth unemployment in parts of Europe and concerns over surveillance remain. Beyond the official sessions, much of the event’s value lies in informal networking and deal-making on the sidelines.

Al-Shabaab has warned Kenya that its attacks are not over, days after a deadly siege at Nairobi’s Westgate mall left 67 people dead. The militant group is said to have tortured hostages, with evidence showing victims had limbs severed or were hanged. It also emerged that Kenyan intelligence officials had warned Cabinet members a year earlier that the mall was a potential target. Kenyan authorities are now facing scrutiny over how the well-coordinated assault was carried out, amid ongoing military tensions with Al-Shabaab in Somalia.

Rukia Shabiby endured decades of isolation and shame after developing an obstetric fistula during a traumatic childbirth at age 13, a condition that left her incontinent and socially ostracized. She eventually found hope at a Tanzanian hospital that provides free corrective surgery, using local ambassadors and mobile money transfers to help poor rural women reach the facility. After treatment, patients regain their dignity and many receive vocational training in skills like sewing and jewelry-making. These women often return to their communities as advocates, spreading the message that the condition is treatable and encouraging others to seek help.

The article highlights the deadly plight of African refugees attempting to cross from Egypt into Israel, with many dying in the desert or being shot by border guards. Those who survive often fall into the hands of Bedouin traffickers, who subject them to brutal torture, rape, extortion, and forced labor. A human rights worker in El Arish regularly recovers and buries the bodies of unidentified migrants, while local authorities appear unable or unwilling to stop the smuggling networks. The region remains lawless, leaving refugees trapped in a cycle of violence and exploitation with little hope of escape.

A shortage of lethal injection drugs contributed to a continued decline in U.S. executions, with only 39 carried out in 2013—a 10 percent drop from the prior year and just the second time in two decades the annual total fell below 40. States struggled to obtain execution drugs after European manufacturers banned their use, forcing reliance on new drug combinations or loosely regulated compounding pharmacies and prompting court delays. Maryland became the sixth state in six years to abolish capital punishment, while death sentences also hit historic lows and public support waned. Although some legal experts believe the Supreme Court may eventually reconsider the constitutionality of the death penalty, there are no current signs the justices will take up the issue soon.

A Shanghai-based “death experience” game is set to open in September 2014, using special effects and an escape-room format to simulate dying. Participants who lose face a fake cremation, moving through a conveyor-belt incinerator with heat and light effects before entering a womb-like capsule to symbolize rebirth. The founders, who also run a hospice support organization, tested the experience themselves in a real crematorium and hope the attraction encourages people to reflect on life and confront death more openly. The project was crowdfunded successfully, showing strong public curiosity about mortality in China.

A new SARS-like coronavirus has claimed another life, with a 39-year-old Saudi man dying shortly after hospitalization, bringing the WHO’s recorded total to 15 cases and nine deaths. The patient had no known contact with infected individuals, prompting investigations into other exposure sources. The virus causes severe respiratory symptoms and can lead to pneumonia or kidney failure, and while most cases are in the Middle East, a few have appeared in the UK through family transmission. Health officials believe the virus likely originated in bats but stress that it does not spread easily among people, so no travel restrictions are recommended.

Although speaking time in presidential debates often draws attention, experts say it is rarely decisive; shorter answers can be just as effective as longer ones. The upcoming debate’s extended format may suit President Obama’s paragraph-style explanations, but it also risks exposing him to mistakes, while Mitt Romney’s discipline could help him if he stays composed. Ultimately, the candidates’ authenticity and how the media and campaigns frame the debate afterward are more important than how long they speak.

The White House is warning that failing to raise the debt ceiling by October 17 could trigger a catastrophic default, but many Republicans openly doubt that deadline and dismiss the threat as exaggerated. They argue the U.S. can avoid default by prioritizing interest payments, and some see the debt limit as leverage to force spending cuts or changes to the health care law. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew insists there are no good options once borrowing authority runs out, and most economists agree that hitting the limit could cause severe economic damage. With no clear precedent, uncertainty dominates, and nervous investors have already sent stock markets falling.

The Defense Department has formally charged Majid Shoukat Khan, a Pakistani national held at Guantanamo Bay, with offenses including conspiracy, murder, attempted murder, terrorism support, and espionage. He is accused of aiding al Qaeda after 9/11, including plotting to bomb U.S. gas stations, preparing a suicide mission targeting Pakistan’s president, and funneling money to a group linked to a deadly hotel bombing in Jakarta. If convicted, Khan could receive a life sentence. His lawyers have alleged he was tortured while held in secret CIA custody, though the CIA has denied any wrongdoing.

A leading obstetricians’ group has updated the definition of a full-term pregnancy, replacing the broad 37-to-42-week range with more specific categories. Under the new guidance, 37 to just under 39 weeks is “early term,” 39 to just under 41 weeks is “full term,” 41 to just under 42 weeks is “late term,” and 42 weeks or more is “postterm.” The change reflects evidence that fetal brain and lung development continues through the final weeks, with the best newborn outcomes occurring at 39 to 40 weeks. As a result, the group stresses that elective deliveries before 39 weeks should only happen when continuing the pregnancy poses significant health risks to the mother or baby.

At a Davos panel on emerging markets, officials and business leaders agreed that while the BRICS countries are highly diverse, their large consumer bases still offer strong investment returns. China remains a growth leader at around 8%, driven by urbanization, whereas Brazil is struggling with low growth despite recent reforms and a rising middle class. Attention is shifting to next-tier economies like Mexico and Nigeria, which offer new opportunities but still face challenges such as corruption and over-reliance on the U.S. or oil. Long-term prospects remain solid, as low vehicle ownership rates in developing nations point to substantial future demand.

At the annual St. Petersburg economic forum, Vladimir Putin presented his economic agenda for his new presidential term, focusing on reducing reliance on oil, using sovereign funds for infrastructure, and addressing high interest rates and capital flight. German Chancellor Angela Merkel joined him on stage, where both leaders showed firm stances on foreign policy, including sharp exchanges over Syria and Turkey. Despite their differences, the two emphasized a desire to strengthen business ties between Russia and Germany. The event highlighted Putin’s push for economic reform while signaling Russia’s continued assertiveness on global issues.

Despite official restrictions, some Iranian cafes and restaurants defied the ban on broadcasting World Cup matches, allowing men and women to watch together in public. Women expressed joy and excitement at sharing the experience, which is rare because mixed-gender sports events have been prohibited since 1979. Authorities had warned venues against showing the games and used measures like censored billboards and delayed TV broadcasts to limit female visibility. The push for equality continues, with women sneaking into a volleyball match disguised as fans and a female vice president investigating the ban.

More than one million signatures have been collected in the effort to recall Wisconsin’s governor, nearly double the number required to trigger an election. The recall drive stems from Governor Scott Walker’s controversial law stripping most public employees of collective bargaining rights, which sparked massive protests. Democratic officials submitted the signatures, setting up what would be Wisconsin’s first gubernatorial recall. Walker remains confident, noting that most voters did not sign the petition and expressing hope they will trust him again.

House Democrats are using a procedural tactic to force a vote on raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10, even though they acknowledge it will not succeed in the Republican-controlled House. The move is largely an election-year strategy to put Republicans on the defensive by framing them as opposing a popular measure that helps working families. Republicans counter that a wage hike would cost jobs and argue voters care more about the economy and Obamacare. Public polling shows broad support for the increase, and both parties are citing a nonpartisan report to back their positions.

Amid stalled immigration reform in Congress, dozens of Democratic lawmakers are pressing President Obama to use executive action to halt deportations of undocumented immigrants, arguing he has the legal authority to do so and pointing to his past deferral program for young immigrants. The push gained momentum after a heckler confronted Obama in San Francisco, though the President has maintained he lacks such power. While Obama has deported more people than previous presidents, his administration now prioritizes convicted criminals and serious violators over everyday workers. The Senate has passed comprehensive immigration legislation, but the House has not taken it up, leaving the issue unresolved.

A Navy veteran and legal permanent resident, Howard Dean Bailey, was deported to Jamaica in 2012 after a 1997 drug conviction triggered immigration laws that mandate removal for certain felonies. He is among thousands of former service members who have been deported, a largely overlooked issue even amid national debates on immigration and veterans. Immigration advocates argue that while enforcement agencies have some discretion, immigration judges do not, and they are urging the Obama administration to prioritize military service in deportation cases. Bailey’s family continues to fight for his return, describing his exile as devastating and isolating.

Casey Anthony told mental health experts in pretrial depositions that she may have been drugged and sexually assaulted at a party in 2004, leading to her pregnancy with Caylee. The newly released records also show she claimed her father blamed her for Caylee’s death, took the child’s body, and that she had been sexually abused by him as a child. Anthony was acquitted of murder but convicted of lying to investigators, while her father has consistently denied all allegations of abuse and involvement in Caylee’s death.

Mali’s Festival au Desert, held near Timbuktu on the edge of the Sahara, offers a unique blend of Tuareg culture, camel racing, and desert blues, far removed from typical music festivals. This year’s event went ahead despite security concerns following the kidnapping and killing of tourists in the area, though travel warnings kept many visitors away. The lineup mixed regional artists with international stars, including a surprise appearance by Bono, while local groups like Tartit, formed by Tuareg women, captured the festival’s authentic spirit.

Scientists have moved a step closer to synthetic life by constructing a redesigned chromosome and successfully placing it inside brewer’s yeast, where it functioned and was passed on to offspring. The team made hundreds of genetic alterations, streamlining the chromosome by removing repetitive and “junk” DNA. This work goes beyond earlier achievements with synthetic bacteria because yeast is a more complex eukaryotic organism, sharing many genetic features with humans. The breakthrough could eventually lead to engineered yeast cells capable of producing medicines, vaccines, or fuels.

Fashion designer L'Wren Scott was found dead in her New York apartment on Monday in an apparent suicide; she was 49. Her assistant discovered her body after receiving a text from Scott that morning. The news left her longtime partner, Mick Jagger, "completely shocked and devastated," and the Rolling Stones canceled their scheduled Perth concert. Tributes poured in from celebrities, highlighting Scott's talent, generosity, and impact as a designer.

Linda Lwanga, a British-born designer and former electrical engineer, moved to Uganda to launch Zanaa, a luxury accessories brand that repurposes discarded ankole cow horns and other traditional African materials into high-end jewelry. Her work supports local artisans and promotes sustainable practices by transforming waste into sellable products for international markets. However, operating from Kampala presents challenges, including shipping delays, poor infrastructure, and difficulty accessing trade information. Lwanga believes that improved regional trade agreements, like those under COMESA, could help her business grow and gain global recognition.

The Ebola outbreak in Liberia has devastated communities, leaving many children orphaned, including a young boy who lost 13 relatives. The country’s health system is overwhelmed, with many hospitals closed and patients left untreated outside clinics, while health workers lack adequate safety equipment and training. Burial teams face horrific scenes, such as infants found beside deceased mothers, as they work long hours under dangerous conditions. In response, communities are adopting preventive measures, including temperature checks and changes to church practices, though fear remains widespread.

The EU’s decision to lift economic sanctions on Myanmar, while keeping an arms embargo, signals a belief that democratic reforms have succeeded. However, the article argues this overlooks ongoing state-backed persecution of Rohingya Muslims, including killings, arson, mass arrests, and forced displacement. Despite Myanmar’s claims of inter-communal violence, evidence points to government complicity in ethnic cleansing, with Rohingya denied citizenship and humanitarian aid. The author warns that international praise for Myanmar’s political opening ignores the Rohingya’s suffering and endangers their lives.

The article presents a ten-day mindfulness plan to combat the stress and gloom of January, drawing on techniques from an Oxford-based program. It explains that mindfulness involves paying full, non-judgmental attention to the present moment, which helps people see thoughts and feelings as temporary. The suggested daily activities include mindful eating, walking, breathing exercises, gratitude practices, and even going to the movies, all designed to reduce anxiety and increase well-being. Ultimately, the guide emphasizes that by practicing these habits, people can ease stress, boost mental clarity, and rediscover simple pleasures.

International inspectors are now overseeing Syria's initial steps to dismantle its chemical weapons program, with crews using cutting tools to disable warheads, bombs, and mixing equipment at nearly 50 sites. Despite this progress, a defected Syrian general has cast doubt on the regime's intentions, claiming that President Assad is hiding stockpiles and moving some chemical agents to Iraq and Lebanon—allegations those countries deny. The destruction effort stems from a unanimous UN Security Council resolution requiring Syria to eliminate its arsenal, a diplomatic deal brokered by the US and Russia that prevented military strikes following a deadly sarin attack near Damascus.

A gunman opened fire at a mall in Happy Valley, Oregon, killing two people and wounding a teenage girl before taking his own life as police arrived. Authorities identified the shooter as 22-year-old Jacob Tyler Roberts, saying they found no connection between him and his victims and that his motive remained unclear. The injured 15-year-old underwent surgery and was expected to recover, while friends and school officials expressed shock, describing Roberts as a polite and popular young man. The two deceased victims were remembered as devoted family members and friends who put others first.

Former Rutgers student Dharun Ravi has apologized for his role in spying on his gay roommate, Tyler Clementi, who later died by suicide, and has decided to voluntarily begin his 30-day jail sentence rather than wait for an appeal. He will appear in court to formally waive his right against double jeopardy so he can start serving his punishment, which also includes probation, community service, and restitution. Prosecutors have called the sentence too lenient and are appealing, but legal experts say the appeal is unlikely to succeed given the judge’s broad sentencing discretion under state law.

Tuberculosis remains a serious public health threat in the United States, and diabetes has become a major new driver of the disease. Diabetes weakens the immune system, making people far more likely to develop active TB and suffer worse outcomes, including drug resistance and death. The convergence of these two epidemics is especially visible along the U.S.-Mexico border and in states like California, Texas, and Florida, yet many diabetes care providers are unaware of the risk. To prevent reversing decades of TB control progress, the article calls for routine TB screening among diabetes patients, greater awareness and education, and stronger government investment in research, diagnostics, and treatments.

Former President George W. Bush and his wife expressed relief and happiness after learning that Dick Cheney’s heart transplant surgery was successful, offering prayers for his full recovery. The 71-year-old former vice president underwent the procedure in Virginia after being on the transplant waiting list for nearly two years, with his family expressing gratitude to the anonymous donor. Cheney has a long history of heart problems, including multiple heart attacks and prior procedures such as a pacemaker and a heart pump. He served as Bush’s influential vice president from 2001 to 2009, and a documentary about his polarizing career was in the works.

Mitt Romney’s Republican National Convention speech aimed to introduce himself, humanize his image, and contrast himself with President Obama, but it drew mixed reviews. Some analysts felt he succeeded in appearing warmer and more relatable, while others argued he offered vague policy ideas and failed to make a strong substantive case for his presidency. The night was also marked by unusual moments, including Clint Eastwood’s rambling performance and Marco Rubio’s widely praised introduction, which overshadowed parts of the program. Overall, the convention helped soften Romney’s public image, but left questions about his specific plans and the campaign’s ability to seize its biggest moment.

James Shigeta, a trailblazing Asian-American actor, passed away at age 81 in Los Angeles. Over a five-decade career, he broke barriers in Hollywood, with memorable roles in films such as "Die Hard," "Flower Drum Song," and the animated "Mulan." He also appeared extensively on television in popular series like "Hawaii Five-O" and "Fantasy Island." His agent remembered him as a dear friend and a major star who paved the way for Asian-American performers.

Men are just as likely as women to struggle with excess weight, but diet advertising has long focused on women, discouraging many men from seeking help. New campaigns from major weight-loss companies now explicitly target men, aiming to tap into a largely underserved market. Beyond marketing, men like Jeff Romig and Lloyd Dinwiddie show that lasting change often requires personal motivation, accountability, and support from others. Romig even left a stressful job to prioritize his health, while Dinwiddie relies on an online community to stay on track.

Satellite images have identified two possible pieces of debris from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 in a remote stretch of the southern Indian Ocean, offering investigators a more specific target after weeks of searching vast corridors. The objects, measuring roughly 24 meters and 5 meters, were spotted far off the coast of western Australia, but the area is extremely difficult to reach and operate in due to its distance, deep waters, and unpredictable weather. Poor visibility and strong winds could hamper air and satellite efforts, while ocean conditions and currents may also affect the debris' movement. Search crews likely have only a few days to locate the objects before conditions make recovery even more unlikely.

Donna Summer, the iconic “Queen of Disco,” passed away at age 63 after battling cancer, surrounded by family in Florida. She rose to fame in the 1970s with hits like “Love to Love You Baby,” “Hot Stuff,” and “Bad Girls,” and later proved her range by crossing into rock, R&B, and inspirational music. A five-time Grammy winner, she was remembered by fellow artists and industry figures as a groundbreaking vocalist whose sound defined an era. Her family requested donations to the Salvation Army in her memory.

Actor Lee Thompson Young was found dead in his Los Angeles apartment on Monday morning in an apparent suicide, according to his manager. The 29-year-old actor was best known for starring in Disney’s “The Famous Jett Jackson” and more recently played Detective Barry Frost on TNT’s “Rizzoli & Isles.” His manager and the show’s executive producer paid tribute to him, describing him as a kind, gentle person whose loss has deeply affected colleagues and loved ones.

Novak Djokovic and Petra Kvitova were named the ITF world champions for 2011, recognizing their standout seasons. Djokovic dominated men’s tennis with three Grand Slam titles and a 43-match winning streak, while Kvitova captured her first major at Wimbledon, won the WTA Championships, and helped the Czech Republic claim the Fed Cup. The awards also honored the Bryan brothers in men’s doubles and Peschke and Srebotnik in women’s doubles. Both singles champions were praised for combining national-team success with exceptional individual achievements.

Two Brooklyn men were freed after 21 years behind bars when new DNA evidence cast doubt on their convictions for a 1992 triple murder. The evidence, discovered under the victim’s fingernails, matched a later crime committed while both men were already imprisoned, proving they could not have been involved. Their original convictions relied on confessions obtained under coercion when they were teenagers. The district attorney acknowledged that the new findings would likely have led a jury to a different verdict, prompting their release.

Dr. Kermit Gosnell was convicted of first-degree murder for killing newborns with scissors at his Philadelphia clinic and could face the death penalty. He was also found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for a patient who died from an anesthetic overdose, along with numerous illegal late-term abortion charges. The trial exposed horrific conditions, including unsanitary procedures and unlicensed staff, intensifying national debate over abortion. Both anti-abortion and abortion-rights advocates claimed the verdict supported their broader views on the issue.

A Veterans Affairs doctor has come forward with allegations that the Phoenix VA health system is forcing combat-injured veterans from Iraq and Afghanistan to wait up to ten months for appointments, directly violating federal rules that grant them priority access. The doctor, Katherine Mitchell, reported the delays to the VA's inspector general, noting that even severely traumatized patients with PTSD or polytrauma were affected. She attributes the backlog to a nationwide shortage of medical providers caused by low pay and slow hiring, which has led facilities to conceal wait times. The claims add to a growing scandal involving secret waiting lists and patient deaths, prompting President Obama to promise accountability and dispatch a senior aide to investigate the Phoenix facility.

Oscar Pistorius’s court-ordered psychiatric evaluation found that he suffers from depression, PTSD, and is a suicide risk, but showed no signs of psychopathy or abnormal aggression. The doctors concluded he was not mentally incapacitated when he killed Reeva Steenkamp and understood his actions were wrong, though his extreme fear response was seen as plausible given his disability. The defense views the report as supportive of his claim that he mistook Steenkamp for an intruder, while the prosecution maintains he killed her intentionally after an argument. The judge must now decide whether his belief in an intruder was reasonable, with possible outcomes ranging from acquittal or culpable homicide to a murder conviction and lengthy prison sentence.

New York City is considering a proposal to raise the minimum age for purchasing tobacco products from 18 to 21, a move supporters hope will curb youth smoking. Backers argue that since most smokers start young and tobacco is highly addictive, older teens need protection from lifelong addiction. Opponents worry about lost tax revenue, enforcement difficulties, and restrictions on personal choice. Officials project the measure could significantly reduce smoking among teens and young adults, though experts note education programs are also essential.

More than 150 doctors and medical professionals urged President Obama in an open letter to let civilian physicians treat Guantanamo Bay detainees, arguing that the prisoners rightly distrust military doctors who are force-feeding them. The hunger strike, now involving over 100 of the 166 detainees, stems from their indefinite detention and protest against conditions. The letter followed the government’s release of the names of 46 prisoners held indefinitely, most of them Yemeni, after a lawsuit by the Miami Herald. Obama has renewed his pledge to close the prison, which human rights groups have long condemned.

The young Indian woman who was brutally gang-raped on a New Delhi bus in December has died at a Singapore hospital, succumbing to severe organ failure and brain injuries. Her death has intensified public outrage and grief, with protesters demanding justice and stronger measures to protect women. Six suspects, including the bus driver and a minor, remain in custody. In response, Indian leaders have pledged to strengthen laws and improve women's safety, while the case has highlighted the broader epidemic of sexual violence and harassment across the country.

A new documentary claims that death row inmate Glen Rogers, not O.J. Simpson, carried out the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, alleging Simpson waited nearby while Rogers committed the killings. The film relies on statements Rogers made to his brother and a criminal profiler, including claims that Simpson hired him and that he sent a victim’s pin to his mother. Ronald Goldman’s family strongly rejected the allegations, and the LAPD said it remains confident Simpson was the killer, though it would look into Rogers’ claims. Critics also suggest Rogers may have fabricated the story to delay his execution.

Ex-SAS soldier Andy McNab argues that psychopathic traits, particularly focus and ruthlessness, can be an advantage in leadership, especially in the corporate world. He coaches executives to set aside empathy and concentrate on the mission, drawing parallels between the boardroom and combat. The article notes that psychopathic tendencies are more common among CEOs, as capitalism often rewards such behavior. However, McNab emphasizes that his goal is not to turn everyone into a psychopath, but to help leaders strike a balance and understand their own decision-making processes.

Dick Cheney’s relentless media campaign to rewrite his record is both appalling and politically useful for Democrats, since he is overshadowing more credible Republicans while refusing to admit any mistakes. The article catalogs his failures, including ignoring terrorism warnings before 9/11, making false claims to justify the Iraq War, and pushing policies that weakened America. Unlike Hillary Clinton, who openly admitted her Iraq War vote was wrong, Cheney shows no remorse—his only stated regret is a vague reference to his misspent youth. Even his hunting accident, in which he shot a companion, reportedly drew no apology, reinforcing the image of a man unable to accept responsibility.

Coca-Cola reported a slight profit decline last year as global soda demand weakened, with overall volume growth falling short of its targets. To counter shrinking sales, the company continues investing heavily in marketing, leaning on the enduring mystique of its “secret recipe” to maintain consumer interest. The recipe’s legend—protected in a high-security vault and known to only a few—helps position the brand as special and valuable, even though the formula has never been patented. Experts argue the exact recipe matters less than the brand’s iconic status, since loyal customers would still choose the original over cheaper imitations.

Japanese artist Megumi Igarashi, known as Rokudenashiko, was arrested in Tokyo for allegedly distributing digital files that could be used to 3D-print models of her genitals, which she created as part of a crowdfunded art project. She argues the work is fine art meant to challenge Japan’s taboo around female genitalia, unlike the more accepted depictions of penises in pop culture. Critics point to the country’s strict obscenity laws, noting that Japan only recently banned child pornography and still allows explicit anime and manga. Her arrest has sparked an online petition and support from lawyers who say the detention is unjust and a matter of freedom and equality.

The fragile ceasefire in eastern Ukraine is already under threat after shelling near key cities just days after it took effect. The truce is strained because neither side fully controls the various volunteer and nationalist militias involved, and the agreement lacks clear terms and enforcement mechanisms. Some factions may deliberately seek to undermine the peace process, while unresolved issues like rebel disarmament and regional autonomy remain. The coming days will determine whether negotiations proceed or whether violence escalates, potentially prompting stronger Western sanctions and a NATO response.

Iraqi officials are investigating a video that appears to show Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi delivering a sermon in Mosul, with both Iraqi and U.S. authorities analyzing it to confirm its authenticity. If verified, it would be one of the first known videos of the elusive militant, who has rarely been seen publicly. The release follows unconfirmed reports that he was killed or wounded in airstrikes, and it coincides with the group’s declaration of an Islamic caliphate, in which he was named Caliph Ibrahim. The video’s authenticity has not been independently confirmed.

Cell phones can be a lifeline during disasters, as seen when wireless networks largely survived Hurricane Irene, but sudden emergencies like tornadoes may temporarily disrupt service. To stay prepared, people should keep phones charged with backup or hand-crank chargers, maintain updated contacts, and know how to use text messaging and social media when voice calls fail. Low-tech backups like printed contact lists and simple prepaid phones are also valuable, as are cloud-based tools for sharing emergency documents. Ultimately, the key is planning ahead so you can communicate and access information during the critical period after a crisis strikes.

A new survey of British travelers reveals that many airline loyalty members never redeem their miles, often due to restrictions like blackout dates and high earning requirements, making the programs a source of frustration rather than reward. Reward seat availability also varies sharply by carrier, with some airlines offering seats consistently while others rarely do, partly because selling miles to partners is highly profitable. However, some programs, such as Air France-KLM’s, provide better value through promotions and partner redemptions. Ultimately, measuring whether these schemes truly build loyalty is difficult, yet airlines continue to rely on them as a competitive necessity.

Luxury pet hotels are surging in popularity as owners increasingly treat their animals like family and spend heavily on premium care. These resort-style facilities offer high-end suites, pools, gyms, spa treatments, webcams, and even chauffeur services, with prices ranging from about $38 to $200 per night. The boarding and grooming industry has nearly doubled in the past decade, and demand for upscale pet services remains strong despite economic downturns. Experts expect this trend to keep growing as pet ownership rises and owners devote more disposable income to pampering their pets.

The article highlights the growing prominence of drones in modern militaries, illustrated by the presence of former Israeli drone pilot Lior Peleg at the Singapore Airshow, who now trains new UAV operators. It notes that drones have expanded from a small fraction to nearly a third of U.S. military aircraft, with predictions of further growth, as they are cheaper and ideal for dull, dirty, or dangerous missions. The piece also explores the shifting role of humans in combat, with some experts arguing that remote operation can improve decision-making, while others stress the continued need for critical thinking. Ultimately, drones are becoming part of an interconnected network of systems, reshaping military operations and the profile of the modern pilot.

With Halloween falling on a Monday, the article suggests using the weekend to decorate the home with creative, do-it-yourself projects rather than standard store-bought items. Ideas include spray-painting oddly shaped pumpkins to look like candy corn, wrapping foam wreaths in autumn-colored yarn, and making garlands from doilies or coffee filters for a vintage, slightly eerie feel. It also offers matching costume concepts for moms and babies, such as a chef with a lobster-in-a-pot baby, along with other budget-friendly decorating tips like creepy terrariums and personalized dinnerware. Overall, the piece emphasizes that simple handmade touches can make Halloween decor sophisticated, whimsical, and fun for families.

Disgraced cyclist Lance Armstrong admitted in a televised confession to using performance-enhancing drugs throughout his career, saying he felt ashamed and accepted blame for his actions. He expressed a desire to compete again, arguing he deserved that chance, while also suggesting his lifetime ban was harsher than penalties given to other dopers. Armstrong spoke of the personal toll, including stepping down from his cancer charity and telling his children to stop defending him. Critics, however, viewed the confession as incomplete, urging him to testify under oath and name others involved in the doping network.

Donald Sterling has agreed to sell the Los Angeles Clippers to former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer for a record $2 billion, according to his attorneys, signaling a resolution to the ownership dispute. The sale still requires NBA approval, though Ballmer has said he would keep the team in Los Angeles. Sterling had previously fought the deal and sued the league, but that lawsuit is expected to be withdrawn. The agreement comes after Sterling was banned and fined for racist remarks that sparked widespread outrage.

The Los Angeles Clippers owner, Donald Sterling, is under renewed scrutiny after audio recordings surfaced in which he allegedly made racist remarks. This controversy is not new, as Sterling has previously faced multiple legal accusations of discrimination, including a wrongful termination lawsuit from former Clippers executive Elgin Baylor, who claimed Sterling ran the team with a “plantation” mentality. He also settled a federal housing discrimination case over refusing to rent apartments to Black and Hispanic tenants, and faced a separate tenant lawsuit alleging discriminatory practices. Despite these past allegations, Sterling has denied wrongdoing, and Clippers officials have said the recording does not reflect his true beliefs.

A California probate judge has cleared the way for Shelly Sterling to sell the Los Angeles Clippers to Steve Ballmer for a record $2 billion, ruling that she properly removed her husband Donald from the family trust. Donald Sterling’s lawyers said he plans to appeal, but legal experts doubt the appeal will succeed. The NBA welcomed the decision, while Shelly expressed relief and hope the sale closes soon. Donald still faces separate lawsuits over the league’s actions and his removal, stemming from the racist remarks that led to his lifetime ban.

Donald Sterling has filed a $1 billion federal lawsuit against the NBA, challenging the league's decision to ban him for life and force the sale of the Los Angeles Clippers following his racist remarks. The lawsuit argues the NBA's actions are unconstitutional and breach contract, while also questioning the validity of the recording that triggered the scandal. This legal move comes as the NBA and Sterling's estranged wife, Shelly, had already agreed to sell the team to Steve Ballmer for $2 billion, a deal now threatened by the litigation. Additionally, reports that Sterling is mentally incapacitated have surfaced, though his lawyer denies this, further complicating the question of who controls the franchise.

Donald Sterling has issued a public apology for his racist remarks but claims he was provoked and manipulated into making them, saying he does not consider himself a racist. The NBA has banned him for life and fined him, and team owners are moving toward forcing a sale of the Clippers. Sterling insists he made a serious mistake and hopes to be forgiven, while also suggesting his comments stemmed from jealousy over a female friend. Meanwhile, his estranged wife, Shelly, says she will fight to keep her 50 percent ownership stake in the team.

Francesca Ramsey, a black YouTuber, found that a single video about race brought her massive popularity but also typecast her and attracted racial hostility. Minority creators on YouTube often face vicious, race-targeted comments far more than other users, reflecting broader societal racism rather than a unique platform problem. YouTube offers moderation tools, but many creators choose to ignore or block haters instead of engaging. Both Ramsey and fellow creator Andre Meadows emphasize building loyal fan communities that help police comments and drown out the negativity.

In his U.N. address, Netanyahu urged world leaders to apply the same urgency they show against ISIS to confronting Iran and Hamas, arguing that Iran must not be allowed to develop nuclear weapons. He described militant Islamist groups as interconnected threats, comparing them to a spreading cancer and to the Nazis in their ambition for world domination. Netanyahu also insisted that ISIS and Hamas share the same extremist ideology, a point he said many coalition members overlook. In response, PLO official Hanan Ashrawi accused him of distorting facts and unfairly blaming victims.

Sunscreen remains a vital defense against rising skin cancer rates, and dermatologists recommend choosing a broad-spectrum formula with at least SPF 30, ideally higher for those at greater risk. Most people apply far too little, so experts advise using two coats and paying special attention to easily missed areas like the nose, ears, and scalp. Antioxidant-infused sunscreens can offer extra protection, but sunscreen alone isn't enough—seeking shade, wearing protective clothing, and avoiding peak sun hours are equally important. It’s never too late to adopt these habits, as consistent protection now can significantly reduce future skin damage.

A Thai airline’s provocative Facebook campaign featuring bikini-clad women sparked both praise and criticism, highlighting how Asian carriers often use youthful, attractive cabin crews as part of their branding. Unlike Western airlines, which face stricter anti-discrimination laws and emphasize service attitude over looks, many Asian airlines operate in legal environments that allow appearance and age requirements. While experts doubt that beauty directly boosts profits, the attention raised brand awareness and shifted passenger demographics for Nok Air. Ultimately, the article suggests that Asian carriers’ superior service standards, not just their glamorous image, are what truly set them apart.

Douglas McAuthin McCain, a 33-year-old American from a Minneapolis suburb, was killed while fighting alongside ISIS in Syria, a transformation that shocked his family and friends. Those who knew him described him as a kind, quiet basketball lover who had converted to Islam years earlier and was searching for purpose. Although his past included only minor legal issues, U.S. officials had been monitoring him due to his associations with suspected extremists, and he had traveled through California, Sweden, and Turkey before reaching Syria. His relatives insisted he was not a terrorist, but his social media activity suggested growing sympathy for the militant group.

The article explains that U.S. presidential debates are rare, televised events held every four years, beginning with the 1960 Nixon-Kennedy matchup. It notes that while debates rarely decide elections, memorable moments—such as Reagan's witty retorts, Gore's visible sighs, or Perry's "oops"—can shape public perception. The piece also outlines the typical format of three debates plus a vice-presidential face-off, and assesses Obama and Romney as capable but flawed debaters. Ultimately, it suggests debates matter more for their theatrical moments and potential gaffes than for changing many voters' minds.

Despite soaring tuition and student debt, most families still view college as the essential route to career success and social status. However, recent data shows that a degree no longer guarantees strong earnings or employment, with many graduates facing unemployment or underemployment while skilled manufacturing jobs go unfilled. This disconnect suggests that traditional higher education may be out of step with labor market needs. Yet the rise of free, high-quality online education from initiatives like Coursera and ED-X could soon transform the system, making college more accessible and affordable while challenging the conventional four-year university model.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is launching a new pilot study to reassess cancer risks near nuclear facilities, updating a decades-old analysis that found no elevated risk. The National Academy of Sciences will examine six nuclear power plants and one fuel facility in a $2 million, two-to-three-year project, with possible expansion to all U.S. reactors. Although the NRC does not expect to find increased cancer rates from radiation releases, it sees the study as a way to address ongoing public health concerns. The nuclear industry has opposed the effort, arguing that other cancer causes could overshadow any potential impact and that the study is unlikely to yield definitive scientific conclusions.

A TransAsia Airways ATR 72 crashed while attempting to land on Taiwan’s Penghu Islands amid stormy weather, leaving as many as 47 people feared dead. The aircraft, carrying 58 passengers and crew, went down near Magong Airport and struck a residential area, setting homes on fire. Dozens were reported missing and at least a dozen were hospitalized, with officials noting the casualty figures were still changing. The cause was under investigation, though strong winds from Typhoon Matmo were suspected as a contributing factor.

Dozens of concertgoers, mostly teenagers, were hospitalized after Avicii’s Boston show, with officials citing dehydration, drugs, and alcohol as contributing factors. The venue was reportedly hot, and worried parents gathered outside as ambulances transported patients. This follows a similar incident at the Electric Daisy Carnival in Las Vegas, where Avicii also performed, and which saw hundreds treated and one death. The events highlight growing concerns about safety at large electronic dance music concerts.

The article explores the debate over whether parents should allow their children to taste alcohol at home before the legal drinking age. While some research suggests supervised drinking may reduce binge drinking, other studies indicate that parental offers of alcohol can increase the likelihood of early or heavy drinking. Experts are divided, with some advocating for teaching responsible drinking at home and others stressing that underage drinking should be discouraged until the brain is fully developed. Ultimately, the piece emphasizes the importance of open communication and responsible parental modeling over a one-size-fits-all approach.

A Spanish train driver was speaking on the phone with railway staff just before the derailment that killed 79 people, according to court officials. The train was traveling at nearly twice the speed limit for the curve, and the driver has been charged with multiple counts of reckless homicide and injury. He was released under conditions, including suspension of his train license and weekly court appearances. Experts suggest the phone conversation may have distracted him from taking manual control of the train, and victims were honored at a memorial service.

A 13-year-old student in Florida was brutally attacked by three older youths on a school bus, and while the driver called dispatchers for help, he did not physically intervene, citing school policy and safety concerns. The driver, who retired shortly after the incident, said stepping in could have endangered himself and other students. Although police criticized his failure to act, prosecutors determined no charges were warranted because he followed district policy, which only required him to contact dispatch. The victim suffered a broken arm and black eyes, and the attack reportedly stemmed from the boy reporting one of the assailants for trying to sell him drugs.

The article argues that U.S. drone strikes are counterproductive, fueling widespread anger and resentment rather than enhancing security. It highlights UN findings of civilian deaths, including an imam who opposed al Qaeda, and stresses the complete lack of transparency and accountability in the covert campaign. The piece also notes that Yemeni authorities have voted against the strikes, yet the U.S. and UK continue them with impunity. Ultimately, it warns that this secretive policy alienates local populations and undermines the very people and democratic values the West claims to support.

Yemen’s parliament has voted, in a largely symbolic move, to demand an end to U.S. drone strikes after a mistaken attack on a wedding convoy killed at least 14 people. The vote reflects growing public anger, though Yemen’s government is unlikely to change its stance since it relies on drones for operations in remote areas where its own forces cannot reach. Critics point out that such strikes have killed many civilians and may actually strengthen al Qaeda by fueling resentment among local tribes.

California’s severe drought has renewed attention on water scarcity and is pushing farmers, startups, and researchers to develop new conservation technologies. Although Silicon Valley investors are hesitant to fund long-term water projects, innovation hubs in places like Milwaukee and other global centers are advancing solutions such as data-driven agricultural monitoring, sonar-based well tracking, and simple devices like plastic trays that cut tree water use. Agriculture, which consumes most of the water supply, is a key focus, with companies using aerial imaging and big data to help farms irrigate more efficiently. The crisis is also raising public awareness that water availability, not just cost, is the real issue, and it is forcing the industry to innovate.

Senators pressed Dr. Mehmet Oz about promoting weight-loss supplements on his show despite weak scientific support, specifically calling out green coffee beans and Garcinia cambogia. Lawmakers, led by Sen. Claire McCaskill, argued his endorsements gave false hope and helped fuel deceptive marketing. Oz defended his approach as being a cheerleader for viewers but acknowledged using exaggerated language and said he would be more cautious and publish a list of products he believes in. The article also notes that weight-loss supplements are not FDA-approved and that regulators warn consumers to be skeptical of products promising easy weight loss without diet or exercise.

At the Dubai Airshow, the three major Gulf carriers—Emirates, Etihad, and Qatar—placed massive aircraft orders, including a landmark deal for Boeing 777X jets and Airbus A380 superjumbos, cementing their status as dominant global airlines. While these purchases signal the Gulf carriers' growing power and strategic advantage, they also raise industry-wide fears about overcapacity, as older planes will likely be passed on to smaller airlines that may cut fares to fill seats. Historically, such capacity gluts have worsened industry downturns, leaving weaker carriers vulnerable. The Gulf Three, however, are well-positioned with new hubs, global route networks, and independent growth plans, making them the clear winners while others worry about the future.

Durham has reached a settlement with three former Duke University lacrosse players who were falsely accused of sexual assault in 2006. As part of the agreement, the city will contribute $50,000 to the North Carolina Innocence Inquiry Commission. Durham maintains that its police acted properly and points to former District Attorney Mike Nifong, who was disbarred and jailed for misconduct, as the responsible party. The players were fully exonerated in 2007, but not before the team’s season was canceled and the coach lost his job.

Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands has announced she will abdicate on April 30, exactly 33 years after her coronation, passing the throne to her eldest son, Prince Willem-Alexander. In a televised address, she expressed deep gratitude for the public’s support and confidence in her successor and his wife, Princess Máxima. The Dutch prime minister praised her reign, noting her personal warmth and dedication. Beatrix, who turns 75 this week, will step down while remaining active in public life.

A Dutch court has ruled that the Netherlands is legally responsible for the deaths of more than 300 Bosnian Muslim men who were forced out of a UN-protected Dutch compound in Srebrenica in July 1995 and later killed by Bosnian Serb forces. The court found that Dutch peacekeepers acted unlawfully by cooperating in the men’s removal, given that they knew the men were at risk of genocide and could have saved them by allowing them to stay. The state must compensate the families of the victims, though the court cleared it of liability for thousands of other men who fled and were killed, as well as for broader failures before the enclave fell. The ruling builds on a previous Supreme Court decision and comes as war crimes trials of Bosnian Serb leaders continue.

Volcanoes are both breathtaking and hazardous, offering travelers a chance to witness Earth’s raw power while learning about its geological history. Volcanologist Rebecca Williams highlights several top destinations, including Ecuador’s Tungurahua, Italy’s Mount Etna and Pantelleria, Hawaii’s Kilauea, Iceland’s Eldfell, and Antarctica’s Mount Erebus. She emphasizes that while these active sites can be spectacular, visitors should always respect local safety warnings and check current conditions before exploring. From glowing lava lakes to historic eruptions that shaped landscapes, each volcano provides a unique glimpse into nature’s destructive and creative forces.

A new study shows that the Early Start Denver Model, a play-based behavioral therapy for toddlers with autism, can normalize brain activity and improve social functioning, not just ease symptoms. In the trial, children who received ESDM showed brain responses to faces similar to typically developing peers, unlike those given standard community interventions. Researchers say this demonstrates that early therapy can alter brain development and behavior, reinforcing the importance of early screening and diagnosis. The findings also suggest brain-wave measurements might eventually help detect autism risk before behavioral signs appear.

A series of small earthquakes near California’s Mammoth Mountain has prompted the U.S. Geological Survey to label the activity “volcanic unrest.” Although dozens of quakes up to magnitude 3.8 occurred in just two days, experts say such swarms are typical for the region, though this one is larger than recent events. Seismologists believe rising fluids from deep in the crust are triggering the quakes, and they continue to monitor the area with tools like a newly installed gas station. The volcano remains at normal/green alert levels, and its last eruption was roughly 57,000 years ago.

Earthships are self-sufficient, off-grid homes designed by Michael Reynolds, built from natural and recycled materials like tires, bottles, and cans. They generate their own power, manage water and sewage on-site, and use natural ventilation for heating and cooling. Originally constructed in New Mexico, these homes have spread worldwide and are also used in urban settings. Reynolds now aims to build entire Earthship cities that are more affordable and sustainable than conventional infrastructure.

A large observational study found that people who regularly ate nuts had a lower risk of dying from major diseases, including heart disease, cancer, and respiratory conditions. Those who consumed nuts at least seven times per week had about a 20 percent lower death rate over the study period compared to non-consumers. Nut eaters also tended to be leaner, more active, and less likely to smoke, though the researchers stressed the findings show a correlation rather than a proven cause-and-effect link. The study was partly funded by a nut industry foundation, but that group had no role in the research or conclusions.

The World Health Organization has announced a coordinated response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, including establishing a sub-regional control center in Guinea and improving surveillance, community engagement, and cross-border communication. The outbreak has caused hundreds of cases and deaths across Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia, with spread driven by traditional practices, such as home care and funeral customs, as well as extensive travel. Uganda has introduced screening measures for travelers from affected countries, while experts stress that the disease is not easily transmitted and can be contained with basic hygiene and avoiding contact with infected bodily fluids. However, weak health systems, fear, and distrust remain major obstacles to controlling the epidemic.

Contact tracing in the Ebola outbreak is severely hampered because many patients hide their contacts or are not fully honest, with CDC estimates suggesting that 40 to 60 percent of contacts may go unidentified. Fear plays a major role, as rumors spread that being listed leads to death, and some families conceal sick relatives at home. This gap is dangerous because a single missed contact can reignite transmission, and health workers often lack the resources to follow up even with known contacts. As a result, response efforts are struggling to contain chains of infection, especially in communities where trust in health systems is weak.

Armed attackers, motivated by fear of Ebola, raided a health facility in Monrovia, causing infected patients to flee, though some later returned and no injuries were reported. The attack highlights widespread panic surrounding the outbreak, which has killed hundreds across West Africa. In response, Liberia has received doses of the experimental drug ZMapp to treat infected doctors, while also closing borders and running public education campaigns. Neighboring Cameroon has similarly suspended flights to and from Nigeria as part of broader containment efforts.

President Obama said the U.S. must treat Ebola as a national security priority and indicated he would likely deploy military resources to West Africa to set up isolation units and protect health workers. He warned that failing to act could allow the virus to mutate and become a greater threat to the U.S., and he urged international mobilization. The comments followed criticism from Doctors Without Borders and an appeal from an American Ebola survivor for global help. The outbreak is concentrated in several West African countries, with a roughly 50% fatality rate.

The Ebola outbreak has killed 142 people across Guinea and Liberia, according to the World Health Organization, with the virus remaining confined to those two countries. Suspected cases in Sierra Leone have all tested negative. This marks the first time Ebola has appeared in West Africa, and the spread has been described as unprecedented by aid groups. The virus, named after a river in the Democratic Republic of Congo, is among the deadliest known, with a high fatality rate.

The current Ebola outbreak in West Africa is the largest ever recorded, with high mortality and no approved treatments or vaccines despite decades since the disease emerged. The virus spread across borders and into cities, making containment far harder than in past rural outbreaks. While experimental vaccines exist, testing them during an active epidemic raises serious ethical and practical concerns, and the WHO has rejected such trials in affected communities. Some experts argue for targeted use in healthcare workers, who face the highest risk, and for stockpiling proven vaccines to better prepare for future outbreaks.

President Obama’s U.S.-Africa summit is overshadowed by the deadly Ebola outbreak in West Africa, which forced the leaders of Liberia and Sierra Leone to cancel their attendance. International organizations have pledged hundreds of millions of dollars to contain the epidemic, but the virus continues to threaten vulnerable economies through reduced trade, travel restrictions, and disruptions to mining and agriculture. While research on Ebola treatments and vaccines has received some funding—partly due to bioterrorism concerns—experts note that the lack of a strong commercial incentive and weak local infrastructure hinder progress. The outbreak’s broader economic damage is expected to deepen as companies pull back and flights are suspended.

Two American Ebola patients who received the experimental drug ZMapp have recovered and been released from an Atlanta hospital, raising hopes amid the largest Ebola outbreak on record. However, ZMapp is not an approved treatment, and no proven cure or vaccine exists yet. The drug, developed by Mapp Biopharmaceutical, uses lab-engineered antibodies and had only been tested in monkeys before being given to humans. As the outbreak has killed more than half of those infected, global health officials are debating the ethics of using unapproved treatments and racing to develop vaccines and therapies.

The Ebola outbreak in West Africa continues to worsen, with hundreds of cases and deaths reported across Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia. The World Health Organization has called for urgent action and is deploying expert teams, while aid groups warn that the epidemic is out of control and spreading to cities, partly due to travel and weak health systems. Although there is no cure or vaccine, early treatment has helped lower the death rate from the usual 90 percent to about 60 percent. The outbreak will be considered contained only after 42 days pass with no new infections.

A Liberian man being treated for Ebola in Lagos, Nigeria, has died, intensifying concerns that the outbreak could reach Africa’s most populous country. The regional epidemic has already caused hundreds of deaths across Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia, according to health officials. In a related development, a prominent Sierra Leonean doctor involved in fighting the outbreak has also contracted the virus. The disease spreads through contact with bodily fluids, putting healthcare workers at heightened risk, though early treatment has lowered the current death rate to about 60 percent.

A new Pew report finds that while most U.S. public libraries now lend e-books and borrowing has grown sharply, many library card holders are unaware this service exists. E-book borrowers generally report satisfaction, though some face waitlists or device compatibility issues. Budget pressures are pushing libraries to prioritize e-book purchases, even as publisher pricing and lending restrictions create challenges. Libraries are also exploring services like lending pre-loaded e-readers and offering classes, especially to reach underserved groups.

Pew research shows that e-books are encouraging more reading among American adults, with e-book users reading significantly more books than those who stick to print. These digital readers also tend to purchase books rather than borrow them, and many report spending more time reading since adopting the format. Although print remains the most common choice overall—especially for children’s books and lending—e-readers and tablets have become widespread. The technology also offers important accessibility benefits for people with visual or literacy challenges, and as device costs drop, e-books may help bridge the digital divide.

A multi-state E. coli outbreak linked to raw clover sprouts has sickened 17 people across five states, with Washington state reporting the most cases. Health officials believe the source is Evergreen Fresh Sprouts, LLC of Idaho, though the company has not issued a recall and its owner says FDA tests came back negative. Nearly half of those infected were hospitalized, though no deaths have occurred. The CDC and state health agencies are urging consumers to avoid raw clover sprouts from the company, highlighting that sprouts are prone to bacterial contamination due to their growing conditions.

Rachel Hope endured severe PTSD stemming from childhood sexual abuse and a near-fatal accident, leaving her with debilitating flashbacks and depression that standard therapy failed to resolve. Seeking relief, she contacted psychiatrist Dr. Michael Mithoefer, who was running a carefully approved clinical trial testing whether MDMA, or Ecstasy, could be used safely in a therapeutic setting. The article also traces MDMA’s history, from its early use by therapists to enhance emotional processing, to its emergence as a party drug and subsequent federal ban. Hope’s story highlights the promise of re-examining banned substances through rigorous medical research as a potential path to healing trauma.

Ecuador has defiantly rejected U.S. pressure over Edward Snowden’s asylum request by renouncing preferential trade benefits under the Andean Trade Promotion and Drug Eradication Act. President Rafael Correa framed the move as a stand against U.S. arrogance and defended Ecuador’s right to consider the asylum petition. However, critics and business leaders warn the decision could damage bilateral relations and deter investment, especially since the trade deal was already expected to expire. Ecuador has offered to compensate the United States with $23 million annually, while insisting its decision on Snowden will be made independently.

Ecuador has revived its nearly defunct national railway with a major investment, and the centerpiece is Tren Crucero, a luxury tourist train running between Guayaquil and Quito. The four-day journey uses restored steam locomotives and new carriages to traverse the Andes, passing dramatic sites like the Devil's Nose switchbacks and the Avenue of the Volcanoes. The government hopes the service will bring economic benefits to communities along the route, which have struggled since the railway’s decline. With hotels and excursions included, the trip is aimed at affluent tourists and offers a rare way to experience the country’s highland landscapes and culture.

Edward Snowden’s father publicly defended his son, insisting that Edward acted out of love for his country and a desire to inform Americans about government surveillance. He argued that critics are wrongly focusing on his son as the “sinner” instead of the wrongdoing revealed by the leaked documents. He urged his son to remain in Russia until a fair trial could be guaranteed, despite U.S. assurances that the death penalty would not be sought. The father also called on President Obama to drop the charges, emphasizing that national character is defined by ethical conduct, not just legality.

Egypt has filed charges against seven Coptic Christians in the U.S. and a Florida pastor for allegedly promoting an anti-Islam video that mocked the Prophet Mohammed, with accusations including insulting Islam and inciting sectarian strife. The charges are largely symbolic since the accused are outside Egypt, but the film has fueled violent protests across the Muslim world, including the Benghazi attack that killed the U.S. ambassador. In response, al Qaeda's North African affiliate urged attacks on American representatives, while U.S. and Libyan officials investigated the Benghazi assault. The unrest also triggered protests in several countries and prompted heightened security at U.S. diplomatic missions.

An Egyptian court has sentenced the Muslim Brotherhood's leader and hundreds of his supporters to death over violent riots that followed the ouster of President Mohamed Morsy, with 37 death sentences now final. The mass verdicts, part of a broader crackdown on the Islamist movement ahead of next month's elections, have drawn sharp domestic and international condemnation, including from the U.N. and Western officials who questioned their fairness. The Brotherhood rejected the rulings as politically motivated revenge by the military-installed government, which has also banned secular opposition groups. The sentencing underscores Egypt's deep instability since Morsy's removal, with authorities intensifying repression against both Islamists and secular activists.

Egypt’s military chief signaled he would run for president if the public requested it, as the country prepared for a constitutional referendum that would strengthen military authority. The vote comes amid deep divisions following the ouster of President Mohamed Morsy, whose supporters accuse the military of reviving authoritarian rule. Morsy remains in detention and faces trial, while the government has designated the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist group and cracked down on its protests. The situation reflects Egypt’s ongoing political instability and the military’s central role in shaping its future.

An Egyptian court has sentenced seven Coptic Christians living abroad to death in absentia for their alleged involvement in producing an anti-Islam film that sparked widespread outrage. The movie, which insulted the Prophet Muhammad, triggered violent protests across several Muslim countries, including an attack in Libya that killed the U.S. ambassador. The filmmaker, an Egyptian-American, was separately sentenced in California to a year in prison for violating probation in an unrelated fraud case. The death sentences would only be enforced if the defendants return to Egypt.

Egypt’s intelligence chief is leading urgent mediation efforts between Israel and Hamas to end the five-day conflict and avert an Israeli ground offensive in Gaza. Hamas has signaled willingness to halt rocket fire in exchange for an end to Israeli strikes and the lifting of the blockade, while Israel has massed troops near the border and authorized reservists, warning it may launch ground operations. The fighting continues with heavy Israeli airstrikes and ongoing rocket attacks, including toward Tel Aviv, as international leaders urge restraint. Casualties have mounted, with dozens of Palestinians and several Israelis killed since the operation began.

Egyptian security forces clashed with Muslim Brotherhood supporters in several cities on Friday during protests against the government and the upcoming constitutional referendum, which would prohibit religious political parties. The demonstrators, who are demanding the reinstatement of ousted President Mohamed Morsy, also called for a boycott of the vote, while authorities used tear gas to disperse marches in Giza and Suez. The unrest comes amid a broader government crackdown on the Brotherhood, which was declared a terrorist organization, and as Morsy faces trial on charges related to inciting violence. The military-backed government defends its actions by blaming the group for attacks on churches and state facilities, while Morsy’s supporters accuse the authorities of returning to authoritarian rule.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi is working to restore Egypt’s regional influence and crush Islamist militancy, continuing a long-standing military establishment pattern of opposing groups like the Muslim Brotherhood. His government has taken a central role in Gaza cease-fire efforts, not as a neutral broker but as a partner aligned with Israel against Hamas and other militant factions. Egypt’s geographic border with Gaza and its security concerns in Sinai and along the Libyan frontier further drive its involvement. At the same time, Sisi is using this position to secure international financial backing and economic relief for Egypt’s struggling economy.

The initial market optimism following Egypt's military takeover has quickly dissipated as the transition mirrors the disorder of the first uprising, with violent clashes between security forces and Morsy supporters further destabilizing the situation. The economy is under severe strain, with foreign reserves down to a three-month import buffer, while unemployment and the budget deficit both hover around 13% and growth remains nearly stagnant. International financial relief has proven difficult to secure, as IMF loan negotiations remain deadlocked and Gulf aid is contingent on shifting political alliances. The political process is also unraveling, as the Salafist Al Nour party's withdrawal from talks threatens the military's proposed six-to-nine-month transition timeline.

Egypt’s newly elected president, Mohamed Morsi, plans to appoint a woman and a Christian as vice presidents, a historic first for Egypt. His adviser also stressed that Egypt will not become an Islamic Republic and that minority rights will be protected. Meanwhile, Morsi’s election rival Ahmed Shafik left Egypt for the UAE, with his lawyer saying no legal cases are pending against him. In a separate development, an Egyptian court struck down a rule allowing the military to arrest civilians without warrants and scheduled hearings on other contested military council decisions.

Egypt’s presidential election is scheduled for May 26–27, with army chief Abdel Fattah el-Sisi running after resigning from the military. He led the ouster of elected Islamist President Mohamed Morsy last year, a move that made him popular among many Egyptians seeking stability but deeply unpopular with Islamists who view it as a coup. The country remains torn and violent, as shown by a recent attack in Sinai that killed a soldier and wounded three policemen.

The trial of three jailed Al Jazeera journalists in Egypt has been postponed until May 22, with their bail requests denied. They face terrorism-related charges linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, which they deny, saying they were only doing their jobs. The proceedings were marked by disputes over excessive fees for evidence, allegations of prisoner mistreatment, and the sudden resignation of two defense lawyers who accused Al Jazeera of exploiting the case. Human rights groups have condemned the trial as part of a broader crackdown on press freedom in Egypt.

Eileen Brennan, the Oscar-nominated actress best known for her role as the tough drill sergeant in “Private Benjamin,” has died at age 80 after battling bladder cancer. Over her career, she played memorable character parts in films such as “The Last Picture Show,” “The Sting,” and “Clue,” and earned multiple Emmy nominations for TV work including “Will & Grace.” She also faced serious personal challenges, recovering from a severe car accident and addiction, and surviving breast cancer. She is remembered by her family as funny, caring, and truly one of a kind.

Formula E, a new electric-car racing series set to debut in 2014, aims to challenge Formula 1 while promoting clean urban mobility. The races will be held in city centers worldwide to highlight the practicality of electric vehicles and help reduce air pollution. Organizers are in talks with global cities, with Rio de Janeiro already confirmed, and plan to feature 10 teams and 20 drivers in the inaugural season. The series, backed by motorsport’s governing body, is intended to boost public interest in sustainable transport and inspire younger generations.

German company e-volo has successfully completed the first manned test flight of its unconventional electric Multicopter, a 16-rotor aircraft powered by lithium batteries. The brief 90-second flight served as a proof of concept, with the pilot controlling the craft using a joystick. Despite its awkward appearance, the vehicle is reportedly easy to handle and can carry about 80 kilograms. The developers envision future uses such as air taxis, search-and-rescue operations, and eventually widespread personal transport.

A Maine veterinarian who devoted his life to caring for elephants died after one of the animals apparently crushed him in an accident at his sanctuary. The 56-year-old founder of Hope Elephants was found dead in the corral, with officials attributing the death to chest compression injuries and ruling out aggressive behavior by the elephant. He had established the nonprofit to rehabilitate two retired circus elephants, both weighing around 8,000 pounds, using therapies like ultrasound and hydrotherapy. His organization mourned his loss, describing his passion for animals, especially elephants, as boundless.

Eliot Spitzer, who stepped down as New York governor amid a prostitution scandal, is seeking a political comeback as New York City comptroller. He acknowledged his past mistakes but hopes voters will give him a second chance, citing years of productive work since his resignation. Spitzer believes his experience as state attorney general makes him well-suited to expand the comptroller's role. He also noted that his wife supports his return to politics, though she may not join him on the campaign trail.

Eli Wallach, the prolific character actor known for roles in classics like “The Magnificent Seven” and “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly,” has died at age 98. Over a career spanning more than six decades, he appeared in over 150 film and television productions, often playing villains or rough-edged figures. Despite his Hollywood fame, Wallach preferred live theater and originated roles in major stage works, earning a Tony Award. He is survived by his wife of 66 years, their three children, and grandchildren.

Elliot Rodger’s lengthy manifesto centered on his rage over lifelong virginity, which he blamed on women, and his bitter envy of wealthy, sexually successful men. The document detailed his belief that winning the lottery was his only escape, and after that failed, he turned to planning violence.
