He described buying multiple guns, practicing at a shooting range, and preparing an attack he called the “Day of Retribution.” His plan began with killing his roommates, whom he resented, before targeting others he believed had enjoyed the pleasures he was denied.

At 86, Elmore Leonard revisits his beloved character Raylan Givens in his latest novel, “Raylan,” which coincides with the third season of the hit TV adaptation “Justified.” Leonard praises the show’s portrayal of the laid-back U.S. Marshal, crediting actor Timothy Olyphant and the writers for capturing his style. He also reflects on his enduring creative drive, noting that writing remains his greatest joy and that he continues to draw inspiration from everyday life. Despite decades of success, Leonard shows no signs of slowing down, already working on a new book.

Elmore Leonard, the acclaimed crime and western novelist known for his sharp dialogue and offbeat characters, has died at age 87 following a stroke. Over a prolific career spanning more than four decades, he wrote dozens of books, many of which became major films such as “Get Shorty,” “Jackie Brown,” and “Out of Sight.” His distinctive minimalist style, shaped partly by crime writer George V. Higgins, made him a Hollywood favorite and earned him prestigious literary honors late in life. He was still working on his 46th novel at the time of his death.

Elon Musk has proposed a futuristic high-speed transit system called the Hyperloop, which would use vacuum tubes and magnetic levitation to move passengers between distant cities at extraordinary speeds. The concept revives an old idea, and a Colorado-based company called ET3 is already developing a similar evacuated-tube system, though its claims remain uncertain. Musk sees the Hyperloop as a better alternative to California’s costly and slow high-speed rail project, but he is unlikely to lead its development directly because of his commitments to Tesla and SpaceX. Instead, he plans to make the technology open-source and collaborate with partners who share his vision.

Elton John has weighed in on the church’s stance on same-sex marriage, saying he believes Jesus would have supported it because his message was one of love, compassion, and inclusion. He praised Pope Francis for focusing on humanity and acceptance, while criticizing church traditions like priestly celibacy and bans on gay clergy as outdated. John also urged the Church of England to embrace modern times and follow that more inclusive example. He added that his own wedding to David Furnish will be a small, low-key celebration taking advantage of new marriage laws.

Atlanta Hawks controlling owner Bruce Levenson is giving up his stake in the team after an offensive 2012 email resurfaced in which he made racially charged comments about the franchise’s struggles to attract white season-ticket holders. He suggested that the predominantly Black audience at games was scaring away white fans and proposed changes such as adding white cheerleaders and playing music familiar to white audiences. Levenson self-reported the email to the NBA, which investigated and deemed his remarks unacceptable, with Commissioner Adam Silver acknowledging his remorse. The league will oversee the sale process while Hawks CEO Steve Koonin manages day-to-day operations.

A no-bid $433 million HHS contract for a smallpox drug was awarded to Siga Technologies, a company with ties to Democratic Party figures, sparking internal government concerns over its high profit margin. Emails revealed that officials deemed the projected 180% return "outrageous" and pushed for a major discount, but the contracting officer was replaced after Siga requested more senior negotiators. The deal drew bipartisan scrutiny, with lawmakers questioning both the lack of competition and the drug's unproven effectiveness, while HHS defended the award as necessary and fairly priced.

At Davos 2014, business leaders are moving away from broad enthusiasm for emerging markets and adopting a more selective approach, recognizing that these economies now vary widely in governance and growth prospects. Some large nations like China, Nigeria, and the Philippines are advancing quickly, while slower reformers such as Brazil, Russia, and Turkey face stagnation and public unrest. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s reduction of bond purchases has also triggered capital outflows from developing economies, adding uncertainty. Still, investors see fresh potential in regions like Southeast Asia and especially Africa, where infrastructure and consumer demand are expected to drive future growth.

Emma Watson delivered a widely shared United Nations speech launching the HeForShe campaign, urging men to join the fight for gender equality and reclaiming the word "feminism" from stigma. Her celebrity platform helped draw rare mainstream attention to the cause, alongside other high-profile figures like Beyoncé. However, the article stresses that despite this visibility, concrete progress remains limited in areas such as media representation, film roles, and pay equity. Ultimately, the challenge is turning celebrity advocacy into real-world change that benefits women globally.

The 2014 Emmy nominations were led by “Game of Thrones” with 19 nods, while “Breaking Bad” received a final round of recognition. HBO’s “True Detective” earned a drama-series spot despite its anthology format, and Netflix solidified its awards presence with 31 nominations. Notable snubs included “Orphan Black” star Tatiana Maslany, though newcomers like “Fargo” and actors such as Matthew McConaughey and Chiwetel Ejiofor gained attention. In comedy, “Modern Family” faced fresh competition from “Orange Is the New Black” and “Silicon Valley,” with hopes high for Amy Poehler to finally win.

After 50 days of conflict, Israel and Hamas agreed to an Egyptian-brokered, open-ended ceasefire. The deal includes easing Israel’s blockade of Gaza to allow humanitarian aid and construction materials, with further indirect talks planned on issues like demilitarization, a seaport, and prisoner releases. However, the agreement largely mirrors the 2012 truce and leaves major demands unresolved, so neither side achieved a clear victory. The war exacted a heavy toll, with thousands of Palestinian and dozens of Israeli deaths, widespread displacement, and significant political damage for both Hamas and Israeli leadership.

The CDC has confirmed over 100 cases of Enterovirus D68 across at least 11 states, with Alabama and Indiana among the latest to report infections. Health officials believe the actual number is likely higher, since many similar respiratory viruses go untested. The virus is especially concerning for children with asthma, as it can worsen breathing difficulties. Several other states are also investigating possible clusters and have sent samples to the CDC for confirmation.

Mattel has launched Entrepreneur Barbie, a new version of the doll available in four ethnicities and equipped with a tablet, smartphone, and briefcase, aiming to encourage young girls to pursue business careers. The company partnered with eight real-life female entrepreneurs to promote the doll and reinforce the message that girls need visible role models. However, the release also drew criticism, with detractors arguing that Barbie’s unrealistic body proportions and pink, hyper-feminine styling undermine the empowering message. This backlash echoes previous controversies, such as Barbie’s appearance in the Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue, yet Mattel remains defiant in its marketing approach.

The EPA has introduced a new proposal to set the first national carbon pollution limits on newly built power plants, with separate standards for coal and natural gas facilities. Existing plants would not be affected yet, though separate regulations for them are expected soon. Supporters argue the rules encourage cleaner technology, while critics from the coal industry claim the limits are unachievable and would effectively block new coal plants. The proposal will undergo a 60-day public comment period and hearings.

The EPA has issued new federal rules requiring coal- and oil-fired power plants to limit emissions of mercury and other hazardous pollutants for the first time. Officials and environmental advocates hail the move as a major public health victory, estimating it will prevent thousands of premature deaths and deliver billions in health benefits. However, industry groups, some Republicans, and presidential candidates argue the regulations could hurt jobs, raise costs, and strain the electric grid. Power plants will have three years to comply, with possible extensions for installing pollution-control technology.

In a stunning primary upset, little-known economics professor Dave Brat defeated House Majority Leader Eric Cantor in Virginia’s 7th Congressional District, delivering a major victory for the tea party and shaking Republican leadership. Cantor’s loss—despite vastly outspending Brat—highlighted grassroots anger over issues like immigration and perceptions that he had lost touch with conservative voters. The result sends shockwaves through the GOP, disrupts leadership succession plans, and effectively ends any near-term prospects for House action on immigration reform. It also signals that voter discontent can outweigh campaign money and establishment support.

Shin Dong-hyuk, the only known person born inside a North Korean prison camp to escape and survive, is the subject of journalist Blaine Harden’s biography “Escape from Camp 14.” The book reveals the brutal conditions of North Korea’s hidden labor camps, where Shin endured starvation, torture, and was forced to betray his own mother after being conditioned to follow camp rules. He eventually escaped at age 23 and now lives in Seoul, working to raise global awareness about the camps. Harden’s account offers a rare, harrowing look into one of the world’s most secretive and repressive regimes.

Estonia has emerged as a European leader in digital innovation and economic stability, having built its IT sector from scratch after independence. Its low government debt and disciplined fiscal approach stand in contrast to other eurozone nations, and it now contributes to bailouts for wealthier countries that failed to follow fiscal rules. With projected growth outpacing major economies like Germany and France, Estonia's recovery from its post-Soviet struggles is evident. While the broader eurozone still faces a slow recovery, Estonia's success serves as proof that early reforms and adherence to rules yield faster growth.

Most children in the U.S. receive medications that have only been tested in adults, forcing doctors to guess at safe and effective pediatric doses. Pediatric clinical trials are scarce because drug companies see little profit in them, despite incentives like extended patents. The article raises concerns that industry-funded research tends to favor sponsors, making it an unreliable guide for children's health. It argues that nonprofit and public health organizations should take the lead in pediatric drug research instead of leaving it to commercial interests.

A student-led campaign at Ohio University aimed to spark conversation about racial stereotypes in Halloween costumes by featuring students holding images of offensive getups. Although it drew global attention and positive dialogue, it also became the target of Internet memes that mocked and trivialized the message, including a particularly racist image. The organizers received both support and hate mail, with critics accusing them of being oversensitive. They defended the campaign, arguing that stereotypes are harmful and that the backlash itself shows why such discussions remain necessary.

Etihad Airways has agreed to acquire a 49% stake in struggling Italian carrier Alitalia, making it the largest shareholder and marking one of the biggest foreign investments in a European airline. The deal involves an upfront payment of around $760 million, with additional funds pledged through 2018, and is expected to include significant job cuts while addressing Alitalia’s heavy debt burden. This move is part of Etihad’s broader strategy to expand its global network by investing in multiple airlines and cutting costs through shared services. The key challenge will be whether Etihad can successfully turn around Alitalia and other loss-making partners while boosting its own passenger base.

The article argues that while Cyprus’s financial crisis has sparked global alarm, the country’s economy was fundamentally sound until its banks made heavy, ill-advised investments in Greek debt. It criticizes the EU-led bailout plan for unfairly taxing ordinary depositors, including those with insured accounts, while shielding risk-taking bankers from the full consequences. The piece also highlights the political and economic tensions surrounding Cyprus, including Russian deposits and money-laundering accusations, which it suggests are being used to justify harsh terms. Ultimately, the author warns that such heavy-handed treatment of a small eurozone member could undermine faith in the European project.

France’s far-right National Front topped the vote in France for the first time in a nationwide election, part of a broader surge by Euroskeptic and far-right parties across Europe in the European Parliament elections. The results were described by French officials as a political earthquake, reflecting widespread voter discontent with mainstream parties and their handling of the economic crisis. Although centrist blocs are projected to keep a majority in the parliament, the gains give nationalist groups a stronger platform to influence debate and committee leadership. The outcome signals growing public demand for national control over policy and greater skepticism toward the European Union.

The European Union has announced a new military mission in the Central African Republic aimed at restoring security in and around the capital, Bangui, with plans to eventually hand over responsibility to UN or African forces. The operation is intended to protect vulnerable civilians and create conditions for delivering humanitarian aid. This comes amid ongoing violence and instability that began after rebels ousted President François Bozizé, leading to ethnic cleansing and attacks by Christian militias. Despite the presence of African Union and French troops, civilian casualties and atrocities have continued, prompting urgent international action.

The article draws a playful parallel between Euro 2012 and the eurozone crisis, noting that Germany’s disciplined, efficient play mirrors its austerity-driven leadership, while struggling bailout nations like Portugal, Ireland, and Greece have had shaky starts. It also highlights the cautious draw between Spain and Italy, two countries vulnerable to contagion, and the use of football as a lens for economic analysis, with banks predicting a German victory. The piece further suggests that football’s intense national pride underscores the limits of European integration, while the tournament may briefly distract markets from the continent’s financial troubles.

European authorities are increasingly concerned about the threat posed by returning jihadists who have fought with extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, warning that the risk of attacks in Europe is now higher than at any time since 9/11. Recent cases, such as the arrest of a Frenchman in Cannes with bomb-making materials and the fatal shooting at a Brussels Jewish museum, highlight the difficulty of tracking these individuals. Poor intelligence-sharing between European countries and the ease of travel within the bloc have allowed suspects to slip through the cracks, despite some being on watch-lists. With hundreds of EU citizens having joined the fighting and some already returning home, officials are calling for stronger cooperation and better tracking mechanisms to prevent small-scale but deadly attacks.

A year after the eurozone crisis dominated discussions at the Ambrosetti Forum, the mood has shifted to cautious optimism as economic growth returns. However, major challenges persist, particularly high unemployment, with leaders stressing the need for job creation and stronger ties between education and businesses to help young people. There is also a growing call for greater European cohesion and political unity to remain competitive globally. Despite the improved outlook, experts warn that political instability and complacency could still threaten the recovery.

The euro’s architects argue that Europe would have fared far worse without the single currency, despite the recent debt crisis, and they stress the need for stricter enforcement of fiscal rules among member states. As the Maastricht Treaty approaches its 20th anniversary, its defenders highlight the EU’s expansion into Eastern Europe and the economic benefits of open borders and a larger market. Critics, however, contend that the currency project was overly political and contributed to reckless lending and the debt crisis. While the eurozone has returned to growth, the future remains uncertain, with possible treaty changes and the U.K. seeking to renegotiate its membership.

Economists view the European Central Bank’s latest rate cut as a desperate measure that is unlikely to revive the eurozone’s struggling economy. While President Mario Draghi reaffirmed readiness to act, he stopped short of launching bold new stimulus programs, leading some analysts to question whether the ECB has exhausted its options. Political hurdles, such as German elections and legal concerns, along with fears that intervention reduces pressure for structural reforms, are seen as barriers to more aggressive action. Ultimately, experts argue that troubled countries must implement their own reforms rather than rely on the central bank to resolve the crisis.

The U.S. and European Union are set to launch negotiations on an ambitious free-trade agreement called the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership, with talks expected to begin by late June and conclude within roughly two years. The deal aims to eliminate remaining tariffs and harmonize regulations, potentially becoming the largest bilateral trade pact ever negotiated. Supporters argue it would boost economic growth and create jobs on both sides of the Atlantic without requiring public spending, while also addressing stalled global trade talks at the WTO. Estimates suggest the agreement could significantly increase GDP for both economies by removing trade barriers and aligning standards.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun evacuating over 10,000 residents from a danger zone around Mount Mayon after officials raised the alert level to critical, warning that a hazardous eruption could occur within weeks. The volcano has shown heightened unrest, including glowing lava, rockfalls from its summit dome, and low-level volcanic earthquakes. Mayon, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, has a history of deadly eruptions, including past events that caused significant casualties.

A United Airlines Boeing 737 heading from Chicago to Orange County was diverted to Wichita, Kansas, after an evacuation slide unexpectedly deployed in the rear cabin during the flight. The aircraft carried 96 passengers and five crew members, and no injuries were reported since everyone was seated at the time. Passengers described hearing a loud pop and noted that the crew remained calm and cabin pressure appeared normal. The incident echoes previous in-flight slide deployments on other airlines, including a JetBlue flight in November and a 2008 campaign plane carrying Barack Obama.

Andy Coulson, a former News of the World editor and ex-communications chief for David Cameron, told the Leveson Inquiry he was unaware of phone hacking during his editorship and denied any improper dealings with News Corp. He acknowledged that relations between politicians and the press were too close, but rejected claims of a political deal with Rupert Murdoch in exchange for newspaper support. Coulson also admitted holding £40,000 in News Corp. shares while working for Cameron, though he said he saw no conflict of interest. The inquiry continues, with former News International chief Rebekah Brooks due to testify next amid the wider hacking scandal.

A new report by international war crimes prosecutors and forensic experts claims to provide direct evidence that Syria’s government systematically tortured and killed detainees, based on thousands of photos smuggled out by a defector. The images reportedly show emaciated bodies and signs of strangulation and beatings, with a numbering system suggesting killings were ordered and tracked by state security services. The authors say the evidence could support charges of crimes against humanity, though they acknowledge the International Criminal Court would need a UN Security Council referral, which is unlikely due to Russia’s veto. The report’s release comes ahead of peace talks, and the team insists the defector was credible and the photos authentic.

A former Florida sheriff’s deputy who had been a fugitive for decades was arrested in Alaska after authorities say he used his deceased stepbrother’s identity to obtain a driver’s license and unemployment benefits. The man, wanted since the early 1990s on charges of raping a child, had been living under the assumed name in Eagle River. Federal officials learned of the identity theft through the Social Security Administration. He now faces federal identity theft charges and could be extradited to Florida, where he potentially faces the death penalty.

A former girlfriend of Christopher Dorner said she feared she could have been a target after learning he was the suspect in a deadly manhunt, which is why she chose to speak publicly. She described him as someone who internalized stress from his law enforcement career, though she stressed that his actions were unjustifiable. While shocked by the killings, she said she was not entirely surprised given his emotional struggles. She also recalled that he routinely kept firearms around her home, which she had attributed to his job as a police officer.

A former Los Angeles elementary school teacher has pleaded no contest to 23 felony counts involving lewd acts on children and received a 25-year prison sentence. The abuse, which took place between 2005 and 2010, involved 23 victims aged 7 to 10, and included disturbing incidents with photographs and food. The school district has already paid nearly $27.3 million to settle 58 related lawsuits, with additional cases still pending. Officials expressed relief that the legal proceedings are concluding and hope remaining families can find resolution and healing.

A pregnant economist and statistician used her research skills to test common pregnancy advice and found that many widely believed rules are not fully supported by evidence. Moderate caffeine intake appears safe, and the recommended age-based cutoff for prenatal testing is overly simplistic since the decision should reflect personal values about risk. She also found that sex does not effectively induce labor, while epidurals do slightly prolong the pushing stage by about 15 minutes. However, the warning against unpasteurized soft cheeses is justified due to the real risk of listeria.

A spinal cord stimulator implanted for paralysis unexpectedly restored sexual function in a paralyzed man, dramatically improving his quality of life. This benefit highlights a growing debate: many paralyzed individuals prioritize sexual function and bladder/bowel control over walking, and surveys confirm these "secondary conditions" are their top concerns. Researchers and advocates argue these issues are underfunded and deserve more research attention, since they greatly impact daily dignity and health. The man now hopes for a shift in research priorities, saying he would gladly trade walking for these restored functions.

The article discusses how psychiatry often struggles with complex cases, using filmmaker Jason Russell’s public naked breakdown as an example. It explains that his behavior was a classic sign of a manic episode, which is commonly linked to bipolar disorder but can also be triggered by stress, sleep loss, drugs, or medical conditions. The piece notes that mania is usually treatable, sometimes even with a single good night’s sleep. It concludes that Russell’s reported diagnosis of "brief reactive psychosis" is merely descriptive and offers little insight into the cause or long-term outlook.

Michael Jackson was likely suffering from severe sleep deprivation in the months before his death, according to a Harvard sleep expert testifying at the wrongful-death trial. The expert said the singer’s nightly use of the anesthetic propofol for 60 days eliminated REM sleep, producing symptoms such as paranoia, memory loss, and physical decline, and could have proven fatal even without the overdose. The testimony supports the Jackson family’s claim that AEG Live bore responsibility by hiring and pressuring Dr. Conrad Murray, while AEG argued it had no knowledge of the dangerous treatments. The case centers on whether the concert promoter’s actions contributed to Jackson’s death.

A blurry photo taken at a Southern California beach shows a dark shape swimming near children, sparking disagreement among shark experts. One expert identifies it as a juvenile great white shark based on the dorsal fin, while another argues it is a dolphin because the tail appears flat. The image was captured by a mother whose son noticed the figure after they left the beach. Regardless of what it was, experts note that young great white sharks are common in the area and pose little threat to swimmers.

Legal experts are split on whether Amanda Knox could be extradited to Italy after its top court overturned her acquittal in the murder of Meredith Kercher. Some argue that a U.S. extradition treaty bar against double jeopardy protects her since she was acquitted in the U.S. system, while others believe Italy may pursue retrial and that she could be convicted. A former prosecutor predicts Italian authorities won't seek extradition due to flaws in the original case, but a Harvard law professor disagrees, warning that an Interpol notice could restrict her travel and that she might face conviction in a new trial. The case also raises concerns about media bias, with criticism that Knox received favorable coverage because of her appearance while the victim was overlooked.

The deputy leader of al Qaeda, Abu Yahya al-Libi, was killed in a CIA drone strike in Pakistan, marking a significant blow to the group’s core leadership. A Libyan religious scholar and key propagandist, he had gained influence after escaping U.S. custody and used his clerical authority to justify the organization’s actions. His death removes one of the few figures capable of replacing the group’s top leadership, though regional affiliates remain a concern. The strike also highlights ongoing tensions over U.S. drone operations in Pakistan, which have drawn criticism over civilian casualties and sovereignty issues.

A former PTA president in Washington state has been federally charged with producing and distributing child pornography after allegedly recording the sexual assault of an 8-year-old girl at an elementary school and sharing the video online. Investigators were alerted by authorities in Denmark and Australia, and a GPS tag in the video matched the school’s location, leading to the man’s arrest. He had previously faced similar charges in 2009, but those were dismissed. Police searched his home, seized computers and a phone, and he remains in custody awaiting a detention hearing.

Dharun Ravi, the former Rutgers student convicted for using a webcam to spy on his gay roommate, Tyler Clementi, turned himself in at a New Jersey jail to begin a 30-day sentence. Clementi died by suicide after learning about the invasion of privacy. Ravi apologized and said he accepted the sentence to move forward, while prosecutors argued the punishment was too lenient and are appealing. The judge defended the term, saying prison was not appropriate for this case.

The article details the lives and deaths of three Americans killed in the attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, alongside Ambassador Chris Stevens. Tyrone Woods was a decorated former Navy SEAL and paramedic who served in dangerous diplomatic posts, while Glen Doherty was another ex-SEAL who had been searching for missing anti-aircraft missiles and was remembered for his adventurous spirit and compassion. Sean Smith, a Foreign Service information officer and Air Force veteran, was widely known in the online gaming community as "Vile Rat," a skilled diplomat in the game EVE Online. Their backgrounds highlight a mix of military service, protective duty, and personal dedication, with tributes from officials and loved ones emphasizing their courage and character.

The U.S. Department of Transportation and FAA have issued a new final rule aimed at reducing pilot fatigue by increasing the minimum rest period before duty to 10 hours, with at least eight of those hours reserved for uninterrupted sleep. The rule also imposes stricter weekly and monthly limits on flight duty and actual flying time, and requires 30 consecutive hours off each week. It updates regulations based on fatigue science, including factors like start time and time-zone crossings, and follows the 2009 Continental Flight 3407 crash where fatigue was a contributing factor. The rule takes effect in two years and is supported by pilots' unions, though they criticized the exclusion of cargo pilots from the same standards.

The FAA has approved BP’s drone operations in Alaska, marking the first authorized commercial drone flight over land in the U.S. The unmanned aircraft, flown by AeroVironment, will inspect roads, pipelines, and equipment at Prudhoe Bay, with strict limits on visibility, daylight, and line-of-sight operation. This follows earlier FAA permission for drone flights over Arctic waters and reflects the agency’s cautious approach to integrating drones into national airspace. Meanwhile, the FAA is also expanding drone research sites and considering exemptions that would allow film and TV production companies to use drones.

Russian national team coach Fabio Capello has rejected calls to exclude Russia from international football over its annexation of Crimea, insisting that sport should remain separate from politics. He was responding to U.S. senators who urged FIFA to ban Russia from the 2014 World Cup and strip it of the 2018 hosting rights, a move that prompted Russian officials to make a counter-demand against the U.S. Capello also acknowledged that Russia’s strong medal showing at the Sochi Winter Olympics has increased expectations and pressure on his squad for the World Cup. He stressed the need to develop younger players to refresh an aging team and expressed hope that Russia could surprise people in Brazil.

Fabrice Muamba, who retired after his heart stopped during a match, is urging FIFA to put player safety first when deciding when to hold the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. He warns that the country’s extreme heat and humidity pose serious health risks to players and fans alike. His concerns echo those of FIFA’s former inspection chief, who had cautioned that summer temperatures in Qatar would be unsafe for spectators. Muamba also hopes his experience will lead to better heart screening and wider access to defibrillators in stadiums and public places.

Facebook is introducing a new audio-recognition tool that lets users automatically identify and tag music, TV shows, or movies in their status updates by listening through their phone’s microphone. Similar to Shazam, the feature will roll out to U.S. users on Android and iOS in the coming weeks. It aims to make sharing easier while also giving Facebook more data to personalize ads. Users can control visibility, turn the feature off, and friends can preview song clips or see specific show episodes to avoid spoilers.

Facebook unveiled a new feature called Graph Search, which lets users pose natural-language questions to surface people, photos, places, and interests across its network. The beta tool is rolling out gradually and will only show content already shared with the user, addressing privacy concerns. It currently lacks mobile support, an API, and non-English versions, and will rely on Bing for results outside its scope. The company sees it as a new way to navigate Facebook’s data rather than a direct competitor to web search engines like Google.

WhatsApp, recently acquired by Facebook for $19 billion, is introducing free voice calling to its messaging platform, starting with Apple and Android devices in the coming months. The announcement came at Mobile World Congress, where CEO Jan Koum emphasized the goal of affordable communication. WhatsApp also reported strong growth, with 465 million monthly users and 330 million daily users, and remains especially popular in markets like India and Brazil. This expansion puts it in direct competition with services such as Skype and traditional mobile carriers.

Freediving is gaining popularity among young Emiratis, who are drawn to the ocean’s silence and the chance to explore underwater without bulky scuba gear. The sport carries cultural echoes of the UAE’s pearl-diving heritage, though today it is pursued for passion rather than livelihood. However, experts warn that many participants lack proper training, and recent deaths off Dubai highlight the risks. Despite these dangers, advocates point to a strong safety record in organized competitions and describe the sport’s free-falling sensation as its biggest thrill.

The writer describes a fading attachment to their iPhone, comparing it to a long-term relationship that has lost its excitement. They recall the thrill of early models, especially the iPhone 4, but feel let down by later incremental updates like the iPhone 4S. Tempted by newer Android and Samsung devices, they admit the passion is gone, though they will stick with their current phone until their contract allows an upgrade. At that point, they may switch carriers and phones, while still appreciating what the iPhone first offered.

Shirley Temple Black, the beloved child actress who became one of Hollywood’s biggest stars, has died at age 85 from natural causes at her California home. She rose to fame in the 1930s with hits like “Little Miss Marker” and “Curly Top,” becoming the top box-office draw for four consecutive years. After retiring from film, she served as a U.S. diplomat, including ambassador to Ghana and Czechoslovakia. She is remembered both for her iconic performances and her later public service.

Two British tourists were found dead on a beach in Koh Tao, Thailand, after suffering severe head injuries, and police are treating the case as murder. The victims’ families have expressed deep grief, remembering the young woman as joyful and the young man as a talented artist. Investigators are searching for a British man who shared a room with the male victim, while also seeking an Asian man seen in CCTV footage near the bar where the pair were last spotted. Robbery has been ruled out, and the killings mark the island’s first homicide in at least eight years.

After years of struggling with her weight and related health problems, Gabi Rose decided to make a permanent change following a terrifying asthma attack. She transformed her family’s eating habits by cooking healthier meals at home and cutting out processed foods, while the whole family became more active through sports, gym workouts, and races. Together, Rose, her husband, and daughter lost 300 pounds, though she emphasizes that keeping the weight off is the hardest part. Rose now helps others lose weight through a medical program and public speaking, and her daughter has also become an inspiration to other young people.

Kenneth Bae’s mother says her son seems changed after 15 months in North Korean captivity, and she fears for his mental state after seeing him on television. Bae’s reported confession and claim of good treatment are suspected by his family to be coerced, given North Korea’s history of forced statements. His sister expressed mixed emotions but hope that his public appearance signals progress, and the family is urging North Korea to show mercy. Bae, a Washington state man and father of three, was arrested in 2012 while leading tours in the country.

The family of the 9-year-old girl involved in the accidental shooting of an Arizona gun range instructor is devastated and has requested privacy as they cope with the tragedy. The instructor, Charles Vacca, was killed when the girl lost control of an Uzi while he was helping her fire it. Authorities are treating the death as an industrial accident and do not expect to file charges. The incident has sparked public debate over whether children should be allowed to handle high-powered weapons at commercial shooting ranges.

Gary David Goldberg, the acclaimed TV creator behind “Family Ties” and “Spin City,” has died at 68 from a brain tumor at his California home. Over his career, he earned seven Emmy nominations and won two, including for “Lou Grant” and “Family Ties.” He was remembered warmly by stars such as Michael J. Fox, Courteney Cox, and Charlie Sheen, who credited him as a mentor and major influence on their careers. Goldberg also wrote and produced several films, including “Must Love Dogs” and “Bye Bye Love.”

Japanese driver Kamui Kobayashi is returning to Formula One in 2014 with Caterham, helped by a crowdfunding campaign from fans after he lost his previous seat. He will partner Swedish rookie Marcus Ericsson, who says his F1 dream has come true. Kobayashi thanked supporters, saying their donations gave him strength and will also help Caterham develop during the upcoming season. The new campaign features major technical rule changes, with testing set to begin in Spain before the season opener in Australia.

Airbus has announced a major upgrade to its successful A330 jetliner, unveiling the A330neo series at the Farnborough Airshow to better compete with Boeing’s 787 Dreamliner. The new models feature Rolls-Royce engines, aerodynamic improvements, and weight reductions that promise a 14% drop in fuel consumption per seat. While Boeing has questioned the accuracy of those efficiency claims, Airbus expects the revamped aircraft to boost profits and sell at least 1,000 units, drawing on the strong performance of its earlier A320neo program. The A330neo also adds passenger-friendly touches like wider seats and upgraded in-flight entertainment to attract buyers.

Vin Diesel has confirmed that the seventh “Fast & Furious” film will still be made, despite a production delay, and announced a new release date of April 10, 2015. He shared a photo of his final scene with the late Paul Walker, noting the emotional significance of completing the movie. The film was originally scheduled for July 2014 but was paused after Walker’s death in a car crash during the Thanksgiving holiday. Walker’s role was central to the franchise, which has earned billions worldwide, making the film’s completion a major financial and emotional undertaking.

An American father, Michael Shannon, has spent nearly 12 years fighting to see his two sons after his ex-wife took them from Maryland to Egypt without his knowledge. Despite U.S. court orders granting him custody, he has been powerless because Egypt is not a signatory to the Hague Convention, and the State Department offered little help. His ex-wife, Nermeen Khalifa, disputes his account, claiming she fled to protect herself and the boys, and insists he could visit them if he wanted. Shannon, who recently caught a first glimpse of the boys as teenagers, remains hopeful they will one day return to the U.S. on their own.

After years of legal delays, terrorism charges have been refiled against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and four other defendants in the 9/11 attacks, potentially exposing them to the death penalty. Families of victims, like Jim Riches, who lost his firefighter son, expressed cautious hope that the trial will finally proceed, though they remain frustrated by the prolonged political and legal battles. Riches, who previously traveled to Guantanamo Bay and heard Mohammed boast about his role, wants the world to witness the men face justice. He also noted that while he is willing to testify, no outcome can bring his son back.

Dr. William Petit, the sole survivor of the 2007 Cheshire home invasion, testified at the trial of Joshua Komisarjevsky, recounting how he was beaten, bound, and taken to the basement while hearing his wife and daughters being attacked. He described escaping and later learning that his wife was raped and strangled and his two daughters died of smoke inhalation. Prosecutors presented evidence including 911 calls, a bank withdrawal attempt, and photos of Petit’s injuries, while Komisarjevsky’s defense argued he only intended to steal and that his co-defendant, Steven Hayes, committed the murders. Hayes was already sentenced to death for his role in the crimes.

The internet has become a transformative global force for communication, innovation, and economic growth, but this open environment is now endangered by authoritarian governments seeking greater control. Many nations are using an upcoming UN telecommunications conference to push for measures that could legitimize censorship, restrict anonymity, and impose financial barriers on online services. The article argues that internet governance should remain in the hands of engineers, companies, and users through a multi-stakeholder model, rather than being decided solely by governments. Preserving the current open, market-driven approach is essential to ensuring the internet continues to expand freely and benefit humanity.

Children as young as three are absorbing harmful cultural messages that equate thinness with worth, leading to weight anxiety and fat-shaming among kids. This early weight stigma can harm self-esteem and even affect focus and healthy development. Parents can counter these pressures by modeling positive attitudes toward food and bodies, having open conversations, and teaching respect for people of all sizes.

The FBI paid out $2.1 million in rewards for information that led to the capture of fugitive James “Whitey” Bulger and his companion Catherine Greig, while keeping the tipsters’ identities confidential. The arrests followed a public awareness campaign designed to reach people who might recognize Greig, including television ads and billboards. Bulger faces charges including involvement in 19 murders, and Greig is accused of helping him hide for years; both have pleaded not guilty.

The FBI recovered a stolen Henri Matisse painting, “Odalisque in Red Pants,” during an undercover operation in Miami Beach, nearly two decades after it disappeared from a Venezuelan museum. Two suspects, one from Miami and one from Mexico City, were arrested while attempting to sell the artwork, valued at $3 million, for $740,000. The painting was reportedly brought into the U.S. from Mexico, and authorities have charged the pair with transporting and possessing stolen property. Venezuelan officials have begun efforts to secure the painting’s return.

The FBI is looking into threats made against Bowe Bergdahl’s parents amid the intense backlash over his release. The controversy centers on accusations from former soldiers and a fallen soldier’s mother that U.S. troops were killed while searching for Bergdahl, though Pentagon officials say there is currently no evidence to support those claims. Bergdahl disappeared in 2009, and an Army investigation later concluded he left his post deliberately, but officials have not definitively ruled it a desertion.

The FBI is investigating after a crew member discovered a deceased newborn in a guest cabin aboard a Carnival cruise ship. The infant was found on Wednesday while the ship was docked in St. Maarten, where local authorities took custody of the body and spoke with the 20-year-old American mother. When the ship returned to Florida, FBI agents searched two cabins and interviewed passengers and crew. No charges have been filed, and the mother, who remained in St. Maarten, is expected to return to the U.S. soon.

The FBI and Justice Department have launched a broad review of thousands of historical criminal convictions to determine whether faulty forensic hair analysis led to wrongful convictions. The review was prompted by concerns that FBI experts may have overstated the certainty of hair evidence in trial testimony. It follows a recent case where DNA testing exonerated a man who spent 22 years in prison for a 1981 rape. The Justice Department is partnering with the Innocence Project and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers to conduct the review, though the timeline and total number of cases remain unclear.

An FBI counterterrorism official testified that the bureau should have interviewed Maj. Nidal Hasan after learning of his emails with radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, though he doubted political correctness played a role or that an interview would have prevented the Fort Hood attack. The testimony followed an independent report that criticized how the FBI handled the Hasan case, including poor information sharing and failure to follow up on leads. Lawmakers questioned whether the FBI was too cautious, but the official noted al-Awlaki was interviewed after 9/11 with no evidence of prior knowledge, and a passport fraud warrant against him was dropped for lack of proof. The FBI said it has since made changes, while Hasan's military trial was set to begin in August.

The FBI determined that white powder found in letters sent to several New Jersey hotels near the Super Bowl venue and to former Mayor Rudy Giuliani’s Manhattan office was not dangerous. Tests showed the substances were harmless, including cornstarch in one case, and no injuries were reported. The incidents prompted hazmat and bomb squad responses amid heightened security before the game, though authorities are still investigating whether the letters are connected and are coordinating with Canadian officials.

A man wanted for the 2010 murders of a young mother and her two-year-old son in New York has been arrested in Nicaragua and returned to the U.S. He surrendered at the U.S. Embassy in Managua just one day after being added to the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list. Authorities say the suspect, an MS-13 gang member, lured the victims into the woods before killing them, allegedly because the mother had ties to rival gangs. He is scheduled to appear in federal court at the end of March.

The FBI, working with hundreds of law enforcement agencies across more than 100 cities, rescued 168 children and arrested 281 pimps in a nationwide anti-sex-trafficking operation. Officials stressed that these victims are American children exploited in local communities, not distant cases. Since 2008, such efforts have led to nearly 3,600 children rescued, over 1,450 convictions, and millions of dollars in seized assets. Authorities also urged the public to report suspected abuse, saying a single tip could change a child’s life.

The FDA has approved a new bionic arm called the DEKA, developed by Segway inventor Dean Kamen with DARPA funding and inspired by Star Wars. Unlike traditional prosthetics, it uses muscle signals to enable multiple precise movements, such as handling eggs, using keys, and zipping coats. It is designed for people with certain upper-arm amputations and was tested in a study where about 90% of users could perform tasks they couldn’t with their previous prosthetics. The approval allows the device to be legally marketed and sold in the U.S., offering amputees greater independence.

The FDA is investigating counterfeit versions of the cancer drug Avastin that reached 19 U.S. medical centers, though no patients appear to have been harmed. Commissioner Margaret Hamburg stresses that current laws limit the FDA’s ability to quickly seize and destroy fake drugs, and she is pushing for stronger authority, better tracking of the global drug supply, and harsher penalties for counterfeiters. She also warns that ongoing shortages of cancer medications could encourage illegal gray markets to fill gaps. The FDA has improved early warning systems and, through increased reporting, has already helped prevent around 115 drug shortages.

The FDA has announced a new initiative to phase out the use of certain antibiotics in livestock for growth promotion, citing the growing public health threat of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The agency’s plan relies on drug companies voluntarily removing production-related uses from labels and requires veterinary oversight for remaining therapeutic uses. Recent FDA testing found antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a large share of meat samples, and critics argue the voluntary approach is too weak, while industry groups have expressed support. The move is part of broader FDA efforts to address food safety and preserve the effectiveness of antibiotics for human medicine.

The FDA has proposed new rules to extend its authority to e-cigarettes, cigars, hookahs, and other tobacco products, which would establish a minimum purchase age of 18, require health warnings, ban vending machine sales and free samples, and mandate FDA product registration and review. The move comes amid rising youth use of e-cigarettes, increased poison control calls, and concerns about the unknown health risks of nicotine vapor and liquid nicotine toxicity. While some industry leaders support the regulations as beneficial for adult consumers and responsible manufacturers, critics argue the FDA acted too slowly and must finalize the rules quickly to prevent further harm to young people.

An FDA advisory panel has unanimously recommended that a Roche HPV DNA test become the primary screening tool for cervical cancer, replacing the traditional Pap test as the first step for women aged 25 and older. Since HPV causes nearly all cervical cancers, the test can detect high-risk strains earlier and more directly than the Pap smear, which looks for abnormal cells. The Pap test would not disappear entirely, and some experts caution that more research is needed to see how HPV-only screening compares with current co-testing methods. The FDA usually follows such advisory recommendations, which could shift standard cervical cancer screening practices.

The article recounts the aftermath of the 2012 Port Said stadium disaster, where over 70 Al Ahly fans were killed, and the subsequent court verdict sentencing 21 people to death. While the verdict brought tears of joy and relief among the Ahlawy ultras in Cairo, it sparked outrage and deadly clashes in Port Said, where residents believed the accused were scapegoats. The violence led to a curfew imposed by President Morsy, but protesters defiantly marched, viewing the verdict as a political maneuver rather than true justice. The event deepened the rift between the state and both fan groups, leaving a cycle of vengeance and unresolved anger.

In Bangladesh, where child marriage is widespread, a 16-year-old girl named Humaiya Akhter is actively campaigning to end the practice after seeing many friends married young. The problem is global, driven by poverty, gender inequality, and insecurity from conflict or climate change, and it often harms girls by limiting education and increasing health risks. Although many countries have laws against child marriage, enforcement is weak, especially in crisis-affected areas. Experts say lasting change requires education, stronger legal implementation, and whole communities committing to protect girls.

Fabrice Muamba’s future in professional soccer is uncertain after he collapsed during a match, with a heart specialist saying it is doubtful he will play again. The Bolton midfielder remains in critical condition, but prompt on-field treatment, including rapid resuscitation and defibrillation, greatly improved his chances of survival. Doctors are now more concerned about possible brain damage than his heart, and whether he will wake up fully neurologically intact. The next two days are considered crucial, and his cardiac arrest was likely caused by an undetected heart condition despite routine screening.

A federal judge ruled that Oregon’s voter-approved same-sex marriage ban was unconstitutional, citing violations of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. The state’s attorney general had already declined to defend the ban, and same-sex couples began receiving marriage licenses shortly after the decision. Supporters celebrated the ruling as a historic victory for family recognition, while opponents filed an appeal. The decision adds to a growing wave of court rulings favoring same-sex marriage, with numerous similar cases still moving through the courts nationwide.

A Georgia mother moved to Colorado with her severely epileptic daughter after doctors gave her months to live, and the girl improved dramatically on a low-THC cannabis oil that reduced her seizures and allowed her to speak and walk for the first time. A new U.S. House bill would exempt such low-THC cannabis strains from federal drug laws, potentially letting families use the treatment without relocating. Supporters argue no family should have to split up to access a promising therapy, while critics note there are no published studies proving cannabis treats seizures. The bill reflects growing political momentum for medical marijuana, though federal law still classifies it as having no accepted medical use.

Governor Chris Christie is now facing a federal inquiry into whether he misused Superstorm Sandy relief funds on a tourism advertising campaign that featured him and his family. The investigation adds to his existing political troubles from the George Washington Bridge lane-closure scandal, which has already led to the firing of two aides. Federal auditors are examining the bidding process and the higher cost of the winning ad contract, which Democrats argue diverted money from storm recovery and gave Christie an unfair political boost. Christie’s office maintains the campaign was properly approved and helped promote New Jersey’s recovery, but any finding of misconduct could damage his potential 2016 presidential prospects.

A top federal railroad official has raised serious safety concerns about Metro-North following a deadly derailment in the Bronx, citing four major accidents in under seven months that caused five deaths and about 129 injuries. The Federal Railroad Administration has ordered the MTA to quickly adopt a confidential close-call reporting program, which has proven effective on other rail lines, and is considering further federal oversight actions. The MTA says it is fully cooperating and has pledged to work with federal agencies to improve safety while reviewing its own safety culture.

Federal authorities are still trying to identify a man who has mailed hundreds of harmless white-powder envelopes since 2008, mostly avoiding detection by leaving no fingerprints. They believe he is a man over 30 who may seem eccentric and could have ties to mental health facilities. Recently, he has shifted his focus from government offices to schools, sending over 20 such letters to elementary schools and childcare centers in the past two weeks. Although the powder has never been dangerous, the costly screening process has prompted officials to offer a $150,000 reward for information leading to his arrest and conviction.

U.S. federal authorities are asking museums and collectors to check their collections for artifacts tied to a New York dealer accused of involvement in a $20 million antiquities theft ring from India. The dealer, Subhash Kapoor, was arrested in Germany and extradited to India, where he faces charges for allegedly possessing looted temple relics, including stone and bronze statues from Tamil Nadu. Investigators recovered items from his storage units, some of which had been displayed in major international museums, and noted that while the pieces hold great monetary value, they are culturally priceless to their countries of origin. The case stems from a 2007 tip about smuggling, and U.S. agencies say they have since returned thousands of artifacts to nations around the world.

Senator Dianne Feinstein has accused the CIA of improperly searching computers used by Senate Intelligence Committee staff during an oversight investigation into the agency’s post-9/11 detention and interrogation program. She said the move may have violated federal law and constitutional oversight duties, and criticized CIA Director John Brennan for refusing to apologize. Brennan strongly denied the allegations, calling them false and beyond the realm of reason, while some lawmakers demanded a full investigation and warned of serious consequences if the claims are true. The dispute highlights ongoing tensions between the CIA and Congress over access to classified documents and the fate of the committee’s torture report.

Senate Intelligence Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein expressed anger that the FBI failed to inform congressional intelligence committees about its investigation into CIA Director David Petraeus’s extramarital affair, calling the omission atypical. She raised national security concerns, particularly whether his mistress Paula Broadwell had access to classified information. Feinstein also noted that an FBI whistleblower had alerted House Majority Leader Eric Cantor before the president was briefed. The committee plans to investigate the FBI’s handling of the matter and may subpoena a report from Petraeus’s trip to Benghazi.

The release of Bowe Bergdahl has sparked deep anger among many soldiers who served with him, as they accuse him of desertion and blame his disappearance for the deaths of several troops during the manhunt. While the Obama administration celebrated his return and focused on his health and reintegration, former comrades are demanding a military trial and public accountability. The circumstances of his capture remain unclear, and his release in exchange for Guantanamo detainees has intensified the backlash. Meanwhile, his hometown and some officials urge patience, arguing that he has already suffered enough and that the full story has yet to be told.

Protesters disrupted a St. Louis Symphony performance by staging a peaceful flash mob during Brahms' Requiem, singing a modified protest song demanding justice for Michael Brown. Around 50 paying audience members took part, unfurling banners and distributing information before leaving quietly. The demonstration drew mixed reactions, with some applause and some hostile comments. Unlike a similar protest at a Cardinals game, this one ended without arrests or confrontation.

After closing his world-renowned restaurant elBulli, chef Ferran Adria is launching the elBulli Foundation in Barcelona, a broad project dedicated to creativity rather than cooking. It will include a gastronomy research lab, an online food encyclopedia called BulliPedia, courses, and a visitor center. Adria sees the venture as a way to share his “theory of everything” and help people apply creative thinking to any field. He also plans exhibitions on the creative process and will serve only a handful of meals each year.

Japanese rail company JR East has enlisted renowned car designer Ken Okuyama to style its new luxury sleeper train, the Cruise Train, launching in spring 2017. The 10-carriage train will carry just 34 passengers and feature private suites, observation cars, a dining car, and a lounge, with interiors inspired by traditional Japanese culture. It will also include a split-level deluxe suite and the ability to run on both electrified and non-electrified tracks. The train follows in the tracks of JR Kyushu’s earlier Seven Stars luxury service, which launched in 2013 and offers high-end multi-day trips around Kyushu, with bookings managed by lottery due to high demand.

Ferrari has extended Felipe Massa’s contract through the 2013 Formula One season, ending speculation about his future. The Brazilian, who has been with the team since 2006, said he was delighted to continue with his “racing family.” Ferrari hopes the early confirmation of its 2013 lineup will allow Fernando Alonso to focus fully on chasing the drivers’ title, while team officials praised Massa’s recent return to competitive form after his serious injury in 2009.

Ferrari’s new team principal, Marco Mattiacci, says he would gladly welcome Ross Brawn back to the team, praising the former technical director as an iconic and highly respected figure in Formula One. Brawn, who helped Ferrari dominate in the early 2000s and later transformed Mercedes into a championship-leading team, is currently taking a break from the sport. Ferrari has struggled in recent years, with its last constructors’ title in 2008 and last drivers’ crown in 2007, while Mercedes now leads both championships. Mattiacci is focused on rebuilding Ferrari with current technical director James Allison, and it remains unclear whether Brawn would return.Ferrari’s new team principal, Marco Mattiacci, says he would welcome Ross Brawn back, calling him an iconic and highly respected figure in Formula One. Brawn previously guided Ferrari to multiple titles and later helped Mercedes become a dominant force, but he is currently on a break from the sport. Ferrari has struggled recently, with no constructors’ title since 2008 and no drivers’ championship since 2007. Mattiacci is focused on building a strong team with James Allison as technical director, and it remains uncertain whether Brawn would accept a return.

The U.S. improved its grade on the March of Dimes preterm birth report card, moving from a D to a C, with about 40,000 fewer premature births between 2006 and 2009. The national preterm birth rate now stands at 12.2%, still above the 9.6% target for 2020, which only Vermont has met. Experts attribute persistent gaps to poverty, limited health care access, and social conditions, and suggest that better prenatal care, fewer elective C-sections, and reduced multiple births from fertility treatments could help. Prematurity remains a leading cause of newborn death and costs over $26 billion annually.

FIFA faces accusations of sexism after former reform committee members alleged officials pressured them not to nominate women to lead the investigation into the 2018 and 2022 World Cup bidding process. The role ultimately went to Michael Garcia, who was not on the original shortlist and was reportedly recommended through Interpol. Garcia has called for his full report to be published, but FIFA president Sepp Blatter has refused, citing confidentiality rules. The controversy highlights ongoing criticism of FIFA’s lack of transparency and resistance to reform.

Rita Mrwebi, South Africa’s female welterweight champion, is training hard at Johannesburg’s Hillbrow Boxing Club to defend her title in August, a crucial fight since boxing is her main income and she rarely gets bouts without sponsors. The gym, founded by former boxer George Khosi, offers free training to keep local youth away from the dangers of drugs and crime in the tough Hillbrow neighborhood. Mrwebi says boxing kept her disciplined and away from trouble, and she hopes to one day become a promoter to help other young boxers succeed. The club has become a vital community anchor, producing champions and giving at-risk children a positive outlet.

Fierce clashes continued on Tripoli’s outskirts as rival militias battled for control of the international airport, marking some of the heaviest violence since the 2011 uprising. The fighting, which involved Misrata-backed forces and Islamist militias against the Zintan-based group that has held the airport, has killed civilians and caused widespread damage, including to parked aircraft. International actors, including the UN and the US, voiced alarm and evacuated staff, warning that Libya faces a major escalation and possible collapse into a failed state. The weak central government acknowledged it may need international help but stopped short of requesting foreign military intervention.

The film industry mourns Sarah Elizabeth Jones, a 27-year-old camera assistant killed in an on-set train accident while working on Gregg Allman’s biopic. In her memory, colleagues launched the “Slates for Sarah” movement, sharing clapboard photos that drew tens of thousands of supporters worldwide. Her name was also added to the Oscars’ In Memoriam segment. The tragedy has sparked broader conversations about improving safety standards on film sets.

Joseph Ruskin, a prolific character actor with roles in numerous films and television series, passed away at age 89 in Santa Monica from natural causes. His career spanned major productions like "The Magnificent Seven" and "Star Trek," while also maintaining deep roots in theater, from his early post-Navy performances to recent stage work in Los Angeles. Beyond acting, Ruskin was a dedicated union leader, serving on the Screen Actors Guild board for over two decades and advocating for the merger that created SAG-AFTRA. He is remembered by colleagues as a consummate professional who supported fellow actors throughout his long career.

Finnair is introducing a traditional sauna in its upcoming premium lounge at Helsinki Airport, aiming to offer top-tier passengers a memorable Nordic experience. The lounge, designed with Finnish furnishings and seasonal video projections, includes separate areas for work, relaxation, and bathing. While saunas are typically enjoyed nude in Finland, guests are advised to use towels. This marks a return for the airline, as a previous airport sauna was closed years ago due to financial reasons, but Finnair now expects the expanded lounge to make it a success.

Finnish Prime Minister Jyrki Katainen says the eurozone crisis stems from countries failing to follow the bloc’s rules, and that this neglect has come at a heavy cost. He points to upcoming measures such as a European Central Bank-supervised banking union and the European Stability Mechanism as steps toward a safer, more sustainable currency union. While lower borrowing costs in countries like Ireland and Portugal suggest returning confidence, Katainen cautions against declaring the crisis over. He stresses that restoring competitiveness through reforms, as seen in Spain and Ireland, remains essential, though such changes take time to deliver results.

The election of Pope Francis, the first Latin American pope in history, sparked joy and pride across the Americas, especially among Catholic communities in Argentina, Mexico, and the United States. Many faithful saw his selection as long-overdue recognition of Latin America's large Catholic population and expressed hope that his papacy would bring greater attention to the region's poverty and struggles. The choice also resonated with U.S. Latinos, who noted that Francis, as the son of migrants, understands the migrant experience firsthand. Overall, his election was viewed as a powerful symbol that the Church is truly universal and that Latin American Catholics are now fully represented.

Massachusetts has approved 20 medical marijuana dispensary licenses, marking the first such approvals since voters legalized the drug in 2013. Officials selected the winners from 100 finalists through a strict review process focused on public safety, business viability, and patient care. Eight additional applicants were deemed qualified but had their proposed locations rejected, and they may reapply in counties without a licensed dispensary. Patients with a doctor’s written certification will register online, and while the dispensaries remain illegal under federal law, they will serve those with conditions such as cancer, AIDS, and chronic pain.

A Long Island couple’s marriage nearly collapsed under the strain of the husband’s untreated post-traumatic stress after his Iraq deployment, which fueled anger, heavy drinking, and panic over small mistakes. They found help at a pioneering clinic where veterans and their family members receive coordinated treatment together, rather than separately through the VA system. This shared approach allowed both partners to be honest and rebuild trust, and they credit the clinic with saving their marriage. The center also aims to reduce stigma by offering free, integrated care for the whole family.

Iowa social conservative leaders held a private meeting to try to unite behind a single Republican alternative to Mitt Romney ahead of the state's caucuses, fearing a split conservative vote would hand him the nomination. They focused on four candidates—Bachmann, Perry, Gingrich, and Santorum—while setting aside Cain and Paul over concerns about their consistency and experience. Organizers acknowledged the effort was still in early discussion and faced challenges, including the need for organization and funding. Another meeting was planned, though at least one attendee said her group would not endorse any candidate before the caucuses.

Senate leaders remained deeply divided as the year-end fiscal cliff deadline approached, with negotiations continuing over how to avoid automatic spending cuts and tax hikes that could harm the economy. A key sticking point emerged when Republicans briefly demanded changes to Social Security inflation adjustments, but they later dropped that condition after Democrats rejected it. Vice President Joe Biden and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell took the lead in last-minute talks, while President Obama blamed Republicans for blocking tax increases on the wealthy. Lawmakers on both sides expressed cautious optimism that a partial deal could still be reached before the midnight deadline.

Five infants in El Paso have tested positive for tuberculosis after being exposed to an infected nurse at Providence Memorial Hospital, where more than 850 babies and 43 healthcare workers were potentially affected. Health officials stress that the infants do not have active TB, and four of the positive results may be due to the BCG vaccine rather than actual infection. All exposed infants are receiving treatment as a precaution, while the infected nurse is no longer working and is undergoing care. Hospital leadership has publicly apologized and committed to addressing the situation.

On the second-to-last day of the Sochi Olympics, the U.S. men’s hockey team was shut out 5-0 by Finland in the bronze medal game, a disappointing end after earlier defeating Russia. The Netherlands continued its speed skating dominance by winning gold in both men’s and women’s team pursuit events. In alpine skiing, Austria took the top two spots in the men’s slalom, while Norway swept the women’s 30-kilometer cross-country race. Russia’s Vic Wild and Austria’s Julia Dujmovits claimed gold in the parallel slalom competitions.

A great internship is defined less by pay or perks and more by the effort and mindset an intern brings to the role. Students emphasize the importance of taking ownership of meaningful projects, embracing structured programs, and building strong relationships with supervisors and mentors. Even unpaid positions can be invaluable when they offer hands-on experience, networking opportunities, and a sense of purpose. Ultimately, a successful internship provides concrete talking points and practical skills that help launch a student’s career.

Malawi may lack the tourist numbers of its neighbors, but it offers its own unique appeal, from friendly locals and stunning sunsets to the vast, fish-rich waters of Lake Malawi. The country is also emerging as a quieter safari destination, where visitors can see elephants, hippos, and diverse birdlife without the crowds. Its history is tied to explorer David Livingstone, and travelers can trace his routes or visit historic missions. Meanwhile, most Malawians live in rural villages, where traditional lifestyles and homemade drinks like sweet beer remain central to daily life.

The Republican presidential debate in Washington was notable more for substantive clashes than flashy moments. Newt Gingrich drew sharp criticism from Mitt Romney after proposing a limited path to legal status for long-term undocumented immigrants, highlighting a major rift between the two front-runners. Jon Huntsman and Michele Bachmann delivered strong performances, especially on foreign policy and national security issues, while Ron Paul stood alone with his antiwar and non-interventionist views. The candidates largely agreed on staunch support for Israel, whereas Herman Cain remained largely subdued and failed to make a significant impact.

The article highlights how female executives are revitalizing major food and beverage brands, focusing on CNN’s feature with Campbell Soup CEO Denise Morrison. Morrison has modernized the 144-year-old company by acquiring Bolthouse Farms and expanding into healthy products and new soup flavors to attract millennials. It also profiles other influential women, including PepsiCo’s Indra Nooyi, lifestyle guru Martha Stewart, cookbook author Donna Hay, and the sisters behind Goldilocks Bakery, who have each built or transformed their brands through innovation and strategic growth.

The future of money will be shaped by a shift from profit-only motives to a broader 4P model encompassing people, planet, and purpose, enabled by mobile tech. Alternative currencies like Bitcoin and local digital pounds will grow, challenging traditional banks. Mobile payments are driving financial inclusion, especially in Africa and India, where they empower the unbanked. Ultimately, connected devices and transparent networks will create a more collaborative, equitable global economy.

Flesh-eating bacteria are rare but can cause rapid, severe tissue destruction when they enter the body through cuts or trauma. Many bacterial types, including Aeromonas and Group A Strep, can trigger this condition, often exploiting wounds or even bruises to reach the bloodstream. Treatment requires urgent, aggressive surgery to remove infected and surrounding tissue, along with antibiotics. Although cases are uncommon and not systematically tracked, doctors advise monitoring wounds for increasing pain, redness, or drainage.

Search teams have moved the hunt for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to a new area in the Indian Ocean after radar analysis suggested the plane was flying faster than previously thought, meaning it likely traveled less far south. This new lead is considered the most credible yet, and additional aircraft are joining the search. Recent satellite images from several countries have spotted floating objects, but none have been visually confirmed as wreckage. Meanwhile, families remain frustrated by the lack of answers, and the pilot’s son has rejected speculation that his father was responsible, as investigators say they have found no clear motive.

A Florida man has been arrested for allegedly fatally shooting his wife and then posting a photo of her body on Facebook alongside a confession. He later surrendered to police and is being held without bond on a first-degree murder charge. In his statement to authorities, he claimed the couple argued and that he shot her in self-defense after she attacked him. Police found the couple’s 10-year-old daughter unharmed in the home, and Facebook removed the graphic post and disabled the man’s account.

A Florida man who ran from a traffic stop early Thursday was captured hours later after being bitten by an alligator. The 20-year-old had abandoned his car and escaped on foot, but sought treatment at a hospital for wounds to his face and arm. Police arrested him there and he faces charges including fleeing police and driving without a license. The encounter occurred near a water treatment plant, highlighting the gator's presence in local waterways.

A Florida man was cited after attempting to trade a live four-foot alligator for a 12-pack of beer at a convenience store in Miami. The clerk refused and called police instead of making the swap. The alligator was unharmed and released back into the wild, while the man now faces misdemeanor charges for possessing and selling an alligator. Authorities described the incident as highly unusual.

A previously healthy 17-year-old boy died from the flu after his condition rapidly worsened during a family Christmas trip. What began as mild symptoms turned into a high fever, kidney failure, and a staph infection that caused septic shock. Despite hospital care and intubation, he passed away days later. His family was devastated, and after his death, the college acceptance letter he had been waiting for arrived in the mail.

Forbes’ latest billionaires list no longer includes Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, marking the first time since 2009 that the Sinaloa cartel leader has been excluded. The magazine suggests that much of his wealth is now being spent on security for himself and his family, and it could not verify his finances. Despite the drop, Guzmán remains a major global drug figure and is still wanted by authorities following his 2001 prison escape. The 2013 rankings also set a record with 1,426 billionaires, led by Mexico’s Carlos Slim.

Eileen Ford, co-founder of Ford Models, has died at 92 due to complications from meningioma and osteoporosis. She and her husband launched the agency in New York in 1946, transforming the modeling industry and helping pave the way for the era of the supermodel. The agency honored her as an “icon and pioneer” whose influence on fashion and beauty was immeasurable. Ford Models noted that her passion and drive built it into one of the world’s leading agencies.

Mayor Bloomberg’s proposal to ban large sugary drinks in New York City has sparked debate over personal freedom, but the deeper issue is whether targeting just one dietary item is scientifically justified. While sugary beverages are linked to weight gain, research suggests that other foods like French fries and processed meats have a stronger association with obesity, making the policy’s focus seem arbitrary. Obesity stems from a complex mix of genetics, environment, and diet, so singling out soft drinks may not produce meaningful public health results. The ban could be a modest step toward reducing portion sizes, but its shaky scientific foundation may lead to disappointment if no measurable impact emerges.

The article highlights a growing hotel trend of offering complimentary bicycles so guests can explore local areas. It features ten hotels around the world that provide free loaner bikes, each with unique perks—from Portland’s bike with a beer tap and Paris’s classic wicker-basket rides to electric bikes in Santa Barbara and tandem cycles in Palm Springs. Other examples include properties in Canada, Mexico, New York, Vermont, Texas, and Kenya, where bikes range from stylish city cruisers to mountain bikes, often with added conveniences like boxed lunches or scenic routes. Overall, the piece emphasizes how these bike programs enhance travel experiences by promoting eco-friendly, active sightseeing.

Craft beer is rapidly gaining popularity in South Africa, particularly in the Cape Town region, as a wave of small, independent microbreweries emerges to meet growing consumer demand for distinctive flavors.
