Despite the overwhelming market dominance of large industrial brewers like SABMiller, these new craft producers are differentiating themselves by using local ingredients to create fresh, unique brews and by promoting their products at beer festivals. The movement is driven by a consumer shift toward quality over quantity, with drinkers appreciating the variety and care that goes into craft beer compared to mass-produced options. Ultimately, the success of this sector hinges on passion and a commitment to showcasing the artistry of beer, rather than on competing directly with the big corporations.

Tito Vilanova, the former Barcelona head coach, has passed away at age 45 after a long battle with cancer. He took over from Pep Guardiola in 2012 and guided Barcelona to the Spanish league title in his sole full season, despite undergoing treatment for the disease. His death prompted an outpouring of grief and tributes from the club, players, and the wider football world. Barcelona opened a space for fans to pay their respects and planned a memorial ceremony in his honor.Tito Vilanova, former Barcelona coach, has died at 45 after a prolonged battle with cancer. He led the Catalan club to the Spanish league title during his brief tenure, having taken over from Pep Guardiola in 2012. His passing drew widespread tributes from the football community, including former players and rivals. Barcelona opened a condolence area at the Nou Camp and planned a memorial ceremony.

Four former Blackwater guards have been re-indicted on manslaughter charges in connection with the 2007 Baghdad shooting that killed 17 unarmed civilians. The men deny the allegations, maintaining they acted in self-defense after coming under fire. The case was originally thrown out over withheld evidence, but an appeals court later reinstated it, allowing prosecutors to pursue new charges. The incident fueled international condemnation and prompted Iraq to restrict the use of private security contractors.

A former boyfriend of Sharon Bialek has publicly corroborated her claim that Herman Cain groped her in 1997, saying she told him about the incident soon after it happened. Cain continues to strongly deny all accusations of sexual misconduct, and his wife has defended him, saying he respects women. Meanwhile, new polling shows Cain’s support among Republicans has dropped significantly since the allegations emerged, with many Americans tending to believe the accusers.

Former first lady Barbara Bush, age 88, was admitted to a Houston hospital for treatment of a respiratory-related issue. Family spokesman said she is in good spirits, receiving excellent care, and has had visits from her husband and family. Bush is remembered for championing literacy and founding the Barbara Bush Foundation for Family Literacy in 1989. Her hospitalization comes after a history of health challenges, including Graves’ disease, heart surgery, and a prior ulcer surgery.

A former “Ice Road Truckers: Deadliest Roads” cast member, Tim Zickuhr, was arrested in Las Vegas on charges including kidnapping and extortion after an alleged dispute with a sex worker. Police say he locked her in a closet and demanded money, threatening to kill her if payment wasn’t brought; the threat was made to an undercover officer’s phone. Zickuhr’s attorney denies the allegations and questions the woman’s credibility. He is scheduled to appear in court in May.

Two former Navy SEALs working as private security contractors were killed in Benghazi after leaving a safe annex to assist colleagues during the initial assault on the U.S. Consulate. They helped evacuate staff and recovered the body of a State Department employee who died from smoke inhalation. After returning to the annex, they were killed in a second, more intense attack involving rocket-propelled grenades and mortars. Both men were experienced veterans with multiple deployments, and they were later honored by President Obama and Secretary Clinton.

Former New England Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez was charged with first-degree murder in the shooting death of Odin Lloyd and was ordered held without bail. Prosecutors alleged Hernandez drove Lloyd to a remote industrial area and orchestrated the killing, citing surveillance footage and other evidence, while his defense argued the case was circumstantial. The Patriots released Hernandez shortly after his arrest, and the NFL expressed deep concern over his involvement. Hernandez also faces weapons charges, and the investigation remains ongoing, including questions about two other men seen with him.

Former NFL linebacker Junior Seau died Wednesday at age 43 from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound at his home in Oceanside, California. Police responded to a call from his girlfriend and found him with a chest wound; he was pronounced dead at the scene. Seau was a 20-year NFL veteran known for his intense play, 12 Pro Bowl selections, and time with the Chargers, Dolphins, and Patriots. His death came after a 2010 domestic violence arrest and a previous incident in which he drove his car off a cliff.

A judge has ordered the preliminary seizure of Aaron Hernandez’s Massachusetts home amid a wrongful death lawsuit filed by the family of Odin Lloyd, the man Hernandez is accused of murdering. The New England Patriots have indicated they will not pay the $3.25 million owed to Hernandez under his contract, which was terminated after his arrest. Hernandez has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, while also facing scrutiny over alleged gun trafficking and a separate civil claim from a man who says Hernandez shot him in the face.

A former employee of Donald Sterling has filed a lawsuit accusing him of sexual harassment, making racist remarks about her ex-husband and children, and firing her after she objected. The suit also claims he promised her $10,000 a month as a caretaker but withheld wages and pressured her for sex. Her lawyer says there is supporting evidence, including voicemails and texts, while Sterling’s attorney dismisses the claims as baseless. The case adds to Sterling’s legal troubles following the leaked audio that led to his NBA ban and the forced sale of the Clippers.

The FBI has placed a former Washington, D.C., private school teacher on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in connection with child pornography charges. He is accused of using a hidden camera in his classroom’s adjacent bathroom and allegedly possessing and producing illicit images of children. Authorities believe he may be working as a tutor or nanny and have offered up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest. The FBI warns that he is considered dangerous because he may still have access to children.

Jim Oberstar, a longtime Democratic-Farmer-Labor congressman from Minnesota, has died at age 79. He served the state’s 8th District for 36 years, becoming the state’s longest-serving House member and chairing the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. National and state leaders, including former Presidents Obama and Clinton, praised his dedication to infrastructure, Minnesota, and Haiti. Oberstar lost his seat in the 2010 Republican wave and is survived by his wife, children, and grandchildren.

After a historic trial, Egypt’s former president Hosni Mubarak was sentenced to life in prison for his role in the deadly crackdown on pro-democracy protesters during the 2011 uprising, while he and his sons were cleared of corruption charges. The verdict marked the first time a leader ousted in the Arab Spring was personally brought to justice, drawing both outrage and approval from crowds inside and outside the courtroom. Mubarak, who ruled Egypt for three decades under emergency laws and was once a key Western ally, was toppled after an 18-day revolution. His conviction underscored that even long-entrenched autocrats are not above the law, though Egypt’s political future remains uncertain as the military council prepares for a contentious presidential runoff.

After more than two decades away, Mexico will rejoin the Formula One calendar in 2015, as confirmed by F1 chief Bernie Ecclestone. The race is set to take place at the upgraded Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico City, though an official date has not yet been announced. The deal was celebrated by race organizers and by Mexican drivers Sergio Perez and Esteban Gutierrez, who see it as a major moment for their country. Mexico’s last Grand Prix was held in 1992, and the circuit previously hosted F1 events in the 1960s and from 1986 onward.

Syrian activists have turned to video documentation and social media to expose the regime’s brutal crackdown, especially since journalists are barred from covering the conflict freely. They carefully verify footage by naming locations, dates, and recognizable landmarks to counter government claims that the videos are fake. Activists rely on cell phones, hidden cameras, and satellite devices, often smuggling footage across borders at great personal risk, and some have been killed while filming. Their efforts have been recognized internationally, including with a Reporters Without Borders prize, as they strive to ensure the world bears witness to the violence.

The Army psychiatrist convicted for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13 people has reportedly written to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, requesting citizenship in the Islamic State. His attorney confirmed the two-page letter was sent recently, though it was first reported by Fox News. Hasan, who is on military death row and paralyzed after being shot by police, carried out the attack on unarmed soldiers preparing for deployment to Afghanistan. During his trial, he offered no defense and claimed the soldiers were participating in an illegal war.

The sentencing phase of Maj. Nidal Hasan’s court-martial has begun, with emotional testimony from survivors and victims’ families describing the lasting trauma of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting. Hasan, who was convicted of 13 murders and 32 attempted murders, faces possible execution, and prosecutors are presenting aggravating evidence to support the death penalty. Representing himself, Hasan has declined to mount a defense or cross-examine witnesses, and he has previously indicated he would accept death as a martyr. The case is complicated by the rarity of military executions, as the last one occurred in 1961 and most military death sentences have been overturned on appeal.

A U.S. soldier accused of planning a bombing at Fort Hood has claimed in his first interview that he initially targeted Fort Campbell, where he was stationed. He said he intended to abduct and execute a senior officer on July 4th and had purchased items like handcuffs and a cattle prod, but abandoned the plan after military police learned of his gun store visits and he went AWOL. The soldier, who has pleaded not guilty to charges including attempted murder and use of a weapon of mass destruction, also faced child pornography charges and had sought conscientious objector status. His statements could not be independently verified due to a gag order.

Foster Farms is recalling boneless chicken products distributed to several major retailers across eight western states due to possible salmonella contamination. The chicken was produced in early March and may still be in consumers’ freezers, though likely no longer on store shelves. The recall follows a confirmed salmonella illness in California linked to the products, but a consumer advocacy group argues the action is too limited and fails to fully protect public health. Salmonella infections can be serious or even life-threatening for vulnerable individuals.

ISIS militants seized the strategic border town of Al-Qaim and three other towns in Iraq’s western Anbar province, placing them along a key highway to Baghdad and raising fears of an advance on the capital. Their success has been bolstered by support from some Sunni tribes, while Iraqi forces awaited reinforcements and the first U.S. military advisers. In Baghdad, thousands of Shiite militiamen staged a show of force, reflecting deep sectarian tensions, and deadly bombings struck the capital. The escalating violence has displaced more than a million Iraqis this year, and U.S. officials warned that military action alone cannot succeed without a more inclusive Iraqi government.

A journalist who broke the story about James Holmes’ notebook may face jail if she refuses to reveal her source. A judge has delayed the decision until it is determined whether the notebook is admissible in court. The reporter argues that disclosing her source would destroy her career and credibility. Legal experts say the case could discourage investigative journalism by making reporters fear legal consequences for protecting confidential sources.

Islamist militants in Nigeria have released a video showing a French family abducted in Cameroon, with armed Boko Haram fighters demanding the release of jailed members and threatening to kill the hostages if demands are not met. France strongly condemned the footage, with its foreign minister describing the images as shocking and showing extreme cruelty. The kidnapping has heightened concerns that Westerners may be targeted by Islamist groups in Africa following France’s military intervention in Mali. French authorities are working to secure the family’s release.

France’s military action in Mali is not a departure from its foreign policy but reflects its long-standing willingness to intervene abroad when necessary. French doctrine balances support for UN-sanctioned, multilateral interventions with national interests and post-colonial sensitivities. While France often invokes human rights and international law to justify action, it is more reluctant to intervene in former colonies to avoid appearing neo-colonial. In Mali, pragmatism prevailed because advancing Islamist fighters posed an urgent threat, prompting direct French military engagement despite earlier hesitation.

The latest Gaza conflict has continued for over three weeks, with Palestinian casualties far exceeding Israeli losses due to the dense urban combat and the effectiveness of Israel’s Iron Dome. Israel has expanded its strikes beyond military targets to include Hamas-linked institutions and Gaza’s infrastructure, while neither side appears willing to accept the kind of UN-brokered ceasefire that ended previous rounds. Israel is determined to destroy Hamas’s tunnels and rocket arsenal, while Hamas continues firing and uses guerrilla-style tactics, despite facing a much harder time rearming because Egypt’s new government has cut off its smuggling routes and political support. The fighting is likely to end only when Israel believes it has inflicted enough damage to make Hamas militarily ineffective, rather than through a negotiated truce.

Franz Beckenbauer, the German football legend, has been provisionally banned by FIFA for 90 days for refusing to cooperate with an ethics investigation into the controversial World Cup bidding process that awarded the 2022 tournament to Qatar. The suspension comes amid ongoing corruption allegations surrounding FIFA, including past bribery scandals and renewed claims against Qatari official Mohamed bin Hammam. Separately, FIFA president Sepp Blatter has faced backlash after signaling he may seek another term, while Interpol has deployed teams to Brazil over concerns about match-fixing and illegal betting during the World Cup.

The music video for Duologue’s “Memex” is striking because its hyper-realistic images are not photographs but a virtual 3D scan of actor Beryl Nesbitt. London studio Marshmallow Laser Feast created it using 94 cameras, photogrammetry, and high dynamic range lighting to capture the skin in extreme detail. The team sees the result as a high-resolution digital sculpture rather than a tool for traditional film or games. Their broader goal is to use such realistic virtual humans in immersive art installations that push the boundaries of virtual reality.

After nearly two years in captivity, American journalist and author Peter Theo Curtis has been freed by the Syrian rebel group al-Nusra Front. His mother confirmed his identity by asking about a detail only he would know from his doctoral dissertation, and she immediately reached out to the mother of slain journalist James Foley before sharing the news. U.S. officials said Washington was not directly involved in negotiations, though private efforts helped secure his release. His release came just days after Foley’s execution by ISIS, and Curtis is now safe and expected to reunite with his family.

Open textbooks are gaining traction as a cost-saving alternative to traditional course materials, with professors customizing free digital resources to better fit their classes and students accessing them conveniently on devices. Their adoption is growing, especially at community colleges, where textbook costs place a heavy financial burden on learners. However, some educators remain hesitant due to concerns about editorial quality, though publishers are addressing this by adding peer review and oversight. Supporters argue that even imperfect free textbooks are preferable to expensive ones that students often skip, ultimately improving access and learning outcomes.

Clermont Foot has made history by naming Helena Costa as the first female head coach of a French professional men's team, a landmark appointment for European football's top leagues. Costa, who previously managed the Iran women's national team and led Benfica's male youth side, will take charge next season. The article also highlights other pioneering women in football roles while noting the sport's lingering sexism, referencing past derogatory comments made by male broadcasters about female officials.

The controversy began when footballer Nicolas Anelka used the “quenelle” gesture, associated with the French comedian Dieudonné, bringing the comedian’s long history of anti-Semitic and inflammatory rhetoric into the national spotlight. Dieudonné, who denies being anti-Semitic, has faced multiple convictions for incitement to hatred and is also under investigation for tax fraud and money laundering. The French government, led by Interior Minister Manuel Valls, moved to ban his performances, but the decision sparked a legal and public debate over censorship and free speech. While many believe Dieudonné has crossed the line from comedy into political extremism, the bans have also increased his notoriety and ticket sales.

Former French President Nicolas Sarkozy has been formally placed under investigation on suspicion of corruption and influence peddling, becoming the first former French leader to be held in police custody in such a case. He denied any wrongdoing, saying he had never acted against republican principles and felt a desire to humiliate him. The probe reportedly centers on whether he obtained confidential legal information from magistrates in exchange for offering one of them a prestigious position. His lawyer and a magistrate were also placed under investigation, and the case could threaten any political comeback, though officials stressed the presumption of innocence.

The French government has been dissolved after internal conflict, with President François Hollande requesting Prime Minister Manuel Valls to assemble a new cabinet. The upheaval was triggered by Economy Minister Arnaud Montebourg’s public criticism of the country’s economic direction, which was viewed as a direct challenge to Hollande and Valls. Hollande emphasized that the new government must stay aligned with his chosen policy course. Both leaders are facing weak public support, with Hollande holding record-low approval ratings and Valls also losing popularity.

French President François Hollande acknowledged personal turmoil over allegations of an affair with actress Julie Gayet, saying he and partner Valérie Trierweiler were going through painful moments but insisting private matters should remain private. He said he would clarify the situation before the couple’s upcoming U.S. state visit, which includes a White House state dinner. The scandal has dominated headlines, drawn criticism from opposition figures, and overshadowed his economic policy announcements, while Trierweiler remains hospitalized following the report.

Valerie Trierweiler, the former partner of French President François Hollande, has released a tell-all book about their relationship and its painful end. She recounts her distress after tabloid photos suggested Hollande’s affair with actress Julie Gayet, including a moment when he stopped her from taking sleeping pills and her subsequent hospitalization. Trierweiler also describes confronting Hollande about the rumors, his denials, and her feelings of being sidelined and dehumanized during his presidency. The book arrives as Hollande’s popularity is low, and he reportedly was dismayed by its publication.

Julie Hermann, recently appointed Rutgers athletic director to restore the program after a coaching abuse scandal, now faces her own allegations of verbal and psychological abuse from former University of Tennessee volleyball players she coached in the 1990s. The former players claim she used “mental cruelty” and made degrading comments, though Hermann denies the accusations and says she was an intense but not abusive coach. Rutgers’ president has reaffirmed support for her, while New Jersey’s governor plans to discuss the matter with the university. The controversy also revived a past case involving a $150,000 jury award over a pregnant assistant coach’s firing, which Hermann says she misspoke about regarding a video.

Corey Griffin, a friend of the man who inspired the Ice Bucket Challenge, died in a diving accident off Nantucket shortly after helping raise $100,000 for ALS charities. The 27-year-old was pulled from the harbor by an off-duty lifeguard and later pronounced dead. The viral campaign, started by Pete Frates and his former teammates, has drawn widespread participation and significantly boosted donations to the ALS Association. The article highlights Griffin's dedicated fundraising efforts and the challenge's success in raising millions for the cause.

The article uses the NFL harassment case between Richie Incognito and Jonathan Martin as a springboard to explore the broader issue of toxic friendships. It explains that such relationships often lack mutual respect and can be marked by competition, belittlement, or a harmful dynamic that mirrors unresolved personal issues. Experts suggest that while ending a long-standing friendship is difficult due to shared history and mutual friends, it may be necessary if the relationship consistently brings one down. They advise trying to create distance first, and if that fails, ending the friendship thoughtfully and directly rather than impulsively.

Myanmar is undergoing a gradual, deliberate transition from decades of military rule and isolation toward political and economic openness, a shift widely seen as irreversible. The government has introduced reforms such as elections, press freedom, and foreign investment, while still navigating deep internal divisions, including ethnic conflict and communal violence. The country is actively courting global powers to reduce its heavy reliance on China, attracting investment from the U.S., Japan, India, and Europe. Despite immense potential in tourism, agriculture, and energy, Myanmar faces major hurdles in infrastructure, institutional capacity, and reconciling a still-powerful military with democratic aspirations.

Published in 1971, “Our Bodies, Ourselves” grew out of discussions among a small group of women in Boston and became a landmark feminist health guide, selling millions of copies worldwide. The book broke taboos by candidly addressing topics such as sex, abortion, lesbianism, and masturbation, which sparked bans and outrage but also filled a critical gap in women’s health information. In an interview, longtime editor Judy Norsigian reflected on the book’s feminist roots, the progress made against sexism and medical paternalism, and the persistent challenges women still face, including poverty and violence. The latest edition updates sexual and reproductive health across the lifespan, adds new material on gender identity, and remains a trusted resource amid widespread misinformation.

The EU’s new sanctions against Russia, triggered by the downing of Flight MH17, include a ban on future arms deals, though existing contracts like France’s Mistral warship sale are exempt. Russia is largely self-sufficient in defense production, so the embargo will not immediately weaken its military, especially since its main arms customers, India and China, are not taking part. However, the loss of European high-tech defense electronics and Ukrainian subcontractors could create longer-term problems for Russia’s defense industry.

The article argues that the Royal Navy’s effectiveness stems not from rigid command but from cultivating “soft skills” such as trust, respect, and cheerfulness, which are forms of emotional intelligence. These qualities, rather than technical management, are what motivate people and build resilient, high-performing teams. The author applies this military philosophy to business, urging leaders to develop a strong culture, clear intent, and genuine care for employees, especially in tough times. Ultimately, improving workplace leadership through these principles boosts employee engagement, productivity, and commercial success.

Under Xi Jinping, China has unexpectedly pursued a more assertive and proactive foreign policy, moving away from the traditional reactive stance of his predecessors. This new approach is marked by a willingness to challenge U.S. influence in Asia, as seen in the East China Sea and South China Sea, and to introduce new diplomatic language like the "Chinese dream" and "new type of great power relations." Xi has also expanded China's engagement in Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Korean Peninsula, prioritizing national interests and energy security over old mantras of non-interference. Overall, his strategy signals a more self-confident China that is increasingly willing to act on the global stage and redefine its role as a great power.

The art world has made notable progress in recognizing female artists, with more women nominated for major prizes, leading major museums, and achieving high auction prices than in the past. However, significant gender disparities remain, particularly in the upper echelons of the market, where a "glass ceiling" persists and art by women still sells for less than work by men. Online sales platforms and certain museums are helping democratize access and visibility for female artists, while some curators say gender balance is becoming more intuitive. Still, many contemporary female artists prefer to focus on their work rather than emphasize gender, even as economic gaps linger.

Mark Shuttleworth, the South African space tourist and tech entrepreneur, recalled how Nelson Mandela used a phone call from space to brighten the final days of a terminally ill teenage girl, showing his selfless focus on others. Shuttleworth said Mandela’s real lesson was the need to seek the good in everyone, even in divided or troubled times. He also spoke about the future of commercial space travel, predicting suborbital flights within two years and interplanetary trips within a decade. Back on Earth, his company Canonical had just signed its first mobile partnership to bring its Ubuntu operating system to phones, positioning it to challenge major platforms.

Robert Ondrovic discovered his late father’s vintage photographs from the 1964 World’s Fair in Queens, New York, capturing both family moments and the event’s futuristic architecture. The images evoke nostalgia for a bygone era, with details like period clothing and the iconic IBM Pavilion. The discovery coincides with the fair’s 50th anniversary, and while the Unisphere still stands, volunteers are working to preserve the New York State Pavilion. Ondrovic shared the photos publicly as a way to remember the experience and celebrate the fair’s lasting legacy.

Dr. Robin Hanbury-Tenison argues that the most thrilling exploration opportunities are on Earth rather than in space, pointing to the rainforest canopy, undiscovered caves, and coral reefs as key frontiers. He emphasizes that true exploration means contributing to science and conservation, not just visiting as a tourist. By reading deeply, respecting local communities, and offering practical help at research stations, anyone can become an explorer-scientist, even without a science degree. This mission is increasingly urgent because habitats like rainforests are being destroyed before their secrets are fully understood.

Edward Snowden, the former NSA contractor living in exile in Russia, will appear remotely at this year's South by Southwest Interactive Festival in Austin. He is scheduled to speak with an ACLU technologist about mass surveillance and how the tech community can protect user privacy through new tools. The festival has also lined up teleconference appearances from Glenn Greenwald and Julian Assange, both of whom helped publicize Snowden's leaked documents. The event highlights privacy and government surveillance as central themes of this year's programming.

A man wanted for what authorities call Florida’s largest gold robbery was arrested in Belize while trying to cross the border illegally. He allegedly stole over 100 pounds of gold flakes from a victim in 2012, and his court-ordered ankle monitor placed him at the crime scene. After being released on bond, he fled and remained at large until immigration officials captured him in 2014. He now faces multiple charges, though the stolen gold has never been recovered.

Candace Cameron Bure’s new book focuses on managing her roles as a working wife and mother, while also addressing her long marriage to hockey player Val Bure. She clarifies that her use of “submissive” is based on a biblical definition, meaning strength under control rather than weakness, and that she willingly lets her husband lead major family decisions. She emphasizes that she still voices her opinions and considers herself equal in importance, though their roles differ. The former “Full House” star also hints that a reunion remains possible if fans want it.

The killing of Ukrainian nationalist commander Oleksandr Muzychko has deepened tensions within the country, with his Right Sector allies accusing the interior minister of murder and alleging that corrupt officials may be acting on Moscow’s behalf. His funeral drew emotional mourners who viewed him as a hero and a Robin Hood figure, while the group’s leader warned that any Russian invasion would be met with guerrilla warfare. The incident highlights the fragile unity of Ukraine’s post-revolution leadership and the growing influence of radical nationalist forces, which have alarmed both Russia and the West. Amid fears of a Russian incursion, Right Sector is positioning itself as a defender of national independence, even as concerns about its ideology persist.

Vice principal Kang Min Kyu, who survived the Sewol ferry disaster, took his own life two days later, overwhelmed by guilt after many students died. In a note, he accepted blame for the tragedy, saying the trip was his idea, and requested that his body be cremated and his ashes scattered where the ferry sank. His quiet funeral drew students and mourners who defended him, noting his deep care for students and arguing he should not be blamed. His death sparked widespread sorrow and sympathy across South Korea.

Sid Caesar, a pioneering comedian of 1950s television, has died at age 91 after years of health problems. He was best known for "Your Show of Shows" and "Caesar's Hour," which featured groundbreaking sketch comedy, parodies, and pantomime, and launched the careers of legendary writers like Mel Brooks, Neil Simon, and Carl Reiner. Caesar's innovative work helped shape TV comedy and influenced later shows and films, though the intense pressure of live weekly production led to a long struggle with addiction that he eventually overcame. He is remembered as a comic genius who brought laughter to audiences worldwide.

Pamplona’s San Fermín festival is a unique, chaotic celebration that must be experienced firsthand, as Ernest Hemingway’s grandson explains. Hemingway was drawn there after hearing Gertrude Stein’s symbolic interpretation of bullfighting, and he returned nine times, finding in the fiesta the danger, camaraderie, and release from writing that he needed. The festival’s essence is spontaneity and impermanence, captured in the local saying that the party is in the streets. For the author, experiencing Pamplona brought him closer to his grandfather and taught him to embrace life’s unpredictability and creativity.

The Gaia space telescope has been launched to create the most detailed three-dimensional map of the Milky Way, using a billion-pixel camera capable of measuring stellar distances with extraordinary precision. The mission will chart roughly a billion stars, along with millions of quasars and numerous objects in our solar system, at a total cost of about one billion euros. By building on earlier space observatories, Gaia aims to provide a reliable foundation for understanding the galaxy’s structure, history, and evolution. It is also expected to discover thousands of exoplanets, supporting future efforts to study atmospheres and seasonal changes on distant worlds.

Photographer David Gulden is known for raw, black-and-white images of East African wildlife, capturing animals in unglamorous, intimate moments rather than idealizing them. His work, praised for combining documentary and fine-art traditions, reflects deep patience—he spent three years using a camera trap to photograph the elusive mountain bongo. Gulden’s path began with a childhood safari and mentorship from photographer Peter Beard, and he now lives near Nairobi, where he can quickly reach wilderness areas. He favors unusual angles and techniques, once even having a rhino charge his vehicle, an experience that left him uninjured but destroyed his gear in a separate fire.

Viator is launching two new “Game of Thrones” themed tours this summer, one in Dubrovnik, Croatia, and another in Belfast, Northern Ireland. The Dubrovnik tour highlights King’s Landing locations such as the city walls and Lovrijenac Fortress, while the Belfast tour includes sites like Dark Hedges, Dragonstone, and the Giant’s Causeway. The tours are independent of the show and feature guides knowledgeable about the series. Prices start at $72 for the Dubrovnik walking tour and $110 for the Belfast excursion.

Shaquille O’Neal has shifted his focus from basketball to fighting diabetes, a cause that became personal after watching family members struggle with the disease. He is especially concerned about rising childhood obesity and stresses the importance of prevention through healthy eating and daily exercise. O’Neal also wants to help those already living with diabetes and has invested in a product designed to manage low blood sugar more healthily. His message emphasizes that taking action now is essential to reversing the trend.

The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation has pledged $50 million to combat the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, where more than 2,200 people have died, mainly in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The funds will support emergency response efforts and accelerate work on treatments, vaccines, and diagnostics. The World Health Organization warns the outbreak is worsening, especially in Liberia, with new cases rising rapidly and treatment centers quickly overwhelmed. In response, the United States has announced additional funding and health worker support, while President Obama called the crisis a national security priority, citing the risk of the virus mutating and spreading more easily.

After years of campaigning, same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales, with the first ceremonies taking place at midnight. Among the first couples were Andrew Wale and Neil Allard, who had waited five years to marry and saw the day as a historic milestone. While the law marks significant progress, the couple noted that discrimination still exists, and they hoped their wedding would send a message of support to LGBTQ people in countries where such rights remain under threat.

Elite sprinters Tyson Gay and Asafa Powell have both tested positive for banned substances, marking another major doping scandal in track and field. Gay, who withdrew from the world championships, said he unknowingly put his trust in someone and was let down, while Powell tested positive for the stimulant oxilofrine and insisted he has never intentionally cheated. Jamaican sprinter Sherone Simpson also revealed a positive test for the same substance. The cases follow the recent doping suspension of Veronica Campbell-Brown, casting a shadow over the sport ahead of the world championships in Moscow.

A Gaza fisherman discovered a large bronze statue in the sea, initially mistaking it for a body, and later realized it was an ancient artifact believed to depict the Greek god Apollo. The statue was taken by a local armed group and listed for sale online, prompting an investigation by Gaza’s antiquities and interior authorities for illegal trafficking. Officials have since secured the statue, rejecting any sale, and plan to restore and display it, with international help offered from Geneva. Meanwhile, the fisherman, who hoped the find would make him rich, now seeks a reward instead.

Amid renewed international calls for a ceasefire, violence in Gaza has escalated, with Palestinian officials reporting dozens killed, including children at a refugee camp and hospital, while Israel confirmed the deaths of ten of its soldiers. Prime Minister Netanyahu vowed to continue the military campaign until Hamas’s tunnel network is destroyed, rejecting negotiations while attacks persist. World leaders, including the U.S. and European allies, urged a lasting truce, but diplomatic efforts have stalled, with Palestinians demanding an Israeli withdrawal. Meanwhile, Israel denied responsibility for a deadly strike on a U.N. school, claiming an errant mortar round was fired at militants in the area.

The Gaza zoo in Jabalya has been devastated by the recent Israel-Hamas conflict, leaving many animals dead and survivors traumatized and starving. Staff lack the funds to feed or properly care for the remaining animals, with lions reportedly going up to 15 days without food. A CNN crew provided some relief by buying chickens for the lions, but the zoo’s broader situation remains dire. While the park is allegedly linked to Hamas and may have been near rocket launchers, the immediate crisis is that surviving animals face hunger and disease amid Gaza’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.

A major U.S. pertussis outbreak in 2012 highlighted the disease's serious threat to infants, who are too young to be fully vaccinated and often catch it from family members, especially parents. Adults and adolescents may have mild, lingering coughs and unknowingly spread the infection to vulnerable babies, leading to severe illness and even death in young children. Health experts recommend that adults, particularly those in close contact with infants, get a Tdap booster because childhood immunity fades over time. A public awareness campaign encourages parents, grandparents, and caregivers to get vaccinated to help protect infants from this potentially fatal disease.

A new book by Lillian Tong showcases the Pinang Peranakan Mansion’s collection of Straits Chinese gold jewelry, highlighting the intricate fusion of Malay, Chinese, Indian, and European influences. These ornate pieces, often combining materials and motifs from across the world, served as symbols of status and identity for wealthy Peranakan families. The jewelry reflects a broader cultural blend in architecture, fashion, and design that peaked between 1900 and 1940. Ultimately, the collection illustrates a creative era when designers freely mixed diverse traditions into distinctive, hybrid works.

Retired Marine General John Allen has been appointed by Secretary of State John Kerry to coordinate the international coalition against ISIS, a role that returns him to a challenging mission. Allen brings extensive relevant experience, including commanding U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan and leading the Sunni Awakening strategy in Iraq that turned tribal forces against al Qaeda. His career also includes diplomatic work on Israeli-Palestinian peace efforts and senior posts at U.S. Central Command. Although his nomination for NATO commander was briefly derailed by the Petraeus email scandal, he was cleared of any wrongdoing before retiring.

A South Carolina teen was told by the DMV to remove his makeup for his driver’s license photo, with officials citing a policy that bars applicants from altering their appearance in a way that could misrepresent their identity. The 16-year-old, who identifies as gender non-conforming and regularly wears makeup, was reportedly told he looked like he was wearing a disguise and did not look “like a boy should.” A transgender rights group has stepped in, arguing that the DMV’s action violated his free speech rights and that he should be allowed to be photographed as himself. The group is urging the DMV to let him retake the photo without forcing him to change his appearance.

The article discusses the gender pay gap debate sparked by the firing of New York Times executive editor Jill Abramson, with the publisher denying pay disparity played a role. It highlights Boston’s ambitious initiative to become the first U.S. city to eliminate the wage gap through a voluntary corporate compact and a detailed set of strategies. Experts argue that closing the gap is not only about fairness but also economic competitiveness, as women increasingly dominate the highly educated workforce. The piece also notes that women often avoid salary negotiations due to social backlash, underscoring the need for systemic change alongside individual action.

The article highlights the growing adoption of "genius hour" in schools, a concept inspired by Google’s 20% time policy that gives students dedicated class time to explore their own passions. Teachers use this approach to encourage student-driven learning, creativity, and risk-taking, emphasizing that failure is an acceptable and valuable part of the process. Examples include students researching sneaker preferences, writing novels, and building projects, with educators noting that this freedom helps students become more engaged, confident, and independent learners. While some students initially struggle with the open-ended format, teachers and parents see it as a meaningful break from rigid, test-focused education.

George Clooney says married life feels wonderful after tying the knot with lawyer Amal Alamuddin in a small Venice ceremony. The couple’s wedding is featured in People magazine with exclusive photos, highlighting her custom Oscar de la Renta gown and his Giorgio Armani tuxedo. Around 100 guests, including celebrities like Bono and Matt Damon, attended the intimate event, which the bride’s mother described as legendary. The couple, who share interests in travel and humanitarian work, say they are excited about their future together.

A Florida jury acquitted George Zimmerman of all charges in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, accepting his claim of self-defense after a trial that reignited intense national debate over race and justice. The verdict drew emotional reactions from both families, with Martin’s parents expressing grief while Zimmerman’s relatives voiced relief but acknowledged the tragedy. Authorities and advocates urged calm, though concerns were raised about Zimmerman’s safety, and the NAACP called for federal civil rights charges. The case highlighted broader questions about racial profiling and the treatment of young Black men in the criminal justice system.

George Zimmerman, in a recent CNN interview, said he still faces death threats and controversy but believes only God is his ultimate judge. He maintains he acted in self-defense in Trayvon Martin's death, though he regrets going out that night and cannot discuss the killing due to a federal investigation. Since his acquittal, he has faced legal troubles, a canceled charity boxing match, and criticism for selling his artwork, while expressing a desire to become a lawyer to prevent similar injustices. He also denied racism, saying critics don't know the real him.

George Zimmerman’s parents are suing comedian Roseanne Barr for posting their home address and phone number on Twitter, claiming the disclosure forced them to flee their home and live in hiding. The lawsuit alleges Barr’s tweet was a reckless call for vigilante action that caused severe emotional distress and invaded their privacy. The post came shortly after their son was involved in the fatal shooting of Trayvon Martin, a case that had drawn intense national scrutiny. Barr has not yet publicly responded to the lawsuit.

Shellie Zimmerman, wife of acquitted Trayvon Martin shooter George Zimmerman, pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor perjury charge. She was sentenced to one year of probation, 100 hours of community service, and must apologize in writing to the judge. Prosecutors said she falsely claimed the family was indigent during her husband’s 2012 bond hearing, though he actually had around $135,000. The plea came as George Zimmerman’s legal team prepared to seek reimbursement from Florida for trial expenses, a request allowed under state law for acquitted defendants.

Jury selection has begun in Florida for the trial of George Zimmerman, the neighborhood watch volunteer charged with second-degree murder in the 2012 shooting of unarmed teenager Trayvon Martin. The case, which ignited national debates over race and gun laws, stems from Zimmerman’s claim that he acted in self-defense after Martin attacked him. Initially released without charges, Zimmerman was later prosecuted after public outcry led to the appointment of a special prosecutor. He has pleaded not guilty and remains free on bond while his defense prepares to argue that the shooting was justified.

Aimee Copeland, the Georgia woman who contracted a severe flesh-eating infection after a zip-line accident, has reached a major milestone by breathing entirely without ventilator support. Her father reports that she remains in good spirits, joking and showing her usual personality despite having undergone multiple amputations, including both hands and her remaining foot. The family has praised her extraordinary courage, noting that she accepted the surgeries with remarkable composure. The article also mentions another woman, Lana Kuykendall, who is recovering from the same rare bacterial infection after giving birth to twins.

Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble believes the eurozone is in much better shape than before, though its problems are not fully resolved, and he does not foresee additional bailouts. He stressed that a stronger Europe depends on all member states boosting competitiveness rather than relying on financial support from others. His remarks come as Germans prepare to vote in September, with many weary of funding rescues for struggling eurozone nations. While the eurozone is showing signs of recovery and market confidence has improved, Schaeuble acknowledged Greece may need further help, but ruled out new debt haircuts.

German officials are seeking about $8,000 from Justin Bieber to cover expenses for the capuchin monkey he left behind in Munich after bringing it on tour without proper documentation. The costs include the animal’s care, vaccinations, and transport; the monkey, named Mally, is now housed at a zoo in northern Germany. Since Bieber missed the deadline to reclaim the pet, it became government property, and authorities made the payment demand public after failing to reach him. He will need to settle the bill when he next enters Germany, or he could be denied entry or have other property seized.

German prosecutors have charged a 93-year-old man as an accessory to murder in at least 300,000 deaths at Auschwitz, where he allegedly worked as camp staff. His duties included removing luggage from arriving prisoners and counting cash from their belongings, which helped the Nazis profit from the killings. The charges focus on the deportation of around 425,000 Hungarian Jews in 1944, at least 300,000 of whom were murdered. A regional court will now decide whether the case goes to trial.

President Vladimir Putin reportedly told German Chancellor Angela Merkel that he had ordered a partial pullback of Russian troops from the border with Ukraine, a move that could ease tensions following Russia’s annexation of Crimea. The United States called the reported withdrawal a welcome preliminary step but urged Russia to speed it up and engage with Kyiv. Meanwhile, Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev visited Crimea to announce economic integration measures, including higher salaries and a special economic zone. Despite the apparent de-escalation signal, Ukrainian officials said Russian forces were still repositioning, and Western leaders remained cautious about Moscow’s intentions.

Germany's World Cup-winning captain Philipp Lahm has announced his retirement from international football, just days after lifting the trophy in Brazil. The 30-year-old, who earned 113 caps over a decade, will continue playing for Bayern Munich. His decision, revealed in an open letter, drew widespread praise from coach Joachim Löw, teammates, and Chancellor Angela Merkel, who lauded his leadership and versatility. Lahm retires at the peak of his career, having also captained Germany since 2010 and played a key role in their triumph.

Gerry Conlon, one of the Guildford Four wrongly convicted for the 1974 IRA pub bombings in England, has died in Belfast at age 60 after a period of illness. He spent 15 years in prison before the convictions were overturned in 1989, and his fight for justice was dramatized in the film *In the Name of the Father*. Britain formally apologized in 2005, acknowledging the case as a miscarriage of justice. Tributes from political figures praised Conlon as a tireless campaigner for justice who later supported other victims of wrongful conviction.

The article examines the powerful inner circle surrounding Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, highlighting how family members have become increasingly central to the regime as pressure on it has grown. It profiles key relatives, including his influential mother Anisa, his British-born wife Asma, his hard-line younger brother Maher who commands elite military units, and his sister Bushra, who wields behind-the-scenes political influence. The piece also notes the roles of brother-in-law Asef Shawkat, who was killed in a 2012 bombing, and the deaths of Bashar's two brothers, which ultimately paved his own path to the presidency. Overall, it portrays a ruling dynasty that has relied on family loyalty to maintain its decades-long grip on power.

The article marks the 150th anniversary of the Battle of Gettysburg, a pivotal and bloody clash in July 1863 that ended with Confederate forces retreating. It highlights the establishment of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, where Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address, and the later creation of the Gettysburg National Military Park, now a major historic site with thousands of monuments and visitors. The piece also includes practical visitor information, such as tours and fees, and features a park ranger who shares personal reflections on the battlefield's historic landscapes and the enduring significance of sacrifice.

Three Ghanaian entrepreneurs turned a classroom project into Dropifi, a customer-feedback tool designed to replace traditional contact forms by providing businesses with insights, sentiment analysis, and social media integration. Within about two years, the startup became the first African company accepted into Silicon Valley’s 500 Startups accelerator, a milestone the founders say exceeded their original ambition of building a global company from Ghana. Their early success was fueled by winning startup competitions, which brought initial funding and eventually connected them with 500 Startups’ founder. Now serving thousands of clients worldwide, the team aims to strengthen its presence in the U.S. and international markets before eventually becoming a leader in Africa.

After more than five years in captivity, Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit was freed in exchange for over 1,000 Palestinian prisoners, sparking widespread joy across Israel and among Jewish communities worldwide. His release followed years of public campaigns, including protests, marches, and international calls for his freedom. Shalit thanked Egypt for mediating the deal and expressed hope that it would advance the peace process, while also saying he would support releasing Palestinian prisoners as long as they did not return to fighting Israel. Despite the celebration, many Israelis felt bittersweet emotions, as the agreement meant freeing prisoners convicted of involvement in attacks against Israelis.

Russell Johnson, the actor famed for playing the Professor on “Gilligan’s Island,” has died at age 89 from natural causes at his Washington state home, surrounded by family. Although he had a varied career in film and television, including sci-fi classics and Westerns, he remained best known for the sitcom role. A World War II veteran, he used the G.I. Bill to study acting and later advised young performers to focus on preparation and perseverance. His former co-star Tina Louise paid tribute, saying he would be remembered as part of American pop culture history.

A 4-year-old girl who was abducted, raped, and severely injured in central India has died in a hospital, prompting renewed anger across the country. Police arrested a 35-year-old man who allegedly confessed to the assault. The case follows the recent rape of a 5-year-old in New Delhi and comes months after the fatal gang rape of a young woman on a bus, which had already sparked nationwide protests. The incidents have intensified public outrage and drawn renewed attention to India's high number of reported child rape cases.

An 11-year-old Christian girl in Islamabad was arrested on blasphemy charges after allegedly burning pages of the Quran while collecting paper for cooking fuel. Police say she is illiterate and unaware the pages were from the holy book, while reports that she has Down syndrome remain unconfirmed and were denied by local authorities. A mob of about 150 people threatened to burn Christian homes, prompting other families to flee. Pakistan’s president has requested an urgent report and warned against misuse of the blasphemy law, while critics and politician Imran Khan condemned the arrest and demanded her release.

At Jared Loughner’s sentencing, Mark Kelly, speaking for his wife Gabrielle Giffords, condemned politicians for avoiding meaningful action on gun laws and for being intimidated by the NRA. He noted that Loughner legally obtained a high-capacity firearm despite a history of troubling behavior, while Giffords continues to recover from severe injuries. The article argues that closing loopholes like unlicensed private gun sales and barring high-risk individuals—such as violent misdemeanants and repeat alcohol offenders—would reduce gun violence. These measures are backed by most gun owners and even many NRA members, contradicting the notion that such reforms are politically dangerous.

Actor Cory Monteith, best known for his role as Finn Hudson on “Glee,” was found dead in his Vancouver hotel room at age 31; police said foul play was not suspected, and an autopsy was scheduled. Colleagues remembered him as a warm, dedicated presence on set and the emotional core of the show. Monteith had been open about past substance abuse and had entered rehab earlier that year. Tributes poured in from castmates, while his girlfriend Lea Michele asked for privacy during the difficult time.

A massage therapist who accused John Travolta of assault at the Beverly Hills Hotel has retained Gloria Allred, one day after being dropped from a federal lawsuit over date confusion. The original suit now proceeds only with a second accuser from an Atlanta hotel, whose lawyer insists he has strong evidence and witnesses. Travolta’s legal team dismisses both claims as baseless, noting the first accuser’s timeline was disproven and arguing the second accuser’s own emails do not mention Travolta. The case remains contentious, with the actor’s attorney confident the remaining allegations will also collapse.

The new "Godzilla" has generated strong anticipation, but critics are divided on the final result. Many reviewers feel the human storyline—featuring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Taylor-Johnson—is weak, overly dramatic, and poorly connected to the monster action. However, the creature sequences and director Gareth Edwards' approach to building tension and awe have earned praise, with some calling it a satisfying summer blockbuster. The film's distinctive sound design, which used massive speakers and slowed-down roars, also adds to its unique appeal.

Food waste and obesity have risen in parallel, driven by larger portions and a tendency to consume more than our bodies need. This waste carries severe environmental costs, including squandered water resources, significant greenhouse gas emissions, and billions in economic losses, with the problem extending beyond the U.S. to countries like Canada and Britain. However, the issue is entirely preventable through smarter consumption, smaller portions, composting, and redirecting surplus food to those in need. Individual choices and industry efforts together can reduce waste and create lasting global benefits.

For tennis legends Steffi Graf and Andre Agassi, their Olympic gold medals mean more than any Grand Slam title. Graf’s 1988 Seoul victory was especially historic because she won all four majors that same year, creating the “Golden Slam,” while Agassi cherished his emotional 1996 triumph on home soil in Atlanta. Both describe the Olympic podium experience as uniquely powerful, with Agassi also honoring his father’s Olympic dreams. They remain deeply connected to the Games, and Agassi sees Wimbledon’s Olympic tennis as a thrilling challenge for today’s stars like Djokovic and Federer.

A golf cart operator at the U.S. Open was arrested after allegedly striking a state trooper and fleeing the scene. The driver, 59-year-old Thomas Lineberry, faces multiple charges including felony assault on an officer, hit-and-run, impaired driving, and resisting arrest. The trooper suffered a minor leg injury and was treated, while Lineberry was released after posting a $3,000 bond. NBC Sports confirmed the individual was a volunteer who is no longer assisting with the production, and said it would wait for the full facts before commenting further.

Alicia Rhett, one of the last surviving cast members of “Gone With the Wind,” has died at age 98 in Charleston, South Carolina. She played India Wilkes in the 1939 classic but chose not to pursue Hollywood fame, instead returning to Charleston to build a career as an artist. Rhett was also known for her deep Southern roots, being the great-granddaughter of a prominent secessionist senator. She passed away peacefully of natural causes, surrounded by friends.

Once hailed as a transformative leader for Nigeria, President Goodluck Jonathan has seen his popularity collapse within months due to mounting crises. His decision to end fuel subsidies sparked widespread protests, while his handling of Boko Haram violence and perceived indecisiveness have drawn heavy criticism. Supporters argue his cautious, consultative style is misunderstood, but many Nigerians feel change is coming too slowly. The once-celebrated "man of the people" now faces deep public disillusionment and accusations of weak leadership.

Tooth decay is a widespread chronic disease influenced by both genetics and environment. About 60% of cavity risk is linked to genetic factors, including sweet preference, enamel strength, taste perception, saliva composition, and oral bacteria. The remaining 40% comes from environmental factors, with sugary drinks being the biggest contributor and fluoride the strongest protective measure. Good dental hygiene and fluoride exposure remain essential, but genetics can make some people more vulnerable than others.

Google has launched a new subscription music service, Google Play All Access, at its I/O conference. It merges a vast catalog with users' uploaded music and offers personalized recommendations through its Listen Now feature, which learns listening habits over time. The service also includes human-curated radio stations and gives users more control over upcoming songs compared to rivals like Pandora. Priced at $9.99 per month after a free trial, it has no free, ad-supported tier.

Nevada has become the first state to grant a license for self-driving cars, with Google receiving the initial approval. The autonomous vehicles rely on cameras, sensors, and detailed mapping to navigate without a driver, though a person can still take control if needed. Google had already completed over 200,000 miles of computer-driven testing before the state issued the special red license plate featuring an infinity symbol. For now, these vehicles are limited to testing, but Nevada plans to introduce green plates for autonomous cars once they become available to the public.

Google is adding prescription lenses and new Titanium frame designs to Google Glass, responding to the most requested feature and aiming to make the device more appealing before its broader release. The frames cost $225, with separate $150 sunglasses options, though the Glass hardware itself remains unchanged and is not designed for quick frame swapping. The move also raises concerns about wearers being unable to remove the glasses without losing vision, as well as ongoing issues with movie theaters and driving regulations. Google is addressing costs through a vision insurance partnership and plans to work with third-party eyewear companies in the future.

Google confirmed that the mysterious barge in San Francisco Bay is not a data center or party venue, but rather an experimental interactive space for showcasing new technology. The structure, built from shipping containers, is believed to serve as a floating showroom for products like Google Glass and may be part of a fleet of mobile event spaces. This disclosure follows days of speculation and secrecy, with the project reportedly intended to compete with Apple’s retail stores.

Google unveiled a new self-driving car prototype that is built entirely from scratch, with no steering wheel or pedals—just a stop-and-go button. It seats two passengers, has a top speed of 25 mph, and prioritizes safety through sensors that eliminate blind spots and detect objects far beyond human range. The vehicle’s friendly, smiley-face front design adds a playful touch. Google plans to build about 100 test models soon, with the technology expected to reach consumers by 2020.

Google has introduced an invite-only beta service called Google Domains, aimed at helping small businesses register and manage web addresses. This move puts it in direct competition with former partners like GoDaddy, which has struggled financially despite its large customer base. The service offers features such as free private registration and access to new domain endings, with plans to eventually integrate users into Google’s broader products and advertising ecosystem. Although the domain market has seen limited growth, Google’s existing influence could help it succeed where smaller rivals face challenges.

Gordon Willis, the celebrated cinematographer known as “The Prince of Darkness,” has died at age 82. He was renowned for his masterful use of light and shadow in landmark films such as “The Godfather,” “Manhattan,” and “All the President’s Men,” helping define the 1970s New Hollywood era. Though he received only two competitive Oscar nominations, he earned an honorary Academy Award in 2009 for his exceptional command of light, color, and motion. Willis was also remembered as a meticulous perfectionist who insisted on controlling every aspect of his images.

A leaked video from Pedrinhas prison in northeastern Brazil shows three inmates who had been beheaded, with other prisoners displaying the bodies. The jail had already faced scrutiny after 62 killings in 2013, and a judge reported severe abuses including overcrowding and sexual coercion of female visitors by gang leaders. The violence stems from conflict between rival inmate factions from the capital and the interior. In response, federal authorities agreed to move the leaders of these groups to federal prisons.

A secret federal surveillance court judge rejected the Obama administration’s bid to keep NSA phone metadata longer than the current five-year retention limit. The judge ruled that the government’s stated reason—preserving records for possible civil litigation—did not justify further privacy intrusions, especially since the civil plaintiffs had not asked for the data. The decision comes amid ongoing debate over bulk phone record collection, which was exposed by Edward Snowden and prompted Obama to propose moving such data out of direct government control.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force has issued draft recommendations advising against using hormone therapy—estrogen alone or with progestin—as a preventive measure for chronic disease in menopausal women. The guidance stems from evidence showing the risks, such as stroke, dementia, blood clots, and certain cancers, outweigh potential benefits like fracture prevention. It does not apply to younger women managing menopause symptoms or those who had surgical menopause. The recommendations reinforce a shift in practice that began after the Women’s Health Initiative trial revealed the therapy’s harms.

Indigenous hunter-gatherers in the Congo Basin have long lived on forest land without legal rights, leaving them vulnerable to displacement by logging, mining, and conservation projects. To address this, organizations like Rainforest Foundation UK and Cameroon’s Centre for Environment and Development train communities to map their traditional lands using GPS technology. These maps serve as evidence in negotiations with governments and companies, helping secure access to vital resources and even leading to greater rights within national parks. The mapping efforts also highlight that indigenous communities are effective stewards of the rainforest, supporting both their survival and conservation.

Senator Lindsey Graham easily won South Carolina’s Republican primary, clearing the 50% threshold to avoid a runoff despite a fragmented field of challengers. His victory contrasted sharply with House Majority Leader Eric Cantor’s upset loss in Virginia, though Graham also differed from Mississippi’s Thad Cochran, who faced a tea party-backed runoff. Graham benefited from a large campaign fund, a divided opposition, and a strong grassroots effort, while his critics focused on immigration reform and other past votes. He is now the heavy favorite in the general election against Democratic state Senator Brad Hutto.

Malcolm Shabazz, the 29-year-old grandson of civil rights leader Malcolm X, died in a Mexico City hospital after being severely beaten early Thursday morning. Authorities are treating the case as a homicide and have launched an investigation, noting he had been drinking at a recreational venue before the attack. His family mourned his loss, remembering him as kind and hopeful, while former acquaintances expressed shock and grief.

Greek authorities have charged a Roma couple with abducting a young girl known as Maria, whose DNA has not matched any profiles in Interpol’s global database. The case has sparked international interest, with agencies in the U.S., Canada, and Europe checking missing-child files against the girl’s details. The couple claims they adopted her from her biological mother, but police suspect documents were falsified and have suspended several officials. Investigators are also examining possible trafficking links and widespread discrimination against Roma communities as the search for her true identity continues.

Simone Battle, the 25-year-old singer and former "X Factor" contestant known for her role in the girl group G.R.L., was discovered dead in her West Hollywood residence on Friday. The exact cause of death has not been released, though an autopsy is scheduled for the weekend. In the wake of her passing, heartfelt tributes from her bandmates and Pitbull, who collaborated with the group on a hit single, praised her talent and generous spirit. Battle, a Los Angeles native who studied at USC, had credited Whitney Houston as her inspiration and also appeared in a 2012 film.

After nearly four decades, Exodus International, the prominent Christian ministry that claimed to help gay people change their sexual orientation, is closing its doors. The organization issued an apology to the LGBTQ community for the harm and judgment it had caused, with its president, Alan Chambers, expressing regret for his role in that hurt. The group had already been moving away from conversion therapy, a practice condemned by major psychological associations. In its place, the board plans to launch a new ministry called Reduce Fear, focused on fostering welcoming and loving church communities.

The article examines the risks and implications of releasing Guantanamo Bay detainees, focusing on the swap of five prisoners for Bowe Bergdahl. It notes that while some freed detainees have returned to terrorism—roughly 17% confirmed and more suspected—officials argue these particular men have been out of action for years and will be closely monitored by Qatar. The piece also highlights political disagreement, with critics like John McCain condemning the trade as dangerous, while the White House defends it as urgent and necessary. Additionally, it points out broader concerns about indefinite detention, the high cost of the facility, and the fact that many detainees were never charged with crimes.

Omar Khadr, the former Guantanamo detainee and only remaining Western prisoner there, has been transferred to Canada to serve the rest of his eight-year sentence at a maximum-security prison in Ontario. His case remains deeply divisive: some Canadians believe his punishment was too light, while others argue he should have been treated as a child soldier because he was captured at age 15 and allegedly abused. Khadr’s transfer followed a 2010 plea deal in which he admitted to killing a U.S. special forces soldier in Afghanistan, and U.S. officials said the repatriation took about a year to negotiate due to legal and political sensitivities. Human rights groups welcomed the move but urged Canada to investigate his claims of torture and address the violations he suffered.

Rapper Gucci Mane, legally Radric Davis, has been sentenced to over three years in federal prison after pleading guilty to illegally possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. The sentence also includes three years of supervised release, a $5,000 restitution payment, and a requirement to undergo mental health treatment upon release. The case stemmed from an incident in which police found him armed and making threats while under the influence, and officials emphasized his lengthy criminal history involving guns and violence. His legal troubles also include past arrests for assault, traffic violations, and a murder charge that was ultimately dropped.

Hungarian cuisine offers a rich, affordable blend of European and Middle Eastern influences, making it a paradise for food lovers but a challenge for dieters. The article highlights iconic dishes such as goulash, paprika chicken, stuffed cabbage, and savory pancakes, along with sweet treats like Dobos cake and chimney cake. It also provides specific restaurant recommendations across Budapest and other towns for experiencing these traditional foods. Overall, the piece serves as a culinary guide to Hungary's hearty, paprika-heavy comfort food and indulgent desserts.

Many people misjudge how much alcohol qualifies as heavy drinking; federal guidelines define it as eight or more drinks per week for women and 15 or more for men. Excessive drinking is linked to roughly 88,000 adult deaths annually, mostly among men, and can lead to chronic disease, addiction, and other harms. Definitions vary across agencies, and experts note the labels are imprecise, but binge drinking—especially among college students—is a growing concern due to risks like violence and impaired brain development. Drinking patterns matter too, as moderate daily drinking may carry some health benefits while heavy or binge drinking is clearly harmful.

A former Rutgers student, Dharun Ravi, was convicted on all charges, including bias intimidation and invasion of privacy, for secretly using a webcam to spy on his gay roommate, Tyler Clementi, who later died by suicide. Ravi now faces up to 10 years in prison and possible deportation to India, with sentencing scheduled for May. The case drew national attention to cyberbullying and helped prompt stricter New Jersey anti-bullying laws, as well as broader legal scrutiny of unauthorized webcam use in the social media era.

Airline alliances remain vital for profitability and business travel, with most major European carriers belonging to Star, Skyteam, or Oneworld. The entry of Qatar Airways into Oneworld marks the first time a Gulf carrier has joined an alliance, intensifying competition among the three groups as they vie for members and partnerships. While Emirates and Etihad prefer codeshare deals rather than full membership, this has created tensions—such as Air Berlin’s position between Etihad and Oneworld—though alliances are reluctant to lose members. Meanwhile, smaller carriers like Royal Brunei are choosing to retreat from direct competition with Gulf airlines and focus on regional strengths instead.

The Gulf of Mexico’s summer dead zone this year spans about 5,000 square miles, slightly smaller than the recent average but still far larger than the reduction target scientists hoped to reach by 2015. This oxygen-depleted area forms when nutrient runoff from agriculture and wastewater triggers algae blooms that consume oxygen, forcing fish and shrimp to flee while killing bottom-dwelling organisms and harming biodiversity. Researchers say little progress has been made toward shrinking the zone, and achieving meaningful change would require broader adoption of improved farming practices. The Gulf’s dead zone is the second-largest human-caused example worldwide, and such zones cost U.S. seafood and tourism industries tens of millions of dollars annually.

Authorities revised their account of the Las Vegas shooting, saying police officers—not the gunman’s wife—fired the fatal shot that killed Jerad Miller after he and Amanda Miller ambushed two officers and a Walmart shopper. The couple, who held anti-government views and left extremist symbols and messages on the officers' bodies, had prior police contacts without raising red flags. Investigators noted that while the Millers expressed anti-police ideology online, nothing predicted their violent turn. The fallen officers, Igor Soldo and Alyn Beck, were remembered as devoted family men and community-oriented police officers.

A gunman opened fire inside a crowded Colorado movie theater during a midnight screening of the new Batman film, killing 12 people and wounding dozens more. The suspect, identified as James Holmes, had dyed his hair red and told police he was "the Joker," and his apartment was found booby-trapped with incendiary devices. Police recovered multiple legally purchased weapons, including an AR-15 rifle, and believe the suspect acted alone. The attack has prompted heightened security at theaters and an outpouring of grief from officials and the film's cast and crew.

Two gunmen stormed a college campus in Kano, Nigeria, detonating explosives and opening fire in a lecture hall, killing at least 13 people before being fatally shot by police. The attack fits a pattern of violence by Boko Haram, the Islamist militant group whose name means “Western education is forbidden” and which has repeatedly targeted schools and students. The incident follows other deadly assaults on educational institutions, including the mass abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok and bombings at medical and polytechnic schools. Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan condemned the attack and vowed to strengthen security efforts against terrorism.

Loyalists of former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh launched mortar attacks on Sanaa’s international airport, forcing a halt to all flights. The unrest followed a major military overhaul by President Hadi that removed several Saleh relatives from top posts, including former air force commander Mohammed Saleh al-Ahmar, who refused to step down and threatened to target aircraft. In a related escalation, the residence of a senior opposition leader was shelled, with opposition figures calling it retaliation for the military reforms. The violence underscores ongoing tensions as opposition factions insist on complete military restructuring before engaging in national dialogue.

Gunmen attacked a remote mountaineering camp at the base of Nanga Parbat in Pakistan, killing 11 people, including 10 foreign tourists and a local guide. The victims were from China, Ukraine, Slovakia, Lithuania, Nepal, and the United States. The Pakistan Taliban claimed responsibility, saying the assault was revenge for a US drone strike that killed its deputy leader and a protest against international drone policy. Pakistan’s prime minister condemned the attack and ordered an investigation into the incident.

An American cardiologist of Pakistani origin was shot dead by gunmen on motorcycles while visiting a graveyard in Punjab, Pakistan, where he had been volunteering to treat heart patients. The doctor, a member of the persecuted Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, was killed alongside his wife and young son, though the motive remains unclear. His death marks the second killing of an Ahmadi in Pakistan this year, following the recent murder of a community member in police custody. The family plans to bury him in Canada, while community leaders condemned the ongoing hate and discrimination against Ahmadis in Pakistan.

Militants believed to be from Al-Shabaab carried out a deadly assault on Mpeketoni, a town near Kenya’s coast, attacking a World Cup viewing and nearby residential areas with guns and machetes. The Kenyan Red Cross reported at least 48 deaths, while officials blamed the al Qaeda-linked group, though no one immediately claimed responsibility. The attack follows a series of recent incidents, including grenade explosions in Nairobi that killed at least 10 people. Kenya has faced repeated Al-Shabaab retaliation since sending troops into Somalia in 2011.

Suspected Boko Haram militants carried out a nighttime attack on a college dormitory in northeastern Nigeria, killing at least 40 students.
