Italian Prime Minister Enrico Letta’s coalition comfortably survived a Senate confidence vote after Silvio Berlusconi abruptly abandoned his attempt to bring down the government, following signs that many of his own lawmakers would defy him. Letta had warned that political instability would deepen Italy’s economic troubles and derail needed reforms. A lower-house confidence vote was still expected, but Letta was not seen as seriously threatened there. Berlusconi’s political future now looks uncertain as a parliamentary committee prepares to consider stripping him of his Senate seat after his tax fraud conviction.

A secretly recorded video from a migrant center on Lampedusa, showing an aid worker spraying a naked man with treatment for scabies in view of others, has triggered widespread condemnation across Europe. Italian and EU officials called the scene degrading and unacceptable, prompting an official inquiry and promises to investigate conditions at the facility. The camp manager defended the staff, saying migrants had removed their own clothes to speed up the process, though he admitted the situation should have been handled differently. The controversy adds to ongoing concerns about overcrowding and substandard conditions at the island’s detention center, already under scrutiny after recent migrant shipwrecks.

A migrant boat carrying up to 500 people capsized and caught fire near the Italian island of Lampedusa, killing at least 110 people, with 154 survivors rescued. The vessel, believed to have departed from Libya with Eritreans, Somalis, and Ghanaians aboard, highlights the ongoing peril faced by refugees crossing the Mediterranean. The tragedy prompted calls from the UN, Amnesty International, and Pope Francis for stronger search-and-rescue efforts and greater action to prevent future loss of life. Lampedusa, located close to North Africa, has long been a primary entry point for migrants, and deadly shipwrecks in the region remain a recurring crisis.

Italian Prime Minister Enrico Letta has stepped down after less than a year in office, with the president accepting his resignation. His departure follows pressure from his own Democratic Party, led by Matteo Renzi, who argued that a new government was needed to push through reforms. Renzi is expected to be asked to form a new government, though his ability to secure support remains uncertain. The change adds to Italy’s long-running political instability, as no leader has been elected since 2008.

Lawyers for Silvio Berlusconi have formally requested that he be allowed to perform community service instead of serving a one-year tax fraud sentence, with a Milan judge expected to decide soon. Because of his age, the former prime minister will not go to prison, leaving community service or house arrest as the options. Berlusconi, a longtime polarizing figure in Italian politics, is also appealing a separate conviction for abuse of power and paying an underage prostitute. The request comes shortly after he was forced to reverse course and support the government in a confidence vote when his own party refused to follow his lead.

Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, gave birth to a baby boy on Monday, with Prince William by her side; the child is third in line to the British throne. The birth sparked widespread celebrations outside Buckingham Palace and drew congratulatory messages from leaders including Prime Minister David Cameron, the Obamas, and Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper. The baby’s name has not yet been announced, and he will be known as His Royal Highness Prince of Cambridge. The event also highlighted a recent change in succession rules ensuring a first-born daughter would not be overtaken by a younger brother, and retailers expect a significant boost from royal-themed merchandise.

Sir Robert Edwards, the British scientist who co-developed in vitro fertilization, has died at age 87. His work with Dr. Patrick Steptoe led to the birth of the world's first "test-tube baby" in 1978, and since then IVF has brought millions of children into the world. Despite facing criticism from religious groups, Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in 2010 and knighted the following year. He is remembered as a visionary researcher whose work transformed reproductive medicine.

Jackie Gingrich, the first wife of former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, has died in Atlanta at age 77 after a long battle with cancer. She was the mother of his two daughters, and their divorce in 1980 later became a recurring issue during his political career, especially his 2012 presidential run. A mathematics teacher and devout church volunteer, she was remembered as a determined, warm, and accomplished woman who prioritized family and faith. Her funeral home obituary highlighted her pioneering role as a woman in math and her dedication to her grandchildren and community.

The Jackson family feud escalated as Janet, Jermaine, and Randy Jackson confronted Michael Jackson’s children at the family home, with video showing a tense exchange over Paris Jackson’s phone use. The dispute centers on 82-year-old Katherine Jackson, who was reported missing but later found safe in Arizona, though her grandchildren say they still haven’t spoken to her. Sheriff’s deputies broke up a separate scuffle, and no arrests were made, but a battery report was filed. Meanwhile, authorities are investigating allegations that Katherine may have been emotionally and financially mistreated by family members, which she has denied.

Fans of Michael Jackson erupted in celebration outside the courthouse after a jury convicted Dr. Conrad Murray of involuntary manslaughter in the pop star’s death. Murray had administered the anesthetic propofol, which combined with sedatives to kill Jackson. Family members and supporters called the verdict a victory and said justice had been served, while online reactions mixed relief with sadness over the tragedy. Jackson’s estate also praised the jury’s decision, saying the justice system had worked.

An Egyptian court has again refused bail for three Al Jazeera journalists held on terrorism-related charges, a case widely condemned by human rights groups. The reporters—Peter Greste, Mohamed Fahmy, and Baher Mohamed—rejected accusations of links to the Muslim Brotherhood, insisting they were only doing their jobs. The hearing also highlighted concerns about Fahmy’s untreated shoulder injury and Baher’s wish to be present for his child’s birth. The trial has been postponed until April 10, amid broader concerns that Egypt is suppressing press freedom.

Iranian actress Marzieh Vafamehr has been freed after an appeals court reduced her one-year prison sentence to three months and overturned her 90-lash punishment. She had been convicted over her role in the film “My Tehran for Sale,” which included scenes showing her without a mandatory head covering and appearing to drink alcohol. Amnesty International and the film’s producers confirmed her release, with producers voicing support for artists facing punishment in Iran. Rights groups remain concerned, noting that several other filmmakers are still detained in Tehran’s Evin Prison.

By imprisoning Yulia Tymoshenko, President Yanukovych triggered broad international outrage and inadvertently strengthened the opposition, turning her into a powerful symbol of democratic resistance. The case has deepened geopolitical tensions, as Russia pushes Ukraine toward its customs union while the EU conditions a key trade agreement on her release. Yanukovych has hinted at legal changes that could free her, but parliament has resisted, leaving Ukraine’s democratic future uncertain. The episode has damaged the country’s reputation, raised concerns about judicial fairness, and forced a choice between closer European integration and isolation.

China’s anti-corruption campaign has reached its highest-ranking target yet with the investigation of former security chief Zhou Yongkang, signaling President Xi Jinping’s willingness to go after senior “tigers,” not just low-level “flies.” While the public largely supports the crackdown, there are concerns about political instability within the Communist Party and complaints from ordinary officials losing fringe benefits. Analysts argue that without deeper systemic reforms—such as public asset disclosure, an independent judiciary, and a free media—corruption will likely persist. The case underscores that building a clean, rule-of-law-based government remains an ongoing challenge.

James Avery, best known as Uncle Phil on “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,” has died at age 68 due to complications from open-heart surgery. His former co-stars paid tribute, remembering him as a beloved mentor and a groundbreaking presence for African Americans on television. Beyond the iconic sitcom, Avery had a wide-ranging career in film, TV, and voice acting, including roles in “L.A. Law,” “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles,” and an upcoming film at Sundance. He is survived by his wife, mother, and stepson.

James Patterson, one of the world’s most prolific and successful authors, continues to dominate bestseller lists with numerous books released yearly through collaborations with co-writers. Beyond writing, he is deeply committed to philanthropy, recently donating 200,000 books to troops overseas and advocating for children’s reading through initiatives like ReadKiddoRead.com. His upcoming novel, "Guilty Wives," follows four women accused of murder in France, while the film adaptation of his Alex Cross series, starring Tyler Perry, is also generating excitement. Patterson remains highly productive, drawing from a large reservoir of story ideas and maintaining a disciplined writing routine.

Jane Kean, best known for playing Trixie Norton in the 1966 revival of “The Honeymooners,” has died at age 90. She passed away in Burbank, California, after being hospitalized for a fall that caused a hemorrhagic stroke. Kean had a long career across stage and television, and she previously worked with Jackie Gleason in vaudeville before reuniting with him on the show. Her family remembered her as an independent and vibrant performer who remained active into her later years.

Former Japanese Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama visited South Korea to meet surviving comfort women and acknowledge Japan’s wartime atrocities, offering personal remorse for their suffering. The visit highlights the ongoing dispute, as survivors and Seoul demand a formal government apology and direct compensation, while Tokyo insists the matter was settled by a 1965 treaty. Murayama is remembered for his landmark 1995 apology, which current Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has suggested revising. Tensions remain high due to Abe’s nationalist actions and territorial disputes between the two countries.

A year after the devastating earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima nuclear disaster, Japanese Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda offered a somber reflection, emphasizing the need to learn from the accident and share its lessons internationally. He acknowledged criticism from an independent panel that Japan concealed the most severe risks, including fears of a possible Tokyo evacuation. On energy, Noda reaffirmed Japan’s shift away from nuclear dependence, with nearly all reactors offline and new investment in renewables, while warning that energy shortages could hurt the economy. He also highlighted pressing challenges such as reconstruction, a strong yen, heavy public debt, an aging population, and political instability, while defending his unpopular plan to raise the sales tax.

Japan’s nuclear regulator has upgraded the status of a radioactive water leak at the Fukushima Daiichi plant to a level 3 “serious incident” on the international nuclear event scale, marking the most severe alert since the 2011 disaster. The decision came after the government criticized the plant operator’s response as reactive and pledged to take a more active role in addressing the crisis. The operator, Tepco, continues to struggle with massive volumes of contaminated water, including groundwater seeping into the Pacific and hundreds of thousands of tons stored in temporary tanks, one of which was the source of the leak. The cause of the leak has not yet been identified.

Japan intervened in currency markets for the third time this year to weaken the yen after it hit its strongest level against the dollar since World War II. The finance minister said the move was necessary because an overly strong yen would harm the export-reliant economy, especially as it still recovers from the March earthquake and tsunami. The intervention briefly pushed the yen down, but analysts questioned how long the effect would last, noting that its success depends on whether Japan continues to act.

Japan has launched its largest warship since World War II, an 820-foot vessel designed to carry helicopters, though officials insist it is not an aircraft carrier and will not operate fighter jets. The ship’s debut comes amid ongoing territorial disputes with China over islands in the East China Sea, which have fueled military tensions and frequent confrontations between the two countries. China responded by warning Japan against military expansion and urging it to follow a path of peaceful development. The launch also coincided with the anniversary of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, a day marked by ceremonies and calls to remember the consequences of nuclear war.

Japan’s iconic Shinkansen, once a symbol of postwar innovation, is now aging and facing stiff competition from European and Chinese high-speed rail networks. In response, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe is championing maglev technology, which can reach far higher speeds and has already set world records. However, the proposed maglev line between Tokyo and Nagoya carries a massive price tag and faces skepticism due to Japan’s declining population and uncertain future demand. Japan is also pitching the technology to the U.S. for a New York–Washington route, but doubts remain about whether the project will gain traction.

Japan is considering a new safety measure to test breast milk from new mothers in Fukushima Prefecture for radiation, following public concern over the nuclear disaster. The plan is still being developed, and officials have not finalized details. Recent government surveys found trace amounts of radioactive cesium in some mothers’ milk, though experts say the levels were too low to harm infants. The proposal is part of broader safety efforts after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Japan has allocated $29 million from its tsunami reconstruction fund to bolster security for its whaling fleet, a decision that has drawn sharp criticism from Greenpeace, which argues the money should go to disaster victims. Fisheries officials defend the spending as vital support for a whaling-dependent community devastated by the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, noting local residents view whaling as central to their recovery. The fleet departed for its annual hunt with the largest Coast Guard escort ever provided, following last season’s disruption by Sea Shepherd activists. The move comes amid ongoing international opposition to Japanese whaling, including a legal challenge brought by Australia.

For the first time, aircraft have become involved in the ongoing territorial dispute between China and Japan over the East China Sea islands, after a Chinese patrol plane approached the area and prompted Japan to scramble fighter jets. The incident marks an escalation in tensions that have simmered since Japan’s government purchased the islands in September, leading to repeated incursions by Chinese ships and verbal standoffs with Japanese coast guard vessels. Japan called the flight “extremely regrettable” and lodged a diplomatic protest, while China said the plane was conducting a routine joint air-sea patrol to assert its sovereignty claim. The United States has urged a peaceful resolution but acknowledged the islands fall under its mutual defense treaty with Japan.

Two and a half years after the Fukushima disaster, the crippled plant is still leaking highly radioactive water, and the Japanese government has pledged $470 million to address the ongoing crisis after criticizing TEPCO's temporary, "whack-a-mole" approach. The leaks stem from hastily built storage tanks and contaminated groundwater seeping into the Pacific, with radiation readings far exceeding safe limits. Experts argue that TEPCO has lacked a sustainable long-term strategy, and proposed fixes like freezing the ground around the reactors are untested on this scale and not viable for decades. The most practical solution, they say, is to treat the contaminated water using existing technology and release it, since the vast ocean would quickly dilute it.The Fukushima plant remains dangerously unstable more than two years after the disaster, with TEPCO facing criticism for relying on makeshift fixes while radioactive water continues leaking from storage tanks and groundwater into the Pacific. The Japanese government has pledged $470 million to tackle the problem, but its proposed measures, including freezing the ground around the reactors, are untested and seen by experts as unsustainable long-term. Radiation levels near the leaking tanks are extremely high, posing risks to workers, though the contamination is not considered a direct threat to Tokyo. Experts argue the only viable approach is to treat the water with existing technology and release it into the ocean, where it would quickly dilute.

Turkey and Japan have signed a $22 billion agreement to construct a nuclear power plant in Turkey’s northern Sinop province, marking a significant boost for Japan’s nuclear sector after the 2011 Fukushima disaster. The project, led by Japanese and French firms, will use an advanced third-generation reactor design. Turkish and Japanese leaders emphasized that safety lessons from Fukushima have been incorporated, despite both countries being earthquake-prone. The deal also includes plans for a joint Turkish-Japanese technical university.

TEPCO has been effectively nationalized after the Japanese government approved a $12.5 billion bailout, giving it majority control of the utility, which was devastated by the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. The company has pledged a 10-year restructuring plan that includes major cost cuts, a proposed electricity rate increase, and efforts to restart some nuclear reactors. Meanwhile, Japan is currently without any nuclear power for the first time in 40 years, as all reactors remain offline. Government and business leaders warn that a prolonged nuclear shutdown could severely damage Japan's economy, with some describing the situation as a potential national crisis.

Japan announced it would release three Australian anti-whaling activists who boarded a Japanese patrol vessel in Antarctic waters, while insisting the annual whale hunt would continue. The activists were detained after climbing aboard to protest the hunt, but Japanese officials said they had not been violent and had no history of disruptive actions with Sea Shepherd. Australia, which opposes the hunt, said it had sought assurances for the men’s safety but acknowledged the incident occurred outside its territorial jurisdiction. Japan also lodged a diplomatic complaint urging Australia to prevent similar boardings in the future.

Japan has announced it will resume its controversial whale hunt in the Southern Ocean this winter, sending a Fisheries Agency patrol boat to protect its vessels from interference by the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society. The decision follows last season’s hunt being cut short after activists disrupted operations, though Japan maintains the program is for scientific research. Sea Shepherd has vowed to return with more than 100 people to block the fleet, while Australia has condemned the hunt and is pursuing legal action at the International Court of Justice to end it permanently.

Golfer Jason Day has revealed that eight members of his family, including his grandmother, an uncle, and six cousins, were killed when Typhoon Haiyan devastated the Philippines. In a statement, the world No. 18 expressed deep sadness and gratitude for support, while asking for privacy and urging awareness for relief efforts. The typhoon has left nearly 4,000 people dead, with many more still missing. Despite the tragedy, Day is expected to compete alongside Adam Scott at the World Cup of Golf in Melbourne.

Jay Z’s “Made in America” festival is expanding to take place in both Los Angeles and Philadelphia over Labor Day weekend, marking its first West Coast edition. While fans hoped for a joint announcement with Beyoncé, that didn’t happen, though the event is still significant, with Los Angeles expecting around 50,000 attendees. City officials acknowledged logistical hurdles in hosting the downtown LA event, and past festivals have brought major economic benefits to Philadelphia. The lineup hasn’t been revealed yet, but Jay Z hinted at diverse genres, leaving the possibility of Beyoncé performing again.

Jazz guitarist and vocalist Carline Ray has died in New York City at age 88. A Juilliard graduate, she first gained prominence with the all-female International Sweethearts of Rhythm and later performed with notable bandleaders such as Duke Ellington’s orchestra and Erskine Hawkins. Throughout her career, she advocated for greater recognition of women in jazz and was honored with several awards, including the Mary Lou Williams Women in Jazz Festival Award. She released her debut solo album in 2013 and is survived by her daughter and sister.

JB Holmes won the Wells Fargo Championship at Quail Hollow, his first PGA Tour victory since 2008, finishing one stroke ahead of Jim Furyk. His win was especially meaningful given his recovery from brain surgery in 2011 and later ankle and elbow injuries. Justin Rose and Phil Mickelson failed to mount serious challenges, while Brendon de Jonge and Rory McIlroy impressed with strong comebacks despite earlier poor rounds. Holmes held his nerve under pressure, capping a remarkable return to top form.

Jeffrey Pollack, a filmmaker and producer known for directing “Booty Call” and “Above the Rim” and for producing “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,” was found dead on a jogging trail in Hermosa Beach, California, at age 54. Police said foul play is not suspected, and the cause of death has not yet been determined. Beyond his work on the hit sitcom, Pollack partnered with Benny Medina in Handprint Entertainment, representing stars like Mariah Carey, Tyra Banks, and Jennifer Lopez. He also collaborated with Jeff Beacher on the Beacher’s Madhouse shows, with Beacher remembering him as a close friend and mentor.

Jenson Button initially criticized Lewis Hamilton after their collision at the German Grand Prix, but later admitted he had overreacted once he reviewed the race. Hamilton, who charged from 20th to finish third, damaged his front wing while trying to pass Button and also made contact with Valtteri Bottas. Hamilton apologized for the incident, explaining he believed Button was giving him room to overtake. Nico Rosberg won the race, extending his championship lead over Hamilton to 14 points, though Hamilton remains confident in the title fight.

Former U.S. Representative Jesse Jackson Jr. was sentenced to 30 months in prison for conspiring to misuse about $750,000 in campaign funds for personal luxuries such as vacations, furs, and collectibles. His wife, Sandi Jackson, received a 12-month sentence for filing false tax returns related to the scheme. The judge acknowledged their genuine remorse and cooperation, handing down a lighter sentence than prosecutors requested. Jackson apologized in court, saying he misled the American people, and expressed hope for redemption.

A group of intoxicated teenagers boarded a school bus in Sydney and subjected Jewish children, ages 5 to 12, to anti-Semitic abuse and violent threats, leaving the students terrified and in tears. The youths fled before police arrived, but five were arrested the next day and later released to their parents without charges, while police awaited a sixth suspect. Authorities described the attack as random and opportunistic, though Jewish community leaders condemned it as sickening, especially because the victims were young children. In response, officials and Jewish groups began discussing increased security measures for school buses.

Ji Cheng is set to make history as the first Chinese cyclist to compete in the Tour de France, riding for Giant-Shimano after years of professional racing in Europe. His participation is seen as a milestone that could boost competitive cycling's popularity in China, where road cycling has struggled to gain traction despite past Olympic success in track events. While cycling in China has declined as a daily transport mode, a growing middle class is embracing it for recreation, and experts believe Ji's performance could inspire more interest and investment in the sport. Ji himself hopes his journey will encourage more Chinese riders to pursue professional careers in Europe.

Jim Carrey delivered a commencement address at Maharishi University of Management, where he shared some of his artwork and offered graduates advice about embracing their true potential. He spoke about how his father’s decision to play it safe in accounting ultimately failed, inspiring Carrey to take chances and pursue what he loved. He also mixed in humor, joking about the school’s meditation breaks, and received an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree.

Jimmy Carter turns 90, and while his presidency is often judged harshly due to economic struggles and the Iran hostage crisis, his 1976 campaign was built on restoring public trust after Watergate. He promised to open government, limit lobbyist influence, and push ethics reforms, later signing the Ethics in Government Act. Though his legacy is overshadowed by failures, his message about the importance of trustworthy leadership remains relevant today.

J.K. Rowling is returning to the wizarding world, but not with a new Harry Potter book or a story about Harry himself. She will make her screenwriting debut with a film adaptation of *Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them*, focusing on the adventures of its author, Newt Scamander. Rowling emphasizes the movie is neither a prequel nor a sequel, but rather an extension of the magical universe, set in New York 70 years before Harry’s story begins. The film is planned as the first in a new series, part of a broader creative partnership with Warner Bros.

Jennifer Lopez performed a birthday song for Turkmenistan’s president at a private corporate event hosted by a Chinese oil company, a decision her spokesperson said was made without knowledge of the country’s human rights record. The event was not government-sponsored or political, and the birthday greeting was a last-minute request from the corporate host. Human Rights Watch has described Turkmenistan as one of the world’s most repressive countries, with the government controlling nearly all public life. The singer’s team stressed she would not have attended had she been aware of such issues.

Former “Good Morning America” host Joan Lunden was diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer, a rare and aggressive form, after an ultrasound following a clear mammogram revealed two small tumors. Though initially frightened and tempted to keep the news private, she chose to go public and sought multiple medical opinions before beginning chemotherapy. She also decided to shave her head before hair loss began, saying it helped her feel empowered rather than like a victim. Lunden stresses that breast cancer varies widely among women and that additional screening like ultrasound can be vital for those with dense breast tissue.

Joan Rivers, the pioneering and acerbic comedian known for her self-deprecating early routines and later her cutting celebrity commentary, has died at age 81, a week after suffering cardiac arrest. Rising from stand-up comedy to become a talk-show host and red-carpet fixture, she built a career on saying what others only thought, often courting controversy with her blunt insults. Her path included a famous falling-out with Johnny Carson, personal tragedy with her husband’s suicide, and a later resurgence alongside her daughter Melissa on “Fashion Police.” She leaves a legacy as a trailblazer who influenced generations of bold female comics.

Joan Rivers was honored at a star-studded, theatrical funeral in Manhattan that matched the irreverent, showbiz style she had requested. The service featured celebrity guests, comedic moments, and musical performances instead of traditional eulogies. Rivers died at age 81 following complications from a medical procedure, and her death is under state investigation. The event reflected her lifelong desire to make people laugh, even in death.

Joan Rivers is still on life support five days after going into cardiac and respiratory arrest during a throat procedure at a Manhattan clinic. Her daughter Melissa expressed gratitude for the public’s support, noting that the family remains hopeful. Rivers, 81, was hospitalized in critical condition, and her upcoming work commitments, including “Fashion Police” tapings, were canceled. Just before the incident, she had performed a comedy show in which she joked about dying onstage.

A former grain silo in Johannesburg has been transformed into an affordable student housing complex called Mill Junction, featuring stacked shipping containers that add extra floors and give the building a distinctive, Jenga-like look. The project provides budget-friendly accommodation for nearly 400 students, helping address high university dropout rates linked to a shortage of decent, affordable housing near campuses. It includes shared kitchens, study spaces, free WiFi, and a rooftop social area, while also repurposing materials and preserving the city’s architectural heritage. Developers say the initiative revitalizes the area by keeping old structures in use and maintaining the character of historic neighborhoods.

The upcoming 18th Chinese Communist Party Congress marks a historic leadership transition, with Xi Jinping poised to replace Hu Jintao at the helm. The opaque succession process has been marked by intense political maneuvering, highlighted by the abrupt demotion of Hu's protégé, Ling Jihua, following a scandal involving his son. This incident has fueled speculation about factional struggles, particularly between the camps of former President Jiang Zemin and the outgoing Hu, as well as the rising influence of the Communist Youth League faction in shaping the future leadership lineup.

Jodie Foster has secretly married her girlfriend, Alexandra Hedison, over the weekend, as confirmed by her representative. The couple had been dating for nearly a year, and Hedison is a photographer and actress who previously dated Ellen DeGeneres. Foster, known for guarding her privacy, has long avoided public discussion of her personal life, notably declining to make a big coming-out speech at the 2013 Golden Globes. She has previously emphasized the importance of privacy, having been in the public eye since childhood.

Joe McGinniss, the investigative journalist and author, has died at age 71 after a two-year battle with prostate cancer. He was best known for “Fatal Vision,” his controversial account of the Jeffrey MacDonald murder case, and “The Selling of the President 1968,” which exposed Richard Nixon’s media-driven campaign strategy. McGinniss also drew attention with his 2010 book about Sarah Palin, which prompted a threatened lawsuit. He leaves behind his wife, five children, and seven grandchildren.

President Obama has chosen John Brennan, his top counterterrorism adviser, to lead the CIA, highlighting the administration’s reliance on drone strikes and special operations rather than large-scale military force. Brennan has been the key architect of the drone campaign, which has recently shifted focus from Pakistan to Yemen, where strikes have increased despite growing local and international criticism. The policy faces legal and ethical questions, particularly over civilian casualties and the targeted killing of an American citizen, even as officials argue drones are precise and lawful. The same approach may soon extend to Mali, where al Qaeda-linked militants have gained ground.

John Henson, son of Muppets creator Jim Henson, has died at age 48 after a sudden, massive heart attack, according to The Jim Henson Company. He passed away Friday at home with one of his daughters nearby. A longtime board member and shareholder, he was known for playing the beloved Muppet character Sweetums. His death follows the passing of his mother, Jane Henson, last April, and his father, who died in 1990.

Secretary of State John Kerry stated that coalition airstrikes have halted ISIS’s advance and likely prevented the fall of Baghdad and Irbil, but they have not defeated the group. He emphasized that the military campaign will be lengthy and requires a broader strategy, including rebuilding Iraqi forces, securing local support, cutting off financing, and countering extremist ideology. Kerry also defended U.S. airstrikes in Syria under international law, noting that the Syrian government was unwilling or unable to address the threat. Additionally, he acknowledged that U.S. personnel are already on the ground in various roles, while declining to confirm the death of the Khorasan Group’s leader.

Kevin McEnroe, the 27-year-old son of tennis legend John McEnroe and actress Tatum O'Neal, was arrested in Manhattan on drug charges after police observed what they believed to be a drug deal. He was found carrying suspected cocaine, anxiety medication, and several types of painkillers, leading to two counts of criminal possession of a controlled substance. Although prosecutors requested bail, a judge released him without bail, and he is scheduled to return to court in October. The arrest echoes his mother’s own 2008 drug-related arrest, highlighting a recurring legal issue within the family.

John Sheardown, the Canadian immigration officer who sheltered and helped six American diplomats escape Iran during the 1979 hostage crisis, has died at age 88. His son confirmed he passed away in an Ottawa hospital after battling Alzheimer’s and cancer. Sheardown played a central role in the covert “Canadian Caper” rescue, housing the fugitive diplomats alongside Ambassador Ken Taylor until they were smuggled out in early 1980. Though the film *Argo* dramatized the mission, it omitted his contributions, and he remained humble about his heroic actions.

The Jonas Brothers have abruptly canceled their upcoming tour, citing a serious conflict within the group. A spokesperson explained that the split stems from fundamental disagreements over their musical direction. Refunds will be issued to ticket holders, and while the band had recently reunited and planned a new album, the future of that project is now uncertain.

A Jordanian court has cleared radical cleric Abu Qatada of conspiring to bomb an American school in the late 1990s, though he remains in custody while a separate case involving an alleged 2000 millennium bombing plot is still pending. The cleric, who was deported from the UK last year after a lengthy legal fight, had been convicted in absentia in Jordan on two explosion-related conspiracy charges. His removal from Britain was delayed partly by European court concerns that evidence obtained through torture could be used against him. Abu Qatada has consistently denied the accusations.

Radical cleric Abu Qatada has been deported from the UK to Jordan, where he now faces trial and has denied charges related to past bomb plots. Jordanian officials have pledged a fair trial and respect for human rights, while the UK government welcomed his removal after years of legal efforts. His deportation was previously blocked by European courts over concerns that torture-tainted evidence could be used against him. UK authorities have long accused him of supporting terrorist groups and fundraising for extremists, allegations he has consistently denied.

Veteran journalist Marie Colvin was killed in Syria while trying to retrieve her shoes after rockets struck the makeshift press center where she was staying. The American-born Sunday Times correspondent had been reporting from the besieged Homs neighborhood of Baba Amr, where she described Syrian forces shelling civilians and denying the existence of military targets. Her mother believes she was deliberately targeted, and the attack also killed French photographer Remi Ochlik. In her honor, Colvin’s family has established a fund to support charities she cared about.

Despite hopes that three jailed Al Jazeera English journalists would be released, an Egyptian court sentenced them to more than seven years in prison, sparking widespread international condemnation and expressions of solidarity from news organizations and journalists worldwide. U.S. and other Western officials urged Egyptian authorities to consider pardons, but President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi refused to intervene, insisting the judiciary was independent. The journalists and their colleagues expressed heartbreak and anger, vowing to keep campaigning until the three are freed.

Juan Martín del Potro will be away from tennis for an extended period after confirming he needs surgery on his left wrist, scheduled for Monday. The Argentine, who previously missed eight months following a similar operation on his right wrist in 2010, struggled with the injury again at the 2014 Australian Open, where he exited in the second round. He admitted the decision is difficult and that recovery will be challenging, but expressed gratitude for the support he has received. Since returning from his earlier wrist surgery, Del Potro has won 11 titles, including the Sydney International in January.

A federal judge has ended a temporary halt on force-feeding a Guantanamo detainee, explaining that she could not allow him to die despite concerns about the painful methods used. The ruling also speeds up the review of the detainee's request to stop the feedings, which he considers abusive. The detainee, a Syrian man held for over a decade without charges and cleared for release, had refused food and water, causing his health to decline rapidly. The judge acknowledged the risk of unnecessary suffering but concluded that preserving his life took precedence.

A Los Angeles judge has granted Kerri Kasem temporary conservatorship over her ailing father, radio host Casey Kasem, citing serious concerns for his safety and well-being. The court also ordered authorities to locate him after his daughter claimed his wife, Jean Kasem, may have taken him away. This ruling follows a long-running family dispute over Casey Kasem’s care, with his children previously accusing Jean of isolating him and blocking them from seeing him. The 82-year-old former “American Top 40” host suffers from Parkinson’s disease and possible Parkinson’s dementia.

A Pakistani court granted bail to Rimsha, a 14-year-old Christian girl accused of blasphemy for allegedly burning Quran pages, a case that has intensified religious tensions. Her release was secured with a roughly $10,000 bail paid by a minority-rights group, though the judge’s written order was due the next day. The case shifted when police said a local cleric had planted extra Quran pages to strengthen the accusation against her, and he now faces his own blasphemy and evidence-tampering charges. Rimsha’s family had already fled their home due to the uproar surrounding the case.

A Georgia judge rejected Usher’s ex-wife’s emergency request for custody of their children after their five-year-old son nearly drowned in a pool. The judge ruled the incident, while serious, did not create an emergency requiring removal from Usher’s care, and he praised the aunt who was supervising at the time. The boy remains hospitalized but is improving. The ex-wife testified about ongoing concerns over communication and caregiving, while Usher said he keeps her informed about the children’s schedules and medical visits.

A federal judge struck down Kentucky’s refusal to recognize same-sex marriages performed in other states, ruling that the policy violates constitutional equal protection. The judge emphasized that religious or traditional justifications cannot legitimize discrimination against gay and lesbian couples. The decision did not address whether Kentucky must issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples. A Kentucky Baptist leader condemned the ruling, warning it undermines the state constitution and moral order.

A federal appeals court has declined to rehear a landmark ruling that struck down California’s Proposition 8, keeping in place a stay on same-sex marriages while the case moves toward the U.S. Supreme Court. The original decision found the voter-approved ban unconstitutional under the 14th Amendment, and supporters of the measure have vowed to appeal. Gay-rights advocates welcomed the court’s action, calling it a step toward restoring marriage equality in California. The case is part of a broader national debate, with similar legal challenges pending and growing political support for same-sex marriage, including from President Obama.

A Texas judge drew widespread criticism for sentencing a 20-year-old man convicted of raping a 14-year-old girl to just 45 days in jail and probation, citing the victim's sexual history and claiming she was not the victim she appeared to be. The judge also ordered the offender to do community service at a rape crisis center, which refused to accept him, saying a convicted rapist would be inappropriate there. Prosecutors and victim advocates warned that the lenient sentence and focus on the victim's background could deter other sexual assault survivors from coming forward. The victim said she was devastated, and the judge later recused herself as prosecutors pushed for stricter probation conditions.

A judge has ordered an investigation into the welfare of Paris Jackson following her apparent suicide attempt, which left the 15-year-old hospitalized for evaluation. The inquiry will look into recent media reports about her well-being and may also examine the role of co-guardian T.J. Jackson, who has been accused of being absent from the family home. A lawyer for the family dismissed that claim as false, insisting T.J. remains actively involved.

A century after the assassination that sparked World War I, the article draws parallels between 1914 and today, noting a similar power shift toward Asia and rising tensions driven by China's growing influence and challenges to the U.S.-led order. However, it argues that a major-power war is far less likely now due to key differences: the lingering memory of the world wars, the deterrent effect of nuclear weapons, the existence of international institutions like the UN, and the continued resilience of U.S. power. While flashpoints such as the South China Sea and Taiwan carry risks, the global balance and institutional safeguards make a repeat of 1914 improbable.

Jurors have begun deliberating in the trial of Joshua Komisarjevsky, the second man charged in the 2007 Connecticut home invasion that left three family members dead. Prosecutors argue he was the mastermind behind the attack, while his defense maintains he never intended for anyone to die. He faces 17 charges, including murder, and could receive the death penalty if convicted. The case follows the conviction and death sentence of his alleged accomplice, Steven Hayes, in 2010.

Prosecutors and defense attorneys delivered closing arguments in the trial of Joshua Komisarjevsky, with the state portraying him as the mastermind of a brutal 2007 Connecticut home invasion that left three family members dead, while his lawyer argued he never intended for anyone to die. The jury is set to begin deliberations on 17 charges, including murder, kidnapping, and arson, and Komisarjevsky could face the death penalty if convicted. His co-defendant, Steven Hayes, was already sentenced to death for his role in the crime. The defense sought to shift blame to Hayes, emphasizing that Komisarjevsky did not kill anyone directly and even took actions that may have slowed the fatal fire.

The sentencing phase has begun for Joshua Komisarjevsky, the second man convicted in the 2007 Connecticut home invasion that killed Jennifer Hawke-Petit and her two daughters. The jury must decide between life in prison and the death penalty, with defense attorneys emphasizing his traumatic childhood and lack of prior violence as mitigating factors. Prosecutors are expected to argue that aggravated circumstances justify execution, and closing arguments are not anticipated until after Thanksgiving. The victims’ family, including survivor William Petit, has expressed relief at the conviction, describing Komisarjevsky as a sociopath and highlighting the broader issue of violence against women.

The involuntary manslaughter trial of Dr. Conrad Murray in Michael Jackson’s death is set to begin with opening statements, after a judge barred the defense from showing a video of Jackson’s 2009 concert announcement to illustrate his health and mental state. Murray’s legal team acknowledged the ruling limits their case but vowed to present a strong defense, relying on witnesses to testify about Jackson’s declining health in the months before his death. The first prosecution witness will be “This Is It” producer Kenny Ortega, while the newly seated jury—composed of seven men and five women—will hear the case. Murray faces up to four years in prison if convicted in connection with Jackson’s death from a propofol overdose.

Jurors failed to reach a verdict on whether convicted home-invasion killer Joshua Komisarjevsky should receive the death penalty, and deliberations are set to resume. He was found guilty of multiple charges, including murder and kidnapping, in the 2007 attack that killed a mother and her two daughters. His defense argued for life in prison, citing his troubled childhood, lack of prior violence, and good behavior behind bars. The jury must decide between execution and life without parole, while his accomplice, Steven Hayes, has already been sentenced to death.

A U.S. Justice Department investigation found that Albuquerque police have engaged in a long-standing pattern of excessive and unconstitutional force, including deadly shootings of unarmed or mentally ill individuals. The report highlights cases such as the killing of a 19-year-old who was shot again while lying on the ground and a veteran with PTSD who threatened suicide. It also criticizes the department for using Tasers and other force against people who posed minimal threats, especially those in mental health crises. The findings point to systemic failures in training, supervision, and accountability, with internal oversight largely ineffective, and recommend broad reforms.

The Justice Department released a legal opinion defending President Obama’s recess appointments, arguing that pro-forma Senate sessions do not interrupt a recess long enough to prevent such appointments. The opinion covers Richard Cordray’s appointment to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and three NLRB members. Republicans, led by Senator Chuck Grassley, strongly rejected the reasoning and hinted at possible Senate retaliation. The unusual public release of the opinion is expected to intensify partisan conflict over executive power.

The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that a New York town’s practice of opening board meetings with prayer is constitutional, citing historical tradition and finding the invocations did not coerce participation. The decision was narrow, with the majority emphasizing the specific circumstances, while two conservative justices argued even subtle pressure would not invalidate such prayers. Dissenting justices warned that allowing government-sponsored sectarian worship could divide citizens along religious lines. The ruling upheld the town’s policy against a lower court decision, but left many broader questions about religious expression in civic life unresolved.

The Supreme Court heard arguments in a consolidated set of cases challenging the EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from stationary sources such as power plants. The dispute centers on whether the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to set emissions standards for these sources, with opponents arguing the rules exceed executive authority and could eventually affect schools and small businesses. During the hearing, the justices appeared divided over how much deference to give the EPA’s interpretation of ambiguous statutory language, with key swing votes likely to decide the outcome. A ruling, expected by June, could have major implications for climate policy and the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress.

The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that President Obama’s recess appointments to the National Labor Relations Board were unconstitutional because the Senate was not truly in recess during its brief pro forma sessions. The narrow decision limits presidential power to bypass Senate confirmation, though it still allows recess appointments under certain conditions. The ruling could invalidate many NLRB decisions and also affect a similar appointment to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Political leaders from both parties claimed partial victory, while the White House expressed disappointment.

The Supreme Court unanimously struck down a Massachusetts law that created fixed buffer zones around abortion clinics, ruling that it violated free speech rights by closing off too much public sidewalk. The decision was narrow, leaving room for the state to create a less restrictive law, and did not invalidate all clinic protest regulations. The Court acknowledged the state's interest in safety and access but found the law went too far in restricting speech. The ruling may prompt other states with similar buffer-zone laws to revisit them.

The Supreme Court has agreed to review whether the EPA can impose stricter greenhouse gas emission limits on stationary sources such as power plants, consolidating six appeals from industry and state opponents. The Court declined to hear broader challenges to the EPA’s overall authority on carbon emissions, a move environmental groups hailed as a positive sign. Supporters argue the regulations are necessary to combat climate change, while critics, including Texas, accuse the agency of overreach and harming the economy. A decision is expected by June, adding to another major environmental case already on the Court’s docket this term.

Justin Bieber is under investigation by Los Angeles police after an alleged attempted robbery at a batting cage, reportedly involving a dispute over a cell phone. Authorities say the incident occurred Monday night, though the complaint was filed the next day. A source close to Bieber downplayed the situation, describing it as a normal encounter with overzealous fans. The accusation adds to a string of recent legal troubles for the singer, including prior arrests and investigations.

Justin Bieber was the night’s biggest winner at the American Music Awards, taking home three honors including artist of the year, and he brought his mother onstage while thanking her for her support. He also addressed critics, saying he plans to stay in the music industry for a long time. The show paid tribute to the late Dick Clark, the awards’ creator, with a musical memorial, while host Ryan Seacrest noted the event still reflects Clark’s vision. Other highlights included Psy teaming up with MC Hammer for a viral dance mashup, and wins for artists like Taylor Swift, Nicki Minaj, and Carrie Underwood.

Justin Bieber addressed recent rumors on Twitter, pushing back against allegations that he tried to grab a woman’s phone at a Los Angeles batting cage. He insisted the truth would prevail and urged fans not to believe the reports, while also saying he tries to stay kind despite unfair treatment. A source close to the singer downplayed the incident, saying he was just hanging out with friends and that the accusation was blown out of proportion. Bieber’s representative declined to comment, but he maintained that he has thick skin and will keep trying to be the person his mother raised.

Justin Bieber’s legal team is urging Los Angeles prosecutors to treat the January egg-throwing incident at his neighbor’s home as a misdemeanor, arguing it was a prank and he has no criminal record. However, sheriff’s investigators are pushing for a felony charge because the damage was estimated at around $20,000. Meanwhile, Bieber has sold his California mansion and relocated, while still facing separate DUI and assault cases. Legal experts suggest that even if he is charged, he would likely receive probation, fines, or community service rather than jail time.

Justin Bieber’s path from teen idol to adult celebrity has been rocky, marked by constant public scrutiny and a series of missteps, including alleged drug use, tardiness, and a recent battery accusation. Unlike earlier pop stars who had peer groups to share the spotlight, Bieber faces this transition largely alone, with every personal moment becoming headline news. His struggles echo those of other young stars like Miley Cyrus, who also faced harsh judgment while growing up in the public eye. Supporters argue that Bieber is simply navigating fame and manhood under immense pressure, and that the relentless criticism may be unfair.

A Florida judge ruled that police booking video of Justin Bieber must be released to the media under the state’s open records law, but ordered a court technician to blur his genitals before publication. The footage, recorded after Bieber’s January arrest on DUI and related charges, includes a segment where he appears to be urinating in a jail cell. The judge said the public has a right to see the video, but Bieber is still entitled to basic dignity. Additional photos and earlier video of Bieber have already been released, and his next court hearing is scheduled for March 11.

Parents of older kids and teens can use Justin Bieber’s arrest as a springboard for meaningful conversations about drugs, alcohol, and reckless driving, rather than avoiding the topic. Experts suggest parents listen more than lecture, asking young people what they think about celebrity behavior and what truly makes someone admirable. The episode also offers lessons about separating talent from poor choices, recognizing that mistakes don’t define a person, and understanding that fame and outside approval don’t guarantee happiness. Ultimately, the goal is to help kids develop their own judgment and self-worth without idolizing celebrities.

Amid rampant tabloid speculation about Justin Bieber’s behavior during his South American tour—including unverified claims that he visited a Brazilian brothel—the singer has urged fans to focus on his music rather than gossip. A short video of Bieber sleeping, posted by a young woman, has only fueled online debate, with devoted fans defending him and skeptics reading more into the footage. The article stresses that little is actually known about his private life, since his team rarely comments and paparazzi images are often ambiguous. Ultimately, it highlights the intense public scrutiny Bieber faces as he transitions from teen idol to adulthood, while his career continues to thrive.

Authorities have seized Justin Bieber’s iPhone as part of an investigation into an alleged egg-throwing attack on a neighbor’s home, looking for messages or videos that show him bragging about the incident. The search is focused only on the egg attack, not on any personal photos or drug-related texts. The damage is estimated at $20,000, which could lead to felony vandalism charges. Separately, a houseguest, rapper Lil Za, was arrested on drug charges after deputies found suspected ecstasy and Xanax during the raid.

Juventus moved eight points clear atop Serie A with a 2-0 victory over Livorno, thanks to two quick goals from Fernando Llorente, putting the title within reach after a recent loss. Milan also won 2-1 at Genoa. In England, Sunderland’s survival hopes were badly damaged by a 5-1 defeat at Tottenham, leaving them bottom of the Premier League and seven points from safety.

The suspect in the Kansas City-area shootings faces hate crime charges even though his victims were Christian, because federal law focuses on the offender’s bias rather than the victims’ actual identity. Authorities say the gunman, a longtime white supremacist, targeted Jewish facilities and made anti-Semitic statements, including shouting "Heil Hitler" after his arrest. Prosecutors are confident in the evidence and plan to present federal hate crime charges to a grand jury. If convicted, the suspect could receive a life sentence.

Prince William and Catherine, the Duchess of Cambridge, introduced their newborn son to the public outside a London hospital, with the couple noting that they were still choosing a name. The baby boy, who is third in line to the British throne, was born Monday and has already drawn widespread celebrations across the UK, including gun salutes, bell ringing, and patriotic light displays. Well-wishers and world leaders, including the Obamas, offered congratulations, while the couple’s families expressed their joy. The new parents appeared relaxed and described the moment as emotional and special.

Kate Winslet has welcomed her third child, a baby boy, born on December 7 at a hospital in Sussex, England. Both mother and son are reported to be doing well. The actress already has two children from previous relationships, and she shares the new baby with her husband, Ned Rocknroll, whom she married in 2012. The couple had announced they were expecting earlier in the year.

Katy Perry has been recognized by the RIAA as the most decorated digital artist in history, with 72 million paid digital singles sold—far surpassing Rihanna and Taylor Swift. The organization, which began tracking digital sales in 2004 and later added streaming, honored Perry with numerous gold, platinum, and multiplatinum digital awards. Her catalog, including hits like "Dark Horse" and "I Kissed a Girl," helped cement this milestone. RIAA’s chairman praised her talent, drive, and strong connection with fans as key to her historic achievement.

The article stresses the importance of having a dedicated storm preparedness area and understanding the key difference between weather watches and warnings, with warnings indicating imminent dangerous conditions and watches meaning they are possible. It advises taking proactive steps before a storm, such as securing the home, preparing an emergency kit, and having an evacuation plan. A comprehensive list of essential supplies is provided, including water, non-perishable food, medications, flashlights, and important documents. Finally, it outlines crucial safety measures to follow after the storm, like avoiding floodwaters, reporting downed power lines, and checking food for spoilage.

Kelsey Grammer launched his verified Twitter account with a self-appointed mission to fix grammatical errors, using the hashtag #KelseyGrammerGrammar. He quickly began correcting fans, such as pointing out the proper use of "it's" in a tweet about his movie. The initiative was well-received, with fans praising his efforts and even William Shatner playfully acknowledging his arrival. The overall tone is lighthearted, positioning Grammer as a humorous enforcer of proper grammar on the platform.

An American mother was granted a rare visit to North Korea to see her son, Kenneth Bae, who has been imprisoned there for nearly a year on charges of subversion. During their emotional six hours together, he told her he was being treated fairly, but she fears his improved appearance masks a fragile health condition that could not withstand a return to hard labor. She is pleading for amnesty and forgiveness, apologizing on his behalf, while acknowledging the family feels powerless to secure his release. The visit highlights the ongoing ordeal for Bae’s family, especially as diplomatic tensions make high-profile intervention unlikely.

Kenya is marking 50 years of independence with nationwide celebrations, including a photography contest organized by Nairobi photographer Mutua Matheka and Samsung. The initiative invited Kenyans to submit images capturing the country’s cultural and historical heritage, with over 2,000 entries received and the top 25 displayed in a public street exhibition. Matheka emphasized that the project aimed to showcase Kenya through its own people’s eyes, highlighting both pride in progress and the need to reflect on past mistakes. The overall message is one of hope and national reflection, celebrating how far the country has come while looking ahead to the next 50 years.

Kenyan security forces moved to end a deadly siege at an upscale Nairobi mall, where Al-Shabaab militants killed at least 68 people and wounded over 175, with a small number of hostages still believed held. The attackers, estimated at 10 to 15 gunmen, included suspects from several countries, and U.S. authorities were investigating claims that Americans were involved. Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, who lost a nephew in the attack, vowed to swiftly and painfully punish those responsible. The assault was the deadliest terror attack in Kenya since the 1998 U.S. embassy bombing, and came amid ongoing tensions over Kenya's military operations in Somalia.

The release of closed-circuit television footage from Nairobi’s Westgate Mall attack reveals gunmen calmly moving through the complex, firing at random, pausing to pray, and communicating by phone as shoppers fled or hid in terror. The video shows attackers moving between the supermarket and parking lot, rounding up hostages, and shooting the wounded, while the death toll reached at least 67. The footage aligns with Al-Shabaab’s claims of involvement, though many details remain unresolved, including the exact number of assailants and whether those seen were killed or captured. Officials have given conflicting figures, and with part of the mall collapsed, authorities admit that key answers may still lie buried in the rubble.

Kenyan and Somali forces have seized control of the northern half of Kismayo, a key Somali port city, as part of an ongoing offensive against Al-Shabaab. The military has carried out airstrikes and destroyed militant bases while working to consolidate its position before advancing further. Al-Shabaab has claimed it ambushed Kenyan troops and inflicted heavy losses, but Kenyan officials dismiss these reports as propaganda. The port is strategically important to the militants for smuggling and charcoal trade, and many civilians have fled the city amid the fighting.

A major fire at Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport has disrupted operations at East Africa’s busiest aviation hub, threatening Kenya’s key economic drivers of horticulture exports and tourism. Authorities are working to restart international flights by moving traffic through the domestic terminal, while flower growers have been urged to delay harvesting due to limited cold storage at other airports. The disruption comes at a sensitive time for Kenya’s tourism industry, which was already recovering from security and election-related setbacks, and major Gulf carriers have suspended flights. The longer the terminal takes to rebuild, the greater the risk to Kenya’s export revenues and its ambitious tourism growth targets.

Kenyan forces serving with the African Union in Somalia have seized the strategic town of Afmadow from Al-Shabaab, a key militant stronghold and logistical hub. The capture is seen as a major step toward advancing on Kismayo, the group’s main bastion in southern Somalia. In related operations, Kenyan naval forces killed 14 militants near Kismayo, while 20 others surrendered in Fafadun. The offensive reflects continued pressure on Al-Shabaab, despite its ongoing ties to al Qaeda and ability to stage attacks in Mogadishu.

Kenya’s Prime Minister Raila Odinga stated at Davos that his government will not negotiate with al-Shabaab and insists the militant group must unconditionally release Kenyan hostages. This follows al-Shabaab’s demand that Kenya free all Muslims held on terrorism charges. Odinga called terrorism an international issue requiring a unified African and global response. He also expressed confidence that Kenya’s upcoming elections would not trigger the violence seen five years ago, citing institutional reforms.

The deadly standoff at Nairobi’s Westgate Mall continued into a fourth day, with Kenyan officials claiming control even as gunmen, including snipers, remained inside and sporadic gunfire and smoke persisted. The attack, claimed by Al-Shabaab, has left at least 62 dead and dozens missing or wounded, while Kenyan authorities reported arresting several suspects and tightening border security. Kenya’s foreign minister suggested the assault bore the hallmarks of al Qaeda and said some attackers may have been young Americans of Somali or Arab origin, though U.S. officials said they had no definitive confirmation. The siege has drawn international condemnation and pledges of support, with Kenyan leaders vowing to punish those responsible for the terror.

Kenya held a state funeral in Nairobi for Wangari Maathai, the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, who died of cancer at 71. Mourners, including top government officials, gathered at a park where she often protested, and the ceremony featured tree planting and prayers. Maathai was honored for her environmental activism, especially her Green Belt Movement, which planted millions of trees and empowered women, and she requested cremation with her ashes placed at a peace institute. Her death came just before three women activists, including two Liberians, received the Nobel Peace Prize, continuing the legacy she championed.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry announced a breakthrough in Middle East peace efforts, saying an agreement had been reached to resume direct final-status negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians. The plan, presented during Kerry’s regional shuttle diplomacy, could lead to initial talks in Washington within days. Israeli leaders welcomed the development as an end to years of stagnation, while Hamas rejected the initiative as futile. Major disputes over borders, settlements, Jerusalem, security, and Palestinian refugees remain unresolved.

Secretary of State John Kerry stated that several countries, both in the Middle East and beyond, are ready to join U.S.-led airstrikes against ISIS if needed, though he did not name specific nations. He reiterated that the administration does not plan to deploy U.S. ground troops, instead relying on local Iraqi forces and Syrian rebel groups, with the White House emphasizing efforts to train and equip those fighters. However, Republican Senator Lindsey Graham sharply criticized the strategy, arguing that defeating ISIS would require a substantial American ground presence and that the U.S. cannot outsource its security.

Decades after Robert Kennedy stood with Cesar Chavez in California, New York farm workers still lack basic labor rights due to historical exclusions from New Deal protections. The author visited upstate New York and documented severe abuses, including grueling hours, no overtime, substandard housing, sexual assault, and child labor. A bill extending standard labor protections to farm workers has repeatedly passed the State Assembly but is blocked in the Senate by special interests. The author urges New York lawmakers to bring the Farmworkers Fair Labor Practices Act to a vote, framing it as a moral continuation of the fight for justice.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held four hours of talks in Paris, but failed to reach an agreement on withdrawing Russian troops from Ukraine’s border. Both sides acknowledged their differences over the crisis while pledging to keep seeking a diplomatic solution. They discussed possible cooperation on issues such as minority rights, constitutional reform, and internationally monitored elections, though Kerry stressed that real progress depends on Russia pulling back its forces and that Ukrainians must be included in any decisions. Lavrov reiterated Russia’s openness to broader cooperation and floated the idea of a federal structure for Ukraine, while the West remained wary amid reports of a significant Russian military buildup and ongoing sanctions.

Secretary of State John Kerry clarified that the U.S. is only communicating with Iran, not coordinating or cooperating militarily, after his earlier remarks sparked speculation about a potential alliance. He emphasized that no options are off the table in addressing the threat from ISIS, but any U.S. assistance to Iraq is about supporting the Iraqi people, not Prime Minister Maliki. Kerry also noted that the U.S. had been monitoring the militants' advances and is working with regional allies through diplomatic and nonlethal means. He stressed that the coming days and weeks are critical, and the U.S. is committed to diplomatic efforts to honor the sacrifices of past service members.

Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani has signaled openness to joining a new Iraqi government, despite pressing Kurdish independence in talks with U.S. officials. Secretary of State John Kerry said Iraqi leaders recognize the need to move past sectarian divisions and that a unified, inclusive government is essential for U.S. military support to succeed against ISIS. Kerry stressed that without a viable political solution, any American intervention would be severely limited, though the U.S. reserves the right to act militarily if necessary. He also defended the administration’s decision to avoid strikes on Syria, citing the successful removal of Syria’s declared chemical weapons.

Kevin Bacon initially disliked the "Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon" game, feeling it was a joke at his expense, but he has since come to appreciate it. The game, created by Brian Turtle and two college friends in 1994, connects any actor to Bacon through shared movie roles and anticipated the rise of social media. Over time, Bacon embraced the phenomenon, launching the charity site SixDegrees.org and acknowledging that his many ensemble films make him a natural hub for such connections. Today, the game remains popular through websites and Google searches that calculate a celebrity's "Bacon number."

Despite government claims of victory, residents and witnesses reported that ISIS still controlled Tikrit, with heavy shelling and fierce clashes ongoing. The militant group declared a caliphate, renaming itself the Islamic State and urging Muslims to pledge allegiance. Iraq received Russian fighter jets as Prime Minister al-Maliki criticized the US for delaying F-16 deliveries, while Washington dismissed the blame and indicated it would not intervene militarily until a new Iraqi government was formed. Human rights groups documented atrocities on both sides, including mass graves and kidnappings by ISIS and extrajudicial killings by government forces.

A 14-year-old Filipino-American boy who was kidnapped by suspected Abu Sayyaf militants in the Philippines last July has been freed after about five months in captivity. He managed to escape while his guards were sleeping and walked for two days before being found and turned over to U.S. forces. His mother and cousin had already been released in previous months. Officials and family members expressed relief and joy, with authorities vowing that those responsible will be prosecuted.

A Colorado study intended to examine playground injuries unexpectedly revealed a more alarming pattern: a significant number of children were being seriously injured or killed by firearms in everyday, non-mass-shooting incidents. The data showed that gunshot wounds were far more severe than other childhood injuries, with higher rates of intensive care and death, and many were self-inflicted. The researchers highlight that children's easy access to guns is a critical public health issue. They also point to a lack of federal funding for gun violence research, which has hindered progress in prevention, unlike the successful public health campaigns that reduced car crash deaths.

The Aedes aegypti mosquito is a major driver of the global dengue fever epidemic, a disease with no vaccine or cure that now threatens over 100 countries. In response, scientists are developing genetic modification techniques to control the insect, such as releasing engineered males whose offspring die before maturing. These methods have shown high suppression rates in field trials, leading to the first commercial approval in Brazil, with other genetic strategies also being explored. While many researchers advocate for broader trials and deployment, critics warn that the ecological risks and trial data are not yet fully understood or verified.

Kim Jong Un cast his vote in North Korea’s parliamentary election alongside his sister, Kim Yo Jong, marking her first official public appearance and fueling speculation about a generational shift in the regime’s leadership. The election, in which Kim was unanimously elected with full turnout, was dismissed by critics as a political spectacle, while North Korea defended it and lashed out at U.S. criticism of its electoral system. Observers suggest Kim Yo Jong’s prominent role may signal her rising political influence, possibly taking over responsibilities once held by her aunt, Kim Kyong Hui. However, analysts believe Kim Kyong Hui’s political relevance has faded, though she remains protected as a family member.

Despite being on the market only a few weeks, Amazon's Kindle Fire is projected to become the world's second-best-selling tablet by year's end, even as it faces criticism. Users have reported Wi-Fi and internet connection problems, and usability expert Jakob Nielsen issued a harsh review, citing clunky web browsing, an uncomfortable, heavy design, screen glare, and a poor magazine-reading experience. However, commentators counter that the device's low $200 price, compared to the iPad's $500, along with its portability, make it an appealing budget option. Many believe consumers will accept its shortcomings in exchange for a much lower cost, especially in a tough economy.

Character actor Dennis Burkley has died at age 67, reportedly passing in his sleep at his Los Angeles home. Known for a long career spanning over 130 film and TV credits, he was recognized for voice work on “King of the Hill” and roles in “My Name is Earl,” “Mask,” and “Tin Cup.” His agent remembered him as a versatile performer who balanced comedy and drama with a surprisingly tender side. Burkley, who had recently been semi-retired and focused on voice projects, is survived by his wife and two children.

Researchers examining the remains of King Richard III have discovered evidence that he was infected with intestinal roundworms, as parasite eggs were found in soil samples near his pelvis. The findings, published in the Lancet, add a surprising personal detail to the monarch, whose skeleton was identified through DNA and other evidence after being found under a parking lot in Leicester. While such infections were common in his era and still affect many people worldwide, they are now rare in Britain. Richard III, who died in battle in 1485, is scheduled to be reburied in Leicester Cathedral.

Kitty Wells, who died at 92, was remembered as the pioneering "Queen of Country Music" and the first female superstar of the genre. Her 1952 hit "It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels" challenged traditional gender norms and became a massive success despite being banned from the Grand Ole Opry. That song opened doors for women in country music, inspiring legends like Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn, Reba McEntire, and Dolly Parton. Wells' decades-long career and influence cemented her legacy as a trailblazer for generations of female country singers.

The article uses a CNN newsroom “douche jar” as a playful lens to examine self-promotional and obnoxious behavior on Twitter. It highlights tools like Klouchebag that rate users’ “douche” scores and cites a study finding that only about a third of tweets are considered worth reading, with boring content disliked even more than arrogant posts. The piece also mentions satirical Twitter accounts that mock pompous figures, suggesting such parody offers a way to laugh at self-importance. Ultimately, it reflects on how Twitter encourages a bit of egotism, while acknowledging that even the author is not immune.

Kobe Bryant and his wife, Vanessa, have reconciled and are dropping their divorce proceedings, announcing the news on social media. Vanessa had filed for divorce in 2011, but the couple now say they are looking forward to their future together as a family. Their relationship had previously drawn public attention in 2003, when Vanessa stood by Kobe after he was accused of sexual assault; those criminal charges were later dismissed and a civil lawsuit was settled. The couple have two daughters.

Kumano, Japan, is renowned for its handmade brushes, producing 80% of the country’s total output through traditional artisan techniques. The town’s annual Brush Festival, held on the autumn equinox, honors the souls of used brushes in a ritual cremation and draws thousands of visitors. Brush-making began there about 160 years ago, and while calligraphy brush demand has declined, local companies now craft high-end makeup and paint brushes using the same methods. The festival features demonstrations, food stalls, and a procession up a 99-step path decorated with thousands of brushes.

Syria’s Kurdish minority has exploited the power vacuum created by the civil war to take control of several northern areas, notably around Qamishli and near Aleppo, raising fears in Turkey because of the dominant role of the PYD, a group linked to the PKK. The Syrian regime initially tolerated the PYD as a lever against Turkey, but the Kurds have since pursued a “third way,” backing neither the government nor the rebels. Turkey is deeply alarmed by the prospect of a PKK-friendly zone along its border and has warned of military action, while the U.S. shares concerns about PKK haven. At the same time, rival Kurdish factions are competing for influence, and the situation could destabilize not only Syria but also Turkey, Iraq, and Iran.

Labor Day marks the unofficial end of summer, with millions of Americans expected to travel for the holiday weekend despite a slight rise in gas prices. The article highlights key workforce statistics, including the size of the labor force, average commute times, and persistent gender gaps in earnings. It also notes the impact of government employment programs, particularly in helping veterans and displaced workers find jobs. Additional figures cover health insurance coverage, union membership, and the tradition of wearing white after Labor Day.

IMF chief Christine Lagarde has cautioned European leaders not to become complacent after the eurozone returned to modest growth, urging them to press on with banking union and structural reforms to sustain job creation.
