She noted that Europe has recently avoided market scrutiny due to focus on U.S. fiscal issues, but warned that this should not lead to inaction. Lagarde also stressed that tackling high youth unemployment, particularly in countries like Spain and Greece, must be a top priority, though analysts say meaningful action may have to come from national governments rather than the EU budget.

Italy held a national day of mourning after more than 100 refugees, mostly from Eritrea, died near Lampedusa, but the tragedy is not an isolated accident—it reflects decades of failed migration policy. The article argues that smugglers are not the root cause; people are forced to risk their lives because they lack safe, legal routes to asylum and face oppression, poverty, and visa barriers. It calls on EU and national leaders to move beyond tougher policing and military patrols, and instead create accessible legal channels, fair asylum procedures, and clear rescue obligations. Ultimately, the crisis demands a fundamental rethinking of sovereignty, humanitarianism, and Europe's responsibility toward migrants.

An internal review determined that eight Los Angeles police officers violated the department's deadly force policy when they shot two women during the manhunt for ex-officer Christopher Dorner. Police Chief Charlie Beck said the incident fell short of the required standard, noting that an officer mistakenly believed the sound of a newspaper hitting the ground was a gunshot, which triggered the shooting. The victims, Margie Carranza and Emma Hernandez, were delivering newspapers at the time, with Hernandez shot twice in the back and Carranza injured by broken glass. The city later approved a $4.2 million settlement for the two women, while Dorner, who had killed four people, died in a cabin fire following a standoff.

CBS News and “60 Minutes” formally apologized for a report on the 2012 Benghazi attack, admitting their primary source, security contractor Dylan Davies, was not credible. Davies, who used the pseudonym Morgan Jones, had claimed he reached the compound during the assault, but his account conflicted with what he told the FBI. The network acknowledged it was wrong to air his story, and the publisher of Davies’ book, “The Embassy House,” suspended its release. The retraction came after the report had fueled Republican criticism of the Obama administration’s response to the attack.

A major global study on tobacco use finds that nearly half of men in many developing countries use tobacco, while women in these regions are beginning to smoke at younger ages. The research highlights a shift in the tobacco epidemic from industrialized nations to low- and middle-income countries, where industry marketing increasingly targets women and youth. Experts say this trend demands urgent policy action, as the World Health Organization warns that continued smoking rates could cause up to one billion deaths this century. Although some countries have made progress through stricter regulations, weaker governments in poorer nations often struggle to resist tobacco industry influence.

Larry Speakes, the former acting White House press secretary during the Reagan administration, has died at age 74 at his Mississippi home after a long illness. He stepped into the role in 1981 after press secretary James Brady was seriously wounded in the assassination attempt on President Reagan. Speakes held the position until 1987 and later wrote a book about his time in the White House. He is survived by a daughter and two sons.

Air travel is often stressful, but for some people it leads to lasting love. The article shares three stories of couples who met at airports or on flights: a former flight attendant connected with a ramp agent after a plane delay, a woman found love with a man at an airport bar while traveling home, and another woman who went on a solo trip specifically hoping to meet someone ended up finding her future husband before reaching the resort. In each case, an unexpected airport encounter turned into a serious relationship and marriage.

The Vatican has announced that Pope John Paul II will be canonized as a saint, along with Pope John XXIII. John Paul II, who served from 1978 to 2005, was known for his global popularity and extensive travel, and his path to sainthood was unusually quick, aided by the approval of two attributed miracles. John XXIII is recognized for convening the Second Vatican Council, which modernized the Catholic Church. A date for the canonization ceremony has not yet been set.

Hawaii officials have issued an emergency declaration as lava from Kilauea Volcano threatens a Big Island community, with the flow advancing to within about a mile of the Ka'ohe Homesteads subdivision. The lava could reach the area within a week and may cross Highway 130, potentially isolating nearby communities from the rest of the island. While evacuations have not been ordered, road access to the subdivision is now restricted to residents only. Kilauea, one of the world's most active volcanoes, has been erupting continuously since 1983.

The U.S. military launched airstrikes in Syria, drawing concern from Senator Tim Kaine, who argued the action needed congressional approval. Lawmakers were away from Washington campaigning for the midterms, and while some supported the strikes, others questioned the president’s legal authority to act without a new vote. The participation of five Arab nations in the operation helped ease some concerns, and many members were privately relieved they did not have to cast a difficult vote before the election. Critics like Representative Justin Amash condemned congressional leaders for leaving town without debating or voting on military action.

Despite a judge and multiple doctors declaring Jahi McMath brain-dead, her family's attorney claims the 13-year-old is stabilizing and improving under new medical care after being released from a California hospital. Medical experts counter that true brain death is irreversible, so any improvement would indicate a misdiagnosis. The family has kept her location private, citing threats and the need for quiet, as the case continues to fuel national debate over the legal and ethical definition of death.

One of two massage therapists suing John Travolta for sexual battery has withdrawn from the case after giving the wrong date for the alleged incident, a move Travolta’s lawyer says fully clears the actor. The remaining accuser, who claims Travolta groped him at an Atlanta hotel, still plans to pursue his case, with his attorney citing witness support and emails he says back the allegation. Travolta’s legal team disputes the credibility of those emails, noting they do not mention the actor or the alleged misconduct. The plaintiff’s lawyer, however, argues the case will show a pattern of behavior involving many other massage therapists.

In Cairo, lawyers for Mohamed Morsy and other Muslim Brotherhood defendants requested a new panel of judges, arguing that the soundproof glass cage used in court prevented private communication with their legal team and was humiliating. The defense also challenged the legitimacy of the proceedings, calling the charges politically motivated and accusing the military leadership of crimes related to the 2013 coup and subsequent crackdown. Morsy, who maintains he is still Egypt’s legitimate president, dismissed the trial as a farce and repeated his refusal to recognize the court’s authority. The judge adjourned the case until Monday, with no immediate decision on the recusal request.

A lawyer for three of the five men accused in the fatal New Delhi bus assault says he has advised them to plead not guilty, though he fears they may face pressure to change their plea. The trial has been closed to the public after heated scenes in court, where some lawyers objected to defending the suspects. The five adult defendants face charges including murder, rape, and kidnapping, and could receive the death penalty. A sixth suspect is being handled separately in juvenile court, while the victim died in a Singapore hospital weeks after the attack.

Prosecutors are making a final effort to keep Oscar Pistorius in custody as his bail hearing resumes, following the removal of the lead investigator, Hilton Botha, who faces attempted murder charges from a separate 2011 incident. The prosecution's case has been weakened by admitted police errors, including possible crime-scene contamination and mishandled evidence, which the defense argues amounts to a collapse of the state's case. Pistorius maintains he shot his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, by mistake, believing she was an intruder. Meanwhile, Nike has suspended its sponsorship deal with the athlete, and the ANC Women's League has criticized authorities for granting him special treatment in detention.

A leaked phone call between Estonia’s foreign minister and the EU’s top diplomat has stirred controversy after the minister relayed a doctor’s claim that Ukraine’s new coalition, not ousted President Yanukovych, may have orchestrated the deadly sniper attacks in Kiev. The Estonian minister confirmed the recording was authentic but stressed he was only passing along concerns heard during a visit, not endorsing the opposition’s involvement. The leak is seen as part of a broader information battle, following a separate intercepted call in which a U.S. official reportedly criticized the EU’s handling of the crisis.

Travelers face a growing array of hidden fees from airlines, hotels, and rental car companies, including charges for baggage, ticket changes, resort amenities, and even in-flight drinks. These fees help companies keep base prices low while boosting profits, but they often leave customers frustrated and make true cost comparisons difficult. However, many of these charges can be avoided with careful planning, such as choosing fee-free carriers, using co-branded credit cards, joining loyalty programs, or booking through knowledgeable travel agents. Ultimately, staying informed and strategic is key to minimizing the impact of these extra travel costs.

The author, who has Asperger’s, pushes back against media speculation linking autism to the Newtown shooter, calling such claims false and harmful. He shares how he was bullied and stigmatized as a child, and describes founding an online community for autistic people to counter isolation. He emphasizes that research shows autistic individuals are no more violent than others and are often more likely to be victimized. The piece urges the public to reject damaging stereotypes and instead focus on compassion and shared humanity.

Spanish authorities arrested a wealthy Lebanese mayor on suspicion of attempting to pay poor immigrants for liver tissue needed for his own transplant. Officials described it as the first detected case of organ trafficking in Spain, involving accomplices who recruited and tested nine vulnerable people. A Romanian immigrant was deemed a medical match, but the transplant was blocked at a Barcelona hospital because he was not a relative or close friend of the mayor, as Spanish law requires. The mayor later received a liver from his son, while investigators warned that organ trafficking remains a form of exploitation that no country is immune to.

Kipchoge Keino rose to global fame at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics by winning the 1,500 meters, and he went on to earn more Olympic and Commonwealth medals while setting world records. Now in his seventies, he has shifted his focus to philanthropy, drawing on his own childhood loss of his mother to open an orphanage and schools in Kenya. He later founded a sporting academy to nurture young athletic talent. His main goal is to give underprivileged children confidence, self-respect, and the chance for a better life.

Charlie Haden, the acclaimed jazz bassist and Grammy winner, passed away at age 76 after a long illness, surrounded by family. With a career spanning more than seven decades, he was a key figure in free jazz through his work with Ornette Coleman and also led his own ensembles. Haden’s musical range extended from jazz to country and world music, reflecting his roots as a child performer in his family’s country band. In 2012, he was honored as an NEA Jazz Master for his contributions as a musician, composer, and educator.

Van Cliburn, the celebrated American pianist, has died at age 78 after battling bone cancer. He became a symbol of Cold War pride when he won the International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow in 1958, shortly after the Soviet Union’s Sputnik launch, and was honored with a ticker-tape parade in New York. His triumph was seen as a boost to U.S. morale and helped ease cultural tensions between the two superpowers. Over his long career, he performed for every U.S. president since Harry Truman and left a lasting legacy in classical music.

A Chicago hotel has shut down and drained its pool, hot tub, and fountain after two people died from Legionnaires’ disease linked to the property. Health officials have confirmed eight cases among guests since mid-August, though they believe there is no ongoing risk. They are urging anyone who stayed there and has flu-like symptoms to see a doctor for prompt testing and treatment. The disease, a bacterial infection spread through water mist, is not contagious between people and can be fatal in a small percentage of cases.

A recently rediscovered Leonardo da Vinci painting, “Salvator Mundi,” is one of only about 15 known surviving works by the artist and has been restored to excellent condition. It will be publicly exhibited for the first time in centuries at London’s National Gallery, alongside other Leonardos. A CNN special follows Nick Glass as he examines the painting in New York, speaks with its restorer and experts, and explores da Vinci’s life and legacy. The program also considers whether such a discovery could happen again and what the work’s true value is.

Michela Obama’s fashion choices are more than superficial; they demonstrate that style can coexist with intelligence and substance. Her wardrobe reflects confidence, practicality, and a commitment to personal authenticity, offering lessons in mixing affordable and designer pieces, building a timeless closet, and embracing bold colors. Beyond personal style, her fashion supports emerging designers and mirrors America’s cultural diversity, while also promoting an active, healthy lifestyle. Ultimately, her approach to dressing is both historically significant and accessible, showing that looking good and making a meaningful impact are not mutually exclusive.

The response to the Arapahoe High School shooting reflected lessons learned from Columbine, as officers entered the building immediately to confront the gunman rather than waiting outside. A school resource officer and security guard quickly closed in on the shooter, who turned the gun on himself within about 80 seconds, likely preventing further casualties. Lockdown procedures and the active-shooter protocol developed after Columbine were key to keeping students and staff safe. The incident also underscored the importance of training all school employees, since a janitor’s quick actions helped evacuate the intended target and alert authorities.

The viral drinking challenge known as Neknominate, which originated in Australia, has spread globally through social media, prompting participants to film themselves consuming large or unusual alcoholic drinks and then daring others to top them. The trend has turned deadly, with several young men dying after taking part, leading health experts to warn that heavy drinking impairs judgment and increases danger. In response, politicians and parents are urging schools to help young people resist peer pressure, while critics argue that social media platforms like Facebook should take more responsibility for hosting such content.

LeWeb founder Loic Le Meur is considering “digital hippies” as a possible theme for his next tech conference, describing a growing movement of entrepreneurs who prioritize happiness over wealth, fame, and power. Inspired by Burning Man, he notes these digital hippies embrace simplicity, sustainability, and the sharing economy, as seen in platforms like Wikipedia, Airbnb, and Lyft. He also highlights a renewed interest in hardware and 3D printing as a way to disrupt traditional supply chains. Despite the theme’s risk with sponsors, Le Meur values Davos for its unique access to global leaders and the chance to gather fresh ideas.LeWeb founder Loic Le Meur is exploring “digital hippies” as a possible theme for his next conference, pointing to entrepreneurs who value happiness over wealth, fame, and power. Inspired by Burning Man, he sees this movement embracing simplicity, sustainability, and the sharing economy through platforms like Wikipedia, Airbnb, and Lyft. He also notes a shift back to hardware and 3D printing, which could disrupt traditional supply chains. Although the theme might worry sponsors, Le Meur finds Davos valuable for meeting global leaders and gaining new ideas.

Lewis Hamilton won the Spanish Grand Prix by just over half a second from Mercedes teammate Nico Rosberg, taking over the lead in the Formula One championship for the first time this season. It was Hamilton’s fourth consecutive victory and his first in Spain, while Mercedes secured another dominant one-two finish. Hamilton admitted Rosberg was quicker but managed his car’s balance to hold off the late pressure, while Rosberg felt one more lap could have changed the result. Red Bull’s Daniel Ricciardo finished a distant third, as Mercedes extended their commanding leads in both championships.

Lewis Hamilton has signed a three-year deal with Mercedes for the 2013 Formula 1 season, ending his long association with McLaren. Michael Schumacher will leave the team, with Hamilton partnering Nico Rosberg, while Sergio Perez moves to McLaren to race alongside Jenson Button. The announcement resolves weeks of speculation and marks a major driver shake-up. Meanwhile, the 2013 race calendar was released, though the New Jersey Grand Prix remains uncertain due to track readiness concerns.

Fierce clashes between rival Libyan militias continued around Tripoli's international airport, prompting the weak interim government to consider requesting international military intervention. The fighting has caused numerous casualties, heavy damage to aircraft and infrastructure, and led the United Nations to evacuate its staff from the capital. The government has ordered militias to withdraw from the airport area but lacks the strength to enforce it, as armed groups remain powerful and divided. The international community has expressed concern and urged a political dialogue to resolve the crisis.

Libyan officials were called before parliament to address worsening violence in Benghazi after a bombing killed an intelligence officer and his young son, with his wife and infant injured. The government pledged to improve security, starting with Benghazi, and the UN condemned the ongoing assassinations. The attacks are attributed to Islamist extremists and militias, while critics point to the government's failure to enforce law and hold perpetrators accountable. Widespread public frustration persists over the state's inability to curb the escalating instability.

Libya’s General National Congress voted overwhelmingly against Prime Minister-elect Mustafa Abushagur’s proposed crisis cabinet, leading to his automatic dismissal less than a month after his appointment. The rejected plan was a downsized government, which Abushagur said he was forced to form along regional quota lines rather than on merit, and he blamed political blocs for imposing unrealistic conditions. The congress decided to keep the existing interim government in place while it delays setting a new timeline for choosing a replacement. The political deadlock comes amid deep instability in Libya, including security threats, militia influence, and public frustration over the slow pace of rebuilding.

Frankel, one of the greatest racehorses ever, retired undefeated after a brilliant career and now commands enormous stud fees as a breeding stallion. His former jockey, Tom Queally, describes him as a once-in-a-lifetime talent with exceptional speed, intelligence, and a calm temperament. While life after Frankel has been a transition, Queally accepts that no horse will ever match him but remains motivated to pursue new goals in racing. He is at peace with being forever linked to Frankel and expects the horse’s legacy to endure through his offspring.

A 13-year-old Haitian girl named Rose Matrie continues to pursue her education despite living in a home damaged by the 2010 earthquake and facing her family’s financial struggles. Her parents find it difficult to pay school fees for her and her siblings, a common challenge in Haiti where public education is limited and private schooling is costly. Organizations like Plan International USA are working to improve access to education by building schools, training teachers, and providing supplies so that costs do not keep children out of the classroom. Supporting girls’ education initiatives through donations and awareness campaigns can help students like Rose Matrie reach their potential.

Kowloon Walled City was a densely packed, largely unregulated Hong Kong settlement that grew from a former fortress into a vertical maze of interconnected buildings housing tens of thousands. Photographer Greg Girard, who documented it before its 1994 demolition, recalled both its chaotic conditions and the ordinary lives of residents living within. Architect Aaron Tan studied the community and admired its resourcefulness, especially its self-managed water system, which he saw as proof that residents could solve problems creatively without formal design. Though the city was torn down and replaced by a park, its legacy endures through films, games, and its influence on architects who embrace organic, unplanned urban life.Kowloon Walled City was a densely packed, unregulated Hong Kong settlement that grew from a former fortress into a towering maze of interconnected buildings. Photographer Greg Girard documented its chaotic conditions, noting that despite the lack of safety codes and dark, cramped spaces, residents led ordinary lives. Architect Aaron Tan admired the community’s ingenuity, particularly its self-managed water system, which showed how residents solved problems collectively. Although demolished in 1994 and replaced by a park, the Walled City’s legacy lives on in films, games, and as an inspiration for architects who value organic, unplanned urban spaces.

Cardiff University operates a specialized lightning laboratory that simulates in-flight lightning strikes on aircraft parts, using copper mesh to limit damage. Meanwhile, Cranfield University studies ice formation on wings and engines in an icing tunnel, exploring protective measures like wire mesh. Both research efforts aim to improve aircraft safety and performance under extreme weather conditions.

The article recaps reader reactions to several recent stories. Commenters criticized the difficulty of getting HIV tests, with one person describing having to pretend to be gay to receive a test. A discussion about model Kate Upton’s fitness drew heated defenses of her body against accusations of being overweight. Another debate centered on Chicago’s violence, where readers argued over whether guns, poverty, or parenting were to blame, while a story about a woman needing multiple organ transplants prompted hopes for medical advances in growing organs.

Barcelona’s new president has firmly stated that Lionel Messi is not for sale and plans to negotiate a new contract to keep him as the club’s highest-paid player. Messi, who has been central to Barcelona’s success with numerous league and Champions League titles, remains a top priority despite reported interest from Paris Saint-Germain. The statement comes amid recent turmoil after former president Sandro Rosell resigned over an investigation into the Neymar transfer. The new leadership is working to reassure fans by emphasizing stability and commitment to key players.

The latest round of Syria peace talks in Geneva ended with little progress, as the warring sides could only agree on an agenda for future talks, not on key issues. The main deadlock centers on the Syrian government’s insistence on addressing terrorism first, while the opposition demands talks on a transitional government. Meanwhile, President Obama and Jordan’s king discussed the refugee crisis and possible U.N. pressure on Damascus, with the U.S. urging Russia to take a more constructive role. The only notable achievement so far has been a limited cease-fire allowing aid and evacuations in Homs, even as violence and the humanitarian catastrophe continue across Syria.

Facing a rare bone cancer as an adult, the author was treated in a pediatric oncology unit, where she initially felt out of place. Surrounded by children enduring harsh treatments, she was deeply inspired by their bravery, resilience, and focus on normal life rather than illness. Their hopeful perspective made her stop complaining about aging and taught her to face treatment with courage. She contrasts this with the more somber adult cancer ward, and she calls for greater funding and research to help children battling cancer.

The article humanizes the 239 passengers and crew of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, emphasizing that they were far more than a tragic statistic. It highlights the diversity of those aboard—ranging from a two-year-old child to a 76-year-old, and including engineers, artists, a stuntman, pilgrims, and vacationers from many nations. Through brief profiles, it shows the personal stories and deep loss felt by their families, such as a father who promised his children chocolates, a painter heading to an exhibition, and a captain remembered as a devoted family man. Ultimately, the piece underscores the profound human toll behind the mystery, as loved ones cling to hope amid the agonizing lack of answers.

The article emphasizes that MH17 victims likely lost consciousness instantly from explosive decompression, sparing them prolonged suffering, while the real anguish falls on their families. It calls for the United Nations to secure the crash site and protect evidence and bodies from looting and interference, ensuring dignified identification and farewells. Drawing lessons from Lockerbie, it warns against revenge and stresses the need for impartial international justice, rather than powerful nations acting as accuser and judge. The author also suggests that relatives may find support in established victim-assistance groups and that the truth should be pursued through trusted international institutions like the ICC.

Lollapalooza is expanding to the Middle East, with its first Israeli edition scheduled for August 2013 in Tel Aviv’s Yarkon Park. This makes Israel the festival’s third international host, following Chile and Brazil. The event is deliberately set for Tuesday through Thursday to avoid the Jewish Sabbath, when many observant attendees would not attend. Founder Perry Farrell also hinted at possible future plans for Jerusalem, as part of his vision to grow the festival globally.

Lollapalooza 2012 is set to draw 100,000 fans daily to Chicago’s Grant Park, with a sold-out lineup that pairs rock acts like Black Sabbath and the Red Hot Chili Peppers with electronic headliners such as Avicii and Justice. Founder Perry Farrell notes that DJs now command rock-star-level fees, reflecting their rise as major festival draws. To recreate the event’s original intimacy, Farrell is emphasizing late-night after-parties across the city, extending the festival beyond the park. He also hints at future growth, including international expansion and a surprise headliner for next year’s event.

Prime Minister David Cameron has pledged to hold a referendum on Britain’s EU membership if he wins the next election, a move that has drawn criticism from European leaders who reject the idea of a selective “à la carte” relationship. London Mayor Boris Johnson defended the promise as a democratic necessity, noting Britons haven’t been consulted since 1975, and predicted the UK would ultimately remain part of the free trade zone. He also dismissed French efforts to shift eurozone financial activity away from London, arguing that European capitals recognize the benefits of having a global financial powerhouse in the British capital.

Some 2012 London Olympic torchbearers are listing their used torches on eBay, with several selling for over $150,000 despite the fact the burners are disabled after the relay. Organizers note the torches belong to the runners, who bought them at a discounted price, and urge online buyers to verify authenticity. The relay continues across the UK with crowds turning out, featuring both celebrities and community members chosen for their achievements. The flame will eventually reach the opening ceremony, where the final runner will light the Olympic cauldron.

Families of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 face the uniquely painful ordeal of mourning loved ones whose remains may never be found, a situation experts compare to past disasters like TWA Flight 800 and 9/11. Psychologists say relatives must eventually find a way to make peace without the closure of recovered bodies, a process described as a "living loss" that can be more torturous than confirmed death. Some next of kin, such as a Chinese widow who has not told her young sons, are struggling to cope with the uncertainty. Grief counselors emphasize that while this challenge is immense, survivors can learn to carry their loved ones in their hearts and still find a path forward.

Louisiana has changed its lethal injection protocol for the upcoming execution of Christopher Sepulvado, adopting the same two-drug combination used in a recent Ohio execution because it cannot obtain pentobarbital. Sepulvado’s legal team plans to appeal the method of execution, not the death sentence itself. The controversy stems from Ohio inmate Dennis McGuire’s execution, during which he gasped and convulsed for about ten minutes, prompting concerns that the drug combination may amount to cruel and unusual punishment. The switch was anticipated by defense attorneys, who had predicted the state would struggle to secure the preferred drug.

Rachel Jeantel’s testimony in the George Zimmerman trial sharply divided public opinion, with reactions often reflecting viewers’ own backgrounds and biases. Critics saw her as hostile and unreliable, while supporters viewed her as a grieving teenager under immense pressure. Many negative judgments emerged before cross-examination, suggesting that perceptions of her appearance and speech influenced credibility more than her actual testimony. Ultimately, her impact on the case likely hinges on whether the jury saw her as a stereotype or as a sincere young woman in mourning.

The W hotel chain now offers a $3,000 “social media wedding concierge” service at its New York properties, which documents the planning process, live-tweets the ceremony, and ensures guests use a unified hashtag before compiling the best posts into a keepsake book. While the service has drawn mockery, it reflects the growing tendency to broadcast major life milestones online, and it can help faraway relatives follow along. However, some photographers worry that constant posting could distract from the ceremony and exclude guests who aren’t active on social media. The hotel also offers the opposite option—collecting guests’ phones—for couples who prefer an unplugged wedding.

The article highlights the plight of same-sex binational couples in the U.S., who are blocked from sponsoring their partners for immigration because federal law doesn't recognize their marriages. It profiles individuals like Melanie Servetas, who left her American life to live in Brazil, and others considering exile in Canada due to visa expirations. The piece underscores the high stakes of the Supreme Court's pending rulings on DOMA and Proposition 8, as well as a proposed Senate amendment that could grant immigration equality. For these couples, the legal uncertainty forces agonizing choices between love and country.

Premiere in 1994, "Friends" remains hugely popular in reruns, retaining a devoted audience even a decade after it ended. While the show has been criticized for its lack of diversity, its enduring appeal lies in the cast's chemistry and the comforting, familiar world of the characters' apartments and coffee shop. To mark the 20th anniversary, Warner Bros. recreated Central Perk in New York, where actor James Michael Tyler recalled that the original set was dismantled immediately after the final scene. He also shared that he kept Gunther's tie from the last episode, which the cast signed at the wrap party.

China and Malaysia are signaling a return to normal relations after tensions over the missing MH370 flight, with officials from both sides stressing cooperation and dismissing the harsh accusations made by some Chinese relatives as not representing official views. Malaysia has also confirmed China’s role in the investigation team. The strong economic partnership remains a key priority, as China is Malaysia’s largest trading partner and a major source of tourists. Experts believe the diplomatic friction was largely media-driven and that bilateral trade will stay stable, given China’s reliance on Malaysian raw materials and components.

Lupita Nyong'o and Gwendoline Christie have been added to the cast of “Star Wars: Episode VII,” with Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy expressing enthusiasm about the growing ensemble. They join previously announced actors such as John Boyega, Daisy Ridley, and Adam Driver, while original stars Mark Hamill, Harrison Ford, and Carrie Fisher are set to return. Nyong'o, who recently won an Oscar for “12 Years a Slave,” celebrated the news on social media.

A CDC inspection of the Silver Shadow cruise ship in Alaska resulted in a failing health score after crew members reportedly hid large amounts of food in their cabins to avoid detection. The vessel received an 82, below the satisfactory threshold, prompting the cruise line to express disappointment and call the incident an anomaly. Although the CDC verified the complaints and disposed of the food, it lacks enforcement power, so the ship faced no fines and continued its voyage. The episode adds to broader concerns about cruise industry safety, though customer satisfaction surveys still show generally positive ratings for major lines.

TripAdvisor has released its annual Travelers’ Choice Attractions Awards, ranking the world’s top landmarks and parks based on traveler reviews from the past year. Machu Picchu in Peru was named the world’s top landmark, while Stanley Park in Vancouver took the title of top park globally. The lists feature many religious and historic sites, and several U.S. military memorials rank highly among American landmarks. However, the results also sparked surprise due to notable omissions, including the Statue of Liberty, the Grand Canyon, and Egypt’s pyramids.

After more than a decade as a Mac user, the author is surprisingly eager for Windows 8, Microsoft’s major overhaul of its operating system. The redesign replaces the traditional Start menu with a touch-friendly “Metro” tile interface that offers live updates, while still keeping the classic desktop available for traditional apps. Although using the beta on a laptop involves a learning curve, the author finds the experience impressive and praises Microsoft for taking a bold step toward the future of computing. Whether consumers will embrace the gamble remains uncertain, but the author believes Microsoft must be doing something right.

Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees, most of which are found only on the island, have long been central to both its unique ecosystem and local communities, providing food, medicine, and shelter. However, these trees and the island’s extraordinary biodiversity are increasingly threatened by deforestation driven by slash-and-burn farming, logging, and charcoal production. Although the government has launched conservation and reforestation efforts and expanded protected areas, experts argue that key baobab habitats remain unprotected. Without stronger action and changes in local practices, Madagascar risks losing more of its irreplaceable forests and the unique species that depend on them.

A fourth U.S. death has been linked to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, the fatal human form of mad cow disease, after a Texas patient who had traveled extensively in Europe and the Middle East tested positive. Health officials noted that all U.S. cases of this rare brain illness are believed to have originated from exposure abroad, and they stressed there is no public health risk in Texas. The disease differs from classic CJD, which is not connected to mad cow disease and affects fewer than 400 Americans annually. The infection is caused by consuming beef products contaminated with prions from cattle with bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

Samuel Wong’s family-owned Chinese shipyard is trying to move upmarket by building mid-sized luxury yachts under the Accelera brand, hoping to challenge established European makers. The company leverages lower labor costs to sell its vessels at about a third of the price of Western competitors, but it faces skepticism from status-conscious buyers who doubt Chinese-built quality. This effort reflects a broader shift in China’s industry toward higher-value branded goods, though domestic yacht makers still struggle against foreign rivals and regulatory hurdles. While some Chinese firms are buying Western yacht brands to gain prestige, Wong is betting on gradual acceptance of his homegrown label.

A British woman was found dead in a hotel room days after a Sky News reporter confronted her about allegedly sending abusive messages online to the family of missing girl Madeleine McCann. The woman, identified as Brenda Leyland, had used the Twitter handle “Sweepyface” and denied any wrongdoing during the on-camera exchange. Police said her death was not being treated as suspicious and that a file was being prepared for the coroner. Separately, Scotland Yard was reviewing allegations of malicious communications directed at the McCann family, though no one had been interviewed in connection with that investigation.

Charlie Hebdo’s Paris office was set on fire early Wednesday, just before the satirical magazine was set to release a cover lampooning Islamic law with a cartoon of the Prophet Muhammad. The publisher blamed a Molotov cocktail attack, while French officials strongly condemned the violence and reaffirmed their commitment to press freedom. The incident comes amid heightened tensions over France’s Muslim community and follows threats against the magazine, whose website was also hacked by a group claiming to act in defense of Islam.

The Maker Faire, rooted in the DIY maker culture, has grown from a Bay Area gathering into a globally exported brand, with its original California event drawing over 120,000 attendees. While Maker Media organizes major fairs in New York and Rome, it also supports more than 120 smaller community-run events worldwide, up from 60 the previous year. The festival blends entertainment with hands-on learning, featuring attractions like Arduino projects, 3-D printing, and interactive exhibits, while emphasizing science and engineering for families. Organizers highlight the event’s role in getting children engaged in creative, hands-on activities, especially as schools move away from such experiences.

Saudi women are focusing their efforts on economic empowerment as a strategic priority, seeing it as beneficial both for themselves and for the kingdom’s goal of reducing reliance on oil and foreign labor. Despite high female unemployment and weak global rankings for women’s economic participation, the article argues that growth alone is insufficient and must be paired with inclusive reforms. Civic changes that increase women’s visibility—such as appointing them to the Shura Council, allowing them to vote, and easing mobility—are essential for creating role models and driving further progress. Ultimately, women’s economic integration is presented as a crucial step for both gender equality and national transformation.

The attack on Malala Yousufzai underscores the widespread dangers girls face in pursuing an education, as violence—both in communities and within schools—remains a major barrier worldwide. Many girls are kept out of school due to fear of sexual assault, early marriage, or harassment, while those who do attend may still face abuse from teachers. However, education can actually reduce girls' vulnerability to violence and open doors to better opportunities. To create lasting change, governments and organizations must invest directly in girls, enforce protections against teacher abuse, provide safe spaces, and recruit female teachers.

People differ in emotional resilience because their brains are wired with two opposing systems—one that gravitates toward threat and negativity, and another that draws them toward positivity and reward. These patterns shape whether someone tends toward pessimism or optimism, and they influence how everyday events are interpreted. However, the brain is not fixed; thanks to neuroplasticity, repeated thoughts and experiences can physically reshape neural circuits, much like London cab drivers grow a larger hippocampus through intensive navigation training. This means that by consciously training the mind, people can shift toward a more optimistic outlook, which, especially when balanced with realism, supports better health, success, and well-being.

Local currencies are experiencing a revival as communities seek to boost local spending and address economic inequality, with new digital technologies making them easier to use. Success depends on a clear purpose, a dedicated volunteer team, and strong early engagement with local businesses and residents. Practical steps include running design competitions, securing funding, and gaining official support, but the real challenge lies in sustaining momentum after launch. Long-term viability requires continuous promotion, creative incentives, and building deep relationships with major local institutions to integrate the currency into everyday spending.

Malala Yousafzai marked her 16th birthday by delivering her first major public address at the United Nations, where she called for universal access to education and spoke out against the Taliban’s efforts to silence girls. She said she holds no hatred toward the gunmen who shot her, emphasizing that violence and fear had been replaced by strength and courage. Yousafzai urged world leaders to protect children’s and women’s rights, end conflicts, and guarantee free compulsory education for every child. She also presented the U.N. chief with a petition signed by millions supporting the millions of children worldwide who are denied schooling.

Malala Yousafzai has spoken out against Boko Haram’s abduction of Nigerian schoolgirls, saying such attacks stem from a fear of women’s empowerment. She called the kidnapped girls her “sisters” and urged global action, joining the #BringBackOurGirls campaign and launching a Nigerian girls’ education initiative through her fund. Malala also criticized Boko Haram’s interpretation of Islam, insisting the religion supports education and dignity for women. The Nigerian government, meanwhile, has faced backlash for its slow response and has accepted U.S. military assistance in the search.

The article outlines eight unresolved questions surrounding the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over rebel-held eastern Ukraine. Key uncertainties include who fired the missile, whether the plane was mistaken for a military target, and why civilian aircraft were allowed to fly over an active conflict zone. Investigators also face major obstacles, including rebel control of the crash site, the status of the black boxes, and the recovery and handling of victims' remains. Finally, the incident poses a diplomatic dilemma for Russia, as its response could either trigger severe international sanctions or damage Putin's domestic standing.

After weeks of searching, authorities have yet to find any confirmed wreckage from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, with recent leads like orange objects and debris turning out to be fishing gear and a jellyfish. Frustrated families are demanding concrete evidence, especially after receiving mixed signals about whether passengers could still be alive. The multinational search effort is expanding, with more ships and aircraft scouring the southern Indian Ocean, though officials acknowledge they are working with limited information. Meanwhile, time is running out to locate the flight recorder before its beacon battery dies, as the search continues without a set deadline.

Malaysia Airlines is allowing passengers to cancel or change their tickets without fees following the MH17 disaster, with the option valid until July 24 for travel through year-end. The airline is also retiring the MH17 flight number, renaming the Amsterdam–Kuala Lumpur service MH19 out of respect for the victims. Other carriers have rerouted flights away from Ukrainian airspace, and Singapore Airlines has apologized for a social media post that was perceived as insensitive amid the tragedy.

After more than a month of searching, authorities have yet to find any trace of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, but they are focusing on new hope: underwater signals detected by an Australian naval vessel that could be from the plane's black boxes. Officials caution that the pings are unconfirmed and have not been heard again, though the search area has been narrowed to a smaller zone in the Indian Ocean. Time is a critical factor because the locator beacons' batteries were expected to last about 30 days. Despite cautious optimism, no physical wreckage has been found, and investigators are still piecing together what happened after the jet vanished from radar.

A Malaysian court has approved the extradition of an Iranian suspect, Masoud Sedaghatzadeh, to Thailand for his alleged role in the February Bangkok bombings. He plans to appeal the decision in a higher court. The explosions, which caused no deaths, were reportedly aimed at Israeli diplomats, and Thai police say evidence includes CCTV footage linking him to the blast site. Two other Iranian suspects are in Thai custody, while two more remain at large.

A Malaysian appeals court has reversed Anwar Ibrahim’s earlier acquittal and found him guilty of sodomizing a former aide, a charge he has long dismissed as politically motivated. His party allies condemned the ruling as a rushed injustice aimed at preventing him from participating in upcoming elections. The case stems from a 2008 allegation, and the original trial judge had rejected the DNA evidence as unreliable. Anwar, a prominent opposition leader with a history of past convictions, now faces a possible prison sentence of up to 20 years.

Malaysian opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim confirmed that the missing MH370 pilot was a party member and a distant relative, but rejected claims that the plane’s disappearance was a political protest over his own prison sentence. He accused the Malaysian government of promoting that theory to distract from its poor handling of the crisis. A political analyst similarly dismissed the political motive as a red herring, noting there was no evidence and that such a silent protest would be unprecedented. Malaysian officials declined to respond to Anwar’s allegations.

Malaysia has agreed to return a diplomat to New Zealand to face charges related to an alleged sexual assault, ending a tense dispute between the two countries. The official, who had left New Zealand using diplomatic immunity, is accused of burglary and assault with intent to commit rape in Wellington. New Zealand authorities said he will be arrested upon arrival and brought before a court. The case had sparked public outrage, and while New Zealand’s foreign minister apologized for miscommunication over the envoy’s status, he maintained that Malaysia had acted in good faith throughout.

Andrej Pejic, the model known for his androgynous runway work, has come out as a transgender woman named Andreja after undergoing gender reassignment surgery. She says she always wanted to be a girl and hid her true identity while growing up, but now feels fully herself. Pejic has also begun acting, with roles in a David Bowie short and Sofia Coppola’s upcoming film, and she chooses to keep the details of her surgery private, echoing fellow trans celebrity Laverne Cox. She is speaking publicly to inspire others and says her career will now adapt to her authentic life.

Islamist militants linked to al Qaeda in northern Mali have again destroyed revered mausoleums in Timbuktu, asserting that such shrines are idolatrous. The attack, the latest in a series against the city's historic tombs, drew international condemnation. Mali has been destabilized since a coup earlier this year, enabling rebels to seize the north, and the U.N. Security Council has approved a resolution paving the way for a possible military intervention to reclaim the region.

France’s rapid military intervention in Mali succeeded in ousting Islamist militants from key towns, but the harder part is just beginning: jihadists have melted into the desert and mountains, threatening a guerrilla campaign of bombings and ambushes. The mission to stabilize Mali is complicated by a weak and divided national army, ethnic Tuareg grievances, mutual accusations of atrocities, and a poorly equipped African peacekeeping force that lacks airpower and mobility. French officials acknowledge that military action alone cannot secure lasting peace, so they are pushing for political dialogue, army reform, and elections, while trying to peel moderate Tuareg factions away from extremists. Without addressing the underlying regional and ethnic tensions, analysts warn, Mali could easily slide back into crisis despite its recent military gains.

Malta’s foreign minister says the country can no longer afford to support the large number of migrants held in its overcrowded detention centers, adding that many migrants damage the facilities and do not help their own situation. He is urging other European Union members to show solidarity through a fair system of relocating recognized refugees across member states. The minister also argues that Malta bears a disproportionate burden compared to other EU countries and stresses the need to tackle the root causes of migration and prevent human trafficking. The appeal comes as thousands continue to cross the Mediterranean, with many rescued near Italian and Maltese shores.

NFL star Adrian Peterson is dealing with legal trouble after being charged with injuring his young son by spanking him with a switch, an act his lawyer frames as discipline similar to Peterson’s own upbringing. At the same time, the man accused of fatally abusing another of Peterson’s children has been released on a $2 million bond, though Peterson has maintained that child’s death was accidental. Peterson denies being a child abuser, while the NFL has placed him on paid leave as the case proceeds. Despite his off-field struggles, the summary should note his on-field achievements, including an NFL MVP award and a record-setting rushing performance.Adrian Peterson, an NFL star, is facing child abuse charges for using a switch to spank his young son, an act his lawyer defends as parental discipline. Meanwhile, the man charged in the death of another of Peterson’s children has been released on bail, even though Peterson has maintained that earlier death was accidental. Peterson denies any wrongdoing and has been placed on paid leave by the NFL while the legal case unfolds. Despite these personal troubles, he remains a celebrated athlete, known for his record-breaking rushing performance and an NFL MVP award.

Your brain is constantly rewiring itself through experience, and this neuroplasticity means change is always happening—either by your choice or by default. By understanding how your brain works, you can make deliberate “neurochoices” that build healthy habits, while unchecked patterns can lead to harmful addictions. To manage your brain during stress, you can shift your focus toward solutions, breathe steadily to calm your body, and consciously relax to access clearer thinking. Ultimately, taking an active role in shaping your brain helps you create the life and outcomes you want.

An American man returning from overseas was arrested at JFK Airport on weapons charges after federal authorities linked him to online support for ISIS. Donald Ray Morgan, who had been living abroad, is accused of illegal weapons possession and trafficking, in violation of his probation. Officials described him as an “aspirational” ISIS sympathizer rather than someone involved in active plots, though prosecutors argued he may have trafficked guns to the group. A judge denied bail, citing tweets suggesting he intended to travel to Syria or Iraq.

Malcolm Glazer, the American businessman who owned both the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Manchester United, has died at the age of 85. He turned the struggling Buccaneers into a Super Bowl-winning franchise, but his 2005 purchase of Manchester United sparked fan anger because it loaded the club with heavy debt. Despite the controversy, United enjoyed major success under his ownership, claiming multiple Premier League titles and a Champions League trophy. His family will continue to run both teams, and tributes have highlighted his impact on the NFL and the Tampa Bay community.

Manchester United announced that Sir Alex Ferguson will retire at the end of the season after 26 years as manager, with Everton’s David Moyes widely expected to be named his successor. Ferguson leaves as the most successful manager in British football history, having won over 30 trophies and transformed the club into a global commercial powerhouse. His farewell comes after securing this season’s Premier League title, and he will remain at the club as a director and ambassador. The announcement marks a major transition for the club, as his successor faces the daunting task of following an iconic and highly decorated leader.

Former South African President Nelson Mandela is back home after a hospital stay and is doing well, according to his granddaughters, who say he is alert, reading the newspaper, and spending time with family. They strongly denied social media rumors that he is near death, calling such speculation hurtful and insensitive. The family thanked supporters worldwide for their prayers and asked for privacy as Mandela continues recovering at home. The 94-year-old anti-apartheid icon remains in good spirits, though he has largely stayed out of public view since 2010.

Nelson Mandela’s 95th birthday is being celebrated worldwide, especially in South Africa, even as he remains hospitalized in critical but stable condition with a lung infection. The day, recognized as Nelson Mandela International Day, encourages people to spend 67 minutes in public service, reflecting Mandela’s years of activism. Festivities include a poster exhibition at the University of Pretoria featuring 95 works from international designers, with proceeds going to a children’s hospital trust. Many South Africans are joining in tributes, hoping for his recovery and honoring his legacy of humanity and charity.

A Moroccan man was sentenced to 30 years in prison for plotting to bomb the U.S. Capitol, a scheme disrupted by an FBI sting in which he received a suicide vest and gun that were made inoperable. Prosecutors pushed for the maximum penalty, citing the seriousness of the plot and recent attacks on U.S. personnel, while defense lawyers argued he was manipulated by undercover agents and had no desire to harm Americans. The judge imposed the harshest sentence allowed under the plea agreement, noting concerns about whether he might repeat such actions in the future. El Khalifi, who was in the U.S. illegally, had considered multiple targets before settling on the Capitol and will be deported to Morocco after serving his sentence.

The article begins by noting that New York’s first Manhattanhenge of 2014 was obscured by clouds, though additional viewing dates were still upcoming. It then shifts to showcasing spectacular sunset destinations around the world, including Myanmar, Kenya, Australia, Italy, the Grand Canyon, Dubai, China, Taiwan, Greece, Easter Island, Cambodia, and Hawaii. Each location is highlighted for its unique scenery and atmosphere at dusk. The piece also invites readers to share their own favorite sunset spots in the comments.

In a pretrial hearing at Fort Meade, the military judge ordered prosecutors to provide the defense with a redacted Defense Intelligence Agency damage assessment related to the WikiLeaks disclosures, a modest win for Private Bradley Manning. Manning faces multiple charges, including aiding the enemy, and could receive life in prison if convicted. His defense team is seeking dismissal of ten charges, arguing that the Espionage Act language is unconstitutionally vague and that Manning had authorized access to the classified networks. Additional hearings are set to continue, including witness testimony on how damage assessments are produced.

A Wisconsin entrepreneur is offering his vacation home for 100 million Dogecoins, the meme-inspired cryptocurrency that began as a Bitcoin parody. Although far less valuable than Bitcoin, Dogecoin has gained a loyal community and real-world use, including fundraising efforts and business transactions. The seller sees it as a viable payment method and believes the currency has room to grow alongside other digital coins. While no offers have been made yet, the listing has generated significant attention for Dogecoin.

The family of Marlon Brown, a Florida man killed in May when a police cruiser ran him over during a foot chase, has publicly released dashcam footage in hopes of prompting criminal charges against the officer involved. The officer, James Harris, had been pursuing Brown over a seatbelt violation, and the incident ended when Brown fell and was struck by Harris’s vehicle. A grand jury declined to indict Harris on a vehicular manslaughter charge, and he was later fired from the police force. Although the city paid Brown’s family $550,000 in a settlement, they are pushing for further legal accountability, arguing the use of the vehicle amounted to reckless conduct.

A Georgia man charged with murder in the hot-car death of his 22-month-old son faces a probable cause hearing to determine if he should remain jailed. Police allege the father left the child in a hot SUV for hours while at work, and investigators have noted internet searches about children dying in hot cars. The boy’s mother has publicly supported her husband, who called into the funeral from jail. The medical examiner has indicated the death was consistent with hyperthermia and suggested homicide, though toxicology results are still pending.

The jury for Jerry Sandusky’s trial has been selected, with many members having personal or professional ties to Penn State, including professors, graduates, employees, and a current student. Several jurors know potential witnesses or have followed the case closely, but most said they could remain impartial. The judge acknowledged that such connections were unavoidable in the local community. The trial is set to begin with opening statements on Monday.

Baylor basketball player Isaiah Austin’s NBA hopes ended after a physical revealed he has Marfan syndrome, a genetic disorder that weakens connective tissue and can dangerously enlarge the heart and aorta. The condition also explains his tall, slender build and past eye problems, including blindness in one eye. Although the diagnosis crushes his pro basketball dreams, it may save his life by allowing him to manage the condition and avoid fatal complications, unlike volleyball player Flo Hyman, who died from an undiagnosed aortic tear. Millions may be unaware they have the disorder, but with proper medical care and lifestyle adjustments, those affected can live longer, healthier lives.

Maria de Villota, a pioneering female Formula One driver and former Marussia reserve driver, has died at the age of 33. She was found dead in a hotel in Seville, where she was promoting her autobiography, and her family confirmed that her death was caused by the severe neurological injuries she sustained in a 2012 crash during a test session. That accident had cost her her right eye and left her with serious head trauma. Tributes poured in from across the F1 world, with teams and officials honoring her courage, determination, and inspirational spirit in the face of adversity.

Marina Abramovic is staging a major new performance piece in London, where she will spend over two months in the gallery for eight hours a day, creating art purely through energy and presence rather than physical objects. The exhibition builds on her reputation for intense audience connection, recalling her famous MoMA retrospective where thousands waited to sit silently with her. Her decades-long career has been marked by extreme physical endurance and a disciplined approach rooted in her strict upbringing, while her mainstream fame has not diminished her radical artistic ambitions. For this show, she asks visitors to leave their devices behind, urging them to experience the moment fully rather than document it.

U.S. Marines stationed in Italy and Spain have been placed on heightened alert as a precaution ahead of expected large protests in Egypt this weekend. They are prepared to deploy within an hour if needed to protect American personnel and facilities, while additional Marines are positioned on Navy ships in the Red Sea for potential evacuation support. Officials stress this is contingency planning, not an indication of imminent action, and note that U.S. forces are better positioned than during the 2012 Benghazi attack. The U.S. Embassy in Cairo will be closed Sunday and Monday, and American citizens have been advised to avoid protest areas and limit movement.

The Pentagon has relocated around 200 crisis-response Marines from Spain to a base in Sicily as a precaution due to the worsening security situation in North Africa. The force, equipped with Ospreys and cargo aircraft, is positioned to respond quickly to regional threats, including protecting U.S. embassies and potentially operating in Yemen. Officials stress the move is unrelated to the Nigerian schoolgirl rescue mission and is part of broader efforts to maintain flexible military options. The deployment reflects lessons from past attacks on U.S. facilities, such as the 2012 Benghazi incident.

A pregnant 19-year-old Marine wife disappeared in Southern California after going to Joshua Tree National Park to scout photo spots. Extensive ground and air searches have found no trace of her, though her car was later located near the military base where her husband is stationed. Police now consider the case suspicious and homicide detectives are leading the investigation, but no charges have been filed. Her mother, who learned of the pregnancy only after the disappearance, remains desperate for her daughter’s return.

Mark Harmon has teamed up with Stand Up to Cancer and the Cancer Research Institute for a new public service announcement promoting immunotherapy, which uses the body’s own immune system to fight cancer. Motivated by friends affected by the disease, Harmon emphasizes the importance of raising awareness about these treatments. Recent studies presented at a major cancer conference have shown meaningful progress in the field. The two organizations have also funded a collaborative research team to further explore how the immune system can be harnessed against cancer.

The family of Marlise Muñoz, a Texas woman declared brain dead while pregnant, won a legal battle to have her removed from life support against a hospital's interpretation of state law. In their first national interview, they said they fought to honor her known wishes, as she had never wanted to be kept alive by machines. They hope their story encourages other families to have clear end-of-life conversations and to make their own decisions, rather than leaving such matters to politicians. The family also expressed anger that the case was used for political debate, emphasizing that the ordeal was deeply personal and not a platform for others' agendas.

The article highlights a same-sex couple in Washington, D.C., who are legally married under local law but are denied federal benefits because of the Defense of Marriage Act, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman. Their case is part of a Supreme Court appeal over whether DOMA violates constitutional equal protection. The Obama administration has refused to defend the law, leaving House Republicans to argue for its constitutionality. The couple describes the personal and financial hardships of being treated as legal strangers by the federal government, and they hope the Court will end that inequality.

NASA’s Curiosity rover has provided the strongest evidence yet that ancient Mars could have supported microbial life. By analyzing clay-rich mudstone in Gale Crater’s Yellowknife Bay, scientists confirmed that a lake once existed there, containing the essential chemical ingredients for life. The rover also measured the age of a Martian rock for the first time, showing that habitable conditions existed around 4 billion years ago. Although Mars later became cold, dry, and highly radioactive, these findings deepen understanding of its past environment and will help guide future human missions.

NASA’s Curiosity rover landed safely on Mars after a complex descent, marking a major engineering success and drawing widespread praise. The rover is in good condition and will begin exploring Gale Crater and Mount Sharp to assess whether Mars ever had conditions suitable for microbial life. Initial images have been received, and while full scientific work will take time, the mission is seen as a significant achievement for NASA and a boost for future space exploration.

Rachel Jeantel, the friend who was on the phone with Trayvon Martin before his death, expressed anger and disappointment at George Zimmerman's acquittal, calling the verdict unjust and insisting Martin was calm and nonaggressive. She argued that race was central to the case, suggesting a white teen in a hoodie would not have been treated the same way. Jeantel also criticized Zimmerman's defense for not having him testify, calling it weak, and dismissed claims that marijuana made Martin dangerous. Though her testimony faced credibility challenges and public scrutiny over her speech and demeanor, one juror said she felt sympathy for Jeantel, who seemed overwhelmed and out of place in the trial.

Typhoon Bolaven struck Okinawa with its most powerful winds in nearly five decades, bringing gusts over 250 kilometers per hour and torrential rain. The storm, which is enormous in size, caused residents to shelter in concrete buildings designed for such extreme weather. After passing Okinawa, Bolaven is now threatening the Korean peninsula, where landfall could occur soon. Meanwhile, its interaction with Typhoon Tembin is altering Tembin's path, potentially pulling it toward China and causing another landfall in Taiwan.

MasterChef runner-up Joshua Marks, who struggled with bipolar disorder and a recent schizophrenia diagnosis, died by suicide at age 26. His family says he could not get the long-term mental health care he needed and that easy access to a gun made his death possible. They described his final months as a desperate battle with mental illness, marked by a previous self-inflicted gunshot and arrest, and are now calling for better treatment options and stricter gun access. His mother found him in an alley after a neighbor reported he was walking with a gun.

Arnold Palmer’s 1962 Masters win marked the start of a standout year that cemented his status as a global golf icon, as he overcame a playoff to claim his third Green Jacket and later added another British Open title. The article also traces golf’s greatest seasons through history, highlighting legendary figures such as Bobby Jones, Byron Nelson, Ben Hogan, Jack Nicklaus, Tom Watson, Nick Faldo, and Tiger Woods, each of whom defined their era with remarkable achievements. These players not only dominated competition but also shaped the sport’s legacy through record-breaking performances and lasting influence.

Maxine Powell, the longtime Motown grooming coach, has died at age 98. She shaped the poise and public image of legendary acts like Diana Ross, Marvin Gaye, and the Supremes, teaching them manners, style, and confidence. Motown founder Berry Gordy and Smokey Robinson both praised her as an essential, one-of-a-kind figure whose influence helped define the label’s polished appeal. Her legacy endures through the artists she mentored.

Maya Angelou is remembered above all for her powerful use of language, which she wielded in both writing and speech to move audiences deeply. Among her most notable public moments were reading her poem at President Bill Clinton’s 1993 inauguration, receiving the Literarian Award at the 2013 National Book Awards, and delivering tributes at Coretta Scott King’s 2008 funeral. She also shared her poetry as a keynote speaker at the 2012 Children’s Defense Fund conference. Her words continue to resonate long after her passing.

Senator John McCain urged the U.S. to lead international airstrikes against Syrian government forces to establish safe havens and better equip opposition fighters, arguing that military aid alone is insufficient to end the bloodshed. He acknowledged the risks and the lack of cohesion among rebel groups, but insisted the U.S. must act to shape a favorable outcome. Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts advanced as UN officials and envoy Kofi Annan prepared to visit Damascus, even as violence continued and the death toll rose. The article also highlights growing Iranian support for the Syrian regime, U.S. sanctions on Syrian state media, and the ongoing humanitarian crisis, with thousands of civilians killed and displaced.

Chris McDaniel, the Mississippi state senator who lost the Republican runoff to Thad Cochran, announced he will soon file a legal challenge, claiming thousands of voting irregularities and uncounted absentee ballots. He defended his campaign's reward offer for evidence of voter fraud and condemned racist remarks made on a Cochran campaign call, distancing his campaign from the caller. The Cochran camp dismissed the allegations as exaggerated and demanded proof, accusing McDaniel of prolonging the fight for attention. McDaniel said he would respect court decisions but has not decided whether to endorse Cochran if the challenge fails.

Reality television increasingly depends on female confrontations and physical altercations to attract viewers, with shows like "Jersey Shore," "The Bachelor," and "Real Housewives" using catfights as a ratings staple. While audiences claim to be annoyed by the constant drama, they still tune in and even enjoy the shock value, often choosing sides between feuding cast members. Producers acknowledge that although fights aren't scripted word-for-word, they deliberately create tense situations likely to spark conflict. As competition among hundreds of reality shows intensifies, producers keep raising the bar on aggression to capture attention, leaving experts questioning how far the genre will go.

The article explores the rising problem of "mean girl" behavior among younger girls, fueled by online culture and hyperfeminine pressures. Experts advise parents to model supportive female relationships, explicitly teach empathy and the golden rule, and focus on building their daughters' self-worth rather than labeling others. Avoiding the "mean girl" label itself is also important, as it can prevent kids from learning to handle conflict constructively. Ultimately, parents are urged to reflect on their own behavior and stay actively involved in guiding girls through friendship challenges.

In northern Yemen, Houthi militants attacked a Sunni town in Sa'ada before dawn, killing at least 24 people and wounding dozens more, with witnesses saying the area was under siege and medical help was blocked. The assault targeted a Sunni religious center and came amid failed mediation efforts and rising sectarian violence. The Houthis, who have expanded their control across several provinces, rejected the recent power-transfer agreement signed by Yemen's president. The attack followed the president's formal departure after months of protests, part of the broader Arab Spring upheaval.

President Dmitry Medvedev has ordered an investigation into reported voting irregularities in the recent parliamentary elections, following large street protests. Although he disagreed with the demonstrators' demands, he instructed officials to verify compliance with election laws at polling stations. The ruling party, United Russia, lost significant ground but maintained its majority, while tens of thousands protested in Moscow and St. Petersburg, calling for a new vote. Earlier demonstrations had led to hundreds of arrests.

Scientists have identified a new dinosaur species, Torvosaurus gurneyi, from fossils in Portugal, making it the largest land predator known from Europe. Previously mistaken for a North American relative, the species is distinguished by fewer teeth and lived about 150 million years ago. Its existence supports the idea that Europe and North America were briefly connected during the Late Jurassic, allowing animals to mix before geographic separation led to distinct species. This formidable carnivore, with nearly four-inch teeth and a large skull, was likely the top predator of its tropical environment.

The newly launched superyacht Azzam has overtaken Roman Abramovich’s Eclipse as the world’s largest, measuring 590 feet and costing $605 million. Its owner remains unidentified, though speculation points to a wealthy Middle Eastern buyer. In addition to its record-breaking size, Azzam is also the fastest superyacht afloat, with a top speed above 30 knots. The vessel was designed and engineered by top European firms, but many details of its lavish interior are still being kept secret.

Boeing has recently advanced its sustainable aviation fuel efforts through three key initiatives: promoting “green diesel” as a low-carbon biofuel, launching a biofuel supply chain in the United Arab Emirates with a demonstration flight, and reporting promising research on saltwater-tolerant desert plants called halophytes. The company emphasizes diversifying biofuel sources and regions to reduce cost volatility and meet aggressive industry targets for carbon-neutral growth by 2020 and a 50% emissions cut by 2050. Green diesel stands out because it is already produced in large volumes and costs about $3 per gallon with incentives, though it still needs regulatory approval for jet use. Critics argue that biofuel production can compete with food crops and may emit more carbon than it saves, but Boeing insists it only pursues feedstocks that do not compete with food production resources.

A robot band called Z-Machines, created by University of Tokyo engineers, features a towering humanoid guitarist with 78 fingers, a drummer with 22 arms, and a laser-playing keyboardist. British electronic artist Squarepusher composed music for the group, whose debut album includes tracks exploring whether machines can produce emotionally engaging music. The project highlights the eerie, fascinating boundary between human and machine, while acknowledging that human creators still control the robots. Despite the novelty, the inventor suggests robot performers won't replace human musicians anytime soon.

Mel Gibson has publicly expressed sympathy for Shia LaBeouf following the actor’s recent arrest and erratic behavior, saying he relates to the pain of being judged under public scrutiny. Drawing on his own experience with controversy, Gibson noted that people are quick to criticize troubled celebrities but that LaBeouf is likely going through a difficult personal transformation. He also voiced confidence in LaBeouf’s recovery, especially after the actor sought treatment for alcohol addiction, and said he believes LaBeouf will ultimately be fine.

Two Pussy Riot members were briefly detained by police in Sochi on suspicion of a hotel theft, but were released after questioning with no charges filed. The women, Maria Alyokhina and Nadezhda Tolokonnikova, alleged that officers used physical force and dragged them while they waited for a lawyer. They were in Sochi to protest restrictions on free speech and record an anti-Putin song, having recently been released from prison after a controversial conviction.

The Justice Department has confirmed that the U.S. may legally kill an American citizen overseas if that person is a senior operational leader of al Qaeda or an associated force, provided an imminent threat exists and capture is not feasible. The policy, outlined in a confidential memo, has been used to justify drone strikes such as the 2011 killing of Anwar al-Awlaki, who was never charged with a crime. While the administration defends the strikes as lawful under congressional authorization and war principles, civil liberties groups and some lawmakers argue the policy grants the president excessive power without judicial oversight. Critics are urging the release of the full legal opinions behind the memo to clarify the limits of executive authority.

The sinking of the Sewol ferry devastated a South Korean high school community, as most of the victims were students from Danwon High School. Many bodies remained unidentified, described only by clothing or personal items, while the school and nearby neighborhoods became sites of mourning with flowers, yellow ribbons, and heartfelt notes. The tragedy also brought grief to local residents and business owners who knew the students, and the school reopened only for senior students with mental health support available. Parents and teachers struggled with profound loss, clinging to memories of their children and calling out for them in grief.

A Drexel University student died from the same strain of serogroup B meningitis linked to the Princeton University outbreak, after having close contact with Princeton students about a week before falling ill. This death has raised concerns that the outbreak strain may still be circulating in the Princeton community, though no new cases have been reported there since an unlicensed vaccine was administered starting in December. Health officials are investigating the student’s contacts and providing antibiotics, while noting that vaccinated individuals could still carry and transmit the bacteria. No related cases have been reported at Drexel.

A rare, non-contagious fungal meningitis outbreak has sickened at least 119 people and killed 12, with cases linked to contaminated steroid injections used for back pain.
