The tainted medication was traced to the New England Compounding Center, which has recalled its products, and health officials expect the number of cases to grow. Those who received the injections since May and develop symptoms such as headache, fever, stiff neck, or sensitivity to light are urged to seek medical attention. Federal and state agencies are investigating the source of the contamination, which occurs when fungal spores are injected directly into the spine.

A South African court sentenced four men to 18 years each for the 2006 murder of 19-year-old lesbian Zoliswa Nkonyana, with the judge ruling that the killing was driven by hatred of her sexual orientation. After receiving credit for time served, the men will remain imprisoned for 14 more years. Rights advocates welcomed the ruling as the first time in South Africa that sexual orientation discrimination was treated as an aggravating factor in a criminal case. They hope the sentence sends a strong signal across Africa, where homophobic violence and discriminatory laws remain widespread despite South Africa’s legal protections.

Phil Mickelson pulled out of the Memorial Tournament on Friday, saying he was mentally fatigued after a demanding stretch that included four events in five weeks and personal travel. His decision followed a poor opening round of seven-over-par 79, his worst score at that course. He explained that he needs to rest and recharge to be at his best for the upcoming U.S. Open, where he will focus his preparation next.

The latest court ruling in Italy has again convicted Amanda Knox and Raffaele Sollecito for the murder of Meredith Kercher, prolonging a legal saga that has overshadowed the victim herself. Kercher’s family says they may never know exactly what happened the night she died and acknowledge the case could continue to Italy’s Supreme Court. They stress that Meredith, not the defendants, should be remembered, describing her as a generous, vibrant young woman whose life was cut short. Despite the intense media focus on Knox, those close to Kercher remain committed to honoring her memory and seeking justice.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel said U.S. spying on her phone and other allies has severely damaged transatlantic trust, insisting that words alone are not enough and that concrete changes in U.S. surveillance practices are needed. She stressed that spying among friends is unacceptable, a message she conveyed directly to President Obama, who assured her the U.S. is not monitoring her communications and has ordered a review of intelligence-gathering methods. The controversy, fueled by Edward Snowden's leaks, has angered European leaders, prompting calls for stronger EU data protection rules and adding surveillance concerns to the summit agenda. The U.S. has defended its intelligence activities as standard practice while acknowledging the disclosures have strained key alliances.

Chancellor Angela Merkel told Germany’s parliament that resolving the eurozone crisis requires a genuine fiscal union and treaty changes, warning that the process will be lengthy and that the crisis reflects a failure of trust and politics. She ruled out a split between euro and non-euro countries and rejected Eurobonds as a quick fix, insisting instead on stronger budget coordination and transparency. Opposition leaders criticized her approach, accusing her of overstepping while planning domestic tax cuts. Despite the challenges, Merkel remained hopeful, comparing the effort to a marathon that demands endurance rather than speed.

The first U.S. case of MERS has been confirmed in Indiana, involving an American health care worker who recently returned from Saudi Arabia. The patient is hospitalized in stable condition and isolated, and officials stress the risk to the public remains very low since the virus does not spread easily among people. Health authorities are investigating the case and will contact fellow travelers as a precaution, though they are not considered high risk. The case highlights the global reach of MERS, which has caused hundreds of infections and dozens of deaths, mostly linked to the Arabian Peninsula.

A new study detected MERS coronavirus genetic material in air samples taken from a camel barn linked to an infected camel and its owner, who later died. The viral strain matched the one found in the camel and the patient, suggesting the virus can be present in airborne particles. However, experts caution that finding viral RNA in the air does not prove the virus is infectious or easily transmitted through aerosols. More research is needed to determine whether airborne transmission plays a significant role in spreading MERS.

Federal regulators issued an emergency order requiring Metro-North to take immediate safety measures after a fatal derailment in the Bronx. The train entered a sharp curve at nearly three times the speed limit, and the engineer may have dozed off. The order mandates signal system upgrades to enforce speed limits and requires two qualified crew members in the cab at major speed-reduction zones until those changes are made. The railroad must also submit a broader safety action plan by the end of the year.

A deadly Metro-North derailment near New York, caused by an engineer’s apparent inattention, has reignited debate over whether advanced automation should take over critical safety tasks from humans. Experts say positive train control technology, which uses GPS and computers to enforce speed limits and prevent crashes, would likely have stopped the accident, but railroads have resisted it due to cost and implementation delays. Similar questions are emerging in aviation and self-driving cars, where automation can reduce human error but raises concerns about expense, complacency, and pilots or drivers losing understanding of the systems. Ultimately, while automated safety technology is increasingly seen as the future, experts caution that it must be designed to support human judgment rather than replace it entirely.

Mexican church leaders have publicly revealed that drug cartels attempted to extort a major Catholic seminary in Mexico City, demanding thousands of dollars under threat of killing priests. While such extortion attempts against parishes are increasingly common, public acknowledgment of them is rare, and church officials are urging people to report threats rather than pay. The Catholic Church in Mexico has long faced dangers from cartel violence, including past assassinations and threats against clergy who speak out against drug trafficking. Church leaders plan to raise these ongoing risks to priests and congregations during an upcoming meeting with Pope Francis.

Amnesty International reports that the decapitated editor of a Mexican border newspaper was likely killed by a drug cartel in retaliation for her social media activity. The body of María Elizabeth Macías was found in Nuevo Laredo alongside a message warning that others who use social networks to report on crime could face the same fate. Amnesty noted that two other people had recently been killed under similar circumstances, suggesting an intimidation campaign against online commentators. The killing, which made Macías the fourth female journalist murdered in Mexico this year, has intensified concerns about the dangers of reporting on drug violence.

Mexican officials announced the arrest of 18 suspected gang members tied to kidnappings and murders in Guerrero state, with 13 of them being active federal police officers. The government condemned the officers’ actions as a betrayal of public trust and reiterated a zero-tolerance stance on corruption. The arrests add to Acapulco’s troubles, which have included recent storm damage and a high-profile assault case. Official data also highlights widespread kidnapping across Mexico, though most incidents go unreported.

Mexican authorities confirmed the killing of Zetas cartel leader Heriberto Lazcano Lazcano in a shootout with marines, marking a major victory in the government’s long-running offensive. However, his body was later stolen by gunmen, and analysts are divided on whether his death will significantly disrupt the cartel, since leadership had reportedly already shifted to another figure. The Zetas remain a dominant and violent trafficking organization, responsible for mass murders, migrant killings, and other atrocities across Mexico. The killing underscores both the government’s progress in targeting top capos and the enduring challenge of reducing cartel violence.

During Felipe Calderón's presidency, more than 26,000 individuals disappeared in Mexico amid escalating cartel violence and government crackdowns. The new administration of Enrique Peña Nieto has established a task force to locate the missing, calling it a top priority. Human Rights Watch has linked Mexican security forces to at least 149 of these disappearances, describing the situation as one of the worst crises of its kind in Latin American history. While the government acknowledges the scale of the problem, it remains unclear if it will effectively investigate and prosecute those responsible.

Mexican President Felipe Calderón reaffirmed his commitment to the military-led crackdown on drug cartels, vowing to keep fighting organized crime through the end of his term. He argued that cartels pose a threat to democracy by trying to influence elections, and he highlighted the capture or killing of numerous top criminals as evidence of progress. In response to mounting criticism over human rights abuses, including a recent complaint filed with the International Criminal Court, Calderón dismissed the allegations as false and insisted his government had acted against any confirmed violations.

Thieves in Mexico stole a truck carrying radioactive cobalt-60, a medical isotope that could also be used in a dirty bomb, but authorities recovered the material days later in a remote area. The container had been opened, raising concerns about radiation exposure, and the suspects remain at large, possibly unaware of the danger. Cleanup may take weeks, and Mexican officials are considering international assistance. The incident highlights the serious security and health risks posed by mishandled radioactive materials.

In Mexico’s Michoacan state, armed vigilante groups, formed to combat the Knights Templar cartel amid perceived state failure, have escalated tensions after federal forces were sent to disarm them, leading to clashes and standoffs. The government’s intervention has been inconsistent, with critics accusing authorities of acting more like referees than peacekeepers as violence continues. Analysts warn the unrest could spread to other regions, especially where cartels are deeply entrenched and state presence is weak. Additionally, officials caution that these self-defense groups, despite initially noble intentions, could devolve into criminal organizations themselves.

A large team of international investigators and monitors has finally reached the Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 crash site in eastern Ukraine to begin recovering remains and evidence, after ongoing fighting had made the area too dangerous. The team, the biggest to access the site so far, used a route negotiated with the OSCE and benefited from a brief Ukrainian cease-fire, though hostilities have since resumed nearby. Many victims' bodies are still scattered in the debris field, and officials stress that time is critical for the recovery and investigation. The effort unfolds amid continued accusations against Russia over its support for rebels, new Western sanctions, and parallel talks on releasing hostages and securing safe access to the site.

The downed Malaysia Airlines flight in eastern Ukraine left a devastating scene, with wreckage and victims scattered across fields near the Russian border. The area was controlled by pro-Russian separatists, and even battle-hardened fighters appeared shocked by the scale of destruction. Rescue and investigation efforts were hindered by armed groups and overwhelmed local resources, while the debris was so fragmented that identifying victims and evidence seemed largely a matter of chance. The crash, which killed all 298 people aboard, marked a tragic escalation in a region already torn by conflict.

Malaysia is sending investigation teams to the MH17 crash site in eastern Ukraine to recover victims' remains still scattered in the area, coordinating with Australia, Ukraine, and the Netherlands. Leaders from Malaysia and Australia stressed the importance of an international probe and ensuring those responsible are brought to justice. Dutch investigators are set to release a preliminary report soon, with a final report expected within a year. The site was previously controlled by pro-Russian separatists, and while responsibility remains unclear, the U.S. and Ukraine have accused the rebels of shooting down the plane.

A new crowdfunding campaign launched by relatives of missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 passengers aims to raise $5 million for a private investigation into the plane's disappearance. The effort, promoted through a dramatic video, seeks to uncover new clues and offer a reward for information, with funds managed by a committee that includes family members and private experts. Some relatives have expressed frustration with the official search, which has found no wreckage and is set to resume later with private contractors. Malaysian aviation officials have said they do not object to the campaign and would welcome any findings it produces.

After months of pressure from families, raw satellite data from the missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 may soon be made public. Inmarsat and Malaysian officials announced they are working to release the communication logs and analysis details, though no timeline was given. Relatives remain cautious, saying they need to see real action, while analysts believe the data could validate some theories and eliminate others. The release is seen as a step toward greater transparency amid criticism over the search’s focus on the southern Indian Ocean.

Malaysian authorities released satellite communication logs from missing Flight 370, but the documents omit key technical details and the model used to determine the plane's final path, drawing criticism from experts and relatives who say independent verification is impossible. Inmarsat, which provided the data, insists the information is sufficient for third-party experts to reach their own conclusions and that gaps are not significant. Families of passengers remain frustrated by the lack of full transparency and are calling for independent analysis. The release comes as the underwater search is paused, with no wreckage found after more than two months.

Officials announced that the next stage of the MH370 search will be an expanded underwater operation covering 60,000 square kilometers, involving private contractors and costing roughly $56 million over several months. Aerial searches are being suspended since any floating debris is now likely waterlogged and has sunk, while the earlier submersible scans of the ocean floor found no trace of the aircraft. Meanwhile, frustrated relatives of the 239 people aboard, dissatisfied with Malaysian authorities' handling of communication, plan to voice their concerns at Boeing's shareholder meeting.

Malaysian officials publicly released the final voice communication from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, along with new radar and satellite data, during a briefing for relatives of Chinese passengers. The recording captured the last exchange between the cockpit and a radar controller, while the timeline showed the plane was off course and that the airline made an unanswered call to the cockpit hours later. Officials calculated that the aircraft ran out of fuel around 8:12 a.m., just after its final satellite "handshake" at 8:11 a.m., indicating it was far south of its planned route. The briefing marked a more cooperative tone with families, who said they were making progress in their search for answers.

An independent autopsy commissioned by Michael Brown’s family found that he was shot at least six times, all from the front, including four wounds to his right arm and two to his head, with no signs of close-range firing. The findings do not resolve the conflicting accounts of the shooting, as they could be interpreted either as Brown confronting the officer or as him having his hands raised. Family attorneys argue the evidence supports arresting the officer, while community leaders warn the report may heighten tensions. A separate federal autopsy has also been approved as the investigation continues.

In a Los Angeles wrongful death trial, a former associate producer testified that Michael Jackson appeared extremely frail and said God was speaking to him days before his death, prompting fears he was dying and urgent pleas for hospitalization. The lawsuit against AEG Live claims the company negligently hired and supervised Dr. Conrad Murray, who was later convicted in Jackson's death, while AEG argues Jackson himself chose and controlled the doctor. Testimony also highlighted Jackson's creative genius, his excitement for the "This Is It" tour, and the close bond he shared with his children. The jury heard emotional accounts of his deteriorating condition alongside memories of his artistic vision and family life.

In the wrongful death lawsuit against AEG Live, jurors saw evidence that Michael Jackson's physical condition severely declined in the weeks before his death, including an email describing how he could no longer perform the 360-degree spins he had mastered years earlier. The family argues AEG negligently hired and supervised Dr. Conrad Murray, who gave Jackson the propofol that caused his fatal overdose. AEG counters that Jackson himself chose Murray and that executives were unaware of the dangerous treatments. The trial also featured conflicting testimony over whether Jackson could still perform the spin move during rehearsals for his planned "This Is It" concerts.

Paris Jackson, Michael Jackson’s 15-year-old daughter, was hospitalized early Wednesday after cutting her wrist; a suicide prevention hotline call from her home prompted emergency responders. Family sources described the incident as a possible cry for help, though her attorney said she was physically fine and receiving appropriate care. The episode comes as Paris faces emotional pressure as a witness in the wrongful death lawsuit against AEG Live, with her deposition described as an intense grilling over her father’s death. Her family has asked for privacy, and her mother, Debbie Rowe, also requested respect for Paris’s privacy during this difficult time.

Katherine Jackson testified in the wrongful death case against AEG Live, saying she wants to know the truth about her son’s death and disputing negative characterizations of him, including claims that he was lazy or a “freak.” The lawsuit argues AEG negligently hired or supervised Dr. Conrad Murray, who was convicted in Michael Jackson’s death, while AEG maintains Jackson controlled Murray and the company was unaware of the dangerous treatments. Testimony included estimates that Jackson could have earned over a billion dollars from touring and endorsements, though AEG’s lawyers dismissed those projections as fabricated. The trial is expected to continue into mid-September, with AEG’s defense indicating it will not call Murray to testify.

Debbie Rowe, Michael Jackson’s ex-wife and the mother of two of his children, is expected to testify in the wrongful death lawsuit against AEG Live. The trial centers on claims that the concert promoter hired Dr. Conrad Murray, whose use of propofol led to Jackson’s fatal overdose. Although Rowe has largely avoided public attention since their divorce, her close personal history with Jackson may offer rare insight into his life. The article also notes that after years of estrangement, she reconnected with her children following Jackson’s death and has been especially supportive of their daughter Paris.

Michael Sam, a standout defensive lineman from the University of Missouri, has publicly come out as gay, making him a potential historic first as an openly gay player in the NFL draft. He revealed that his teammates had known since August and emphasized his desire to be accepted for who he is. Despite some concerns about his athletic limitations, his agent believes his honesty will not hurt his draft chances, and the NFL has voiced support for him. The announcement adds to a growing wave of LGBTQ athletes coming out and coincides with broader federal recognition of same-sex marriage.

Michael Schumacher's medically induced coma is being gradually lifted as doctors begin the lengthy process of waking him, over a month after his severe head injury from a skiing accident in the French Alps. His management confirmed the change while stressing that no further updates would be provided and asking the media to respect the family's privacy. The Formula 1 community has shown widespread support, with former teams Mercedes and Ferrari sending messages of encouragement. Investigators previously concluded that speed was not a factor, attributing the crash to Schumacher striking a rock hidden beneath the snow.

Michael Schumacher, the seven-time Formula 1 world champion, was in critical condition after a serious skiing accident in the French Alps left him with severe head injuries. He was airlifted to a hospital in Grenoble, where he underwent emergency brain surgery after arriving in a coma. The accident occurred on an off-piste slope, and although he was wearing a helmet, the exact cause remains under investigation. News of the crash prompted widespread concern from the motorsport community, as the former Ferrari star had retired from F1 in 2012.

Michael Schumacher has regained consciousness and left the Grenoble hospital where he was treated after a severe skiing accident, according to his management. He has been moved to a university hospital in Lausanne, Switzerland, to begin a long rehabilitation process. Investigators concluded that he struck a rock hidden under the snow while skiing off-piste, causing his fall and head injury. His family has requested privacy during his recovery and thanked the public for their support.

Michelle Bachelet has won Chile’s presidential runoff decisively, capturing about 62% of the vote against conservative rival Evelyn Matthei. In her victory speech, she pledged to focus on improving education and promoting equality, while emphasizing that she would govern for all Chileans. Bachelet, who previously served as the country’s first female president and later led UN Women, will assume office in March. Her return marks a significant political comeback in the South American nation.

Michelle Knight, one of three women held captive by Ariel Castro for over a decade, delivered a powerful and defiant statement at his sentencing, describing her 11 years of torment and her determination to move forward. She revealed that she never stopped thinking about her son and credited fellow captive Gina DeJesus with saving her life through their friendship. Knight also recounted how she was forced to deliver Amanda Berry’s child under threat of death. Though she said she can forgive Castro, she declared she will never forget, and that his true punishment will be living with the memory of his crimes while she reclaims her life.

Ariel Castro lured Michelle Knight into his Cleveland home by offering her a puppy, then held her captive for 11 years alongside two other women. During her imprisonment, she endured severe abuse, including being chained, beaten, and starved, but she survived by holding onto hope of reuniting with her son. Castro was eventually convicted and sentenced to life in prison, but he took his own life shortly after. Knight has since become the most outspoken of the victims, sharing her harrowing story publicly in an interview to reclaim her voice and show her resilience.

Michelle Knight, one of three women held captive by Ariel Castro for years, revealed new details of her abuse in a televised interview, describing being hung and bound like an ornament, chained with a motorcycle helmet, and punished after an escape attempt. She also recounted being starved and beaten to induce miscarriages, and said she helped deliver Amanda Berry’s child. Knight said speaking out has been liberating and that she wants to give other families hope, showing resilience despite enduring severe physical and emotional trauma.

Michelle Obama, during her China tour, spoke at Peking University about the importance of study abroad programs, framing them as vital to U.S. foreign policy and international relations. She encouraged students from all economic backgrounds to participate, noting that such exchanges help address global challenges and foster people-to-people connections. Obama highlighted the growing role of technology in enabling citizen diplomacy without travel, while also acknowledging that study abroad should be accessible to all, not just privileged students. Her remarks also touched on the strong educational exchange between the U.S. and China, with Chinese students being the largest international group in America.

Escaped Michigan inmate Michael David Elliot was arrested in Indiana, ending a manhunt that began after he fled prison by slipping under fences. During his escape, he abducted a woman at knifepoint and forced her to drive him away, but she managed to call 911 from a gas station bathroom while he tried to break in. She escaped unharmed, and authorities later tracked down the vehicle before capturing Elliot. He was serving multiple life sentences for a 1994 murder conviction involving four victims.

Mick Jagger playfully mocked the Monty Python troupe in a video, calling their reunion a money-making attempt by aging comedians and joking that their best days were long past. The five surviving Pythons are reuniting for live shows in London, their first together since 1980, with performances selling out quickly and extra dates added. The comedians, all in their seventies, say these will be their final shows and plan to perform classic sketches alongside new material. They acknowledged reuniting largely for financial reasons but expressed excitement about working together again.

Wadah Khanfar, the former head of Al Jazeera, describes the current Middle East turmoil as unprecedented and unlikely to end soon, driven by the collapse of state structures and the merging of political Islam with terrorism. He argues that the suppression of the Arab Spring, combined with the Syrian civil war, created a vacuum filled by extremist groups like ISIS, whose rapid advance in Iraq exposed the weakness of Western-imposed borders. Khanfar warns that a broad arc of crisis could spread from Iraq to Libya, ultimately threatening Gulf states, and criticizes Western support for authoritarian leaders as both unethical and ineffective. He urges the West to rethink its strategic approach, including accepting the possible redrawing of borders and reassessing Iran's role in the region.

Production of the Gregg Allman biopic *Midnight Rider* has been suspended after camera assistant Sarah Elizabeth Jones was fatally struck by a freight train in Georgia; six other crew members were also injured. The production company withdrew its filming permits in Savannah following the incident. In response, the film community has launched a tribute campaign, sharing photos and messages on social media and urging the Academy to include Jones in the Oscars' In Memoriam segment. Allman and other industry figures have also expressed their condolences.

A powerful late-season tornado outbreak swept across several Midwestern states, causing widespread destruction, particularly in Washington, Illinois, where hundreds of homes were damaged or destroyed. At least eight people were killed and many more injured, with the storm packing EF-4 winds and leaving over 600,000 customers without power. Survivors described harrowing moments as their houses were torn apart around them, yet many escaped serious physical harm. The severe weather also disrupted travel, including flight cancellations and a delayed NFL game in Chicago, before the system moved offshore.

A migrant ship sank in the Mediterranean between Libya and Lampedusa, killing at least 10 people, while 70 others were rescued and search efforts continued. The vessel was carrying migrants from North Africa, a route that has become increasingly deadly as thousands attempt the crossing to Europe. The incident echoes a similar shipwreck in the same area two months earlier. Amnesty International reported at least 1,500 migrant deaths in the Mediterranean last year and criticized European policies for hindering timely rescue operations.

Mike Parker, a key figure in the rise of the ubiquitous Helvetica typeface, has died at age 84. Although he did not design the font, he directed its development for Linotype machines, helping it become an industry standard. Helvetica, created in 1957, was celebrated for its clarity and rational design, fitting the postwar emphasis on legible, modern communication. Parker later co-founded the digital font company Bitstream and remained a devoted advocate for elegant typography throughout his career.

Mikhail Kalashnikov, the Soviet inventor of the AK-47 assault rifle, has died at the age of 94. He created the weapon in the 1940s, and it became renowned for its simple, durable design that worked reliably in harsh conditions. The rifle was widely adopted by Soviet-aligned militaries and revolutionary groups, becoming one of the most iconic and common firearms in the world. Kalashnikov maintained that he designed the weapon to defend his country, not to cause harm.

Mikhail Khodorkovsky, the former Russian oil tycoon and Kremlin critic, has been released from prison after more than a decade and flown to Germany, where he was reunited with his son. He stated that he had requested a pardon from President Putin but emphasized that the issue of admitting guilt was not part of the discussion. The United States welcomed his release while urging Russia to strengthen its judicial system and human rights commitments. His release came through a broader amnesty, just months before Russia hosts the Winter Olympics in Sochi, and follows years of international criticism over what many viewed as a politically motivated prosecution.

Miley Cyrus and Liam Hemsworth have called off their engagement, according to the actor’s representative. The couple, who got engaged in 2012 after meeting on a film set, had faced persistent breakup rumors and denials earlier this year. Recent speculation intensified after Cyrus reportedly unfollowed Hemsworth on Twitter. Both stars are now focusing on upcoming projects, including Hemsworth’s "Hunger Games" sequel and Cyrus’s new album.

Miley Cyrus’s VMA stand-in for homeless youth, Jesse Helt, is wanted in Oregon for violating probation tied to a 2011 criminal trespass conviction. Authorities say they will arrest him if encountered, though they are not actively searching due to limited staff. Helt used the awards stage to spotlight the struggles of homeless young people, while Cyrus responded to the media attention by defending him and directing fans to donate to a Los Angeles homeless charity.

Miley Cyrus has clarified that her recent hospitalization was not due to a drug overdose, but rather a severe allergic reaction to antibiotics prescribed for a sinus infection. The health scare forced her to postpone several European tour dates, though she has since recovered with the help of vitamins and honey. During a London press conference, she emphasized her healthy lifestyle, stating she avoids alcohol and drugs before performing and takes her tour seriously. She described herself as a model of good health and called the ordeal the worst two weeks of her life.

Miley Cyrus’s European tour has hit a snag as her severe allergic reaction to an antibiotic has flared up again, forcing her to postpone shows in Amsterdam and Antwerp to late June. The singer had previously been hospitalized in April, which led to the rescheduling of her North American dates to August. Her representatives say doctors have advised against travel while the reaction persists, though she still hopes to perform in London in early May.

Militants have circulated a tipsheet listing 22 ways to evade American drone strikes, including hiding under trees, avoiding cell phones, scattering when drones approach, and using decoys or jamming gear. The document, found in Mali and online, reflects deep anxiety among jihadists about drone attacks, which have disrupted operations and made recruitment harder. While some tactics may help in certain environments, former military officials argue drones remain highly effective and that the list actually exposes militant methods, allowing countermeasures to be developed. Drone strikes have killed thousands, including civilians, fueling resentment in countries like Pakistan and Yemen.

The U.S. military has not executed a service member since 1961, even though death sentences are still handed down for serious crimes. The case of Ronald Gray, a soldier convicted of multiple murders and rapes, shows how close executions can come but are ultimately blocked by last-minute legal appeals. Experts point to the military’s unique justice system—where commanding generals can override juries and personnel changes slow the process—as a key reason for the reluctance to carry out executions. With Army Major Nidal Hasan facing a possible death sentence for the Fort Hood shootings, his case may add to the five men already on military death row, though actual execution remains unlikely.

Egyptian military police entered Tahrir Square to enforce a cleric-brokered truce, but calm quickly broke down as protesters clashed with security forces, leading to continued tear gas and rock-throwing. The unrest, part of ongoing demonstrations demanding the ruling military council step down, has left at least 35 dead and thousands wounded. Authorities arrested hundreds, including three American students, while the UN condemned the excessive use of force and called for an independent investigation. The violence has deepened uncertainty over Egypt’s political transition just days before parliamentary elections.

Egyptians display a striking mix of political views, with unusually high support for both military rule and Islamic law compared with other Middle Eastern nations, according to a survey released during the country’s constitutional referendum. The vote follows the army’s removal of President Mohamed Morsy, and the findings highlight deep societal divisions. Over time, Egyptian backing for democracy grew sharply before the Arab Spring, while support for Sharia as the sole basis of law declined, though it remained relatively strong. Despite favoring military leadership in some measures, most Egyptians still say democracy is a good system, and the army chief has signaled he may run for president.

The full D.C. Circuit will rehear the military convictions of two Guantanamo detainees, a rare en banc review requested by the Obama administration after panels overturned the verdicts. The case centers on whether the men can be prosecuted for providing material support to terrorism and conspiracy, crimes that were not defined under U.S. law when the alleged conduct occurred before the 2006 Military Commissions Act. The earlier rulings held that such retroactive charges violate the Constitution's ban on ex post facto laws, allowing only pre-existing offenses or war crimes to be tried. The outcome could shape the legal limits of the military tribunal system and may ultimately be decided by the Supreme Court.

Both warring sides in Syria agree that the historic minaret of the 12th-century Great Umayyad Mosque in Aleppo has been completely destroyed, but they sharply disagree on who is responsible. Opposition groups accuse government forces of shelling the landmark, while the Syrian government claims al-Qaeda-linked rebels planted explosives there. The mosque is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its destruction highlights the ongoing conflict's toll on the country's cultural heritage.

University of Washington researchers demonstrated a noninvasive brain-to-brain connection, where one scientist’s thoughts transmitted over the internet triggered another scientist’s hand movement. However, the work is unpublished and has drawn skepticism from experts, who note it lacks the conscious choice and feedback needed for true brain-to-brain communication. Earlier rodent studies have shown more advanced two-way brain interfaces, while the human experiment remains a one-way signal. The researchers hope to expand the technology and explore practical uses, such as surgical training or assisting disabled individuals.

The remains of the former U.S. Navy ship Guardian have been fully removed from a Philippine reef after the last and largest section, its stern, was lifted onto a barge. The vessel had run aground in January, causing significant damage to about 4,000 square meters of the protected Tubbataha Reef, a UNESCO World Heritage site. With the hull gone, salvage teams are shifting focus to collecting debris and assessing the reef’s condition for restoration. The ship had already been decommissioned and replaced by the USS Warrior, and an investigation into the grounding, reportedly linked to a navigational chart error, is still ongoing.

Kirsten Haglund, who became Miss America at 19, turned her personal battle with anorexia into a platform for advocacy. Her eating disorder began at age 12, fueled by the intense pressure of ballet training and a desire for control during a turbulent time. After years of struggle and treatment, she entered pageants as part of her recovery and unexpectedly won the national title. She now works to raise awareness and help others access treatment through her foundation.

The parents of missing American journalist Austin Tice have issued an emotional public appeal, urging his captors to release him so the family can be reunited for Christmas. Tice disappeared in Syria in mid-August while reporting on the country’s uprising, and U.S. officials believe he was detained by Syrian authorities as he prepared to leave. His parents describe him as deeply connected to the Middle East and its people, and they are asking whoever is holding him to show compassion and let him come home.

Seven Cameroonian athletes disappeared from the London 2012 Olympic Village, prompting speculation that they intended to defect. A Cameroon Olympic official attributed their likely flight to inadequate training facilities and limited support at home, which left athletes feeling unable to compete fairly. The missing group included a female footballer, a swimmer, and five boxers, and their photos made front-page news in Cameroon. The incident fits a broader pattern of Cameroonian athletes seeking better opportunities abroad, a trend linked to the country's poverty and lack of sports infrastructure.

The discovery of the three Israeli teenagers' bodies in the West Bank has sharply escalated tensions, with Israel directly blaming Hamas for their abduction and deaths and vowing to retaliate. Israeli leaders have pledged to take strong action against Hamas, while a Hamas spokesman warned that any attack on Gaza would open "the gates of hell." The incident has drawn international condemnation, including from the U.S., the Vatican, and the U.N., with calls for restraint and continued cooperation between Israel and the Palestinian Authority. In response, Israel has conducted airstrikes in Gaza and intensified security operations, raising fears of further violence.

Mississippi is seeking to execute Michelle Byrom for the 1999 murder of her husband, a case marked by her son’s repeated confessions to the killing, which a jury never heard due to her defense attorneys’ errors. Her son, who testified against her in a plea deal and later denied shooting his father, was released from prison, while Byrom’s supporters argue she received ineffective counsel and endured a lifetime of abuse. The state’s highest court has yet to confirm the execution date, and her advocates maintain that key evidence, including her son’s confessions, was improperly withheld. If carried out, the execution would make her the first woman put to death by Mississippi in 70 years.

The article recounts the tragic misidentification of a Boston Marathon bombing victim: Krystle Campbell was initially believed to be the survivor being treated, but her friend Karen Rand had been carrying Campbell’s identification. Doctors had used the ID to assume the patient was Campbell, but the family soon discovered the truth—Rand survived while Campbell, 29, was among the three people killed. The piece also highlights Campbell’s strong work ethic and cheerful, outgoing nature, remembered fondly by family and former employers. Her memorial Facebook page drew an outpouring of grief and support, alongside demands for justice.

Mitchell Casado, a soft-spoken Canadian pilot, has become an unlikely TV aviation expert during the MH370 coverage, despite being uncomfortable with on-camera fame. His gift lies in explaining complex flight concepts in plain, accessible language, though his casual style draws online criticism. Casado’s path to flying was difficult: he endured childhood bullying, worked low-wage jobs, and even became homeless after a flight school scam before eventually earning his licenses. While he takes part in dramatic simulator scenarios for television, he stays deeply aware of the real human tragedy behind such disasters.

Over the next decade, smartphones will evolve into far more advanced devices, featuring glasses-free 3D displays that enable immersive browsing and virtual navigation. Security will shift from passwords to multiple biometric methods, including fingerprint, facial, and voice recognition, with the level of authentication tailored to the sensitivity of the task. Phones will also replace physical wallets through secure mobile payment systems, while increasingly intelligent personal agents will anticipate users' needs and deliver personalized information. Additionally, screenless smartphone models and seamless integration with smart surfaces will offer new ways to interact, making connectivity more intuitive and pervasive.

Narendra Modi and his BJP secured a historic landslide victory, winning 282 of 543 seats and a clear majority, with Modi set to be sworn in as Prime Minister on May 21. Outgoing PM Manmohan Singh resigned and gave a farewell address, reflecting on his rise from a poor partition-era childhood while leaving office with a mixed legacy of economic reform and corruption scandals. Modi, known for his pro-business record in Gujarat, faces high expectations to revive India's slowing economy, but his past remains shadowed by the 2002 anti-Muslim violence, though he was cleared by an investigation and has since received a congratulatory call from President Obama.

A year after Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation ignited the Arab uprisings, the region remains in the early stages of a long and difficult democratic transformation rather than a simple seasonal shift. While three dictators have fallen and popular participation has grown, serious challenges persist—including military dominance in Egypt, violent repression in Syria, fragile deals in Yemen, and sectarian tensions in Bahrain. Islamist parties have emerged as major political forces, reflecting the region’s conservative social values after decades of exclusion. The West must adopt more respectful, equal partnerships and support civilian protection, while Tunisia’s power-sharing experiment offers a hopeful model for the Arab world’s future.

Mohamed ElBaradei, a Nobel Peace Prize-winning diplomat, is being considered for the role of interim prime minister in Egypt after the military coup, though his appointment has not been officially confirmed. Known for his international career rather than grassroots politics, he struggled in last year’s presidential election, partly because he was seen as an outsider. Despite this, he remained active in Egypt’s reform movement and opposition. His background includes leading the IAEA, challenging the U.S. on Iraq’s alleged nuclear program, and joining anti-Mubarak protests, which kept him in the military’s attention.

A Florida mother was arrested and charged with felony child neglect for allowing her 7-year-old son to walk alone to a park less than half a mile from home, even though the child had a phone and had checked in with her. The case has drawn attention amid a broader national debate about whether authorities are overreaching by prosecuting parents for what some see as normal, low-risk childhood independence. Florida law does not specify a minimum age for leaving children unsupervised, leaving decisions open to interpretation and causing confusion and fear among parents. Advocates argue that such arrests reflect a troubling trend of criminalizing noncriminal parenting choices.

A 13-year-old Florida girl took her own life after enduring relentless bullying, which began over a dispute involving a boy and escalated into vicious online harassment. Her mother, grieving on what would have been her daughter’s birthday, has vowed to raise awareness about bullying and seek justice. Two teenage girls have been charged with aggravated stalking in connection with the case, though one suspect’s father claims her account was hacked. Separately, the mother of one of the accused girls was arrested on child abuse charges after a video surfaced showing her hitting children.

Malissa Booth left a corporate management career after being laid off, and despite skepticism about her age and gender, she became a tattoo artist. She opened a family-friendly shop in Missouri, deliberately avoiding the edgy, male-dominated tattoo culture to make all clients feel comfortable. Her empathetic approach, which focuses on the personal meaning behind each tattoo, has attracted a diverse clientele and built a successful business. Booth says the work is an adventure and she is happier than she was in her corporate job.

Dr. Alfred Brann, a pediatric neurologist, has dedicated his career to reducing maternal and newborn deaths, a mission inspired by his mother's death during his birth. He emphasizes that most newborn fatalities are preventable and that improving women's overall health—not just pregnancy care—is critical. His "systems approach" treats the mother, fetus, and newborn as a continuous unit, and he advocates for implementing proven solutions worldwide. Brann stresses that a healthy pregnancy depends on proper spacing, planning, nutrition, and skilled care, and that women's health outcomes are shaped by factors largely beyond their control.

Nineteen-year-old Lara Prior-Palmer became the youngest and first female champion of the Mongol Derby, the world’s longest horse race across Mongolia’s rugged steppe. The grueling 1,000-kilometer event, modeled on Genghis Khan’s ancient messenger system, requires riders to change horses at 40 nomadic outposts while enduring extreme heat, wind, and exhaustion. Prior-Palmer was declared the winner after the first finisher received a time penalty when her horse failed a post-race veterinary check. The teenager, who plans to study history at university, said the victory was bittersweet because the other rider was devastated.

The Chinese air force has deployed trained macaques at a northern airbase located along a major bird migration route. The monkeys are used to remove bird nests from trees, reducing the risk of birds being sucked into jet engines and causing dangerous accidents. Earlier methods like shooting or using poles and soldiers to remove nests proved ineffective and time-consuming. Unlike those approaches, the monkeys leave a scent that deters birds from rebuilding their nests, making them a lasting solution.

The article details the mysterious death of American engineer Shane Todd in Singapore, which authorities ruled a suicide but his parents believe was murder. They point to a suspicious suicide note, physical evidence from an independent autopsy, and files on his hard drive suggesting he was involved in sensitive gallium nitride research with a Chinese telecom firm. Singapore police have since requested FBI assistance to examine evidence held by the family, while the parents continue to push for a deeper investigation into possible corporate or national security motives.

Claude Nobs, the founder of the Montreux Jazz Festival, has died at age 76 after a skiing accident left him in a coma. He co-founded the renowned Swiss festival in 1967 and became famous for rescuing people during a 1971 casino fire, an event later immortalized in Deep Purple’s “Smoke on the Water” with Nobs referred to as “Funky Claude.” Musicians including Nile Rodgers, George Clinton, and Queen’s Brian May paid tribute, praising his legacy and contributions to jazz, blues, and rock culture. The festival’s official statement honored his audacity, generosity, and lasting impact on the music world.

A Libyan security official said he warned U.S. diplomats days before the Benghazi attack that security was deteriorating and dangerous for foreigners. The assault, which involved heavy weapons and masked gunmen, killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens, whose body was later found after the consulate was overrun and burned. Local militia members helped evacuate Americans to a safe house, but that location also came under attack. Libya’s president acknowledged the government struggles to control extremist groups and called for international assistance.

A new American Cancer Society report shows a 20% drop in U.S. cancer death rates since 1991, with major declines for lung, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancers. This progress is largely attributed to reduced smoking rates, along with better early detection and treatment. However, the report warns that obesity is now a major cancer risk factor and is pushing rates upward, while many Americans still miss recommended screenings or lack access to adequate care. Closing these gaps could save many more lives, especially as the population ages.

Publicis chief Maurice Levy says wealthy people should bear a larger share of the tax burden to help fix public deficits, calling it unjust for the poor to suffer more. He claims many business leaders privately support this view but are unwilling to say so publicly. Levy also urges European leaders to reach clear agreements on the euro crisis and Greece, arguing that restoring trust is essential for economic recovery. Despite the turmoil, he expects modest growth in the eurozone this year rather than a collapse.

More than 100,000 people have applied to Mars One for a one-way trip to establish a human settlement on Mars, with the first crew slated to depart in 2022. The project plans to fund the mission through media and sponsorship, and will narrow applicants to a small multinational team after years of training. However, experts question the feasibility, citing unresolved financial hurdles and serious radiation risks that current technology cannot adequately shield against. Despite these concerns, Mars One’s founder maintains that the mission is achievable and that radiation is not the biggest obstacle.

U.S. forces launched new airstrikes near Iraq’s Mosul Dam, following President Obama’s pledge to intensify action against ISIS after the killing of journalist James Foley. Since August 8, American strikes have totaled 90, with most supporting Iraqi and Kurdish efforts around the dam, which was recently recaptured from militants. Iraqi forces are now working to secure the surrounding area, as concerns remain that damage to the dam could endanger millions downstream. The conflict has displaced up to 1.2 million Iraqis this year, while France has joined relief efforts by sending additional humanitarian aid to the region.

For the second time in two days, militants targeted Pakistan’s busiest airport in Karachi, this time attacking the Airport Security Forces academy before fleeing; no one was killed. The Pakistani Taliban claimed responsibility, saying the attacks were retaliation for government airstrikes and the killing of their former leader. Flights were briefly suspended but later resumed after security forces said the situation was under control. Earlier that day, Pakistani airstrikes in the tribal region near Afghanistan killed at least 15 militants, part of the ongoing cycle of violence.

In 2012, U.S. fertility clinics reported a record number of babies born through assisted reproductive technology, with nearly 62,000 infants delivered via IVF—about 2,000 more than the previous year. This rise stands in contrast to the nation’s overall declining birth rate and likely reflects the trend of women having children later in life, since fertility naturally decreases with age. Success rates were strongly tied to age, with women under 35 having the highest live birth rates, while older women faced sharply lower odds. Despite growing acceptance and medical advances, IVF remains costly and often uninsured, and doctors are increasingly transferring fewer embryos to reduce the risks of multiple births.

Egyptian human rights groups report that 49 men were beaten and held for up to 17 hours by supporters of President Mohamed Morsy after clashes near the presidential palace, though prosecutors later released them for lack of evidence. President Morsy claimed the detainees had confessed to being paid instigators, a statement criticized by Human Rights Watch for blaming victims rather than condemning abuse. Detainees described severe beatings, denial of medical care, and harassment, with some saying their captors acted without fear of accountability. The incident has raised concerns about police complicity and vigilante justice during the political crisis.

Tens of thousands of demonstrators gathered in Moscow to protest the results of the parliamentary elections, which they believe were fraudulent. Many participants were first-time protesters and previously apolitical citizens who were shocked that United Russia won despite few admitting to voting for it. They are calling for the election results to be annulled and a new vote held, while emphasizing they seek free elections, not revolution. Social media played a key role in mobilizing the largely middle-class crowd, who, though not expecting immediate change, feel a new sense of unity and hope.

Hotel concierges often go to extraordinary lengths to fulfill bizarre guest requests, from crafting life-size chocolate statues for a wedding to sourcing camels and delivering Kobe beef for a dog. Other notable feats include arranging a unicorn-themed surprise, a "Hangover"-style party, and scattering a deceased dog's ashes at sea. One concierge even coordinated a secret mariachi proposal on the Golden Gate Bridge and another rushed custom fingerprint art for a wedding. These stories highlight how dedicated staff turn outlandish wishes into memorable experiences.

The World Health Organization warns that cancer is becoming a global crisis, with new cases projected to rise sharply from 14 million in 2012 to 22 million by 2032. The increase is driven by population growth, aging, and the spread of Western lifestyle factors like tobacco use, poor diet, and obesity into lower-income regions. While cancer death rates have dropped in the U.S. and Western Europe thanks to prevention and reduced smoking, many developing countries face rising deaths due to late diagnosis and inadequate care. The report urges stronger prevention efforts worldwide and highlights key personal steps—such as avoiding tobacco, maintaining a healthy diet and weight, exercising, getting vaccinated, and undergoing screening—to reduce cancer risk.

The mother of a 12-year-old Florida girl who died by suicide after relentless cyberbullying is urging parents to recognize that a child may appear happy while suffering privately. She and her lawyer intend to file a wrongful death lawsuit after criminal charges against two girls were dropped. Their attorney is also advocating for "Rebecca's Law," which would hold parents civilly liable for their children's bullying. The mother emphasizes that despite her efforts to stop the harassment, it continued, and she warns other parents to take bullying seriously and never give up.

American midwife Robin Lim was honored as the 2011 CNN Hero of the Year for her work running free maternal health clinics in Indonesia, where many women cannot afford safe childbirth. Her organization, Bumi Sehat, provides prenatal care, delivery services, and medical aid, addressing high maternal and infant death rates linked to unaffordable hospital costs. Lim received $250,000 for her cause, in addition to the $50,000 given to all top 10 heroes. The ceremony also celebrated the other nine honorees for their varied charitable efforts around the world.

In the trial of Shafilea Ahmed’s parents, her mother unexpectedly changed her testimony and accused her husband of killing their 17-year-old daughter, claiming she tried to intervene but was beaten back. The prosecution alleges the couple murdered Shafilea in 2003 because her Western lifestyle brought shame on the family, with their other daughter testifying that she saw them suffocate the teen with a plastic bag. The case has also highlighted the broader issue of honor killings, which experts say occur across many cultures and regions, though prosecutions remain difficult due to silence within communities.

During November, men around the world take part in Movember by growing mustaches to raise money and awareness for men’s health issues, particularly prostate cancer and depression. The movement began in Australia in 2003 and has since expanded globally, with participants following rules like starting clean-shaven and keeping the mustache well-groomed. Fundraising efforts have generated hundreds of millions of dollars, making Movember the largest non-governmental funder of prostate cancer research. The campaign also uses social media and celebratory events to encourage participation and remind men to prioritize regular health screenings.

Bernice King, the youngest daughter of Martin Luther King Jr., is stepping into the public spotlight as the nation marks the 50th anniversary of the March on Washington, opening up about her guarded personal life and the tragedies that shaped her. Now head of the King Center, she addresses long-standing controversies, including family legal disputes over her father’s legacy, criticism over licensing fees for his monument, and her past participation in a march against same-sex marriage, which she now says she would handle differently. Despite her often stoic public image, those close to her describe a warm, humorous woman who has struggled to grieve and live up to impossible expectations. Through it all, she is working to define herself on her own terms, rather than being frozen in the shadow of her famous parents.

MTV has unveiled the nominees for its 2014 Movie Awards, mixing Oscar contenders like “12 Years a Slave” and “American Hustle” with major franchises such as “The Hunger Games” and “The Hobbit.” Alongside traditional categories, the ceremony features quirky awards for moments like best kiss, best fight, and best shirtless performance. A notable inclusion is a posthumous nomination for Paul Walker, recognized alongside Vin Diesel for “Fast & Furious 6.” Fan voting is now open, and the winners will be announced on April 13 at a ceremony hosted by Conan O'Brien.

The 2013 MTV Video Music Awards took place at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn, where a wide range of music videos were honored. Justin Timberlake stood out with multiple wins, including Video of the Year for "Mirrors" and Best Direction for "Suit & Tie." Other major winners included Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, and Macklemore & Ryan Lewis, who took home several awards across different categories. The ceremony also recognized emerging talent and technical achievements in areas like choreography, editing, and visual effects.

Bolton Wanderers midfielder Fabrice Muamba was clinically dead for 78 minutes after collapsing during an FA Cup match, requiring 15 defibrillator shocks before his heart restarted. Despite the severity of the cardiac arrest, the 23-year-old has made a remarkable recovery, now responding in English and French, joking with visitors, and no longer in immediate danger. His treating doctors described the ordeal as miraculous, noting his neurological function looks promising. Meanwhile, Bolton will resume playing this weekend with his family’s support, and the abandoned FA Cup tie has been rescheduled.

Egypt's ousted former president Hosni Mubarak remains in critical but stable condition, drifting in and out of consciousness, with his family by his side; officials dismissed rumors of his death as false. The 84-year-old is serving a life sentence for his role in the deadly crackdown on 2011 uprising protesters, a conviction that sparked widespread outrage. His health struggles have persisted since the trial, where he appeared on a stretcher, and he is currently receiving intensive care under military and prison doctors. The revolt he suppressed ended his 29-year rule and left more than 800 people dead, while he remained a key U.S. ally throughout his tenure.

Former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's health deteriorated after a fall in his prison bathroom caused a blood clot, leading to a coma and reports that he was clinically dead, though his condition later improved and he was taken off life support. His lawyer attributed the crisis to inadequate prison medical care and noted that Mubarak remains hospitalized in intensive care. The health scare unfolded amid political turmoil, as Egypt delayed announcing its presidential election results and the military council moved to expand its legislative authority, raising concerns about the democratic transition. Mubarak, already sentenced to life in prison for his role in suppressing the 2011 uprising, has appealed the verdict.

A new editorial argues that multivitamins and dietary supplements are a waste of money for preventing chronic conditions, citing three studies that found no benefits for heart disease, cancer, or cognitive decline. While the research showed no protective effect and even linked beta carotene to higher lung cancer risk in smokers, some nutrition experts countered that many Americans have poor diets and may need supplements to fill nutritional gaps. The authors acknowledged that supplements are necessary for certain groups, such as pregnant women or people with deficiencies, but stressed that a healthy diet and exercise remain the most important factors.

An Alabama judge dismissed the murder case against Gabe Watson after prosecutors presented their evidence, ruling there was insufficient proof to support the charges. Watson had been accused of killing his wife, Tina, during a scuba-diving trip in Australia shortly after their wedding. He had previously served 18 months in prison there for negligent manslaughter. The judge's decision, which cannot be appealed, drew relief from Watson's family and disappointment from the victim's relatives.

The publisher of the defunct News of the World has reached financial settlements with several prominent figures, including former Downing Street communications chief Alastair Campbell and actor Steve Coogan, over phone hacking. These agreements resolve nearly all outstanding civil claims, though singer Charlotte Church has declined to settle and is heading to court. The hacking controversy forced the paper’s closure and triggered multiple police investigations and an independent press ethics inquiry. No criminal charges have been filed so far.

Music therapy is increasingly used in hospitals and other settings to ease anxiety, distract from pain, and support emotional expression, as illustrated by a child life specialist at Boston Children's Hospital who plays for young patients during stressful procedures. The field, which began with musicians performing for war veterans, has grown into a recognized profession with about 5,000 board-certified therapists in the U.S. Research suggests music can reduce anxiety, boost immunity, and trigger pleasure-related brain chemicals, while therapists use techniques like the "Iso principle" and biofeedback to tailor sessions to individual needs. It has shown particular promise for children with autism, Alzheimer's patients, and veterans with PTSD, with some describing music therapy as life-saving.

The Muslim Brotherhood’s presidential candidate strongly condemned former intelligence chief Omar Suleiman’s late entry into Egypt’s election, calling it an insult to the revolution and warning that any fraudulent victory would trigger mass protests. He reaffirmed that Egypt would honor its international treaties, including with Israel, while criticizing Israel for failing to uphold Palestinian rights, and questioned the timing of an IMF loan under the interim government. The Brotherhood also prioritized easing sectarian tensions and nominated a backup candidate, Mohammed Morsi, amid legal uncertainties over candidate eligibility. Meanwhile, Suleiman’s candidacy faced only symbolic parliamentary opposition, while other candidates were disqualified over past convictions or family citizenship issues.

The family of Jun Lin, a Chinese student killed in Montreal, has traveled from China to support the investigation and mourn, with his mother visibly overcome with grief. Police allege that Luka Rocco Magnotta murdered and dismembered Lin, posted a video of the act online, and mailed body parts to political party offices and schools. Magnotta was arrested in Berlin and is facing extradition to Canada on a first-degree murder charge. Investigators are still searching for missing remains and looking into Magnotta’s online activity, including prior animal abuse allegations.

Authorities placed Myanmar’s second-largest city, Mandalay, under curfew after two nights of deadly clashes between Buddhists and Muslims left two dead and more than a dozen injured. The violence began after a mob attacked a Muslim-owned tea shop following allegations that the owner raped a Buddhist woman, with reports of large armed gangs involved. Analysts point to extremist Buddhist monks and online hate speech as key drivers of the unrest, noting that social media was used to inflame tensions. The incident reflects broader anti-Muslim violence in Myanmar that has threatened its political transition and left many minority communities vulnerable.

Win Tin, a veteran Myanmar journalist and co-founder of Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy, has died at age 85 in Yangon after being hospitalized with a kidney problem. He spent 19 years in prison for his pro-democracy activism, enduring harsh treatment and refusing to make false confessions. Even behind bars, he continued advocating for democratic change, writing to the United Nations and drawing further punishment. His death is mourned as a major loss to Myanmar’s democratic movement at a critical time of transition.

Myanmar’s aging power grid serves only a quarter of its population, leaving many residents, even in Yangon, reliant on generators and facing frequent blackouts. The government now prioritizes using the country’s natural resources for domestic energy needs before exporting, a shift from past policies. Expanding access is a major challenge, but off-grid renewable projects, modeled on successful efforts in Laos, and foreign investment in oil and gas infrastructure offer potential paths forward. Officials aim to raise electricity access from 26% to 60% by 2020, though progress will require significant time and funding.

Investigators are looking into the killing of five goats and seven chickens at an urban farm in Detroit connected to a school for pregnant teens. The animals were found dead in their pen, with two additional chickens discovered injured and removed from the scene. The Michigan Humane Society has taken over the case, but the motive and weapons used remain unclear. Authorities are determining whether criminal charges will be filed.

Nadine Gordimer, the South African Nobel laureate and anti-apartheid literary icon, has died at age 90. Her novels, essays, and stories offered deep insight into the country’s racial divisions, and several of her books, including "Burger's Daughter," were banned under the apartheid regime. She was celebrated both for her moral courage and her literary skill, and she remained an outspoken public voice on political issues into her later years. Her death marks the loss of a writer widely regarded as one of South Africa’s most important cultural and political figures.

Julia Hobsbawm, known as the “queen of networking,” created the Names Not Numbers festival to bring together professionals from varied fields for intensive, face-to-face idea exchange. The multi-day retreat is designed to counteract the rushed, digitally isolated nature of modern work by allowing participants to relax and connect more deeply. Hobsbawm believes such gatherings have grown popular because people still crave personal interaction and intellectual stimulation, even in an age of constant online connectivity. She also sees them as a remedy for information overload, since curated programming lets attendees step back from endless emails and screens.

India is experiencing a wave of optimism, with surging markets, renewed foreign investment, and global leaders courting Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has promised ambitious projects like smart cities, bullet trains, and sweeping reforms. However, the article cautions that India’s past economic promise has often gone unfulfilled, and despite progress, poverty numbers remain stubbornly high due to population growth. The government faces tough structural challenges, including rising subsidies, stagnant tax revenues, and the immense pressure of providing for hundreds of millions of young people. Ultimately, Modi’s biggest test will be managing inflated expectations while delivering a realistic, long-term economic plan.

NASA is preparing for a future mission in the 2020s that would send astronauts to study an asteroid, though there is no immediate threat to Earth. To practice, astronauts are using a large swimming pool in Houston to simulate the low-gravity conditions of an asteroid landing and test tools and spacesuits. The plan involves capturing an asteroid and moving it into orbit around the moon, where astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft would collect samples. These samples could offer insights into the solar system's origins, and the mission would help develop technologies needed for future human trips to Mars.

Ray Price, a legendary country singer known for popularizing the signature “shuffle” rhythm that shaped the Nashville sound, has died at 87. He rose to fame with hits like “Crazy Arms” and “For the Good Times,” and was mentored early on by Hank Williams. Price was celebrated for his distinctive voice and for bringing country music to wider audiences. He passed away after a battle with pancreatic cancer, having been inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1996.

Natalie Westling, a 17-year-old Arizona native and self-described tomboy, has quickly risen in the fashion world after being scouted less than two years ago. Initially uninterested in modeling, she broke through after landing an exclusive to open a Marc Jacobs show, and her bold red hair has since made her a standout on runways and in ad campaigns. Despite her rapid success, she acknowledges the job’s intensity and the hard work behind the glamour. Her career also coincides with new New York regulations protecting underage models, and she credits her mature outlook to being raised by older parents.

The Scripps National Spelling Bee ended in a rare tie, with Sriram Hathwar and Ansun Sujoe both named champions after exhausting the competition’s word list. It was the first co-championship in over 50 years, and both boys successfully spelled exceptionally difficult words in the final round. They described the contest as a battle against the dictionary rather than each other, and President Barack Obama congratulated them on Twitter. The event featured 281 spellers from eight countries and concluded with a live broadcast on ESPN.

NATO and the United States expressed skepticism over Russia’s announcement that it was pulling troops back from Ukraine’s border, noting that similar promises had not been kept in the past and that no withdrawal had been observed. They urged Moscow to follow through, warning that removing forces would be a key step toward de-escalation. NATO also stressed the importance of Ukraine’s upcoming presidential election and called on Russia and pro-Russian separatists to halt violence and allow the vote to proceed. Meanwhile, tensions remained high in eastern Ukraine, with ongoing clashes, reported human rights abuses, and accusations that Russia was backing the separatists.

Europe’s top players face burnout at Euro 2012 after a grueling season, with the English Premier League’s lack of a winter break making its stars especially injury-prone. Sports scientist Craig Duncan argues that GPS tracking during matches could help prevent fatigue-related injuries by monitoring players’ workloads, but FIFA currently bans its use in games. Some fitness experts question whether coaches would ever substitute players based on GPS data or trust its reliability in large stadiums. Meanwhile, research highlights that insufficient recovery time significantly reduces teams’ chances of winning, underscoring the need for better player load management.

The holiday season poses extra risks for people with food allergies, since many festive dishes lack labels and hosts may forget dietary needs. To keep celebrations safe, hosts should retain ingredient labels, prevent cross-contamination, and offer non-food alternatives for guests to bring. Allergic guests should remind hosts in advance, bring their own safe dishes, and always carry rescue medication. With clear communication and careful preparation, families can enjoy holiday gatherings without compromising health.

The article explores the emotional difficulty of grieving during the holiday season, when societal expectations of joy clash with personal loss. It highlights the stories of Tasha Dimling, who honors her late father by sharing a special bottle of wine at his grave, and Kristine Brite McCormick, who copes with the loss of her newborn daughter by lighting candles and displaying a memorial tree. Clinical psychologist Joshua Klapow advises that grieving people should give themselves permission to feel sadness, limit social obligations, and prioritize self-care. He also suggests redefining the holidays as a time of remembrance, since painful memories may resurface each year.

The U.S. Navy now believes the underwater signals that guided the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 likely came from man-made equipment used in the search, not from the plane's black boxes. This reassessment came as the first phase of the underwater hunt ended with no wreckage found after scanning a large area of the Indian Ocean floor. Officials acknowledged the pings could not be definitively ruled out, but said there was no evidence linking them to the missing jet. The next phase of the search, involving private contractors and a much larger area, is expected to begin in about two months.

The U.S. Navy is showcasing futuristic weapons and technologies, including a low-cost laser defense system, an electromagnetic railgun that fires hypersonic projectiles without explosives, and a process to turn seawater into fuel. These innovations are being highlighted alongside the christening of the USS Zumwalt, the Navy's most advanced stealth destroyer, which is far harder to detect on radar and carries long-range guided guns. The laser will be tested this summer, the railgun at sea in 2016, and the fuel technology has already powered a model aircraft, with officials calling these developments game-changing and potentially life-saving.

An 89-year-old Philadelphia man has been arrested and faces possible extradition to Germany over allegations that he served as an SS guard at Auschwitz during World War II. German prosecutors charge him with complicity in the murder of more than 216,000 Jews, citing new evidence that contradicts his long-held claim that he was only a minor perimeter guard with no direct involvement in atrocities. He has lived in the U.S. since the 1950s and previously avoided prosecution due to his age at the time of service. His extradition hearing is set for late August, though legal experts note the process could be lengthy.

Laszlo Csatary, a 98-year-old suspected Nazi war criminal, has died in Hungary, ending legal proceedings against him. He was accused of deporting over 15,000 Jews to Auschwitz and hundreds more to Ukraine during World War II. Discovered living in Budapest in 2012, he was considered the most-wanted Nazi suspect by the Simon Wiesenthal Center, which criticized the delay in bringing him to justice. Csatary had previously lived in Canada before returning to Hungary amid deportation efforts.

An NBC News freelance cameraman working in Liberia has contracted Ebola and is being flown back to the U.S. for specialized treatment. His colleagues, including Dr. Nancy Snyderman, show no symptoms but will return on a private charter and undergo a 21-day quarantine as a precaution. He is the fourth American to become infected with the virus in Liberia, following three others who have all recovered.

Two Princess Cruises ships operating out of Florida reported nearly 500 cases of norovirus over the weekend. The Crown Princess had 394 affected passengers and crew, while the Ruby Princess reported 105 cases. The CDC is assisting with investigations and monitoring sanitation efforts, and both ships were cleaned before returning to sea. Norovirus, which causes stomach illness, spreads easily through contaminated surfaces, food, or water.

Fierce clashes between ISIS and rival rebel factions in northern Syria have killed nearly 700 people in nine days, including civilians, as the al Qaeda-linked group tries to impose strict rule. The infighting has deepened divisions among opposition forces and threatens to shift power toward extremists. At a Paris meeting, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and allies urged Syrian rebels to join upcoming Geneva peace talks, insisting there is no military solution. Meanwhile, the UN humanitarian chief warned of starvation and dire conditions for civilians displaced by the ongoing conflict.

Graca Machel, Nelson Mandela’s wife, was a seasoned public figure in her own right, having served as Mozambique’s first lady and later as its education minister. Though initially hesitant to marry Mandela, she eventually became his partner, and their late-in-life marriage was built on mutual respect and companionship. She had to navigate the challenge of loving the man behind the global icon, and while South Africans were wary of a foreign first lady at first, she won them over with loyalty and grace. Their private wedding on Mandela’s 80th birthday marked the union of two remarkable lives dedicated to public service.
