To honor Nelson Mandela’s birthday, people worldwide shared tributes on social media, describing him as a symbol of courage, freedom, and hope, with many praising his leadership and inspirational legacy. His birthday also marked Mandela Day, a U.N.-backed initiative encouraging people to spend 67 minutes helping others—one minute for each year he fought for justice. The global outpouring included video tributes, blog posts, and trending hashtags, reflecting his enduring impact. Mandela’s life journey, from 27 years in prison to becoming South Africa’s first Black president and a Nobel laureate, continues to inspire generations across the world.

Mandela’s remains were brought to his childhood village of Qunu, where he will be buried after a final journey marked by emotional farewells and public mourning. His family and ANC leaders paid tribute, with his daughter recalling his deep love for the hills and his wish to be laid to rest there. The funeral, expected to draw thousands and international dignitaries, will include traditional Xhosa rites and a private family burial. Heavy security and military presence were arranged to manage the large crowds and honor the late leader’s legacy.

In back-to-back U.N. speeches, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed Iran’s president as a deceptive hardliner and accused Tehran of continuing its pursuit of nuclear weapons, urging world leaders to keep up sanctions. Iran’s representative rejected the claims as baseless, insisting the nuclear program is peaceful and calling for an end to the economic penalties. The exchange followed recent U.S.-Iran engagement, including a historic phone call, though both Washington and Jerusalem stressed that Iran must prove its intentions through verifiable actions. Iran also pointed out that Israel possesses weapons of mass destruction and has not signed the nonproliferation treaty.

In an interview, Prime Minister Netanyahu defended Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a necessary response to relentless Hamas rocket fire and cross-border attack tunnels, arguing that Israel acts to restore sustainable quiet and security. He rejected claims of disproportionate force, blaming Hamas for civilian casualties by deliberately hiding behind Palestinian civilians and using them as human shields. Netanyahu insisted that any ceasefire must include the demilitarization of Gaza and the destruction of tunnels, while also condemning Jewish extremism and contrasting Israel’s prosecution of such acts with Hamas’s glorification of violence. On Iran, he warned against a bad nuclear deal, arguing that no deal is preferable to one that leaves Iran with the capability to quickly build a bomb.

A secret al Qaeda letter found at Osama bin Laden’s compound outlined a broad plot to attack Western infrastructure and economic targets, including tunnels, dams, pipelines, financial centers, and even German gay pride events. The plan, written by senior operative Younis al-Mauretani, also proposed infiltrating Western companies and universities, using trained pilots to crash planes into facilities, and coordinating with al Qaeda affiliates for funding and support. Bin Laden endorsed the strategy and urged affiliates to cooperate, but al-Mauretani was arrested in Pakistan in 2011 before the plans could be carried out. The document was later shared with German prosecutors for use in a terrorism trial in Dusseldorf.

Brian Moore created the iPhone app Cloak after repeatedly running into his ex-girlfriend in New York. The app uses location data from Instagram and Foursquare to show where acquaintances have recently checked in, allowing users to avoid them and set alerts for people they don’t want to meet. It reflects a growing sense of social fatigue and a desire for more real-life privacy, though it currently works only with those two platforms. The developers plan to add Facebook and possibly Twitter, while advising users to tighten privacy settings to prevent misuse.

During Pope Benedict XVI's trip to Mexico, where he blessed children, a new book by three Mexican authors accused the Vatican of covering up clerical child sex abuse. The book focuses on Marcial Maciel, the late founder of the Legion of Christ, and claims church leaders knew of his abuses for decades but hid them, using leaked Vatican documents and testimony from victims and whistle-blowers. While Benedict had removed Maciel from ministry in 2006, a Mexican cardinal defended the pope's handling of abuse, and Benedict himself urged protection of children without directly addressing the allegations.

Prosecutors have called for the death penalty for four men convicted of the brutal gang rape and murder of a young woman in New Delhi, arguing that the attack's extreme cruelty warrants the harshest punishment. Defense lawyers countered that life imprisonment should be the standard, with execution reserved as an exception, and the judge scheduled sentencing for Friday. The victim's family and protesters outside the court have loudly demanded that the men be hanged, reflecting widespread public outrage. The case has also fueled national debate over violence against women, prompted stricter anti-rape laws, and raised questions about India's use of capital punishment.

A recent gang rape of a young woman on a New Delhi bus has ignited nationwide outrage and renewed fears among women about their safety in the Indian capital. Many female students describe everyday harassment, stalking, and groping, reflecting a broader crisis reflected in sharply rising rape statistics over the past decades. Experts and activists argue that the root causes lie in deep-seated patriarchal norms, son preference, and the treatment of women as sexual objects, which also contribute to female feticide. They stress that legal measures alone are insufficient and that lasting change requires a fundamental shift in societal attitudes and the way boys are raised.

A low-budget American film secretly produced by anti-Islam activists provoked deadly protests across the Muslim world after it depicted the Prophet Mohammed in offensive ways. The filmmaker, who used multiple aliases and was later identified as convicted fraudster Nakoula Basseley Nakoula, misled cast and crew into believing they were making a historical adventure movie. The unrest culminated in an attack on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi, Libya, killing the ambassador and three other Americans. Authorities warned the film could fuel further violence, while those involved said they were shocked and felt deceived by the production.

Astronomers have discovered a new dwarf planet, currently named 2012 VP113, whose orbit lies far beyond Pluto in a remote region called the inner Oort Cloud. Its extreme distance is puzzling because no known planetary processes could place an object on such a distant, isolated path. The finding suggests that this region may contain many more similar objects and hints at the possible existence of a large, unseen planet influencing their orbits. Scientists say these distant bodies could offer valuable clues about the early formation of the solar system.

The USDA has issued new nutrition standards for snacks sold in schools, replacing candy, doughnuts, and regular chips with healthier options like granola bars, trail mix, and baked chips. The rules limit fat, salt, and sugar in vending machines and snack bars, restrict sugary sports drinks, and require free water where meals are served, with compliance required by the 2014-2015 school year. Part of the effort to combat childhood obesity, the guidelines still allow homemade treats, birthday snacks, and bake sales. Some nutrition advocates worry that many approved items remain processed and high in sugar, while the changes build on earlier school lunch reforms that faced student backlash.

The Obama administration has issued new federal guidelines reaffirming that public schools must admit all children, regardless of their or their parents' immigration status. While schools may request documents to verify a student's age and local residency, they cannot demand proof of citizenship or legal residence. The guidance, rooted in a 1982 Supreme Court ruling, aims to eliminate enrollment barriers for undocumented and homeless students and clarify schools' legal obligations.

European foreign ministers met with Syrian opposition leader Ahmed Moaz al-Khatib and pledged support while condemning President Bashar al-Assad’s actions, warning that any use of chemical weapons would be held accountable. Syria responded by accusing the United States of fabricating chemical weapons claims, while U.S. and European contractors reportedly trained rebels in Jordan and Turkey to secure such stockpiles. Deadly violence continued across Syria, with opposition forces capturing a military base in Aleppo province. Meanwhile, the U.S. moved to designate the al-Nusra Front as a terrorist organization, aiming to isolate extremists and bolster the new opposition coalition.

Somalia marked a historic step in September by electing Hassan Sheikh Mohamud as president in the first home-based vote in decades, a milestone welcomed internationally as a sign of progress. However, the new leader faces immense challenges, including a shattered economy, crumbling infrastructure, and continued militant control over large areas, notably by Al Shabaab. A Somali academic and parliament member, Ahmed Ismail Samatar, acknowledges the heavy burdens ahead but sees growing hope, noting that Somalis are weary of war, Islamist militancy, and warlordism and are yearning for a new beginning.

A 3-year-old boy named Grayson, who was born without a cochlear nerve, became the first child in the U.S. to receive an auditory brainstem implant after a cochlear implant failed to help him. The device, which sends sound signals directly to his brainstem, has given him sound awareness, though doctors are still learning what he can perceive. His adoptive parents, who were determined to help him, joined a small FDA-approved trial at UNC Hospitals involving only 10 children. They hope the procedure will eventually become available to more children with similar hearing loss.

A second inquest into Amy Winehouse’s death has confirmed the original finding that she died from accidental alcohol poisoning. The new hearing ruled her death a “misadventure,” noting that toxicology tests showed a potentially fatal blood-alcohol level and that she had resumed drinking after a brief period of abstinence. The earlier inquest was invalidated because the presiding coroner lacked the proper legal qualifications. Winehouse, a Grammy-winning singer known for her struggles with addiction, was found dead at her London home in 2011 at age 27.

The Obama administration acknowledged that the international community is not currently equipped to respond to ISIS calls for attacks on coalition nations. At this week’s UN General Assembly, President Obama will push for a binding Security Council resolution aimed at tracking and preventing the movement of foreign fighters, though the measure would lack enforcement mechanisms. U.S. intelligence estimates that about 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries have joined ISIS, including roughly 100 Americans, some of whom have returned home and are under surveillance. The White House also plans a separate summit on countering violent extremism to address the broader threat.

A New Jersey teenager has dropped her lawsuit against her parents seeking financial support and college tuition, after returning home and reuniting with them. The judge accepted her decision to dismiss the case as voluntary, bringing the legal dispute to an end. The case had drawn national attention and stemmed from her claims of emotional mistreatment, which her parents denied, saying she left after refusing to follow their rules. The family’s attorney said the case is over and the Cannings now want to move forward as a family.

The World Health Organization reports that the new MERS-CoV virus has infected 49 people globally, with 27 deaths, including recent fatalities in Saudi Arabia. WHO officials have called the virus a worldwide threat that no single nation can manage alone, emphasizing the need for international cooperation. While most cases trace back to the Middle East, limited local transmission has occurred in France and the UK among people who had contact with recent travelers from the region. The virus causes severe respiratory illness and can lead to pneumonia or kidney failure, but much about how it spreads remains unknown.

Western tourism to North Korea has grown significantly over the past decade, prompting the launch of a new mobile app by London-based Uniquely Travel. The app features over 350 geo-tagged destinations, along with historical, cultural, and ethical guidance, and is designed for both prospective visitors and curious armchair travelers. It includes an offline mode for use in North Korea and allows users to compare prices or build custom itineraries. The developers hope to expand the app to other restricted countries, such as Iran and Libya, and may add more language versions if it succeeds.

Scientists at CERN announced the discovery of a new particle consistent with the Higgs boson, a long-sought breakthrough that could explain how particles acquire mass and fill a major gap in the Standard Model of physics. The results, based on data from the Large Hadron Collider, were described as preliminary but sparked excitement among researchers. The discovery follows years of effort, including recent findings from the U.S. Tevatron collider, which narrowed the search but could not confirm the particle. If confirmed, the Higgs boson would represent a fundamental step in understanding the universe's deepest mysteries.

The United States and Iran are launching an additional round of high-level bilateral discussions on Iran's nuclear program, separate from the ongoing P5+1 negotiations in Vienna. This diplomatic push comes as the interim agreement, which eased sanctions in exchange for nuclear rollbacks, approaches its expiration. Significant differences over a comprehensive deal still exist, but the new talks are intended to test whether those obstacles can be resolved. The added consultations are meant to complement, not replace, the broader P5+1 framework.

The U.S. is implementing stricter airport security measures for international passengers flying into the country, prompted by intelligence about new, harder-to-detect explosives. Travelers may have their electronic devices inspected and must ensure they are charged, as devices that cannot power up will be barred from the flight and could lead to extra screening or rebooking. The rules primarily affect flights from Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, with security experts suggesting checks will likely be random rather than applied to everyone. While the measures may cause some inconvenience and raise concerns about delays, analysts expect the heightened scrutiny to ease over time as the perceived threat diminishes.

Despite a player population that is largely Black, the NFL recently filled eight head-coach and seven general-manager openings without hiring a single minority candidate, marking a major setback for diversity. The article highlights Ozzie Newsome, the Ravens’ longtime general manager, as a powerful counterexample—his shrewd personnel decisions and leadership have made Baltimore a consistent contender. His success underscores the broader issue that qualified minority executives exist but are being overlooked. In response, advocates are pushing to strengthen the Rooney Rule by extending it to coordinator positions, while acknowledging that current hiring results have been disappointing.

New research complicates the idea that people without children are happier than parents. One large study found that once factors like income, education, and health are accounted for, parents and childless adults report similar overall life satisfaction, though parents experience both more joy and more stress. Another study found that childless couples are more satisfied with their relationships, while mothers report the highest life satisfaction overall despite being less content with their partnerships. The key takeaway is that relationship happiness often comes down to small, everyday acts of kindness, which can help couples stay connected amid the demands of parenting.

U.S. intelligence agencies disrupted a terrorist plot aimed at bombing an airliner, recovering an explosive device abroad before it posed any threat to American flights. The device resembled past al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula bombs but showed signs of updated techniques designed to evade detection. Officials stressed that the foiled attempt highlights the need for continued vigilance, even as they noted the intended bomber was no longer a danger. Around the same time, a CIA drone strike in Yemen killed a senior AQAP operative linked to the USS Cole bombing, dealing the group a significant setback.

A new portable device called the TransMedics Organ Care System, or "heart-in-a-box," keeps donor organs warm and functioning during transport instead of storing them on ice, which reduces organ damage and may improve patient outcomes. Early U.S. trial results show lower rates of graft dysfunction, shorter ICU stays, and fewer complications after lung transplants. The technology could also expand the donor organ supply by allowing organs to travel farther and potentially enabling doctors to treat or repair damaged organs before transplantation. However, the system is expensive—around $58,000 per use—and is still awaiting U.S. regulatory approval.

The article responds to a personal account of living with Crohn's disease, acknowledging the severe physical and social challenges of the condition. However, it emphasizes that major medical progress has transformed Crohn's from a poorly understood illness into a manageable one. New therapies, improved monitoring, and a proactive treatment approach now allow many patients to achieve remission, avoid surgery, and live full, normal lives. The authors stress the importance of early, effective intervention and express optimism about future treatments and the ongoing search for a cure.

A new White House report warns that climate change is already affecting the U.S. and will intensify, bringing more flooding, drought, and wildfires depending on the region. The Obama administration is using the assessment to push for urgent action and public awareness, despite strong Republican opposition and skepticism from fossil fuel allies. The report highlights rising sea levels, Southwestern drought, and longer fire seasons as major threats, while noting that many cities are beginning to invest in adaptation. Officials argue that public support for climate action is growing, even as polls show the issue remains less urgent to many Americans than economic concerns.

Federal prosecutors charged 48 people in connection with a $500 million scheme in which Medicaid patients, including those with HIV and other serious conditions, were paid cash to sell their prescription medications. The drugs were then resold to pharmacies and wholesalers across multiple states, often at high markups. Officials described it as a “double-dip” fraud that defrauded taxpayers, pharmaceutical companies, and legitimate pharmacies while endangering patients who received mishandled or expired drugs. Authorities also seized millions of dollars in prescription pills stored in unsafe conditions and urged anyone affected to contact the FBI.

New York City’s Board of Health has approved a mandate requiring children under age five in licensed preschools and day care centers to get a flu shot, one of Mayor Bloomberg’s final health measures. Officials say the policy addresses low vaccination rates and the high risk young children face from flu complications, while also reducing community spread. The decision is controversial, with some advocacy groups threatening a lawsuit and repeating debunked claims linking vaccines to autism. The flu vaccine, available as a shot or nasal spray, must be administered by December 31.

A federal judge has overturned the kidnapping conspiracy conviction of former NYPD officer Gilberto Valle, ruling that his online communications about abducting, torturing, and eating women were fantasy role-play rather than a genuine criminal plot. Valle, who spent 21 months in custody and faced life in prison, was ordered released on bail with GPS monitoring and a mental health evaluation. Prosecutors plan to appeal the decision. The judge acknowledged Valle’s messages were deeply disturbing and misogynistic but said they were insufficient to prove a real agreement to commit kidnapping, especially since no one was actually abducted.

The deadly East Harlem explosion was likely caused by a natural gas leak from a 127-year-old cast iron pipe, according to investigators who found high gas concentrations in the soil. Experts say the incident highlights a broader national problem: aging, leak-prone gas mains in older U.S. cities are increasingly dangerous and have led to frequent explosions. While utilities like Con Edison are replacing old cast iron pipes with plastic and spending heavily on maintenance, thousands of miles of vulnerable pipe remain in service. Cold weather and shifting soil make these old lines especially prone to cracking, and recent studies have found potentially explosive methane levels beneath other major cities as well.

New York City’s Board of Health has approved a measure banning the sale of sugary drinks larger than 16 ounces at restaurants and similar venues, aiming to combat obesity and related diseases. Mayor Michael Bloomberg championed the rule, linking large sugary beverages to rising obesity, diabetes, and heart disease, while noting the city’s high healthcare costs. The soda industry and critics argue the ban is an overreach and that consumers should make their own choices. The regulation takes effect in six months, with enforcement through restaurant inspections, and does not apply to grocery stores.

New York has become the latest state to legalize medical marijuana after Governor Andrew Cuomo signed the Compassionate Care Act, permitting doctors to prescribe non-smokable cannabis for specified serious conditions. The law establishes a tightly regulated, patient-focused program with safeguards such as criminal penalties for fraud and the governor’s power to suspend it over public safety concerns. New York is now the 23rd state, plus Washington, D.C., to allow medical cannabis, though some supporters worry the 18-month rollout is too slow for patients with urgent needs. Critics, meanwhile, argue the measure was driven more by politics than sound medical policy.

A federal judge ruled that the NYPD’s stop-and-frisk policy is unconstitutional, finding it disproportionately targeted Black and Latino people and violated Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights. The court ordered reforms, including requiring reasonable suspicion, appointing an independent monitor, and testing body cameras in high-stop precincts. City officials strongly disagreed, denied racial profiling, and vowed to appeal, arguing the policy helped reduce crime. Mayor Bloomberg said he hoped the appeal would delay implementation until after he leaves office.

The engineer involved in Sunday’s fatal New York train derailment has been identified as William Rockefeller Jr., a veteran locomotive operator with nearly 11 years on the job who rose from a janitorial position at Grand Central. Colleagues describe him as honest, dedicated, and well-liked, with no prior disciplinary issues, and he is fully cooperating with investigators. A union representative said Rockefeller apparently dozed off and realized the danger too late, and the crash killed four people and injured dozens more. He has not been charged, and his lawyer notes he is a family man and former volunteer firefighter who is deeply shaken by the tragedy.

The NFL Players Association is working with the league on a proposed $100 million, 10-year research partnership with Harvard University focused on diagnosing, treating, and preventing player injuries and illnesses. Unlike earlier efforts centered mainly on brain trauma, this initiative would take a broader look at the full range of physical and mental health issues affecting players over their lifetimes. The plan involves studying a large group of current and former players, then conducting deeper evaluations on the healthiest and least healthy among them. Funding would come from the players' share of league revenues, and the project is expected to be announced during Super Bowl week.

French footballer Nicolas Anelka has been suspended for five matches and fined £80,000 by the English FA for using the controversial “quenelle” gesture during a Premier League match. The gesture was deemed offensive and linked to ethnic or religious references, though the disciplinary panel concluded Anelka was not anti-Semitic and did not intend to promote hatred. He was also ordered to complete an educational course. Anelka denied the charges and has seven days to appeal the ruling.

Nigerian police reversed an earlier ban on protests supporting the more than 200 schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram, clarifying that peaceful demonstrations were never prohibited and that only an advisory had been issued due to security concerns. The initial ban, announced by Abuja’s police commissioner, had sparked public outrage and threats of legal action from protest groups. Authorities maintained that the advisory was meant to prevent potential infiltration by criminals or insurgents, not to suppress citizens’ rights. The girls remain missing, and the government continues to face criticism over its response to the abduction.

Boko Haram’s escalating attacks across northern Nigeria have left many survivors traumatized, including Daniel Ayuba, who was severely wounded by a bombing in Maiduguri and still carries physical and emotional scars. The militants have grown bolder, carrying out mass kidnappings, bombings, and shootings, such as the abduction of nearly 200 schoolgirls and a deadly bus station blast near Abuja. The violence has driven a state of emergency in the northeast, while both Boko Haram and the Nigerian military face accusations of brutality. Despite his suffering, Ayuba considers himself fortunate to be alive and remains haunted by the ongoing bloodshed.

The rescue of the 276 abducted Nigerian schoolgirls is extremely difficult due to the time already lost, the likelihood they have been split into small groups and moved across Nigeria’s porous borders into neighboring countries. The Nigerian military’s poor handling of the crisis, lack of intelligence and equipment, and history of heavy-handed tactics further complicate efforts, while Boko Haram’s ruthless leader, Abubakar Shekau, has rejected negotiations and threatened to sell the girls. Airstrikes or ground assaults are risky given the hostages’ numbers and the militants’ entrenched positions, so international help, mainly from the U.S. and others, is focusing on intelligence and negotiation support.

Nigerians are protesting to demand government action after Boko Haram militants abducted around 230 schoolgirls from Chibok over two weeks ago, with nearly 190 still missing. Demonstrations have taken place in Abuja and Lagos, while relatives accuse authorities of failing to respond effectively. The military says it is committed to the rescue but warns that some information may be misleading and that a cautious approach is needed to protect the hostages. The abductions have sparked a social media campaign under #BringBackOurGirls, highlighting Boko Haram's opposition to women's education.

A 24-hour curfew was imposed in Adamawa State, Nigeria, after three days of sectarian violence left more than 30 Christians dead, with authorities fearing retaliatory attacks by Christian youths. The attacks, which occurred in the cities of Yola and Mubi, have been linked to the militant group Boko Haram. President Goodluck Jonathan condemned the violence and urged Nigerians to remain peaceful, while also defending his government’s decision to remove fuel subsidies, a move that has sparked nationwide protests. He promised oversight to ensure the savings from subsidy removal are used prudently for national development.

Nigeria is grappling with overlapping crises, including escalating religious violence in the north, separatist unrest in the oil-rich south, and a nationwide strike triggered by the government’s sudden removal of popular fuel subsidies. President Goodluck Jonathan faces intense pressure, with critics questioning the timing of the subsidy cut amid rising sectarian tensions and widespread poverty. The government is caught in a difficult bind: reversing course could signal weakness to militants, while enduring the strike risks severe economic disruption, since oil exports fund most of the national budget. Meanwhile, fears of broader ethnic and religious conflict have prompted prominent Nigerian figures to urge calm, as the country’s deep-seated divisions come to the fore.

At 23, Gossy Ukanwoke launched Beni American University, Nigeria’s first private online institution, offering flexible programs for graduates, working professionals, and aspiring entrepreneurs. The idea grew from his earlier educational social network, and the school now serves around 200 students with affordable short online courses. A major hurdle has been Nigeria’s requirement for a physical campus, so Ukanwoke purchased land in Benue State to build one in the coming years. Driven by a belief that education is essential for progress, he promotes the university mainly through social media and student referrals.

Nigerian military officials say they have killed a suspected Boko Haram leader who had been impersonating the group’s deceased figurehead, Abubakar Shekau, in recent clashes near Maiduguri. The announcement comes after past claims of Shekau’s death were retracted when he reappeared in videos. In related operations, dozens of militants surrendered, while others were killed or captured. President Goodluck Jonathan also addressed the U.N. Security Council, highlighting Boko Haram’s ties to global terror groups and the severe toll of its insurgency, including thousands of deaths and the mass abduction of schoolgirls from Chibok, for whom negotiations for release are ongoing.

North Korea has withdrawn its invitation for the U.S. special envoy to visit and negotiate the release of detained American Kenneth Bae. Bae, imprisoned on charges of plotting against the government, has reportedly suffered serious health decline while in custody. The envoy had been expected to request humanitarian clemency so Bae could return home for medical care. The sudden reversal leaves Bae’s fate uncertain amid ongoing tensions between the two countries.

Critics are largely impressed by the ambition and boldness of Darren Aronofsky’s “Noah,” even when they find its execution uneven. The film is praised for its striking visuals, serious spiritual themes, and Russell Crowe’s strong performance, but reviewers note its dark tone and morally complex protagonist make it hard to root for anyone. Many describe it as a strange blend of biblical epic and visionary art film that defies easy categorization, with some calling it magnificent and others finding parts ridiculous. Despite controversy over its loose handling of scripture, most agree Aronofsky has crafted a thought-provoking, serious spectacle that stays with viewers.

Doris Lessing, the Nobel Prize-winning British author, has died at age 94. She is best remembered for her groundbreaking 1962 novel *The Golden Notebook*, a landmark feminist work. Drawing on her childhood in Southern Rhodesia, she wrote over 50 books and was praised for her fierce intellect and storytelling. Lessing passed away peacefully at her London home, leaving behind a legacy as one of the great writers of her generation.

The Vatican has denied reports that a cardinal or a woman are also under investigation in the leak case, saying only the pope’s butler, Paolo Gabriele, has been formally charged with aggravated theft. Gabriele is accused of stealing confidential documents that were later passed to journalist Gianluigi Nuzzi, whose book exposed internal Vatican disputes, including concerns about corruption and mismanagement. While the Vatican has not disputed the documents’ authenticity, it considers their publication a criminal breach of privacy. The investigation is ongoing, and questions remain about whether any trial would be held in Vatican City or Italy due to the city-state’s limited judicial and detention capacity.

Eskom’s CEO defends South Africa’s heavy reliance on coal, arguing it has been essential for energy security, economic growth, and expanding electricity access, and he rejects criticism as misinformed. Coal supplies about 86% of the country’s energy and has helped make South Africa the continent’s largest economy, while its share of global emissions remains small. He stresses that South Africa is committed to a lower-carbon future and has clear emissions targets, but developing countries still need affordable, reliable power. The long-term plan includes a mix of energy sources, with renewables and nuclear playing major roles alongside coal to meet baseload demand.

After years of intense media scrutiny, Amanda Knox was freed by an Italian court, overturning her conviction for the murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher. The case had become a global pop culture spectacle, driven by sensational headlines, social media, and Knox’s photogenic image, which overshadowed the facts. Experts noted that the investigation was flawed and that the public’s fixation on Knox’s appearance, rather than the evidence, contributed to her wrongful conviction. Meanwhile, the media frenzy continued, with outlets competing for interviews and the Kercher family expressing concern that Meredith had been forgotten in the coverage.

The thriller “No Good Deed” took the top spot at the domestic box office in its debut, earning about $24.5 million—nearly double its production budget—with Idris Elba and Taraji P. Henson starring. “Dolphin Tale 2” opened in second place with roughly $16.6 million, falling short of the first film’s opening weekend. “Guardians of the Galaxy” slipped to third with $8 million, though it has now surpassed $300 million domestically and internationally. Meanwhile, “Let’s Be Cops” remained a strong earner for Fox, and the limited-release drama “The Drop” posted an impressive per-screen average.

Copenhagen Zoo has again sparked public outrage by euthanizing a family of lions to make room for a new male, echoing its earlier controversial killing of a giraffe. The zoo defended the action as necessary to prevent inbreeding, but critics are calling for boycotts. However, the article argues that such killings are an inevitable consequence of keeping animals in confined captive spaces with limited genetic diversity. The real solution is to stop supporting zoos altogether, since their conservation and education claims are weak, and instead focus on protecting animals in their natural habitats.

Poland’s Bledow Desert, often called the Polish Sahara, is a natural oddity in an otherwise green, forested country. The EU is funding a conservation project to stop the desert from disappearing by cutting down trees and removing vegetation that have caused it to shrink. The desert originally formed after 13th-century deforestation exposed deep glacial sand, and it later served as a WWII training ground for German troops. Supporters argue it is a unique regional attraction worth preserving, with plans to boost tourism despite questions about why a desert should be saved.

The Army has begun investigating Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl’s disappearance, but he has not yet been read his rights or given a lawyer because investigators see no evidence of misconduct during his captivity. His reintegration debriefings focus on the time after his capture, and if he says anything incriminating, the process would stop so he could be informed of his rights. The formal probe, led by Maj. Gen. Kenneth Dahl, must be completed within 60 days, and Bergdahl would likely be interviewed last. Meanwhile, he continues to receive military pay, including back pay from his years in captivity, unless it is determined he deserted.

Recovery efforts are getting underway in Moore, Oklahoma, after Monday’s devastating EF5 tornado killed at least 24 people, including 10 children, and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes. With all missing people now accounted for, local leaders are pushing for new requirements for storm shelters in homes and schools, arguing that safer buildings could save lives in future tornadoes. Federal officials, including President Obama, have pledged ongoing support for the long rebuilding process, while communities like Joplin, Missouri, which suffered its own deadly tornado two years ago, are sending help. The storm’s damage is expected to result in billions of dollars in insurance claims, and officials warn that additional funding may be needed if more disasters strike.

India is facing a severe crisis of sexual violence, with recent brutal gang rapes and murders in Uttar Pradesh highlighting the epidemic. Conviction rates for rape are declining despite rising reported cases, and many crimes go unreported due to stigma and distrust of authorities. Political leaders have made insensitive remarks, reflecting deep-rooted patriarchy and gender inequality that also limit women's economic and educational opportunities. To address this, the article calls for cultural change, stronger law enforcement, faster justice, and greater protection and support for victims.

Two separate cruise ships this week reported norovirus outbreaks, with Princess Cruises’ Caribbean Princess cutting its trip short due to fog after 178 passengers and crew fell ill, while Royal Caribbean’s Explorer of the Seas saw nearly 700 cases. The virus, which causes stomach pain, nausea, and diarrhea, is highly contagious and spreads through contaminated food, surfaces, or close contact. There is no specific treatment, but most people recover with hydration, though young children and the elderly face higher risks. Prevention relies on frequent handwashing with soap and water, since hand sanitizer does not kill the virus, along with disinfecting surfaces and avoiding shared items.

Severe flooding triggered by unusually early and intense monsoon rains has devastated northern India, especially the mountainous state of Uttarakhand, killing up to 150 people and leaving more than 60,000 stranded. Officials likened the disaster to a "Himalayan tsunami," with rescue operations hampered by persistent bad weather and submerged villages making it difficult to determine the full extent of casualties. The heavily damaged pilgrimage town of Kedarnath saw its revered temple remain standing while surrounding structures were wrecked, and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, after an aerial survey, cautioned that the death toll could climb. The extreme weather also affected New Delhi, where the Yamuna River surged to its highest level since 2010 and forced thousands to relocate.

North Korea has withdrawn its invitation for a U.S. envoy to discuss the detained Korean-American Kenneth Bae, prompting disappointment from Washington. Bae, sentenced to 15 years of hard labor on charges related to missionary activity, was recently moved back to a labor camp after a hospital stay, which his family called devastating. The U.S. reiterated its demand for his release and noted that civil rights leader Jesse Jackson has offered to travel to Pyongyang to seek Bae’s freedom. The cancellation comes amid rising tensions over upcoming U.S.-South Korea military drills, which North Korea condemns as invasion preparations and has threatened to use as a reason to call off planned inter-Korean family reunions.

China and North Korea both rejected a UN report accusing Pyongyang of crimes against humanity, with Beijing calling it politicized and detached from reality and potentially blocking any ICC referral. The report, based on a yearlong investigation, documented widespread abuses such as torture, forced killings, and starvation, urging international action. North Korea dismissed the findings as fabrications by hostile forces and defectors, while China defended its repatriation of North Koreans and questioned the report’s credibility. Despite the damning evidence, the report’s authors warned that meaningful change in North Korea remains unlikely without decisive global response.

North Korea conducted a brief live-fire exercise near the disputed western maritime boundary with South Korea, prompting a strong warning from Seoul that it would respond with force if the drills crossed into its territory. No shells landed in South Korean waters during the roughly 15-to-20-minute drill, which Pyongyang had announced in advance. The exercise came amid heightened tensions following President Obama’s visit to the region, with South Korean officials reporting that North Korea had completed preparations for a possible nuclear test. The situation was further complicated by the detention of an American tourist and the threat of additional sanctions from Washington.

North Korea announced it no longer considers the 1953 armistice that ended the Korean War valid, following new U.N. sanctions over its recent nuclear test. The country also severed a direct emergency communication line with South Korea at the border. This is not the first time Pyongyang has declared the truce void, as it has made similar threats in the past. The move raises concerns about renewed hostilities, especially given the U.S. military presence in South Korea.

North Korea launched 25 short-range rockets into the sea from its east coast, which South Korea interpreted as a protest against ongoing joint military exercises with the United States. The projectiles were identified as aging, unguided Soviet-designed FROG rockets. The United States joined South Korea in urging Pyongyang to stop actions that raise tensions, while North Korea defended the launches as legitimate self-defense.

North Korea has released 75-year-old Australian missionary John Short, who was detained last month for distributing religious materials. State media said he was expelled out of leniency and consideration for his age, and he has since arrived in Beijing. The article also notes that North Korea often pressures detainees into making false confessions, and it highlights the ongoing detention of Kenneth Bae, a Korean-American still held by the regime.

U.S. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel warned that North Korea's recent provocations are pushing toward a dangerous confrontation, while affirming that Washington is fully prepared to respond to any attack. Intelligence suggests Pyongyang may be readying multiple missile launches, possibly without advance notice, heightening regional anxiety. Despite the threats, South Koreans remain largely unfazed, though the North has escalated tensions by withdrawing workers from a joint industrial zone and being blamed for cyberattacks. The situation reflects a stark contrast between foreign alarm and domestic calm on the peninsula.

North Korea is holding parliamentary elections that are widely seen as a formality to reinforce the ruling system, with Kim Jong Un running for a symbolic seat. While the vote is dismissed by critics as a political spectacle, analysts will examine the list of deputies for signs of shifts in power and purges. The elections also function as a de facto census, helping authorities identify defectors who have left the country. Ultimately, experts say the process is designed to project legitimacy and popular support for the regime.

North Korea has released a new propaganda video depicting a simulated missile strike on Washington, D.C., targeting the White House and Capitol. The video arrives amid heightened tensions following new U.N. sanctions over North Korea’s latest nuclear test, and Pyongyang has responded with threats of a preemptive nuclear attack. Analysts note that North Korea remains far from having the capability to strike the U.S. with nuclear missiles, though the Pentagon is still adding West Coast missile interceptors as a precaution. This is not the first such video, as an earlier one used footage from a video game before being taken down.

South Korean defense officials say North Korea appears ready to conduct a nuclear test at any time, based on recent satellite imagery showing active excavation and equipment movement at the Punggye-ri test site. The officials believe Pyongyang is only waiting for a political decision to proceed. The warning follows North Korea’s failed rocket launch in April, which drew international condemnation and led to the collapse of a U.S. food-for-nuclear-freeze deal. Tensions remain high, with North Korea vowing to continue its nuclear program and the United States warning that another test would be a serious mistake.

North Korea has threatened military action against the United States and South Korea as the allies began their annual joint exercises, with state media claiming its forces are prepared for war with nuclear-armed capabilities. The drills come shortly after U.S.-North Korea talks ended without notable progress, marking the first high-level contact since Kim Jong Un assumed power. In a related show of resolve, Kim visited frontline military units and warned of a powerful retaliatory strike against any territorial intrusion. Washington has maintained that the exercises are defensive, while Pyongyang views them as preparation for an attack.

North Korea launched a long-range rocket on Friday despite international warnings, but the missile broke apart shortly after liftoff and crashed into the sea. The failure was an embarrassment for Pyongyang, especially since state media unusually admitted the launch did not place a satellite into orbit. The United States, South Korea, Japan, and others condemned the action as a disguised ballistic missile test and a violation of U.N. resolutions, warning of further isolation. The launch came as North Korea celebrated the centenary of founder Kim Il Sung and sought to solidify the leadership of his grandson, Kim Jong Un, raising concerns that additional provocations, possibly a nuclear test, could follow.

North Korea has confirmed that Kenneth Bae, the American sentenced to 15 years of hard labor, has been moved to a special prison. Bae was arrested in November and is accused of attempting to overthrow the regime, while the U.S. and his family insist he was simply a tour operator. Despite repeated U.S. requests for amnesty and a personal appeal from Dennis Rodman, North Korea has refused to release him, stating he is not a bargaining chip. The situation remains strained amid ongoing tensions over North Korea's nuclear activities and its harsh penal system.

North Korea has announced it will launch unspecified “special actions” aimed at destroying South Korea’s president and government, claiming the operation would take only minutes and use unprecedented methods. The threat was accompanied by state media propaganda, including imagery of attacks on a caricature of President Lee Myung-bak. The announcement appears to be a response to South Korea’s recent disclosure of a cruise missile capable of reaching any target in North Korea. It also follows North Korea’s failed long-range rocket launch earlier this month, which had already heightened regional tensions.

After nearly 170 years, one of the two ships from Sir John Franklin’s ill-fated 1845 expedition has been discovered in the Canadian Arctic. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper announced that the find resolves one of Canada’s greatest historical mysteries, though it is not yet known whether the wreck is the Erebus or the Terror. The discovery was made on September 7 using a remotely operated underwater vehicle deployed by Parks Canada. Harper highlighted the discovery as a historic moment that reinforces Canada’s Arctic sovereignty, noting that Franklin’s expedition helped establish the country’s claim to the region.

Kenyan counterterrorism officials are investigating a Norwegian citizen of Somali descent as a possible suspect in the Westgate mall attack, with alleged ties to senior Al-Shabaab commander Ikrima. Ikrima, who reportedly spent time in Norway and recruited for the militant group in Europe, was the target of a failed U.S. Navy SEAL raid in Somalia. The case has renewed concerns about Al-Shabaab’s ability to radicalize and recruit within Western diaspora communities. Experts warn that small, isolated extremist networks in countries like Norway, the U.S., and the U.K. remain a key security threat.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continued without success after the jet vanished en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, with no wreckage located despite extensive aerial and naval efforts. Unconfirmed oil slicks spotted in the Gulf of Thailand offered a possible lead, but authorities stressed they had not verified the finding. The investigation has been complicated by the discovery that at least two passengers’ passports were stolen, though officials said there was no confirmed link to terrorism. With 239 people aboard, including many Chinese and Malaysian nationals, authorities cautioned that determining what happened could take a long time.

A Bhoja Air passenger jet carrying 127 people crashed while approaching Islamabad in poor weather, with no survivors found. The Boeing 737-200 had flown from Karachi and went down in a residential area near a military airbase, scattering debris across several villages. Investigators recovered the flight data recorder and are examining whether bad weather, aircraft condition, or equipment failures played a role. Pakistani officials expressed grief and launched an inquiry, while the airline defended the plane’s airworthiness.

A Philadelphia jury has deadlocked on most counts in the landmark trial of two priests, prompting the judge to order further deliberations after 12 days. Monsignor William Lynn, the first senior church official prosecuted in such a case, is accused of shielding abusive priests, while the Rev. James Brennan faces charges of attempted rape. Both defendants have pleaded not guilty. The case is historic because it targets a church administrator for failing to stop abuse, not just the alleged abusers.

Congressman Roger Williams, then a 14-year-old boy, met President John F. Kennedy in Fort Worth on the morning of November 22, 1963, shaking his hand just before Kennedy departed for Dallas. He was in Latin class later that day when he learned of the assassination, a moment he says changed the country forever. Williams credits that brief encounter with inspiring his own path into public service, despite his conservative politics differing from Kennedy’s. He still vividly remembers the President’s kind words and considers the meeting a deeply emotional turning point in his life.

NSA Director Keith Alexander defended the agency’s surveillance programs at the Black Hat conference, claiming they helped thwart 54 terrorist attacks worldwide, including 13 in the U.S. He addressed privacy concerns by emphasizing that phone metadata collection excludes call content and that internet surveillance targets foreign actors, with strict oversight and limited analyst access. Alexander faced heckling from some attendees who accused him of lying, but he maintained that the programs are lawful and necessary for connecting intelligence dots. He also suggested that leaks by Edward Snowden could weaken future counterterrorism efforts by exposing methods to adversaries.

Edward Snowden’s father visited him in Moscow for the first time since the NSA leaker fled the U.S., saying his son deserves a Nobel Peace Prize and defending him as a whistleblower. The elder Snowden expressed uncertainty about his son’s whereabouts and future plans, noting Edward has kept a low profile while adjusting to life in Russia. He thanked Russia and President Putin for granting asylum, and said he hopes to visit again, while making clear he loves and supports his son.

The Montana-based 341st Missile Wing, which oversees around 150 Minuteman III nuclear silos, has removed its security forces commander, Col. David Lynch, after the unit received an unsatisfactory rating on a safety and security inspection. The failure stemmed from tactical-level errors unrelated to nuclear operations, and the wing was not stripped of its nuclear mission certification. Lynch had led more than 1,200 personnel across four squadrons. The lapse follows a similar inspection failure at Minot Air Force Base earlier this year that led to the removal of 17 personnel.

The U.S. faces a looming energy shortfall over the next two decades as aging coal and nuclear plants retire while electricity demand rises, threatening economic stability. Renewables alone cannot solve the gap because they need backup when conditions are unfavorable, making nuclear power a reliable and clean alternative. Advanced reactor designs and the existing nuclear industry’s strong safety record position nuclear energy as a key solution, despite past setbacks and financial hurdles. To avoid an energy crisis without sacrificing clean air, nuclear power must remain central to national energy policy.

The article describes an Israeli nurse at Barzilai Medical Center who was shocked to find her wounded son among soldiers brought from Gaza, not having known he was deployed there. The day marked the deadliest in the conflict so far, with 13 Israeli soldiers and dozens of Palestinians killed, many in the Shaja'ia assault. The hospital, located near the border, has ramped up surgical capacity and treats both soldiers and Palestinian patients amid ongoing rocket threats. Overall, the war has killed hundreds of Palestinians, most estimated to be civilians, along with 18 Israeli soldiers and two civilians.

Nu Skin, a US-based skincare company, is treating 16,000 employees from Greater China to a lavish corporate trip in the United Arab Emirates. The event is expected to inject about $20 million into the local economy, with arrangements including chartered flights, thousands of hotel rooms, and visits to major landmarks. The trip marks the company’s 30th anniversary and rewards its top sales performers, with Dubai having won the hosting bid over several other cities.

A Manhattan grand jury is looking into whether the fatal beating of a 62-year-old man in Union Square should be prosecuted as a hate crime. The suspect, Martin Redrick, allegedly made a racial threat before attacking the victim, who later died from head injuries; two other men were also hurt when they tried to intervene. Redrick is currently charged with assault, and authorities are considering upgrading the charges to include hate crime or manslaughter. His lawyer noted that no psychiatric evaluation has been conducted, while friends remembered the victim as a kind and caring man who helped others and looked after his elderly mother.

The NYPD has acquired two pairs of Google Glass to explore how the wearable technology might assist police work, though the devices are only being tested and have not been used in active patrols. The department is part of a broader effort to review emerging tech for potential law enforcement applications. Similar experiments are underway in firefighting, where apps could provide building details, thermal imaging, or record incident footage. However, the device’s ability to capture photos and audio has also raised privacy concerns.

The Obama administration announced it will halt deportation of undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, provided they meet criteria such as age, continuous residence, education or military service, and a clean record. The policy grants eligible individuals a two-year reprieve and work permits, potentially affecting around 800,000 people. Latino and immigrant advocacy groups praised the move, while Republicans condemned it as an overreach and amnesty, arguing it bypasses Congress. President Obama defended the action as a temporary, fair measure and urged lawmakers to pass the DREAM Act for a permanent solution.

President Obama will use his State of the Union address to make economic inequality a central theme, aligning with Pope Francis’s view that wealth disparity is a moral issue. The issue has gained international traction, and Obama’s upcoming meeting with the Pope underscores their shared focus on fighting poverty and inequality. Left-of-center leaders in several countries are also seizing on public discontent over stagnant living standards and economic hardship. Historical patterns suggest that as the lingering effects of the 2008 crisis persist, center-left parties may gain political ground.

President Obama will make history as the first U.S. president to visit Myanmar, during a broader Asia trip that also includes Thailand and Cambodia. His visit is meant to acknowledge Myanmar’s recent democratic progress while encouraging further reforms. He is scheduled to meet President Thein Sein and democracy advocate Aung San Suu Kyi, whose party has re-entered politics after years of military rule. The U.S. and other Western nations have begun easing sanctions in response to Myanmar’s reforms, though officials stress that more work remains for a full transition to democracy.

President Obama and British Prime Minister David Cameron are scheduled to attend an NCAA tournament game in Ohio, where they will also take part in a joint halftime interview. Obama has launched a March Madness bracket challenge on his campaign website, inviting supporters to predict the tournament winner and compare their picks with his. This comes after past Republican criticism over Obama’s public bracket selections, including his incorrect 2011 championship prediction. Beyond the basketball outing, the leaders’ meeting will include serious discussions on issues like Afghanistan and Syria, and they co-authored an op-ed emphasizing the strength of the U.S.-U.K. alliance.

Most Americans struggle to understand basic health insurance terminology, and a recent study found that only a small percentage of insured individuals could correctly define key terms or calculate out-of-pocket costs. This lack of knowledge is especially concerning as millions of uninsured people will soon need to choose plans under the Affordable Care Act. Experts warn that misunderstanding insurance language can lead to poor and expensive coverage decisions. The article highlights essential terms—such as deductible, co-pay, co-insurance, premiums, and in-network providers—to help consumers navigate their options.

The article explains that the Affordable Care Act will allow millions of uninsured Americans, like Amy Braun-Gross, to obtain health coverage despite pre-existing conditions. It outlines key enrollment details, including the open enrollment period, the individual mandate with penalties for going uninsured, and the health insurance marketplaces where people can compare plans. Subsidies and tax credits are available to help lower-income individuals afford coverage, and various exemptions exist for those who cannot comply. The piece also emphasizes the importance of meeting the December 24 deadline for coverage starting January 1 and advises consumers to shop carefully for the plan that best fits their needs.

The term "Obamacare" evolved from a Republican attack line into a phrase Democrats later tried to embrace, with President Obama himself using it to argue that he genuinely cares. Its use in Congress spiked dramatically, and the upcoming Supreme Court ruling on the health law could reshape public perception, potentially turning the label positive if the law is upheld. However, experts note that the word still triggers negative associations for many, and the law’s cumbersome official name has made it harder to defend. Ultimately, the debate centers less on the law’s text and more on how it is framed and communicated.

The Supreme Court’s ruling on the individual mandate shifts attention to the real challenge of health reform: curbing rising health care costs. While the mandate itself will not significantly reduce spending, the Affordable Care Act includes numerous measures aimed at improving quality and efficiency, such as Medicare payment reforms and incentives for better hospital care. These systemic changes are preferable to proposals that simply shift costs onto states and individuals. The decision clears the way for pursuing innovative solutions to make health care spending more sustainable.

Despite South Carolina’s political resistance to the Affordable Care Act, two young food-truck owners in Greenville see the health insurance exchanges as a welcome improvement over their current costly, limited coverage. They represent the healthy, younger enrollees whose participation is essential to making the law work by balancing costs for older and sicker patients. Although they have avoided serious illness, one has already faced expensive out-of-pocket treatment, and both view buying insurance as a smart long-term investment in their future health. They plan to shop for a plan that is both affordable and comprehensive, hoping the new system delivers the security their current policies lack.

President Obama met with the Dalai Lama at the White House despite strong objections from China, reaffirming U.S. support for preserving Tibet’s religious and cultural traditions and encouraging dialogue between the Dalai Lama’s representatives and Beijing. The White House reiterated that the U.S. considers Tibet part of China and does not support Tibetan independence. China condemned the meeting as interference in its internal affairs and warned it would seriously harm U.S.-China relations. The Dalai Lama, who denies seeking independence, has met with Obama twice before, and such meetings have consistently drawn sharp criticism from Beijing.

President Obama traveled to Estonia to reassure NATO allies along Russia’s border that the alliance will defend them against any aggression, emphasizing that Ukraine’s crisis would not be repeated in NATO territory. At the upcoming NATO summit in Wales, leaders are expected to bolster Eastern European defenses with rotating troops and equipment, while also pressing member states to increase defense spending. The summit will also address the threat from ISIS, following the group’s killing of a second American journalist, and the future of NATO’s role in Afghanistan after combat troops withdraw.

President Obama announced plans to push other nations to contribute more to the Ebola response, warning that a weak international effort would cost lives. He indicated that new airline passenger screening measures would be introduced both in West Africa and at U.S. entry points. While he downplayed the risk of a major Ebola outbreak in the United States, he stressed that global cooperation is essential. His remarks came after the first U.S. Ebola diagnosis and a separate infection in Spain.

President Obama announced an expanded U.S. military campaign against ISIS, including airstrikes in Syria as well as Iraq, and the deployment of additional American military advisers to Iraq. He emphasized that the strategy would not involve U.S. combat troops on the ground and aimed to build an international coalition to degrade and ultimately destroy the militant group. The speech drew mixed reactions, with many lawmakers supporting the tougher approach while some liberals and war-weary Americans remained cautious. Obama also sought congressional backing for arming and training moderate Syrian rebels as part of the broader effort.

President Obama announced the U.S. will arm and train Syrian rebels to fight ISIS, while reiterating that American ground troops will not be used in combat. Congress approved his plan, and U.S. military leaders are finalizing airstrike targets in Syria, with France also joining air operations in Iraq. Meanwhile, ISIS has seized more Kurdish villages near the Turkish border and continues to spread propaganda and commit atrocities, including the killing of hostages. The U.S. is building an international coalition to degrade the group without another large-scale ground war.

President Obama marked the 60th anniversary of the Korean War armistice by honoring fallen and surviving veterans, stressing that the conflict should not be forgotten and that those who served deserve recognition and care. He laid a wreath at the Korean War Veterans Memorial and reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to recovering and accounting for troops still missing in action. Obama called the war a victory, noting that South Korea’s freedom and prosperity stand in sharp contrast to the repression and poverty in the North. Meanwhile, North Korea held its own military parade in Pyongyang to mark what it calls “Victory Day.”

President Obama announced new U.S. sanctions against major Russian banks, energy and defense firms, as well as separatist groups, saying Russia had not taken real steps to end the conflict in Ukraine. European leaders also signaled plans to tighten their own measures, reflecting growing Western pressure. In response, President Putin warned the sanctions would backfire and seriously damage U.S.-Russian relations, while accusing Washington of encouraging continued fighting. U.S. officials also repeated allegations that Russia was supplying weapons and maintaining thousands of troops near the Ukrainian border.

President Obama acknowledged that he should have anticipated the negative reaction to playing golf right after condemning the beheading of journalist James Foley, admitting that the visual impact of his actions matters. He explained that the performative side of the presidency does not come naturally to him, though he understands its importance. Obama also expressed that the killing deeply affected him, especially after speaking with Foley’s grieving family. He conceded that the demands of the job have left him sleep-deprived at times.

Afghans are closely watching the U.S. presidential election, but many feel the war in Afghanistan has been sidelined in the campaign, with candidates avoiding serious debate about the country’s future. Their main concerns are the candidates’ positions on Pakistan and their plans for the U.S. troop withdrawal after 2014, since Afghanistan’s economy and stability remain deeply tied to American support. The article also highlights President Hamid Karzai’s strained relationship with the Democrats and his warmer ties with Republicans, though analysts doubt even a Romney win would restore close relations. Ultimately, the enduring symbol of America’s ambiguous legacy is Kabul’s “Bush Market,” which is likely to keep its name no matter who wins.

President Obama clashed with a heckler in San Francisco who urged him to halt all deportations, with Obama insisting he lacks the legal authority to do so and must enforce the law. Immigration advocates argue he could use executive discretion, and legal experts note that while the president has some leeway in enforcement, a blanket stop would likely overstep his authority. Obama has previously used this discretion to protect certain groups, such as young Dreamers and parents of citizens, but has still deported record numbers overall, focusing mainly on criminals and serious violators. The broader political debate remains unresolved, as comprehensive immigration reform is stalled in Congress and Republicans have announced hearings on the administration's enforcement policies.

President Obama asked Congress to delay a vote on military action against Syria while pursuing a new Russian-backed diplomatic plan for Syria to surrender its chemical weapons, while insisting the U.S. military maintain pressure as leverage. He argued that a limited, targeted strike was necessary to enforce international norms and deter chemical weapons use, but ruled out ground troops or a prolonged campaign. The address came amid strong public and congressional opposition, with many lawmakers skeptical of U.S. involvement. Obama stressed that diplomacy could only succeed if the threat of force remained credible, though the Russian initiative still lacked details and faced doubts about whether it was a genuine solution or a stalling tactic.

The Supreme Court delivered a significant environmental win by upholding the EPA’s Cross-State Pollution Rule in a 6-2 decision, affirming federal authority to regulate coal-fired power plant emissions that drift across state lines. The ruling backed the agency’s interpretation of the Good Neighbor Provision, allowing it to require upwind states to reduce pollution harming downwind states. Supporters highlighted potential health benefits, including preventing tens of thousands of premature deaths, while opponents, including industry groups and some states, argued the regulations were costly and overreaching. Justice Scalia issued a sharp dissent, accusing the majority of enabling bureaucratic overreach.

President Obama announced a new $100 million research initiative aimed at deepening understanding of the human brain and developing treatments for disorders such as Alzheimer’s, epilepsy, and traumatic brain injury. The project, called the BRAIN Initiative, would fund advanced tools to observe brain activity in real time and explore how thought, learning, and memory work. The proposed funding, included in the upcoming federal budget, would support multiple government agencies and private partners, though it may face challenges amid spending-cut pressures. Officials hope the research could lead to transformative breakthroughs in how brain disorders are treated and prevented.

Danish Prime Minister Helle Thorning-Schmidt sparked global attention by taking a selfie with President Obama and UK Prime Minister Cameron at Nelson Mandela’s memorial service. While some British media criticized the gesture as inappropriate, many Danes saw it as harmless and reflective of their leader’s down-to-earth style. The article also highlights Thorning-Schmidt’s background, including her marriage to Stephen Kinnock and her historic role as Denmark’s first female prime minister. Overall, the reaction suggests a cultural divide, with Danes viewing the moment as a relatable, human act rather than a breach of decorum.

The White House expressed shock after President Obama viewed the video of Ray Rice assaulting his then-fiancée, while top officials said Rice’s indefinite suspension appeared justified. Lawmakers, especially female senators, sharply criticized NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell for initially handing down a lenient two-game ban and demanded a true zero-tolerance policy for domestic violence. Some threatened congressional hearings if the league fails to police itself, and former FBI Director Robert Mueller was appointed to investigate how the NFL handled the case. The controversy grew amid additional domestic abuse allegations involving other NFL players, prompting calls for teams to bench those under investigation.

President Obama told congressional leaders he believes he already has the legal authority to expand military action against ISIS without a new vote, while still asking for public backing to demonstrate national unity. Lawmakers appear unlikely to hold a formal vote before the midterm elections, partly due to political risks, though some argue existing war powers from the post-9/11 era are sufficient. The administration is developing a broader strategy that includes airstrikes in Syria, supporting Iraqi forces, building an international coalition, and aiding moderate Syrian rebels. Obama is set to address the nation to outline the threat and his plan to defeat the militant group.

President Obama formally requested congressional approval for limited U.S. military action against Syria in response to an alleged chemical weapons attack, arguing that the use of such weapons demands a firm international response. The decision shifts the crisis into a domestic political debate, with Congress set to hold hearings and vote after returning from recess. While U.S. officials expressed confidence in the evidence against the Syrian government, U.N. inspectors were still analyzing samples, and global reactions were divided. Syria’s government dismissed the threats, and opposition figures worried that inaction could embolden the regime.

President Obama reaffirmed that U.S. forces will not take on a combat role in Iraq, emphasizing that American support will be limited to airstrikes, training, and intelligence assistance for local partners. Secretary of State John Kerry echoed this stance, asserting that the U.S. would have enough allies for the campaign, though no nations had offered ground troops. The message was complicated by Joint Chiefs Chairman General Martin Dempsey, who said he might recommend U.S. advisers accompany Iraqi troops under certain conditions, while Iraq’s prime minister insisted foreign troops were not welcome on the ground. Meanwhile, the House approved a plan to arm and train Syrian rebels, even as the administration faced criticism over mixed signals and the lack of a clear strategy.

Fifty years after JFK’s Cold War speech in Berlin, President Obama’s visit comes at a reversed moment: Germany is now Europe’s economic anchor while Britain and France struggle, and Washington increasingly needs Berlin to step up globally. The article argues Obama should push Germany beyond its post-war reluctance to use hard power and toward leadership in three key areas: resolving the euro crisis, advancing the transatlantic trade deal, and taking on a stronger NATO security role. Germany’s past remains a sensitive burden, but its current strength and stability make it the natural partner to revive the European project and help shape global rules. Ultimately, the visit is less about American reassurance to Germany and more about urging Germany to accept the responsibilities of its new standing.

President Obama pressed Iraqi leaders to resolve their political divisions, warning that military action alone cannot defeat the insurgency without an inclusive government representing Shiites, Sunnis, and Kurds. As Sunni militants from ISIS advanced toward Baghdad and displaced hundreds of thousands, the U.S. began deploying military advisers to assess Iraqi forces and set up joint operations centers. U.S. officials also signaled doubts about Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki’s ability to unite the country, given his Shiite-dominated leadership.

The United States and Ukraine warned Russia against military intervention in Crimea, with President Obama stating that any violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty would be costly and destabilizing. Ukraine accused Russian forces of attempting to seize airports in the region, calling the presence of armed troops an invasion, while Russia insisted its actions were in line with existing military agreements. Diplomatic efforts intensified, including calls between U.S. and Russian officials, as concerns grew over separatism and possible annexation. Meanwhile, ousted Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych resurfaced in Russia, denouncing the new interim government as illegitimate and vowing to continue his fight for Ukraine’s future.

President Obama warned Syria’s government that using or moving chemical or biological weapons would cross a U.S. “red line” and trigger serious consequences, including a possible military response. He stressed that Washington had communicated this clearly to all parties in the region and had prepared contingency plans. The warning highlighted Syria’s large chemical weapons arsenal, while noting that its biological program is believed to be research-only. The statement came amid ongoing heavy violence, with scores killed, including a Japanese journalist, as the conflict entered its 18th month.

A new study finds that most adult dogs and cats in the U.S. are overweight or obese, with the problem worsening over the past year. Excess weight raises risks for serious conditions like diabetes, arthritis, and cancer, and can shorten pets’ lives. Many owners do not recognize their pets are too heavy, reflecting a growing “fat pet” norm tied to overfeeding, calorie-dense food, and lack of exercise. Experts stress gradual weight loss under veterinary guidance, along with healthier treats and regular activity, to improve pets’ health and longevity.

A new study shows a significant 43% drop in obesity among children ages 2 to 5 over the past decade, even though overall obesity rates for older children and adults remained largely unchanged. The findings were announced alongside new proposed rules to restrict advertising of high-calorie foods and drinks in schools, part of Michelle Obama’s Let’s Move! initiative. The campaign has driven changes in school meals, snack regulations, and childcare guidelines, with some early signs of progress. Still, officials stress that childhood obesity remains a major challenge and more work is needed.

Occupy London protesters are marking 100 days of their camp outside St Paul’s Cathedral, arguing that they have shifted public debate on capitalism and inequality, even as a court has ordered them to leave. While some acknowledge the physical occupation may have run its course, they insist the movement will continue through community outreach and future actions. Meanwhile, Occupy activists are also present in Davos, where they contrast their inclusive, people-focused protest with the exclusive World Economic Forum, though there are tentative signs of dialogue between the two sides.

Pediatric obsessive-compulsive disorder affects about 1 in 100 children, often emerging around ages 10 to 12, and involves persistent fears and repetitive rituals that can disrupt daily life. The International OCD Foundation has launched a new website featuring young people’s stories to help kids and families recognize symptoms and find support. Treatment commonly includes cognitive behavioral therapy—especially exposure therapy that frames OCD as a “bully” to fight—along with medication, which studies show can be especially effective when combined. Personal accounts highlight that while OCD can be managed and symptoms may ease, children often experience ups and downs, and support from therapy, family, and peers is crucial.

Nadya Suleman, mother of 14, says she would consider acting in an adult film if it paid well and required no kissing or physical contact, as she struggles to support her family. She recently filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy and faces foreclosure on her California home, but remains determined to provide a stable, safe future for her children. Suleman defended her parenting, noting that social workers found no issues and that her children are healthy and happy despite media criticism. She hopes to eventually build a business empire and become a role model, though she acknowledges the challenges ahead.

The OECD’s latest economic outlook describes a divided global recovery, with the U.S. gaining momentum thanks to stimulus measures while the eurozone remains held back by austerity, debt crisis fallout, and weak credit conditions. Europe is expected to face continued recession and rising unemployment, including severe youth joblessness, while the U.S. and Japan see improving labor markets.
