The opposition accused the Syrian government of deliberately targeting children, while U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry condemned the assault and acknowledged that President Assad had strengthened his position, though the conflict remains a stalemate. The mosque had been repurposed as a classroom because other schools were destroyed or filled with displaced people. The broader Syrian civil war has now claimed over 100,000 lives since 2011.

Oprah Winfrey celebrated the graduation of the first class from her South African leadership academy, where all 71 graduates—girls from impoverished and traumatic backgrounds—were accepted into universities. The $40 million school provides free, high-quality education and support to hundreds of girls. Despite past controversies, including an abuse scandal, Winfrey remains committed to her mission. She now plans to use this model to expand educational opportunities for millions of underprivileged girls worldwide.

Oprah Winfrey visited Jaipur, India, for its literary festival and described the country as the most fascinating place she has ever seen, saying she plans to return many times. She expressed interest in interviewing Deepak Chopra in India and reflected on her past conflict with author James Frey, noting she had shown him more harshness than she would show murderers. Regarding Salman Rushdie’s canceled appearance due to security threats, Winfrey said she avoids getting involved in others’ political decisions and does not support banning books, though she understands safety concerns. She also revealed that a long-standing personal goal to visit India, represented on her vision board, finally came true.

Oracle Team USA continued its remarkable America’s Cup comeback by winning a fifth consecutive race against Emirates Team New Zealand. Despite this surge, New Zealand still leads the series 8-6, while Oracle began the defense with a two-race penalty for illegal boat modifications. Oracle must now win the remaining three races to retain the cup, starting with race 17 on Tuesday. Both skippers acknowledged the strong performance, with Oracle citing momentum and New Zealand remaining confident.

A shooting at Reynolds High School in Oregon left one student dead and a teacher injured before the suspected gunman, also a student, died from a self-inflicted wound. The victim was identified as 14-year-old freshman Emilio Hoffman, who was killed in a locker room. The injured teacher helped initiate the school’s lockdown despite being hurt, and officials credited the quick response with preventing further casualties. The tragedy reignited national debate over gun violence, with President Obama urging Americans to demand stronger action from Congress.

Osama bin Laden’s son-in-law, Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, is standing trial in a civilian U.S. court in Manhattan, accused of acting as al Qaeda’s public spokesman after the September 11 attacks and helping recruit fighters. Prosecutors argue he agreed to deliver bin Laden’s message of violence while the World Trade Center was still burning, making him a key figure in spreading the terror network’s call to arms. The defense counters that the case relies on fear rather than evidence, emphasizing that Abu Ghaith was not directly involved in the 9/11 plot. If convicted, he faces life in prison.

Osama bin Laden’s son-in-law, Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, appeared in a New York federal court and pleaded not guilty to charges that he conspired with al Qaeda to kill Americans. He served as al Qaeda’s spokesman after the September 11 attacks and had been arrested in Jordan following reported detention in Turkey. While U.S. officials portrayed the arrest as a victory against terrorism, some analysts argued that Abu Ghaith was not a major al Qaeda figure. His civilian trial also drew criticism from Republicans who believed he should have been treated as an enemy combatant.

Crime scene photos from Oscar Pistorius's bathroom have surfaced, showing blood trails, a bloodied toilet, and bullet holes, just before his court date. The images appear to contradict or support different narratives: Pistorius claims he shot through the door fearing an intruder, while prosecutors argue it was premeditated murder after an argument. The authenticity of the photos is unconfirmed, and their release raises concerns about police misconduct. The investigation has already been marred by errors, including the lead detective facing his own charges and mishandling of evidence.

In the murder trial of Oscar Pistorius, a neighbor and doctor testified about the aftermath of the shooting, describing how he found Reeva Steenkamp fatally wounded and heard Pistorius say he mistook her for a burglar. The athlete broke down in court as the graphic details were recounted. Defense lawyers worked to cast doubt on witness accounts, suggesting screams heard by neighbors may not have come from Steenkamp and that sounds could have been from Pistorius breaking down the bathroom door. Pistorius maintains he killed her accidentally, while prosecutors argue the shooting was intentional following an argument.

The prosecution in Oscar Pistorius's murder trial announced it will rest its case early next week after calling just a few more witnesses, a move that could allow the defense to begin presenting its case or seek dismissal. Key ballistics testimony suggested Steenkamp was shot in the hip first, then hit in the arm and head while in a defensive position, though the defense disputed this sequence. The case hinges on whether Steenkamp had time to scream between shots, which would undermine Pistorius's claim that he fired believing she was an intruder. The trial, built largely on circumstantial evidence, will ultimately be decided by a judge rather than a jury.

Oscar Pistorius was involved in an altercation at a Johannesburg nightclub after another patron confronted him about his murder trial, and he later said he regretted going to a public place. The incident was followed by his first tweets in some time, including messages about helping others, a passage on love from Viktor Frankl, and a prayer for those in pain. The posts drew mixed reactions, with some questioning his decision to be out in public while on trial. His murder trial remains adjourned until August 7, when closing arguments are set to begin.

The murder trial of Oscar Pistorius has been extended until mid-May, with a brief recess scheduled in April after all parties agreed to the new dates. Pistorius admits to fatally shooting Reeva Steenkamp but denies murder, claiming he mistook her for an intruder and acted in self-defense. The prosecution unexpectedly indicated it may rest its case early next week after calling only 18 of a possible 107 witnesses. The case has drawn intense media attention, and the outcome could range from a lesser negligence-based conviction to a life sentence for premeditated murder.

South African model Reeva Steenkamp was shot and killed by her boyfriend, Olympic athlete Oscar Pistorius, on Valentine’s Day, a tragedy that followed her own social media posts about feeling safe and urging women to speak out against violence. Pistorius admitted to the shooting but claimed he mistook her for an intruder; he was ultimately convicted of culpable homicide. Steenkamp was a successful model and law graduate with a rising public profile, and her relationship with Pistorius had shown both affection and signs of tension. Her death highlighted issues of gender-based violence in South Africa and cut short a promising life and career.

A South African judge has ordered Oscar Pistorius to undergo psychiatric evaluation before his murder trial can proceed, indefinitely postponing proceedings. The decision follows testimony from a defense psychiatrist suggesting the athlete has suffered from generalized anxiety disorder since childhood due to his amputations. While Pistorius does not claim insanity, the judge ruled the testimony raised enough doubt about his mental state to require expert assessment. The evaluation could influence the verdict or sentencing, with possible outcomes ranging from acquittal by reason of mental illness to a finding that his mental health is irrelevant.

Oscar Pistorius broke down in court as a pathologist described the fatal wounds suffered by Reeva Steenkamp, who died from multiple gunshots, including a head wound that likely killed her instantly. Pistorius maintains he shot her by mistake, believing she was an intruder. The trial also heard from a security guard and a former girlfriend, with the defense seeking to cast doubt on the prosecution’s case. Pistorius faces murder and firearms charges, and the judge alone will decide his fate.

Oscar Pistorius is selling the Pretoria home where Reeva Steenkamp was fatally shot, using the proceeds to cover mounting legal expenses after his murder trial ran longer than expected. The prosecution is nearing the end of its case, and Pistorius may testify in his own defense as early as next week. He admits to firing the fatal shots but denies murder, claiming he mistook Steenkamp for an intruder and acted in self-defense. The financially strained athlete, who has not competed since the charges, says he could never return to the property.

Oscar Pistorius's trial for the murder of Reeva Steenkamp centers on whether he intentionally killed her or mistakenly believed she was an intruder. He faces premeditated murder and multiple gun-related charges, with a judge rather than a jury deciding the case. If convicted of premeditated murder, he could receive a life sentence, while a lesser culpable homicide conviction might result in a shorter or even non-custodial sentence. The trial also highlights broader issues in South Africa's justice system, including prison conditions and unequal access to legal resources.

After a grueling cross-examination of Oscar Pistorius, the defense began presenting its own witnesses to challenge the prosecution's murder case. A forensic expert testified that a key wound on Reeva Steenkamp may have been caused by a magazine rack rather than a bullet ricochet, though the state prosecutor aggressively questioned his credibility. The defense continues to argue that Pistorius fired in fear of an intruder, not intentionally after an argument, and even introduced a Valentine's Day card from Steenkamp to show their relationship was loving. If convicted of premeditated murder, Pistorius faces life in prison, with the trial expected to run until mid-May.

CNN readers correctly predicted four of the six major Oscar categories in their pre-awards poll. They accurately chose "Argo" for best picture, Daniel Day-Lewis for best actor, Jennifer Lawrence for best actress, and Anne Hathaway for best supporting actress. However, their picks for best supporting actor and best director were off, as Christoph Waltz and Ang Lee took those honors instead. Overall, the readers' predictions were largely on target, with only two misses among the top awards.

Michael Moss’s new book exposes how the processed food industry deliberately engineers products with optimal levels of sugar, salt, and fat to make them irresistible, contributing to the obesity epidemic. He reveals that companies use tactics like the “bliss point” for sugar, fat’s appealing “mouth feel,” and specially shaped salts to maximize flavor impact. The book also highlights how marketing to children, such as Lunchables, capitalized on kids’ desire for control, while government agencies like the USDA often promote the very foods their nutrition guidelines warn against. Moss advises shoppers to stick to lists, focus on fresh foods, and read nutrition labels carefully, while noting that industry pressure and consumer demand may be pushing food giants toward healthier changes.

The author reflects on the legacy of their father and grandfather, who inspired awe for the ocean, but acknowledges that today the focus has shifted to the severe threats of climate change, pollution, and overfishing. Despite these dangers, they argue that the ocean should be seen as a source of hope and practical solutions rather than despair. A healthy ocean is essential for oxygen, food, climate regulation, and economic stability, and restoring it is achievable through better management, conservation, and sustainable practices. Ultimately, the future of the ocean depends on both collective action and individual choices, which can determine whether it becomes a symbol of loss or of renewed possibility.

President Felipe Calderón leaves office amid deep public division over his six-year war on drug cartels, which he defended as necessary despite widespread violence and tens of thousands of deaths. Protesters condemned his legacy as devastating, while supporters credited him with taking on organized crime and maintaining economic stability. Calderón also faced criticism over human rights abuses and was recently announced as a Harvard fellow, a move that drew objections from a Mexican researcher. Incoming President Enrique Peña Nieto has signaled a shift in strategy, focusing on reducing violence rather than continuing the same military-led approach.

Outgoing Mississippi Governor Haley Barbour issued full pardons to four inmates serving life sentences for murder, along with one burglar, all of whom had worked as trusties at the governor’s mansion. The pardons have sparked outrage among victims’ families, who say the offenders served far less time than their crimes warrant and that they received little or no warning before the releases. Relatives of one victim noted they were told just days earlier that the inmate would not be paroled, making the sudden pardon especially shocking. Barbour’s office did not respond to requests for comment before his successor’s inauguration.

A Tokyo assemblywoman was subjected to sexist heckling from male lawmakers while advocating for better support for women, including shouts telling her to marry and asking if she could bear children. The incident sparked widespread outrage and calls to identify the offenders, with the politician describing the remarks as deeply hurtful. It also highlighted persistent gender inequality in Japan, where women face workplace discrimination and low representation in leadership roles. Despite government initiatives like “Womenomics,” significant gaps in pay and managerial positions remain.

An online auction of items allegedly collected from the scene of Paul Walker’s fatal car crash—including sunglasses, a fire extinguisher, and debris—has sparked outrage among fans. The authenticity of the belongings, especially the sunglasses, has not been verified, and local police have expressed doubt that they were actually Walker’s. The auction site reportedly crashed due to heavy traffic, and a petition was launched to halt the sale. Meanwhile, production on “Fast & Furious 7” is set to resume in Atlanta, with the studio planning to retire Walker’s character rather than kill him off.

A Sri Lankan domestic worker, Rizana Nafeek, was executed in Saudi Arabia for the death of her employer’s infant, a crime she maintained was a tragic accident. Rights groups argued she was a minor at the time, had no proper legal representation, and was forced to confess, but appeals for clemency from her family, the Sri Lankan government, and human rights organizations were rejected. Her case has drawn international criticism and is seen as part of a broader pattern of Saudi Arabia executing foreign migrant workers and individuals convicted of crimes committed as minors.

An independent group of experts has released its own analysis of satellite data, concluding that Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 likely crashed in the southern Indian Ocean at a location hundreds of miles southwest of the area previously searched. Using five separate computer models, the group pinpointed a tight cluster of possible positions and recommended that the official search focus there. The experts acted ahead of a BBC documentary and an upcoming Australian announcement to ensure their findings were seen as independent. Meanwhile, Australian authorities are finalizing their own reassessment of the data and expect to announce a revised search zone by the end of June.

Many cancers detected through screening may never become life-threatening, yet the term "cancer" triggers aggressive treatment even when unnecessary. Experts argue that overdiagnosis and overtreatment stem from outdated diagnostic standards, defensive medicine, financial incentives, and a culture that equates finding abnormalities with providing care. While some overtreatment is accepted as a trade-off for saving lives, screening also causes harm through false positives and anxiety. The National Cancer Institute recommends reserving the word "cancer" for dangerous lesions, focusing screening on high-risk groups, and reducing unnecessary tests and biopsies.

World powers and Iran announced a framework for further nuclear negotiations after several days of talks in Vienna, with both sides agreeing on the issues that must be addressed in a final deal. Technical experts will meet in early March, followed by another round of high-level discussions in mid-March, as they work toward a comprehensive agreement. The talks build on an interim accord that eased sanctions in exchange for limits on Iran’s nuclear activities, but key disputes remain, including Iran’s refusal to consider dismantling its nuclear facilities. Western officials stress that any final deal must include concrete, verifiable steps to ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

Hurricane Carlotta intensified into a Category 2 storm as it approached Mexico's southwestern Pacific coast, bringing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph. Hurricane warnings were issued for a stretch of coastline from Salina Cruz to Acapulco, with dangerous storm surge, coastal flooding, and life-threatening flash floods and mudslides expected, particularly in Oaxaca. The storm was moving northwest and had begun moving over land, so it was not forecast to strengthen further and was expected to weaken on Saturday.

A small landscape bought by chance in a Canterbury auction lot for about $46 and stored away for ten years has been identified as a genuine John Constable, now valued at over $390,000. The owner’s son initiated an investigation after noticing a faint signature, and an art expert spent a year authenticating the piece through detailed analysis. Experts believe Constable painted it as a gift for his father-in-law, and it had never been publicly exhibited. The painting is currently kept in a bank vault, with hopes to restore it and eventually show it in a museum.

Pakistan has condemned a suspected U.S. drone strike in North Waziristan that killed three people, calling it a violation of its sovereignty and international law, and said it would address the matter through diplomatic channels. The attack occurred amid already strained U.S.-Pakistan ties, following a parliamentary demand for an end to such strikes and a recent NATO incident that killed Pakistani soldiers. While Pakistan views the strikes as illegal, the U.S. has defended them as lawful and effective counterterrorism measures, with President Obama arguing they are more precise and less intrusive than other military options.

Pakistan marked a historic milestone as its democratically elected government became the first to complete a full five-year term, despite the country’s long history of military coups and political instability. The ruling Pakistan Peoples Party struggled throughout its tenure with corruption allegations, chronic power cuts, food shortages, terrorist attacks, and sectarian violence, while also facing public anger over perceived U.S. influence. The government’s survival was aided by the military’s decision to stay out of politics and President Asif Ali Zardari’s willingness to shift power to the prime minister and provinces. Meanwhile, former President Pervez Musharraf announced plans to return from exile and lead his party in the upcoming elections, leaving uncertain whether Pakistanis would welcome him back.

A Pakistani political party official has publicly identified the CIA director and the agency’s station chief in Pakistan as part of a police complaint over a recent drone strike. The strike, which killed several people in northwest Pakistan, has prompted a murder investigation, though U.S. officials have not confirmed the allegations. The move echoes a past incident when the CIA recalled its top spy in Pakistan after being publicly identified. The party, led by Imran Khan, is also pressing the government to cut U.S. ground supply routes unless drone strikes stop.

Imran Khan, a leading candidate in Pakistan’s upcoming election, was injured in a fall from a forklift at a campaign rally, suffering spinal fractures and a head wound but no neurological damage. From the hospital, he urged citizens to vote, while his main rival suspended campaigning as a gesture of respect. The election has been overshadowed by deadly violence, with the Pakistani Taliban claiming responsibility for multiple attacks on political events that have killed dozens in recent days.

Pakistan’s Senate has approved a symbolic, non-binding resolution calling for former military ruler Pervez Musharraf to be arrested and tried for treason over unconstitutional actions during his rule. The move adds political pressure on Musharraf, who has been in self-imposed exile since 2008 and recently planned to return for elections. His party dismissed the resolution as meaningless. Musharraf also faces arrest in connection with the 2007 assassination of Benazir Bhutto, a charge he denies.

The Pakistani Taliban have claimed responsibility for an acid attack on a college van in northern Pakistan, severely burning two female students and warning that girls pursuing education will face similar violence. The attack is part of the group's broader campaign to block girls from schooling, following the recent shooting of education activist Malala Yousufzai. Local officials say the assailants also fired on the vehicle, wounding others. The article also highlights acid violence as a wider problem in Pakistan, including a separate case in which a teenage girl died after her parents allegedly attacked her over family honor.

Malala Yousufzai, a 14-year-old Pakistani activist, is recovering after being shot by the Taliban for speaking out in favor of girls' education. Her attack has sparked worldwide rallies and support for her cause. Various organizations, including UNICEF and other education-focused groups, are working to expand schooling for girls in Pakistan, and an online petition has been launched to demand education access for all children globally.

Pakistan launched a ground assault in Miranshah, the capital of North Waziristan, marking a new phase in its ongoing military campaign against militants near the Afghan border. The operation, which began with airstrikes on June 15, aims to permanently eliminate militant groups, including the Pakistani Taliban and the Haqqani network. At least 15 militants were killed in the latest raids, adding to more than 376 deaths since the offensive began. The fighting has displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians, with nearly half a million people registered at camps and receiving aid.

Pakistani authorities are still hunting for two young gunmen and the man believed to have driven them to the attack on teenage education activist Malala Yousufzai. The interior minister said the suspects had carefully studied her routine, and he defended the investigation while rejecting calls for a military response. Malala is recovering in a British hospital, and officials have promised enhanced security for her and her family when they return to Pakistan. The government also said it would cover her treatment costs and allow her to remain in the UK as long as needed.

Pakistan’s military offensive in North Waziristan has left the main town of Miranshah largely deserted and in ruins, with most residents gone and daily life silenced. The army says the operation, Zarb-e-Azb, has cleared 80% of the area, uncovering militant tunnels, bomb-making materials, and compounds linked to terror groups, while claiming hundreds of fighters have been killed. However, many militant leaders reportedly escaped into Afghanistan, and over 876,000 people have been displaced. Adding to the uncertainty, a newly emerged militant group has claimed control over parts of the region and vowed to resist, signaling that the conflict is far from over.

Pakistan’s Supreme Court has formed a judicial panel to investigate the so-called “Memogate” scandal, overruling the government’s preference for a parliamentary inquiry. The controversy stems from an alleged memo by civilian officials, reportedly seeking U.S. help to prevent a military coup after the killing of Osama bin Laden. The court’s decision is a setback for President Asif Ali Zardari’s administration, whose former ambassador to Washington has denied involvement, and it deepens long-standing friction between civilian leaders and the military. The affair has intensified political turmoil in Pakistan, already strained by U.S. relations following the bin Laden raid and NATO airstrikes.

Pakistan’s upcoming election is seen as a historic democratic step, with millions of new voters and a record number of female candidates, even as the country faces deep problems such as terrorism, corruption, poverty, and economic instability. The ruling Pakistan People’s Party, led by Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, is seeking a rare second term, while main challengers include former prime minister Nawaz Sharif and cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, whose campaign was disrupted by a fall that may boost his support. The election is also marked by severe Taliban violence targeting political parties, which has made campaigning dangerous and forced some leaders to stay away. Notably, Pervez Musharraf is barred from running, and the vote will mark Pakistan’s first civilian-to-civilian transfer of power.

Pakistan announced it would reconsider its cooperation with the United States and NATO following a cross-border airstrike that killed 24 of its soldiers at military checkpoints. In response, Islamabad closed NATO supply routes into Afghanistan and demanded the U.S. vacate an airbase used for drone operations. U.S. and NATO officials expressed regret and pledged a thorough investigation, while Pakistan condemned the attack as unjustified. The incident further deepened existing tensions between the two countries.

Israeli airstrikes on Gaza have killed at least 172 Palestinians, mostly civilians, including children and people at a disability center, while Hamas continues firing rockets into Israel. Civilians are trapped between Israeli evacuation orders and Hamas instructions to stay, with many fleeing to U.N. shelters and reporting they have no safe options. Israel has rejected international calls for a ceasefire, saying it will keep striking militant targets, while Hamas shows no sign of stopping its rocket fire. Diplomatic efforts have stalled, and violence is also rising in the West Bank, deepening the broader conflict.

UNESCO has designated the ancient West Bank village of Battir as a World Heritage Site and simultaneously placed it on the List of World Heritage in Danger. The decision, made during a committee meeting in Qatar, highlights concerns that an Israeli separation barrier could cut off farmers from their ancestral lands. Battir is valued for its 2,000-year-old Roman-era terraces and traditional irrigation systems. The article also notes that the U.S. has limited influence at UNESCO due to withheld funding after Palestine was granted full membership.

Pamela Anderson publicly disclosed at a Cannes Film Festival event that she was sexually abused as a child, beginning at age six when a female babysitter molested her, and later raped at 12 by a 25-year-old acquaintance. She made the revelation while launching her animal rights foundation, explaining that she had kept the trauma secret to avoid burdening her struggling mother. Anderson said her deep connection with animals and nature became her refuge and source of strength during those difficult years.

Defense Secretary Leon Panetta condemned newly published photos of U.S. soldiers posing with dead Afghan insurgents, saying the behavior violates American values and military regulations. The Los Angeles Times published the images after receiving them from a soldier who said they showed leadership failures that endangered troops. NATO and U.S. military officials also denounced the photos as an isolated incident and said an investigation is underway. The publication comes amid a series of incidents that have strained U.S.-Afghan relations, including the burning of Qurans and alleged mass killings by a U.S. soldier.

Efforts to curb the illegal wildlife trade increasingly focus on reducing consumer demand, not just enforcing laws. A notable example is a WildAid campaign featuring Yao Ming, which helped cut shark fin soup consumption in China by 50 to 70 percent. The article also highlights a new public service announcement in Vietnam, funded by reader donations, aimed at discouraging the consumption of pangolin scales and meat. These demand-side campaigns show promise in protecting threatened species by shifting public attitudes and creating social stigma around wildlife products.

A Philadelphia couple had their home seized by authorities under civil forfeiture laws after their adult son was arrested for selling a small amount of heroin, even though the parents were never charged with a crime. The practice allows police to take property linked to drug activity without a conviction, and Philadelphia has used it far more aggressively than other parts of Pennsylvania, seizing millions in assets. Supporters argue the law deters crime and removes illegal profits, while critics contend it violates property rights and due process by forcing owners to prove their innocence. The couple regained access to their home only after agreeing to bar their son from the property, but they remain in legal limbo and fear losing their house again.

A Federal Trade Commission review found that most mobile apps marketed to children provide little or no privacy information, leaving parents unable to determine what data is collected or how it is used. The report noted that Apple and Google require developers to disclose such details but do not enforce those rules. Key concerns include in-app purchases, social media connections, location tracking, and aggressive advertising that may share data or add charges. The FTC has signaled it may take stronger action, having already fined one developer for violating children’s privacy rules.

The family of a 10-year-old Pennsylvania girl with cystic fibrosis is urging U.S. health officials to waive a policy that prevents children under 12 from receiving priority for adult lung donations. The girl has been waiting 18 months and is in critical need of a transplant, and her family argues the rule is discriminatory and blocks doctors from using more readily available adult lungs. Several lawmakers have joined the appeal, asking the health secretary to allow an exception so medical professionals can decide if adult lungs could save her life. While the secretary has said she cannot intervene in individual cases, she has agreed to review the policy.

Amid budget pressures and shifting post-Cold War needs, aircraft makers are increasingly converting existing manned planes—such as business jets and crop dusters—into surveillance drones rather than designing new aircraft from scratch. Examples showcased at the Paris Airshow include Piaggio’s HammerHead, Iomax’s ArchAngel, and Aurora’s Centaur, which can switch between piloted and remote operation. Experts note that adapting already-certified aircraft is faster and easier than gaining approval for new unmanned designs. Separately, AgustaWestland unveiled Project Zero, an experimental electric tilt-rotor aircraft intended not for production but as a testbed for future aviation technology.

In mid-September, six neighboring countries across Central America and Mexico celebrate their independence from Spain, with five Central American nations marking the occasion on September 15 and Mexico on September 16. The festivities feature vibrant parades, street parties, and family gatherings, as captured in reader-submitted photos from past and present celebrations. Images highlight diverse traditions, from masked and costumed performers in Guatemala to young dancers in Nicaragua and Honduras, where participants express national pride through music and dance. In Honduras, the day also offers orphans a chance to join the parades, reflecting the deep community spirit and passion behind the events.

Travelers sometimes end up in the wrong place because of confusingly similar destination names. A couple is suing British Airways after flying to the Caribbean island of Grenada instead of Granada, Spain, and another passenger had the same mix-up the previous week. The article also highlights other travel errors, including flights to the wrong country, state, and airport due to similar-sounding names or code confusion. These incidents show that even with modern technology, destination mix-ups remain surprisingly common.

The acquittal of George Zimmerman in Trayvon Martin's death sparked nationwide protests and outrage, with demonstrators in several cities demanding federal civil rights charges and changes to Florida's Stand Your Ground law. Many activists and ordinary citizens expressed deep sorrow and fear that the verdict legitimizes racial profiling and vigilante violence, while some protests turned destructive, leading to arrests and heightened police presence. Civil rights leaders urged peaceful action and respect for Martin's memory, even as some conservative voices defended the jury's decision. The case has intensified a broader national debate over race, self-defense laws, and the justice system.

A South Korean pastor and his wife have been arrested on suspicion of starving three of their children to death, believing the children were possessed by evil spirits after overeating during Lunar New Year. The couple allegedly cut the children’s hair, beat them, bound their limbs, and gave them only water for over a week, resulting in all three dying on the same day. Their bodies were discovered nine days later, and the parents reportedly prayed for the children’s resurrection. An eight-month-old daughter survived and was placed into care; police plan to send the case to prosecutors.

After receiving experimental stem cell injections in his spine, an ALS patient named Ted Harada reported significant improvements in strength and breathing, allowing him to stop using a cane. The Emory University trial was designed primarily to test the safety of the procedure, not its effectiveness, and involved only a small group of patients. While researchers cautioned against overinterpreting the results, they noted that some participants appeared to experience slower disease progression, with one showing possible improvement. Based on the encouraging safety data, the team is seeking approval to advance the study by injecting stem cells higher into the spinal cord.

Two HIV patients who received bone marrow transplants to treat lymphoma have shown no detectable virus in their blood for weeks after stopping antiretroviral therapy, according to Boston researchers. While encouraging, experts caution that this is not a cure and that the risky procedure is not a practical option for most people with HIV. The cases echo the earlier “Berlin Patient” but differ because those donors did not have the rare HIV-resistant genetic mutation. Researchers say the findings could still offer valuable insights for future HIV cure strategies.

A patient in California is being tested for possible Ebola exposure as a precaution, though health officials consider the case low-risk and the patient is isolated in a specialized hospital room while awaiting CDC test results. No confirmed Ebola cases exist in the state. The development follows a recent negative test in New York, and two American aid workers infected in Liberia are currently receiving care at Emory University Hospital. The article also notes that Ebola spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids, not through air or water, and that there is no approved drug treatment, with care focused on supportive measures.

Patrick Awuah left a lucrative career at Microsoft to return to Ghana and found Ashesi University, driven by a belief that Africa needs a new generation of ethical, innovative leaders. The university blends technical majors with liberal arts, enrolls a diverse student body, and aims to transform the continent by reshaping how its future leadership is educated. Awuah sees this as a catalytic effort, noting that the small percentage of Ghanaians who attend college will eventually run the country, so their education is crucial. His long-term hope is that African universities will compete not just on academic excellence but on producing principled graduates who can drive meaningful change.

The families of two men allegedly killed by Aaron Hernandez are suing the New England Patriots and team ownership to block any payment of the $3.25 million guaranteed to Hernandez, arguing the money should be preserved for the victims. The $6 million wrongful death lawsuit, which also names the Patriots and Kraft Enterprises as co-defendants, stems from the 2012 fatal shootings of Daniel de Abreu and Safiro Furtado. The families’ attorney says Hernandez has already received over $11 million and that some of his assets should be set aside for compensation. Hernandez, who is also charged in a separate murder, has pleaded not guilty, while the NFL Players Association has filed a grievance over the unpaid sum.

Celebrity chef Paula Deen is invoking last month’s Supreme Court ruling on same-sex marriage to argue that a former employee’s racial discrimination lawsuit should be dismissed, claiming the white plaintiff lacks legal standing. Her lawyers cite the high court’s decision that private backers of California’s Proposition 8 did not have standing to appeal. The plaintiff, Lisa Jackson, responds that her case is not about the slur but about a pattern of disrespect and abuse toward people Deen considered inferior. Regardless of the legal outcome, Deen has already faced major professional fallout, including lost endorsements, the cancellation of her Food Network show, and the shelving of her cookbook.

A solar energy initiative in Africa is using a pay-as-you-go model to bring affordable, clean electricity to off-grid rural communities. Customers purchase scratch cards for about a dollar a week to access power stored in solar battery packs, replacing costly and polluting kerosene lamps. The program has already expanded to several countries, improving daily life and productivity for households. Its developers aim to scale up the technology, eventually powering larger appliances and significantly cutting carbon emissions across the continent.

ActiveHours is a startup offering an app that lets hourly workers access wages they’ve already earned before their official payday, bypassing the need for high-interest payday loans. Unlike traditional lenders, it charges no mandatory fees and instead relies on voluntary tips from users. The company has grown quickly and attracted investor interest, though experts warn it could face abuse and the “free rider” problem since donations are optional. Its founder argues the real issue is the outdated payday system itself, and the goal is to give workers control over money they’ve already earned.

A stabbing attack at a Pennsylvania school complex left 21 people injured and led to the arrest of a 16-year-old student on attempted homicide charges. School staff, including an assistant principal who tackled the suspect, along with students and other employees, were praised as heroes for their quick actions. The incident deeply shook the small, tight-knit community, where residents expressed shock and heartbreak over the violence. Officials closed the high school for several days and arranged counseling for students and staff.

Peaches Geldof, the 25-year-old daughter of musician Bob Geldof and TV presenter Paula Yates, was found dead at her home in Kent, with police treating the death as sudden and unexplained pending a post-mortem. Her family, including her husband Tom Cohen, expressed deep grief, noting that she leaves behind two young sons. Geldof had been a TV host and social media personality, and her death drew tributes from celebrities. The article also notes the tragic family history, as her mother died of a heroin overdose in 2000.

Pennsylvania’s governor announced plans to sue the NCAA, arguing that the sanctions imposed on Penn State over the Jerry Sandusky scandal unfairly punish students and the university rather than the convicted abuser or those who enabled him. He also criticized the university-commissioned Freeh report as incomplete, while the NCAA defended its actions as justified and supportive of the victims. The $60 million fine is meant to fund child sexual abuse prevention and victim support, though Pennsylvania lawmakers want all of it spent within the state. Sandusky himself was convicted and sentenced to decades in prison, while Penn State has said it will continue complying with the NCAA’s requirements.

A new government audit found that roughly 83,000 Defense Department employees and contractors with security clearances owe about $730 million in delinquent federal taxes, raising espionage concerns because financial distress can make people vulnerable to foreign intelligence recruitment. The report notes that many accrued their tax debt after receiving clearances, and that thousands had IRS liens or faced collection actions. Investigators struggle to identify such risks because IRS privacy rules limit how tax data can be shared with clearance officials. The intelligence community agrees that tax debt should be more accessible during background checks, but technological and privacy obstacles remain.

The article explores the persistent embarrassment many women feel about menstruation, highlighted by the author’s own awkwardness asking for tampons. It focuses on a viral HelloFlo ad called “Camp Gyno,” which reframes getting a period as a proud milestone and aims to reduce shame. The piece also features mothers who are determined to talk openly with their daughters, contrasting with past generations’ silence and misinformation. Overall, it suggests that while periods remain somewhat taboo, attitudes are gradually shifting toward openness and empowerment.

Former Pakistani military ruler Pervez Musharraf, who seized power in a 1999 coup and ruled until 2008, now plans to return from exile in late January despite facing arrest. His comeback is tied to launching a new political party and rebuilding support, but he is threatened by a warrant related to Benazir Bhutto’s assassination. Musharraf’s lawyers dismiss the case as politically motivated, while he insists he will risk returning and trust the judiciary to act fairly.

A British singer living in Paris was unexpectedly launched into the American music scene when she recorded Tony Hatch’s song “Downtown,” which became a number-one hit in the U.S. and made her part of the 1960s British Invasion. She balanced her rising career with family life, spending more time in America and enjoying the energy of the era’s music and audiences. While she appreciated the excitement, she stayed focused on her work and family rather than the wild party scene. The songs from that period have lasted, and she still performs them with fondness, grateful to have been part of a movement led by the Beatles.

Pharrell Williams has been officially confirmed as a new coach for Season 7 of "The Voice," according to an NBC announcement. Fans had long hoped for this move, especially after his standout performance as a guest mentor for Usher's team in 2013. NBC executives praised his recent musical achievements, including his Oscar-nominated song "Happy" and his Grammy-winning work with Daft Punk, calling him a natural fit for the show. Williams responded enthusiastically, saying the experience would be a lot of fun.

Philip Chism, the teenager charged with murdering his Massachusetts math teacher, is now accused of assaulting an employee at the youth detention facility where he is being held. The attack reportedly occurred Monday, though officials have not disclosed the extent of the worker’s injuries or what prompted the incident. Chism, who was 14 at the time of the teacher’s death, is charged as an adult with raping and killing Colleen Ritzer in a school bathroom in 2013. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Philippine forces conducted a pre-dawn airstrike on the southern island of Sulu, killing around 15 militants, including a Malaysian terror suspect on the FBI’s most-wanted list and two other senior figures. The dead were identified as members of Jemaah Islamiyah and the Abu Sayyaf group, with the U.S. having offered a $5 million reward for the Malaysian militant. Officials described the operation as brief and precise, though they noted that identifying the bodies was still underway. The article also recalls past cases where Philippine authorities prematurely announced the deaths of fugitives who later resurfaced.

Typhoon Hagupit is barreling toward the central Philippines, threatening the same region devastated by Super Typhoon Haiyan just over a year ago. Haiyan was historically the most powerful tropical cyclone ever recorded at landfall, with wind speeds reaching up to 315 kilometers per hour. The Philippines is especially susceptible to such storms due to its geography, dense coastal population, and widespread poverty, which leaves many communities with weak infrastructure and limited resources. The country regularly faces deadly typhoons and other disasters, and the economic and human toll from these events is often severe.

After 15 years of negotiations, the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front have reached a preliminary framework agreement to create a new autonomous Muslim region called Bangsamoro in the south. The deal aims to end decades of separatist insurgency by bringing the rebels into the political process and shifting their focus from armed struggle to development. It outlines key arrangements for governance and revenue sharing, with the new region expected to replace the current one by 2016. International leaders, including officials from the U.S. and UK, welcomed the agreement as a significant step toward lasting peace.

The Philippines announced it will bring its South China Sea dispute with China to international arbitration, saying diplomatic efforts have been exhausted. The move challenges China’s extensive territorial claims in the resource-rich waterway, which is also contested by Vietnam, Malaysia, and others. Tensions have been high since a prolonged naval standoff last year, while China continues regular patrols to reinforce its sovereignty claims. The United States has urged restraint, though it avoids taking sides on sovereignty, as separate frictions persist between China and Japan over islands in the East China Sea.

In the aftermath of Super Typhoon Haiyan, Tacloban’s Catholic priests took on the grim task of blessing the dead scattered across the ruined city, while struggling with their own grief and the difficult question of why God allowed such suffering. Many survivors found comfort in church services and prayer, even as they faced destroyed homes, missing loved ones, and scarce aid. Churches became vital centers of shelter, food, and community support, though the handling of corpses remained harsh and undignified, with bodies placed in mass graves. Despite the devastation, clergy and residents tried to hold onto hope, emphasizing that while the city was battered, its people were not defeated.

A grieving mother in Tacloban says she has lost all will to live after her sons disappeared in Typhoon Haiyan’s storm surge, as she searches desperately for their bodies. The disaster has killed nearly 4,000 people, displaced millions, and left widespread destruction, looting, and violence. International relief efforts are ramping up, with U.S. and British military assets delivering food, water, medicine, and medical aid to the stricken region. While aid distribution is slowly improving, the Philippine government faces criticism for its slow and disorganized initial response to the catastrophe.

Phoenix VA leaders denied maintaining a secret waiting list or covering up delays, but a whistleblower doctor and other insiders contradicted them, alleging that over 1,400 veterans were hidden on an off-the-books list, documents were shredded, and at least 40 veterans died awaiting care. The officials acknowledged that some veterans on waiting lists died but said there was no proven link to delayed treatment and insisted they had requested an inspector general review. The controversy has prompted President Obama to order an investigation and sparked calls from Congress for the Phoenix VA director’s resignation, though she has said she will remain in her role.

Three Phoenix VA officials, including the system’s director, were placed on administrative leave after an investigation by CNN alleged that a secret waiting list hid long delays and that more than 40 veterans died awaiting care. VA Secretary Eric Shinseki said the allegations are unacceptable and ordered an independent review, while the officials denied the claims. The whistleblower, Dr. Sam Foote, said the off-the-books list began in early 2013 and that top managers knew about it, despite their denials. The controversy has drawn White House and congressional attention, with calls for hearings and resignations.

The Phoenix VA director remains on paid status over a month after President Obama vowed accountability for record-falsification, though acting VA Secretary Sloan Gibson says she and two others have been removed from their posts while termination proceedings continue. Gibson confirmed efforts are underway to recover the director’s $9,000 bonus and announced no senior Veterans Health Administration officials will receive performance bonuses this year. He is pushing systemic reforms—such as expanded clinic hours, overtime, and new space—to reduce wait times, but cannot promise when all veterans will be seen within 30 days. He also stressed protecting whistle-blowers and pledged to discipline officials found guilty of misconduct.

Dutch designer Dave Hakkens has proposed Phonebloks, a modular smartphone whose individual components can be swapped out or upgraded instead of discarding the entire device, aiming to combat the growing global e-waste crisis. The concept has drawn massive public attention and celebrity support, though experts and critics question its practicality, citing potential higher costs, bulkier design, and battery limitations. Some also argue that easier upgrades might not necessarily reduce waste, while others believe the idea’s popularity could pressure major manufacturers to build more sustainable, longer-lasting products. Despite skepticism, Hakkens sees the enthusiasm as proof that people want environmentally friendlier phone options.

In the ongoing British phone-hacking trial, prosecutors presented a handwritten “target evaluation” list from private investigator Glenn Mulcaire that included Kate Middleton and other notable figures. Former News of the World editors Rebekah Brooks and Andy Coulson, along with several former employees, face conspiracy charges over illegally intercepting voicemails of well-known people. They are also accused in connection with hacking the phone of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler. The scandal previously prompted a major public inquiry into press ethics led by Lord Justice Leveson.

A new book by wedding photographer Thea Dodd and GayWeddings.com president Kathryn Hamm aims to help photographers capture same-sex couples more authentically. It challenges traditional posing conventions that assume heterosexual gender roles and offers practical guidance, such as handling matching attire and avoiding crushed boutonnieres. The authors emphasize planning conversations with couples to understand their dynamic and natural positioning, while noting that basic composition principles like height placement still apply. Ultimately, the book seeks to improve photographers' skills for all couples by encouraging them to move beyond outdated assumptions.

The American Medical Association has officially classified obesity as a disease, a move aimed at shifting how the medical community approaches prevention and treatment. With nearly a third of U.S. adults and many children affected, the designation could boost research funding, expand insurance coverage for obesity care, and reduce stigma. However, some experts worry it may encourage quick fixes or medication over lifestyle changes. The decision also aligns with renewed congressional efforts to broaden obesity treatment options for Medicare patients.

A Frontier Airlines flight diverted to Cheyenne, Wyoming, due to bad weather, leaving passengers stranded for nearly two hours without food. The pilot called a local Domino's and ordered 38 pizzas to feed all 160 people on board. The pizzas were delivered directly to the plane and handed out by flight attendants. The airline praised the pilot, saying such thoughtful actions are typical of their crew.

A pizza deliveryman who unknowingly became a highlight of the Oscars has described his shock at being called onstage by host Ellen DeGeneres to serve celebrities like Brad Pitt and Julia Roberts. He said the surreal moment felt like the American dream. The unexpected publicity has caused a surge in business across all locations of the pizzeria, with owners scrambling to keep up with demand. DeGeneres also gave the deliveryman a $1,000 tip during her own show.

The wreckage of a plane that disappeared off Venezuela’s coast in January has been found, nearly six months later. The aircraft carried Italian fashion executive Vittorio Missoni, his wife, and four others, all now presumed dead. Recovery efforts are underway, aided by a U.S. vessel with specialized oceanographic equipment. The Missoni brand, known for its colorful knitwear, remains a major Italian fashion house that Vittorio helped lead with his siblings.

"Playing for Change" is a global music initiative founded by producer Mark Johnson that unites street musicians from over 25 countries to promote peace and cross-cultural connection. Their collaborative covers, such as "Stand By Me," became viral hits and led to a bestselling album. The movement expanded into a foundation that builds music schools for underprivileged youth, mainly in Africa, providing education and job opportunities. It has also partnered with the United Nations on original songs to raise awareness about global unity and shared challenges.

Satao, a beloved 45-year-old elephant in Kenya’s Tsavo National Park known for his enormous tusks that reached the ground, was killed by poachers using poisoned arrows. His mutilated body was identified through distinctive features like his ears and the mud patterns on his skin. His death highlights the devastating impact of the global illegal ivory trade, driven largely by demand in Asia and the United States, which has led to tens of thousands of elephants being killed each year. Conservationists warn that this surge in poaching not only endangers wildlife but also threatens tourism-based livelihoods and helps fund armed groups through ivory-for-arms deals.

Indian police arrested seven men for allegedly gang-raping a woman on a bus in Punjab, an attack that closely mirrors last month's fatal Delhi bus rape. The victim was the sole passenger when the bus passed her stop, and the driver and helper took her to a location where five others joined them in assaulting her overnight. Unlike the Delhi case, which sparked nationwide protests and a government pledge for stricter laws, this latest incident has not triggered public outrage. The article also notes that reported rapes in India have risen sharply over the decades, though many cases go unreported due to stigma.

In Afghanistan, police rescued a 15-year-old girl who had been imprisoned and brutally tortured by her in-laws after she refused to be forced into prostitution. The victim, married off months earlier, was starved, had her nails and hair pulled out, and suffered severe health issues before being hospitalized. Her in-laws were arrested, but her husband escaped. The case underscores the ongoing abuse and violence faced by Afghan women, despite broader societal progress since the Taliban's fall.

Ahead of President Vladimir Putin's visit, New Delhi authorities sealed off the central government district following two days of violent protests over the brutal gang rape of a young woman on a bus. The demonstrations, marked by clashes with police, tear gas, and water cannons, prompted Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to appeal for calm while acknowledging the public's justified anger and vowing to ensure women's safety. The victim remained in critical condition after further surgery, and the incident has ignited nationwide outrage, with protests also occurring in other states. In response, Indian officials have pledged stricter laws and faster trials for rape cases, with some lawmakers advocating for the death penalty.

A Georgia magistrate ruled there is enough evidence to proceed with murder and child cruelty charges against Justin Ross Harris, who is accused of leaving his toddler son in a hot car for seven hours. Testimony revealed explicit messages to multiple women, internet searches about hot-car deaths and a "child-free" forum, and behavior that prosecutors called self-centered and suspicious. The defense countered that the child's death was a tragic accident, pointing to Harris's partial deafness and the ease of distraction, while his wife continues to support him. Harris remains in custody without bail as the case moves forward.

The article revisits the 1960 murder of Irene Garza, a Texas schoolteacher, with strong evidence and witness testimony pointing to the late priest John Feit, who died without facing charges. Despite two independent witnesses claiming Feit confessed, the district attorney blocked prosecution, questioning their credibility, and a grand jury declined to indict. The victim's cousins spent decades investigating and pushing for justice, believing the church protected Feit and covered up the crime. The case remains a symbol of how institutional power and legal caution can stall accountability.

The suspect in the Aurora movie theater massacre appears to have spent months preparing, as evidenced by a steady stream of deliveries to his home and workplace and the booby-trapped apartment he left behind, which police described as designed to kill. The attack during a Batman screening left 12 people dead and dozens wounded, with the gunman using multiple legally purchased firearms and thousands of rounds of ammunition. Authorities safely cleared the explosives from his residence after evacuating nearby buildings, while the community began mourning and planning vigils. The suspect is in custody and is expected to appear in court, as President Obama also planned to visit the affected area.

Eddie Ray Routh, a 25-year-old Marine veteran with a history of mental health struggles, is charged with fatally shooting Chris Kyle and Chad Littlefield at a Texas gun range. Routh had previously been hospitalized for psychiatric evaluation and had spent time in VA facilities, and authorities believe the victims were trying to help him cope with PTSD. After the shooting, Routh fled in Kyle’s truck and later told relatives he had “traded his soul for a truck” before being arrested. Kyle, a former Navy SEAL and author of “American Sniper,” was known as the deadliest marksman in U.S. military history and had become an advocate for fellow veterans.

A Queens man accused of carrying out five Molotov cocktail attacks across the New York City area is being psychologically evaluated after showing erratic behavior, according to police. He faces multiple charges, including arson as a hate crime, after allegedly targeting an Islamic center, a Hindu temple, a grocery store, and two homes. Investigators say his apparent motives were personal grudges, such as being denied restroom access at the mosque, being banned from a store for shoplifting, and disputes with acquaintances. No one was injured, but the attacks have raised alarm, and officials have condemned them as contrary to the city’s values.

Pakistani police in Karachi arrested a senior Taliban commander, Abdul Qayyum Mehsud, along with three other suspects, after a tip-off, seizing weapons, explosives, and suicide vests. Mehsud, once a bodyguard to former Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud, is accused of orchestrating suicide bombings, kidnappings, and other attacks in the region. The arrests highlight Karachi’s role as a key hub for militant fundraising and logistics, with some seminaries serving as recruiting centers. The article also notes growing divisions among Taliban factions, which may weaken the group, despite recent efforts to form a unifying council backed by the Afghan Taliban leadership.

A grenade and gun assault on a private school in Karachi killed the principal and wounded eight others, including students and a teacher. Pakistan’s interim prime minister condemned the attack as cowardly and stressed that targeting schoolchildren, especially girls, showed the terrorists’ brutality. The incident is part of a broader pattern of violence against educators in Pakistan, including the recent killing of a female teacher and the earlier shooting of girls’ education activist Malala Yousafzai. The attack has renewed international concern, with UN officials and education advocates urging stronger protection for students and teachers.

Sudanese protesters took to the streets for a fourth consecutive Friday, rallying against soaring prices and demanding the government's removal. Security forces responded with tear gas and arrests, particularly around a mosque in Omdurman that has become a protest hub. The demonstrations began over economic austerity measures and have been fueled by Sudan's severe economic crisis following South Sudan's secession, which cost the country most of its oil revenue. President Omar al-Bashir has dismissed the protesters as troublemakers, while rights groups have called for the release of those detained.

Authorities in Los Angeles County have reopened the 1981 drowning death of actress Natalie Wood after receiving what they describe as substantial and credible new information, though they stress that her husband, Robert Wagner, is not a suspect. The renewed inquiry follows fresh statements from the yacht captain, Dennis Davern, who claims Wagner delayed calling the Coast Guard and influenced what those aboard told investigators. Wood’s sister, Lana Wood, has long pushed for the case to be revisited and says she hopes the truth will finally emerge. Officials maintain the death is still officially ruled an accidental drowning, and legal experts say criminal charges remain unlikely.

Police presence in Ferguson is being reduced now that the immediate unrest has calmed, but officials stress that rebuilding community trust is far from complete. The protests stem from the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown by a white officer, which intensified long-standing racial tensions between the Black community and the largely white police force. While state troopers and the National Guard are pulling back, the commander leading the security response says officers are now focused on listening and building better relationships. The operation has drawn criticism over heavy-handed tactics like tear gas and military-style equipment, though local police defended those measures as necessary given the violence that emerged.

The high youth turnout in Scotland’s independence referendum, especially among first-time voters aged 16 and 17, shows that young people will engage when they feel the stakes are meaningful. In contrast, American millennials have grown increasingly disillusioned with politics since their historic mobilization for Barack Obama in 2008. Polls indicate low trust in government and weak enthusiasm for the upcoming midterms, with many young voters seeing few genuine choices. To reverse this trend, the article argues that political leaders must give young Americans a reason to believe their participation matters.

Egypt’s presidential election concluded after a voting extension aimed at boosting turnout, though reports indicate few voters showed up in Cairo. The race pitted former army chief Abdel Fattah al-Sisi against Hamdeen Sabahy, with both candidates objecting to the extra day and Sabahy’s campaign withdrawing poll monitors due to alleged arrests and assaults. Human Rights Watch argued that a prolonged crackdown on dissidents had stripped the election of credibility. The vote followed the military’s ouster of President Mohamed Morsy, with al-Sisi having resigned from the military to run.

Pope Benedict XVI has announced his resignation, citing advanced age and declining strength as the reason he can no longer adequately fulfill his papal duties. His departure, effective February 28, marks the first papal resignation in nearly 600 years. A conclave of cardinals is expected to convene in March to elect his successor before Easter. After stepping down, the former pope will reportedly live at Castel Gandolfo and later a Vatican monastery, dedicating himself to prayer and reflection.

Pope Benedict XVI used his Christmas Eve Midnight Mass homily to urge the faithful to look beyond the holiday’s commercial trappings and rediscover its spiritual core. He called on people to embrace humility and simplicity, comparing the low entrance to the Bethlehem stable to the humble attitude needed to find faith. The 84-year-old pope also took part in traditional Christmas Eve rituals, including lighting a peace candle and unveiling a large nativity scene in St. Peter’s Square. He was set to deliver his Christmas Day blessing, “Urbi et Orbi,” the following day.

Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI has confirmed he will attend the upcoming canonization ceremony for Popes John Paul II and John XXIII, joining Pope Francis in a rare public appearance by two popes. The event is notable because Benedict’s presence alongside Francis is highly unusual, given that he resigned the papacy rather than leaving office through death. The two men being made saints both rose from modest beginnings—one from a poor Italian farming family and the other from industrial Poland—to lead the Catholic Church. Large crowds, including many cardinals, bishops, and heads of state, are expected in St. Peter’s Square for the ceremony.

Pope Benedict XVI used his Christmas address to urge peace and dialogue in conflict-ridden regions, including Syria, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Mali, Nigeria, and Egypt. Speaking to about 50,000 people in St. Peter’s Square, he called for an end to violence, protection of civilians, and political solutions to wars. He also appealed to China’s new leaders to respect religious freedom and recognize the positive role of religions in society. Throughout his message, the pope emphasized hope and trust in God even amid suffering and difficult circumstances.

Pope Francis addressed the conflict with ISIS by affirming that it is permissible to stop an unjust aggressor, though he carefully avoided endorsing bombing or war, instead emphasizing that the means must be evaluated. His remarks sparked media speculation about a possible crusade, but the Pope was drawing on the Catholic just-war tradition, which views force as a last resort for protecting the vulnerable. He also stressed the importance of international consensus through the United Nations, warning against unilateral action and the dangers of mission creep. Ultimately, Francis sought to balance ancient moral teachings with modern multilateralism, cautioning against the rhetoric of religious war.

Pope Francis drew worldwide attention after embracing and praying over a man visibly affected by neurofibromatosis, a painful genetic disorder that causes tumors, during a general audience in Vatican City. The tender moment, which took place in St. Peter’s Square, quickly spread on social media and drew praise, even from atheists. It also reinforced the Pope’s ongoing message about the importance of reaching out to the poor, sick, and vulnerable. The encounter was the latest in a series of heartfelt gestures that reflect his commitment to practicing the compassion he preaches.

Pope Francis invited the Israeli and Palestinian presidents to the Vatican for a joint prayer for peace during his Middle East visit, urging both sides to recognize each other’s right to exist as states. He called for renewed commitment to a two-state solution and warned against unilateral actions that undermine peace efforts. In Bethlehem, he also met Palestinian refugees, prayed at Israel’s separation barrier, and appealed for the protection of Christians in the region. His broader trip emphasized interfaith unity and the urgent need to resolve conflicts, including the Syrian crisis.

Pope Francis left a playful voicemail for a Carmelite convent in Lucena, Spain, after the nuns missed his New Year’s Eve call while praying. The nuns shared the message with a Spanish radio network and later managed to speak with him when he called again. During the conversation, he encouraged them to remain hopeful, warning that sadness can lead to spiritual apathy. The call also marked the community’s 400th anniversary and reflected Francis’s reputation for warmth and closeness to ordinary people.

Pope Francis has selected a group of eight cardinals from various continents to advise him on reforming the Catholic Church, specifically focusing on updating the Vatican’s governing constitution for the Roman Curia. The advisory group, which includes only one member from the Curia itself, will hold its first meeting in October and has no legislative authority. Its creation comes amid ongoing calls for change following church scandals, and is seen as a sign that significant reform may be ahead.

Pope Francis has chosen to remain in a modest two-room suite at the Vatican’s Casa Santa Marta hotel rather than move into the grand papal apartment, though he still uses the Apostolic Palace for official duties. This decision reflects his well-known preference for simplicity, as he also avoided luxurious housing and transportation while archbishop in Buenos Aires. Continuing that humble approach, he will celebrate the Holy Thursday foot-washing ritual at a youth detention center instead of the traditional grand basilica. His actions reinforce his call for a Catholic Church that is poor and focused on the marginalized.

Pope Francis marked Holy Thursday by washing the feet of a dozen young inmates, including women and Muslims, at a youth detention center in Rome, choosing a simple service over the traditional grand basilica setting. The act reflected his emphasis on humility and his focus on reaching out to society’s forgotten and marginalized. During the day’s earlier Mass at St. Peter’s Basilica, he urged priests to stay close to their congregations and be attentive to everyday struggles. He also called for an end to violence in the Central African Republic and prayed for a peaceful political resolution there.

Pope Francis made his first pastoral visit as pontiff to the Italian island of Lampedusa, a key entry point for migrants crossing from North Africa, to honor refugees who died at sea and draw attention to their plight. He condemned what he called “global indifference,” urging greater fraternal responsibility and criticizing a culture of comfort that ignores the suffering of others. During the visit, he met with migrants, prayed at the site of a deadly shipwreck, and celebrated Mass at an altar built from the wood of refugee boats. The trip highlighted broader issues such as human trafficking, the divide between rich and poor, and the need for a more unified European response to immigration.

Pope Benedict XVI is making his first visit to Mexico, his first to Spanish-speaking Latin America, but the trip is being overshadowed by the enduring popularity of his predecessor, John Paul II, who is still deeply loved there. Many Mexican Catholics feel less excitement about Benedict's visit, and a recent poll shows most are not as enthusiastic as they were for past papal visits. Additionally, the 85-year-old pope will skip Mexico City due to health concerns about the high altitude, a decision that has disappointed some residents. Despite this, there is hope that Mexicans will come to appreciate Benedict as they did John Paul, and some, like a young girl attending the mass, are eagerly looking forward to seeing him.

Pope Francis has reportedly agreed to attend the World Meeting of Families in Philadelphia in September 2015, which would mark his first visit to the United States as pontiff. Archbishop Charles Chaput announced the pope’s intention, though the Vatican has not yet issued an official confirmation and is still considering other possible U.S. stops, including New York and Washington. A visit would carry special significance for the nation’s growing Hispanic Catholic population, as Francis would be the first Latin American pope to address them in Spanish. The trip could also coincide with the U.N. General Assembly, raising speculation that he might speak there as well.

Pope Francis has reportedly told Vatican officials he intends to travel to the U.S. for the 2015 World Meeting of Families in Philadelphia, though the Vatican has not made an official announcement. A visit would carry special significance for the nation’s growing Latino Catholic population, as he would be the first Latin American pope to address them in Spanish. The trip would also highlight the Church’s focus on family issues amid global debates over same-sex marriage, a topic he recently discussed with French President Hollande. Speculation suggests Francis could combine the visit with an address to the United Nations in New York, but no firm plans have been confirmed.

Pop-up hotels are emerging as a flexible alternative to traditional lodging, often set up in unusual structures like tents, yurts, or shipping containers at events and historic sites. Companies such as The Pop-Up Hotel and Snoozebox have found success by offering portable, high-end accommodations that connect guests to their surroundings or serve major gatherings. A more innovative proposal from architecture firm Pink Cloud aims to turn vacant office buildings into temporary hotels, addressing high office vacancy and hotel shortages in cities like New York. This concept would be quick to assemble, cheaper for guests, and adaptable to different locations and events, potentially even serving as a branded promotional space.

Amid Europe’s economic crisis, Portugal has positioned itself as a leader in reform, arguing that fiscal discipline must be paired with structural changes to boost competitiveness and job creation. The government has implemented wide-ranging measures, including privatization, labor reform, reduced bureaucracy, and energy liberalization, while also approving a growth strategy centered on industrial renewal. This strategy focuses on lowering taxes, easing administrative burdens, improving vocational training, and expanding financing for small and medium enterprises. Ultimately, Portugal emphasizes that sustained recovery depends not only on government action but also on the commitment of businesses, workers, and researchers to invest and innovate.

Per Se, a three-Michelin-starred New York City restaurant, was downgraded from an A to a C after a February health inspection racked up 42 violation points. The critical violations included missing hand-washing supplies in food-prep areas, improper food temperatures, and eating or tobacco use near food preparation. Chef Thomas Keller responded by saying the restaurant will contest the findings at a hearing and will display a “Grade Pending” sign in the meantime. The restaurant, known for its $310 nine-course tasting menu, maintains that it continues to uphold high standards.

The article explores why many parents avoid discussing race and class with their children, despite the urgent need highlighted by events like the Ferguson protests. It features perspectives from parents of color who teach their kids about racial bias and how to interact with police, as well as white parents confronting the reality of white privilege. Experts and parents argue that racial tolerance requires deliberate effort, such as exposing children to diverse cultures and having open, ongoing conversations. Ultimately, the piece emphasizes that overcoming racism depends on facing discomfort and talking honestly about race with the next generation.

A major power grid failure in northern India caused the country’s worst blackout in a decade, cutting electricity to seven states and more than 350 million people. The outage disrupted rail and road travel for hours, stranding passengers and worsening traffic in New Delhi, while partial power was restored after about six hours. The government ordered an investigation, and officials noted the region had not seen a full grid collapse in ten years. The crisis highlighted India’s chronic electricity shortages and prompted business leaders to urge urgent reforms to close the widening gap between energy supply and demand.

Prabowo Subianto, who has rejected the official outcome of Indonesia's presidential election and accused the election commission of widespread fraud, is preparing to file a legal challenge with the Constitutional Court on Friday. Official results showed rival Joko Widodo winning with 53% of the vote, though Prabowo's camp claims irregularities at tens of thousands of polling stations put millions of votes in question. His brother clarified that Prabowo never actually withdrew from the race, despite earlier remarks suggesting otherwise. Meanwhile, international leaders have congratulated Jokowi, who is urging national unity ahead of his October inauguration.

An Australian radio station has pledged at least 500,000 Australian dollars to a memorial fund for Jacintha Saldanha, the nurse who died after a prank call about the Duchess of Cambridge. The station, 2DayFM, faced intense public criticism and advertiser backlash over the hoax, and its owners said all advertising profits through year-end would go to the family. The two DJs involved issued tearful public apologies, saying they never expected the call to be put through. Meanwhile, the hospital treating the duchess set up its own memorial fund, and police investigations into the nurse's death continued.

Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, has been released from a London hospital after being treated for severe morning sickness, and will continue recovering at Kensington Palace. Her hospitalization led to the early public confirmation of her pregnancy, which is still in its early weeks.
