Prince Charles expressed joy at becoming a grandfather and made light of a prank call scandal involving Australian DJs who obtained private health details. The royal baby will be third in line to the throne, and recent succession changes mean gender will not affect the line of succession.

A 16-year-old pregnant leukemia patient in the Dominican Republic died after her chemotherapy was delayed for about 20 days because doctors feared the treatment could harm the fetus, which would violate the country’s strict abortion ban. Her mother says medical officials failed to prioritize her daughter’s life and pleaded for an exception to the law. The teen eventually received treatment but suffered a miscarriage, cardiac arrest, and could not be revived. Her case has intensified national debate over the Dominican Republic’s constitutional protection of life from conception.

The Obama administration has launched a coordinated federal initiative to address the growing threat of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, including an executive order creating a task force to develop a national action plan. A new five-year strategy and advisory council aim to improve surveillance, accelerate research on new antibiotics and diagnostics, and promote alternatives to antibiotics in agriculture. The plan also includes financial incentives, such as a $20 million prize for rapid diagnostic tests, to help combat resistant infections. With thousands of deaths and millions of illnesses linked to drug-resistant germs each year, officials stress that success depends on both developing new treatments and using existing antibiotics more responsibly.

During his first visit to Khartoum since South Sudan’s independence, President Salva Kiir met with Sudanese leader Omar al-Bashir and both agreed to negotiate final settlements on unresolved issues such as borders, oil revenue sharing, security, and the disputed Abyei region. They announced the creation of joint committees with timetables to address these matters. The meeting came amid rising tensions over conflicts in border areas, but both presidents stressed their commitment to peaceful resolution and rejected war as a solution.

In the Philadelphia clergy abuse trial, pretrial arguments centered on whether jurors could hear that a third priest, Edward Avery, pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 10-year-old altar boy, especially if defense attorneys challenge the victim’s credibility. The two remaining defendants—Reverend James Brennan, accused of attempted rape, and Monsignor William Lynn, the first high-ranking church official charged with endangering children by reassigning abusive priests—pleaded not guilty. The judge suggested prosecutors might call Avery to testify and also questioned why more victims had not come forward until recently. Jurors also heard testimony about another former priest’s sexual abuse of a teenager, and prosecutors planned to call Monsignor Kevin Quirk, who oversaw Brennan’s 1996 church trial.

The Church of England will now permit men in civil partnerships to become bishops, provided they remain celibate, as same-sex sexual activity is still considered sinful. This decision extends the existing policy that allows celibate gay priests, while maintaining that clergy must adhere to church teachings on sexuality. Meanwhile, women remain ineligible for the episcopate, as previous efforts to approve female bishops failed. The church continues to define marriage as between a man and a woman and would be barred from conducting same-sex weddings even if Parliament legalizes them.

The article argues that a prolonged Republican primary is beneficial, not harmful, to the party's chances in the general election. It contends that extended contests boost voter engagement and enthusiasm, citing historical examples like the 2008 Democratic race and Ronald Reagan's 1980 nomination to show that drawn-out primaries can strengthen a party's eventual nominee. The piece also suggests that competitive primaries in key states have previously produced stronger Republican candidates and that current GOP enthusiasm is higher than Democratic enthusiasm. Ultimately, it frames the ongoing primary as a way to build momentum and contrast Republican solutions with President Obama's failed policies.

A Primark customer in Northern Ireland discovered a handwritten note hidden in a pair of trousers, allegedly from a Chinese prisoner claiming to work 15-hour days under slave-like conditions. The shopper reported the finding to Amnesty International, which said the claim is disturbing but difficult to verify. Primark denied using forced labor, noting the garment was sold years ago and that inspections of the supplier found no violations, though it has launched an investigation. Similar notes reportedly found in clothing in Wales have also raised concerns, amid broader allegations of forced labor in Chinese detention facilities.

Prime Minister Julia Gillard has announced that Australia’s next federal election will be held in September, much earlier than required, in an effort to end speculation and encourage a more measured national debate. The unusually long lead-up has drawn criticism, with commentators warning that a lengthy campaign could exhaust voters and backfire politically. Gillard’s decision also reflects her political position, as she seeks to maximize the advantages of incumbency while managing internal party tensions and a challenging opposition led by Tony Abbott. The campaign will focus on issues such as taxation, regulation, and individual freedoms.

Mark Shand, the brother of Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall and brother-in-law of Prince Charles, has died in New York from a head injury sustained in a fall. His family, including the Duchess and Prince Charles, expressed deep devastation over the sudden loss. Shand was widely known as the chairman of the Elephant Family conservation charity, where he worked to improve treatment of Asian elephants and combat poaching and habitat destruction. He was also an author whose book inspired a BBC documentary.

Prince Harry and Cressida Bonas have ended their two-year relationship, putting an end to widespread speculation that they were headed for marriage. The split was amicable, and they reportedly remain close friends. Bonas, who felt increasingly uncomfortable with media attention and wanted to pursue her own career, had been under pressure from constant scrutiny and marriage rumors. Harry is expected to attend a friend’s wedding in the U.S., and some observers note that, like Prince William and Kate, the couple could potentially reunite in the future.

Royal analysts have dismissed the latest conspiracy claim that British special forces assassinated Princess Diana, comparing the enduring theories to those surrounding JFK. The allegation, reportedly from a soldier’s in-laws, is being reviewed by London police, though officials stress it is not a formal reinvestigation. Experts point to prior exhaustive inquiries that found no evidence of foul play, attributing the crash to a drunk driver. They also note the timing of the claim, just before the anniversary of Diana’s death and a new film, as proof of her lasting media appeal.

In his first interview since becoming a father, Prince William playfully described baby George as a lively “rascal” who dislikes sleeping, while noting that Catherine has handled most nighttime duties. He admitted he was eager to return to his RAF job partly to catch up on rest, and revealed he had practiced installing the car seat to avoid any mishaps. William also shared that he changed George’s first diaper as a “badge of honor” and hopes to pass on his passion for African wildlife to his son. Above all, he said his family is now his top priority, and parenthood has already changed him emotionally in unexpected ways.

The principal of Danwon High School has been dismissed in connection with the Sewol ferry disaster, though officials did not disclose specific reasons. The school suffered devastating losses when the ferry sank in April, killing 292 people overall, including 244 students and 10 teachers from the school. The removal was delayed because authorities were focused on responding to the tragedy. Earlier, the school’s vice principal, who survived the sinking, had died by suicide, expressing guilt over surviving while so many perished.

The U.S. is quietly pursuing diplomatic efforts to secure the release of Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, the only American soldier held captive in Afghanistan, as his health declines and the troop withdrawal deadline approaches. These sensitive talks, conducted through intermediaries, create tension between the longstanding policy of not negotiating with terrorists and the military’s commitment to leave no soldier behind. A major obstacle is the Taliban’s demand for the release of Guantanamo Bay detainees, which faces resistance in Congress and concerns that such a trade could encourage future captures. While officials deny active negotiations, they acknowledge that a prisoner exchange may be the only viable option before the window for rescue closes.

The deadly assault on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi is believed to have been a pre-planned military-style attack carried out by roughly two dozen militants, likely from the al Qaeda-linked Imprisoned Omar Abdul Rahman Brigades. The group had previously claimed attacks on the consulate and other Western targets in eastern Libya, and the assault came shortly after al Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri urged followers to avenge the death of senior militant Abu Yahya al-Libi. U.S. and Libyan sources suggest the attackers used a protest as cover, though the ambassador was probably not specifically targeted. The incident highlights al Qaeda's growing foothold in eastern Libya, where jihadist and Salafist groups have exploited the security vacuum since the fall of Moammar al-Gadhafi.

Louis Freeh’s internal review of Penn State’s handling of the Sandusky scandal is focusing on how Joe Paterno used his influence to keep player discipline and misconduct within the football program, away from public view. Emails show Paterno insisted on being the sole authority over player punishments and resisted involving campus officials, while a former student affairs administrator described his behavior as manipulative and abusive. Investigators are also examining whether Paterno’s preference for handling matters internally affected the decision not to report the 2001 shower incident involving Sandusky to authorities. The review suggests this culture of secrecy may have enabled Sandusky’s abuse to continue.

Raffaele Sollecito, convicted alongside Amanda Knox for Meredith Kercher's murder, saw his acquittal overturned when Italy's highest court ordered a retrial, reigniting what he described as a nightmare. He consistently maintained his innocence, calling the charges baseless and the prosecution's key evidence an illusion. In his memoir, he admitted to poor decisions, including smoking marijuana and trusting police, while expressing a deep desire to be forgotten and live a normal life. The retrial, he said, meant his life remained a living hell.

Palm oil, produced mainly by Malaysia and Indonesia, is a hugely profitable ingredient in countless consumer goods, as highlighted by a major Malaysian company’s successful stock market debut. However, environmental groups warn that the industry drives severe deforestation, especially of carbon-rich peatlands, which releases large amounts of greenhouse gases and destroys wildlife habitats. While consumer pressure has led some companies to adopt more sustainable practices, and Indonesia has introduced a deforestation moratorium, the industry remains controversial. Supporters note that palm oil also plays a significant economic role, lifting rural incomes and contributing substantially to national GDP.

Uyghur economist Ilham Tohti went on trial in Xinjiang on charges of separatism, nine months after his detention, with his lawyers saying he denies the allegations and has long advocated peaceful dialogue and ethnic harmony. The trial took place under heavy security, and rights groups expressed concern that prosecuting a peaceful critic could worsen ethnic tensions in the region. The case unfolds against a backdrop of recurring violence in Xinjiang, which Beijing attributes to Uyghur separatists, and a broader government crackdown on dissent.

The World Health Organization has proposed stricter sugar limits, recommending that added and free sugars make up less than 5 percent of daily calories, down from the previous 10 percent guideline. This change responds to rising concerns that excess sugar, especially in sweetened drinks and processed foods, contributes to obesity, chronic disease, and dental problems. Most Americans consume far more than the suggested amount, often without realizing it because sugar is hidden in everyday products like bread, soup, and yogurt. To help consumers, the FDA has proposed updating nutrition labels to clearly list added sugars, and the WHO is accepting public comments on the draft until the end of March.

Pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine have rejected President Vladimir Putin’s request to postpone their planned May 11 referendum on greater autonomy, insisting they will proceed with the vote. The European Union condemned the move as illegitimate and warned it could escalate the crisis, while Ukraine’s interim government said it would only talk with those not involved in violence. Meanwhile, NATO and the White House said there was no evidence that Russia had withdrawn troops from Ukraine’s border, despite Moscow’s claims. The situation remains tense amid ongoing clashes, and a new poll shows most Ukrainians, including in the east, still favor keeping the country unified.

Ukraine’s acting government issued a deadline for Crimea’s pro-Russian leaders to release hostages, but it passed without action after armed supporters stormed the Ukrainian navy headquarters in Sevastopol and detained its commander. In response, Kyiv announced new measures against Russia, including a visa regime, plans to leave the Commonwealth of Independent States, and preparations to evacuate military personnel if Crimea is designated a demilitarized zone. NATO warned that Russia’s actions in Crimea could be part of a broader strategy that might extend into eastern Ukraine, while the U.N. chief prepared to visit both Russia and Ukraine to push for a peaceful resolution. Meanwhile, Russia moved forward with formal steps to annex Crimea, despite international condemnation and sanctions.

The CEO of the ferry company whose vessel sank off South Korea last month has been arrested on charges of negligence and violating maritime safety laws. Investigators allege that the ferry was carrying more than twice its legal cargo limit and that poorly secured cargo caused it to capsize. The company had reportedly operated the ferry with excess cargo on 139 prior trips, earning millions in additional profits. The disaster killed at least 269 people, with dozens more still missing.

Los Angeles County sheriff’s investigators have formally recommended that prosecutors charge Justin Bieber with felony vandalism for allegedly throwing eggs at a neighbor’s home in January, causing about $20,000 in damage. The district attorney’s office said no charging decision will be made this week. A felony charge would require Bieber to appear in court, whereas a misdemeanor could be handled by his lawyer. The singer is also facing separate misdemeanor charges in Miami Beach and Toronto.

California’s attorney general has formally opposed Sirhan Sirhan’s latest bid for freedom, arguing that the evidence against him remains overwhelming. While conceding that his lawyers may show a second gun was fired, she contends that this does not prove his innocence or undermine his conviction. She also dismissed the defense’s claim that Sirhan was hypno-programmed into acting as a diversion, calling that theory speculative and not widely accepted. The filing maintains that even if another shooter was involved, Sirhan could still be held legally responsible under California law.

Prosecutors allege that Aaron Hernandez used coded language during jailhouse phone calls to discuss the killing of Odin Lloyd, and they have requested access to those recordings and visitor logs. The defense has opposed the move, calling it an unjustified “fishing expedition.” Court filings also note that Hernandez’s fiancée and cousin, both charged as accessories, visited him in jail. Authorities believe Hernandez was involved in Lloyd’s murder, and surveillance footage reportedly shows him with a gun shortly after the crime.

Authorities are asking tattoo artists who may have worked on Aaron Hernandez between early 2012 and mid-2013 to come forward, hoping the tattoos could yield evidence in the 2012 killings of two Boston men. The former NFL player faces first-degree murder charges in that case, while already jailed for the separate 2013 murder of Odin Lloyd. Investigators are keeping the specific tattoos confidential to avoid tainting potential statements, and the artists are treated as witnesses, not suspects. Hernandez also faces additional charges related to shots fired at three other people during the 2012 attack.

Prosecutors revealed that the Boston Marathon bombs were built using Christmas lights as fuses, model-car parts for remote detonation, and powder from hundreds of fireworks, suggesting the suspects had training or help. The court filing also included a note allegedly written by Dzhokhar Tsarnaev while hiding in a boat, in which he sought to justify the attack. Much of the document focuses on the legal fight over his hospital interrogation, with prosecutors arguing it was necessary due to possible accomplices and ongoing public danger, while defense lawyers claim he was coerced and denied his rights.

The EPA has issued a landmark rule imposing the first federal limits on mercury and other toxic air pollutants from coal- and oil-fired power plants. Agency analyses indicate the health benefits far outweigh compliance costs, with projections of thousands of prevented premature deaths, heart attacks, and childhood respiratory illnesses. The rule has drawn opposition from industry and Republican lawmakers concerned about higher electricity bills and plant retirements, while supporters call it a historic public health achievement. The regulation culminates a lengthy policy battle that spanned multiple administrations and reversed an earlier Bush-era decision to use a cap-and-trade approach instead of direct emissions limits.

Protesters in Ukraine and Venezuela are using the walkie-talkie app Zello to coordinate demonstrations privately, avoiding public social media. In Venezuela, the app reportedly stopped working on the state-run ISP, leading Zello to suspect government interference and to release an update designed to bypass the block. Venezuelan authorities have denied involvement, while users are turning to VPNs to circumvent restrictions. The situation highlights how governments can target communication tools and how developers and citizens adapt to evade such measures.

In central Cairo, demonstrators clashed with police near Tahrir Square, throwing Molotov cocktails as officers responded with similar force. The protesters denounced both the current government and the Muslim Brotherhood, accusing them of continuing the repressive tactics of ousted leader Hosni Mubarak. The unrest coincided with the anniversary of deadly street battles that killed dozens the previous year, for which no one has been held accountable. No immediate injuries were reported in the latest violence.

Thai anti-government demonstrators managed to disrupt Sunday’s national vote in a Bangkok district by blocking access to ballot boxes, forcing a delay for tens of thousands of voters. The standoff followed a violent clash in which gunmen opened fire near protesters and police, leaving several people wounded. The protests are part of a long-running campaign against Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra, whose party is expected to win the election despite the opposition’s rejection of the vote. The ongoing political turmoil has raised fears of instability, damaging Thailand’s tourism and investment climate.

In Sao Paulo, thousands clashed with riot police during a protest against a public transit fare hike, with officers using tear gas and rubber bullets. The demonstration, held exactly one year before the World Cup, resulted in over 100 injuries and more than 120 arrests. It was part of a broader wave of protests across Brazilian cities, where demonstrators accused police of excessive force and said no warning preceded the crackdown. The fare increase, from 3 to 3.20 reais, was described by many protesters as the breaking point amid rising costs.

Canadian authorities are preparing for possible protests at an event near Vancouver where former U.S. presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton are speaking. Amnesty International has urged Canada to arrest Bush over alleged war crimes related to enhanced interrogation techniques, though it acknowledged the challenge. Activists have also promoted an "Occupy Surrey" protest similar to the Occupy Wall Street demonstrations. Canadian officials have dismissed the arrest call, with the immigration minister accusing Amnesty of ideological cherry-picking.

Psy’s latest single “Hangover,” featuring Snoop Dogg, has gained over 31 million YouTube views in just three days, though it trails the explosive records set by his earlier hits “Gangnam Style” and “Gentleman.” The music video, filmed near Incheon to fit Snoop’s tight 18-hour schedule, shows the duo on a drunken, traditional Korean escapade involving drinking games, a bathhouse, karaoke, and an amusement park. Psy explained that he requested the collaboration through manager Scooter Braun, co-directed the video to give it a fresh feel, and praised Snoop for his professionalism during the demanding shoot. He also promoted the song on “Jimmy Kimmel Live” and teased an upcoming EP, with the lead single “Daddy” expected this summer.

Pulitzer Prize-winning author Oscar Hijuelos passed away at age 62 due to sudden cardiac arrest. He made history as the first Latino writer to win the fiction Pulitzer for his 1989 novel *The Mambo Kings Play Songs of Love*, a work he felt gave him creative freedom and helped open publishing doors for other Latino authors. His early years included a serious childhood illness that shaped his recurring themes of identity and belonging. He also wrote several other notable novels, including *Empress of the Splendid Season* and *The Fourteen Sisters of Emilio Montez O'Brien*.

The FDA has announced a preliminary decision to revoke the generally recognized as safe status of partially hydrogenated oils, the main source of artificial trans fats, which could eventually lead to a ban on their use in processed foods. These fats, linked to higher heart disease risk, have already been largely reduced by manufacturers and some local regulations, but the FDA says consumption still poses a public health concern. The agency has opened a comment period to gather input on how quickly food companies could phase out these ingredients if the rule is finalized. Health organizations have praised the move, noting that eliminating artificial trans fats could prevent thousands of heart attacks and deaths each year.

President Obama and Vladimir Putin spoke by phone amid escalating tensions over Ukraine, with Obama urging Russia to withdraw troops from the border and engage directly with Kyiv to de-escalate the crisis. The call came as Russia rejected a UN General Assembly resolution declaring Crimea's secession referendum invalid, while Western officials warned of a significant Russian military buildup near Ukraine. Meanwhile, ousted Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych resurfaced to call for regional referendums, and Yulia Tymoshenko announced her presidential run as the IMF offered Ukraine a multibillion-dollar bailout to stave off bankruptcy. The situation remained fraught, with fears of further Russian incursions into eastern Ukraine despite international sanctions and diplomatic efforts.

Ukraine has launched its first formal military operation against pro-Russian separatists in the east, retaking an airport after an ultimatum for militants to disarm expired. In response, Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that Ukraine is on the brink of civil war, echoing concerns from Russian officials about the government's actions. The escalation has deepened international alarm, with NATO and the EU urging Russia to pull back troops and help de-escalate the crisis. Diplomatic efforts are now focused on upcoming four-way talks in Geneva aimed at reducing tensions.

Vladimir Putin was inaugurated for a new presidential term amid heavy security and protests, after an election that international observers and opposition figures said was marred by fraud. He quickly nominated Dmitry Medvedev, his predecessor and ally, for prime minister. Under constitutional changes, Putin’s new six-year term could allow him to stay in power until 2024, longer than any Soviet-era leader since Stalin. Meanwhile, police arrested hundreds of demonstrators, including prominent opposition leaders, after anti-Putin rallies turned violent.

President Vladimir Putin announced he intends to pardon jailed former oil tycoon Mikhail Khodorkovsky, citing a personal appeal from Khodorkovsky and humanitarian reasons, including his mother’s illness. The move comes shortly after Russian lawmakers approved a broad amnesty and as international attention focuses on Russia’s human rights record ahead of the Sochi Winter Olympics. Khodorkovsky, imprisoned since 2003, has long maintained his prosecution was politically motivated. His son expressed skepticism, saying he had not confirmed the report and noting that dealings with Putin are often personal.

President Putin questioned the logic of Western nations supplying arms to Syrian rebels, warning that such weapons could end up with extremist groups like al-Qaeda’s affiliate, Jabhat al-Nusra. He reiterated his stance that only a Syrian-led political dialogue can ensure a lasting solution, while rebels claimed to have received heavy weapons from supportive nations. The remarks highlighted ongoing tensions at the G8, where Putin remained the sole backer of President Assad. Separately, Putin outlined Russian plans to boost economic growth and curb tax evasion, while German Chancellor Merkel expressed concern over Turkey’s EU bid amid its crackdown on protesters.

President Vladimir Putin indicated that Edward Snowden may be softening his stance on Russia’s conditions for asylum, noting that his recent statements suggest a shift, though the outcome remains uncertain. Snowden, who is seeking temporary asylum in Russia while hoping to reach Latin America, has reportedly said he no longer intends to harm U.S. interests. Putin also claimed that the United States effectively trapped Snowden in Moscow by revoking his passport, leaving him unable to travel. Meanwhile, journalist Glenn Greenwald warned that Snowden still holds sensitive documents that could be a major embarrassment to the U.S. government if released.

Qatar’s 2022 World Cup organizers have issued an updated workers’ charter in response to criticism over migrant labor conditions, claiming tangible progress and citing consultations with the International Labour Organization. While they highlight improved wages, accommodation, and inspections, human rights groups remain skeptical, noting that the kafala system—which restricts workers’ freedom to change jobs or leave the country—has not been reformed. The response follows pressure from FIFA and damning reports of abuse and high construction fatalities, with critics urging that protections apply to all migrant workers, not just those on World Cup projects. Separately, FIFA is still weighing whether to move the tournament to winter due to Qatar’s extreme summer heat.

Qatar’s preparations for the 2022 World Cup remain clouded by allegations of severe mistreatment of migrant workers, including claims of forced labor, unsafe conditions, and preventable deaths. A senior Qatari official rejected the “slave state” label as outrageous, while acknowledging that labor protections are still being developed and enforced in a rapidly growing nation. Labor unions and rights groups warn that thousands of workers could die before the tournament unless international pressure forces meaningful change. FIFA is now expected to address worker rights and the possibility of moving the event to cooler months.

FIFA has given Qatar a February 12 deadline to submit a detailed plan showing concrete steps to improve migrant workers' conditions on World Cup construction projects. The demand follows an Amnesty International report exposing widespread abuses, which FIFA President Sepp Blatter called unacceptable. FIFA official Theo Zwanziger is overseeing the monitoring process and has consulted human rights groups, with updates expected at upcoming meetings. Separately, FIFA is still weighing whether to move the 2022 tournament to winter due to Qatar's extreme summer heat.

Qatar’s 2022 World Cup organizers remain open to moving the tournament to winter if the international football community reaches a consensus, despite their original plan to host in summer. Concerns about extreme heat have fueled discussions, with UEFA president Michel Platini backing a November-December schedule to avoid disruption and conflicts with the Winter Olympics. The event’s awarding to Qatar has also been clouded by controversy, including allegations of corruption and concerns over the country’s treatment of gay fans.

Amid ongoing controversy over Qatar hosting the 2022 World Cup, former FIFA governance insider Alexandra Wrage has called for a fresh vote, arguing that only a rerun can restore trust in the selection process. She points to persistent corruption allegations, the unresolved question of moving the tournament to winter, and concerns over migrant workers' conditions as key issues. Wrage also criticizes FIFA for lacking transparency and resisting meaningful reform, though she doubts a new vote will actually happen. Her remarks come as FIFA faces renewed scrutiny from ethics investigations and fresh media reports of financial dealings tied to the original bid.

A powerful earthquake near the Iran-Pakistan border has killed at least 34 people and injured 80 others in Pakistan, where rescue operations involving military and paramilitary forces are underway. In Iran, officials initially reported casualties but later clarified that no deaths occurred, though about a dozen people were injured and treated. The quake, measured around magnitude 7.8, struck a rural and sparsely populated area, prompting a state of emergency in Iran's Saravan region. Widespread tremors were felt across southern Pakistan and as far as Abu Dhabi, but no damage was reported at Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant.

Zara Tindall, Queen Elizabeth II’s granddaughter, is expecting her first child with her husband, former England rugby captain Mike Tindall. The baby will be the Queen’s fourth great-grandchild, joining the children of Zara’s brother Peter Phillips and the upcoming child of Prince William and Catherine. Zara, an Olympic equestrian medalist, plans to compete in the 2016 Rio Games. The palace also confirmed that Prince William and Catherine’s baby will be styled as a royal prince or princess of Cambridge.

A week after Staff Sgt. Robert Bales allegedly killed 16 Afghan villagers, anger and grief persist in Afghanistan while Bales is held in pretrial confinement at Fort Leavenworth. His defense team says his family is shocked but stands by him, describing him as a devoted husband and experienced soldier. Bales had multiple combat deployments, suffered injuries including a brain trauma, and had a prior dismissed assault charge. Afghan villagers are demanding he be tried in Afghanistan, and President Hamid Karzai warned that the incident has pushed U.S.-Afghan relations to a breaking point.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton is set to testify publicly before congressional committees about the 2012 Benghazi attack that killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Lawmakers are expected to press her on State Department security failures, the administration’s shifting public account of the assault, and whether warnings about militant threats were properly handled. The testimony comes after an independent review found systemic management and security deficiencies, and after criticism of U.N. Ambassador Susan Rice’s initial explanations, which were later attributed to flawed intelligence. Despite the political controversy, Clinton’s public approval ratings have remained strong as she faces what is likely to be one of her most difficult appearances as secretary of state.

A parliamentary report has concluded that racism remains a serious issue in English football, despite notable improvements in the sport’s overall atmosphere. It points to recent high-profile incidents involving players such as Luis Suárez and John Terry as evidence that more work is needed. The report urges the Football Association to take a stronger lead by improving steward training, addressing abuse at grassroots level, tackling homophobia, and increasing diversity among coaches and referees. The FA and other football bodies acknowledged the findings and reaffirmed their commitment to fighting discrimination across the game.

Radical cleric Abu Qatada has been freed on bail in the UK after winning an appeal against deportation to Jordan, where he faces terrorism charges. British authorities have long sought to remove him over allegations that he funded terrorist groups and inspired figures linked to the 9/11 attacks, though he denies the accusations. The UK government expressed strong disagreement with the ruling, saying it had secured assurances about fair legal proceedings in Jordan, and announced plans to appeal.

Rafael Nadal secured his first Cincinnati Masters title by defeating John Isner in two tight tiebreak sets, extending his hard-court winning streak to 15 matches. The victory marked his second consecutive Masters 1000 title and lifted him to world No. 2, pushing Andy Murray down to third ahead of the U.S. Open. In the women’s final, Victoria Azarenka came from a set down to beat top seed Serena Williams, earning a significant confidence boost before the season’s final Grand Slam.

Rafael Nadal claimed the Madrid Open title after Kei Nishikori retired in the third set due to a back injury, with Nadal leading after recovering from a first-set loss. Nishikori had struggled with the injury since his semifinal and, despite his disappointment, was set to break into the world’s top 10 for the first time. In the women’s final, Maria Sharapova staged a comeback after a poor start to beat Simona Halep in three sets, securing her latest clay-court title.

Tropical rainforests in countries like Brazil and Indonesia are being protected for their immense biodiversity, though scientists still do not know exactly how many species depend on them. These ecosystems are ancient and have supported uninterrupted evolution, with some areas, such as Ecuador’s Yasuni National Park, containing extraordinary numbers of species in very small spaces. New species continue to be discovered regularly, highlighting how much remains unknown. Beyond wildlife, rainforests provide essential resources, including food, water, medicine, and thousands of commercial products, while also serving as homes to indigenous peoples.

Jane Jeong Trenka, adopted from Korea as an infant, later learned her adoption was built on false documents that concealed her poor health and misled her birth mother. Her experience reflects South Korea’s long history of sending over 200,000 children abroad, a practice now being challenged by returning adoptees. Trenka and other activists helped pass a 2012 law that discourages overseas adoption, requires verified maternal consent, and allows mothers to revoke decisions, though some adoptees like Steve Choi Morrison defend international adoption and oppose parts of the law. The movement continues, with activists now pushing for better support for single mothers in South Korea.

Senator Rand Paul sharply criticized President Obama at the Values Voter Summit, accusing him of acting like a king and ignoring the Constitution through unilateral executive actions. He specifically condemned the president for launching airstrikes against ISIS without first seeking congressional authorization, calling such behavior illegal and arrogant. Paul also addressed social conservatives by urging a return to traditional values and faith, describing America as facing a spiritual crisis. His remarks blended political attacks with a call for national moral renewal.

Veteran New York Democrat Charlie Rangel narrowly fended off state Senator Adriano Espaillat in a competitive House primary, likely securing his final re-election bid. In Mississippi, Republican Senator Thad Cochran survived a tea party challenge from Chris McDaniel, aided by Democratic and African-American voters in the runoff. Elsewhere, James Lankford won Oklahoma’s Senate primary, Anthony Brown clinched Maryland’s Democratic gubernatorial nomination, Bob Beauprez won Colorado’s GOP gubernatorial primary, and Curt Clawson took Florida’s special House election.

Sister Somalia, founded by Fartuun Adan, is the first rape crisis center in Somalia, offering medical care, counseling, and emotional support to survivors of sexual violence. Adan returned to her war-torn homeland after years in Canada, risking her safety to help women and children who faced widespread rape in displacement camps. Despite threats and deep social stigma, she persisted and was honored with the U.S. Secretary of State’s International Women of Courage Award. With a new government acknowledging the issue, Adan remains hopeful for a future where Somali women can live in peace and dignity.

The article highlights the widespread use of rape and sexual violence as a weapon of war in Syria, describing common patterns such as assaults at checkpoints and the deliberate destruction of families. It emphasizes the severe cultural consequences for survivors, including honor killings, forced marriages, and suicide, which compound the trauma. The author’s organization is documenting these incidents on a live map to preserve evidence for future war crimes trials, though many victims are killed or die after attacks. The piece calls on the international community to support survivors and Syrian civil society, and to push for accountability through the International Criminal Court.

Remote camera traps in a Vietnamese forest reserve have captured images of a live saola, one of the world’s rarest large mammals, often called the “Asian unicorn.” The species, which resembles an antelope but is related to cattle, had not been seen in the wild in Vietnam since 1998. Conservationists hailed the sighting as a historic breakthrough and evidence that protection efforts are working. They also noted that saolas remain threatened by wire snares set for other wildlife, though forest patrols have removed tens of thousands of traps in recent years.

The Turin Shroud was shown on Italian television for only the second time in history, an appearance authorized by former Pope Benedict XVI before he stepped down. The broadcast included a video message from Pope Francis, who reflected on the shroud’s image as a symbol of both suffering and peace. While many Christians revere it as Christ’s burial cloth, scholars and even the Catholic Church acknowledge its authenticity is uncertain, with carbon dating pointing to the Middle Ages. A new app offering a high-definition view of the shroud was also launched, alongside renewed scientific claims that the cloth may date to Jesus’ era, though those findings remain disputed.

The Baltimore Ravens cut running back Ray Rice and the NFL suspended him indefinitely after new surveillance footage emerged showing him punching his then-fiancée in an elevator. League officials, including Commissioner Roger Goodell, said they had not seen the video before it was released publicly, prompting Goodell to replace his earlier two-game suspension with a harsher penalty. The incident also drew sharp criticism of the criminal justice system for allowing Rice to avoid prosecution through a pretrial program. In response to the backlash, the NFL announced a new policy imposing a six-game suspension for domestic violence offenses, with a lifetime ban for a second violation.

Teresa and Joe Giudice, stars of “Real Housewives of New Jersey,” were sentenced in federal court for fraud-related charges they had pleaded guilty to. Joe received 41 months in prison, while Teresa received 15 months, along with forfeiture and fines. Their sentences will be staggered so one parent can care for their four daughters. Additionally, Joe, who is not a U.S. citizen, may face deportation after completing his prison term.

The article examines common questions about artificial sweeteners, explaining that they vary in chemical makeup and are perceived as sweeter than sugar in smaller amounts. It notes that current evidence does not show they cause cancer in humans, despite past rat studies using extremely high doses. While they offer a calorie-free alternative that may aid weight loss, some research suggests diet drinks could confuse the body’s response to real sugar, and excessive intake of certain sweeteners may cause digestive issues. Overall, experts advise moderation and emphasize that a healthy diet with limited sweeteners of any kind is best.

Sean Sasser, known for his groundbreaking same-sex relationship with AIDS activist Pedro Zamora on MTV’s “The Real World: San Francisco,” has died at age 44. He passed away from mesothelioma, a rare cancer diagnosed only a month earlier, after living with HIV for 25 years. Their televised commitment ceremony in 1994 was a historic moment that introduced many young viewers to a gay couple affected by HIV. Sasser continued working as an AIDS educator and activist until his death, and his passing prompted widespread tributes for his legacy of courage and visibility.

The head of the Free Syrian Army claimed that Syrian government forces are moving chemical weapons into Lebanon and Iraq, though these assertions could not be independently verified and were denied by Iraq and questioned by Israeli officials. If true, such movement could challenge previous U.S. intelligence assumptions about the regime's control over its stockpile. The rebel commander also said he discussed the situation with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry, who indicated that the threat of military strikes remains if Syria is not honest in disarmament efforts. Additionally, while the opposition is receiving some U.S. support, the commander expressed doubts that the regime will allow international inspectors to fully dismantle its chemical arsenal, noting that conventional weapons remain the larger cause of casualties.

Shiite Houthi rebels have seized a key tribal stronghold in northern Yemen’s Amran province after intense fighting, forcing the Sunni Hashid tribe to withdraw and regroup. The assault involved heavy artillery and hundreds of reinforcements, leaving dozens dead in recent clashes. Yemen’s president has sent a committee to negotiate a cease-fire as the conflict has killed at least 240 people since January. Separately, a German national was kidnapped in Sanaa, highlighting the country’s growing instability and dangers for foreigners.

General Motors faces intense criticism after delaying recalls affecting millions of vehicles due to faulty ignition switches and power steering issues, with the CEO apologizing for related deaths. The company’s troubles are compounded by a history of missed opportunities and weak global performance compared to rivals, despite a costly government bailout. Long-standing strategic failures, such as abandoning early electric vehicle development and mishandling brands, have left GM struggling with its image and competitiveness. The article suggests that foreign ownership might bring the fresh management and vision needed to run the company effectively.

The Justice Department announced that Google will pay a record $500 million civil penalty for profiting from illegal online prescription drug sales, despite being alerted to the issue as early as 2003. The government said Google allowed U.S. customers to be targeted by online pharmacies that often required no real prescription and charged extra for online consultations. The penalty followed a three-year investigation and was among the largest ever paid by a private company. Of the total, $230 million will go to Rhode Island police departments, with the remainder placed in a Justice Department fund.

In Colorado, where recreational marijuana is legal under state law but still federally prohibited, the Andrews family operates a cash-only pot shop in Denver, navigating banking restrictions and regulatory hurdles. On opening day, their store saw overwhelming demand, with sales reaching $10,000 in just hours and nearly 1,000 customers served, far exceeding expectations. The article highlights the broader "green rush," projecting a $208 million recreational market in Colorado this year and rapid national growth, while noting the family's transition from medical to recreational cannabis and their plans to expand. Despite the chaos, the family remains optimistic about the business's future, even as they adapt to intense demand and ongoing legal complexities.

Vietnam’s dramatic reduction in poverty and hunger shows that strong political commitment and targeted investment in small-scale family farming can be highly effective. Oxfam highlights smallholder agriculture as one of the most reliable paths out of poverty, with successful examples including fair-trade cooperatives in Malawi, a women-led farming initiative in South Sudan, and a Haitian tree-planting cooperative that boosted yields and provided loans. These efforts help farmers gain skills, access markets, and improve their livelihoods, even amid conflict or environmental damage. While progress is promising, Oxfam stresses that such initiatives must be expanded so the world’s poorest farmers can fully benefit.

The official count of Syrian refugees exceeds 500,000, but aid workers say the real number is far higher because many refugees avoid registering out of fear and distrust of officialdom. Some are also deterred by pride, finding it difficult to accept aid after being self-sufficient. The majority live outside camps in crowded urban areas, where they face soaring rents, eviction, and harsh winter conditions without adequate supplies. Aid agencies are struggling to locate and assist these unregistered refugees, whose needs are growing more urgent as the conflict continues.

The conflict in Syria has internally displaced millions, with the U.N. estimating that 4.25 million people are now homeless within the country, about half of them children. Many families have been forced to flee repeatedly after their homes were bombed, leaving them without shelter, food, or medical care. Syria’s healthcare system has been devastated—more than half of its hospitals are damaged or non-operational—and many doctors have fled, making treatment nearly impossible for the injured, including children with severe burns. Aid groups are struggling to deliver relief under dangerous conditions, and the U.N. is pressing for cross-border access and humanitarian pauses to meet the urgent needs of millions.

Federal regulators have approved a new flu vaccine called Flublok, which is produced using insect cells rather than eggs or live influenza virus. This manufacturing method allows for faster production, which could be crucial during a pandemic. The vaccine is approved for adults aged 18 to 49 and offers protection against three flu strains, with an overall effectiveness of about 44.6% against circulating viruses. It will be in limited supply this winter but more widely available next flu season.

A 15-year-old American boy from Florida, Tariq Khdeir, was filmed being beaten and detained by Israeli security forces in Jerusalem, where he was visiting relatives after his Palestinian cousin was killed. His family says he was not involved in clashes and has demanded his release, expressing concern over his treatment and medical care. Israeli authorities have distanced themselves from the incident and announced an investigation, while the U.S. State Department called for a transparent inquiry and accountability. The case has heightened tensions already inflamed by the deaths of Israeli and Palestinian teenagers.

The decades-old sexual abuse allegation against Woody Allen has resurfaced, with his adopted daughter Dylan Farrow publicly repeating her claim that he assaulted her as a child. Her brother Moses Farrow has sided with Allen, alleging their mother, Mia Farrow, manipulated the children and coached Dylan into making false accusations. Ronan Farrow, another sibling, has publicly supported Dylan, while Allen’s lawyer maintains that past investigations cleared him and that Dylan may be acting on implanted memories. The dispute has reopened bitter divisions within the family over the truth of the allegations.

The article highlights how painful memories of Ireland’s sectarian conflict still surface in public life. During his presidential campaign, Martin McGuinness was publicly challenged by a man whose father, a soldier, was killed by the IRA in 1983; McGuinness denied knowing who was responsible and rejected claims he had been on the IRA’s ruling council. Meanwhile, the family of murdered Belfast lawyer Pat Finucane met with Prime Minister David Cameron to renew their demand for a public inquiry, insisting the British state colluded in his killing. The piece underscores that while Northern Ireland’s peace process has moved forward, unresolved cases and old wounds continue to threaten reconciliation.

Rep. Bill Young of Florida, the longest-serving Republican in the U.S. House, died Friday at age 82 due to complications from a chronic injury. The 22-term congressman had just announced his retirement, expressing frustration with partisan gridlock and excessive politics in Congress. First elected in 1970, he served more than four decades in the House and was widely respected for his expertise on defense and his leadership on the Appropriations Committee. His death came shortly after his family said he was gravely ill.

Al Qaeda’s North African branch has reportedly executed a French hostage in Mali, saying the killing was retaliation for France’s military campaign there. The group also warned that French President François Hollande is accountable for the fate of six remaining French captives. France has denied any ransom negotiations, while reaffirming that it is working to secure the hostages’ release. The crisis stems from France’s intervention in Mali after Islamist militants seized territory in the north and threatened to advance on the capital.

The article reveals that former FBI agent Bob Levinson, who vanished in Iran in 2007, was actually on an unofficial CIA mission at the time, contradicting years of official denials that he was there on private business. The Associated Press and Washington Post reported that the CIA concealed his role, leading to internal fallout, firings, and a $2.5 million settlement with his family. His family has criticized the U.S. government for failing to prioritize his rescue, while officials defended their efforts and expressed regret over the story's publication. Levinson's current fate remains unknown, though U.S. sources believe he is alive and likely held by Iranian authorities.

Former Manchester United footballer Eric Cantona was arrested and given a police caution in London on suspicion of common assault. Authorities confirmed the incident involved a man in his mid-40s, and the alleged victim did not need medical treatment. Accepting a caution means admitting the offense, though it is not a criminal conviction. Cantona, now 47, retired from football at 30 and remains a celebrated figure at Manchester United.

Chechen militant leader Doku Umarov, long one of Russia’s most wanted figures, has reportedly died, according to a jihadist website, which named Ali Abu Mohammed as his successor. The claim remains unverified, and no details were given about the circumstances of his death. Umarov led the Caucasus Emirate and was linked to multiple deadly attacks, including the Moscow airport and subway bombings, as well as the Nevsky Express train bombing. He had also urged his followers to disrupt the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi.

A new risk assessment warns that within 12 years, countries facing high or extreme climate vulnerability could account for nearly a third of global economic output, with their combined GDP projected to triple by 2025. The report identifies Bangladesh, along with several Asian cities such as Mumbai, Manila, Kolkata, and Bangkok, as being at greatest risk, despite their strong economic growth potential. Many African and Southeast Asian nations are also highly exposed due to poverty, weak infrastructure, and reliance on agriculture. Experts say the findings underscore the urgent need for a binding global climate agreement to prevent devastating economic and social consequences.

Human Rights Watch has documented a systematic policy of torture by the Syrian government, describing a network of at least 27 detention centers run by intelligence agencies to crush dissent. The report, based on testimony from former prisoners and defectors, details brutal methods such as beatings, electrocution, and mutilation, with victims including children and the elderly. Activists have collected the names of about 25,000 detainees, though the true scale remains unknown. The organization is urging the U.N. Security Council to refer Syrian officials to the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity.

A knife- and axe-wielding mob attacked civilians, a police station, and government buildings in Xinjiang, China, in what authorities described as an organized and premeditated terrorist assault. Police fatally shot dozens of the attackers, and numerous vehicles were damaged or set on fire. The violence occurred in a county that has seen previous attacks, adding to a series of deadly incidents across the region in recent months. The unrest reflects longstanding tensions between Uyghur Muslims and the Han Chinese majority, with Uyghurs alleging discrimination and harsh treatment.

Amnesty International has denounced a reported Saudi Arabian court ruling that would paralyze a man as punishment for causing paralysis in another person, calling the sentence torture and urging that it never be carried out. The case involves Ali Al-Khawahir, who was reportedly 14 when he stabbed and paralyzed his friend a decade ago, and has been ordered to pay roughly $266,000 in compensation to avoid the punishment. Amnesty noted that such retribution falls under Saudi Arabia’s qisas system, which can also include eye-gouging or execution, and argued the sentence would violate the UN Convention against Torture. The reports remain unverified, and Saudi authorities have not commented on the case.

Egyptian security forces are ramping up efforts in North Sinai to locate and free two American tourists and their Egyptian guide who were abducted on Friday. The kidnappers are demanding the release of a relative held by Egyptian authorities on drug charges. One of the hostages is a diabetic pastor from Massachusetts, and his family has appealed for prayers while expressing confidence in the ongoing negotiations. The abduction is part of a broader pattern of such incidents in the region since the 2011 uprising.

Aaron Hernandez, the former NFL player awaiting trial for murder, wrote a letter to a supporter insisting he is innocent and predicting that those who doubted him will regret it. The letter, which he asked not be shared publicly, was sold by the fan to a memorabilia shop and then to TMZ for $18,000. The fan said he sold it to show support and give Hernandez a chance to be heard, while still expressing sympathy for the victim’s family. Authorities confirmed the letter came from the jail, though they could not verify Hernandez’s handwriting.

The body of former Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Jovan Belcher was exhumed so his brain could be examined for signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease linked to repeated head hits. Belcher’s family hopes the tests will explain why he killed his girlfriend and then himself in 2012. CTE can only be confirmed after death, and experts note that brain tissue may have deteriorated during the year he was buried. The case highlights broader concerns about brain damage in football, which led the NFL to settle a concussion lawsuit for $765 million.

Iranian officials announced the arrest of an alleged MI6 agent in Kerman province, claiming the suspect had confessed after multiple meetings with British intelligence both inside and outside Iran. Britain declined to comment on the matter. The announcement came amid a cautious thaw in UK-Iran relations, including a recent visit by an Iranian envoy to Britain. Separately, the article notes fresh reports that a former FBI agent who disappeared in Iran in 2007 may have been working for the CIA, though officials and his family deny this.

Iran marked progress at its Arak heavy water facility by installing key reactor components, with officials hoping the reactor could begin operating in 2014 to produce medical isotopes. However, the United States and the IAEA expressed concern, saying Iran has not provided required design information and is not cooperating sufficiently with inspectors. The IAEA chief noted that talks with Iran have stalled, while Washington warned that the opportunity for a diplomatic resolution would not remain open indefinitely. The reactor is a point of contention because heavy water reactors can produce plutonium, which could be used in a weapons program.

The Islamic State in Iraq and Syria killed at least 270 people, including troops and workers, in an attack on a gas field in central Syria, with dozens more missing. The group has also issued a stark ultimatum to Christians in Mosul, Iraq, demanding conversion, payment of a special tax, or facing execution. Human Rights Watch reports that ISIS is already killing, kidnapping, and threatening religious and ethnic minorities across the region, forcing tens of thousands of families to flee. The militants have seized broad territories in both Iraq and Syria, fueling a sharp rise in civilian and security force deaths in recent months.

ISIS reportedly waterboarded at least four Western hostages in Syria, including slain American journalist James Foley. The technique, long associated with CIA interrogations after 9/11, was used despite U.S. officials declining to confirm the claims out of sensitivity to hostages' families. The report reignites debate over enhanced interrogation methods, which were justified under the Bush administration but later condemned by President Obama as torture and officially ended.

Japan’s health ministry is looking into allegations that workers at the crippled Fukushima Daiichi plant were instructed to shield their radiation dosimeters with lead covers to mask dangerous exposure levels. The reported incident occurred in early December, about nine months after the earthquake and tsunami triggered the nuclear crisis. The utility TEPCO said it learned of the claim from a subcontractor, which also stated the covers were never actually used, though a newspaper reported that some workers did wear them for several hours. Authorities have said they will take firm action if any laws were broken.

Japan has approved the restart of two nuclear reactors in Fukui Prefecture, marking the first such move since all reactors were halted after the 2011 Fukushima disaster. The decision was made despite public opposition, with Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda stating that local consent had been obtained and pledging to work on rebuilding trust in nuclear safety. This restart may pave the way for other reactors to come back online. Japan, which once relied on nuclear power for about 30% of its electricity, has increased fossil fuel imports while its reactors remained offline.

The preliminary Dutch investigation into Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 concludes that the aircraft broke apart midair after being struck by numerous high-energy objects from outside, consistent with an external explosion. The report does not assign responsibility, though it suggests a surface-to-air missile may have been involved, while ruling out technical failure or crew error. Investigators were unable to access the crash site due to ongoing instability in eastern Ukraine, and they noted no evidence that the flight recorders had been tampered with. Further examination of wreckage and foreign objects is still needed to reach a definitive conclusion.

The NSA is reportedly using facial recognition technology on a massive scale, intercepting millions of images daily from emails, texts, social media, and video calls, according to leaked documents from Edward Snowden. The agency captures around 55,000 images suitable for facial recognition each day, though the technology has limitations with low-quality or angled photos. An NSA spokesperson defended the program as necessary for identifying foreign intelligence targets and preventing threats, while declining to say whether images of American citizens from social media were collected.

An independent review board found that the NSA’s Section 702 surveillance program is lawful and effective, but it also raises significant privacy concerns due to the incidental collection of Americans' communications and uncertainty about how much U.S. data is gathered. While the program’s core targeting of non-U.S. persons abroad was deemed constitutional, the board recommended reforms such as stricter targeting criteria, limits on FBI use of the data, and better filtering technology. Intelligence officials praised the report for affirming the program’s national security value, while civil liberties advocates argued the recommendations did not go far enough to protect privacy. The review was prompted by Edward Snowden’s disclosures and is part of a broader congressional and presidential examination of U.S. surveillance practices.

Boko Haram militants carried out deadly raids on several villages in Nigeria’s northeastern Borno State, killing hundreds of people, with local estimates ranging from 400 to 500. The attackers, disguised as soldiers, gathered residents before shooting men and boys, burning homes, and chasing down those who fled; survivors escaped into Cameroon and the Mandara Mountains. A military airstrike briefly pushed the militants back, but they returned once the jet left, leaving bodies unburied and the area under insurgent control. If confirmed, this would be the deadliest assault in Boko Haram’s five-year insurgency, and the group also launched a separate attack on a nearby town, burning a church and government building.

The Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general found that the TSA does not adequately document, monitor, or resolve airport security incidents, leaving the agency without a full picture of vulnerabilities. A review of six major airports showed corrective action was taken for only about half of reported breaches, with Newark performing worst at 42%. The report also highlighted inconsistent reporting practices and a lack of centralized oversight, which hindered efforts to identify trends and improve security. The TSA acknowledged the shortcomings and said it would update its directives to standardize how security breaches are defined and tracked.

A Turkish court has lifted the nationwide ban on YouTube, ruling that blocking the site violated fundamental rights and freedom of expression, though access to 15 specific videos remains restricted. This decision follows the restoration of Twitter, which Turkey's Constitutional Court ordered after finding the ban breached free expression rights. The social media restrictions were imposed by the government in response to leaked wiretap recordings, including a purported conversation about military action in Syria, which officials claimed were part of a campaign of false information. The bans had drawn criticism and were eventually reversed through legal challenges.

Despite the mandatory evacuation around the Fukushima nuclear plant, farmer Naoto Matsumura has remained in Tomioka out of anger and grief, refusing to abandon his contaminated hometown. He stayed initially to care for his livestock and then began feeding the many abandoned pets and farm animals, witnessing horrific suffering and death among them. He criticizes the government and TEPCO for neglecting the exclusion zone and failing victims, while demanding faster decontamination efforts. Though his body is now contaminated, he vows to stay as the town's sole resident to ensure cleanup happens and to die in his hometown.

A new study finds that eating at both fast-food and full-service restaurants leads to higher daily intake of calories, sugar, saturated fat, and sodium compared to eating at home. On average, people who dined out consumed about 200 extra calories per day, and full-service meals were linked to an even greater sodium increase than fast food. The researchers suggest that people do not compensate by eating less elsewhere, and they recommend smaller portions, sauces on the side, and water instead of soda. Ultimately, the authors advise that restaurant meals should be the exception, not the norm, in a healthy diet.

The review describes "The Avengers" as an entertaining but lightweight blockbuster that prioritizes humor and spectacle over epic depth. It notes the film feels opportunistic in uniting its many Marvel heroes, yet succeeds through sharp dialogue and the engaging dynamic of clashing personalities. The standout is Mark Ruffalo's Hulk, who brings both danger and fun to the role. Ultimately, the movie delivers satisfying action and fan-pleasing moments, even if it doesn't elevate the genre beyond its familiar limits.

Billionaire Richard Branson is showcasing his private Caribbean island, Necker Island, through a new photography book by Russell James. The book features over 150 images of the island’s beaches, wildlife, and luxury residences. Branson bought the island in 1978 and later turned it into an exclusive resort that has hosted numerous celebrities and world leaders. Since renting the entire island can cost up to $60,000 a night, the book offers a more affordable way to experience the island’s allure.

Richard Kiel, the towering actor celebrated for his role as the metal-toothed Bond villain Jaws, has died at age 74 in a California hospital. He became a beloved figure in the 1970s through the James Bond films “The Spy Who Loved Me” and “Moonraker,” where his silent, seemingly indestructible character won over audiences. Beyond Bond, Kiel appeared in numerous TV shows and films, including “Happy Gilmore,” and later worked as a writer and producer. Tributes from former co-stars like Roger Moore and Adam Sandler highlighted his kindness and generous spirit, noting his family was with him in his final days.

Amnesty International released a report documenting U.S. drone strikes in Pakistan’s tribal regions, alleging that many victims were civilians, including women and children, and that the attacks may constitute extrajudicial killings or war crimes. The report coincided with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif’s visit to Washington, where he renewed calls for an end to the strikes, calling them a violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty and counterproductive. A separate report by Human Rights Watch raised similar concerns about drone attacks in Yemen, saying some strikes may have violated the laws of war and killed numerous civilians. The U.S. government rejected the allegations, insisting that its counterterrorism operations are conducted lawfully and with great care to avoid civilian harm.

In the Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp near Damascus, severe hunger and lack of medical care have led to dozens of deaths, including children, with activists reporting people resorting to eating grass and animal feed. The camp has been under siege for months, trapped between government forces controlling the entrances and armed rebel groups, while repeated aid deliveries have been blocked by gunfire and restrictions. Residents describe a slow dying process, with extreme food prices, malnutrition, and no safe way to leave due to restrictive travel rules for Palestinian refugees. Humanitarian officials have condemned the situation as a humanitarian catastrophe and war crime, urging all parties to allow safe access for aid.

A protest by around 100 asylum seekers on Nauru turned destructive as they burned their shelters, drawing global attention to Australia’s new policy barring boat arrivals from ever resettling in the country. Under the law, those arriving by sea will be transferred to Papua New Guinea’s Manus Island, where they must wait for refugee status or face return. The move is meant to deter people-smuggling and risky boat journeys, but critics call it inhumane, especially given the harsh conditions asylum seekers already endure on Nauru. The unrest has since subsided, though rioters could face criminal charges, and the policy may also boost the government’s standing ahead of elections.

Police in Buenos Aires arrested at least 30 people after a World Cup celebration turned violent, with vandals smashing storefronts, ransacking a theater, and attacking police and journalists. Authorities responded with water cannons and tear gas, leaving 15 officers and several others injured. The unrest came as fans gathered to honor Argentina’s run to the final—its first since 1990—even though the team lost to Germany in extra time. Lionel Messi was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player, and fans remained proud of the team’s effort.

More African professionals are reversing the brain drain, leaving struggling Western economies to pursue opportunities in their home countries, which are experiencing notable economic growth. Nigeria, in particular, has attracted returnees like financial consultant Joshua Egba, who left London after the 2008 crisis and witnessed Nigeria's sustained expansion. Job platforms report rising interest from both Africans and Europeans, especially in sectors like mining, agriculture, and oil and gas. However, challenges such as poor infrastructure, corruption, and daily inconveniences still discourage many skilled diaspora members from returning.

A growing number of foreign families, particularly in the Netherlands, are adopting healthy U.S. infants, often African American, as birth mothers increasingly choose open adoptions with overseas parents. These mothers often hope their children will escape racial prejudice they believe the children would face in America. The trend is driven by U.S. laws allowing birth mothers to select adoptive families, and Dutch families are often more open to maintaining contact and embracing the child's heritage. While international adoptions overall have declined, the number of U.S. children placed abroad has steadily risen, offering birth mothers like Susan a hopeful alternative to poverty or foster care.

A boat carrying asylum seekers from Iraq and Lebanon capsized off Indonesia’s West Java coast, leaving at least 22 dead, including children, while 28 survivors were rescued and dozens more remain missing. The vessel was believed to be heading to Australia’s Christmas Island, a common destination for such risky journeys. Officials suggested the boat may have run out of fuel or been poorly handled by those aboard. The tragedy comes as Australia maintains a strict policy barring illegal immigrants who arrive by boat from ever settling in the country.

Rival armed groups clashed near Tripoli’s main airport, killing nine people and wounding dozens more, while heavy shelling endangered nearby residential areas and forced the suspension of all flights. The violence underscores Libya’s fragile security situation, as the weak interim government struggles to assert control over powerful militias, many of which are nominally state-funded. Islamist brigades claimed to have reached the airport’s perimeter, challenging the Zintan forces that have held it since 2011. International actors, including the United States and the United Kingdom, condemned the fighting and urged all sides to stop hostilities and pursue dialogue.

Robert Downey Jr.'s 20-year-old son, Indio Falconer Downey, was arrested on drug charges after police found cocaine and a smoking pipe during a traffic stop. He was released on bail later that evening. The family's spokesperson attributed the arrest to a likely inherited predisposition to addiction and expressed gratitude to law enforcement, emphasizing that Indio has strong family support and the potential to recover. The statement also drew parallels to Robert Downey Jr.'s own past struggles with substance abuse, which he overcame after years of treatment.

Toronto’s city council voted decisively to strip Mayor Rob Ford of most of his powers and transfer them to Deputy Mayor Norm Kelly, reducing Ford to a largely ceremonial role. The vote came after Ford admitted to using crack cocaine and amid ongoing misconduct allegations. Ford angrily denounced the move as a “coup d’etat,” vowed political revenge, and compared the council’s action to Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait. He also accidentally knocked down a councilor during a recess and apologized, but insisted he will not resign and will let voters decide his future.

Robin Roberts, co-anchor of “Good Morning America,” has revealed she is battling myelodysplastic syndrome, a blood and bone marrow disorder linked to the chemotherapy and radiation she received for breast cancer five years ago. She is beginning treatment and will continue working when possible, though she will take time off for a bone marrow transplant. Her sister is a perfect match as a donor, which greatly improves her chances of recovery. Roberts is also using her announcement to raise awareness about the shortage of marrow donors, particularly for African-American women.

Singer Robin Thicke and actress Paula Patton have announced their separation after nearly a decade of marriage. The couple, who have a young son together, said in a joint statement that they will always love each other and remain best friends. They had previously denied rumors of trouble in their relationship. No further details were provided about a possible divorce.

Robin Williams was cremated and his remains were scattered in San Francisco Bay, as confirmed by his death certificate. The certificate lists the cause of death as pending, though investigators suspect he died by suicide by hanging. He had been receiving treatment for depression and was also coping with early-stage Parkinson's disease, according to his widow. Despite reports of relapse, she emphasized he was sober at the time of his death.

Robin Williams’s widow revealed that he was sober at the time of his death but had been privately battling depression, anxiety, and the early stages of Parkinson’s disease. The Parkinson’s diagnosis added to his fears and emotional burden, as he worried it would limit his ability to cope through exercise. Investigators believe he died by suicide, and his wife expressed hope that his tragedy would encourage others to seek help for their own struggles.

Robotic telepresence technology is set to bring remotely controlled, screen-faced robots into offices, allowing distant managers to move through workplaces and interact with teams as if physically present. While already used in hospitals, its adoption in corporate settings is still emerging, with proponents comparing it to the early days of video calls. The technology faces challenges such as social awkwardness and unresolved etiquette, but researchers are improving realism with features like robotic body language. As prices drop and interfaces become more intuitive, these robots are expected to become a normal part of the future workplace.

A four-year-old girl with arthrogryposis, a condition causing weak muscles and curved joints, has gained new independence through a 3D-printed robotic arm device called the WREX. The exoskeleton uses elastic bands to make her arms feel weightless, allowing her to reach, play, and perform everyday tasks. 3D printing has made the device faster to produce and easier to customize for each child. Her family hopes the technology will continue to improve and help her grow into a fully independent adult.

Each year, over 700,000 Americans suffer a stroke, often leading to paralysis on one side of the body. Researchers at Georgia Tech are developing a brain-controlled robotic arm exoskeleton that responds to patients’ thoughts, with early tests showing promise in rewiring brain signals. Similar brain-computer interfaces could eventually power prosthetic limbs for amputees, while other scientists are working on restoring sensation through virtual touch. These technologies may also find mainstream uses, such as enhancing athletic performance, which could make them more accessible to people with disabilities.

Israel announced a four-hour humanitarian pause in parts of Gaza, but fighting continued as militants kept firing rockets and Israeli forces carried out airstrikes. A U.N. school sheltering thousands of Palestinians was hit, drawing international condemnation and deepening the humanitarian crisis, with widespread casualties, displacement, and critical shortages of power and water. Several Latin American nations recalled their ambassadors from Israel in protest, while Israeli officials defended the military campaign against Hamas. Public opinion polls indicated most Jewish Israelis opposed a cease-fire, and many Palestinians rejected a two-state solution.

Roger Ebert, the Pulitzer Prize-winning film critic known for the “two thumbs up” show with Gene Siskel, died at age 70 after a recurrence of cancer. Despite losing his voice and jaw to earlier treatments, he remained prolific, writing hundreds of reviews and blog posts until the end. He was celebrated for his sharp wit, open-mindedness, and willingness to reconsider films, as well as his deep influence on movie criticism. Tributes from his wife, colleagues, and city leaders highlighted his courage, generosity, and lasting legacy.

Roger Federer says he will skip the French Open if it conflicts with the birth of his third child, prioritizing family over tennis. The 17-time Grand Slam champion has not missed a major since 1999, but he insists that supporting his wife matters more than extending that streak. He is currently competing at the Monte Carlo Masters but remains unsure whether he will play at Roland Garros, which starts in late May. The tournament has also announced a prize money increase, with singles champions set to earn $2.3 million.

Roku, known for its successful streaming players, is expanding by embedding its platform directly into television sets.
