It has partnered with Chinese manufacturers TCL and Hisense to produce Roku TVs, which will feature Roku’s interface and remote without needing an external box. The company plans to work with more TV makers and aims to become the standard smart-TV platform, with the goal of offering these features at little or no extra cost.

Rolf Harris, the 84-year-old former children’s entertainer, was convicted in London of 12 sexual abuse charges involving four females, including a child as young as seven, with offenses dating back to 1970. The case was part of the wider Operation Yewtree investigation into historical abuse by public figures. He was released on bail until sentencing, where the judge warned he could face prison. Police praised the victims’ bravery and said the verdict showed that allegations would be investigated regardless of how much time had passed.

Thousands of African descendants are traveling to Ghana’s Cape Coast Castle as part of “roots tourism,” seeking a tangible connection to the suffering their ancestors endured before being shipped into slavery. The fortress, once a major hub of the transatlantic slave trade, holds harrowing reminders of overcrowded dungeons, abuse, and the infamous “Door of No Return.” The visit resonates deeply with many, including former U.S. President Barack Obama and his family, who made an emotional pilgrimage there. Despite the tragedy, the site also inspires reflection on resilience and the remarkable survival instinct of those who endured such brutality.

Golf star Rory McIlroy and tennis player Caroline Wozniacki have ended their engagement, with McIlroy saying he realized after sending wedding invitations that he was not ready for marriage. He described the split as mutual and amicable, and both athletes are now focusing on their upcoming tournaments. The couple, together since 2011 and engaged on New Year's Day, had been a high-profile pairing in the sports world. Wozniacki acknowledged the difficult moment publicly while thanking supporters for their kindness.

Rory McIlroy rebounded from a poor second round with a 68 at the Scottish Open, keeping him optimistic about his form heading into next week’s British Open at Hoylake. Justin Rose and Marc Warren share the lead at 10 under par, one stroke ahead of Kristoffer Broberg. Meanwhile, Tiger Woods continued his comeback from back surgery with a practice round at Royal Liverpool, saying he has regained his speed and strength. In the Women’s British Open, South Korea’s Park Inbee holds a one-shot lead after a 68, while Charley Hull posted the best round of the day with a 66.

Emmy-winning actress Rosemary Murphy passed away at age 89 in her Manhattan home, with cancer reported as the cause. She was widely recognized for playing Miss Maudie Atkinson in the classic film *To Kill a Mockingbird*. Murphy earned an Emmy for her portrayal of Sara Delano Roosevelt in *Eleanor and Franklin* and received Tony nominations for several stage roles. Over her long career, she also played the mothers of George Washington and John F. Kennedy in television productions, along with appearances in soap operas and films.

The European Space Agency is preparing to select a landing site for its Philae probe, which will attempt the first controlled landing on a comet after a decade-long mission. The agency will narrow the options from five to two candidate sites on Monday, with a final choice expected in October. Engineers face significant challenges because the lander cannot be steered after release, must rely on sunlight for power, and needs a safe trajectory around the comet's irregular, rocky shape. The mission aims to study the comet's composition and could reveal whether comets delivered water or life-building chemicals to Earth.

Iranian President Hassan Rouhani signaled openness to immediate, time-bound nuclear negotiations and reiterated that nuclear weapons contradict Iran’s religious and security principles, while calling for sanctions relief and reduced tensions with the United States. In response, President Barack Obama welcomed Iran’s conciliatory tone but stressed that any agreement must be backed by transparent, verifiable actions, and the two leaders did not meet. The article also highlights ongoing friction over Syria, with Obama pushing for a strong UN Security Council resolution to enforce chemical weapons disarmament and Russia resisting, as well as Brazil’s public condemnation of U.S. surveillance practices.

Hassan Rouhani, a centrist cleric, has emerged as an unexpected wildcard in Iran's presidential race, which was initially expected to be dominated by ultra-conservatives after reformist leaders were barred. By openly criticizing state media censorship and the government's heavy-handed security tactics, he is appealing to supporters of the crushed Green Movement and generating significant momentum. Although he is a longtime insider with ties to the Supreme Leader, his populist defiance could make him a spoiler against hardline frontrunners like Saeed Jalili and Mohammad Qalibaf. Observers say his campaign is gaining ground, and a surprise victory is no longer unthinkable.

A British travel firm is offering an ultra-luxurious 53-day round-the-world rail journey starting in London, priced at $36,500 and limited to around 25 passengers. The first-class itinerary includes iconic trains such as the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express and the Tsar’s Gold Private Train, crossing North America, Asia, and Europe via the Trans-Siberian line. The trip is aimed at wealthy travelers with ample free time, and the company notes it is their longest and most expensive offering. A cheaper, 40-day reverse alternative is also available from another operator.

Queen Elizabeth II’s losing streak at Royal Ascot continued when her horse Bold Sniper was defeated in the Wolferton Stakes on the fourth day, with Contributor taking the win. The previous day, her filly Estimate had also narrowly missed retaining her Gold Cup title. Elsewhere, Rizeena won the Coronation Stakes, Hartnell claimed the Queen’s Vase, and Louis The Pious delivered a 33-1 upset in the Buckingham Palace Stakes.

Queen Elizabeth II’s filly Estimate narrowly missed retaining the Gold Cup at Royal Ascot, finishing just behind Leading Light in a dramatic sprint to the line, with Missunited third and Michael Owen’s Brown Panther fourth. The Queen, dressed in blue, graciously presented the trophy after her horse’s brave career-best effort. Earlier on the same day, Frankie Dettori secured his 49th Royal Ascot victory, while trainer Sir Michael Stoute reached a milestone 70th win at the meeting.

Royal Ascot has boosted its total prize fund to a record $7.5 million in a bid to draw elite international racehorses, though this remains far below major global events like the Dubai World Cup and the Breeders' Cup. The festival's prestige was underscored last year when top-rated horses such as Frankel and Black Caviar competed there. Organizers have also renamed a race in honor of Prince William, while maintaining strict dress codes and royal traditions. Despite the increased purse, Ascot's flagship race still offers significantly less than its richest global counterparts.

The Duchess of Cambridge is pregnant, but the news was announced earlier than usual because she was hospitalized with severe morning sickness, making secrecy impossible. In a break from tradition, the palace revealed the pregnancy immediately, reflecting a more open approach by William and Kate to manage intense media scrutiny. The child will be third in line to the throne, and due to recent changes in succession rules, a girl would not be passed over for a younger brother. The announcement sparked widespread excitement, crashing the royal website within minutes.

The Duchess of Cambridge remains hospitalized in London for severe morning sickness, though her condition is improving, and Prince William has visited her. The palace confirmed the couple is expecting their first child, though the pregnancy is still in its early weeks. The baby will be third in line to the British throne, and recent succession reforms ensuring daughters are not bypassed by younger brothers are already taking effect. The announcement has sparked global attention, with political leaders offering congratulations and bookmakers already taking bets on the baby's name and gender.

The Duchess of Cambridge’s pregnancy confirms the arrival of a second royal child, which is expected to generate global excitement and strengthen the monarchy. Historically, a "spare heir" was essential to secure the succession due to high mortality and unexpected deaths, as several British monarchs were younger sons who became king only after their elder brothers died. A key modern change is that, following legal reforms, a daughter would retain her place in line to the throne ahead of any younger brothers. However, the article notes that being the second child carries a heavy burden, as seen with Princess Margaret and Prince Harry, involving intense public scrutiny, limited privacy, and the challenge of finding a meaningful role.

The article discusses Prince William and Kate’s decision to bring baby Prince George on their three-week royal tour of New Zealand and Australia, using a schedule that lets them return to him most evenings. It contrasts this with Queen Elizabeth II’s 1953 Commonwealth tour, when she left young children at home, and with Princess Diana’s 1983 decision to take William along. The author argues that while Diana is often credited for modernizing royal parenting, the Queen’s earlier difficult choices and willingness to adapt made such changes possible. Ultimately, the piece suggests the Queen deserves much of the credit for the monarchy’s evolution, not just Diana.

Rubin “Hurricane” Carter, the former boxing contender who was wrongfully imprisoned for nearly two decades, has died in Toronto at age 76 from prostate cancer. He spent 19 years in prison for a triple murder before his convictions were overturned, after which he became a leading advocate for the wrongly convicted. Carter was once a celebrated middleweight fighter, but his later life was defined by his fight for justice and his belief that letting go of anger was essential to survival. His story inspired songs, books, and a film, and he is remembered as a courageous campaigner against wrongful convictions.

USA Rugby has announced plans to bid for the 2018 Rugby World Cup Sevens, with a formal proposal expected in early December and a final decision due by mid-2015. Sevens rugby, a faster, seven-a-side version of the sport, is gaining global attention ahead of its Olympic debut in 2016. The U.S. has already formed a bid committee and held early discussions with interested cities. Hosting the tournament would give American fans a rare chance to see a Rugby World Cup on home soil.

Amor Towles, a Manhattan investment professional and first-time novelist, has earned critical acclaim and bestseller status for "Rules of Civility," a nostalgic novel set in late 1930s New York. The story follows Katey Kontent, a sharp, ambitious young woman from a working-class background, as she navigates love, friendship, and high society after a chance encounter and an unexpected accident alter her path. Towles drew inspiration from Walker Evans' candid subway photographs of the era, and the book explores enduring themes of aspiration, self-invention, and how youthful decisions shape a lifetime. While it evokes comparisons to literary classics like "The Great Gatsby," Towles sees his work as a fresh creation built from diverse influences rather than a simple homage.

Mexico’s runner-up, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, has formally challenged the presidential election result, alleging that the winner, Enrique Peña Nieto, and his party secured votes through illegal purchases. He argues that the partial recount failed to address his concerns and that accepting the outcome would mean surrendering his rights. Official tallies gave Peña Nieto 38.21% of the vote against López Obrador’s 31.59%, but the results remain provisional until the electoral tribunal rules by September 6. The PRI has denied the vote-buying accusations, while López Obrador’s refusal to concede echoes his disputed 2006 loss.

The article contrasts the daily lives of two women on opposite sides of the Gaza-Israel conflict: an Israeli woman who has seconds to reach a bomb shelter when rockets hit, and a Palestinian woman in Gaza who has no safe room and can only pray as airstrikes threaten her crowded neighborhood. Both are exhausted by the violence, closely follow the news, and struggle with fear and trauma, while children on both sides grow up accustomed to the sounds of war. Despite the hatred around them, both women express a shared longing for peace and safety for their families, even as they remain trapped in a cycle of escalation. A new technical regulation in the Russia-Belarus-Kazakhstan customs union will require all skin-contact underwear to contain at least 6% cotton, effectively banning most lacy synthetic lingerie from July. Officials say the rule is meant to protect consumers from moisture-related skin issues, but it has sparked anger in Kazakhstan, where women have protested and mocked the policy online. The measure also affects other undergarments and linens, and critics note that most luxury lingerie falls far below the cotton threshold. Under pressure from shoppers and producers, officials have indicated the regulation could be amended.

Russia has condemned Prince Charles over reported remarks comparing Vladimir Putin to Adolf Hitler, calling them unacceptable and accusing the British royal family of using Western media to spread propaganda about the Ukraine crisis. The alleged comment was made during a museum tour in Canada while Charles spoke with a Polish Holocaust survivor about her escape from Nazi Germany. The conversation has not been independently confirmed, and Charles’s representatives declined to comment. In response, Russia’s deputy ambassador requested a meeting with UK officials to address the controversy.

Russia reacted with fury to new U.S. and EU sanctions tied to the Ukraine crisis, with officials calling the measures unlawful, warning of retaliation, and accusing Washington of unfair competition in the arms trade. The expanded sanctions target major Russian banks, energy firms, and defense companies, while the EU also moved toward additional penalties. Tensions escalated further as Ukraine claimed a Russian fighter shot down one of its jets, and the Pentagon reported thousands of Russian troops near the border. Moscow insisted the sanctions would backfire, deepen U.S.-Russia strains, and only worsen the conflict.

Edward Snowden has been granted a three-year residency extension in Russia, according to his lawyer, after his previous one-year asylum expired. He remains active in Russia, working online and speaking about the surveillance programs he exposed. U.S. officials reiterated that he still faces felony charges and should return to face due process, while critics like Hillary Clinton argue he could have sparked public debate without stealing and leaking government secrets.

Russia’s parliament voted overwhelmingly to approve the annexation of Crimea, a move that deepened the standoff with the West. In response, the United States and the European Union expanded sanctions against Russian officials, a major bank, and allies of President Putin, while Moscow retaliated with its own sanctions on U.S. lawmakers. Ukraine’s government vowed never to stop fighting for Crimea’s return, even as it prepared for possible evacuations of its military personnel. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s navy commander was released after being detained by pro-Russian forces, but tensions remained high amid fears of further escalation.

In Sochi, animal rights activists accuse local authorities of poisoning stray dogs ahead of the Winter Olympics, citing witnessed cases of poisoned animals and alleging a campaign to cull the population. City and Olympic officials deny the claims, saying strays are collected humanely by contractors and that a new shelter is available, though activists are skeptical and view it as a publicity move. In response, grassroots volunteers have taken direct action by rescuing dogs, building makeshift shelters, and even transporting animals to other cities. They argue that Russia’s lack of animal protection and sterilization laws is the root cause of the stray dog crisis.

The article contrasts the dominant international account of the MH17 disaster—that pro-Russian rebels shot down the airliner with a Russian-made missile—with a series of conspiracy theories promoted by Moscow and its allies. These alternative narratives include claims that passengers were already dead, a Ukrainian fighter jet was responsible, or that the plane was mistaken for Putin’s aircraft. U.S. officials dismiss the Russian version as propaganda, noting that Moscow has repeatedly spread misinformation throughout the Ukraine conflict. The piece also highlights how Russian state media and even Wikipedia edits were used to shape the story, while some journalists inside Russia resigned over the deliberate distortion of facts.

Russia has recalled its ambassador to NATO and suspended military cooperation with the alliance, citing NATO’s confrontational stance and its plans to strengthen defenses in Eastern Europe following Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Moscow also defended its troop buildup near Ukraine as legitimate exercises. In Ukraine, a government report accused ousted President Viktor Yanukovych of ordering sniper attacks on protesters, with alleged Russian involvement. Meanwhile, Gazprom announced another gas price increase for Ukraine, deepening economic pressure amid the crisis.

President Vladimir Putin has formally annexed Crimea, returning it to Russian control decades after it was transferred to Ukraine. The EU is under pressure to impose broader sanctions, including asset freezes and visa bans on Russian oligarchs close to the Kremlin. However, European leaders must recognize that such measures carry economic risks and could backfire. Trade should remain off the table, as both sides depend heavily on it, especially given Europe's reliance on Russian gas and the fragile state of Russia's economy.

Russian lawmakers approved a bill that would ban Americans from adopting Russian children, a move widely seen as retaliation for the U.S. Magnitsky Act, which imposed sanctions on Russian human rights abusers. The legislation also targets U.S.-funded nongovernmental organizations and U.S. officials accused of human rights violations. The U.S. State Department expressed concern, noting that over 60,000 Russian children have been adopted by American families and that a bilateral adoption agreement was recently implemented. Critics, including Amnesty International, called the measure a childish and dangerous response that could harm civil society and children.

In Rwanda, a national cycling team made up of genocide survivors is using the sport to heal deep emotional wounds and gain global recognition. The team, inspired by the country's traditional wooden bicycles, was established by American cyclists and has helped members channel their painful pasts into disciplined training and competition. One founding member is set to compete in the 2012 Olympics, symbolizing personal triumph and national pride. Their achievements are reshaping both international views of Rwanda and the riders' own sense of identity and hope for the future.

People magazine has reported that Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are expecting a baby in October, though no source is cited and the famously private couple has not confirmed the news. The rumor sparked intense reactions online, with fans expressing heartbreak and sharing memes about the possible pregnancy. Even celebrities joined in, including Ellen DeGeneres, who jokingly congratulated the pair and praised the expected child’s imagined qualities.

A legal dispute over a valuable Andy Warhol portrait of Farrah Fawcett is being decided in court, with the University of Texas claiming she left it to them and Ryan O'Neal insisting it was a personal gift. The trial has delved into the couple's decades-long, on-and-off romance, including their separations, reconciliations, and shared caregiving during illnesses. Witnesses have offered conflicting accounts of Fawcett's intentions, while O'Neal is expected to testify about their relationship to support his ownership claim. The case also highlights the complexities of defining a couple and determining ownership of art given as a gift.

After months of protests and deadly clashes in Ukraine, a negotiated agreement was reached to reduce presidential powers, restore the 2004 constitution, and release opposition leader Yulia Tymoshenko, with new elections promised by December 2014. However, many demonstrators on Kiev’s Independence Square remained dissatisfied, saying the deal did not go far enough and insisting President Viktor Yanukovych must resign. The truce is fragile, as deep anger over the recent bloodshed and uncertainty about the government’s commitments still dominate the atmosphere. While the accord offers a possible path toward peace and European integration, the crisis is far from resolved.

The European Aviation Safety Agency has issued a new directive requiring all Airbus A380 superjumbos to undergo wing crack inspections, expanding an earlier order that applied only to the 20 oldest aircraft. The planes are not grounded, but inspection deadlines vary based on the number of takeoff and landing cycles completed. The order is a precautionary follow-up rather than a response to new damage, and no immediate safety risks have been identified. A permanent solution is being developed with Airbus and is expected by summer.

Jonathan Jansen, the rector of the University of the Free State in South Africa, uses his graduation speech to urge students to respond to the country’s lingering anger with reason rather than rage. Raised in a poor, apartheid-era neighborhood, Jansen credits his parents’ values of dignity, generosity, and racial tolerance for his success and his belief that education is the key out of poverty. He is a sharp critic of South Africa’s failing education system and low academic standards, which he sees as a lingering effect of apartheid’s message of inferiority. His leadership has also been marked by a controversial but principled choice to offer forgiveness and reconciliation to white students involved in a racist incident on campus, reflecting his commitment to mercy over revenge.

Thousands of Salafi demonstrators rallied in Cairo’s Tahrir Square, demanding that President Mohamed Morsy’s government immediately apply Islamic law. The protest highlighted deep divisions over Sharia’s role in Egypt’s new constitution, with Salafists pushing for swift implementation while the Muslim Brotherhood favors a gradual approach. Many Egyptians, as well as the Coptic Christian minority, oppose the religious push, urging instead a focus on economic recovery and fighting corruption. The rally was organized by hardline Islamist groups, while the Muslim Brotherhood and the Salafi Nour Party declined to take part.

A New Jersey judge has ruled that same-sex couples must be allowed to marry, stating that the state’s current civil-union system is unconstitutional because it denies them federal benefits. The ruling, which would permit same-sex marriages starting October 21, came after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down part of the Defense of Marriage Act, prompting federal agencies to recognize only marriages, not civil unions. Governor Chris Christie’s office indicated it would appeal the decision to the New Jersey Supreme Court, arguing the matter should have been left to voters. New Jersey is one of only a few states that offered civil unions but not marriage to same-sex couples.

Samir Khan, an American-raised al Qaeda operative, was killed alongside Anwar al-Awlaki in a U.S. drone strike. He had become a key propagandist by editing the English-language magazine Inspire, which used his understanding of Western culture to radicalize readers and provide practical guidance for carrying out attacks without traveling to training camps. His death, along with al-Awlaki’s, dealt a significant blow to al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula’s efforts to recruit Westerners, as few replacements possess the same language and technical skills.

Samsung has won a legal victory in Australia, allowing its Galaxy Tab 10.1 to go on sale there just in time for the holidays after the country’s High Court rejected Apple’s appeal. The ruling strengthens Samsung’s position in its broader global patent disputes with Apple, including in the U.S. Apple maintains that Samsung copied the iPhone and iPad designs, while Samsung denies the claims and says it can prove its products are distinctive. Additionally, Samsung has filed a separate complaint with the U.S. International Trade Commission seeking to block Apple devices from entering the U.S. over alleged patent violations.

The San Antonio Spurs have made history by hiring veteran WNBA star Becky Hammon as an assistant coach, making her one of the few women to hold such a role in the NBA. Head coach Gregg Popovich praised her basketball knowledge, work ethic, and ability to connect with players, noting she had already spent time with the team. Hammon, who is retiring from a standout WNBA career, said she felt honored and credited the women who paved the way for her, while making clear she expects to be treated like any other coach. Though not the first woman on an NBA staff, her appointment with the reigning champions drew significant attention.

Sand holes at beaches can be deadly, as shown by three U.S. deaths this summer, including a nine-year-old girl who died when a deep hole she was sitting in collapsed and buried her. Rescue efforts are often hampered because loose sand keeps falling back into the hole, making it a technical challenge. Experts note that even a small amount of sand can crush the chest or block the airway, and there are no national rules or tracking systems for such incidents. While rare, these accidents affect both children and adults, prompting calls for greater public awareness and local safety regulations.

Actor Thomas Guiry was arrested at Houston’s Bush Intercontinental Airport after allegedly head-butting a police sergeant when he became upset over being denied boarding a United flight for intoxication. He now faces a felony charge of assault against a public servant. The situation escalated after officers suggested a sobering center, and he allegedly threatened and kicked the officer before the head-butt. Guiry, known for roles in “The Sandlot” and a “Lassie” remake, has continued acting in recent TV shows.

A judge has relaxed Jerry Sandusky’s house arrest conditions, allowing him supervised visits with eight of his grandchildren and time with adult friends, while leaving decisions about the other three grandchildren to a custody court. The judge also rejected prosecutors’ requests to keep Sandusky indoors and to move the trial out of the county, noting no evidence he posed a threat to a nearby school. Sandusky, who faces child sexual abuse charges and has pleaded not guilty, remains under house arrest as he awaits a trial scheduled for May.

The trial of former Penn State coach Jerry Sandusky is nearing its end, with closing arguments expected Thursday after the defense finishes its case. Sandusky faces 51 counts of child sexual abuse involving at least 10 boys over 15 years, and he has denied the allegations. The defense is working to undermine the accusers' credibility, suggesting they have financial motives, and plans to call an expert who may argue Sandusky's behavior stems from a personality disorder rather than predatory grooming. A key remaining question is whether Sandusky will testify in his own defense, which some legal experts believe could be his best chance at convincing a juror to hold out.

The defense in Jerry Sandusky’s child sex abuse trial rested without calling the former coach to testify, leaving closing arguments scheduled for Thursday. Prosecutors also finished their rebuttal, after a psychologist disputed earlier testimony about Sandusky’s mental health. The defense’s final witness contradicted a key accuser’s account of the shower incident, while Sandusky’s wife had testified she saw no abuse. With 51 counts remaining, the case now heads to the jury for deliberations.

Jerry Sandusky’s memoir about his troubled relationship with his adopted son Matt closely mirrors the letters he wrote to alleged victim No. 4, both showing a pattern of mentorship, emotional intensity, and eventual estrangement. Matt Sandusky recently came forward during his father’s trial, claiming he too was abused, and his story echoed the testimony of other accusers who met Sandusky through his charity for at-risk children. The letters to No. 4, described as “creepy love letters,” reveal Sandusky as needy, scolding, and manipulative, and they are considered key evidence in the case. Sandusky, who faces dozens of charges, has denied the allegations and did not testify in his defense.

Saudi Arabia has appointed Prince Salman bin Abdulaziz as the new crown prince, placing him next in line to the throne after the death of his brother, Crown Prince Nayef. Salman, who remains defense minister, also takes on the role of deputy prime minister. The late Nayef was remembered for his hard-line stance and leadership in counterterrorism, particularly against al Qaeda, and has been succeeded as interior minister by Prince Ahmed bin Abdulaziz.

A video showing a British man and his Saudi wife being attacked by Saudi religious police in a Riyadh supermarket parking lot has sparked widespread outrage online. The incident began when the couple used a cashier line reserved for women and families, prompting three men to follow and confront them. The man said he was beaten and kicked on the ground, and his wife was kicked in the stomach when she tried to defend him. Saudi authorities condemned the attack, found the officers acted beyond their authority, and transferred four of them from Riyadh, while the British Embassy provided consular support.

Saudi Arabia is moving forward with plans to build the Kingdom Tower in Jeddah, a skyscraper designed to surpass Dubai’s Burj Khalifa as the world’s tallest building. Construction is set to begin soon, with the tower expected to reach about one kilometer in height and cost over a billion dollars. Engineers face significant challenges, including protecting deep foundations from seawater and managing wind loads, which the design addresses by altering the tower’s shape at different levels. Despite the difficulties, experts believe the project is achievable with current construction technology.

Saudi Arabia has announced it will allow female athletes to compete in the Olympics for the first time, reversing its previous policy and joining Qatar and Brunei in sending women to the London Games. The decision follows pressure from the International Olympic Committee and marks a rare concession in a country where women face broad restrictions, including bans on driving and requirements for male guardian permission. The Saudi embassy said women who qualify will be allowed to participate, though it remains unclear how many will be ready on short notice. Equestrian Dalma Rushdi Malhas, the first Saudi woman to compete in the Youth Olympics, welcomed the move as opening doors for women, even though she will not compete this year due to injury.

Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Bahrain have pulled their ambassadors from Qatar, citing Doha's failure to honor a Gulf Cooperation Council agreement aimed at preventing interference in each other's domestic affairs and curbing support for groups that threaten regional stability. The move follows months of diplomatic efforts and marks a significant escalation in tensions within the GCC. Qatar responded with regret and surprise, stating it would not take reciprocal action and reaffirming its commitment to the security of the Gulf bloc. The rift highlights longstanding friction over Qatar's alleged backing of Islamist movements, such as the Muslim Brotherhood, which other Gulf states view with deep suspicion.

Saudi Arabia has officially permitted girls in private schools to participate in physical education for the first time, with rules requiring modest dress and female Saudi teachers overseeing the activities. The government framed the move as consistent with Islamic teachings, though some observers note that private schools already offered sports programs. It follows broader, cautious reforms, including Saudi women competing in the London Olympics, while many restrictions on women's rights remain in place.

Saudi Arabia’s king has ordered medical care for a 610-kilogram man from a southern border region, arranging his transfer to a Riyadh hospital. The young man, who cannot move on his own, will undergo a weight-loss program that may include surgery if needed. The case draws attention to rising obesity across the Gulf, where countries like Kuwait and Saudi Arabia report some of the highest adult obesity rates in the region. This growing health issue is also expected to drive a sharp increase in Gulf healthcare spending due to lifestyle-related diseases.

A Saudi-born al Qaeda operative known as “Spin Ghul” is being held in New York after his secret extradition from Italy, with charges against him now unsealed. He is accused of conspiring to kill U.S. nationals, bomb U.S. government sites, and provide support to al Qaeda, and could face life in prison if convicted. Authorities say he fought U.S. forces in Afghanistan and later plotted an attack on the U.S. embassy in Nigeria that never materialized. He was arrested in Libya in 2005, released in 2011, then detained by Italian authorities before being handed over to U.S. custody.

Saudi Arabia has reported at least 14 new MERS-CoV infections, with five patients dying within a day, raising the kingdom’s known total to 313 cases and 92 deaths. The sudden rise remains unexplained, though health officials noted a similar uptick occurred around the same time last year. In response, Saudi authorities are intensifying efforts, including a planned WHO meeting, discussions with a drug company about vaccine development, and threats to suspend ambulance workers who refuse to treat patients. Globally, the WHO has confirmed hundreds of cases and nearly as many deaths, with recent infections also appearing in the UAE, Greece, and Malaysia.

Saudi Arabia has conducted a major counterterrorism sweep, arresting 62 suspects linked to al Qaeda affiliates in Yemen and Syria, with authorities still searching for 44 others. The cell was allegedly planning attacks on targets inside the kingdom with al Qaeda's backing. The arrests, made over the past two months, were mostly Saudi nationals and were carried out independently of recent U.S.-led operations in Yemen. Officials emphasized that the operation remains ongoing as they continue hunting additional suspects.

Hungary’s spa culture is deeply rooted in history, dating back to the Romans and shaped by Ottoman influence, and remains a social ritual where locals gather to bathe, chat, and even play chess. Unlike luxury wellness retreats, Hungarian spas emphasize health and function, with many offering affordable admission and basic amenities. Notable destinations include Budapest’s grand Széchenyi complex, the striking white travertine hills of Egerszalók, the underground Cave Bath at Miskolctapolca, and Europe’s largest thermal lake at Heviz. The country also features massive water parks and historic bathhouses, such as Hungarospa and Szeged’s Anna Thermal Bath, blending therapeutic waters with family-friendly attractions.

The author, an HIV-positive gay black man, sees recent victories for gay rights as a hopeful sign, but argues the next crucial battle is ending the stigma around HIV/AIDS. While medical advances have made the disease manageable, most Americans living with it do not receive the consistent care they need, largely because shame and fear keep them from seeking help. To change this, the piece calls for broader education, greater political support, and more celebrity involvement to bring the issue into the open. With the right tools and collective effort, the author believes the HIV/AIDS epidemic in America can finally be ended.

A newly launched iPhone app called Whale Alert provides real-time data on endangered right whale sightings near busy U.S. shipping lanes, helping ship captains avoid deadly collisions. The app combines information from multiple conservation and government organizations and alerts mariners when whales are within a risky distance of their routes. Since right whales number only a few hundred, losing even one, especially a female, can seriously threaten the species. The app has already been widely downloaded and could serve as a model for protecting whales in other regions worldwide.

South Carolina authorities had a history of involvement with Timothy Jones Jr. and his children, with social services documenting concerns about unsafe living conditions and allegations of physical punishment, though the children denied abuse and were not removed from the home. Jones was arrested in Mississippi after a police encounter, and he later led investigators to the bodies of his five children in Alabama. He now faces five murder charges and has waived his initial court appearance. Officials say the children’s remains were wrapped in garbage bags and carried in his SUV for several days before being discovered.

Germany’s finance minister publicly clashed with IMF chief Christine Lagarde after she suggested eurozone countries should soften austerity demands, arguing that the IMF itself had consistently warned about the dangers of high debt. Lagarde, citing new research that austerity’s economic damage had been underestimated, backed giving Greece and Spain more time to meet budget targets and allowing automatic stabilisers to cushion weaker growth. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Angela Merkel signaled possible domestic stimulus measures, including tax cuts, to support Germany’s slowing economy. The dispute highlights growing tensions between Berlin and international institutions over how to balance deficit reduction with growth in struggling eurozone states.

A Colorado school district reversed its decision to label a six-year-old boy’s hand-kiss as sexual harassment after the case drew national outrage. The boy returned to school and his disciplinary record was changed to “misconduct.” His mother said the act was an innocent childhood crush, while the girl’s mother argued the school was right to protect her daughter from repeated unwanted contact. The superintendent defended the district’s response, saying the focus was on stopping the behavior while considering both students involved.

A Massachusetts high school punished an honors student, Erin Cox, for going to pick up a drunk friend, citing its zero-tolerance alcohol policy even though she was sober and police confirmed that. The decision sparked widespread public backlash, with many arguing she should be praised for preventing a potential drunk-driving tragedy. Her family pursued legal action, and while a court initially declined to intervene, they planned further legal steps to challenge the policy. The case highlights a broader debate over whether strict school rules discourage students from helping peers in dangerous situations.

Scientists exploring a remote mountain range in northern Queensland, Australia, have uncovered a "lost world" with at least three new vertebrate species: a leaf-tailed gecko, a golden skink, and a frog that emerges only in the rain. These animals have evolved in isolation for millions of years among massive granite boulders and upland rainforest on Cape Melville. The gecko, considered a primitive relic, is notable for its size and distinct appearance, while the frog breeds in moist rock crevices without needing open water. Researchers say the discoveries are remarkable for Australia and expect future expeditions to reveal more hidden species.

Scientists used optogenetics to implant false memories in mice by reactivating a memory of a safe chamber while giving foot shocks in another chamber, causing the mice to fear the safe chamber. The study shows that false memories rely on the same neural mechanisms as genuine memories, which helps explain why people often believe false memories are real. The findings have implications for understanding memory reliability, particularly in legal cases involving eyewitness testimony, and may inform future research on psychiatric conditions where patients experience a distorted sense of reality.

Scientists have, for the first time, created human embryonic stem cells using a cloning method that inserts skin cell DNA into a donated unfertilized egg. This breakthrough, though an important step, produced cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes, making them useful only for research rather than medical treatments. The ultimate aim is to generate patient-specific stem cells to treat diseases like Parkinson’s and diabetes, but the next hurdle is refining the technique to avoid chromosomal abnormalities. The field still faces challenges, and researchers emphasize the need to better understand egg cell biology to improve reprogramming methods.

The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess for their groundbreaking discovery that the universe’s expansion is accelerating, not slowing down. Their work, based on observations of distant supernovae, revealed that a mysterious force called dark energy makes up about 74 percent of the universe and counteracts gravity. This finding transformed cosmology and suggests the universe will keep expanding indefinitely rather than collapsing. The discovery has become a central puzzle in modern physics, deepening the mystery of what drives cosmic acceleration.

NASA experts say humanity is on the verge of discovering another Earth and signs of alien life, thanks to rapid advances in space technology. The Kepler telescope revealed that our galaxy contains at least 100 billion planets, including the first Earth-sized world in a habitable zone. Upcoming instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope will be able to detect atmospheric gases produced by life, offering the first real chance to identify biosignatures on distant worlds. With nearly every star likely hosting planets, the panel believes finding life beyond Earth is highly probable.

Mexican authorities raided a squalid shelter in Michoacán, Mexico, after parents complained they were denied access to their children, and found nearly 500 minors living in horrific conditions. The children endured physical, psychological, and sexual abuse, were forced to beg, and slept on filthy floors infested with rats and roaches. The shelter’s operator, Rosa del Carmen Verduzco, and eight employees were detained, with allegations that babies born there were registered under her name and that some victims were kept against their will for years. Authorities were working to clean the facility since the children could not be moved immediately.

Scotland votes today in a historic independence referendum, with a record 4.2 million people registered to decide whether the nation should leave the United Kingdom. Polls opened across 32 districts, from remote islands to major cities, and results are expected early Friday morning. Both campaign leaders, Alex Salmond for independence and Alistair Darling for union, have cast their ballots, and turnout is expected to be high. For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are eligible to vote, alongside Commonwealth, Irish, and EU citizens living in Scotland.

With Scotland’s independence referendum days away and polls showing a tight race, the leaders of the UK’s three main parties jointly pledged to grant Scotland broader devolved powers if voters choose to remain in the Union. The pro-independence side, led by Alex Salmond, argues that a Yes vote is a once-in-a-lifetime chance for Scotland to control its own taxes and spending, while unionists warn that separation would be irreversible and economically risky. Key unresolved issues include currency, fiscal policy, and the future of the UK’s nuclear submarine fleet based in Scotland. The United States has also expressed its preference for a strong and united UK, though it respects Scotland’s decision.

A man arrested in Beverly Hills allegedly gave police the name of Stone Temple Pilots singer Scott Weiland, convincing authorities he was the musician. The real Weiland quickly posted a video denying the arrest and saying he had been touring and recording. Police initially stood by their identification, but later admitted a fingerprint check revealed the suspect was actually 44-year-old Jason Michael Hurley. Hurley now likely faces additional charges for providing false information to police.

Swedish filmmaker Malik Bendjelloul, who won an Oscar for his documentary “Searching for Sugar Man,” died suddenly in Stockholm at age 36; police said no crime is suspected. His acclaimed debut film told the story of Sixto Rodriguez, a little-known American singer who became an anti-apartheid icon in South Africa. After running out of funds, Bendjelloul completed the documentary using a low-cost iPhone app. He was remembered by colleagues as a passionate, genuine storyteller who sought meaningful narratives rather than fame.

Rescue efforts for three missing climbers on Nepal’s Mount Manaslu were called off after an avalanche swept through camps, leaving eight confirmed dead and raising fears the toll could reach eleven. The disaster, triggered by a massive falling ice block, also injured twelve climbers and destroyed or damaged dozens of tents. Survivors described being buried in snow and tumbling hundreds of meters, with one American rescued from his tent still in his sleeping bag. Difficult terrain and deep crevasses are expected to hamper any further search or body recovery.

Nigerians took to the streets in largely peaceful protests after the government abruptly ended fuel subsidies, causing petrol prices to more than double overnight. Demonstrators, frustrated by corruption, poor infrastructure, and high living costs, accused officials of imposing the hike without preparation or consideration for ordinary citizens. The government defended the move as necessary for economic reform, saying savings would be invested elsewhere, while protesters demanded the old price be restored. Widespread anger also reflected deeper distrust of the administration, with many linking the issue to unemployment, unreliable electricity, and broader governance failures.

The National Institutes of Health confirmed that former NFL linebacker Junior Seau had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head trauma, after his family donated his brain for research. Seau, who died by suicide at age 43, had never been diagnosed with a concussion during his career, underscoring that CTE can develop even without a documented concussion history. His case adds to a growing list of high-profile football players found posthumously to have the disease, which can cause memory loss, aggression, and depression. In response, the NFL acknowledged the need for more research, while the players' union called for independent medical oversight and safer conditions in professional football.

Two infants born with HIV who received aggressive antiretroviral treatment within hours of birth have shown no detectable virus in their blood, raising hopes for a potential functional cure. The first child, in Mississippi, stopped medication after about 15 months and has remained virus-free for nearly two years, while a California baby is still on treatment, so remission is not yet confirmed. Researchers believe very early therapy may prevent HIV from establishing lifelong viral reservoirs, but they stress that larger clinical trials are needed before changing standard care. The only other known cure, the "Berlin patient," involved a risky bone marrow transplant with a rare genetic mutation and is not a viable option for most patients.

The Netherlands has reported a second MERS case, following the first confirmed a day earlier, with both patients being family members who shared a room during a trip to Saudi Arabia. One of them had visited a camel farm, and both had underlying health conditions that may have increased their susceptibility. The World Health Organization has raised concern about the virus’s spread but has not declared a global health emergency. MERS, which has caused over 570 infections and 171 deaths, has also appeared in the United States in two healthcare workers who had been in Saudi Arabia.

The CDC has confirmed a second U.S. case of MERS, this time in Florida, involving a health care worker who had recently traveled from Saudi Arabia. Officials stress that this case is unrelated to the first one reported in Indiana and that the risk to the general public remains very low. Health authorities are tracing and testing people who may have had close contact with the patient, including airline passengers and hospital staff. The article also notes that MERS has caused over 500 infections globally, with no easy person-to-person spread in community settings, and that camels are suspected as a source of the virus.

Chris Brown’s legal team is positioning his bodyguard as the one responsible for the alleged assault, claiming the guard acted to protect Brown when a man tried to board his tour bus. The defense may also challenge the credibility of a police officer, citing a reported overheard comment that the alleged victim admitted Brown never hit him. The Washington case is critical because Brown is on felony probation in California for the 2009 attack on Rihanna, and any violation could lead to prison time. Meanwhile, Brown has entered a rehab facility, which his lawyers may use to show he is addressing his behavioral issues.

A Reddit user asked medical professionals and first responders to share deathbed confessions they had heard, sparking thousands of unverified but powerful stories. The responses included moments of deep guilt, family secrets, apologies, and heartbreaking final words, ranging from a son learning he was not biologically related to his father to a grandfather confessing he was gay. Some stories were humorous, like a man’s last words about dying naked, while others reflected regret, fear, and the desire to make amends. Overall, the thread showcased the internet’s capacity for genuine, awkward, and moving human connection.

Narendra Modi’s government faces the major challenge of securing India’s growing energy needs, which will require both competition and cooperation with major powers like China, the U.S., and Russia. India is set to become the world’s largest energy demand driver and coal importer within the next decade, yet it still struggles with widespread power shortages and weak infrastructure. Modi’s strategy emphasizes diversifying fuel sources and suppliers, including possible Russian gas pipelines, while relying on coal as the main power source and expanding renewables and domestic shale, though water scarcity limits fracking. His approach to energy diplomacy and domestic supply development will likely define his administration’s success.

U.S. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel visited Afghanistan and said Afghan officials assured him a bilateral security agreement would be signed soon, despite ongoing delays. The pact, which would allow some U.S. and coalition troops to remain after 2014, has been endorsed by Afghan tribal leaders but President Hamid Karzai refuses to sign until after April elections and certain conditions are met. Washington has resisted those conditions, and NATO has warned it may withdraw all troops if no deal is reached. Meanwhile, Karzai is visiting Iran, which has publicly opposed the security agreement.

The Obama administration is increasing security measures for certain international flights heading to the U.S., driven by worries that terrorist groups are creating more advanced explosives that could bypass airport detection. Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson announced that the TSA would implement enhanced screening at select overseas airports, though specific locations and procedures were not revealed. Officials indicated there was no confirmed plot and no immediate changes to carry-on rules, but the heightened vigilance reflects ongoing concerns about al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula’s efforts to develop undetectable bombs, especially after the 2009 underwear bomb attempt.

The article highlights the public misunderstanding of seizures and epilepsy, using Commerce Secretary John Bryson’s recent seizure-related car crash as a catalyst for discussion. It emphasizes that seizures are common—affecting up to 10% of people at some point—and that a single seizure does not necessarily mean epilepsy. Experts and people living with the condition stress that epilepsy is often a hidden disorder, can emerge at any age, and is manageable in most cases, yet stigma and fear of judgment often prevent open conversation. Personal accounts from individuals like Nathan Jones and Kevin Oliver illustrate the vulnerability, embarrassment, and need for public education and empathy.

A study on selfie behavior found that while women generally post more selfies than men, the trend flips after age 40, with men becoming more active. The article suggests this shift may stem from women’s greater insecurity about visible aging, while men over 40 might seek attention or reassurance. It also highlights a broader societal issue: women’s beauty and value are too often tied to youth. The author encourages women over 40 to embrace their appearance and post more selfies, arguing that beauty and worth should be recognized at every age.

The U.S. Senate approved new economic sanctions targeting Iran’s financial institutions, including its central bank, despite strong objections from the Obama administration. Officials warned the measure could raise global oil prices and inadvertently provide Iran with more revenue, undermining efforts to curb its nuclear program. Around the same time, the European Union also agreed to impose additional sanctions on dozens of Iranian entities and individuals. The measure was attached to a defense bill that also included controversial detainee policies, which the president has threatened to veto.

The Senate held a daylong budget debate that was largely symbolic, since none of the proposals had enough support to pass. Republicans forced votes on several budget plans, including President Obama’s and more conservative versions, while Democrats dismissed the exercise as political theater. The president’s budget received no votes, giving Republicans campaign ammunition, while Democrats argued the plans were outdated or would harm social programs. The event highlighted ongoing partisan gridlock, with both sides accusing the other of prioritizing political advantage over real solutions.

Senegal has reported its first Ebola case, a Guinean university student now quarantined in Dakar, making it the fifth country affected in the outbreak. The case emerged shortly after Senegal closed its border with Guinea, though the WHO has cautioned that such travel bans can hinder relief efforts. The outbreak remains centered in Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia, with more than 3,000 cases and over 1,500 deaths recorded. Health workers have been especially hard hit, with hundreds infected and more than a hundred killed.

Lake Retba, a striking pink lake in Senegal, draws West African migrant workers who harvest salt from its highly saline waters, which can exceed the Dead Sea's salt levels. The pink color comes from a micro-algae thriving in the salty environment. Thousands of laborers, mostly men like Moussa Fame from Mali, work long hours with basic tools, protecting their skin with shea butter, while women transport the salt onshore. The harvested salt is largely exported across West Africa, supporting local livelihoods despite the harsh conditions.

A senior al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula operative linked to the 2000 USS Cole bombing was killed in a CIA drone strike in Yemen. The militant, Fahd al Quso, had been among Yemen’s most-wanted terrorists and escaped prison in 2003. The strike coincided with a broader Yemeni military offensive that killed dozens of suspected militants in Abyan province. Yemen’s president vowed to keep up the campaign against al Qaeda until the group is eliminated.

A Missouri couple in their seventies has been charged in connection with cold-case murders dating back decades. The wife is accused of fatally shooting her ex-husband in the 1970s and hiding his body in a mine, while the husband faces murder charges for allegedly killing his ex-wife and her two children in 1980. The arrests came after investigators followed up on the wife’s case and gathered more evidence. Neighbors expressed shock, saying the couple seemed like ordinary, churchgoing people who kept to themselves.

A man serving a mandatory double-life sentence for a nonviolent LSD conspiracy may benefit from new federal clemency reforms. The Justice Department has broadened its criteria to consider low-level drug offenders who have served at least 10 years, shown good conduct, and received sentences that would be shorter under current laws. Thousands of inmates could become eligible, though only a fraction may ultimately qualify. The prisoner, who refused to testify against his father, remains hopeful that President Obama will commute his sentence.

Six Zimbabweans convicted for watching Arab Spring protest videos face sentencing, with delays as their lawyer pleads for leniency. The charges stem from a 2011 academic meeting and carry up to ten years in prison, though critics and opposition figures dismiss the case as politically motivated repression. The government alleges the group plotted an Egyptian-style uprising, while rights activists say the verdict is meant to intimidate dissent under President Mugabe's long rule. The case highlights fears that North Africa's unrest could inspire similar movements in Zimbabwe.

South Korean officials confirmed that three small unmanned drones found near the border in March and April were sent by North Korea. The low-tech aircraft, equipped with consumer-style Japanese cameras, had photographed sensitive military sites, including islands near the demilitarized zone and the presidential Blue House. Although the drones slipped past South Korean air defenses, experts say they have limited range and capability, posing little serious threat. The incident comes amid heightened springtime tensions, including North Korean missile launches and warnings of a possible nuclear test.

FIFA has denied that Sepp Blatter questioned Qatar’s suitability as 2022 World Cup host, after he admitted in an interview that holding the tournament there in summer was a mistake due to extreme heat. The organization clarified that Blatter was only echoing earlier concerns about scheduling, not the choice of Qatar itself. The possibility of moving the event to winter is still under review, though such a shift would disrupt major football leagues and broadcasters. The decision to award Qatar the tournament has also drawn criticism over migrant workers’ conditions and human rights issues.

Serbian Prime Minister Ivica Dacic has expressed strong confidence that Serbia will be the next country to join the European Union, emphasizing the urgency due to the nation's severe economic challenges, including high unemployment and a brain drain. He believes EU membership is vital for attracting foreign investment and boosting industrial productivity, though he acknowledges it is not merely a financial aid package. The accession process is expected to take up to a decade, with experts noting that Montenegro might join before Serbia. Additionally, Dacic stressed the importance of resolving the Kosovo dispute through dialogue prior to joining, a step that could also help ease political tensions and improve economic prospects.

Several unverified eyewitness accounts have emerged in the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, each claiming to have seen the missing jet. Reports include fishermen near Malaysia spotting a low-flying plane, an oil rig worker off Vietnam seeing a burning aircraft, islanders in the Maldives describing a low jumbo jet, and Indonesian fishermen alleging a crash in the Strait of Malacca. However, none of these sightings have been confirmed by officials, and radar data and searches have failed to corroborate the claims. The unsubstantiated reports only deepen the ongoing mystery surrounding the disappearance of the Boeing 777 and the 239 people on board.

The captain and three senior crew members of the sunken South Korean ferry Sewol have been formally charged with murder, as prosecutors say they abandoned the ship while hundreds of passengers remained trapped inside and could face the death penalty. The remaining 11 crew members face lesser charges of abandonment and safety violations. The disaster, which killed over 280 people—mostly students—has sparked public fury over safety lapses and the crew's failure to evacuate passengers. Meanwhile, recovery efforts are becoming more difficult as strong currents and the deteriorating structure of the submerged vessel hamper search operations.

A helicopter carrying emergency personnel returning from the Sewol ferry rescue mission crashed in an urban area of Gwangju, killing five people and injuring one. The victims included pilots, rescue workers, and a mechanic, and the cause of the crash remains unknown. The crew had been supporting the search for victims of the April ferry disaster, which killed at least 292 people, mostly students, with eleven still missing.

A landmark trial has begun in Philadelphia, marking the first time a senior Roman Catholic archdiocese official is being prosecuted for allegedly covering up child sexual abuse by priests. Monsignor William Lynn is accused of endangering children by protecting abusive clergy, including the Rev. James Brennan, who faces his own assault charge. A third defendant, defrocked priest Edward Avery, pleaded guilty just before trial and was sentenced to prison. The case is seen as historic because it extends criminal liability beyond the abusers to church leadership responsible for concealing their crimes.

The article argues that parents who oppose school-based sex education are unrealistic, since young people are already engaging in sexual activity and need accurate information to protect themselves. It praises New York City for requiring sex education, including condom demonstrations, and criticizes abstinence-only advocates for trying to let parents opt out. The author believes both abstinence and safe-sex practices should be taught, as comprehensive education is essential to reducing teen pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. Ultimately, schools must provide this instruction because many parents fail to address these issues honestly at home.

William Boyd’s new novel, *Waiting for Sunrise*, follows an English actor in pre-war Vienna who, while seeking psychoanalytic treatment, embarks on an affair and later becomes entangled in espionage after war breaks out. The story blends sex, spying, and early psychology, featuring Sigmund Freud as a historical cameo. The article also covers Boyd’s recent appointment to write the next James Bond novel, which he plans to set in 1969, imagining what a Bond story by Ian Fleming might have been had he lived. Boyd describes the opportunity as a natural fit given his familiarity with Fleming’s world and the espionage genre.

Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl has transitioned from inpatient care to outpatient treatment at Joint Base San Antonio-Fort Sam Houston as part of his ongoing reintegration following five years in Taliban captivity. His release came in exchange for five Guantanamo Bay detainees, and he is the first junior enlisted soldier to undergo this specific military reintegration program. The process now involves gradually increasing social interaction and continued psychological counseling to prepare him for a return to duty. Meanwhile, an investigation into the circumstances of his disappearance, including allegations of desertion, remains on hold until his reintegration team approves an interview.

Shakhtar Donetsk’s president has warned six players who refused to return to Ukraine after a friendly in France that they will face consequences for breaching their contracts, including potentially hefty release clauses. He urged the players to come back, promising security and saying the club would not put them in dangerous areas. The reigning Ukrainian champions are weakened for their upcoming Super Cup match and cannot play at home in Donetsk because of the ongoing conflict, with the president hoping to host games in Kharkiv instead. The unrest has also forced UEFA to relocate Ukrainian clubs’ European matches to safer cities and prevent Ukrainian and Russian teams from being drawn against each other.

Shakira and Gerard Pique welcomed their first child, a son named Milan, born Tuesday night in Barcelona. The name means “dear,” “loving,” and “gracious” in Slavic, with additional meanings in Ancient Roman and Sanskrit. The couple marked the birth by encouraging donations to UNICEF in lieu of gifts, and the baby was made an honorary member of FC Barcelona, following in his father’s footsteps. Both mother and child are reported to be in excellent health.

A long-distance swimmer in California survived a terrifying great white shark attack near Manhattan Beach after the shark, likely agitated by a fishing hook, bit his torso. He managed to pry the shark off and made it to shore with help, but the trauma may keep him from ever swimming in open water again. The beach pier was closed temporarily as a precaution. While shark attacks have gradually risen over the decades, experts note this reflects more people spending time in the ocean rather than a higher attack rate.

The Middle East's private jet market, though small globally, is fiercely competitive due to the high expectations of its wealthy clientele, who demand a complete luxury experience from start to finish. Operators differentiate themselves through bespoke services, including cultural customization like separate men’s and women’s areas and specific bedroom placements. However, the industry faces a major challenge from the "gray market," where private owners undercut legitimate charter companies by renting out planes without the same regulatory oversight. To counter this, established firms emphasize their safety standards, pilot expertise, and premium service to maintain client loyalty.

Virginia state Sen. Creigh Deeds was stabbed multiple times by his 24-year-old son, who then fatally shot himself. The day before, deputies had responded to a nonemergency call at the home, and the son was taken for a mental health evaluation but released because no psychiatric bed could be found within the required four-hour window, despite beds being available at nearby hospitals. Deeds was hospitalized in good condition, and the incident prompted shock and condolences from Virginia political figures, including Governor Bob McDonnell.

A Las Vegas couple carried out a shooting spree that killed two police officers and a civilian before dying in an apparent suicide pact. Authorities say the attackers held anti-government beliefs, viewing law enforcement as oppressors, and left symbols such as a “Don’t Tread on Me” flag and a swastika, along with a note calling the attack the start of a revolution. The couple ambushed the officers at a pizza restaurant, then moved to a Walmart, where a bystander was fatally shot while trying to intervene. Police believe the pair acted alone and were prepared for a prolonged gunfight, and they are urging the public to report suspicious threats.

A 20-year-old student, Dylan Quick, was arrested after a stabbing spree at Lone Star College’s CyFair campus near Houston that wounded 14 people, several seriously. Authorities said he admitted to having long-held fantasies of killing people and to planning the attack in advance. Witnesses described chaotic scenes as students and staff fled, while some tackled and held the suspect until police arrived. The campus was locked down during the investigation and later reopened, with the incident occurring just months after a shooting at another Lone Star College campus.

Singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow has revealed that she was diagnosed with a noncancerous brain tumor called a meningioma, which she described as a minor setback. The growth was found months ago after she sought medical attention for memory issues, and while it does not require surgery, she will undergo regular scans to monitor it. Crow, who has previously battled breast cancer, reassured fans that she is doing well and feels grateful for their support.

Lyndsey Scott, a high-fashion model who has worked with brands like Prada and Victoria’s Secret, is also a self-taught software developer who creates mobile apps in her spare time. She first learned to code as a teenager on her graphing calculator and later studied computer science in college, though she initially pursued modeling. Scott has developed several iOS apps, including one that helps Ugandan students and another for organizing modeling portfolios, and she sees coding as a way to have creative control that modeling lacks. She also speaks out against stereotypes in tech, encouraging more women and minorities to pursue programming.

Cognitive neuroscientist Martha Farah has built a career bridging brain science and social issues, moving from early work on visual recognition to studying how poverty and social class shape brain development. Her research suggests that stressful, less nurturing childhood environments are linked to altered stress responses and brain structure, though she cautions against viewing these effects as permanent. Farah also highlights the difficulty of funding such work, noting that poverty-related neuroscience receives far less attention than conditions like autism despite affecting many more children. Her ongoing studies aim to trace how socioeconomic disparities influence the brain from infancy onward.

Shezanne Cassim, a U.S. citizen from Minnesota, returned home after spending nine months in a UAE prison for posting a satirical YouTube video about Dubai teenagers. He condemned his treatment, saying he was convicted without evidence in a "kangaroo court" and was not told the charges for months. Cassim believes his detention was meant to intimidate the public and suppress criticism of the government. U.S. officials confirmed he was released to deportation processing after receiving credit for good behavior.

Shia LaBeouf is voluntarily receiving treatment for alcohol addiction, though his representatives clarified he has not entered a rehabilitation facility. This follows his recent arrest in New York after he allegedly disrupted a Broadway performance while intoxicated and was charged with criminal trespass, disorderly conduct, and harassment. The actor has a history of legal troubles, including past arrests for DUI and public intoxication, as well as recent eccentric behavior like wearing a paper bag at the Berlin Film Festival. He is scheduled to appear in court in late July.

In a historic breakthrough, President Barack Obama and Iranian President Hassan Rouhani spoke by phone, marking the first direct U.S.-Iranian leader contact since 1979. Both leaders signaled openness to resolving the nuclear dispute, with Obama stressing that any deal must involve transparent and verifiable Iranian actions in exchange for sanctions relief. The call followed a rare high-level meeting between U.S. and Iranian diplomats and set the stage for continued negotiations between Iran and world powers. While acknowledging deep mistrust and significant obstacles, Obama expressed cautious hope that diplomacy could succeed under Iran's new leadership.

After nearly three years in captivity, the 22 surviving crew members of the MV Iceberg 1 were rescued by Somali forces in a two-week operation, ending the longest known hostage ordeal involving pirates. The hostages, who endured severe conditions including abuse, illness, and limited food, came from several countries and were reported to be in good health. Two crew members died during the hijacking—one killed by pirates and one by suicide. The rescue highlighted ongoing concerns for the 139 people still held by pirates, even as global piracy has declined to its lowest level since 2008.

Shirahama, a historic Japanese seaside resort, offers a mix of traditional onsen bathing—where nudity is mandatory, as at the 1,300-year-old Sakinoyu Onsen—and modern attractions. Beyond the hot springs, visitors can enjoy an Australian-imported white-sand beach, Adventure World’s famous giant pandas, dramatic cliffs and sea caves, and the moon-shaped Engetsu Island. The town is also known for fresh seafood markets and BBQ dining, plus locally produced umeshu plum liqueur. With convenient train access and a range of hotels, Shirahama blends cultural tradition, nature, and family-friendly activities.

The release of “The Dark Knight Rises” was highly anticipated, with advance ticket sales surpassing those of “The Avengers,” but the excitement was overshadowed by a deadly shooting at a midnight screening in Aurora, Colorado. The tragedy prompted Warner Bros. to cancel the film’s Paris premiere and pull a trailer containing theater gun violence, while experts said the attack’s effect on box office revenue was uncertain. Many noted that the film’s global appeal and lack of major competition could limit financial damage, though the immediate focus remained on the victims and their families.
