Many analysts believed the film’s global appeal and lack of major competition would limit financial losses, though the immediate focus remained on the victims. Past franchise tragedy, such as Heath Ledger’s death, did not hurt the series’ legacy, suggesting the film may still endure.

A judge has delayed James Holmes’ scheduled court hearing until December 10 after his defense said he was medically unable to appear, citing a newly developed but undisclosed condition. Holmes was taken to a hospital, though attorneys declined to reveal details, arguing his medical and psychiatric information is privileged. The case involves the Aurora theater shooting, where Holmes is charged with murder, attempted murder, and weapons offenses in the attack that killed 12 and wounded 58. A gag order has kept officials from releasing further information about his condition.

After the deadly attack on the U.S. consulate in Libya, YouTube temporarily restricted access to an anti-Islam video in Egypt and Libya, even though the company said the video did not violate its guidelines. The article argues that Google acted as an arbitrary censor by making this decision on its own, rather than following a legal order or a clear policy. It points out that this approach is inconsistent and risky, especially compared to Twitter’s stance of only withholding content when legally required and doing so transparently. Ultimately, the piece warns that Google’s unilateral move could set a troubling precedent and invite pressure from governments and other groups.

The article explores whether Santa Claus should be portrayed as slimmer given rising childhood obesity rates and his influence as a widely recognized figure. It highlights a professional Santa who lost 88 pounds and now promotes a healthier image, while experts note that weight alone doesn't determine health and that Santa’s traditional roundness is culturally entrenched. The piece acknowledges that changing Santa’s appearance is difficult because of tradition, but suggests families can adapt the story to encourage healthier habits. Ultimately, it argues that Santa could evolve into a positive health role model without losing the magic of Christmas.

Egypt braced for a possible military intervention after President Mohamed Morsy rejected the army’s ultimatum to resolve the country’s political crisis, with deadly clashes between his supporters and opponents killing at least 16 people and wounding hundreds. The military vowed to defend Egypt and threatened to suspend the constitution and sideline the president unless he agreed to a power-sharing deal by Wednesday evening. Morsy insisted he was democratically elected and refused to step down or call early elections, while the opposition accused him of authoritarianism and economic failure. The United States urged new elections but warned the military that a coup would jeopardize U.S. aid.

Sid Bernstein, the promoter credited with introducing the Beatles to American audiences, has passed away at age 95 in New York. He organized the band’s early U.S. performances, including a Carnegie Hall show and their historic Shea Stadium concerts, helping spark the British Invasion. Bernstein took a major risk on the then-unknown group despite initial resistance from radio and financial backers. He also worked with other legendary artists and is survived by his wife, children, and grandchildren.

The penalty phase of Joshua Komisarjevsky’s trial has concluded, with both sides resting; closing arguments are set for Friday, after which the jury will decide whether he receives life in prison or the death penalty. Komisarjevsky was previously convicted of 17 charges related to the 2007 Connecticut home invasion that killed Jennifer Hawke-Petit and her two daughters. His defense argued that he had no prior violent history, had been abused as a child, and has adapted well to prison life. His accomplice, Steven Hayes, was already sentenced to death in a separate trial.

Bobby “Blue” Bland, the influential soul-blues singer, has died at age 83 at his Tennessee home, with his son confirming he passed from natural causes after battling a tumorous stomach condition. Known as a key architect of the modern soul-blues sound, Bland rose to fame with hits like “I Pity the Fool” and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1992. His music remained culturally significant, as Jay-Z later sampled his song “Ain't No Love in the Heart of the City.” Those close to him remembered him as humble and gracious with fans throughout his long career.

A woman known as “Black Madam” has been charged with third-degree murder in the 2011 death of a British woman who died from a silicone injection to her buttocks performed in a Philadelphia hotel room. The defendant, already in custody for a similar illegal procedure, allegedly met the victim through an online ad and charged her $1,800 for the botched operation. Prosecutors say she showed no remorse and continued promoting such procedures, which have raised concerns among health officials about the dangers of unlicensed cosmetic injections. The case highlights the serious health risks of underground body-enhancement practices, which have led to hospitalizations and even death.

Chris Brown faces new misdemeanor charges for a minor hit-and-run and driving without a a license in Los Angeles, adding to his existing legal troubles. He is already on probation for assaulting Rihanna, and this new arrest could lead a judge to revoke that probation. Brown denied the allegations on Twitter, claiming he exchanged information and that there was no damage. Separately, he is also under investigation for an alleged altercation at a nightclub, which his representative has denied.

At a routine probation hearing, Chris Brown’s lawyer stopped him from speaking, joking that Brown shouldn’t talk, which led to a lighthearted exchange with the judge. The singer is three years into his probation for the 2009 assault on Rihanna and has completed his community service and other requirements. The court noted his upcoming travel to Trinidad, and a past positive marijuana test in Virginia was not brought up since it was reportedly tied to his legal medical use in California. Brown is scheduled to return to court for his next progress report in January 2013.

Sharon Jones & the Dap-Kings have postponed their upcoming tour and album release after Jones was diagnosed with stage 1 bile duct cancer. She says the cancer was detected early and is considered operable and curable, and she will undergo surgery soon, followed by a recovery period. As a result, the planned August release of "Give the People What They Want" is delayed. Jones remains optimistic and promises to keep fans updated, with plans to reschedule shows and release the album once she has recovered.

Carmen Zapata, a Mexican-American actress best known for playing a choir nun in “Sister Act” and its sequel, has died at age 86 in Los Angeles due to heart problems. She co-founded the Bilingual Foundation of the Arts in 1973 to promote bilingual theater and Hispanic cultural heritage. Over a six-decade career, she worked extensively on stage and television, beginning on Broadway in the 1940s and later appearing in numerous series. She was also honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was knighted by Spain’s King Juan Carlos.

A roller coaster car at Six Flags Magic Mountain derailed Monday evening after a tree branch fell onto the track, leaving the front car dangling at a steep angle about 20 feet above the ground. All 22 passengers were eventually rescued, with four people injured and two taken to the hospital as a precaution. The incident adds to a history of amusement ride accidents, including a fatal fall at a Six Flags park in Texas and broader statistics showing thousands of ride-related child injuries annually.

A skin cancer drug called bexarotene rapidly reversed memory loss and cleared more than half of Alzheimer’s-related brain plaque in mice, according to a new study. While the results were dramatic, researchers stressed that the drug has not been proven to work in humans and that many Alzheimer’s treatments that succeeded in mice later failed. Because bexarotene is already FDA-approved for cancer, human trials could begin soon, with researchers planning to test it at standard cancer doses. The Alzheimer’s Association is funding the next phase of research, though side effects like increased cholesterol may require lower doses.

China’s Sky City, an 838-meter tower in Changsha, is set to overtake Dubai’s Burj Khalifa as the world’s tallest building, with construction expected to finish in just ten months. The project relies on a prefabricated block assembly method that the builder claims is fast and efficient, though experts and the public have raised doubts about safety and livability. The tower is designed as a self-contained community, housing thousands of residents with schools, hospitals, offices, and entertainment. It reflects China’s broader skyscraper boom, as the country is expected to far surpass the United States in the number of tall buildings by 2022.

A Utah soccer referee died after a 17-year-old player punched him during a youth match, following years of prior violence he had endured in the sport. The man’s daughter said he knew the risks but continued refereeing out of passion, and the family is now in shock. The teenager is in juvenile detention, and authorities plan to upgrade his charges from aggravated assault after the referee’s death. The case echoes a similar fatal attack on a linesman in the Netherlands months earlier.

The Golden Globe nominations were unveiled, with “12 Years a Slave” and “American Hustle” emerging as the front-runners across drama and comedy/musical categories, respectively. Both films earned multiple nods, including best picture, director, acting, and screenplay recognition. Other notable nominees included “Gravity,” “Captain Phillips,” “Nebraska,” and “The Wolf of Wall Street.” The awards ceremony is set to air on NBC on January 12, hosted by Amy Poehler and Tina Fey.

CNN received three honors at the Foreign Press Association Media Awards, winning for its documentary on the Belfast Project, a feature exposing modern slavery in Mauritania, and a film about a rediscovered Leonardo da Vinci painting. Judges praised the winning entries for their compelling storytelling and cultural depth. CNN executives highlighted the recognition as a testament to their journalism, with the Mauritania piece noted for supporting the network’s Freedom Project advocacy. The network also earned nominations for its coverage of Aleppo and its digital innovation.

The stabbing of a 12-year-old girl by two friends seeking to please the fictional online character Slenderman has alarmed parents about children’s ability to separate digital fantasy from reality. Experts note that while most 12-year-olds can distinguish between the two, incomplete brain development, intense peer dynamics, and exposure to violent media may all play a role in extreme behavior. They emphasize that such acts rarely stem from a single cause and that warning signs like social withdrawal or self-harm should be taken seriously. Ultimately, parents are urged to stay engaged, maintain open conversations, and monitor their children’s online activity, even though no approach can guarantee prevention.

A small Colorado town is considering a measure that would let residents shoot down federal drones, with hunting licenses and bounties proposed as part of the plan. Supporters frame it as a symbolic stand against government surveillance and domestic drone expansion, though they admit it is unlikely to be used in practice. Town officials see it as a way to draw attention, tourism, and revenue, while state authorities dismiss it as legally meaningless since federal law prohibits damaging government property.

Small, low-cost Android tablets such as the Kobo Vox, Kindle Fire, and Nook Color are entering the U.S. market at around $200–$250, offering a more affordable and portable alternative to the iPad. These devices could help bridge the digital divide by giving people with limited resources easier access to the web, apps, education, and job opportunities. However, they face challenges including variable device quality, a steep learning curve for Android, and restrictions that may limit access to the full Android app marketplace. Their long-term impact will likely become clearer during the upcoming holiday season and beyond.

Football helmet manufacturers are introducing impact-sensing technology designed to measure the force of hits and alert sideline staff when a player may have suffered a dangerous blow. This innovation comes amid growing concern over head injuries in football, including lawsuits from former players and worries about young athletes. Riddell’s new SpeedFlex helmet integrates sensors that send wireless warnings to coaches, but experts caution that the devices are not always accurate and should not be overtrusted. Companies emphasize that the systems do not diagnose concussions, but rather provide additional information to help guide decisions about player safety.

The article introduces the HapiFork, a smart utensil that tracks how quickly people eat by counting bites and vibrating as a gentle reminder to slow down. It is part of the broader quantified-self movement, where people use technology to measure daily habits and improve their health. The fork syncs data to a smartphone, offers coaching features, and is designed to help prevent overeating by encouraging slower eating, which may reduce risks like obesity and diabetes. The device is being launched through a Kickstarter campaign, with early users helping test its effectiveness in changing eating behavior.

New Jersey’s decade-old smart gun law could soon take effect as personalized firearms that only work for authorized users near the U.S. market. The technology, which uses features like fingerprint recognition or radio-frequency watches, has intensified the gun debate: supporters see it as a safety breakthrough, while opponents argue it forces consumers to rely on unproven devices. Several manufacturers, including Armatix and Kodiak Industries, are close to selling such guns, which would require New Jersey’s attorney general to determine whether the technology meets legal standards. If activated, the law would make smart guns the only handguns sold in the state within three years.

China is poised to overtake the U.S. as the largest smartphone market, driven by falling device prices and cheaper data plans. A key driver is the widespread adoption of smartphones by young migrant workers, who now use them for news, entertainment, and staying connected, replacing old basic phones. This technology is enabling migrants to share their experiences and grievances on social media platforms like Sina Weibo, where they have occasionally won public support, such as in a successful campaign to save a migrant children's school in Beijing. While such activism remains rare and migrants are still largely marginalized, experts see this as a significant sign of potential future social and political engagement.

The digital age has blurred the boundaries between work and home, allowing constant connectivity but also eroding personal time and focus. While workplace flexibility has increased, true time off has declined, and many professionals feel tethered to their devices around the clock. This blending of roles can lead to longer hours and diminished quality in both work and family life, as attention becomes fragmented. Ultimately, the article argues that preserving distinct moments and contexts matters more than ever.

A French company has unveiled a new smart electric toothbrush called Kolibree at CES in Las Vegas. It connects to a smartphone app via Bluetooth to monitor brushing duration, mouth coverage, and technique, turning oral care into a game to motivate children and adults. The device can also share brushing data with social networks or a dentist, and was inspired by its inventor’s desire to verify whether his kids actually brushed. Prices range from $99 to $200, with pre-orders expected this summer.

Acadia National Park in Maine is the easternmost national park in the continental U.S., known for its dramatic sunrises over pink granite and its diverse coastal landscapes. It attracts nearly 2.5 million visitors annually and offers activities like scenic drives, hiking, camping, and wildlife viewing. Park ranger Charlie Jacobi recommends less-crowded trails, birdwatching spots, and notes that visitors should prepare for changing weather and seasonal fees. He also shares unique park moments, such as temporary waterfalls after heavy rain and an unusual helicopter blueberry-picking incident.

Edward Snowden’s chances of avoiding U.S. prosecution appeared to shrink as most of the 21 countries he approached either rejected his asylum request or said he must apply from their territory. Only Bolivia and Venezuela showed sympathy, but neither made a concrete offer, leaving him stranded in a Moscow airport transit zone without valid travel documents. The situation escalated when Bolivia accused France and Portugal of blocking President Evo Morales’s plane over false rumors that Snowden was aboard. Meanwhile, fresh leaks about U.S. surveillance of European officials sparked diplomatic tension and prompted European leaders to demand explanations from Washington.

The U.S. hockey team’s Olympic disappointment deepened when Finland shut them out 5-0 in the bronze-medal game, leaving the Americans without a men’s medal after earlier losses to Canada for both the men’s and women’s teams. Veteran Teemu Selanne scored twice in what was likely his final Olympic appearance, while Tuukka Rask recorded the shutout. Elsewhere, Austria’s Mario Matt became the oldest Olympic alpine skiing champion in the men’s slalom, and Norway’s Marit Bjoergen earned her record 10th women’s Winter Olympic medal. Russia’s Vic Wild made history as the first snowboarder to win two golds at the same Games, and the Netherlands dominated the speed skating team pursuits.

The 2014 Winter Olympics introduced a wave of extreme sports like slopestyle to attract younger audiences, bringing a relaxed, playful culture to the Games. American Joss Christensen, a little-known skier who qualified just before the event, won gold and led a historic U.S. sweep in men’s slopestyle skiing, dedicating his victory to his late father. The new events emphasize fun and personal style over rigid discipline, though some critics dismiss them as stunt-based entertainment. Still, Olympic and U.S. officials back the sports for their spectacle and medal potential.

Although Russia won the most medals overall at the Sochi Olympics, its per-capita performance was unimpressive, placing it outside the top ten. When adjusted for population, smaller countries fared much better, with Norway emerging as the clear leader by winning over five medals per million residents. Slovenia, Latvia, and Austria also ranked highly, while major nations like the United States and Canada dropped significantly in the per-capita standings.

Sochi is undergoing a massive, around-the-clock construction blitz ahead of the 2014 Winter Olympics, causing major traffic detours, dust, and disruption for residents. While infrastructure like roads and hotels remains unfinished, all ten sports venues are built and have already hosted major test events. Organizers insist they are on track and confident, despite concerns about last-minute changes and the warm climate. The biggest lingering risk is a lack of snow, though officials have stored snow and installed snowmaking equipment to guarantee conditions.

Russian figure skater Evgeny Plushenko withdrew from the men’s individual event at the Sochi Olympics due to a recurring back injury, shortly after helping Russia win team gold. He initially suggested the national skating federation had pressured him to compete despite his condition, but later clarified that he was misunderstood due to his limited English and that no pressure was applied. His withdrawal sparked controversy in Russia, with some officials and lawmakers criticizing him, while his wife defended him against media attacks. Plushenko also hinted that he might use his platform to advocate for gay rights in the country.

A newly surfaced jihadist video has threatened the Winter Olympics in Sochi, prompting Russian President Vladimir Putin to vow that the Games will be secure, with tens of thousands of security personnel deployed. The threat follows recent suicide bombings in Volgograd and ongoing Islamist insurgency in the North Caucasus. U.S. lawmakers expressed doubts about safety and called for greater intelligence sharing with Russia. The article also highlights concerns over Russia's anti-gay laws and the $45 billion cost, which critics say was inflated by corruption.

President Obama announced his support for same-sex marriage, a shift from his previous “evolving” stance, following pressure from fellow Democrats and the same day after North Carolina passed a ban on such unions. The move carries political risks in swing states with conservative voters, but may energize his base and appeal to independents seeking conviction. Mitt Romney reaffirmed his opposition to same-sex marriage, drawing a clear contrast with the president. However, analysts suggest social issues, while prominent, are unlikely to decide the 2012 election, as voters remain more focused on the economy and polls rank same-sex marriage low in importance.

Although many parents worry about the negative effects of social media on teens, research and anecdotal evidence suggest it can also boost confidence, strengthen friendships, and help isolated young people find communities with shared interests. Teens often receive supportive comments online, and many report feeling more outgoing and less shy because of social media. It also enables them to engage in social good, from raising money for causes to speaking out against injustice. Rather than banning these platforms, experts encourage parents to guide their children through the digital world, much like having conversations about other sensitive topics.

A new Pew Research survey across 21 countries shows that text messaging is now a global norm, with usage highest in poorer nations like Indonesia and Kenya. The report also highlights a notable gender gap in mobile internet use, particularly in Spain, Germany, and Turkey, where men are far more likely than women to go online via phone. Social networking remained stable in most countries but surged in Egypt and Russia, reflecting the role these platforms played in recent political protests. Overall, social media use is more prevalent in wealthier countries, largely due to higher internet access rates.

A controlled study found that consuming sugary drinks equivalent to about 25% of daily calories rapidly raised LDL cholesterol in healthy volunteers, highlighting the metabolic risks of added sugar. Public health experts argue that sugary beverages are an easy target in the fight against obesity and diabetes, since cutting them out can save significant calories without major lifestyle changes. The beverage industry pushes back, noting that soda consumption has declined and that its products can fit into a balanced diet. While obesity rates have leveled off alongside falling soda intake, experts caution that sweetened drinks are not the sole cause of the epidemic but remain a logical first place to intervene.

After weeks of silence, Beyoncé, Jay Z, and Solange Knowles issued a joint statement addressing the leaked elevator altercation. They acknowledged that both Jay Z and Solange share responsibility for the incident, have apologized to each other, and have moved forward as a family. The statement also denied reports that Solange was intoxicated or behaving erratically, emphasizing that the matter was a private family issue now resolved. They urged the public to let it go and respect their unity.

Thailand’s military seized control of the government after prolonged political unrest, a familiar scenario in a country with a long history of coups. Bangkok residents largely took the takeover in stride, with daily life continuing despite the imposition of martial law and a nationwide nighttime curfew. The political turmoil has taken a heavy toll on tourism, especially in Bangkok, where hotel occupancy and international bookings have dropped significantly. While some travelers remain undeterred and industry experts hope for a quick return to stability, Thailand’s tourism sector faces growing competition and uncertainty.

A U.N.-commissioned study found that the 2010–2012 famine in Somalia killed about 258,000 people, half of them children under five, making it one of the worst famines in recent decades. The report highlighted that the international community responded too slowly despite early drought warnings, while conflict and restricted humanitarian access deepened the crisis. Aid efforts after the official famine declaration helped reduce the worst effects, but millions in Somalia still need urgent assistance. Oxfam stressed that famines are political failures, not natural disasters, and urged world leaders to invest in long-term solutions to prevent any repeat.

African Union and Somali forces have launched a military operation in the Afgoye corridor near Mogadishu, a densely populated area packed with displaced people and controlled by the al Qaeda-linked militant group Al-Shabaab. The offensive aims to push the militants out so residents can access humanitarian aid and eventually return to the capital. The AU reported that three Ugandan soldiers were wounded, denied civilian casualties, and said their troops had advanced five kilometers despite militant resistance. Al-Shabaab, which has long fought Somalia’s weak government, has faced recent losses but continues to carry out attacks in Mogadishu.

Al-Shabaab has rejected Human Rights Watch’s allegations that it recruits child soldiers, arguing that under Islamic law individuals are considered adults at age 15 and therefore obligated to fight if Muslim lands are attacked. However, a new HRW report documents that the militant group has increasingly abducted children as young as 10, forcing them into combat, using them as human shields, and subjecting them to severe abuse, including rape and forced marriage. The report also criticizes Somalia’s transitional government for failing to fully stop its own recruitment of children, though the army chief said mistaken enlistments are discharged. The findings were released just before an international conference in London aimed at addressing Somalia’s instability.

Despite facing severe danger and a shattered sports infrastructure, Somalia’s national women’s basketball team achieved a historic victory over host nation Qatar at the 2011 Arab Games. The players trained under armed guard in Mogadishu due to threats from Al Shabaab militants, who view women’s sports as un-Islamic. Composed of players from Somalia and the diaspora, the team’s respectable performance is being hailed as a powerful symbol of unity and a potential peace-building tool for the war-torn country.

Despite renewed Republican vows to repeal or resist the Affordable Care Act after the Supreme Court upheld it, analysts say health care reform is already moving forward and cannot simply be stopped. Many states have made significant progress toward implementation, and private-sector initiatives are accelerating regardless of political opposition. While some GOP governors refuse to set up insurance exchanges or expand Medicaid, experts argue the federal funding incentives are too attractive for states to reject in the long run. The result will likely be a patchwork of implementation, with the law’s popular provisions already in effect and major changes arriving in 2014.

A graduate student at UC Santa Cruz lost her health insurance after hitting a lifetime cap under her university’s self-funded student health plan, leaving her unable to afford treatment for a rare neurological disorder. Although the Affordable Care Act generally bans such limits, these self-funded student plans are legally exempt from that requirement, and a proposed federal rule would allow them to keep capping benefits. About 300,000 students are covered by these plans, which are cheaper for universities because they cut out insurance companies. Students and advocates are protesting the loophole, arguing that legal technicalities should not deny young people the same protections as other insured Americans.

A South Korean ferry carrying hundreds of passengers capsized, leaving nearly 300 people missing and prompting a frantic rescue effort. In the aftermath, text messages reportedly from passengers described terrifying scenes of darkness, screaming, and final farewells to loved ones. However, police later said they believed messages sent after the sinking were fake, citing cell phone records showing no calls or texts from missing passengers following the disaster. The authenticity of earlier messages remained unclear.

Gerry Goffin, the renowned lyricist best known for his songwriting partnership with Carole King, passed away at age 75 from natural causes. Together, they created enduring hits like “Will You Love Me Tomorrow,” “The Loco-Motion,” and “Up on the Roof.” King paid tribute to him as her first love and a profound creative influence whose words resonated widely. His decades-spanning career produced numerous beloved songs, and he is survived by his wife, children, and grandchildren.

Lockheed Martin is developing the SR-72, a hypersonic successor to the retired SR-71 Blackbird, designed to fly at Mach 6 and carry missiles, unlike its predecessor. The aircraft would be an unmanned drone, and its extreme speed is intended to eliminate enemy reaction time, making speed the new form of stealth. A scaled-down prototype could be tested within five years, with a full-scale version potentially operational by 2030. However, development will likely require significant government funding from agencies like DARPA and the Air Force to move forward.

The adult son of a retired Los Angeles fire chief was arrested for allegedly bribing a TSA agent to let marijuana-laden suitcases pass through security at LAX. The plot was uncovered when a baggage handler noticed a strong odor from a checked bag, leading to the seizure of about 15 pounds of cannabis. The suspect admitted to making several similar trips and paying the officer $500 per bag. Both he and the TSA employee were released on bond and face arraignment in November.

Aaron Hernandez is under fresh scrutiny as a Massachusetts grand jury investigates him for alleged gun trafficking, including the illegal transport of weapons across state lines. As part of that probe, his former college teammate and current Miami Dolphins player Mike Pouncey was subpoenaed after a game. The investigation reportedly involves an assault-style rifle found in a Florida rental car that later turned up in Massachusetts. Hernandez, already facing a first-degree murder charge in the death of Odin Lloyd, is also being examined in connection with a separate 2012 double homicide.

Justin Bieber and his father reportedly ignored repeated requests from a charter flight crew to stop smoking marijuana during a trip from Canada to New Jersey, with the smoke so thick that crew members donned oxygen masks. The pilot claimed the singer and his father became verbally abusive, prompting the crew to keep their distance. Upon landing, federal agents detected a marijuana odor and searched the plane with drug-sniffing dogs, but no drugs were found. Bieber was briefly detained for questioning, adding to his ongoing legal troubles, which include assault, DUI, and vandalism charges.

Jerry Sandusky’s defense will have him evaluated by a prosecution psychologist before trial resumes Monday, after a judge allowed testimony about whether he has a personality disorder. The defense argues that his letters to alleged victims reflect histrionic personality disorder rather than the “grooming” tactics prosecutors describe. The evaluation is meant to let prosecutors prepare rebuttal testimony, and the trial schedule is unaffected. Sandusky, who faces dozens of child sexual abuse charges, maintains his innocence.

U.S. forces captured Ahmed Abu Khatallah, a key suspect in the 2012 Benghazi attack, in a quiet operation near Benghazi aided by Libyan intelligence. He is the first person taken into U.S. custody for the assault that killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Abu Khatallah is being questioned aboard a Navy ship before facing federal charges in the United States, with officials indicating more charges and arrests may follow. The arrest has also reignited political debate over embassy security and the Benghazi response, particularly involving Hillary Clinton.

A handwritten letter believed to be from the suspect in the ambush of two Pennsylvania State Police troopers has been recovered, describing how he carried out the shooting and fled. The letter does not explain a motive, and investigators are unsure whether it was left deliberately or by accident. The suspect, Eric Matthew Frein, remains at large after the September attack that killed one trooper and wounded another, despite a large-scale manhunt. Authorities also found evidence on his computer indicating the attack had been planned for years.

Steve Ballmer has agreed to purchase the Los Angeles Clippers for $2 billion from the Sterling family trust, pending NBA approval. The sale, which would be a record for an NBA franchise, still faces potential hurdles, including Donald Sterling’s consent and the league’s ongoing disciplinary process against him. Sterling’s attorney said his client wants to clear his name after being banned for racist comments and is not motivated by money. If completed, the deal would make Ballmer the team’s new owner, with no plans to move the franchise from Los Angeles.

The U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya, was hit by an improvised explosive device, causing damage to the front gate but no injuries. A jihadist group, the Imprisoned Omar Abdul Rahman Brigades, reportedly claimed responsibility, saying the attack avenged the recent death of senior al Qaeda leader Abu Yahya al-Libi. The group also threatened further strikes against U.S. interests. Washington condemned the attack, urged Libyan authorities to boost security around U.S. facilities, and insisted it would not alter U.S. engagement with Libya.

The United States will begin supplying Syrian rebels with small arms, ammunition, and possibly anti-tank weapons through the CIA, following the White House's determination that the Assad regime crossed a "red line" by using chemical weapons. The move has widened a rift with Russia and Syria, which dismiss the U.S. evidence as unconvincing, while Britain has expressed support. Although rebel leaders are pleading for heavier arms like anti-aircraft missiles, Washington has ruled out sending troops or enforcing a no-fly zone, and remains wary of weapons falling into the hands of extremist factions.

A South African judge has relaxed Oscar Pistorius’s bail conditions, allowing him to travel abroad, consume alcohol, and return to his own home. The court ruled that several restrictions from the original bail order were not part of the written judgment and therefore should not apply. The decision is a win for Pistorius’s legal team and could permit him to compete internationally, including at the Moscow World Championships, while still facing a premeditated murder charge. Prosecutors plan to formally serve an indictment in June, though no trial date has been set.

South African energy firm Sasol is investing up to $14 billion in a Louisiana facility that will use gas-to-liquids technology to convert abundant U.S. shale gas into diesel and other products. The company sees the project as a major opportunity because American natural gas is cheap and the Gulf Coast offers strong infrastructure, while also helping reduce U.S. reliance on foreign oil. Although the technology has existed for decades, it was previously uneconomical, but the current gap between gas and oil prices has revived interest. However, analysts caution that the venture carries financial risk, especially if natural gas prices rise and erase the cost advantage.

Hollywood executives from major studios are touring South Africa to scout locations for future film and TV productions, with stops including the set of the latest "Avengers" movie. The visit aims to promote the country as a competitive production destination, highlighting its diverse landscapes, experienced local crews, and English-speaking workforce. South Africa is also offering financial incentives, such as rebates for on-location and post-production work, to attract international projects. Officials hope the trip will lead to more big-budget productions, which could create jobs and boost the economy.

Rooibos tea, grown only in South Africa’s Western Cape, has evolved from a niche drink into a globally popular beverage, driven by its distinctive taste, aroma, and documented health benefits such as antioxidants and a calming effect. The industry now generates billions in value, with large portions of the annual harvest exported to health-conscious markets worldwide. Producers are seeking legal protection for the rooibos name, similar to geographical indicators like champagne, to safeguard its heritage. Meanwhile, expansion into new markets such as India and China is underway, with companies developing flavored teas, rooibos cappuccinos, and other products while traditional brews remain a favorite.

A large flightless rhea, similar to an ostrich, has been roaming around an English golf course after escaping from its owner five weeks ago. The fast-moving bird has drawn media attention, but local golfers are unfazed and dismiss reports that it is dangerous, saying it simply runs away when approached. Wildlife officials have warned the public to keep their distance due to its sharp claws, though capture efforts have so far been unsuccessful. Some locals suggest the bird may only be caught during mating season with the help of a male rhea.

South Korean prosecutors have expanded their investigation into the Sewol ferry disaster by raiding the offices of the vessel’s operator, Cheonghaejin Marine, along with affiliated organizations and the home of the reclusive billionaire family that controls the company. The death toll has reached 169, with 133 still missing, while 11 crew members, including the captain, have been arrested over their handling of the sinking. Investigators are also looking into the ship’s safety certification and the exact cause of the accident, though no definitive explanation has been established. Meanwhile, grief has spread across the country, with memorials growing for the mostly teenage victims and hopes for finding more survivors fading.

The death toll from South Korea’s ferry disaster has risen to 275, with 29 people still missing, most of them high school students. Rescue divers continue searching the wreck under dangerous conditions, and one diver has died during the effort. Authorities have arrested the ferry operator’s CEO on negligence charges and moved to revoke the company’s licenses. The tragedy has sparked national outrage over safety failures and weak regulation, prompting the president to apologize and promise safety reforms.

A South Korean soldier who fled after killing five fellow troops was captured following a self-inflicted gunshot wound, ending a standoff near the border with North Korea. He was shot in the side but survived and underwent surgery, with authorities saying his injuries were not life-threatening. The soldier, who had been flagged for special monitoring, had exchanged gunfire with military forces and resisted surrender despite pleas from officials and family. He left an apology note for the victims and their families before the apparent suicide attempt, and now faces a military investigation.

South Korea will suspend all Iranian oil imports starting in July, citing an EU ban on insurance coverage for tankers carrying Iranian crude. The move aligns with Western sanctions aimed at pressuring Iran over its nuclear program, which the West suspects is for weapons despite Iran’s denial. South Korea is the first major Asian buyer to fully halt such imports, though it has already reduced them by 40 percent and lined up alternative suppliers in the Middle East.

A Southwest Airlines flight made an emergency descent near Raleigh-Durham after a cabin pressure issue, leading passengers to believe the pilot had announced the plane was going down. The airline explained that the captain accidentally broadcast an internal communication to flight attendants about descending to a lower altitude, which was misheard as a dire warning. Passengers described moments of panic and fear, though the plane leveled off and landed safely. The FAA is investigating the incident, and the airline offered a voucher to one concerned passenger.

The Sovereign is a $132 million superyacht concept from Gray Design, inspired by luxury limousines and aimed at wealthy buyers rather than only royalty. It includes space for a custom-built car garage, which can double as storage for water toys, and offers optional high-end touches like Armani-designed interiors and a grassy area for golf or pets. The vessel also features ten guest suites, a cinema, gym, nightclub, and a circular infinity pool surrounding a glass helipad. Despite its focus on luxury, it is engineered for performance, with a top speed of 30 knots and production expected to begin soon.

Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, has died at age 82 due to complications from cardiovascular procedures. He made history in July 1969 when he commanded Apollo 11 and took his famous "one small step" onto the lunar surface, a moment watched by millions and seen as a major U.S. triumph during the Cold War. After his historic career, Armstrong remained humble and largely avoided public attention, though he inspired generations of explorers and received tributes from leaders including President Obama. His family and admirers remember him not only for his monumental achievement but also for his modesty and dedication to serving a cause greater than himself.

NASA’s IBEX mission has produced the first detailed map of the solar system’s tail, known as the heliotail, which is formed by solar wind and extends far beyond the planets. The tail’s cross-section resembles a four-leaf clover, with different solar wind speeds shaping each lobe, and its overall form is distorted by magnetic forces from interstellar space. These observations provide new insight into the heliosphere’s structure and how the sun interacts with the surrounding galaxy. The data also complements the Voyager spacecraft’s direct measurements, helping scientists understand the solar system’s outer boundaries in a broader context.

The sun is far more active than it appears from Earth, producing solar flares and eruptions that can disrupt satellites, power grids, and communications. The Space Weather Prediction Center monitors sunspots to forecast these events and protect vulnerable industries like aviation and GPS. Although the sun is currently at a modest solar maximum, recent activity has already caused brief radio disruptions. New NASA imagery is improving our understanding of space weather, though much about the sun’s behavior remains unknown.

Spanish police arrested two suspected militants with alleged ties to al Qaeda’s North African branch, though officials said there was no sign of an imminent attack. The two men, an Algerian and a Moroccan, were described as “lone wolves” whose radicalization resembled that of the Boston bombing suspects, including use of online forums and interest in bomb-making information. Authorities said one suspect had praised the Boston attacks and that both had been in contact with AQIM operatives in Mali. The arrests came ahead of the Madrid Marathon, where security had already been increased following the Boston bombings.

After being overlooked for the 2011 global “New 7 Wonders of Nature,” Spain launched its own contest to highlight the country’s natural highlights. More than 82,000 votes narrowed 20 destinations down to seven winners, ranging from rocky islands and volcanic parks to ancient gold mines and lake landscapes. Many of the chosen sites are relatively unknown even to Spanish travelers. As part of the campaign, a team of explorers will be selected to tour all seven locations on a paid two-week trip.

Spain has become the focal point of Europe's financial turmoil, facing soaring borrowing costs, a fragile banking sector, and extreme unemployment. Upcoming announcements on the national budget and bank audits are expected to reveal deeper fiscal strain and potentially massive banking losses. Because Spain is the eurozone's fourth-largest economy, its collapse would threaten far broader global stability than previous bailouts in smaller nations. The crisis stems largely from a real estate bust, regional debt pressures, and ongoing doubts about whether austerity measures can restore confidence.

Despite Spain’s prolonged economic crisis, its tourism sector has remained a rare bright spot, contributing significantly to GDP and recovering to pre-crisis visitor numbers. The industry has adapted by attracting new markets, notably Russian tourists, which has helped create seasonal jobs for locals like former business owners. However, experts warn that Spain’s reliance on the traditional sun-and-sand model is stagnating, with many coastal towns lacking strategic development. To stay competitive, some hoteliers are beginning to push for higher-quality, more diversified offerings beyond mass tourism.

Alvaro Palacios, a celebrated Spanish winemaker, gained international renown for his high-end red wines from the Priorat region, which he helped revive by seeking out old, forgotten mountain vineyards. His portfolio now spans three Spanish wine regions, producing both exclusive, expensive bottles and more affordable wines for everyday drinkers. He emphasizes the importance of exporting and globalizing for Spain’s future, while also selling domestically, and believes the economic crisis taught younger generations this lesson. Known for unconventional methods, he uses mules on steep slopes and avoids a website, confident in his personal knowledge of the world’s best wines.

Mallorca’s capital, Palma, is moving toward a new rule that would fine people for wearing swimwear away from the beach, targeting tourists who wander through town in bikinis or bare-chested. Officials say beach attire is fine on the sand but not in public spaces, framing the measure as part of a broader effort to curb anti-social behavior. While exact fines haven’t been announced, some reports suggest they could exceed $800. The rule would still allow swimwear on streets or boardwalks right next to the beach, so quick trips for ice cream remain acceptable.

The train driver in the Santiago de Compostela derailment has been formally charged with 79 counts of professional reckless homicide and additional injury counts, though he was released under conditions including bail, passport surrender, and a suspended license. Investigators believe the crash was caused by excessive speed, as the train entered a curve at roughly 190 kilometers per hour where the limit was 80. The death toll reached at least 79, with dozens still hospitalized and forensic teams working to identify remains, including those of two American victims. The disaster, which occurred on the eve of a local holiday, has deeply shocked Spain and prompted an ongoing investigation into the cause.

Ray Harryhausen, the legendary stop-motion animator and special-effects innovator, has passed away at age 92. He was celebrated for blending frame-by-frame model animation with live action in classics like "Jason and the Argonauts" and "Clash of the Titans," inspiring major directors such as Steven Spielberg and Peter Jackson. His work, though dated by modern CGI standards, remains influential and admired. Even late in life, Harryhausen believed the art of combining stop-motion with live actors would eventually make a comeback.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims is marking 25 years as a specialized judicial lifeline for former service members disputing VA disability decisions. Though it handles mostly low-profile cases, it has processed tens of thousands of appeals and remains crucial for veterans seeking fair compensation. A typical case involves an Army veteran who missed an appeal deadline while deployed overseas, highlighting how complex and unforgiving the process can be. With a large VA claims backlog and limited legal representation, advocates stress the ongoing need for pro bono support and reforms to simplify the appeals system.

Cargo bikes are emerging as a practical, low-emission alternative to delivery vans in European cities, offering speed, flexibility, and the ability to handle substantial loads while avoiding traffic and urban delivery restrictions. A shift from motorized freight to bikes could replace a large share of city deliveries and supermarket trips, significantly cutting carbon emissions and reducing air and noise pollution. Safety concerns are also addressed, as replacing large trucks—which are disproportionately involved in cyclist fatalities—with cargo bikes could make streets safer. Despite lingering doubts about what bikes can carry, services are already transporting everything from medical supplies to construction gear, and in bike-friendly cities like Copenhagen, tradespeople are increasingly choosing cargo cycles over cars.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers used electrical stimulation of the spinal cord to help four paralyzed men regain voluntary movement in their legs and torsos, a result that surprised the scientists. While the technique does not yet enable walking, it significantly improved patients' bladder, bowel, and sexual function, as well as overall health. The exact mechanism remains unclear, but the findings open new possibilities for paralysis treatment and have prompted plans for further research with additional patients.

Simon Barnett, CNN Digital’s director of photography, reviews thousands of World Cup images daily and emphasizes that technical quality alone isn’t enough—he looks for an original perspective on historically significant moments. He advises amateur sports photographers to choose clean, natural backgrounds, understand the sport to anticipate action, and fill the frame with the subject. Using a long lens with a wide aperture helps isolate the action, and timing is driven by anticipation rather than reaction. Barnett also stresses the importance of not dwelling on missed shots, since focusing on the past can cause photographers to miss new opportunities.

Egypt’s highest court has declared its decision to dissolve parliament as final, rejecting President Mohamed Morsy’s move to reinstate lawmakers. Morsy’s order puts him in direct conflict with the military and the judiciary, though analysts say a full confrontation is unlikely as both sides are cautious. Legal challenges have been filed against the president’s decree, and the court is expected to rule against it. Meanwhile, Morsy’s Islamist supporters back his decision, setting the stage for continued political tension.

Comedian John Pinette died at age 50 in a Pittsburgh hotel room from natural causes related to a condition he was being treated for, with no autopsy planned. He was widely recognized for his role as a carjacking victim in the “Seinfeld” finale, though he had spent over two decades on the comedy circuit. His manager noted that Pinette had struggled with addiction in the past but was sober at the time of his death, and had recently lost a significant amount of weight, which inspired a new comedy act. Fellow comedians remembered him as a kind, generous, and exceptionally funny performer whose loss was deeply felt.

Staples is partnering with Mcor Technologies to introduce a 3-D printing service called Staples Easy 3D, allowing customers to upload designs online and pick up finished objects in stores or have them shipped. The service uses Mcor’s Iris printers, which build items from layered, glued paper and can produce photorealistic color, though the resulting material has a wood-like hardness with some design limitations. This marks the first time a major retail chain has offered 3-D printing, giving the technology broader mainstream appeal. The service is set to launch in the Netherlands and Belgium in early 2013, with other countries to follow.

Arlene Martel, best known to “Star Trek” fans as T’Pring, Spock’s Vulcan fiancée, has died at age 78 from complications following a heart attack. Her distinctive look led to a wide range of TV roles in the 1960s, from spies to Western characters, and she remained a beloved figure at sci-fi conventions for decades. Beyond acting, she was romantically linked to James Dean and Cary Grant early in her life. Her son remembered her as a dedicated working actress who kept pursuing roles and dreams until the end.

Disney Channel is launching the animated series *Star Wars Rebels*, which premieres Friday before settling into its regular Monday slot. The show is set between *Revenge of the Sith* and *A New Hope*, during a time when the Empire is hunting down the last Jedi and a rebellion is just beginning. Its tone is said to align closely with the original trilogy, despite early fan concerns about it being a kids' show. The series arrives amid high anticipation for *Episode VII*, and it has already been renewed for a second season.

Production on “Star Wars: Episode VII” will pause for two weeks in August so Harrison Ford can continue recovering from a broken leg he suffered in an on-set accident. Despite the delay, the film remains scheduled for a December 18, 2015 release. The filmmakers also announced that newcomers Crystal Clarke and Pip Andersen were selected from tens of thousands of applicants through open casting calls, continuing the franchise’s tradition of discovering fresh talent.

The U.S. is sending a special envoy, Ambassador Robert King, to North Korea this week to negotiate the release of detained American Kenneth Bae. Bae, who has been held since November and sentenced to 15 years of hard labor, has suffered serious health problems, including significant weight loss and other ailments. Washington is asking Pyongyang to grant Bae a pardon on humanitarian grounds so he can reunite with his family and receive medical care. The trip comes amid reports that Bae’s condition has worsened, prompting his recent move to a hospital.

New Jersey is assuming control of Camden’s failing public school system after an investigation revealed severe academic and administrative problems, including low test scores, a declining graduation rate, and weak leadership. Governor Chris Christie stated that the state will closely monitor progress and guide financial decisions, emphasizing that the move was made after years of hoping local officials could improve on their own. Despite receiving over $279 million in state funding and spending well above the state average per student, Camden’s performance remains among the lowest in New Jersey. Local leaders, including the mayor and school board president, have expressed willingness to cooperate, and Camden joins several other New Jersey cities already under state oversight.

President Obama announced that states may apply for waivers from the No Child Left Behind Act, allowing flexibility from its strict 2014 proficiency requirements. Georgia, along with several other states, has already submitted or expressed interest in a waiver, proposing an alternative accountability system that uses multiple measures—including science and social studies—rather than relying solely on a single test. State officials argue this approach gives local schools more flexibility and better reflects student performance. States that do not seek waivers will still be required to follow the original law’s mandates.

A century after Gavrilo Princip sparked World War I, his legacy remains deeply divided in Sarajevo: some honor him with statues and T-shirts as a hero, while others condemn him as a terrorist. The recent unveiling of his statue was part of commemorations marking the war's centennial. Princip was just 19 when he fatally shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife in 1914, an act that escalated tensions between Europe's great powers into a devastating continental conflict. The war ultimately cost millions of lives and reshaped Europe's political order.

Stay-at-home fathers are a growing demographic, and many women find them attractive because they appear nurturing, engaged, and emotionally supportive. This appeal may have biological roots, as stay-at-home dads often have lower testosterone and a more caring, patient temperament. However, the dynamic is not universally romanticized—some women still carry the bulk of housework, and traditional gender expectations can create tension or feelings of emasculation. Ultimately, the concept of fatherhood is evolving, with parenting and providing now defined by emotional involvement rather than just earning power.

Stephen Colbert has been chosen by CBS to take over as host of “The Late Show” after David Letterman retires in 2015, signing a five-year deal. He will not perform in his familiar “Colbert Report” character, leaving fans to see a different side of him. Letterman endorsed the choice, and CBS praised Colbert as a creative force, while Comedy Central wished him well for the remainder of his current show. The move also means Colbert will shift from his current time slot and no longer follow Jon Stewart, who had previously praised him as a remarkable talent.

Adam Silver, the new NBA commissioner, faced his first major crisis when he banned Los Angeles Clippers owner Donald Sterling for life and fined him $2.5 million over racist remarks. Silver’s swift and firm response drew widespread praise, with many noting his decisive leadership in condemning views that have no place in the league. Known as a consensus builder and advocate for transparency, Silver’s philosophy centers on teamwork and the idea that no individual is bigger than the game. Though he never planned a career in basketball, his deep love for the sport and collaborative style have defined his early tenure.

The U.S. Postal Service is considering a commemorative stamp honoring Steve Jobs as early as 2015, just a few years after his death. He appears on an internal list of approved subjects that also includes cultural icons like Michael Jackson, Jimi Hendrix, and Harvey Milk. The move reflects the agency’s strategy to attract collectors with popular-culture themes and boost revenue, though officials stress the list is not final. If approved, Jobs would be the first figure from the American tech industry to receive this honor.

Lung cancer carries a heavy stigma because of its link to smoking, causing many patients to feel shame and face blame instead of sympathy. Yet it is the leading cause of cancer death and affects many people who never smoked or quit long ago, with air pollution also a major risk factor. Promising treatments, including targeted pills and immunotherapy, have improved outcomes, but lung cancer research remains severely underfunded compared to other cancers. Raising awareness and removing blame are essential to support patients and secure the funding needed for better treatments.

After more than a century, Germany has returned 20 skulls to Namibia that were taken during a brutal colonial conflict in the early 1900s. The remains, believed to belong to Herero and Nama people, were used by German scientists in racist research aimed at proving white supremacy. Their return was marked by emotional ceremonies in both Berlin and Namibia, with officials acknowledging the suffering caused. The repatriation has also revived longstanding tensions, as Namibia seeks a formal genocide apology and reparations, while Germany has expressed regret but refused compensation.

The disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 became more puzzling after it emerged that two passports on the passenger list had been previously reported stolen, raising concerns about possible terrorism. Malaysian authorities apparently failed to check the stolen documents against Interpol’s database, and both Austria and Italy confirmed that the listed citizens were safe and not on the plane. U.S. investigators, including NTSB and FBI personnel, prepared to assist in the search, while officials stressed that no cause—including terrorism—had been ruled out. The jet vanished during what is normally the safest phase of flight, leaving investigators considering both mechanical failure and intentional acts.

A Pakistani man has confessed to killing his first wife years ago so he could marry Farzana Parveen, who was later beaten to death by her own family in a public honor killing. The attack occurred as she was heading to court to affirm her marriage, and her father has been arrested while other relatives remain at large. The case highlights the widespread problem of honor killings in Pakistan, which activists say are underreported and often go unpunished due to legal provisions that allow families to forgive perpetrators or accept financial compensation.

Patricia Lim spent about a decade researching Hong Kong Cemetery and turned its 8,500 graves into a social history in her book "Forgotten Souls." Using tombstone inscriptions and old newspapers, she uncovered stories of colonial Hong Kong’s diverse and often harsh life, from wealthy benefactors and doctors to prostitutes and marginalized Chinese residents. The cemetery reflects the city’s inequalities and dangers, with many buried there having died young from disease or hardship. Her work has also helped descendants solve long-standing family mysteries by connecting them to ancestors buried in the cemetery.

A devoted Dave Matthews fan named Emily Kraus spotted the singer stranded on a roadside in Pennsylvania after his bicycle tire blew out before a show. She and her boyfriend pulled over and gave him a lift to the concert, where they chatted along the way. Grateful for the ride, Matthews invited them to dinner, backstage, and gave them front-row seats. He also signed their tickets with a thank-you note, making the surreal encounter unforgettable.

Fomba Trawally, a Liberian entrepreneur, began his journey with just $200 as a street vendor after returning from exile during the civil war. He built a thriving retail business before launching Liberia’s first paper and toiletry manufacturing company in 2010. Despite major obstacles such as unreliable power and poor infrastructure, his factory has generated over $600,000 in sales, and he prioritizes training local workers rather than hiring relatives. Looking ahead, Trawally aims to expand beyond Liberia, with ambitions to export to African, European, and American markets.

The ceasefire between Israel and Hamas fell apart, and hostilities resumed with rockets fired into Israel and Israeli airstrikes on Gaza. The strikes killed 19 Palestinians, including the wife and young child of Hamas's military leader, who vowed retaliation. Both sides accused each other of derailing the negotiations, which stalled over Israel's demand for Gaza's disarmament and Palestinian calls to lift the blockade and restore access to a seaport and airport. The ongoing conflict has now resulted in more than 2,000 Palestinian deaths and 67 on the Israeli side.

U.S.-led coalition warplanes conducted airstrikes near the Syrian town of Ayn al-Arab, also known as Kobani, targeting an ISIS compound and armed vehicles close to the Turkish border—marking the first such strikes in that area. Turkey, which is not part of the coalition, has repeatedly called for a buffer zone along its border. Elsewhere, a monitoring group reported that strikes near al-Hasakah may have killed civilians, though this could not be independently verified. Meanwhile, Kurdish forces continued to resist ISIS advances near Kobani, and the international coalition expanded as the U.K., Denmark, and Belgium joined the campaign, with Western leaders warning of a prolonged fight.

At age 22, the author suffered a sudden hemorrhagic stroke that paralyzed her right side and impaired her speech, forcing her to relearn basic skills. Although she made a strong recovery, she still lives with lasting effects, including weakness and seizure risk, and faces ongoing health precautions. She admits that over time she has sometimes slipped back into taking her health for granted, but the experience has given her lasting perspective and gratitude. Ultimately, she views the stroke not as a tragedy but as a stroke of luck that shaped her outlook on life.

Some schools are replacing traditional snow days with virtual learning days to make up for weather-related cancellations without extending the school year. Districts like Pascack Valley in New Jersey and Coyle and Cassidy in Massachusetts used online lessons, class discussions, and teacher check-ins to keep students engaged from home. While many students were initially skeptical, participation was high and some even appreciated the flexibility and chance for quieter classmates to speak up. However, such programs depend on reliable technology and student access, which remains a challenge for many districts.

Two new studies provide early evidence that stem cells taken from patients' own hearts can reverse damage caused by heart attacks and heart failure. In the trials, treated patients showed significant improvements in heart function, reduced scar tissue, and even signs of newly grown heart muscle, while control groups saw no such gains. The results challenge the long-held belief that heart damage is permanent, though researchers caution that larger studies are needed to confirm the therapy's effectiveness and bring it closer to standard treatment.

A study found that MTV’s “16 and Pregnant” likely contributed to a 5.7 percent drop in U.S. teen births in the 18 months after it premiered, accounting for roughly one-third of the overall decline during that time. Researchers analyzed TV ratings, Google searches, and Twitter activity, noting spikes in birth control-related discussions alongside the show. They concluded the program made the challenges of teen pregnancy more tangible and encouraged viewers to use contraception. However, the show is not the only factor; economic conditions also played a role, and experts suggest media can serve as effective sex education for teens.

A new national study suggests that sexting among U.S. adolescents may be less widespread than earlier reports indicated, with only about 10 percent of youth surveyed having sent suggestive images and just 1 percent having sent explicit ones. The research also found that older teens were more likely to engage in sexting and that explicit images rarely spread widely beyond their original recipients. While the findings are somewhat reassuring, experts caution that even a small number of affected teens can face serious legal and social consequences, and some researchers believe the true rates may be underreported because teens are reluctant to admit such behavior. Parents are encouraged to talk openly with their children about responsible phone use and the potential legal risks of sharing nude images.

A new study concludes that Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses III was assassinated by having his throat slashed, not by poison or snakebite as previously speculated. CT scans of the mummy revealed a deep knife wound that would have caused immediate death, with evidence suggesting the injury occurred before embalming. The study identifies one of his wives and her son as the conspirators behind the plot, and notes that the son was convicted and forced to take his own life. Genetic analysis also confirmed a familial link between the pharaoh and the suspected son.

A new study suggests that fathers with smaller testicles tend to be more involved in caring for their infants, linking lower testes volume and testosterone to stronger nurturing brain responses. However, experts caution that the findings show correlation, not causation, and that caregiving itself might affect testes size. They also stress that testicle size does not determine sperm production, testosterone levels, or a man's quality as a father. Ultimately, many factors shape fathering behavior, and involved dads come in all shapes and sizes.

Liverpool striker Luis Suarez has been suspended for 10 matches after the Football Association ruled that the standard ban for biting Chelsea’s Branislav Ivanovic was insufficient. The incident, which occurred during a 2-2 draw, led to an additional seven-match ban on top of the usual three, with Suarez’s previous disciplinary record cited as a factor. Liverpool expressed shock and disappointment at the severity, while Suarez apologized directly to Ivanovic and was fined by his club, with the money donated to a Hillsborough support group. The ban is among the longest in English football history, though several players have received harsher punishments.

A Sudanese woman sentenced to death for refusing to renounce her Christian faith has given birth to a daughter while in prison in Khartoum. Her husband, a U.S. citizen, was not allowed to attend the birth, and she remains jailed with her young son as her legal appeal proceeds. The case has drawn widespread international condemnation, with rights groups and foreign embassies urging Sudan to overturn the conviction, which also included a sentence of 100 lashes on adultery charges. The dispute centers on her religious identity, as Sudanese courts consider her Muslim because of her father, despite her having been raised Christian.

Sudan and South Sudan have agreed to withdraw their military forces from a demilitarized border zone, following talks mediated by former South African President Thabo Mbeki in Addis Ababa. Both defense ministers pledged to carry out the pullout from the 14-mile-wide area by the end of the month, with monitoring by a UN peacekeeping force. The agreement marks a step toward easing tensions between the two nations, which have remained at odds over border demarcation, oil exports, and the disputed Abyei region since South Sudan’s independence in 2011. The deal follows international pressure to avoid a return to conflict after clashes in 2012 brought them close to war.

New research presented at an American Heart Association conference estimates that sugar-sweetened beverages contribute to over 180,000 obesity-related deaths globally each year, accounting for about one in every 100 such deaths. Mexico had the highest death rate among large countries, with the U.S. ranking third. The beverage industry challenged the findings, arguing the study was not peer-reviewed and did not prove causation. However, experts maintain that sugary drinks are linked to weight gain and related health risks, and the AHA advises limiting added sugar to reduce these dangers.

A suicide bomber struck outside a mosque in northern Afghanistan as worshippers were leaving Eid al-Adha prayers, killing at least 40 people and wounding more than 50, including children. The attack occurred in Maimana, the capital of Faryab province, where the bomber, reportedly wearing a police uniform, detonated explosives in the crowd. No group immediately claimed responsibility, but Afghan officials blamed Taliban leader Mullah Omar, saying the insurgency aimed to kill as many people as possible. The bombing drew swift international condemnation, with the United States and Pakistan denouncing the violence as a callous disregard for religion and civilian life.

A suicide attack at a wedding ceremony in northern Afghanistan killed at least 17 people, including a sitting member of parliament and the provincial intelligence chief. The lawmaker, Ahmad Khan Samangani, was hosting his daughter's wedding when the bomber struck at the venue's entrance. Casualty figures varied among officials, with some reporting more than 20 dead and dozens wounded. No group immediately claimed responsibility, but authorities suspected the Taliban, and the U.S. Embassy condemned the attack.

Great Smoky Mountains National Park, spanning the border of North Carolina and Tennessee, is the most visited national park in the U.S., known for its ancient peaks, free entry, and remarkable biodiversity. Ranger Caitlin Worth, who grew up with a family connection to the Park Service, recommends arriving at Cades Cove at sunrise to see wildlife, visiting Clingmans Dome for sweeping views, and taking the strenuous Mount Cammerer hike for wildflowers and fall colors. She also favors the Oconaluftee Valley for spotting elk and birds, and credits Gulf Islands National Seashore in Florida with inspiring her career as a ranger.

New Orleans leveraged Super Bowl XLVII as a catalyst to complete major post-Katrina upgrades, investing $1.3 billion in infrastructure such as airport renovations, hotel improvements, Superdome enhancements, and new playgrounds. The event, combined with Mardi Gras, is expected to deliver a significant economic boost, with an estimated $730 million impact over the three-week celebration. Officials view the game as a symbol of the city’s resilience and a milestone in its recovery, while also hoping it will attract record visitors and showcase a safer, cleaner, and more welcoming destination. Long-term, residents are seen as the biggest beneficiaries of the city’s renewed vitality and modernized amenities.

Warner Bros. has announced a follow-up to "Man of Steel" that will bring Superman and Batman together on screen for the first time, with Zack Snyder returning to direct and Henry Cavill reprising his role as Superman. The new Batman has not been cast, and Christian Bale will not return as the Caped Crusader. The film is expected to start production in 2014, and Snyder has hinted the two heroes will be rivals. Christopher Nolan, who directed the recent Batman trilogy, will serve as an executive producer on the project.

The 2010 Supreme Court ruling on campaign finance has enabled super PACs to spend unlimited funds, and their impact is already visible in the 2012 presidential primaries through heavy negative advertising. Experts say this influence will likely be even greater in congressional races, where a few million dollars from a super PAC could tip the balance in close contests and determine control of the House or Senate. These outside groups can act quickly, raise large sums without the same donor disclosure rules, and are often run by former aides of the candidates they support, raising concerns about coordination and circumvention of contribution limits. Beyond elections, there are worries that big donors could gain outsized policy influence, potentially shaping the agendas of successful candidates.

Experts say most children can recover from school shootings if they receive prompt family support and return to normal routines, though younger children are especially vulnerable. Those who lost someone close, witnessed the violence, or faced prior hardships are at greater risk for lasting mental health issues. Common reactions include physical symptoms, anxiety, and clinginess, but open communication and avoiding overexposure to trauma can help. With appropriate interventions and community support, the vast majority of children are expected to regain normal functioning within a year.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate, with conservative justices expressing deep skepticism that the federal government can compel Americans to buy insurance. Liberal justices defended the mandate as necessary to prevent cost-shifting in the health care market. The case is seen as potentially deciding not only the mandate’s fate but also the entire health care law, with protests and political reactions unfolding outside the Court. A final ruling is expected by late June.

The Supreme Court justices released their annual financial disclosures in paper form, revealing that most are millionaires with substantial investments and extensive travel funded by outside groups. Justice Sonia Sotomayor reported rental income from her former New York residence and some credit card debt, while Justice Antonin Scalia logged the most trips, including appearances before the Federalist Society. Several justices also earned extra income from book royalties and university teaching. Meanwhile, transparency advocates criticized the court for not posting the reports online, as the president and Congress do, arguing the paper-only system is outdated.

The Supreme Court declined to revisit its Citizens United ruling, effectively confirming that the decision applies to state-level campaign finance laws as well. In a 5-4 vote, the justices blocked Montana’s attempt to enforce its own restrictions on independent corporate political spending. Dissenting justices argued that states should be able to address corruption concerns, while Republican leaders praised the decision as a win for free speech. Critics, including Democratic officials and reform groups, condemned it for allowing unlimited special-interest money to influence elections.

The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that most undocumented minors who turn 21 while waiting for family-based visas must reapply from the end of the line, losing their place in the queue. The majority deferred to the Board of Immigration Appeals' interpretation of ambiguous immigration law, agreeing with the Obama administration. The case involved a Salvadoran mother whose son aged out during the lengthy process, and the ruling means only a small number of applicants are protected under the Child Status Protection Act.
