The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that a key section of the Defense of Marriage Act is unconstitutional, because it denied legally married same-sex couples the same federal benefits and protections granted to heterosexual spouses. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, emphasizing that the law violated the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of liberty and equal protection, while limiting the decision to couples whose marriages are recognized by their states. The case was brought by Edith Windsor, who faced a large estate tax bill after her spouse died because the federal government did not recognize their marriage. Dissenting justices, led by Antonin Scalia, sharply criticized the ruling, while President Obama and marriage equality advocates celebrated it as a historic victory.

The Supreme Court is set to announce its decision on the constitutionality of President Obama’s landmark health care reform law, saving the highly anticipated ruling for the final day of its term. The central dispute concerns the requirement that most Americans obtain health insurance or face a penalty, which opponents argue oversteps federal authority while supporters say it is essential to making the system work. Lower courts have been divided on the issue, and the ruling is expected to have major consequences for health care delivery and the broader balance of government power. The law remains a deeply polarizing political issue, with public opinion split and the decision likely to influence the upcoming presidential election.

Fifty years after the first surgeon general’s report linked smoking to cancer, the latest report calls for eliminating tobacco use entirely. Although adult smoking rates have dropped from 42% to 18%, millions still smoke, and tobacco-related deaths have risen to 480,000 annually. The report newly links smoking to additional diseases such as diabetes, stroke from secondhand smoke, and several other conditions, while warning that millions of children remain at risk. Officials urge stronger action, including higher tobacco prices, smoke-free laws, cessation programs, and efforts to prevent young people from starting.

Sheryl Sandberg and Getty Images launched the Lean In collection to combat persistent gender stereotypes in media by offering more diverse, empowering images of women in professional and everyday roles. The initiative stemmed from research showing that such portrayals are both socially impactful and commercially successful, with sales of the collection rising significantly. Sandberg pointed to campaigns like Dove’s “Real Beauty” and Pantene’s viral ads as proof that authentic, representative imagery resonates with audiences and drives brand engagement. She urged advertisers to use their reach to depict women as leaders rather than reinforcing outdated clichés.

The head of the NYPD’s intelligence division testified that the department’s post-9/11 Demographics Unit, which monitored Muslim communities in New York, never generated a single lead that launched a terrorism investigation. The testimony came in a long-running lawsuit over police surveillance guidelines, with the unit’s reports focusing on ethnicity, language, and location rather than criminal activity. The NYPD defended the unit as a small operation that helped identify areas of potential threat, while activists and civil rights groups condemned the program as discriminatory and contrary to American values. The disclosure adds to ongoing criticism of the department’s surveillance tactics, which have also drawn scrutiny from federal officials.

A new AT&T survey challenges the stereotype that teens are the main culprits of texting while driving, finding that nearly half of adults admit to the behavior—slightly more than the 43% of teens who acknowledged it. Despite 98% of respondents knowing it is unsafe, many continue, with 40% saying it has become a habit. The findings are part of AT&T’s “It Can Wait” campaign, which aims to curb distracted driving through awareness and pledges. The survey also notes that texting drivers are 23 times more likely to crash, and the problem appears to be worsening.

Teenagers are showing signs of growing disenchantment with Facebook, citing the presence of adults, excessive oversharing, and frequent drama as key reasons their interest is fading. Many are migrating to platforms like Twitter, Instagram, and Snapchat, where they feel freer to express themselves without Facebook's social pressures. Despite this, Facebook remains the dominant social network among teens, who say they stay on it mainly to avoid missing out. Facebook executives downplay the idea of a youth exodus, arguing that teens are simply adding other platforms rather than abandoning Facebook.

A seemingly minor pine needle prick led Percy von Lipinski to develop necrotizing fasciitis, a rare flesh-eating infection that nearly cost him his hand and life. His case echoes recent high-profile infections in patients like Aimee Copeland and Lana Kuykendall, highlighting how even trivial wounds can trigger the disease. Early warning signs include severe, disproportionate pain and fever, and prompt surgical removal of dead tissue is critical for survival. Von Lipinski eventually recovered full use of his hand after a long rehabilitation, but the ordeal left him far more cautious about even the smallest cuts.

The article examines survivor guilt in the aftermath of the Aurora theater shooting, highlighting how survivors struggled with why they lived while others, including children, died. Psychologists explain that such guilt is a common grief response, especially when someone died protecting another, but it can become overwhelming and lead to PTSD or depression. Coping involves processing the event, seeking support from loved ones or professionals, and doing meaningful acts to honor the deceased. Experts stress that persistent symptoms should be treated, and survivors should not let guilt prevent them from moving forward.

A Spanish national was arrested at Málaga airport on suspicion of being an Islamic militant returning from the Syria-Iraq conflict and posing a national security threat. He was linked to an al Qaeda-affiliated network that recruited, trained, and sent fighters to Syria, with ties to groups such as ISIS and Jabhat al-Nusra. Authorities had been monitoring the network, which was based in Ceuta and northern Morocco, and had already jailed several suspects. The arrest highlights concerns that returning fighters could carry out attacks in Spain.

A Swedish radio journalist, Nils Horner, was fatally shot in broad daylight in Kabul just weeks before Afghanistan’s presidential election. He was killed by a gunshot to the head while conducting interviews near a restaurant that had previously been bombed. Colleagues remembered him as a legendary, deeply committed correspondent who gave voice to ordinary people across Asia. The killing highlights the severe security risks as Afghanistan prepares for the April 5 vote, which the Taliban have threatened to disrupt.

Swiss voters narrowly passed a referendum imposing new quotas and limits on foreign residents and workers. The government had opposed the measure, warning it could hurt businesses and strain ties with the European Union, which expressed regret over the decision. The new rules will cap residence permits, including for cross-border commuters and asylum seekers, and require Swiss nationals to be prioritized in hiring. Foreigners make up a significant share of Switzerland’s population and workforce, and the vote reflects public anxiety over recent population growth.

Radio host David “Kidd” Kraddick died suddenly at age 53 while attending a charity golf event in New Orleans for his foundation, Kidd’s Kids, which supports chronically and terminally ill children. Known for his nationally syndicated morning show heard in nearly 100 cities, he had earned multiple industry honors and was widely admired for his philanthropy. His death came shortly after he had jokingly discussed his own final moments on air, and tributes poured in from fans and public figures like Mark Cuban. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed.Need final only.Radio host David “Kidd” Kraddick died unexpectedly at 53 while participating in a charity golf tournament in New Orleans for his foundation, Kidd’s Kids, which sends seriously ill children and their families to Disney World. He was best known for his nationally syndicated morning show, which reached nearly 100 cities, and had received numerous broadcasting awards. His death came shortly after he had humorously imagined his final moments on air, and tributes from fans and figures like Mark Cuban highlighted his generosity and impact. The cause of death was not immediately released.

A Syrian airstrike on a refugee camp in northern Lebanon killed nine Syrians and wounded nine others, according to Lebanese state media. The attack targeted an area near the border in the Bekaa Valley, marking another cross-border incident in the ongoing conflict. Previous strikes and cross-border activity had already drawn warnings from the U.S. and the U.N. Security Council about escalation. The violence has driven hundreds of thousands of Syrian refugees into Lebanon, straining the country and heightening regional tensions.

A coordinated attack in Aleppo killed dozens near a busy square, with the Al-Nusra Front claiming responsibility for using suicide car bombs and gunmen in military attire. The violence underscores Aleppo’s importance as a major battleground in Syria’s civil war, where control of the city carries significant political and economic consequences. Separately, shelling from Syria struck a Turkish border town, killing five civilians and prompting Turkey to fire back at Syrian military positions. In response to the refugee crisis, the UK pledged additional winter aid to support Syrians sheltering in Turkey.

Syrian Foreign Minister Walid Moallem addressed the UN General Assembly, denying that Syria is in a civil war and instead framing the conflict as a fight against terrorism. He pledged that Syria would fully comply with the international chemical weapons convention, while repeating accusations that rebels—backed by foreign states—have used chemical agents. He also expressed support for a political solution but insisted it must not allow terrorism to continue. Meanwhile, UN inspectors are leaving Syria after investigating chemical attacks, and a team from the global chemical weapons watchdog is arriving to verify the accuracy of Syria’s declared stockpile.

Syria’s uprising has included a vibrant nonviolent artistic resistance, with painters, cartoonists, musicians, and puppeteers using creativity to challenge the regime despite severe risks. An Amsterdam exhibition titled “Culture in Defiance” highlights this movement, showing how artists have broken longstanding fears and used both traditional and digital media to reach wider audiences. The regime’s hostility toward art is evident in attacks on figures like singer Ibrahim Qashoush and cartoonist Ali Ferzat, yet many artists remain committed, using humor and documentation to capture daily life under repression. Social media and satirical works such as the puppet series “Top Goon” have helped spread dissent and engage Syrians in unprecedented ways.

The article describes how the Syrian government’s siege on opposition-held Damascus suburbs is causing widespread starvation, with infants and children among the hardest hit. Doctors report rising deaths from hunger and malnutrition, while parents risk sniper fire just to find food. Humanitarian aid is being blocked, and activists and Amnesty International condemn the blockades as a cruel war crime. Although peace talks allowed limited aid into Yarmouk, it is far too little to prevent what many fear will become mass death.

Western nations are weighing military action against Syria following a chemical weapons attack near Damascus, with the U.S. asserting that the Syrian government is responsible. However, the U.K. Parliament voted against joining potential strikes, and the U.N. Security Council failed to reach consensus, leaving the possibility of unilateral U.S. action. British intelligence assessed that the Syrian regime likely carried out the attack, and the U.K. argued that any military intervention would be legally justified on humanitarian grounds. Meanwhile, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad vowed to defend against any aggression, as U.N. inspectors continued gathering evidence.

A Human Rights Watch report based on testimony from 63 Syrian military defectors documents widespread atrocities, including orders to shoot unarmed protesters, torture, looting, and the killing of soldiers who refused to obey. The defectors describe senior commanders, some linked to President Assad’s inner circle, directing brutal crackdowns on civilian demonstrations. The report names 74 officials and urges the UN Security Council to refer Syria to the International Criminal Court. It also highlights Assad’s denial of responsibility, despite evidence implicating his forces, as the death toll from the unrest reaches an estimated 5,000.

The Syrian government has launched a major military assault on Aleppo, using tanks and heavy shelling in the country’s largest city, where rebel forces are putting up fierce resistance. Opposition leaders warned that international allies must act quickly to prevent a massacre and urged them to provide weapons capable of countering the regime’s tanks and aircraft. The offensive has caused dozens of deaths and severe humanitarian conditions, including shortages of food, bread, and medicine, as regime forces tighten their grip. Meanwhile, Russia and Iran continue to back the Syrian government, while international envoys and Western leaders call for a political solution to end the escalating violence.

Human Rights Watch has accused the Syrian government of deliberately and unlawfully demolishing thousands of homes in opposition-held areas of Damascus and Hama, calling the destruction a form of collective punishment. The report says residents were forced to leave before troops used bulldozers and explosives to raze entire neighborhoods, including apartment buildings, with no evidence of combat-related damage. The demolitions, which spanned roughly a year, were allegedly carried out under the guise of urban planning but were supervised by military forces. HRW is urging the government to halt the demolitions, compensate affected residents, and has called on the U.N. Security Council to refer the situation to the International Criminal Court.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has rejected the peace initiative put forward by the joint UN-Arab League envoy, insisting he does not recognize the envoy's authority and will not act until rebels disarm. International diplomatic efforts remain stalled, as Russia and China have blocked a UN Security Council resolution, with Moscow echoing Damascus's claims that armed terrorist groups are responsible for the violence. The conflict has left thousands dead, and a recent massacre in Homs has intensified international outrage, while the opposition is calling for military intervention and a no-fly zone to protect civilians. Meanwhile, tens of thousands have fled the country, and there are reports that Syrian forces have planted landmines near the borders with Turkey and Lebanon.

The Syrian National Council has chosen George Sabra as its new president, though the leadership vote highlighted internal divisions, as no women were elected to its executive body. In a related setback, the Local Coordination Committees announced it was breaking with the SNC, saying the opposition group had failed to reform and live up to its political role. Meanwhile, rebel forces claimed advances in the border town of Ras Al Ain, driving thousands of civilians into Turkey amid intense fighting with government troops. The United States pledged additional humanitarian aid to help Syrian refugees and support health care, including child immunizations, as the conflict’s death toll and displacement continued to mount.

The killing of three senior Syrian officials in a rebel bombing in Damascus has raised new doubts about the durability of President Bashar al-Assad’s rule. Assad, who inherited power from his father after being thrust into succession, was once viewed by the West as a potential reformer but later became known for crushing dissent and backing militant allies. The attack struck a meeting of security and government leaders, prompting Assad to quickly appoint a new defense minister, while opposition supporters celebrated. The violence underscores a prolonged conflict marked by mass casualties, government crackdowns, and growing international pressure on his regime.

Syrian rebels carried out a major bombing in Aleppo, targeting a hotel and nearby buildings used by government forces, with the Islamic Front claiming responsibility. The blast killed at least 14 people and wounded dozens more, while also damaging historical sites in the old city. Syrian state media condemned the attack as terrorism and reported that the army responded by killing many of the attackers, amid an ongoing water shortage in the city. The violence is part of the broader civil war that has devastated Syria since 2011, with over 100,000 people killed.

Powerful Syrian rebel factions, including the al Qaeda-linked al-Nusra Front, have rejected the Western-backed opposition coalition and its newly formed interim government, instead calling for Sharia law as the sole basis of legislation. The move highlights the growing influence of hard-line Islamist groups and further sidelines the moderate opposition, which has suffered recent battlefield setbacks. The infighting has raised alarms in Turkey, which sees extremist groups as a growing security threat along its border. Meanwhile, Western-backed rebel institutions appear increasingly marginalized as jihadi factions gain ground.

The article highlights the severe strain that hundreds of thousands of Syrian refugees have placed on Jordan, particularly in the border town of Mafraq, where a neighborhood now known as "Syria Town" has become a makeshift home for displaced families. Many refugees, like a widow who lost her husband and son to regime forces, live in converted shops without proper doors, while their children abandon school to search for work. Jordanians, already facing high unemployment and economic hardship, are growing resentful as they compete with Syrians for jobs, housing, and water, with some landlords evicting Jordanian tenants to rent to Syrians at higher prices. The crisis is set to be a key topic in talks between President Obama and Jordan's King Abdullah, while international aid remains insufficient and wealthy Syrian expatriates have launched their own relief efforts.

Turkish authorities in Hatay province are pressuring Syrian refugees living in rented homes to relocate to official camps or face forced eviction, with police issuing warnings and demanding signed evacuation papers. Officials say the aim is to better regulate refugee presence and distribute the burden more evenly across Turkey, while the UN reports the regional refugee count has surged past 300,000. The crackdown reflects growing local tensions in Antakya, where sectarian divisions between Alawite residents sympathetic to Assad and Sunni refugees have fueled resentment, protests, and complaints about foreign fighters passing through. Turkey has also tightened its open-border policy, leaving many displaced Syrians stranded at the frontier as authorities build additional camps.

Residents of Homs’ Old District are enduring a nearly two-year siege marked by severe hunger, untreated illness, and crumbling infrastructure, with children and the elderly dying from malnutrition and lack of basic care. While diplomats at the Geneva II talks agreed to a limited evacuation of women and children, the deal has not been implemented and residents reject it as insufficient, demanding that the siege be lifted entirely. The Red Cross warns that a single evacuation cannot address the crisis, and international actors remain deadlocked, with the U.S. accusing the Syrian government of deliberately blocking aid. Activists and doctors say the world’s inaction is condemning thousands to slow, preventable deaths.

Despite the hardships of life in Jordan’s Za'atari refugee camp, 14-year-old Syrian refugee Mizune is determined to keep education alive for children there. She goes tent-to-tent and mosque-to-mosque to persuade both kids and parents that learning is key to rebuilding Syria’s future, earning her the nickname "Malala of Za'atari" and a friendship with the education activist. Her efforts, alongside UNICEF’s school-building, have helped raise school attendance to about 70 percent, though many parents remain reluctant because they hope to return home soon. Amid the ongoing civil war and the camp’s many daily struggles, Mizune remains focused on her dream of becoming a journalist and insists that education must continue no matter the circumstances.

The reported Syrian airstrikes on Iraqi border towns, which killed dozens of civilians, highlight how the conflicts in Syria and Iraq are increasingly intertwined as ISIS extends its reach. Iraqi officials accused Syria of launching the attacks, though both Baghdad and Damascus denied the claims, while the UN confirmed the planes were not Iraqi. The incident underscores the growing sectarian and security crisis, with Iraqi leaders trading accusations and the government struggling to contain militant gains. Meanwhile, fears are mounting that the spread of extremism could further destabilize the entire region.

Syria’s civil war has seen widespread use of child soldiers, with many boys as young as 14 recruited by rebel and jihadist groups. A new Human Rights Watch report documents how these children are pushed into combat, sent to front lines, or pressured into suicide missions, often following relatives or due to dire circumstances. The report calls for the release of all fighters under 18 and warns that those backing such groups may be guilty of war crimes, while also accusing ISIS of using free schooling to recruit children. Pro-government militias were not examined due to security and logistical obstacles.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad says he is open to further U.N. inspections and maintains that rebel forces, not his government, are responsible for chemical weapons attacks. Russia has rejected the U.N. findings as biased and says it has its own evidence implicating the opposition, while the U.N. and Western nations stand by the report pointing to Assad’s regime. Diplomatic efforts to secure and destroy Syria’s chemical arsenal continue, though disagreements remain over possible military consequences for noncompliance. Meanwhile, Assad claims a diplomatic victory and defends the government’s military campaign as a fight against terrorism, even as the conflict’s civilian toll continues to rise.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, in power for 13 years, faces international condemnation and possible military action over alleged chemical weapons attacks, yet he remains defiant and refuses to step down. Initially welcomed as a reformer after succeeding his father, his rule has been marked by unfulfilled promises, state-controlled media, and a brutal crackdown on protests that escalated into civil war. Analysts describe him as deceptive and reliant on a tight-knit family and Alawite minority network, with his public image carefully managed. Despite more than 100,000 deaths and stalled peace efforts, Assad shows no intention of leaving power.

Syria is holding a presidential election during an ongoing civil war, a vote widely dismissed as illegitimate by the opposition and Western nations and expected to hand President Bashar al-Assad another term. The two challengers are little-known figures, and the election will not be monitored by Western or international bodies, with large portions of the country outside government control and millions displaced or unable to vote. There are also serious concerns about violence and low turnout on election day. Ultimately, the vote is likely to reinforce Assad’s grip on power and make a negotiated political transition even less likely.

Syria has submitted an initial declaration of its chemical weapons stockpile to the international watchdog, with a fuller disclosure expected soon. The review process is being fast-tracked because of the country’s conflict, and a key OPCW meeting has been delayed to allow more time to assess the information. Meanwhile, U.S. intelligence reports indicate Syrian forces are moving chemical weapons, though it remains unclear whether they are consolidating them for handover or attempting to conceal them. The diplomatic push to secure and destroy the arsenal continues amid urgent warnings from U.S. officials, even as the threat of military action remains on the table.

Veteran journalist Nick Paton Walsh has been honored with an Emmy and an Edward R. Murrow Award for his coverage of the Syrian conflict, particularly his reports from Aleppo. His work captured the daily terror of indiscriminate shelling and the chaotic, improvised street fighting in the city's ancient districts. The awards recognized his distinctive, poetic writing, which stood in stark contrast to the grim realities he documented and offered a fresh perspective on the war's brutality. His reporting also included a piece on self-immolation among young women in Afghanistan.

The Syrian ambassador announced that the country’s own investigation into the Houla massacre will conclude within days, reiterating the government’s denial of involvement and blaming armed terrorist groups. In contrast, Western officials maintain that pro-government Shabiha militias carried out the killings, with the U.S. calling the evidence clear-cut. The diplomatic fallout has intensified, as several countries expelled Syrian diplomats and Syria responded in kind, while Russia and China rejected military intervention and defended their stance. Meanwhile, international efforts to pressure President Assad continue, with the U.N. envoy warning that Syria is at a tipping point amid ongoing violence.

The article argues that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad is being wrongly viewed by some Western nations as the lesser evil compared to extremist opposition groups, when in fact his regime exhibits clear fascist characteristics. It warns that the international community's reluctance to confront Assad could lead to future military aggression, potentially against Saudi Arabia, driven by an ideology that defies rational calculation. Drawing parallels to Saddam Hussein and Nazi Germany, the piece highlights Assad's brutal atrocities, indoctrination, and use of sectarian division as evidence of his fascist nature. Ultimately, it urges the world to recognize that fascism, not just terrorism, poses a grave threat in the Middle East.

The U.S. State Department has downgraded Thailand to its lowest human trafficking ranking for the first time, citing persistent failures to combat modern slavery despite years of warnings and waivers. The decision places Thailand alongside countries like North Korea and Syria, reflecting concerns over forced labor in its seafood industry, sex trafficking, and corruption that enables abuse. Thai officials expressed disappointment, arguing that their enforcement efforts, including more convictions and inspections, have improved, but U.S. authorities maintain that results remain insufficient. The report also highlights the vulnerability of Rohingya refugees and other migrants, urging Thailand to show tangible progress to avoid further consequences.

The article celebrates the 50th anniversary of James Bond and the upcoming release of "Skyfall" by highlighting seven real-world travel destinations featured in the franchise. These locations range from Istanbul and the Bahamas to Key West, Paris, the Swiss Alps, Austria, and the Canadian Arctic. Each spot is tied to memorable Bond scenes, such as underwater caves, mountain chases, and iconic landmarks. The piece emphasizes how these exotic settings have long been a key part of the films' appeal, offering fans a chance to experience Bond-style adventure firsthand.

The article reflects on the author’s last-minute conflict that prevents her from bringing her daughter to Take Our Daughters and Sons to Work Day, despite valuing the event’s purpose. To help other parents, she offers practical advice: make the experience meaningful rather than babysitting, plan engaging activities, keep close supervision, avoid putting children to work, and use snack time to discuss what they learned. The goal is to balance fun with realism so children gain genuine career exposure without disrupting the workplace.

Two childhood friends in Uganda turned their shared interest in advertising into a digital media startup called Camouflage Media, offering digital screens and social media management for businesses. They were inspired by the limitations of static posters and saw digital ads as a more cost-effective and engaging alternative. Despite early struggles with coordination and deadlines, the company now serves major clients like Standard Chartered and MTN and is close to turning a profit. The founders see untapped potential in Uganda and hope to expand into classrooms and outdoor advertising, aiming to spark a digital revolution across Africa.

The Taliban has claimed responsibility for shooting down a U.S. Black Hawk helicopter in Helmand Province, Afghanistan, killing all four American crew members on board. A U.S. military official noted that the aircraft was flying in poor weather and that enemy fire had not been ruled out as the cause. The incident adds to a history of deadly helicopter losses in Afghanistan, including an August crash that killed 30 U.S. troops and was also attributed to insurgent fire.

In rural Afghanistan, schools have become a battleground in the conflict between the Taliban and the government. The Taliban has shut down some schools in retaliation for government policies, while allowing others to reopen only after forcing changes to the curriculum, such as expanding religious instruction and reducing subjects like English. Teachers and students face pressure and monitoring from Taliban minders, though some accept the changes. The government admits it is showing flexibility to keep schools operating, reflecting wider anxieties about Taliban influence as international forces withdraw.

A Taliban commander in North Waziristan has declared a ban on polio vaccinations for children until the United States halts drone strikes in the region. The Taliban statement argued that the drone campaign is more harmful than polio and criticized the U.S. for funding eradication efforts while conducting deadly attacks. The decision follows previous controversies linking a fake CIA vaccination drive to the hunt for Osama bin Laden, which damaged trust in immunization programs. It remains uncertain how widely the ban will affect polio eradication efforts, since the commander’s influence is mainly limited to North Waziristan.

The article addresses the difficult challenge parents face in talking to children after mass shootings, such as the Oregon school attack. It highlights how some parents choose to initiate the conversation to prevent fear from peers, while others with very young children may wait. Experts advise offering reassurance about safety, being honest without false promises, and tailoring discussions to the child’s age. Parents are also urged to limit exposure to graphic news coverage and accept that some questions, like “why,” may have no clear answer.

When speaking with someone who has an invisible chronic illness, well-meaning comments like “you look good” or “just stay positive” can feel dismissive and hurtful. Such remarks may invalidate their daily struggles and damage the relationship. Instead, it’s better to offer genuine empathy, admit you don’t fully understand, and provide practical support like bringing a meal, running errands, or simply listening. Asking about their sources of hope and strength can also be a meaningful way to show care and respect their experience.

The Tanzanian government plans to evict the Maasai from Loliondo to create a large conservation corridor, which officials say is needed to protect wildlife and grazing lands. The Maasai, who have lived there for generations, argue the move would strip them of vital dry-season grazing and is tied to hunting concessions granted to an Emirati-owned company. They have refused to leave, calling the plan a death sentence and vowing to resist even at the cost of their lives. The government maintains the land belongs to the state, while Tanzania's parliament has scheduled a debate to address the escalating dispute.

A math teacher at Sparks Middle School was killed when he intervened during a shooting by a student armed with a semiautomatic weapon, according to his brother, who said the teacher likely tried to talk the gunman down. The teacher, a former Marine and Nevada Air National Guard member, was remembered as a selfless person who always helped others and loved his students. Two 12-year-old students were also wounded in the attack. The community mourned the loss, with many honoring him as a hero and a dedicated educator.

In Cairo’s Tahrir Square, thousands of protesters remained camped out after another night of violent clashes with riot police, with tear gas filling the streets and ambulances carrying away the wounded. The demonstrations have left dozens dead, and many young protesters blamed the security forces for provoking the unrest, pointing to the killings that sparked their anger. Some government workers, however, criticized both the protesters and Egypt’s ruling military council, saying the military had repeated the mistakes of ousted President Mubarak by responding too slowly and inadequately. The confrontations continued as protesters threw stones at police, who fired tear gas canisters that bore markings indicating they were made in the United States.

American skiers Ted Ligety and Mikaela Shiffrin carried their Olympic momentum into the World Cup circuit, each winning their signature events on Saturday. Ligety triumphed in the giant slalom in Slovenia for a record sixth time at that venue, while Shiffrin dominated the slalom in Sweden to secure the season-long discipline title. Shiffrin became the first woman to earn eight World Cup victories before turning 19. Meanwhile, Marcel Hirscher finished fourth to keep his lead over Ligety in the GS standings and also narrowed the gap in the overall World Cup race.

Five months after being shot by the Taliban for advocating girls’ education, Malala Yousafzai has returned to school in Birmingham, England, where she is recovering. The 15-year-old called it a dream come true and expressed hope that all girls would one day have the same opportunity. She was attacked in Pakistan’s Swat Valley in October, and after multiple surgeries, she continues her rehabilitation in Britain. Her activism has drawn international attention and renewed commitments to defend girls’ rights.

A Brazilian teenager has set a new Guinness World Record for the fastest text message typed on a touchscreen phone, completing a difficult 25-word sentence in 18.19 seconds. He developed his rapid texting ability after breaking his desktop computer and relying solely on his smartphone. The record was achieved using the Fleksy keyboard app, whose makers brought him to New York for the attempt. Despite his speed, the teen says he does not consider himself addicted to his phone.

A 12-year-old girl turned a school assignment into a two-year project to build a tiny house, with her parents’ support. After her father died suddenly in a car accident, the unfinished house became a way for her and her family to cope with grief. With help from friends and community members, she completed the 128-square-foot home, gaining confidence and practical skills along the way. The experience taught her that finishing the project was about resilience and remembering her father, not just construction.

A 16-year-old student attacked classmates with kitchen knives at a Pennsylvania high school, wounding 20 students and a security officer before being subdued by an assistant principal. The suspect was charged as an adult with attempted homicide and other offenses, though his lawyer indicated he may seek a psychiatric evaluation and a move to juvenile court. Authorities have not established a motive, but noted the teen made statements suggesting he wanted to die. Several victims were seriously injured, and the school community was left in shock by the rare mass stabbing.

Zach Sobiech, an 18-year-old with terminal bone cancer, passed away surrounded by loved ones after his song “Clouds” went viral and drew massive support for children’s cancer research. His music, written after his diagnosis, inspired a celebrity lip-sync tribute organized by actors from SoulPancake’s “My Last Days.” Throughout his illness, Zach became known for his wisdom and gratitude, urging others to start living before facing death. His family and fans remember him as a young man who taught many how to appreciate life’s blessings despite hardship.

The father of the teenage stowaway who survived a flight from California to Hawaii in a jet’s wheel well says his son is a good child facing the challenges of adapting to American life after fleeing war-torn Somalia. The teen, identified by his father as Yahya Yusuf, reportedly lost consciousness during the near-five-hour flight and was found in Maui, where he has been recovering in state custody. The boy told investigators he had been trying to reach his mother in Somalia and had no idea which plane he boarded. His father plans to travel to Hawaii to bring him home and has asked for privacy.

A new meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry found that teens who use cannabis daily before age 17 are over 60% less likely to finish high school than non-users. The study also linked frequent adolescent marijuana use to much higher risks of later cannabis dependence, suicide attempts, and use of other illegal drugs, with effects increasing alongside frequency of use. While the authors noted the evidence did not prove marijuana directly caused depression, suicide, or welfare reliance, they urged policymakers to carefully evaluate cannabis reforms to prevent increased teen use and related harms.

The upcoming trial of two Steubenville High School football players accused of raping a teenage girl has thrust the struggling Ohio town into the national spotlight. The case, fueled by social media evidence and pressure from activist hackers, has sparked accusations of a cover-up and special treatment for the team. In response, local leaders have defended the community and its police force, arguing that the town's reputation has been unfairly tarnished by the incident. The case has also highlighted how deeply the town's identity is tied to its football team, even as residents grapple with the serious allegations.

A 14-year-old student at a Brooklyn middle school is suing New York City for $16 million after he lost vision in one eye from an attack by several boys in the school cafeteria. The lawsuit claims school officials failed to provide adequate supervision, despite the student’s prior complaints about being bullied. Two of the alleged attackers have been arrested and face school discipline. The teen has undergone two unsuccessful surgeries and may need a cornea transplant.

After breaking his glasses and struggling for a week without them, teenager Yash Gupta realized how much children with poor vision miss out on education. At age 14, he founded Sight Learning, which collects donated used eyeglasses from optometrists and distributes them to young people in need. So far, the organization has provided nearly 10,000 pairs of glasses to children in countries such as India, Mexico, and Haiti. Gupta, who also helps at eye clinics and plans to expand to U.S. inner cities, hopes to inspire other young people to make a difference in their communities.

The shooting death of 15-year-old Hadiya Pendleton, a Chicago honor student and majorette who had performed at President Obama’s inauguration events, has become a focal point in the national gun violence debate. Her killing was referenced during a Senate Judiciary hearing and a White House press briefing, with officials citing it as another example of the gun violence plaguing American cities. Pendleton was the 42nd murder victim in Chicago this year, and police have made no arrests. Lawmakers and city leaders used her death to renew calls for action, saying the country has an obligation to prevent such tragedies.

Kevin Trudeau, the former infomercial pitchman known for promoting dubious health and wealth advice, has been sentenced to 10 years in federal prison. The sentence stems from criminal contempt charges after he violated a 2004 court order by airing misleading infomercials and misrepresenting a weight-loss book. During sentencing, the judge sharply criticized him for a long history of deceit, and prosecutors described him as an unrepentant con artist. Trudeau, who has been in custody since his 2013 conviction, plans to appeal the decision.

A 7-year-old Black student in Oklahoma was sent home from school because her dreadlocks violated the dress code, prompting her parents to withdraw her and the school to later revise the policy. The author connects this incident to broader societal biases that treat Eurocentric features, like straight hair, as the standard of beauty, leaving natural Black hairstyles unfairly stigmatized. In response, she organized a digital care package filled with photos and messages from over a hundred women and girls with locs to reassure Tiana that her hair is beautiful. The piece ultimately urges adults to actively affirm the beauty and worth of Black girls, so they don’t internalize harmful standards.

Former Temptations singer Richard Street has died at age 70 in Las Vegas due to a blood clot in his lung, after experiencing back pain and breathing difficulties. His wife confirmed his death, noting he fought hard for his life. Street was the second former Temptations member to pass away this month, following Damon Harris. Known for his contributions to classic songs like “Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone,” he is survived by his wife and four children.

A Tennessee man has been indicted on federal charges of wire fraud and extortion for allegedly claiming he possessed stolen tax returns of Mitt Romney and his wife. Prosecutors say he demanded $1 million in Bitcoin from the Romneys’ accounting firm, threatening to release the returns if not paid. He also sent a flash drive purportedly containing encrypted tax files and posted online messages referencing the fictional character Dr. Evil. The charges stem from incidents during the 2012 presidential campaign, when Romney’s refusal to release more tax returns was a contentious issue.

Bud Adams, the longtime owner of the Tennessee Titans franchise and a co-founder of the American Football League, has died at age 90. He owned the team for over five decades, beginning with the Houston Oilers, who won two AFL titles before joining the NFL and later relocating to Tennessee. Under his ownership, the franchise made one Super Bowl appearance, losing to the St. Louis Rams in January 2000. His death came just days after former Oilers coach Bum Phillips passed away, and former coach Jeff Fisher remembered Adams as a pioneer who helped grow the game.

The Democratic Republic of Congo is set to release delayed presidential election results amid rising tensions, as opposition leaders reject preliminary figures that put incumbent Joseph Kabila ahead. The main challenger, Etienne Tshisekedi, has alleged fraud and vowed not to accept the outcome, while citizens and observers report high anxiety and anticipation. At least 18 people have died in election-related violence, and analysts warn that a disputed result could trigger broader instability in a region still recovering from past conflicts. The country’s vast mineral wealth has not prevented chronic poverty and unrest, making the political stakes especially high.The Democratic Republic of Congo is set to release delayed presidential election results amid rising tensions, as opposition leaders reject preliminary figures that put incumbent Joseph Kabila ahead.
