A federal report found antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the majority of raw meat samples, with ground turkey the most contaminated at 81 percent, followed by pork chops, ground beef, and chicken. Public health experts warn that the widespread use of antibiotics in livestock—not just to treat illness but also to promote growth—is fueling resistance and reducing treatment options for human infections. The FDA defends current oversight and emphasizes that antibiotics remain important for animal health, while industry groups argue resistance trends are not clearly rising. Officials advise that proper cooking and careful handling of raw meat can help prevent foodborne illness.

North Korea appears to have carried out a third underground nuclear test, triggering global seismic detection, though analysts say key details like yield or bomb type may remain unclear. The test follows North Korea’s recent long-range rocket launch and its defiance of U.N. condemnation, heightening concerns that further tests could help it miniaturize warheads for missiles. Underground testing is generally safer than above-ground detonations, but radiation leaks remain a risk, as seen in past incidents. International monitoring networks, using seismic and atmospheric sensors, are expected to detect the event even if no radiation escapes.

Actress Catherine Zeta-Jones has voluntarily checked into a health care facility, with her publicist saying she is committed to regular care to maintain her well-being, though the specific reason was not disclosed. She previously sought treatment for bipolar II disorder in 2011. The article also explains that bipolar II is a treatable but less severe form of bipolar disorder, involving depression and hypomania, and notes that former Congressman Jesse Jackson Jr. has also been diagnosed with the condition.

The Balkans are facing their most severe flooding in over a century, with dozens of deaths already confirmed and more victims anticipated as waters recede. The crisis is worsened by the danger of unexploded landmines from the Bosnian war being dislodged. A slow-moving weather system called a cutoff low dumped months of rainfall in just days, and flooding is expected to persist for at least another week. The swollen rivers have disrupted trade, damaged hydroelectric facilities, and contaminated drinking water supplies across the region.

Hamas’s objectives in the ongoing conflict with Israel include its long-standing aim of destroying Israel, though that goal is widely seen as unrealistic, as well as more immediate demands such as lifting the Israeli blockade, opening border crossings, and releasing Palestinian prisoners. The group also seeks to strengthen its domestic standing by presenting itself as resisting Israeli occupation and settlement expansion. These goals remain unmet, which helps explain why a lasting cease-fire has not been reached. Hamas frames its demands as necessary for Palestinian protection and dignity, while analysts note that the conflict also serves its political and media interests.

Robin Williams’s wife revealed that he had been in the early stages of Parkinson’s disease at the time of his death. Parkinson’s is a progressive nervous system disorder that impairs movement, often starting with tremors and stiffness, and it occurs when dopamine-producing brain cells die off. While the exact cause remains unclear, researchers believe genetics and environmental factors both play a role. There is no cure, but treatments such as levodopa, deep brain stimulation, and experimental cell transplants can help manage symptoms.

Scientists have confirmed the existence of the Higgs boson, the long-sought particle that helps explain how matter acquires mass, following years of experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. The discovery validates a theory proposed in the 1960s by Peter Higgs and Francois Englert, who were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work. The particle works through an energy field that interacts with other particles, giving them different masses. While not the final answer to all questions in physics, it fills a crucial gap in the Standard Model and deepens our understanding of the universe’s fundamental structure.

The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928, is a long-standing religious-political movement advocating governance based on Islamic principles rather than secularism, and it has influenced similar groups across the Middle East. After decades of suppression, it rose to power when Mohamed Morsy became Egypt's first democratically elected president in 2012. However, his presidency quickly lost public support amid economic decline, security failures, and accusations that the Brotherhood was monopolizing state institutions and imposing its Islamist agenda—a process critics called "Brotherhoodization." Massive protests in 2013 reflected widespread discontent, though the group's history of resilience suggests it may endure despite losing political control.

A new study suggests that certain high-glycemic foods may trigger addictive-like brain responses, similar to drugs. Researchers found that meals causing rapid blood sugar spikes and crashes activated the nucleus accumbens, a brain region linked to addiction, leading to renewed hunger and cravings. This challenges the idea that overeating is purely a matter of willpower, pointing instead to biological drivers. While the debate over food addiction continues, the findings hint that limiting high-glycemic foods could help reduce cravings and support weight management.

A rare strain of enterovirus, EV-D68, is causing severe respiratory illness and hospitalizations among children in the U.S. It starts with cold-like symptoms but can escalate to breathing difficulties, particularly for kids with asthma, though there is no specific treatment beyond supportive care. The virus spreads through close contact and contaminated surfaces, so health officials emphasize handwashing and disinfecting as key prevention measures.

Violent conflict between rival mining unions in South Africa is threatening the country’s economy, prompting Anglo American to suspend all operations at its Rustenburg sites. The unrest stems from a turf war between the militant AMCU and the ruling-party-aligned NUM, set against worker demands for sharply higher wages. The deadliest flashpoint was the Marikana massacre, where police killed 34 strikers, intensifying scrutiny of President Jacob Zuma and fueling comparisons to apartheid-era violence. The turmoil has also severely disrupted Lonmin’s production, costing millions and leaving workers unpaid.

The MH17 crash site in eastern Ukraine remains unsecured and vast, raising serious concerns that crucial evidence is being disturbed or destroyed. Armed rebels have hindered investigators, making an already unprecedented forensic operation even more difficult. Experts stress that preserving the wreckage is essential to determine whether the plane was hit by a missile and to establish accountability. Meanwhile, recovering and identifying victims’ remains is the top priority, with forensic teams relying on DNA, dental records, and other methods.

The overuse of antibiotics in livestock for growth promotion and disease prevention has significantly contributed to the rise of drug-resistant infections that threaten human health. Although the FDA has acknowledged the issue, its response has been limited to voluntary measures, and it has failed to enact strong regulations despite decades of scientific evidence and recommendations. Other countries, like Denmark, have shown that reducing antibiotic use in farming does not harm agricultural productivity. Ultimately, consumers can help by choosing antibiotic-free meat, but broader government action is still needed to curb this public health threat.

If convicted of premeditated murder, Oscar Pistorius would face a starkly different reality from his luxury lifestyle, as South African prisons are severely overcrowded, with inmates often sharing cramped cells, enduring 23-hour lockdowns, and suffering from poor sanitation and medical care. His case has also sparked criticism over alleged preferential treatment, since he was held at a police station and allowed visits outside normal hours, unlike other suspects. Experts note that while South Africa’s laws protect prisoners’ rights, enforcement is weak, and systemic delays leave many suspects jailed for long periods before trial. If sentenced, Pistorius would serve at least 25 years before parole eligibility, though his legal team is fighting to prevent that outcome.

Amanda Knox, now in the U.S., vowed to fight the Italian appeals court’s guilty verdict and refused to return to Italy willingly, saying she was shocked by the reversal. Legal experts are divided on whether she could be extradited, citing tensions between U.S. double-jeopardy protections and the U.S.-Italy extradition treaty, with some suggesting politics and her public support may play a role. The Kercher family welcomed the conviction of Knox and Raffaele Sollecito for Meredith Kercher’s 2007 murder, though they acknowledged the case may still face further appeals. Any extradition or final resolution is expected to take a long time, with the next legal steps likely months or more away.

Ecuador has granted Julian Assange political asylum, but this does not resolve his situation since he remains trapped in its London embassy and would be arrested by British police if he stepped outside. The UK has refused safe passage and still intends to extradite him to Sweden, while Assange fears being sent onward to the U.S. on espionage charges. British authorities are unlikely to forcibly enter the embassy, as that would set a dangerous diplomatic precedent, so the standoff could continue for a long time.

More than a month after Michael Brown's death, the case remains unresolved, with no charges filed yet. A St. Louis County grand jury is reviewing evidence to decide whether Officer Darren Wilson should face charges, while the U.S. Justice Department is conducting two civil rights investigations—one into the shooting and another into broader police practices in Ferguson. These federal probes could take a long time, as similar cases have lasted years. Meanwhile, Ferguson officials have proposed a citizen review board to ease community tensions, but critics say it is too weak, and protests have continued.

The article distinguishes between immigrants, who voluntarily relocate for better opportunities, and refugees, who are forced to flee due to danger. It explains that refugees can seek asylum in the U.S., but must prove they face targeted harm based on specific grounds. Many Central American migrants are escaping gang and drug violence, though not all violence qualifies for refugee status. A 2008 U.S. law granting children full immigration hearings is cited as a major factor behind the surge of unaccompanied minors crossing the border.

The Supreme Court upheld the individual health insurance mandate by ruling that the penalty for not having coverage functions as a constitutional tax, not a criminal penalty. Chief Justice Roberts noted that the payment is collected by the IRS through normal tax filing and is modest enough that many people may choose to pay it instead of buying insurance. The Court also decided that the Anti-Injunction Act did not block the challenge because Congress had labeled the requirement a penalty rather than a tax. Finally, the justices emphasized they were not judging the policy’s wisdom, only its constitutionality.

Apple is expected to unveil the next-generation iPad at its upcoming event, facing growing competition from cheaper tablets like the Kindle Fire and Nook Tablet, as well as new Windows-based devices. While the company has not confirmed details, rumors point to a high-resolution retina display, the inclusion of Siri, a possible lower-cost model, and an improved camera. Some analysts also speculate that Apple could surprise observers by announcing an integrated Apple TV instead, though a new iPad remains the most likely focus.

Amal Alamuddin, a prominent international human rights attorney, is reportedly engaged to George Clooney, a surprising turn given the actor’s long-held stance against remarrying. Known for her impressive legal career, which includes representing high-profile clients like Julian Assange, Alamuddin is also noted for her beauty, multilingualism, and global experience. The couple has kept their relationship low-key, but her law firm has publicly congratulated them, while Clooney’s representative has not confirmed the news.

The Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crash was likely caused by an approach that was too slow, with the aircraft far below its target speed and stalling just before impact. The pilot, though experienced overall, had very little time in the Boeing 777 and was making his first landing at San Francisco; the glideslope equipment was also out of service, forcing a visual approach. Investigators found both engines were running at impact, and the tail section separated from the aircraft, while most of the fire damage occurred after the plane skidded to a stop. Two Chinese teenagers died, and authorities are looking into whether one was struck by an emergency vehicle, as well as broader questions about pilot training and crew coordination.

Greece is holding a second election in six weeks after May’s vote produced no clear winner and coalition talks failed. The race is expected to be tight between the pro-austerity New Democracy party and the leftist Syriza, which opposes the bailout terms and has gained support from public anger over harsh spending cuts. The outcome will be closely watched across Europe because it could determine whether Greece remains in the eurozone or risks losing international financial support. Even with a pro-bailout government, the country faces deep economic challenges, and the possibility of a Greek exit from the euro remains a serious concern.

Reality singing competitions often serve as platforms for career reinvention, but Britney Spears is using "The X Factor" not to boost album sales, but to rebuild her public image and reconnect with fans. After years of limited personal exposure under a conservatorship, her reported $15 million judging role offers a chance to show her personality and regain the relatable fame she once had. However, experts warn that her success depends on appearing genuine and unscripted, as a robotic or rehearsed persona could backfire. If she comes across as authentic, the show could revive her stardom and draw huge ratings.

Synthetic drugs sold under innocent names like spice or bath salts are highly dangerous, manmade substances often marketed as legal household products. Because manufacturers constantly alter their chemical formulas, these drugs evade existing laws, making their contents unpredictable and their health effects potentially severe. The DEA warns that these products are especially popular among teenagers and have been linked to violent behavior, hospitalizations, and deaths, including recent cases in Colorado. Authorities are struggling to keep pace with the ever-changing compounds and are working to raise awareness and curb the profitable, underground trade.

A three-year-old Arizona girl with an IQ above 160 has joined Mensa, reading at a fifth-grade level and teaching herself Spanish from an iPad. The article explains that IQ tests measure reasoning and problem-solving abilities but do not capture creativity, practical skills, or emotional readiness. It also notes that IQ can shift over time due to environmental factors, and that average scores have risen across generations, a trend known as the Flynn Effect. Ultimately, a high IQ does not guarantee success; perseverance, curiosity, and work ethic are equally important.

Western governments, especially the United States, have avoided officially calling Egypt's military ouster of President Mohamed Morsy a "coup" because doing so would trigger cuts to the $1.5 billion in annual U.S. aid and damage ties with a key regional ally. While the military's action fits the technical definition of a coup, officials point to the massive popular protests and the military's promise of new elections as signs of public support. The Obama administration has urged a return to democratic rule without explicitly demanding Morsy's reinstatement, reflecting a delicate balancing act. Some legal scholars argue this may be a "democracy-promoting" coup, since the military responded to popular opposition and installed a civilian interim leader rather than seeking to consolidate power.

Cyberbullying affects a significant number of teens and often comes from peers within their social circle rather than strangers, making it a persistent issue that can occur anytime and leave lasting emotional scars. Victims may face anxiety, depression, and even thoughts of skipping school or suicide, with effects sometimes extending into adulthood. Experts emphasize preserving digital evidence and involving schools, parents, and technology tools to address the problem, though responses are not always effective. Some young victims have turned their experiences into advocacy, using online platforms and organizations to raise awareness and push for better reporting mechanisms on social media.

The article highlights two high-profile cases where young brain-dead patients are kept on ventilators amid family disputes with hospitals—one family hoping for a miracle, the other seeking to honor the patient’s wishes. Ethicists argue that misleading terms like "brain death" and "life support" create false hope and confusion, since brain death is legally and medically final. The cases also expose legal complications, especially in Texas, where a law prevents withdrawal of treatment from a pregnant patient. Experts call for clearer communication and a broader public conversation about the meaning of death, the limits of medical technology, and how to balance ethical, legal, and faith-based perspectives.

Argentine President Cristina Fernandez has been out of the public eye for weeks, with no recent public appearances or social media activity, sparking questions about her health and who is actually running the country. Her aides insist she is still in charge and working daily, but the silence has fueled speculation about whether she is recovering, avoiding political difficulties, or preparing for a political transition. Some observers compare the situation to the death of her husband, former President Nestor Kirchner, suggesting she may be prioritizing her health. Meanwhile, officials like Cabinet Chief Jorge Capitanich have stepped in as the public face of the government, and many citizens are growing anxious over the lack of clear leadership.

South Korean authorities are facing criticism as fugitive billionaire Yoo Byung Eun, believed to have controlled the company behind the Sewol ferry disaster, continues to evade arrest. He is wanted for questioning over alleged embezzlement, tax evasion, and other irregularities linked to the sinking that killed nearly 300 people. Investigators have raised the reward for his capture and are searching properties tied to his religious group, while his daughter has been detained in France. The case has sparked public outrage, with President Park Geun-hye accusing Yoo’s family of mocking the law instead of taking responsibility.

Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson remained the world’s busiest passenger airport in 2012, handling over 95 million travelers, followed by Beijing and London Heathrow. Global passenger traffic rose 4.4 percent to more than 5.7 billion, according to Airports Council International. Atlanta also led in aircraft takeoffs and landings, while Chicago O’Hare and Los Angeles followed. In cargo, Hong Kong retained the top spot, with Memphis and Shanghai next.

Transparency International’s 2013 Corruption Perceptions Index shows that most of the 177 countries surveyed scored below 50, indicating widespread perceived corruption in the public sector. Afghanistan, North Korea, and Somalia ranked as the most corrupt, while Denmark and New Zealand were seen as the cleanest. Notable shifts included Syria’s sharp decline amid its civil war, Myanmar’s major improvement following political reforms, and a slight rise for the UK, while the U.S. and China held steady. The report emphasizes that weak institutions and lack of accountability worsen perceptions, and it urges greater openness to combat corruption.

Street painting, or chalk art, traces back to 16th-century Italian Madonnari who drew on streets for coins, a tradition that faded after World War II but was revived in 1973 by a festival in Curtatone, Italy. This revival inspired a global movement of chalk festivals where artists create large-scale, temporary works—ranging from copies of famous paintings to original 2-D and 3-D pieces—directly on pavement. These events emphasize public accessibility and the unique experience of watching art emerge before audiences, with festivals now held across North America, Europe, Mexico, and Australia. Notable examples include the Sarasota Chalk Festival, Santa Barbara’s I Madonnari festival, and the original Fiera delle Grazie in Italy, which remains the most prestigious.

The second-in-command of al Qaeda, Abu Yahya al-Libi, was killed in a CIA drone strike in Pakistan, marking one of the most significant blows to the group since Osama bin Laden's death. U.S. officials described him as a key operational planner and religious authority whose expertise would be very difficult to replace, further weakening an already degraded central al Qaeda leadership. While some jihadists expressed doubt about his death and insisted the fight would continue, the strike was part of an intensified U.S. drone campaign. Meanwhile, the United States remains concerned about the growing strength of al Qaeda affiliates in places like Yemen.

An Iraq war veteran with PTSD and paranoia scaled the White House fence and entered the grounds while carrying a knife, later telling authorities he wanted to warn the president about a collapsing atmosphere. He was arrested and is facing charges, though his former stepson said he meant no harm and needed more mental health support. A separate attempted entry occurred the following day, heightening concerns about security lapses. The Secret Service faced criticism from lawmakers, launched a review of the incidents, and planned to increase security measures around the White House.

The White House has officially confirmed that Syrian government forces have used chemical weapons, including sarin gas, against rebels, declaring that this crosses a longstanding international red line. In response, the United States will expand the scope and scale of its assistance to the opposition, including direct support for the rebel military council, though no final decision has been made on a no-fly zone or directly arming the rebels. The administration maintains that the Assad government controls the chemical weapons stockpile and that there is no credible evidence the opposition has used such agents, contradicting Syrian claims. The announcement comes as rebel forces face mounting losses, and concerns persist about the presence of al-Qaeda-linked militants among the opposition and the security of Syria's chemical arsenal.

Catherine Greig, the longtime companion of fugitive James “Whitey” Bulger, pleaded guilty to charges of harboring a fugitive and identity theft for helping Bulger evade capture for 16 years. Prosecutors stressed that the plea was not a lenient deal and that the case against Bulger remains a priority. Bulger, who is accused of multiple murders, was arrested in 2011 in Santa Monica after FBI agents tricked him into leaving his apartment. Greig now faces up to five years in prison on each count.

A World Health Organization report estimates that air pollution caused about 7 million deaths globally in 2012, making it the world’s largest single environmental health threat. Most of these fatalities were linked to heart disease, stroke, respiratory illness, and lung cancer, with indoor smoke from solid cooking fuels accounting for more than half of the deaths. The hardest-hit areas were Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific, and women and children in developing countries were especially vulnerable to household smoke. Outdoor air pollution contributed roughly 3.7 million deaths, predominantly in low- and middle-income countries, largely from vehicle and industrial emissions.

The article reviews the American cases in the current Ebola outbreak, highlighting the latest patient, NBC cameraman Ashoka Mukpo, who arrived at Nebraska Medical Center for treatment. It also recounts the experiences of other infected Americans, including Dr. Kent Brantly, Nancy Writebol, and Dr. Rick Sacra, all of whom survived after receiving experimental treatments and supportive care. A fourth patient, an unnamed WHO doctor, was treated at Emory University Hospital, while Patrick Sawyer remains the only American to have died from the virus. The piece emphasizes the use of biocontainment units and experimental drugs in treating these patients.

The World Health Organization reports that the Ebola outbreak remains confined to Guinea and Liberia, with suspected cases in neighboring countries like Sierra Leone, Mali, and Ghana still unconfirmed. Guinea has seen the majority of infections and deaths, while Liberia has reported a smaller number of cases. Health officials describe this as an especially difficult outbreak because it is West Africa’s first encounter with Ebola, leading to fear and misinformation. Response efforts are focused on tracking contacts, deploying staff, and supplying protective equipment to contain the virus.

A 16-year-old Pennsylvania student, Alex Hribal, is accused of stabbing or slashing 20 students and a security officer at his high school, leaving his community stunned because he was considered a typical, well-liked teenager with no prior record. His attorney says Hribal is scared, remorseful, and possibly unaware of his actions, and plans to seek a psychiatric evaluation and a move to juvenile court. Authorities have not identified a motive, though they are examining his computer and have noted he had little online presence. Hribal is being held without bail, as officials argue he poses a threat and had expressed a desire to die.

Alix Catherine Tichelman, a 26-year-old model and aspiring writer who also worked as an escort, is accused of injecting Google executive Forrest Hayes with heroin and then calmly leaving him to die aboard his yacht. She appeared in court facing charges related to his death, and her social media profiles paint a complex picture of a woman who wrote dark poetry about addiction and demons. Authorities are also reexamining the overdose death of her former boyfriend, Dean Riopelle, which occurred just months before Hayes’ death. Tichelman has not yet entered a plea.

A new poll suggests about a quarter of Americans believe God influences which teams win sporting events. The article humorously explores this idea, noting that if true, God must favor historically successful franchises like the Yankees while abandoning long-suffering teams such as the Cubs and Bills. It also highlights that both Super Bowl teams have devout players, making it hard to predict divine favor. Ultimately, the author hopes God is not concerned with football outcomes but rather with helping those in genuine need.

The article focuses on Justin Ross Harris, the Georgia father charged with murder and child cruelty after his 22-month-old son died in a hot car. Despite public interest, few details have emerged because authorities, his family, and his lawyer are not providing information. His background includes work at Home Depot, a previous police dispatcher role, and a university degree. Meanwhile, some acquaintances and online supporters have defended him as a devoted father and husband, though their petition to drop the charges was later closed.

The suspect in the Oklahoma beheading attack, identified as Alton Nolen, is expected to face formal charges after allegedly killing one woman and wounding another at the food plant where he had just been fired. Although his family describes him as a kind, nonviolent person who was raised in a loving home, court records show a prior criminal history involving drugs and resisting arrest. His social media activity had shifted to Islam-related content, including references to beheadings, but authorities say there is no confirmed link to terrorism. Investigators suggest workplace grievances, such as being denied a raise and reprimanded for proselytizing, may have played a role.

The article outlines the international coalition assembled to combat ISIS, which has seized territory across Syria and Iraq. It details contributions from regional partners like Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkey, and Jordan, as well as Western allies including the UK, France, Australia, and Germany. These nations are providing a range of support, from airstrikes and military equipment to training for local forces, humanitarian aid, and efforts to counter extremist propaganda. The coalition’s actions involve both direct military engagement and broader strategic measures to weaken the militant group.

After months on the run, Saif al-Islam Gadhafi was captured by rebel fighters in Libya’s southern desert, ending loyalist hopes of a Gadhafi return to power. He had been a prominent defender of the regime during the uprising and was wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity. Despite his Western education and reformist image, he remained loyal to his father and vowed to fight to the end. It is still uncertain whether he will face trial in Libya or be handed over to the ICC.

A Southern California family of four who vanished in 2010 were later found buried in the Mojave Desert, shifting the case from missing persons to homicide. Despite early clues like their abandoned SUV near the Mexican border and a possible border-crossing sighting, investigators were unable to solve the disappearance for years. The victims’ relatives and a private investigator questioned the official handling and pointed to suspicious details, including a delayed missing-person report and a puzzling cellphone call. Authorities say the case remains open, but they have not named any suspects or identified a clear motive.

Samsung’s new Galaxy Gear smartwatch may seem unnecessary, but it represents the next major shift in the wireless industry. Rather than replacing the smartphone, the watch acts as a convenient remote control that pairs with Samsung phones and tablets, letting users check messages and apps at a glance. The broader vision is that the cloud will connect all personal devices, making the watch an essential part of a tightly integrated ecosystem. Samsung beat Apple to market with this idea, though Apple is expected to follow, and the smartwatch is likely to succeed as companies compete to lock customers into their platforms.Samsung’s new Galaxy Gear smartwatch may seem unnecessary, but it represents the next major shift in the wireless industry.
